text: EverQuest II is a 3D fantasy massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG) originally developed and published by Sony Online Entertainment for Microsoft Windows PCs and released in November 2004. It serves as a sequel to the original EverQuest, which was released five years earlier, and includes updated graphics, more streamlined gameplay, and an abundance of voice acting featuring actors such as Christopher Lee, Heather Graham, Minnie Driver, Wil Wheaton, Dwight Schultz, Richard Horvitz, Alan Dale, and Danica McKellar. According to SOE, the game featured 130 hours of spoken dialog recorded by 266 voice actors in October 2004, with additional dialog added through updates, including player voice emotes introduced in September 2005 via the Desert of Flames expansion. The music, composed by Emmy-award-winning Laura Karpman and recorded by the FILMharmonic Orchestra Prague, spans over ninety minutes and features unique themes for each location, aiming for a cinematic feel; the expansions Echoes of Faydwer and Rise of Kunark include themes from the original EverQuest arranged by Inon Zur, and Rise of Kunark introduced a new combat music system with 14 contextual themes based on enemy strength and battle tide. The game is set in an alternate future 500 years after the original EverQuest's events, functioning as a parallel universe that diverges at the conclusion of the Planes of Power expansion, allowing both games to develop independently without interfering with each other. Characters and locations from the original are altered by centuries of war and destruction, and players can access familiar places and characters through "heritage items" obtained via heritage quests. Each player creates a character in the 3D world of Norrath, choosing from races such as human, barbarian, dwarf, erudite, ogre, iksar, troll, gnome, half elf, high elf, halfling, Vah Shir, wood elf, dark elf, Kerra, Ratonga, Sarnak, Fae, and Arasai, with the Froglok race initially locked until a server-wide quest was completed. Players select one of four archetypes—Fighter, Scout, Priest, or Mage—and choose a class at level 10 and a subclass at level 20, though this system changed in 2006 so that the final class is selected at character creation. Characters gain experience through quests, exploration, and monster kills, with no experience loss or level loss upon death; instead, they respawn with full gear at revival locations, though a minor experience debt is repaid, and gear degrades after 10 consecutive deaths, requiring repair for a fee. The game emphasizes quests, with over 6,000 existing, and supports player interaction through grouping (up to six players), raids (up to 24), voice chat, mail, global chat, a marketplace, and tools like "looking-for-group" and "looking-for-work." Guilds are central to gameplay, with experience bars and levels up to 150 earned primarily through "writs" and killing epic monsters, unlocking rewards such as housing, mounts, house items, apparel, titles, guild halls, and a hosted website with forum and bank features. Guild recruitment tools are integrated, and players can maintain houses. A secure commission system allows players to sell crafting skills or use the common market to sell finished items. The game originally operated on a subscription model, but in July 2010, a free-to-play version called EverQuest II Extended was released on a separate server, funded by microtransactions or optional subscriptions. By November 2011, the subscription service was fully cancelled, transitioning all servers to free-to-play with microtransactions as the revenue stream. In February 2005, the game partnered with Pizza Hut, allowing players to order pizza via the "/pizza" chat command, a promotion that ended but generated significant press. In June 2005, Station Exchange—an official auction system on designated servers—was introduced, and in December 2008, Station Cash, a real-money trading (RMT) feature, was added. In January 2009, EverQuest II became available on Steam through a collaboration with Valve. In March 2006, SOE ended its Chinese and Korean operations for EverQuest II, which were managed by Gamania, with beta access ending on March 29 and all accounts moved to US servers by March 30. In October 2012, Krono was introduced as a real-money purchase option that grants 30 days of Gold subscription and can be traded or gifted, offering a safer alternative to purchasing SC cards. The game was nominated for "Best Massively Multiplayer Online Game" at GameSpot's 2004 awards and runner-up for "Best Persistent World Game" at IGN's 2004 awards, both losing to World of Warcraft. It was named the seventh-best computer game of 2004 by Computer Games Magazine and won "Most Improved Game" at GameSpy's 2006 awards for the addition of PvP servers and the Echoes of Faydwer expansion. After adopting free-to-play in 2011, it won "Best Bang for the Buck" at Massively's annual awards. EverQuest II reached 100,000 active accounts within 24 hours of release and grew to over 300,000 in January 2005, with a subscriber peak of 325,000 in 2005. As of September 2020, it had 21,000 subscribers and 29,000 monthly active players. EverQuest II: East, an alternate edition for East Asia, was developed by Sony Online Entertainment and launched in April 2005, featuring localized tutorials, a separate "SOGA Model" character design, and proprietary missions, but failed due to poor localization; Gamania terminated its operations on March 29, 2006, and all Chinese, Taiwanese, and Korean accounts were transferred to US servers. In February 2015, Sony Computer Entertainment sold Sony Online Entertainment to investment company Inception Acquisitions, which rebranded the studio as Daybreak Game Company, which continues to develop and publish EverQuest II. The game has been used in academic studies to analyze virtual economic behavior, with findings showing real-world patterns in production, consumption, and money supply, and that less than one percent (0.43%) of players are Platinum Farmers, with over 77% of them being Chinese. It received mostly positive reviews, earning an 83 out of 100 average on Metacritic, with critics noting it as more convenient and forgiving than the original, though less groundbreaking, with its extensive voice acting being a major advancement. While praised for its presentation and photorealistic graphics, performance issues were common on higher settings, requiring powerful systems for optimal play. The game's expansions, including Tears of Veeshan (which includes Chains of Eternity), introduce new zones, features, creatures, items, and player races, with access to levels above 92 requiring the purchase of Tears of Veeshan. Free-to-play accounts have access to the same areas as subscription accounts but face restrictions such as limited bag slots, coin limits, quest journal limits, race and class restrictions, and gear limitations, though many restrictions have been removed, including the inability to buy or sell items on the broker, spell tier limits, and the alternate advancement slider. The game's feature set has expanded since its 2004 release, including the introduction of Adventure Packs—smaller digital expansions with plot lines, zones, creatures, and items—though the development team now releases free zones and content instead. Expansions are available through retail or digital download and often include bonus features like in-game creatures. EverQuest II: East used similar settings to the original, with localized content and local language character naming, but most dialogue remained in English except for the novice tutorial, which was localized by Gamania.

text: Chiharu Shiota (塩田 千春, Shiota Chiharu), born in 1972 in Osaka, is a Japanese performance and installation artist who has lived and worked in Berlin, Germany since 1996. Her parents operated a business manufacturing fish boxes, producing a thousand wooden boxes daily, and although they did not directly support her artistic ambitions, they permitted her to formally study art. Shiota studied at Kyoto Seika University in Kyoto from 1992 to 1996, where she studied under contemporary sculptor Saburo Muraoka; she was an exchange student at Canberra School of Art, Australian National University, in 1993, and later attended Hochschule für Bildende Künste, Braunschweig (1997–1999), and Universität der Künste, Berlin (1999–2002), where she also served as Artist in Residence at Akademie Schloss Solitude, Stuttgart. In Berlin, she studied under Rebecca Horn and was influenced by Marina Abramović, who became a significant figure in shaping her artistic development. Her early works, including From DNA to DNA (1994) and Becoming Painting (1994), used materials like woolen threads and red enamel paint applied to her body, marking her first physical artworks and serving as acts of liberation. Shiota's artistic practice spans performance, sculpture, and installation, with her most recognized works being vast, room-spanning webs of threads or hoses that connect abstract networks to everyday objects such as keys, window frames, dresses, shoes, boats, and suitcases. Materials hold symbolic meaning in her work: menstruation blood is used as artistic material, and red threads represent human relationships; thin plastic tubing filled with blood-like liquid symbolizes the umbilical connection, suggesting nurturing and the beginning of life. She draws on psychogeography—the relationship between psyche and space—and has stated that she could not have created major installations like A Room of Memory (2009) and Memory of Skin (2005) without living in Berlin. Shiota has collaborated with choreographers and composers such as Toshio Hosokawa, Sasha Waltz, and Stefan Goldmann. Arriving in Berlin in 1999, she observed the city’s lingering Cold War relics and later focused on abandoned areas, collecting hundreds of old windows from former East Berlin, which she used in House of Windows (2005), exhibited at her solo show Raum at Haus am Lützowplatz and later at the 3rd Fukuoka Asian Art Triennale. She equates windows to skin, exploring physical and interpersonal boundaries in a rapidly changing urban environment, and views her own dislocation as a central theme in her work. Since the 2000s, Shiota has produced cobweb-like installations worldwide, adapting their scale to gallery spaces and incorporating found objects such as beds, dresses, shoes, keys, and chairs. These objects carry personal and lived experiences, and the red or black threads stretch, connect, enclose, and obscure them, reflecting the tangled, tense nature of human relationships. The creation process involves hours of labor by Shiota and her assistants, embedding performative elements into the works. In Dialogue with Absence (2010), an oversized white wedding dress hangs on a wall, with red liquid flowing from peristaltic pumps into it via plastic tubes, evoking themes of womanhood, societal burdens, and possibly her own battle with cancer. For Manifesta 14 in Pristina, she hung hundreds of red yarn threads from the Great Hammam’s ceiling, attracting over 150,000 visitors. She has also engaged in community-based projects, such as Further Memory (2010), a tunnel-like structure on Teshima Island, Japan, constructed from 600 used local windows, echoing House of Windows and reflecting on ecological beauty and the islanders’ connection to nature, offering a sense of hope amid depopulation.

### 🔗 Cause-Effect Chain: The Library Donation and Its Consequences

We will build a clear, memorable cause-and-effect chain that ties **Pedro Antonio de Aragón’s library donation** directly to **personal legacy, burial rights, and a broader historical action** — all of which reinforce the significance of his cultural patronage as a strategic personal goal.

---

#### 🔄 Cause-Effect Chain:

1. **Cause**: Pedro Antonio de Aragón donated his personal library of approximately 3,600 volumes to Poblet Monastery in 1677.  
2. **Effect**: In return, he was granted the right to be buried among the monastery’s venerated figures — a prestigious honor reflecting his status and cultural contributions.

text: Thomas Randolph (1523–1590) was an English ambassador to Elizabeth I of England and spent much of his professional life in Scotland, serving at the courts of Mary, Queen of Scots, and her son James VI. He was involved in marriage negotiations and various political upheavals. Between 1568 and 1569, he was sent on a special mission to Russia, where he visited the court of Ivan the Terrible and secured privileges for English merchants, leading to the formation of the Muscovy Company. Randolph served as a Member of Parliament for New Romney in 1558, Maidstone in 1584, 1586, and 1589, Grantham in 1559, St Ives in 1558 and 1572. Born in 1523 to Avery Randolph of Badlesmere, Kent, and Anne Gainsford (not the lady-in-waiting to Anne Boleyn), he entered Christ Church, Oxford at its foundation, graduated with a B.A. in October 1545 and a B.C.L. in 1548, became a public notary, and was principal of Broadgates Hall (now Pembroke College), Oxford until 1553. Due to Protestant persecutions under Queen Mary, he resigned and retired to France, where he resided in Paris and was influenced by George Buchanan, whom he praised in a letter to Peter Young, tutor of James VI. Among his fellow students in Paris was Sir William Kirkcaldy of Grange. After Elizabeth's accession in 1558, Randolph acted as an agent in Germany before returning to England and purchasing a farm in Kent—the house where he was born. His knowledge of Scottish Protestants in Paris led Elizabeth to employ him in bringing the Earl of Arran from Geneva to England. He sometimes signed his letters with the Latin phrase "Virtus pro divitiis," which he wrote in a copy of John Jewel's Apologia ecclesiae Anglicanae (1562), now held by the University of Edinburgh. Under the name Barnabie and using the codename Pamphilus, he was sent in autumn 1559 to secretly transport James Hamilton, 3rd Earl of Arran, into Scotland. He returned to London on 25 November but was again sent to Scotland in March 1560, where his efforts influenced Protestant opposition to the queen-regent and helped establish an understanding with Elizabeth. His continued role as a confidential agent for Elizabeth, and also for William Cecil, the secretary of state, gave him significant influence in Scottish politics despite lacking diplomatic skill compared to Maitland of Lethington. His numerous letters remain vital sources on the Queen of Scots' court, political plots, and social intrigues. At the marriage of Lord James Stewart and Agnes Keith in February 1562, Mary toasted Elizabeth from a gold cup and presented it to Randolph, discussing the "amity" between England and Scotland; Mary was also sent a portrait of Elizabeth, which Randolph verified. In autumn 1562, Randolph accompanied Mary on a northern expedition that resulted in the defeat and death of George Gordon, 4th Earl of Huntly, and he participated in the campaign, stating he was "ashamed to sit still where so many were occupied." In January 1563, he attended the wedding of James Stewart, Commendator of Inchcolm, and Margaret Campbell at Castle Campbell, describing feasts, banqueting, masking, and running at the ring. In June 1563, he met a servant of Catholic priest John Black at St Andrews, bribed him to reveal correspondence, and copied it. On 5 June 1563, Elizabeth granted him a license to return to England for private business. In April 1563, he was sent to Scotland to entangle Mary in marriage negotiations with Lord Robert Dudley, Elizabeth's favourite; initially unenthusiastic, Mary eventually accepted the proposal after Elizabeth declared her official heir on the condition of marriage. In September 1564, Elizabeth granted Dudley the earldom of Leicester to improve his appeal, and in early 1565, Mary accepted the match. However, Dudley refused to marry Mary and showed passive resistance, which Randolph repeatedly tried to overcome through letters. Elizabeth later withdrew her support for the succession declaration. When Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, became a serious candidate, Elizabeth sought to prevent the marriage, and Randolph received instructions to push for a union with Dudley or another noble; if the proposal was irreversible, he was to report how it would distress her. Randolph reported on a Roman antiquity discovered near Edinburgh at Musselburgh, including an inscribed altar and hypocaust, and courted Mary Beaton, one of Mary's companions. In April 1565, Beaton and Randolph played bowls at Stirling Castle with the queen and Darnley, winning and receiving a ring and brooch worth fifty crowns from Darnley. A letter from Alexander Clark mocked their relationship with nonsense words: "And as to your mistress Marie Beton, she is both darimpus and sclenbrunit, and you in like manner without contrebaxion or kylteperante, so you are both worth little money." Randolph failed to prevent Mary's marriage to Darnley and declined to recognize Darnley's authority. His representations may have contributed to the rebellion of James Stewart, 1st Earl of Moray, known as the Chaseabout Raid. On 16 January 1566, he reported that Mary had withheld the "Matrimonial crown" from Darnley and was now pregnant, noting she felt the movement on New Year's Day and had milk in her breasts. On 14 February 1566, he wrote to the Earl of Leicester that he could not commit to writing about Mary's actions due to fear of appearing "malicieus foolyshe and unadvised." In February 1566, Mary accused him of aiding Moray and her rebels with a gift of three thousand crowns, requiring him to leave the country within six days. He retired to Berwick upon Tweed, where after Riccio's murder, he was accused of writing a book against Mary called Mr. Randolph's Phantasy. He was recalled to England around June 1566 and appointed "Master of the King's Post," later becoming postmaster general. On 2 November 1567, he obtained from Robert Constable an assignment as constable of Queenborough Castle and steward of the manor of Middleton and Merden in Kent. In June 1568, he was sent to Russia to support English merchants, securing privileges from Ivan IV that led to the Muscovy Company's formation; he returned in autumn 1569. Following representations by Regent Moray's agent Nicolas Elphinstone in January 1570, he was sent to Scotland despite uncertain news of Moray's assassination. He remained in Scotland for a year. In October 1573 and April 1576, he conducted special embassies to France. In February 1578, he was sent to Scotland but too late to prevent the fall of James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton. After Morton's imprisonment in 1580, he returned to Scotland to negotiate on his behalf. At a convention of the estates on 20 February 1581, he presented a paper on the Queen's intentions and offers to the King of Scotland and delivered a two-hour speech denouncing Esme Stewart, created Duke of Lennox, as a Roman agent. His bold action only sealed Morton's fate. He then attempted, with Elizabeth's approval, to plot the seizure of Lennox and the young king, but the plot was betrayed, and he fled to Berwick after narrowly escaping death from a shot fired in the provost's house in Edinburgh. His advice directly influenced English policy, advising Elizabeth against military intervention in Scotland against the Lennox government. In January 1586, he was sent on his final mission to Scotland with Thomas Mills to negotiate a treaty between England and Scotland, which he successfully secured through the signature of James VI despite opposition from French diplomat Charles de Prunelé, Baron d'Esneval. In August 1586, Randolph and the Scottish ambassador Archibald Douglas sent male deer and huntsmen to James VI at Falkland Palace; the huntsmen likely included Cuthbert Rayne. He wrote: "I have sent the Kynge two hunting men, verie good and skillful, with one footman, that can hoop, hollow and crye, that all the trees in Fawkland will quake for fear. Pray the Kynge's Majestie to be mercifull to the poor bucks; but let him spare and look well to himself." He presented £4,000 to James VI from Elizabeth, the first regular subsidy, noting that James VI, like previous regents, did not issue receipts for such payments, explaining that princes avoid "bills of their hands" to prevent "danger or reproach." Randolph held the joint offices of Chamberlain of the Exchequer and Master of the Post until his death on 8 June 1590, at age sixty-seven, in his house on St. Peter's Hill, near Thames Street, London, and was buried in the church of St. Peter's, Paul's Wharf. Throughout his embassies, he was frequently short of money and struggled to pay expenses. Despite his significant services, he received no substantial reward beyond these modest offices. The claim that he was knighted in 1571 is not supported by evidence. He is believed to have authored the original short Latin Life of George Buchanan, though this is at least doubtful; he showed strong interest in Buchanan's History and offered financial support for its completion. In July 1593, the Scottish ambassador, with Roger Aston, claimed that Randolph had promised in 1586 to pay James VI an annual subsidy of £5,000, a claim William Cecil deemed unlikely and which prompted a search of Randolph's papers. In late 1571, he married Anne Walsingham, daughter of Thomas Walsingham of Chislehurst and cousin once removed of Francis Walsingham. Before the marriage, on 1 October 1571, he received letters patent from Thomas Walsingham and William Crowner granting custody of the manor and hundred of Middleton and Merden at a rent of 100 pounds per annum to be paid to his wife. In 1572, he was appointed Chamberlain of the Exchequer for life. His friend George Buchanan teased him about the marriage, saying: "If you had been in your right wit, you being once escaped the tempestous storms and naufrage (shipwreck) of marriage, had never entered again the same dangers, for I cannot take you for a Stoic philosopher, having one head inexpugnable (not to be captured) with the frenetic tortures of jealousy, or a careless heart sceptic that takes cuckoldry as thing indifferent." Their children included: Thomas Randolph married secondly Ursula Copinger, daughter of Henry Copinger of Allhallows Hoo, Kent, and Buxhall, Suffolk, and his wife Agnes, daughter of Thomas Jermyn (died 1552); their children are listed. Randolph died in 1590.

text: Machine Girl (sometimes stylized as machin3gir1) is an American electronic music project founded in 2012 by Matt Stephenson, also known as DJ Chaotic Ugly, on Long Island, New York. In 2015, the project expanded into a duo when Stephenson recruited percussionist Sean Kelly to play live drums. Lucy Caputi joined in 2024 as a live guitarist and official member. In 2022, Machine Girl composed the original soundtrack for the video game Neon White, consisting of two parts—"The Wicked Heart" and "The Burn That Cures"—aligned with the game's narrative. In an interview with Revolver magazine, Stephenson described the project as "fucked-up electronic punk" and rejected the "industrial" label for being "very goth, and very black and white," emphasizing its "a lot more colorful" nature. Kerrang! recognized Machine Girl as one of the "bands expanding the definition of hardcore," characterizing them as "a particularly punky and ferocious breed of the electronic sub-genre breakcore that could easily pass for hardcore when they rip it live." Pitchfork defined their sound as "relentlessly smashing together bits of punk, grindcore, rave, industrial, and more," describing it as "unpredictable and dangerous, full of animalistic rage and uncontrollable energy." The project's name originates from the 2008 Japanese film The Machine Girl, which they occasionally sampled on their 2014 album WLFGRL. Stephenson is also a member of the electronic duo Prolaps with Bonnie Baxter from Kill Alters, beginning their collaboration on the track "Vomit" from ...Because I'm Young Arrogant and Hate Everything You Stand For, which they started releasing in 2020. In 2013, Machine Girl began posting self-directed videos on their YouTube channel, starting with the unfinished song "~*•°•.[g0o∂]_[∫3º¥].•°•*~," released on December 20, 2013. Their next upload was on February 7, 2014, for the song "Ginger Claps," nine days before the release of their debut album WLFGRL. On November 4, 2014, they posted a video titled "___________DJPH11252014," promoting a DJ performance at "DJ PHANTASY CLUB" featuring ABSRDST, Doss, DV-i, Ducky, Machine Girl, Ligaments, Legion, and The Magick Report, including a snippet of an early mix of "Loop Version" that later appeared on their 2018 album The Ugly Art. On July 31, 2015, Machine Girl released two videos titled "HEAVEN MIX" and "HELL MIX," featuring visuals by Videopunks and containing snippets from each side of their sophomore album Gemini. The next official music video was for "Bitten Twice," released on May 16, 2017, followed by "Sad Claps" on June 12, 2017. Subsequent visualizers were uploaded for ...Because I'm Young Arrogant and Hate Everything You Stand For (September 24, 2017), MRK90 MIX VOL 1 (December 17, 2017), and The Ugly Art (October 14, 2018). The next music video to be published was for "Fully In It" on August 28, 2020, featuring stop motion animation by Ellie Thatcher. On November 15, 2020, Machine Girl released a video titled "GLOBAL FANDEMIC [MACHINE GIRL SET @ A2B2 NIGHT OF FIRE]" as part of a 24-hour virtual music festival hosted by Andy Morin of a2b2, featuring Matt performing over fan-submitted visualizers and including almost entirely unreleased songs and a shortened version of "Athoth A Go!! text: The Jeffersons is an American sitcom created by Norman Lear that aired on CBS from January 18, 1975, to July 2, 1985, spanning eleven seasons and 253 episodes. Starring Isabel Sanford as Louise Jefferson and Sherman Hemsley as George Jefferson, the show follows a prosperous African-American couple who move from Queens to a high-rise apartment in Manhattan, New York City, due to the success of George's dry-cleaning chain, Jefferson Cleaners. It is a spin-off of All in the Family, where the Jeffersons were neighbors of the Bunkers; George's character was specifically created for Hemsley, who was initially unavailable due to starring in the Broadway musical Purlie, leading Lear to introduce Henry Jefferson, played by Mel Stewart, as George's younger brother until Purlie ended. The Jeffersons premiered the week after the All in the Family episode "The Jeffersons Move Up," which aired on January 11, 1975, and featured Louise, her son Lionel (played by Mike Evans), and George moving into the Colby East high-rise. The show's concept was inspired by feedback from Black Panthers who criticized the portrayal of Black people on television, prompting Lear to develop a series highlighting upward mobility. The series evolved into a traditional sitcom but occasionally addressed serious issues such as alcoholism, racism, suicide, gun control, transgender identity, the KKK, and adult illiteracy, with the epithets "nigger" and "honky" used occasionally, especially in early seasons. The show had one spin-off, Checking In, centered on Florence Johnston (Marla Gibbs), who becomes a hotel cleaning manager, lasting only four episodes before returning to The Jeffersons with the story that the hotel burned down. The Jeffersons shared continuity with E/R, featuring Lynne Moody in a guest role, and Sherman Hemsley guest-starred as George in two episodes of a one-season series. The show ended controversially when CBS canceled it without a proper finale, announcing the cancellation at the upfront presentation the day before the final episode aired on July 2, 1985, nearly two months prior; cast members learned through newspapers, tabloids, or Entertainment Tonight. Isabel Sanford criticized the cancellation as disrespectful. The cast later reunited in a stage play, "The Jeffersons Live: The Movin' On Up Tour," and made guest appearances in later series, including The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air (1995 and 1996) and Tyler Perry's House of Payne (2011). In 1985, Hemsley and Sanford made a joint guest appearance in the Italian comedy Grand Hotel, with their voices dubbed by Enzo Garinei and Isa di Marzio. As of 2023, surviving main cast members include Marla Gibbs, Berlinda Tolbert, Damon Evans, and Jay Hammer. The Jeffersons' theme song, "Movin' On Up," was co-written by Ja'Net DuBois and Jeff Barry, inspired by DuBois's dream of providing her mother with a comfortable retirement. The show changed time slots at least 15 times during its run, most commonly airing on Sunday nights. It initially ranked fourth in its first season, later entering the Top 30, peaking at No. 3 in 1982, and remaining in the Top 20 for several seasons. The series was rebroadcast on CBS from February 4, 1980, to September 25, 1981, and released on DVD by Sony Pictures Home Entertainment from 2002 to 2007, later acquired by Mill Creek and Shout! Factory, with the complete series released in a 33-disc collection in 2014. The Jeffersons earned 14 Emmy nominations, winning two: Marla Gibbs won Best Supporting Actress in a Comedy Series from 1981 to 1985, Sherman Hemsley received a nomination in 1984, and Larry M. Harris won Outstanding Video Tape Editing in 1983; Isabel Sanford was nominated for seven consecutive Best Actress Emmys from 1979 to 1985, winning in 1981, making her the first African-American actress to win that award. The show received five Golden Globe nominations. Critics have criticized it as stereotypical, with Gregory Kane calling it demeaning in 1999. The series had many two-part episodes and was known for its recurring characters, including Tom and Helen Willis (played by Franklin Cover and Roxie Roker), who were an interracial couple; Allan (Jay Hammer) and Jenny (Berlinda Tolbert), who married in 1976 and had a daughter, Jessica; and Paul Benedict as Harry Bentley, a British neighbor with a bad back and a habit of being slammed in the door. Ned Wertimer played Ralph Hart, the tip-hungry doorman, and Danny Wells portrayed Charlie, the bar owner and alcoholic, whose drinking issue was addressed in a season 11 episode. Mike Evans (Lionel) left after the first season, with Damon Evans (no relation) taking over until halfway through season 4, and Evans made his final appearance in "Lionel Gets the Business." Mike Evans and Tolbert returned in 1979–1980, with Tolbert's character pregnant, and Evans appeared in only one more season. The series' eighth season reached No. 3, becoming the first African-American sitcom in years to peak in the top 5. Paul Benedict left for a season and a half in 1981, returning in the final two seasons. The show's ratings declined after 1980, and it ended with the episode "Red Robins" on July 2, 1985. On May 22, 2019, ABC aired a live stage production of Norman Lear's All in the Family and The Jeffersons, featuring Marla Gibbs as Florence Johnston.

text: Anil Biswas (2 March 1944 – 26 March 2006), commonly known as Keru, was an Indian communist politician who served as the secretary of the West Bengal State Committee of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) and as a member of the party's politburo from 1998 until his death in 2006. Born into a middle-class Mahishya family in Darermath village near Karimpur, Nadia district, to Ashutosh Biswas and Prafulla Kumari Debi, he lost his father at a young age. While in high school, he became interested in the Left movement and joined Krishnagar Government College in 1961, where he was influenced by Marxist leaders Harinarayan Adhikari and Dinesh Majumdar and became an active member of the Students' Federation of India, serving as a student leader in college elections. After completing an Honours degree in Political Science, he moved to Kolkata for further studies. He became a full-fledged member of the CPI(M) in 1965 and was arrested under the Defence of India Rules 1962, spending 11 months in prison, during which he completed his master's degree in political science. In 1969, he became a whole-time party member and began his party work as a journalist with Ganashakti, the party's daily newspaper. He was elected to the CPIM West Bengal state committee in 1978 and to the state secretariat in 1982. He edited Ganashakti between 1983 and 1998, during which the newspaper achieved its peak circulation. In 1985, he was elected to the party's Central Committee. In 1998, he joined the politburo, mentored by Pramod Dasgupta, and took over as secretary of the West Bengal State Committee after his predecessor Sailen Dasgupta resigned due to ill-health and old age. He was reelected as state secretary in 2002 and 2005. He also served as editor of Marxbadi Path (The Road of the Marxist), the theoretical quarterly in West Bengal. Known for his strategic acumen, he played a key role in the party's political decisions, including the decision to appoint Buddhadeb Bhattacharjee as Chief Minister of West Bengal in place of Jyoti Basu before the 2000 West Bengal Legislative Assembly Elections—a move that addressed public frustration with over two decades of the same chief minister and led to a major victory for the Left Front despite strong opposition from Mamata Banerjee's TMC. His effective management of media and ground workers during the 2006 West Bengal Assembly Election significantly reduced the opposition's seat count, as he had a deep understanding of public sentiment both in the media and on the ground. It is widely believed that the deaths of Anil Biswas and other key ground leaders like Subhas Chakraborty created opportunities for the opposition to come to power and replace the Left Front. He died on 26 March 2006 after being hospitalized due to a brain haemorrhage on 18 March. According to his last wishes, his body was donated to NRS Medical College and Hospital. He is survived by his wife Gita and daughter Ajanta.

text: Mehbooba Bur Mufti Sayed (born 22 May 1959) is an Indian politician and leader of the Jammu and Kashmir People's Democratic Party (PDP), who served as the 9th chief minister of the erstwhile state Jammu and Kashmir from 4 April 2016 to 19 June 2018. She is the first female chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir. After the revocation of Article 370 of the constitution in August 2019, Mufti was detained without any charges at first and later under the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act. She was the first woman to hold the office of chief minister in Jammu and Kashmir. She formed a coalition government in Jammu and Kashmir jointly with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). She resigned in June 2018 after the BJP withdrew from the coalition. Mufti was the president of the PDP and a member of the Indian parliament, representing Anantnag in the 16th Lok Sabha before being sworn in as chief minister. She also represented Anantnag in the 14th Lok Sabha (2004–09) and has been a Leader of Opposition in the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly. She is the daughter of Mufti Mohammad Sayeed and Gulshan Ara, born in 1959 in Akhran Nowpora, J&K, India. She graduated in English literature from Government College for Women in Jammu and has a law degree from the University of Kashmir. Post 1989, she shifted to N. Delhi and joined the Bombay Mercantile Bank, after which she worked with East West Airlines, before moving back to J&K. She married Javed Iqbal Shah in 1984, but they later divorced. Her ex-husband is the first cousin of her father, Mufti Mohammad Sayeed, meaning that before their marriage, Mehbooba Mufti was Javed Iqbal Shah's niece. She has two daughters, Iltija and Irtiqa. Her ex-husband is a political analyst, an animal-rights activist, and was briefly with the National Conference party. When elections for the state assembly were held in 1996, Mehbooba became one of the most popular members elected from Bijbehara on an Indian National Congress ticket. Her father had returned to the Congress, which he had left in 1987, angry at the alliance that party had formed with its traditional rival in the state, the National Conference. She later served as the leader of the opposition in the assembly, taking on the government of chief minister Farooq Abdullah with asperity. She resigned her assembly seat and went on to contest the parliamentary elections in 1999 from Srinagar, where she lost to incumbent member Omar Abdullah. She won the Pahalgam seat in the state assembly from South Kashmir, defeating Rafi Ahmed Mir, when assembly elections were held again in 2002. She was elected to the Lok Sabha from Anantnag seat in 2004 and 2014. She defeated Mirza Mehboob Beg, who was the incumbent MP, in the 2014 Lok Sabha Elections. After her father's death in January 2016, when he was heading the coalition government in Jammu and Kashmir, she took forward the same alliance with the BJP, the second time the BJP and the PDP formed a government in Jammu and Kashmir. On 4 April 2016, she took the oath and became the first woman Chief Minister of Jammu and Kashmir. On 25 June 2016, she won an Assembly seat in a by-election in Anantnag with the highest margin in any recent elections there and thereafter focused on settling of Rohingyas. On 19 June 2018, she resigned as chief minister of Kashmir. Her government had been an alliance between the Peoples' Democratic Party (PDP) and the BJP, but there was a rift in the alliance in February 2018, when two BJP ministers expressed public support for a man who was alleged to have raped and killed an eight-year-old girl in Kathua District. The BJP's National General Secretary, Ram Madhav, announced the end of the alliance between the BJP and the PDP, saying it was because of the deteriorating security situation. Mehbooba and the state government had tried suspending security operations for Ramadan, but the militants had not reciprocated, and 30 people were killed during the ceasefire. So the BJP withdrew from the alliance with the PDP so that the Indian government could get tough with the militants. When the alliance between the PDP and the BJP ended, Mehbooba resigned as chief minister. Mehbooba said "the muscular policy will not work in Kashmir". She contested the 2019 Lok Sabha elections from Anantnag seat but lost it to Hasnain Masoodi of the National Conference, and later also lost the 2024 Lok Sabha elections from Anantnag - Rajouri seat to Mian Altaf Ahmed Larvi of the National Conference with 2.3 lakh votes. On 5 August 2019, she was detained by the Central government. Her daughter Iltija Mufti took over her mother's Twitter account on the 46th day of detention. In November, Iltija Mufti wrote a letter to the Srinagar Deputy Commissioner to shift her mother to a place better equipped for the valley's winter. In February 2020 she was further detained under the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act. She was released on 13 October 2020. On 25 November 2020, former Jammu and Kashmir chief minister and People's Democratic Party chief Mehbooba Mufti was detained by Jammu and Kashmir Police and was not allowed to visit South Kashmir's Pulwama to meet the family of senior PDP leader Waheed Para, who was arrested by the National Investigating Agency earlier that week. Mufti said that her daughter Iltija Mufti has also been placed under house arrest.

text: Terence Renaud, writing for the Los Angeles Review of Books, notes that given the significant changes in the political landscape since the publication of Empire in 2000, much of Hardt and Negri's project now appears to have concluded its contribution. Nevertheless, the authors effectively highlight the internal challenges a resurgent left faces, such as degenerating into sectarian conflict, authoritarian leadership, and complacency in its self-perception. Hardt and Negri advocate for a self-critical and internally democratic left that continuously questions its own assumptions, emphasizing that to transform society, the left must first transform itself. Between 2016 and 2019, Negri published a three-volume collection of essays translated and compiled into English. The first volume, Marx and Foucault, was released on 16 December 2016, aiming to demonstrate how Marx and Foucault's thought were synthesized, particularly in the context of Italy from May '68 onward. The second volume, From the Factory to the Metropolis, published in February 2018, analyzes the shift from the traditional industrial proletarian 'mass worker' to the contemporary 'socialised worker' and examines the modern 'metropolis' as a space of antagonism between finance capital (operating through rents) and the 'cognitive proletariat,' with the central question being how the 'common' of the latter can be mobilized to destroy capitalism. The third volume, Spinoza: Then and Now, published in February 2020, explores how Spinoza's thought represents a radical departure from past ideas and serves as a vital tool for envisioning politics beyond capitalism. On 29 October 2021, Negri released the first volume of a new trilogy, Marx in Movement: Operaismo in Context, which provides an account of the history of Italian Autonomist (or 'Autonomist Marxist') thought, especially focusing on Negri's development of the concept of the 'social worker' as a way to update Marxism in response to changes since Marx's era of factory-based labor. Negri married Paola Meo in 1962; they had two children, Anna and Francesco, and later divorced. He has another daughter, Nina Negri, from a separate relationship. He met the philosopher Judith Revel in 1996 and married her in 2016. Negri died in Paris on 16 December 2023, at the age of 90. text: Michael John Creutz, born on November 24, 1944, in Los Alamos, New Mexico, is an American theoretical physicist at Brookhaven National Laboratory, specializing in lattice gauge theory and computational physics. His father, Edward Creutz, was also a physicist and was involved in the Manhattan Project at the time of Michael's birth. Creutz earned his bachelor's degree in physics with honor from Caltech in 1966 and completed his graduate studies at Stanford University under a NSF Graduate Fellowship, graduating in 1970. His thesis was conducted at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, with Sidney Drell as his adviser. Following graduation, he served as a research associate at SLAC before joining the Center for Theoretical Physics at the University of Maryland, College Park, as a fellow from 1970 to 1972. In 1972, he joined the High Energy Theory Group at Brookhaven National Laboratory, becoming a senior physicist in 1985 and serving as group leader from 1984 to 1987. In 2003, he became an adjunct professor at the C. N. Yang Institute for Theoretical Physics at Stony Brook University. His research covers various areas in particle physics and mathematical physics, but he is best known for his work on lattice QCD. His 1983 textbook, *Quarks, Gluons, and Lattices*, was the first full-length textbook on lattice QCD and is regarded as a classic in the field. Creutz is a fellow of the American Physical Society and received the Aneesur Rahman Prize for Computational Physics in 2000 "for first demonstrating that properties of QCD could be computed numerically on the lattice through Monte Carlo methods, and for numerous contributions to the field thereafter." In 2009, he was awarded the Humboldt Research Award.

text: Mohinder Amarnath Bhardwaj, born on 24 September 1950 in Patiala, is a former Indian cricketer and cricket analyst, son of Lala Amarnath, the first post-independence captain of India. He served as vice-captain of the Indian team that won the 1983 Cricket World Cup, where he was named Player of the Final and also played a key role in the semi-final, earning Man of the Match honors in both matches. He was part of the Indian squad that won the 1985 World Championship of Cricket. Known widely by players and pundits as the best Indian batsman against express pace, Mohinder received the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award in 2009. He was the second eldest son of Lala Amarnath and Kailash Kumari; his elder brother Surinder was a former international cricketer, younger brother Rajinder a former first-class cricketer, and he has two sisters, Kamala and Dolly. He completed his schooling at MB High School, Mandir Marg, Delhi, and graduated from SGTB Khalsa College, Delhi University. Making his Test debut against Australia in December 1969 as a quick-bowling all-rounder, he was a top-order batsman, primarily playing at No. 3, known for being both attacking and defensive, and for reinventing his game over time. He was also skilled with the ball, bowling swingers and cutters with great control and had a unique run-up where he slowed down as he approached the crease. He played 69 Tests, scoring 4,378 runs at an average of 42.50, including 11 hundreds and 24 fifties, and took 32 wickets at 55.68; in 85 One Day Internationals, he scored 1,924 runs at an average of 30.53, with a highest score of 102 not out, and took 46 wickets at 42.84. Imran Khan of Pakistan and Malcolm Marshall of the West Indies praised his batsmanship, courage, and ability to endure pain. In the 1982–83 series against Pakistan and the West Indies, he scored over 1000 runs in the two series, and despite India losing the first three Tests 3–0, he was the sole saving grace for the batting line-up. Sunil Gavaskar, in his book "Idols," described Mohinder as the finest batsman in the world, and Imran Khan stated in his book "All Round View" that Mohinder was the best batsman in the world during the 1982–83 season and should have played continuously from his debut in 1969 until retirement. The series saw Imran Khan take 40 wickets and jointly win "Man of the Series" with Mohinder, who was instrumental in stabilizing India's batting. Sunil Gavaskar scored 434 runs in one innings during the series. Mohinder made his first Test century at Perth against Jeff Thomson at the WACA, the fastest and bounciest wicket in the world, and followed it with 10 more centuries against top-class fast bowling. In the 1983 World Cup semi-final against England, his accurate seam bowling led to the dismissal of David Gower and Mike Gatting, with only 27 runs given in 12 overs (2.25 per over), the lowest among Indian bowlers, and he scored 46 runs to provide a solid foundation, earning Man of the Match. In the final against the West Indies, India was dismissed for 183 in 54.4 overs, far below the 60-over target, but Amarnath's calm batting provided stability, occupying the crease for 80 balls and scoring 26 runs. Krishnamachari Srikkanth top-scored with 38, followed by Sandeep Patil with 27. India's chances were slim, but the Indian bowling, exploiting weather and pitch conditions, bowled out the West Indies for 140, winning by 43 runs. Amarnath and Madan Lal were joint highest wicket-takers with 3 wickets each, and he was again named Man of the Match for his economical bowling, conceding only 12 runs in 7 overs (1.71 per over), and also took the match-winning wicket. As vice-captain, he held the World Cup aloft in a famous photograph with captain Kapil Dev. Except for 1982–83, Mohinder never held a steady place in the Indian Test side and was frequently dropped, earning the nickname "Comeback Man" of Indian cricket. He was known for his batting technique, temperament, and skill, having experimented with a side-on batting stance. He was admired for his personality, courage, and determination; Vivian Richards called him "one of the nicest men to have ever played the game," and David Boon said "Concede didn't seem to be in his vocabulary." Gideon Haigh noted that despite being hit by Richard Hadlee, Imran Khan, Malcolm Marshall, and Jeff Thomson—suffering a skull fracture, being knocked unconscious, teeth knocked out, and a painful jaw injury—he never stopped hooking and continued playing, with Michael Holding stating that what separated him from others was his ability to withstand pain. During the Bridgetown Test in 1982–83, he retired for stitches after being hit on the head and returned to face Michael Holding, hooking a bouncer to the boundary. However, during the 1983/84 tour of India, the West Indies attack restricted him to just 1 run in six innings, with Holding dismissing him three times for ducks, leading to his drop shortly after his 1983 World Cup success. He played a key role in a famous chase at Queen's Park Oval, Port of Spain, in 1976, scoring 85 in the second innings to take India to the brink of a historic win. He had notable conflicts with the Indian cricket selectors, famously calling them a "bunch of jokers," which often led to his exclusion. Mohinder is the only Indian to be dismissed on handling the ball, first in an ODI on 9 February 1986, and the only Indian to be dismissed for obstructing the field in ODIs; he is also the only international cricketer to have been given out for both handling the ball and obstructing the field. He carried a red handkerchief visibly in his trouser pocket while batting as a superstition. He presented a popular weekly cricket coaching TV program in the late 80s and early 90s titled "Cricket with Mohinder Amarnath," which featured technique presentations and guest speakers, mostly from the Indian national team, and gained a strong following among youth, especially after the 1987 Reliance Cup, broadcast on Doordarshan. The program's title song, "Khel hi hain hamara jeevan...", was very catchy; young Sachin Tendulkar, at 15, was interviewed by Amarnath and later joined the Indian team for the Pakistan tour after a year. Mohinder is married to Inderjit Amarnath and has one daughter. The 2021 Hindi film 83, based on India's 1983 World Cup victory, features Saqib Saleem as Amarnath and Amarnath himself as his father, Lala, and he also played the role of a cricket coach to Saleem's character, Viraj Sharma, in the 2016 film Dishoom.

text: Rosa Whitaker Duncan-Williams is an American lobbyist and former trade negotiator who served as the first Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Africa during the administrations of Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush. She currently operates a consulting firm called The Whitaker Group. Whitaker was born in Washington, D.C., and earned both a master's and bachelor's degree from American University in Washington, D.C., and also studied at the Foreign Service Institute in the United Kingdom and Italy. While serving as a Senior Trade Advisor to Congressman Charlie Rangel, she played a key role in drafting the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which was enacted in 2000. AGOA, America’s first comprehensive trade law targeting Africa, continues to serve as the foundation of U.S. economic policy toward the continent, facilitating billions of dollars in duty-free African products entering the U.S. market each year and supporting job creation and investment across Africa. She co-founded and co-chaired the bipartisan advocacy group AGOA Action Coalition with Jack Kemp. After leaving the U.S. Trade Representative’s office in 2003, Whitaker launched The Whitaker Group, which is headquartered in Northern Virginia and Accra, Ghana, and provides advice on trade, investment, and project development across Africa. The firm, established in 2003, has attracted clients from Fortune 500 companies seeking opportunities in both commercial and human development in Africa. In 2017, Whitaker led The Whitaker Group’s first direct investment in Africa by acquiring shares and management control of Dominion TV, a Pan-African television, entertainment, and multimedia company that broadcasts in 48 African countries via DStv, Africa’s largest satellite platform. The firm has also worked with the authoritarian Faure Gnassingbé regime in Togo. In 2005, Whitaker became involved in a controversy over her firm’s lobbying relationship with the Ugandan government, as The Whitaker Group was contracted by Uganda to enhance its international image at an annual cost of $350,000, making it one of the first well-known firms to manage Uganda’s public relations abroad.

## 📚 **Modernity vs. Classical Contrast Grid**  
*(Based on Leo Strauss’s critique of modernity and recovery of classical political philosophy)*

| **Modernity** | **Classical Tradition** |
|--------------|--------------------------|
| **Machiavelli** – Origin of modern political thought; politics as power, not virtue. | **Socrates** – Philosophy begins with self-knowledge and the question of human nature. |
| **Weber** – Positivism, value-free science, epistemological separation of facts and values. | **Plato** – Philosophy and politics are intertwined; the political life is about virtue and the good life. |

| **Nietzsche** – Rejection of truth, belief in the death of God, will to power, creation of myths. | **Maimonides & Al-Farabi** – Faith and reason can coexist; philosophy and theology are compatible. |
| **Historicism** – All values are historically conditioned; no universal truths. | **Natural Right** – Universal moral principles grounded in human nature (e.g., justice, virtue). |
| **Relativism** – Truths are relative to culture, time, or society. | **Esoteric Writing** – Philosophers write in layers to protect themselves and the public from persecution. |
| **Fact-Value Distinction** – Science is value-free; values are outside of empirical study. | **Philosophy as Dialogue** – The "great conversation" between thinkers across time; philosophy is a living inquiry. |
| **Scientism / Positivism** – Politics is a subject for empirical analysis and social science. | **Philosophy as Praxis** – Politics and philosophy are inseparable; philosophy must engage with the political. |
| **Liberalism** – Freedom as the highest good; individual rights over communal virtue. | **Political Virtue** – The good life is achieved through moral excellence and participation in the polis. |
| **Nihilism** – Belief that all values are meaningless or false. | **The Good Life** – A life of reason, virtue, and harmony with nature and community. |

---

## 🔍 **Strauss’s Critique of Modernity (Arrows to Classical Alternatives)**

We now draw **arrows** from modern ideas to their classical counterparts, showing how Strauss critiques modernity by pointing to classical alternatives.

---

### 1. **Modernity: Machiavelli → Politics as Power, Not Virtue**  
➡️ **Classical Alternative: Socrates & Plato**  
- Strauss argues that Machiavelli marks the beginning of modernity by reducing politics to power and manipulation.  
- In contrast, Socrates (in *The Republic*) sees politics as a pursuit of virtue and the good life.  
- **Arrow**: *Machiavelli → Socrates*  
> *Critique*: Modernity replaces virtue with power; classical philosophy sees politics as a moral enterprise.

---

### 2. **Modernity: Weber’s Positivism & Fact-Value Distinction**  
➡️ **Classical Alternative: Aristotle & Plato**  
- Weber claims science must be value-free; facts and values are separate.  
- Strauss argues this is a **false dichotomy** — values are essential to understanding human nature.  
- Aristotle says humans are "political animals" whose flourishing depends on virtue and justice.  
- **Arrow**: *Weber → Aristotle*  
> *Critique*: Modern science fails to grasp the moral foundations of politics; classical philosophy integrates values into understanding of human life.

---

### 3. **Modernity: Heidegger’s Historicism & Nihilism**  
➡️ **Classical Alternative: Plato & the "Great Conversation"**  
- Heidegger sees history as a process where all truths are temporary; ends in nihilism.  
- Strauss says this is a **misreading of history** — classical thinkers believed in enduring truths.  
- Heidegger’s "end of philosophy" is rejected by Strauss, who sees philosophy as a continuous dialogue.  
- **Arrow**: *Heidegger → Plato (Phaedrus, Republic)*  
> *Critique*: Modern historicism leads to nihilism; classical philosophy assumes a stable human nature and enduring truths.

---

### 4. **Modernity: Nietzsche’s Will to Power & Myth-Making**  
➡️ **Classical Alternative: Maimonides & Al-Farabi**

text: Victoria Manalo Draves (née Manalo; December 31, 1924 – April 11, 2010) was a Filipino American competitive diver who won gold medals in both platform and springboard diving at the 1948 Summer Olympics in London. She became the first woman to earn gold medals in both the ten-meter platform and three-meter springboard events and was the first American woman to win two gold medals in diving, as well as the first Asian American to win Olympic gold medals. Born in San Francisco’s South-of-Market district, she was the daughter of Philippine chef and musician Teofilo Manalo and English maid Gertrude Taylor, who met and married in San Francisco. She grew up with her parents, twin sister Connie, older sister Frankie, and younger brother Sonny, who died as a child. Unable to afford swimming lessons until age 10, she took summer lessons from the Red Cross, paying five cents for pool admission in the Mission District. She played badminton, basketball, and softball in high school and graduated from Commerce High School on Van Ness Avenue in 1942, working temporarily in the Army Port Surgeon's office to support her family. Introduced to diving at age 16 by Jack Lavery, she trained under Phil Patterson at the Fairmont Hotel Swimming and Diving Club, where racial discrimination led her to change her name to Vicki Taylor. Patterson’s military service during World War II caused her to pause diving, during which she worked at the Presidio military base. She later joined the Crystal Plunge in North Beach under coach Charlie Sava and trained with Jimmy Hughes, continuing her 50–100 dive after-school practices even while attending San Francisco Junior College (now City College of San Francisco). At 19, she finished third in her first national AAU diving competition at the Indiana meet in 1943. In 1944, she was befriended by Sammy Lee, who introduced her to Lyle Draves, who coached at the Athens Athletic Club in Oakland. Draves began training with Lyle Draves, adding platform diving to her springboard repertoire. After Lyle Draves left the San Francisco Bay Area due to racism at the Fairmont Hotel, she commuted to Los Angeles, placing second and third at the Outdoor Nationals. In 1945, following her father’s death, she returned to her job at the Army Port Surgeon's office in San Francisco. After the war, she moved permanently to Southern California, married Lyle Draves on July 12, 1946, and won the National Tower Diving Championship (10-meter platform) in 1946, 1947, and 1948. She won a total of five United States diving championships prior to the 1948 Olympics, despite not finishing first in either springboard or platform events at the Olympic trials in Detroit. On August 3, 1948, she won the springboard gold medal in London, followed by the 10-meter platform gold on August 6, becoming the first woman to win both titles. After her Olympic victory, she and her husband visited the Philippines, staying in a Malacañang Palace suite and visiting her father’s relatives in Orani, Bataan, where he was born. She gave platform diving exhibitions at Rizal Stadium and other venues, including for Philippine President Elpidio Quirino, and was named one of Life magazine’s top two U.S. athletes at the 1948 Olympics. After the Olympics, she turned professional, joining Larry Crosby’s “Rhapsody in Swimtime” aquatic show for her debut at Soldier Field in Chicago in 1948, and also performed at the L.A. Coliseum with Esther Williams and at the General Motors convention in Detroit. From 1949 to 1950, she toured the U.S., Canada, and Europe with Buster Crabbe’s “Aqua Parade.” After performing regularly at the El Mirador Hotel in Palm Springs and the Shadow Mountain Resort & Club in Palm Desert, she retired from diving. In the early 1950s, she started a family in Glendale and, with her husband, operated a swimming and diving training program at Indian Springs in Montrose, later moving it to Encino. They lived in Tarzana for 35 years, raising their four sons—David, Jeffery, Dale, and Kim—into skilled divers. Draves worked as a secretary while her husband remained a coach and swimming director. In the mid-1960s, she advocated for the Filipino Education Center as the second wave of Filipino immigrants settled in the South of Market district. In 1968, she joined Jesse Owens, Tommy Harmon, and Sam Hanks at the Sands Hotel in Las Vegas to raise $700,000 for the City of Hope National Medical Center. She was inducted into the International Swimming Hall of Fame in 1969. In 2005, she was named the year’s Most Outstanding Alumnus of City College of San Francisco, receiving her award and speaking at the commencement ceremonies at the SF Masonic Auditorium, where she received a resounding ovation from the graduating students. That same year, she was recognized as one of Los Angeles Athletics Club’s outstanding athletes. In October 2006, a two-acre park in San Francisco—named Victoria Manalo Draves Park—was dedicated in her honor, located on Folsom and Sherman streets, the site of her former Franklin Elementary School, four blocks from where she was born and raised. Draves and her husband moved to Palm Springs, California in 1995. She died on April 11, 2010, aged 85, from pancreatic cancer aggravated by pneumonia. On August 3, 2020, she was honored with a Google Doodle in recognition of her achievements.

text: Jack Dorsey began developing the early idea for Twitter in 2006 while working at the podcasting company Odeo. The concept originated during a "daylong brainstorming session" where Dorsey, then an undergraduate student, proposed using an SMS service to communicate with a small group. The original project code name was twttr, inspired by Flickr and the five-character length of American SMS short codes, with Evan Williams later attributing the name to Noah Glass. The domain twitter.com was already in use, so the team purchased it six months after launching twttr and renamed the service Twitter. The developers initially considered "10958" as the SMS short code but changed it to "40404" for ease of use and memorability. Work on the project began in February 2006, and Dorsey published the first Twitter post, "just setting up my twttr," in March 2006. The first prototype, developed by Dorsey and contractor Florian Weber, was used internally at Odeo, with the full version launched publicly on July 15, 2006. In October 2006, Biz Stone, Evan Williams, Dorsey, and others formed Obvious Corporation and acquired Odeo, including its assets. Williams fired Noah Glass, who remained silent about his role until 2011. Twitter spun off into its own company in April 2007. The service was initially ambiguous in definition, described as a social network or microblogging platform, but evolved into being primarily an information network. The term "tweet" emerged from a search by Craig Hockenberry for a shorter way to refer to posting a Twitter update, later adopted by Blaine Cook. The hashtag was introduced in 2007 by Chris Messina, inspired by Internet Relay Chat and Jaiku, and was eventually adopted by Twitter despite mixed initial reactions. Twitter's popularity surged at the 2007 South by Southwest Interactive (SXSWi) conference, where usage increased from 20,000 to 60,000 tweets per day, and the service won the festival's Web Award with the remark "we'd like to thank you in 140 characters or less. And we just did!" Elon Musk joined as a user in 2009. Twitter won the "Breakout of the Year" Webby Award in 2009 and was named Word of the Year by the Global Language Monitor that same year. By February 2010, users were sending 50 million tweets per day, and by March 2010, over 70,000 applications were registered. In June 2010, about 65 million tweets were posted daily, equating to roughly 750 tweets per second, increasing to about 140 million daily by March 2011. Twitter moved to third place among social networking sites by January 2009. The platform saw usage spikes during major events, such as the 2010 FIFA World Cup, where 2,940 tweets per second were posted after Japan scored against Cameroon, followed by 3,085 after the Lakers' NBA Finals victory and 3,283 after Japan's win over Denmark. A record of 7,196 tweets per second was set during the 2011 FIFA Women's World Cup Final. When Michael Jackson died on June 25, 2009, Twitter servers crashed due to 100,000 tweets per hour containing "Michael Jackson." The highest recorded rate, 143,199 tweets per second, occurred in Japan during a screening of the movie Castle in the Sky on August 3, 2013. In June 2009, Tony La Russa sued Twitter for trade infringement after an impersonation of him, leading to a settlement and the introduction of Verified Accounts. Ashton Kutcher's account became the first with a million followers in 2009. Twitter played a major role in the 2009 Iranian presidential election protests. On January 22, 2010, NASA astronaut T. J. Creamer posted the first unassisted off-Earth Twitter message from the International Space Station. By late November 2010, an average of a dozen updates per day were posted on the astronauts' communal account, @NASA_Astronauts. Twitter acquired Atebits on April 11, 2010, which developed the Apple Design Award-winning Twitter client Tweetie, becoming the official client for iPhone, iPad, and Mac. The Library of Congress began archiving all tweets from 2006 onward, initially archiving all new tweets, though it switched to selective archiving in 2018. From September to October 2010, Twitter rolled out "New Twitter," allowing users to view pictures and videos directly within the platform and introducing a redesigned interface with '@mentions' and 'Retweets' above the stream and 'Messages' and 'Log Out' in a top black bar. The "New Twitter" experience was fully rolled out by November 1, 2010. In April 2011, Twitter tested a new homepage and phased out the "Old Twitter," though a glitch delayed the transition, with the retro homepage remaining until April 20. On December 8, 2011, Twitter introduced the "Fly" design, adding Connect and Discover tabs, a redesigned profile, and timeline, with a layout similar to Facebook. In February 2012, Twitter announced a partnership with Yandex, a Russian search engine, to leverage real-time news feeds. On March 21, 2012, Twitter celebrated its sixth birthday with 140 million users and 340 million tweets per day. In April 2012, Twitter opened an office in Detroit and expanded its Dublin office. In March 2011, a cobra escaped from the Bronx Zoo, leading to the creation of a parody account @BronxZoosCobra, which gained widespread attention. On June 5, 2012, Twitter unveiled a modified logo removing text to feature a redesigned bird. By December 18, 2012, monthly active users had increased by 42% and surpassed 200 million. Pope Benedict XVI joined Twitter on December 18, 2012, using the handle @pontifex, which answers questions via the hashtag #askpontifex. In 2012, "tweet" was added to the Oxford English Dictionary. Vine, a short video service, was launched in 2013. On January 28, 2013, Twitter acquired Crashlytics to expand its mobile developer products. On April 18, 2013, Twitter launched a music app called Twitter Music for iPhone. On August 28, 2013, Twitter acquired Trendrr, followed by MoPub on September 9, 2013. As of September 2013, 200 million users sent over 400 million tweets daily, with nearly 60% from mobile devices. In April 2013, the Syrian Electronic Army hacked the Associated Press account, causing a significant short-term market impact, and later hacked Barack Obama's account. During Super Bowl XLVII on February 3, 2013, Kraft Foods VP Lisa Mann tweeted "You can still dunk in the dark" after a power outage, a moment that became a milestone in daily cultural commentary. Twitter went public in 2013 through an IPO that raised $1.8 billion. 2014 was a difficult year for the company, with market pessimism. In April 2014, Twitter redesigned its site to resemble Facebook, featuring profile pictures and biographies on the left and a full-width header with parallax scrolling, which remained the main desktop layout until July 2019. Growth slowed in 2015. In September 2016, Twitter shares rose 20% after reports of takeover interest, with potential buyers including Alphabet, Microsoft, Salesforce, Verizon, and The Walt Disney Company. The board was open to a deal by the end of 2016, but no acquisition occurred due to concerns over abuse and harassment. In 2017, Elon Musk first expressed interest in acquiring Twitter. In June 2017, Twitter revamped its dashboard to improve the user experience. Vine was shut down in 2017. On April 29, 2018, Solstar sent the first commercial tweet from space using commercial infrastructure during a New Shepard flight. In May 2018, Twitter introduced an algorithm to hide replies deemed detractive, requiring users to click "Show more replies" to view them. From 2015 to 2018, Twitter suspended over a million accounts related to terrorism. In 2018, the tweet length limit was increased from 140 to 280 characters, after a trial in 2017. In 2019, Twitter released another user interface redesign. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, Twitter experienced significant growth but also faced challenges with misinformation. The platform began marking tweets with misleading information and adding fact-check links, though it sometimes incorrectly flagged factual content as misleading. In May 2020, two tweets from U.S. President Donald Trump were marked as "potentially misleading" and linked to fact-checks. Trump responded by signing an executive order to weaken Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. After the January 6 United States Capitol attack, Twitter banned Trump, citing violation of its "glorification of violence" policy, drawing criticism from American conservatives and European leaders. In 2020, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Zhao Lijian pushed pandemic conspiracy theories on Twitter, which is blocked in mainland China but used as a public diplomacy tool by Chinese officials. China's ambassador to South Africa also made these claims on Twitter. In May 2020, Twitter placed fact-check labels on two of these tweets.

text: Jacen Solo is a fictional character in the Star Wars Legends continuity, the son of Han Solo and Leia Organa Solo, nephew of Luke Skywalker, and brother of Jaina Solo and Anakin Solo, as well as cousin of Ben Skywalker. He is a central figure in several novels, especially the New Jedi Order series, and becomes the antagonist of the Legacy of the Force series under the name Darth Caedus. Created for Timothy Zahn's Thrawn trilogy, set five years after Return of the Jedi, Jacen is introduced in the 1991 novel Heir to the Empire as one of a pair of twins Leia is pregnant with, born five minutes after his sister Jaina on Coruscant in the 1993 novel The Last Command. The twins, along with their younger brother Anakin, are sent to safe havens under the protection of Leia's handmaiden, Winter. In Jedi Search, they return to Coruscant at age three and have adventures, including becoming lost in the underworld of Imperial City with C-3PO before being rescued. In The Crystal Star, all three children are abducted by Hethrir, who attempts to brainwash them into becoming Dark Jedi, but they defeat him. In the Young Jedi Knights series, Jacen travels to Yavin 4 for Jedi training, discovers a strong connection to the Living Force, communicates with jungle creatures, keeps a menagerie of animals in his room at the Great Massassi Temple, and befriends the Wookiee Lowbacca and the warrior princess Tenel Ka. In Heirs of the Force and Shadow Academy, they discover a crashed TIE fighter from the Battle of Yavin, fix it with Jaina, and are captured by its pilot Qorl, who lives in the jungle for two decades; they escape, but Qorl also escapes and later discovers the Shadow Academy, a Dark Jedi training ground led by Brakiss and containing the remains of the Dathomiri Nightsisters. The twins and their friends are kidnapped by the Second Imperium, resist the dark side, and are rescued by Luke Skywalker and Tenel Ka. After returning to Coruscant, they reunite with Zekk, fight him several times, and eventually build their first lightsabers, with Jacen using a corusca gem for his focusing crystal. In Lightsabers, Tenel Ka's lightsaber shorts out during a sparring match with Jacen when his blade passes through thin air, severing her arm, causing Jacen to suffer guilt. In Darkest Knight, they visit Kashyyyk with Lowbacca to witness his sister's rites; in Jedi Under Siege, they defeat the Shadow Academy and the Second Imperium on Yavin 4. Throughout the series, Jacen and Jaina continue training, meet new friends like Raynar Thul, and cannot convince Zekk to stay at the Academy. They discover the Diversity Alliance, an alien anti-human group led by Twi'lek Nolaa Tarkona, sister of Oola, who was murdered by Jabba the Hutt in Return of the Jedi. In Jedi Bounty, they are briefly held captive on Ryloth to rescue Lowbacca, who joined the Diversity Alliance; in The Emperor's Plague, they uncover a plot involving General Evir Derricote's deadly diseases hidden in an Imperial storehouse, defeat Tarkona, who dies from one of the plagues, and Bornan Thul dies from the plague before his son's eyes. In Return to Ord Mantell, they visit the planet to watch a race, encounter Czethros, a bounty hunter who once hunted Han, and are ambushed by Black Sun agents, helped by Anja Gallandro, a lightsaber-wielding non-Jedi who blames Han for her father's death, though Solo reveals her father died in a trap. In Trouble on Cloud City, Czethros is revealed as a minor Black Sun leader trying to gain power, and Jacen, Tenel Ka, and Lowbacca are ambushed, with Jacen nearly killed. In Crisis at Crystal Reef, Jaina attempts to capture Czethros while Jacen helps Anja overcome her spice addiction and fight Black Sun; Anja recovers and accepts her father's death, and Jacen realizes she lacks Jedi potential, ending his infatuation when she joins Lando. In the New Jedi Order series, Luke takes Jacen as his apprentice, though they disagree on philosophical issues; Jacen believes the Force is a guide to destiny and tells Anakin that the Force is part of something greater. During the Yuuzhan Vong attack in Dark Tide: Onslaught, Jacen believes many Jedi are too aggressive and temporarily abandons his powers, but returns to battle due to his love for his mother, eventually making peace with his father. In Star by Star, Jacen joins a mission to Myrkr to infiltrate a Yuuzhan Vong cloning facility where the invaders create Voxyn; the mission fails with Anakin's death, and Jacen, forced into leadership, uses the Force Meld to unite the team. After destroying the voxyn queen, Jacen is captured by the Yuuzhan Vong under Vergere and Nom Anor, disappearing from the Force. In Traitor, he awakens in the Embrace of Pain, where he learns to use pain to sustain himself under Vergere's tutelage, who was once a Jedi of the Old Republic and met his grandfather, Anakin Skywalker. He works on Yuuzhan Vong ships, heals slaves, and uses a slave seed beneath his flesh to communicate with their technology, escaping by commanding amphistaffs to surround him. Jacen and Vergere flee to Coruscant, where the planet is transformed into a Yuuzhan Vong paradise. Vergere removes the slave seed, but Jacen still senses the Yuuzhan Vong; he is surrounded by warriors, channels Force lightning, runs away, and is later given full Force use by Vergere. He surrenders and becomes the "khattazz al'Yun," or Avatar of God, with Nom Anor intending to use him to sacrifice Jaina, fulfilling a prophecy. Jacen's true allegiance remains his own; when ordered to sacrifice Jedi Ganner Rhysode, he refuses and instead helps Ganner hold off the Yuuzhan Vong, confronting the World Brain and suggesting it work against the invaders. Ganner dies, but Jacen escapes with Vergere. He returns to the New Republic as a hardened man, joins Admiral Kre'fey's fleet, and participates in a successful deception at Ebaq 9, where Vergere dies. Her spectral form appears to him afterward. As the Galactic Alliance forms, Jacen accompanies Luke into the Unknown Regions to seek a solution to the Yuuzhan Vong threat, playing a key role in finding Zonama Sekot and convincing the planet to join the fight. He kills Supreme Overlord Onimi, using the Force as a conduit, after nearly being killed by Shimrra, and begins to believe he is beyond good and evil, marking the start of his fall. After the war ends, Jacen tells Luke he plans to travel the galaxy to learn more about the Force. On a five-year journey, he enters a realm of the Force known as beyond shadows, trained by a sect called the Mind Walkers, and gazes into the Pool of Knowledge, which holds the Throne of Balance, where all future events are shown. He sees a dark man ruling the galaxy and becomes determined to prevent this future. Following this, Jacen begins his descent into the dark side. In Dark Nest, he feels a Force urge, follows his sister to the Unknown Regions to help the Killik against a Chiss invasion, returns to Galactic Alliance space, and travels to the Hapes Cluster to ask Tenel Ka to assist with the conflict, sending a fleet of Hapan Battle Dragons to protect the Killiks. In The Unseen Queen, Tenel Ka gives birth to his daughter, Allana, who is attacked by the Gorog; Jacen repels the attack, uses the Force to send Tenel Ka's grandmother into a coma, and sees a vision of a never-ending war with the Killiks at its center. Determined to prevent it, he provokes the Chiss into destroying the Killiks, though he later reveals he does not know who started the war in the vision. While recovering, Jacen urges Luke to embrace his darker emotions, but Luke refuses and defeats Plo and Raynar Thul without using the dark side. In the novel, Jacen watches holovideos of his grandparents, Anakin Skywalker and Padmé Amidala, seeing Anakin fall to the dark side and Padmé die in childbirth due to Anakin's actions; Jacen sympathizes with Anakin's desire to protect his wife and reminds Luke that Anakin was a fallible human. In Betrayal, Jacen begins training his cousin Ben in the Force. After a mission to Adumar ends in a life-threatening attack, they return to a dinner party at their parents' home, where Han expresses concern over Corellia's independence. Luke orders Jacen and Ben to disable the Centerpoint Station, which Thrackan Sal-Solo, Han's cousin, is using; Ben disables it while Jacen distracts Thrackan, ensuring a partial victory.
