The knockout stage featured 16 teams advancing from the group stage, consisting of four rounds—round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, and the final—with each round eliminating half the teams. Any draw at 90 minutes was followed by 30 minutes of extra time, and if the scores remained level, a penalty shoot-out determined progression. In the round of 16, each group winner (A to H) was paired against the runner-up from another group. The round was marked by controversial refereeing decisions, prompting FIFA President Sepp Blatter to apologize to England and Mexico for the errors, stating that "you can win some and you lose some," and promising to re-open discussions on goal-line technology and video replays, with the first opportunity to discuss it occurring at the July business meeting. The three quarter-finals between European and South American teams all ended in European victories: Germany defeated Argentina 4–0, the Netherlands came from behind to beat Brazil 2–1 (marking Brazil’s first loss in a World Cup match outside Europe since 1950), and Spain won 1–0 over Paraguay to reach the final for the first time since 1950. Uruguay, the only South American team to reach the semi-finals, advanced after a 1–1 draw with Ghana, which missed a penalty in extra time following Luis Suárez’s handball on the line. The Netherlands qualified for the final for the third time with a 3–2 win over Uruguay, and Spain reached their first final with a 1–0 victory over Germany, making it the first World Cup final without Brazil, Italy, Germany, or Argentina, and ensuring a new champion as neither Spain nor the Netherlands had previously won the tournament. Germany defeated Uruguay 3–2 to secure third place, holding the record for most third-place finishes (4), while Uruguay holds the record for most fourth-place finishes (3). The final was held on 11 July 2010 at Soccer City, Johannesburg, where Spain defeated the Netherlands 1–0 in extra time, with Andrés Iniesta scoring the goal in the 116th minute—the latest winning goal in a FIFA World Cup final. This victory gave Spain their first World Cup title, making them the eighth team to win it, the first new winner without home advantage since Brazil in 1958, and the first team to win after losing their opening match. The final saw 14 yellow cards, more than doubling the previous record set in 1986, and John Heitinga was sent off for a second yellow card. The Netherlands had a key chance in the 60th minute when Arjen Robben was released by Wesley Sneijder to face Iker Casillas, who saved the shot. Iniesta broke the deadlock with a volleyed shot from a pass by Cesc Fàbregas. This result marked the first time two teams from the same continent won consecutive World Cups (after Italy in 2006), and Europe reached 10 titles, surpassing South America’s nine. Spain became the first European nation to win a World Cup not hosted on European soil and the first team since West Germany in 1974 to win as European champions. Spain also set a record for the fewest goals scored by a World Cup-winning team (eight), the fewest goalscorers (three: Villa with five, Iniesta with two, Puyol with one), and the fewest goals conceded (two, equaling Italy in 2006 and France in 1998), and became the first team to win the World Cup without conceding a goal in the knockout stage. The four top scorers in the tournament each scored five goals, all from teams finishing in the top four—Spain, the Netherlands, Germany, and Uruguay. text: The 2010 UEFA Champions League final was an association football match played at the Santiago Bernabéu Stadium, home of Real Madrid, on 22 May 2010, to determine the winners of the 2009–10 UEFA Champions League. It was the first Champions League final to be held on a weekend, rather than the traditional Wednesday. The match was won by Inter Milan, who defeated Bayern Munich 2–0, completing the treble—a feat never before achieved by any team from either Italy or Germany. This victory marked Inter's third European Cup title and their first since 1965; it was also their first final appearance since 1972 and the first time an Italian team had reached the final since A.C. Milan's win in 2007. Bayern, who had last won the competition in 2001, were the first German side to reach the final since Bayer Leverkusen in 2002. The 2010 final was the first not to feature an English side since Porto beat Monaco in 2004, due to Manchester United being eliminated by Bayern Munich in the quarter-finals on away goals. The Santiago Bernabéu Stadium had previously hosted three European Cup finals: in 1957, 1969, and 1980. The venue was selected by the UEFA Executive Committee in Vaduz, Liechtenstein, on 28 March 2008, based on criteria including stadium capacity, facilities, and security, and the decision to play the final on a Saturday was made at a meeting in Lucerne on 30 November 2007. The stadium, opened in 1947, had a capacity exceeding 75,000 initially, increased to 125,000 in 1954, reduced to 90,800 after renovations for the 1982 FIFA World Cup, and later reduced to just over 75,000 after conversion to an all-seater stadium in 1998, with a slight increase to just over 80,000 in 2006; only around 75,000 seats were available for the 2010 final. Each finalist was allocated 21,000 tickets, with 11,000 available to the general public, and applications ran from 8 to 19 March 2010 via a random lottery, including 2,000 children's tickets from each club and 1,000 from the public, plus 500 for children at the UEFA Champions Festival. A ticketing launch event was held in Madrid on 5 March 2010, attended by Emilio Butragueño, Esperanza Aguirre, and representatives from UEFA, the Royal Spanish Football Federation, and Real Madrid, with Aguirre receiving the first ticket from players Cristiano Ronaldo and Raúl. A trophy handover ceremony took place at the Palacio de Cibeles on 16 April 2010, where Johan Cruyff and Joan Laporta returned the trophy to UEFA president Michel Platini, who then handed it to Ángel María Villar Llona and Alberto Ruiz-Gallardón for display until the final. The official match ball, the Adidas Finale Madrid, was unveiled on 9 March 2010 and featured a "Starball" design with gold stars incorporating elements from the logos of the last 10 Champions League finals, each with a red border referencing the Spanish flag and a white base matching Real Madrid's kit. The referee was Howard Webb of England, supported by Darren Cann and Mike Mullarkey as assistant referees and Martin Atkinson as the fourth official, all from England. Inter started without any Italian players, while Bayern began with five German internationals, including Franck Ribéry, who was suspended for three matches after being sent off in the semi-final, and Thiago Motta, suspended for two matches. The match opened with the UEFA Champions Festival on 15 May 2010 at Parque del Retiro, culminating in a match between former Spanish players and European ex-professionals on the final day. The UEFA Champions League Anthem was performed by Peruvian tenor Juan Diego Flórez. Inter won 2–0 with both goals scored by Diego Milito in the 35th and 70th minutes; the first followed a long clearance flicked down by Milito to Wesley Sneijder, who returned the pass to Milito, and the second came after Milito collected a pass from Samuel Eto'o and beat Daniel Van Buyten. Milito was substituted before the end of the match and was applauded by Inter supporters, stating the win brought "incredible happiness" and that his team deserved the victory. She acknowledged that a year is too short to undo centuries of patriarchal norms embedded in homes, institutions, and laws, and that police responsiveness is driven by fear of censure rather than duty. Women in urban India still feel unsafe and often wear clothing that covers their bodies to feel safe. Public officials and commentators frequently claim that women who wear "skimpy" clothing or go out with men "invite" attacks, thus denying it is rape. In reality, most women avoid Western clothing due to fear of sexual assault. As society and the Indian government have failed to address the root causes, women adopt safety strategies such as ignoring sexual commentary, avoiding eye contact, dressing more modestly, and refraining from going out at night, which has led to women avoiding public spaces, including public transportation, reinforcing the expectation that women should stay at home. text: After Jyoti Singh's death on 29 December 2012, widespread protests erupted across India, including in Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Mumbai, Bhubaneswar, and Visakhapatnam. Many mourners carried candles and wore black dresses; some pasted black cloth across their mouths. The following day, a large number of people protested near Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, where minor clashes occurred between protesters and police, leading to the removal of some demonstrators. A one-day hunger strike was observed at Jantar Mantar, and all roads leading to India Gate were closed, with areas where protests had gathered previously made off-limits to the public. Protesters spread papers with graffiti and slogans condemning the incident and demanding stricter laws and faster justice. The BJP renewed its call for a special parliament session to discuss the case and adopt stricter laws on crimes against women. New Year's celebrations in Delhi were significantly scaled back, with the Indian armed forces and several clubs and hotels cancelling their parties. The protests also spread across South Asia, with marches and rallies in Nepal, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. In Nepal, hundreds of demonstrators in Kathmandu called for legal reforms and a change in attitudes toward women. In Bangladesh, the human rights group Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) said the Delhi protests had energized demonstrations against sexual violence, noting that men were now participating and that the protests included people from diverse social backgrounds. In Paris, people marched to the Indian embassy, handing over a petition calling for action to make India safer for women. An author for the South Asia Analysis Group described the protests as expressions of middle-class angst stemming from a breakdown of the social contract between the middle class and the liberal state. New Delhi has the highest number of sex crimes among India's major cities, with police data showing an average of one rape reported every 18 hours; reported rape cases increased by nearly 17 percent between 2007 and 2011. Only one of the 706 rape cases filed in Delhi in 2012 resulted in a successful conviction. Between 16 December and 4 January, the Delhi Police recorded 501 calls for harassment and 64 for rape, but only four were followed up with inquiries. The regional program director for U.N. Women South Asia stated that rape cases occur in nearly all cities and rural areas, with victims often dying immediately due to the brutality of the crime, calling the incident a wake-up call. Members of Indian parliament demanded severe punishment for the perpetrators. Sushma Swaraj, then Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, stated that the rapists should be hanged. Sonia Gandhi, Chairperson of the ruling United Progressive Alliance, visited Safdarjang Hospital to meet doctors and obtain updates on the victim’s health. Mayawati, chief of the Bahujan Samaj Party, said proper investigation was needed and that action should be so strict that no one would dare commit such acts again. Jaya Bachchan, an actress and member of the Rajya Sabha, said she was "terribly disturbed" and "ashamed" and felt "helpless" for not being able to act. Meira Kumar, then Speaker of the Lok Sabha, stated that a new law should be introduced and passed to ensure women's safety, emphasizing that existing laws were insufficient and that stricter laws were needed. Delhi’s then Chief Minister, Sheila Dixit, said she lacked the courage to meet the victim and described Delhi as a "rape capital," calling for senior police officials to be held accountable and for the immediate establishment of fast-track courts to handle rape cases swiftly. Three constables who refused to act on Ram Adhar’s robbery complaint were suspended for dereliction of duty. On 24 December 2012, Prime Minister Manmohan Singh issued his first official response, appealing for calm and stressing that violence would serve no purpose. He assured the public that all efforts would be made to ensure women’s safety and expressed empathy, saying as a father of three daughters he felt the incident deeply. He cancelled all official events to celebrate the new year as a tribute to Nirbhaya. Then Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, Akhilesh Yadav, announced a ₹2 million (US$24,000) financial package and a government job for the victim’s family. President Pranab Mukherjee’s son, Abhijit Mukherjee, argued that the women protesters were not students, comparing the situation to the "Pink Revolution" in Egypt, and claimed he saw many "beautiful women" among them, though he expressed doubt about their student status. The remark was widely condemned as sexist; his sister Sharmistha and their father, the president, disapproved. Maharashtra Chief Minister Prithviraj Chavan also expressed disapproval. Abhijit quickly withdrew and apologised. Spiritual guru Asaram Bapu provoked public criticism by claiming the victim was to blame for her assault, saying she could have stopped it by chanting God’s name and falling at the attackers’ feet. Several celebrities, including Preity Zinta, Shah Rukh Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Amitabh Bachchan, and Farhan Akhtar, expressed outrage on social media, demanding the rapists be castrated or hanged. The incident was featured in the first episode of the second season of Satyamev Jayate, hosted by Aamir Khan, which also addressed other rape cases and the suffering of survivors at the hands of police, medical staff, and the public. The American embassy released a statement on 29 December 2012, offering condolences to Nirbhaya’s family and reaffirming its commitment to ending gender-based violence globally. Nirbhaya was posthumously awarded one of the 2013 International Women of Courage Awards by the US State Department, with the citation stating that her personal ordeal, perseverance in fighting for justice, and her family’s bravery were helping to reduce the stigma and vulnerability that drive violence against women. Indian politician Mulayam Singh Yadav opposed making rape a capital offence, saying "Boys will be boys. Boys commit mistakes." Two years later, in response to his comments and another rape incident in Uttar Pradesh where his party was in power, UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon said "We say no to the dismissive, destructive attitude of, 'Boys will be boys'" and stated that violence against women must never be accepted, excused, or tolerated, asserting that every girl and woman has the right to be respected, valued, and protected. UN Women called on the Government of India and the Government of Delhi to take radical reforms, ensure justice, and provide robust public services to make women’s lives safer. In response to Western media criticism of India, Jessica Valenti, writing in The Nation, argued that rape is also common in the United States, but US commentators deny or minimize its systemic nature while attacking India for a supposed rape culture. Activist Eve Ensler, who organized One Billion Rising, said the gang rape and murder was a turning point in India and globally, noting that she had never seen sexual violence break through public consciousness so dramatically, appearing on every newspaper’s front page, in college discussions, and in restaurants, and that India was leading the world in fast-tracking laws, sexual education, and examining patriarchal structures and masculinity. In the aftermath, female tourism to India fell by 35% compared to the previous year, according to an ASSOCHAM industry survey. The UK Foreign Office revised its travel advice and advised women against traveling alone. In 2014, Finance Minister Arun Jaitley stated that one incident of rape in Delhi was enough to cost the country billions in lost tourism. In response to the protests, central and state governments announced measures to improve women’s safety. The Government of Karnataka launched a 24/7 dedicated helpline (1091) operated by state police for sexual abuse complaints and considered setting up fast-track courts for pending cases. The Government of Tamil Nadu announced a 13-point action plan, treating sexual assault as a grave crime, assigning top police officials to probe such cases, and conducting daily hearings in fast-track courts with women prosecutors appointed as government counsels. The Jammu and Kashmir government announced plans to revise state laws on sexual offenses and gender crimes. The Government of Himachal Pradesh established state and district-level committees to review progress in cases of crimes against women. Despite these responses, Singh endured significant hardship during and after the protests, facing a demeaning medical examination, a harsh court cross-examination, salacious media coverage, and an insensitive societal response, including from people who knew her. On 22 December 2012, a judicial committee headed by J. S. Verma, a former Chief Justice of India, was appointed by the central government to submit a report within 30 days suggesting amendments to criminal law to address sexual assault. The committee urged the public, legal professionals, NGOs, and women’s groups to share views on possible legal amendments to ensure quicker investigations, prosecutions, trials, and enhanced punishments for extreme sexual assaults. The committee held its first meeting on 26 December 2012 and received over 6,000 emails with suggestions. The report was submitted after 29 days, having considered 80,000 suggestions, and identified government and police failures as the root cause of crimes against women. It recommended reviewing the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 in conflict zones and setting the maximum punishment for rape as the death penalty, rather than life imprisonment. The committee did not support lowering the age of adulthood from 18 to 16. On 26 December 2012, a Commission of Inquiry headed by former Delhi High Court judge Usha Mehra was established to identify lapses, determine responsibility, and suggest measures to make Delhi and the National Capital Region safer for women. On 1 January 2013, a task force headed by the Union Home Secretary was formed to examine women’s safety in Delhi and review the functioning of the city police. On 3 February 2013, the Criminal Law (Amendment) Ordinance, 2013 was promulgated by then President Pranab Mukherjee, amending the Indian Penal Code, Indian Evidence Act, and Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, on sexual offences. The ordinance introduced the death penalty for rape. According to Minister of Law and Justice Ashwani Kumar, 90 percent of the Verma Committee’s suggestions were incorporated into the ordinance. Critics argue that key recommendations, including the criminalization of marital rape and trying military personnel under criminal law, were ignored. In a December 2013 interview, Nirbhaya’s parents, Badri Nath Singh and Asha Devi, said they were seeking to change the juvenile law in cases like their daughter’s rape and murder. They petitioned the Supreme Court to try the juvenile in a criminal court instead of a Juvenile Justice court. The juvenile defendant, who was just short of 18 years old at the time of the crime, was sent to a borstal youth detention center for three years and then released. In a March 2015 interview with The Tribune, Women and Child Development Minister Maneka Gandhi said the government was moving forward with a law treating juveniles as adults in grave crimes. On 22 December 2015, the Rajya Sabha passed the revised Juvenile Justice Act, proposing that individuals above 16 years of age accused of heinous crimes be treated as adults in court. On 16 December 2013, the first anniversary of the attack, activists held memorials in New Delhi to honor the victim, widely known as Nirbhaya, meaning "fearless." Women’s organizations lit candles and protested against women’s exploitation. University students and others organized a candlelight march at the bus stand in South Delhi where Nirbhaya and her friend Pandey boarded the bus. At a commemorative prayer meeting, political leaders committed to increasing efforts to improve women’s security. Former Chief Minister Sheila Dikshit, speaking with the victim’s mother, said Delhi’s society and authorities would work together to build a permanent legacy for her daughter, promising to fulfill whatever the family desired and to ensure such an incident would never happen again. The parents said they were proud of their daughter’s courage, which they believe inspired more women to speak out. In December 2014, on the second anniversary, the parents remarked that little had changed: "Nothing in India has changed since 16 December 2012. All promises and statements made by our leaders and ministers have turned out to be shallow. Our suffering gives them their moment in the limelight. My daughter asks me what I have done to get her justice. She asks what am I doing so that many more like her get justice and I wake up to realise how helpless and trivial I am..." On 16 December 2015, the third anniversary of the attack, "Nirbhaya Chetna Diwas" was observed with candlelight vigils, prayer meetings, and other events at Jantar Mantar. In a "brave homage to her daughter," Jyoti’s mother, Asha Devi, said, "My daughter's name was Jyoti Singh and I am not ashamed to name her. Those who commit heinous crimes like rape, their heads should hang in shame, not the victims' or their families'." She spoke out against the upcoming release of the juvenile convict and put forth four demands for justice: the juvenile should be sentenced to death, fast-track courts should be established in all courts to offer speedy justice to sexual assault victims, amendments to the Juvenile Justice Act should be passed, and the Nirbhaya Fund should be used to set up high-quality forensic labs.

text: The 2012 Delhi gang rape and murder, known as the Nirbhaya case, occurred on 16 December 2012 in Munirka, Delhi, when 22-year-old Jyoti Singh, a physiotherapy intern, was gang-raped and tortured in a private bus while travelling with her friend, Awindra Pratap Pandey. The bus, which had only six passengers including the driver, deviated from its route and its doors were shut, prompting suspicion from Pandey, who was then taunted by the group. A scuffle followed, during which Pandey was beaten, gagged, and knocked unconscious with an iron rod, and Jyoti was dragged to the rear of the bus, where she was raped and severely injured with a blunt object—later identified as a rusted, L-shaped wheel jack handle—causing extensive damage to her abdomen, intestines, and genitals. Jyoti attempted to fight back, biting three of the attackers. After the assault, both victims were thrown from the moving bus; one of the perpetrators cleaned the vehicle, which was later impounded. The partially clothed victims were found by a passerby around 11 pm and taken to Safdarjung Hospital, where Jyoti received emergency treatment and was placed on mechanical ventilation. She had numerous bite marks and injuries, and medical staff confirmed penetration by a metal rod. On 27 December, she was flown to Mount Elizabeth Hospital in Singapore for further treatment, where she suffered a cardiac arrest during a six-hour flight and died at 4:45 am on 29 December (2:15 am IST). Her body was cremated on 30 December in Delhi under high police security. The incident sparked widespread national and international outrage, leading to public protests in New Delhi and major cities across India, demanding better women's safety and security. Six men were arrested: Ram Singh, the driver, and his brother Mukesh Singh, both from Ravidas camp; Vinay Sharma, a 26-year-old assistant gym instructor; Pawan Gupta, a 19-year-old fruit seller; Akshay Thakur, a 28-year-old man seeking employment; and the juvenile Mohammed Afroz, 17 years and six months old, from Badayun. The juvenile was convicted under the Juvenile Justice Act and sentenced to three years in a reform facility. The adult defendants—Pawan Gupta, Vinay Sharma, Akshay Thakur, and Mukesh Singh—were found guilty of rape and murder on 10 September 2013 and sentenced to death; the Delhi High Court upheld the verdict on 13 March 2014, and the Supreme Court rejected their final appeals on 18 December 2019. The four adult convicts were executed by hanging on 20 March 2020. Ram Singh died in police custody on 11 March 2013, with authorities stating it was unclear whether it was suicide or murder. The case led to the formation of a judicial committee that reviewed 80,000 public suggestions and concluded that government and police failures were the root cause of crimes against women. In 2013, the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act was passed by President Pranab Mukherjee, introducing new laws and creating six fast-track courts for rape cases. Despite these reforms, critics argue the legal system remains slow, though public discourse on women's safety has significantly increased. The victim's father initially opposed revealing her name, but later stated that he wanted the world to know her real name, Jyoti Singh, to honor her courage and inspire other survivors. In compliance with Indian law, her name was not publicly released initially, and media used pseudonyms such as Nirbhaya, meaning "fearless," Damini, or Delhi braveheart. The Delhi police registered a case against the editor of Mail Today for disclosing her identity under section 228(A) of the Indian Penal Code. A Special Investigation Team, led by Pramod Kumar Kushwaha, was formed to probe the case. The attackers had previously robbed a carpenter, Ramadhir Singh, who reported the incident to three police constables from Hauz Khas, who refused to act, citing jurisdictional issues. The Delhi High Court reprimanded the police for being evasive in their probe status report, and two Assistant Commissioners were suspended for failing to prevent the incident. The government appointed a medical committee on 21 December to ensure Jyoti received optimal care, and on 26 December, a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Manmohan Singh decided to transfer her to Singapore, a decision criticized by some doctors as politically motivated. The juvenile defendant, later renamed Raju in media, was arrested at Anand Vihar terminal and had only met the others that day. The case led to significant changes in public awareness and policy, though the victim's father later expressed regret that justice had not been fully achieved.

On 27 August 2015, Vinay, Akshay, Mukesh, and Pawan were convicted of robbing Ramadhir and sentenced to 10 years' imprisonment. On 5 May 2017, the Supreme Court rejected the convicts' appeal, upholding the death sentence, stating they had committed a "barbaric crime" that had "shaken society's conscience," and the verdict was well received by the victim's family and civil society. Legal experts noted the convicts still had the right to file a review petition. On 9 July 2018, the Supreme Court rejected a review petition by three of the convicts. After Jyoti Singh's death on 29 December 2012, protests were held in Kolkata, Chennai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Mumbai, Bhubaneswar, and Visakhapatnam. Many mourners carried candles and wore black dresses; some pasted black cloth over their mouths. The following day, a large number of people protested near Jantar Mantar, with minor clashes and police removal of some protesters. One group observed a one-day hunger strike. All roads to India Gate were closed, and areas where protests had occurred were made inaccessible. text: A documentary titled *Mile Wide Tornado: Oklahoma Disaster* was released on June 5, honoring three storm chasers and covering the events of the EF5-rated tornado that struck Moore and parts of southern Oklahoma City eleven days earlier, on May 20. The November 2013 issue of *National Geographic* featured a tribute to Tim Samaras, a National Geographic Explorer supported in part by the Society, and included a detailed scientific analysis of the tornado. A team of scientists and veteran chasers conducted a crowd-sourcing survey to collect storm chaser data, such as video, photographs, and GPS logs, creating the largest visual dataset ever assembled on a tornado. This information was combined with radar and lightning data, and the project aims to develop a standardized open-access database for future events. In 2015, software called "Tornado Environment Display" (TED), named after Dr. Ted Fujita, was unveiled to synchronize maps, radar data, and storm chaser footage; Anton Seimon, one of its architects, noted that while it had been used only in relation to the El Reno tornado, it could be applied to future tornadoes with sufficient footage. The tornado moved over mostly open terrain, resulting in relatively light damage—though still significant in isolated areas—according to National Weather Service surveys, with structures sustaining at most EF3-level damage. The Oklahoma City West Livestock Market was described as a "war zone," with several large steel-frame warehouse buildings destroyed, multiple large brick buildings at the Canadian Valley Technology Center heavily damaged or destroyed, and a large metal wind turbine prop blade thrown 100 yards (91 m) into a daycare building, with damage at that site estimated at up to $40 million. One farmstead, including a large barn, cattle barn, three machine sheds, granaries, and the owner’s home, was completely destroyed. Several rural homes were destroyed, large amounts of gravel were blown off roads leaving only dirt exposed, and multiple large metal electrical transmission poles, trees, and vehicles were damaged or tossed. At least 29 buildings and 40 vehicles were damaged or destroyed, with repairs in the El Reno area expected to take at least a year. On June 1, the American Red Cross established a shelter at Redlands Community College in El Reno for storm victims. The following day, Oklahoma Governor Mary Fallin visited damaged areas of El Reno. A state of emergency was already in effect due to the May 20 tornadoes, enabling residents to quickly access emergency aid. Homeless residents were provided temporary housing in shipping containers, each equipped with a kitchen, bedroom, living room, and bathroom. Eight people died in the tornado, all in vehicles. Local hospitals, including OU Medical Center, INTEGRIS Southwest Medical Center, and Mercy Hospital in El Reno, reported at least 115 injured, including five critical patients, with a total of 151 injuries attributed to the event. As the tornadoes approached the Oklahoma City metro, thousands of residents evacuated, possibly due to memories of the May 20 EF5 tornado’s devastation, causing Interstates 35, 40, 44, and 240 to become "parking lots" with chaotic traffic, including people traveling southbound in northbound lanes. It has been suggested that the evacuation was partially driven by a controversial on-air recommendation from KFOR-TV chief meteorologist Mike Morgan, who advised residents without underground shelters to evacuate south of the tornado’s path, contrary to the recommended safety plan of seeking an interior room, bathtub, or closet without windows. Dr. Jeff Masters of Weather Underground stated that if the tornado had tracked directly over one of the congested highways, the death toll could have easily exceeded 500. The tornado’s location was 35°28′45″N 97°54′00″W (35.4792°N 97.9°W).

text: The 2013 El Reno tornado was an extremely large, powerful, and erratic tornado that occurred on the early evening of Friday, May 31, 2013, in a rural area of Central Oklahoma. It was a rain-wrapped, multiple-vortex tornado that peaked at a record width of 2.6 miles (4.2 km), making it the widest tornado ever recorded. The tornado formed at 6:03 p.m. CDT (23:03 UTC), about 8.3 miles (13.4 km) west-southwest of El Reno, and rapidly grew in size and intensity as it tracked through central Canadian County. It remained over mostly open terrain and did not impact many structures, but mobile weather radar measurements revealed extreme wind speeds exceeding 313 mph (504 km/h), among the highest ever observed on Earth, just slightly below the 321 mph (517 km/h) recorded during the 1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado. The tornado reached its maximum width of 2.6 miles as it crossed U.S. 81, surpassing the previous record set in 2004, and then turned northeastward, weakening before dissipating around 6:43 p.m. CDT (23:43 UTC) after tracking 16.2 miles (26.1 km). It avoided densely populated areas near the Oklahoma City metropolitan area. The tornado killed four storm chasers—three professional and one amateur—marking the first known deaths in storm chasing history. These chasers, including TWISTEX scientists and engineers Tim Samaras, Paul Samaras, and Carl Young, were caught off-guard by the tornado’s immense size and erratic movement. Paul Samaras and Young were ejected from their Chevrolet Cobalt by a sub-vortex, while Tim remained buckled in the passenger seat. Local resident Richard Henderson, who took a photo of the tornado before being struck, also died. Other chasers, such as Mike Bettes of The Weather Channel and Reed Timmer, were injured or had their vehicles damaged. A Doppler on Wheels analysis revealed that all teams were hit by an intense internal sub-vortex with winds approaching 200 mph (320 km/h), moving in a complex pattern. The tornado was responsible for eight fatalities and 151 injuries. Due to its size, ferocity, irregular movement, and the storm chaser deaths, it became one of the most studied and infamous tornadoes, with the National Weather Service calling it "the most dangerous tornado in storm observing history." The tornado developed within a larger weather system involving a mid-to-upper level trough and a closed mid-level low pressure area moving east-northeastward, with a strong polar jet over the southern Great Plains. Dewpoints ranged from the upper 60s°F (20°C) to lower 70s°F (20–22°C), temperatures were in the low to mid-80s°F (27–30°C), and CAPE values ranged from 3500 to 5000 J/kg, with deep layer wind shear of 45–55 kn (52–63 mph), creating favorable conditions for severe storms. A Particularly Dangerous Situation Tornado Watch was issued at 3:30 p.m. CDT, and a tornado warning was issued at 5:33 p.m. CDT for Canadian County. The tornado initially formed as multiple sub-vortices, deviated from its path at 6:15 p.m. CDT, looped before resuming east-southeast motion, and killed two people at 6:23 p.m. CDT as it passed south of El Reno across U.S. 81. It then moved into more populated areas of Canadian County, prompting a tornado emergency, before turning northeast and passing over Interstate 40 at 6:42 p.m. CDT, killing two more people. The tornado was on the ground for 40 minutes along a 16.2-mile (26.1 km) path. A strong anticyclonic multi-vortex satellite tornado formed southeast of the primary tornado at 6:28 p.m. CDT and remained on the ground for 15 minutes before lifting at 6:43 p.m. CDT. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) initially rated the tornado EF3 based on damage, but later upgraded it to an EF5 rating based on mobile radar data, with wind speeds preliminarily estimated at over 296 mph (476 km/h), and a revised analysis in 2015 showing peak winds of 313 mph (504 km/h). A 2024 NOAA and University of Oklahoma analysis estimated wind speeds between 115–150 m/s (257–336 mph; 414–540 km/h). Despite the radar-measured wind speeds, NOAA revised the rating to EF3 in August 2013 because ground damage surveys did not support a higher rating, citing the rural nature of the area and the fact that the EF5 wind speeds occurred in sub-vortices that did not impact structures. The tornado’s unusual behavior included abrupt direction changes, rapid expansion to 2.6 miles in about 30 seconds, a swift increase in forward speed from 20 to 55 mph (32 to 89 km/h), multiple vortices, and a translucent outer circulation obscured by rain. This made it a worst-case scenario for storm chasers, with many located in the "bear's cage" area northeast of the tornado, where visibility was good but reaction time was minimal. The wrapping rain bands were part of the tornado’s outer circulation, not a narrow corridor of clear air. Tim Samaras, Paul Samaras, and Carl Young were among the first known tornado-related deaths of professional storm chasers or researchers. Tim drove a reinforced truck, while Carl drove an unmodified Chevrolet Cobalt, which was underpowered and poorly suited for high winds and rain-slicked roads. Mike Bettes had his SUV thrown 200 yards, suffering a broken neck and fractured vertebrae, while Emily Sutton and Kevin Josefy had their vehicle damaged by debris. Billy Prater and his family sought refuge under an overpass, Brandon Sullivan and Brett Wright were struck by barn debris, and Reed Timmer’s vehicle lost its hood. Dan Robinson escaped just ahead of the TWISTEX crew and is believed to be the last person to see Samaras, Paul, and Young. A tour group led by Randy Walton and Mike Phelps escaped after turning around as the tornado approached. A Doppler on Wheels analysis showed that all vehicles entered the tornado through the less intense north/northwestern side and were then hit by the intense internal sub-vortex. In response to the deaths, Kansas Emergency Management Association president Brian Stone called for storm chasing regulations, though implementation remains uncertain. AccuWeather Senior Vice President Mike Smith urged against overreacting, noting that the chasers were the first to die in 40 years and that storm chasing provides vital real-time data. On June 2, dozens of storm chasers coordinated a tribute using GPS transponders to spell out the initials of Tim, Paul, and Carl in North Dakota, South Dakota, and Nebraska. The Discovery Channel aired a special tribute episode titled "Mile Wide Tornado: Oklahoma Disaster" on June 5, honoring the chasers and covering the May 20 Moore tornado. The November 2013 National Geographic cover story featured Tim Samaras and a detailed scientific analysis of the tornado. A team of scientists and veteran chasers launched a crowd-sourcing project to collect video, photos, and GPS logs to reconstruct the event, creating the largest visual data set ever gathered on a tornado. The data is combined with radar and lightning information and aims to develop a standardized open-access database. In 2015, software called "Tornado Environment Display" (TED), named after Dr. Ted Fujita, was unveiled to synchronize maps, radar data, and storm chaser footage.

text: The 2018 FIFA World Cup opening ceremony occurred on Thursday, 14 June 2018, at 3:30 BST (about half an hour before the opening match) at the Luzhniki Stadium in Moscow, Russia, where Russia defeated Saudi Arabia 5–0.[2][3] The official mascot of the tournament was Zabivaka (English: "The one who scores"), a wolf designed to represent fun, charm, and character, which was voted for by a 53% margin.[4] Former World Cup-winning Brazilian striker Ronaldo was also a mascot and was originally intended to deliver the ceremonial first kick, but instead, he passed the official match ball—an Adidas Telstar 18—to the child mascot Zabivaka, who then kicked it off to begin the tournament. The match ball was sent into space with the International Space Station crew in March and returned to Earth in early June.[5] Russian President Vladimir Putin delivered the opening speech, describing Russia as "open, hospitable and friendly" and emphasizing the unifying power of football, stating that it transcends language, ideology, or faith. He concluded by saying: “Our duty is to preserve this power of humanity for generations to come for the sake of developing sports and strengthening peace and mutual understanding between people. I wish all the teams’ success and an unforgettable experience for the fans. Welcome to Russia.” FIFA President Gianni Infantino followed with a speech stating: “Welcome to the FIFA World Cup here in Russia. As of today, for one month, football will conquer Russia and from Russia, football will conquer the world. Enjoy the biggest celebration on earth. Thank you President Putin, thank you Moscow, Spasibo [thank you] Russia.” After the speeches, the ceremony performances began before the Russia vs. Saudi Arabia match.[6][7][8] British pop singer Robbie Williams performed "Let Me Entertain You" and later sang "Feel" and a duet of "Angels" with Russian soprano Aida Garifullina, as performers emerged dressed in the flags of all 32 teams, each carrying a sign with their nation's name. Williams then performed "Rock DJ" in an encore as the pitch was cleared for the match.[9] During the encore, Williams gave the middle finger, prompting Fox in the US to issue an apology, while ITV in the UK had cut away before the incident.[10] While singing "Rock DJ," Williams altered the lyrics to "But I did this for free," replacing "Every night"—the reason for this change remains unexplained. Williams appeared on This Morning on 19 June, explaining that under pressure with only one minute left before kickoff, he performed a one-minute countdown using his middle finger, which he admitted he regrets and cannot trust himself to avoid. When asked if he regrets it, he said: "Yeah, of course, yeah. I cannot trust me. And the last thing I said to my manager before we sat down on the sofa here was, 'what could go wrong,' because I don't know what I'm going to do at any time. There's no, sort of, plan. The plan was, sing in key, don't fall over. That was the plan and 99% of the plan, I pulled off.” He added that nothing actually popped into his head, stating there was a block between him and sense, and only later realized he had done it. A total of 21 foreign heads of state attended the match, marking the largest gathering of leaders for a FIFA World Cup match.

text: The 2019 Rugby World Cup (Japanese: ラグビーワールドカップ2019) was the ninth edition of the quadrennial men's rugby union world championship, hosted in Japan from 20 September to 2 November across 12 venues nationwide. The opening match was held at Ajinomoto Stadium in Chōfu, Tokyo, and the final took place at International Stadium Yokohama in Yokohama. This marked the first time the tournament was held in Asia and outside the traditional Tier 1 rugby nations. The event saw the first match cancellations due to Typhoon Hagibis, which affected three matches because of safety concerns. South Africa defeated England 32–12 in the final to win their third title, matching New Zealand's record and becoming the first team to claim the title after losing a pool-stage match. The defending champions, New Zealand, finished third after defeating Wales in the bronze final. The International Rugby Board (IRB), later renamed World Rugby, invited nations to express interest in hosting the 2015 and 2019 tournaments by 15 August 2008, with 10 unions responding and nine showing interest in the 2019 event. Russia initially bid for both tournaments but withdrew in February 2009 to focus on the 2013 Rugby World Cup Sevens; Australia withdrew on 6 May 2009. The three potential hosts—Italy, Japan, and South Africa—were announced on 8 May 2009. On 28 July 2009, the IRB confirmed England as hosts for 2015 and Japan for 2019, approved by Rugby World Cup Ltd with a 16–10 vote. From late 2013, the IRB, RWC Ltd, JRFU, and Japan 2019 conducted a process of gathering expressions of interest and meeting with potential hosts. In May 2014, 22 municipal and prefectural organizations in Japan expressed interest, with formal bids due by 31 October 2014; 14 bids were received on 5 November. Hong Kong and Singapore expressed interest in hosting matches and were included in Japan's bid but were not among the 14 stadiums announced in 2014. Nissan Stadium in Yokohama and Denka Big Swan Stadium in Niigata declined to bid. The JRFU's original 2009 bid was revised, excluding Chichibunomiya Stadium in Tokyo and including the larger 50,000-seat Nagai Stadium in Osaka. East Osaka City, which took over Hanazono Rugby Stadium from Kintetsu in April 2015, submitted a joint bid with Osaka Municipality to refurbish the stadium. Kamaishi, Hamamatsu, Kyoto, Ōita, Nagasaki, and Kumamoto were not included in the bid. Hosting areas excluded were Hokushin'etsu (Hokuriku and Kōshin'etsu) and Chūgoku (including Hiroshima and Shikoku), with no Chūgoku city hosting in the 2002 FIFA World Cup, though Hiroshima hosted in the 2006 FIBA World Championship. The new National Stadium in Tokyo, built for the 2020 Summer Olympics, was initially planned as the primary venue but was scrapped and rebid in 2015 due to design criticism and rising costs, leading to its completion being delayed. As a result, the opening match was moved to Ajinomoto Stadium and the final to Nissan Stadium in Yokohama. The top three teams from the 2015 World Cup received automatic qualification, with the remaining eight spots filled through regional qualifiers, six of which came from regional groups and two via play-offs. Qualifying groups were Africa, Americas, Asia, Europe, and Oceania. The United States qualified on 1 July 2017 by defeating Canada in a two-leg match as America 1. Fiji and Tonga qualified as Oceania 1 and 2 respectively. Samoa secured the third Oceania spot by defeating Germany in a two-leg tie the following year. Uruguay qualified in January 2018 with a 10-point win over Canada as Americas 2. Romania initially qualified as Europe 1, but after complaints from Spain over ineligible players, all three—Romania, Spain, and Belgium—were penalized, resulting in Russia qualifying and Germany entering a play-off against Samoa. Namibia qualified in August 2018 by defeating Kenya in the Rugby Africa Gold Cup final. The final spot was decided in a repechage tournament in Marseille in November 2018, won by Canada after winning all three of their matches. The pool draw took place on 10 May 2017 in Kyoto, moved from its traditional December slot after the previous World Cup to allow nations more time to improve their world rankings. The seeding system from previous tournaments was retained, with the 12 automatic qualifiers from 2015 allocated based on their World Rugby Rankings on 10 May 2017. The remaining two bands were formed from the eight qualifying teams based on their previous World Cup performance. The 20 teams were seeded according to their world rankings as of that date. The draw involved randomly selecting a ball from a pot, with the first ball assigned to Pool A, the second to Pool B, the third to Pool C, and the fourth to Pool D. Each team submitted a squad of 31 players, the same as in 2015, with the deadline being 8 September, the United States being the last to reveal their squad on 6 September. World Rugby named 12 referees, seven assistant referees, and four television match officials for the 48 matches. The opening ceremony occurred at Ajinomoto Stadium in Tokyo on 20 September 2019 at 18:30 (JST), featuring a showcase of traditional and modern Japanese culture and the evolution of rugby in Japan. Richie McCaw, former All Blacks captain and 2015 World Cup winner, performed a ceremonial handover of the Webb Ellis Cup. Six jet aircraft from Japan Air Self-Defense Force's Blue Impulse aerobatic team flew over the stadium. Kiyoe Yoshioka of Ikimono-gakari performed World in Union, the official song. The tournament was officially opened by Fumihito, Prince Akishino of Japan, with World Rugby chairman Sir Bill Beaumont delivering a speech stating: "Over the next six weeks we will experience the very best of rugby and the very best of Japan as excitement sweeps this great nation. I know Japan will be the most welcoming of hosts, you are the best. The waiting is over and the stage is set. It’s now over to the teams and the fans to make this the best World Cup ever." The 20 teams were divided into four pools of five teams, each playing a single round-robin format of 10 games, with each team playing every other team in the pool once. Teams earned four points for a win, two for a draw, and zero for a loss. A bonus point was awarded for scoring four tries or for losing by seven points or fewer, with both conditions applying if both occurred. The top two teams in each pool advanced to the quarter-finals, and the top three teams qualified for the 2023 Rugby World Cup. If teams were tied on match points, the following tiebreakers applied: if three teams were tied, the criteria were applied to determine first place, then again (starting from criterion 1) to determine second place. The opening match of the tournament was Japan versus Russia in Pool A, with Japan winning 30–10. Kotaro Matsushima scored the first hat-trick by a Japanese player at a World Cup. Kirill Golosnitsky scored the first try of the tournament in the opening match after four minutes, the fastest try ever in a World Cup opening match. Two days later, Ireland defeated Scotland 27–3. On 24 September, Samoa beat Russia 34–9 in Kumagaya. Four days later, Japan defeated Ireland 19–12 in Tokyo, scoring four out of six penalties. World Rugby later admitted three of the four offside penalties were incorrectly awarded. Kenki Fukuoka scored a try in the 58th minute to give Japan a two-point lead after Ireland's Garry Ringrose and Rob Kearney scored the opening tries. Yu Tamura's conversion and fourth successful penalty sealed the win. Scotland recorded their first World Cup victory with a 34–0 win over Samoa in Kobe, with Samoan captain Jack Lam describing the ball as "a bar of soap." Three days later, Ireland defeated Russia 35–0 in Kobe, with five different players scoring tries. Jordi Murphy was substituted in the 27th minute due to a possible rib injury, adding to Irish back row pain after losing Jack Conan. Japan won 38–19 in Toyota with a 85th-minute try from Kotaro Matsushima securing a bonus point. Russia was defeated 61–0 by Scotland, with George Horne scoring a hat-trick, making Scotland the first team in World Cup history to not concede a point in two consecutive matches. A red card to Bundee Aki in the 29th minute reduced Ireland to 14 men, but they won 47–5 over Samoa in Fukuoka, with Johnny Sexton scoring two tries. The Japan–Scotland match was under threat due to Typhoon Hagibis, with the Scottish Rugby Union demanding legal action if cancelled. After an inspection confirmed the match could proceed, Japan won 28–21 with Kenki Fukuoka scoring two tries, becoming the first Tier 2 team to qualify since 2007, topping the pool while Ireland finished second. Pool B began with New Zealand defeating South Africa 23–13. New Zealand scored two tries in four minutes from George Bridge and Scott Barrett, leading 17–3 at half-time. Pieter-Steph du Toit scored a converted try to bring the score to 17–10, but two penalties from Richie Mo'unga and Beauden Barrett sealed the win. In Higashiōsaka, Italy conceded an early try to Namibia but won 25–0 with a bonus point. Italy earned a second bonus-point victory in Fukuoka, scoring seven tries in a 48–7 win over Canada. In Toyota, South Africa defeated Namibia 54–0, scoring nine tries while Namibia managed only a Cliven Loubser penalty in the 23rd minute. New Zealand won 63–0 over Canada at Ōita Stadium, with Brad Weber scoring his first two tries and the Barrett brothers (Jordie, Beauden, and Scott) each scoring a try, becoming the first trio of brothers to start for New Zealand. New Zealand then defeated Namibia 62–0 in Chōfu, with Sevu Reece, Ben Smith, and Anton Lienert-Brown scoring two tries in the second half after Namibia allowed only 24 points in the first half. South Africa defeated Italy 49–3 in Fukuroi, with Cheslin Kolbe scoring two tries. South Africa then beat Canada 66–7, with Cobus Reinach scoring the fastest hat-trick in World Cup history in 11 minutes. The final two matches of the group—New Zealand vs. Italy and Namibia vs. Canada—were cancelled due to Typhoon Hagibis. New Zealand finished top of the pool, South Africa second. Pool C began with Argentina recovering from a 17-point half-time deficit against France at Tokyo Stadium, only for France's Camille Lopez to score a drop goal in the 70th minute to win 23–21. In Sapporo, England won a bonus-point match over Tonga with two tries from Manu Tuilagi. England followed with a 38–0 victory over the United States, with Joe Cokanasiga scoring two tries; the match was marred by the first red card of the tournament, given to United States' John Quill for a shoulder charge to Owen Farrell's head. Argentina rebounded from their loss to France with a 28–12 win over Tonga in Higashiōsaka, scoring all their tries in the first 28 minutes, including a hat-trick from Julián Montoya, before Tonga scored two tries to reduce the margin to 16. After Typhoon Mitag nearly cancelled the match, France lost consistency and allowed the United States to stay in the game before three late tries in the second half secured a 33–9 win in Fukuoka. In Chōfu, England defeated Argentina 39–10, with Tomás Lavanini shown a red card for a high tackle on Owen Farrell's head, forcing Argentina to play with 14 men. France qualified with a two-point win over Tonga at Kumamoto Stadium, after conceding the first 17 points, with Sonatane Takulua and Mali Hingano scoring tries to close the gap to three points, before Romain Ntamack scored two penalties in eight minutes to secure the win. Argentina finished their campaign with a 47–17 victory over the United States in Kumagaya, with Joaquín Tuculet and Juan Cruz Mallia each scoring two tries, their first since 2003. After the England–France match was cancelled due to Typhoon Hagibis, Tonga ended their campaign with a 31–19 win over the United States, converting a match-winning try by Telusa Veainu and securing a bonus point. England finished top of the pool, France second. Pool D opened with Australia defeating Fiji 18–0 in Sapporo after Fiji led by two points at half-time, with Australia scoring four tries in the second half for a bonus point. Wales beat Georgia 43–14 at City of Toyota Stadium, leading 29–0 at half-time and 22–0 after three tries in the first half.

text: On 14 January 2019, a Boeing 707-3J9C, serial number 21128 and registered as EP-CPP, operated by Saha Airlines on a cargo flight crashed at Fath Air Base, near Karaj, Alborz province, Iran. This aircraft was the last civil Boeing 707 in operation. It was owned by the Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force (IRIAF) and had been leased to Saha Airlines. The aircraft was 42 years old at the time of the accident, having first flown on 19 November 1976 and been delivered to the Imperial Iranian Air Force as 5–8312. It was transferred to Saha Airlines on 27 February 2000, re-registered as EP-SHK, and subsequently returned to the IRIAF in December 2015 before being re-leased to Saha Airlines in May 2016 with the registration EP-CPP. The aircraft had suffered substantial damage from an uncontained engine failure on 3 August 2009 during a flight from Ahvaz International Airport to Mehrabad International Airport, Tehran, leading to an emergency landing at Ahvaz, after which it was repaired. The flight was intended to carry meat from Manas International Airport in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, to Payam International Airport in Karaj, Iran, but the crew mistakenly landed at Fath Air Base, likely confusing its shorter runway with the longer Payam runway, as the two are only a few kilometres apart and aligned similarly. A Boeing 707 typically requires a runway longer than 2,500 meters (8,200 feet), but Fath Air Base's runway is only 1,300 meters (4,300 feet). Poor weather conditions were also reported. The aircraft overran the runway, crashed through a wall, and collided with a house in the Farrokhabad neighborhood of Fardis County, Alborz province. Security footage captured the crash and subsequent fire. The houses were unoccupied at the time, and no ground injuries occurred. Fifteen of the sixteen crew members on board died; one, flight engineer Farshad Mahdavinejad, survived but was seriously injured and taken to Shariati Hospital in critical condition. There were no passengers. Early reports indicated either 16 or 17 people on board, all but one of whom died. An investigation was launched, and the cockpit voice recorder, flight data recorder, and control display unit were recovered from the wreckage on 14 January.

text: The 2020 French Open was a major tennis tournament held on outdoor clay courts at Stade Roland Garros in Paris, France, and was the 119th edition of the event. Originally scheduled for 24 May to 7 June, it was postponed due to the COVID-19 pandemic, first moved to 20 September to 4 October 2020, then later adjusted to 27 September to 11 October 2020. This marked the first time since 1947 that the tournament was not held in May–June and the first time since the Open Era that a major tournament was postponed rather than cancelled. The event was part of the 2020 ATP Tour and WTA Tour calendars under the Grand Slam category and was run by the International Tennis Federation. It included men's and women's singles and doubles, as well as junior and wheelchair tournaments. Qualifying matches for singles and doubles began on 21 September, with the main singles draws featuring 16 male and 12 female qualifiers out of 128 players each. The tournament was the only Grand Slam to retain the advantage set in the final set, unlike the Australian Open and Wimbledon, which had switched to tiebreaks. The men's singles title was won by Rafael Nadal, who secured his 13th French Open title and 20th Grand Slam title, defeating Novak Djokovic in straight sets; this victory made Nadal equal Roger Federer's all-time record of 20 Grand Slam titles and marked his fourth consecutive and 13th overall French Open title, with no set lost throughout the tournament. The women's singles title was won by Iga Świątek, who claimed her first WTA singles title by defeating Sofia Kenin in straight sets, becoming the first player from Poland, male or female, and the first player born in the 21st century, male or female, to win a Grand Slam singles title. Świątek also did not drop a set during the entire tournament. The 2020 French Open was also the 124th edition of the tournament and the last Grand Slam event of 2020. It was the first year with a retractable roof on Court Philippe-Chatrier (completed in late 2019), with plans for a roof on Court Suzanne-Lenglen by 2023, and the first year with evening tennis due to floodlights installed on the twelve courts. Because of the September–October sunset in Paris occurring before 8:00 pm CEST, evening matches were possible, with the first women's evening match occurring during Iga Świątek and Martina Trevisan's quarterfinal, and the first men's evening match between Rafael Nadal and Jannik Sinner, which started after 10:00 pm and finished at 1:26 am—marking the first French Open match to end after midnight. The mixed doubles event did not take place, continuing the trend after the US Open. The men's doubles began on 29 September with 16 seeded pairs, and the women's doubles began on 30 September with 16 seeded pairs. In men's doubles, Pavić and Soares won the title in straight sets after defeating Krawietz and Mies in the final, marking their second Grand Slam title. In women's doubles, Hsieh Su-wei and Barbora Strýcová, along with other seeded pairs, were eliminated, and the defending champions Tímea Babos and Kristina Mladenovic successfully defended their title in straight sets. In wheelchair men's singles, Hewett won the title in straight sets, defeating Gérard in the final, securing his fourth Grand Slam singles title. In wheelchair women's singles, Yui Kamiji won her fourth French Open title and 24th Grand Slam title by defeating Momoko Ohtani, 6–2, 6–1. In wheelchair quad singles, Dylan Alcott defeated Sam Schröder in the opening round, and Andy Lapthorne defeated David Wagner in three sets, with the semifinal results leading to the final. The tournament had a maximum spectator capacity of 11,500 across the three main courts, with 5,000 in each of Court Philippe Chatrier and Court Suzanne Lenglen and 1,500 in Court Simonne Mathieu, while qualifying matches were played without spectators. Spectator capacity was reduced to 5,000 in the main courts on 17 September and to 1,000 starting on the eve of the main tournament due to a surge in coronavirus cases. Players were required to undergo two virus tests upon arrival and stay in designated hotels. The Laver Cup, originally scheduled for 24–27 September, was postponed to 2021, conflicting with the initial French Open dates. The men's singles event began on 27 September with 32 seeded players, and the women's singles began on the same date. In the men's singles, 11 seeded players were defeated in the first round, including No. 4 Daniil Medvedev, No. 8 Gaël Monfils, and No. 11 David Goffin, and 10 seeded players lost in the second and third rounds. In the women's singles, 12 seeded players lost in the first round, including No. 9 Johanna Konta, No. 12 Madison Keys, and No. 15 Markéta Vondroušová, and seven more lost in the second round. Serena Williams withdrew before her second round match due to an Achilles injury. In the men's doubles, only one seeded pair lost in the first round, and six of the remaining twelve seeded pairs were eliminated in the third round. In the women's doubles, five seeded pairs and three unseeded pairs advanced to the quarterfinals, with the final between Babos and Mladenovic and Guarachi and Krawczyk, won by the former in straight sets. The field consisted of four players; defending champion Dylan Alcott and Andy Lapthorne received the top two seeds, with the other two players unseeded. In the opening round, Alcott faced wild card entry Sam Schröder in a rematch of the final of the US Open some weeks earlier. Alcott was victorious in two sets. The other semifinal saw Lapthorne defeat David Wagner in three sets, with Lapthorne winning the first and third. The final was played between No. 1 Alcott and No. 2 Lapthorne, with Alcott winning both sets by a score of 6–2 to capture his eleventh Grand Slam singles title. The wheelchair men's doubles competition featured the same eight players as in the singles event. Houdet and Peifer formed the top-seeded pair, while Hewett and Reid were the second seeds. The other pairings were Fernandez with Kunieda, and Cattanéo with Gerard. Houdet and Peifer were beaten 12–10 on a tie-break in their semifinal by Fernandez and Kunieda, after both sides had won a set each, while Hewett and Reid advanced to the final with a straight-sets victory over Cattanéo and Gerard. In the final, Hewett and Reid won the first set on a tie-break before losing the second 6–1, but finished victorious after the deciding tie-break finished 10–3 in their favour. As with the men's competition, the wheelchair women's doubles event featured the same eight players as in the singles event. Two of the four pairs were seeded: Diede de Groot and Aniek van Koot received the top seed, and the second seed went to Yui Kamiji and Jordanne Whiley. In the semifinals, De Groot and van Koot defeated the pair of Kgothatso Montjane and Momoko Ohtani, and Kamiji and Whiley defeated the pair of Marjolein Buis and Charlotte Famin. The final was played between the pair of de Groot and van Koot, the defending champions, and the pair of Kamiji and Whiley. The Dutch pair took the first set 7–6 in a tiebreak, but the latter pair came back to win the second set 6–3 and force the match into a third. text: Three-time defending champion Rafael Nadal defeated Novak Djokovic in the final of the 2020 French Open, winning 6–0, 6–2, 7–5 to claim the men's singles title. This victory marked Nadal’s 13th French Open title and his 20th major title overall, tying Roger Federer’s all-time record for men's singles titles. For the fourth time in his career, Nadal did not lose a set during the tournament, following previous instances in 2008, 2010, and 2017. This was the first time in French Open history that neither the men's nor women's singles champions lost a set in their respective tournaments. Nadal also became the first player, male or female, to win 100 matches at the French Open and only the second man—after Federer at the Australian Open and Wimbledon—to win 100 matches at the same major. Djokovic, who was attempting to become the first man in the Open Era to achieve a double career Grand Slam, would accomplish this feat the following year; however, he suffered his worst-ever defeat in a major final, winning only seven games and losing his first and only bagel (0–6 set). In the third round, Taylor Fritz and Lorenzo Sonego played the longest tiebreak in French Open history, with Sonego winning the third set tiebreak 19–17. Jannik Sinner reached the quarterfinals on his tournament debut, becoming the first man to do so since Nadal won in 2005 and the youngest quarterfinalist since Djokovic in 2006; he was also the first man born in the 21st century to reach a major quarterfinal. Nadal and Sinner’s quarterfinal match was the first men's match at the French Open to start at night, beginning after 10:00 pm CEST and finishing at 1:26 am, making it the first French Open match to end after midnight. text: The 2021–22 season marked the 120th season in the history of Brighton & Hove Albion and their fifth consecutive year in the top flight of English football. The club competed in the Premier League, the FA Cup, and the EFL Cup, exiting both cup competitions in the fourth round. Brighton finished ninth in the league, their highest-ever top-flight finish, surpassing their previous best of 13th place from the 1981–82 season. The season began with three pre-season friendlies: a goalless draw against Rangers at Ibrox on 24 July, featuring former Albion player Connor Goldson; a 3–1 win over Luton Town a week later, with goals from Aaron Connolly, Enock Mwepu, and Percy Tau, managed by former Seagulls player and coach Nathan Jones; and a 2–0 home defeat to La Liga side Getafe on 7 August, following the return of key players like captain Lewis Dunk and Leandro Trossard. Brighton opened the league campaign with a 2–1 victory over Burnley, with goals from Neal Maupay and Alexis Mac Allister, and followed it with a 2–0 win against Watford on 21 August, marking their best start in a top-flight campaign and their first match in front of a full stadium since March 2020. In the EFL Cup second round, they defeated Cardiff City 2–0, with Jakub Moder and Andi Zeqiri scoring their first goals for the club. Their first league loss came on 28 August, a 2–0 home defeat to Everton, with Taylor Richards making his league and Premier League debut. In a first derby match against Crystal Palace on 27 September, Brighton were behind after Trossard conceded a penalty scored by Wilfried Zaha, but Joël Veltman's long ball led to Neal Maupay scoring a 90+5th-minute equalizer. A second league loss occurred on 23 October, a 4–1 home defeat to Manchester City, with the City side scoring their first three goals in 18 minutes. In the EFL Cup fourth round, they lost to Leicester City on penalties after a 2–2 draw, with Mwepu scoring his first goal for the club and Jürgen Locadia making his first start and only second appearance in over two years. On 24 October, Brighton drew 2–2 with Liverpool after coming from 2–0 down, with Mwepu scoring his first league goal. On 20 November, manager Alex Potter made his 100th appearance in charge with a 2–0 away loss to Aston Villa. On 6 December, Brighton were drawn away to West Bromwich Albion in the third round of the FA Cup, to be played on 8 January 2022. Their fixture against Tottenham Hotspur on 12 December was postponed due to high COVID-19 cases in the Spurs squad. Brighton played a 1–0 home loss against Wolves on 15 December, with several absences due to injury, suspension, and COVID-19, and their match against Manchester United on 18 December was also postponed two days before kickoff due to cases in both squads. After a 12-game winless run starting on 19 September, Brighton beat Brentford 2–0 on Boxing Day, moving into the top half of the table and securing a double over the Bees after a prior away win in September. In the FA Cup third round on 8 January, Brighton won 2–1 after extra time against West Brom, with Odel Offiah making his first start and Kjell Scherpen making his debut as goalkeeper. In the reverse fixture against Palace on 15 January, Pascal Groß's penalty was saved by Jack Butland, Maupay's goal was disallowed for a high boot, and Joachim Andersen scored an own goal in the 87th minute after a low-paced pass from Maupay. Brighton were knocked out of the FA Cup in the fourth round on 5 February, losing 3–1 to Tottenham after a Harry Kane double and a Solly March own goal, with Yves Bissouma providing a brief hope before Kane scored his second. Their record-breaking seven-match unbeaten run ended on 15 February in Potter's 100th league match, with a 2–0 away loss to Manchester United at Old Trafford, after Dunk was sent off for denying Anthony Elanga a run on goal—initially shown a yellow card, but VAR reviewed and deemed it a sending-off. After six consecutive defeats, Brighton drew 0–0 with Norwich City on 2 April, with Maupay's penalty narrowly missing the target. A week later, on 9 April, they defeated Arsenal 2–1, with Mwepu scoring and assisting on his first start since a long injury absence, and Moisés Caicedo making his Premier League debut and assisting Mwepu's goal. Seven days later, on 16 April, Trossard scored two goals in consecutive games, including a 90th-minute goal, helping Brighton go six games unbeaten in the capital. On 30 April, Brighton beat Wolves 3–0 at Molineux, reaching 44 points—breaking their previous record of 41—and winning 10 league matches, surpassing their previous record of nine. On 7 May, Brighton defeated Manchester United 4–0 at the AMEX, their biggest ever top-flight result and first home win of 2022, in front of a record crowd of 31,637. Moisés Caicedo and Marc Cucurella scored their first goals for the club, Pascal Groß scored his first of the season, and Trossard scored one and assisted two others, ending Brighton's hopes for UEFA Champions League qualification in the 2022–23 season. At the end-of-season awards, Marc Cucurella won both Players' Player and Player of the Season, Jeremy Sarmiento won Young Player of the Season, Enock Mwepu won The Seagulls Goal of the Season for his 20-yard strike against Liverpool in October. Brighton finished ninth after beating West Ham 3–1 in the final match, with Joël Veltman scoring his second goal for the club. The victory brought their points total to 51, 10 points above their previous record, and 42 goals—the most in a Premier League season. The final took place on 28 May 2022 in Paris, where Liverpool, who had previously faced Real Madrid in 1981, lost 0–1 as Vinícius Júnior scored the only goal. The club's spending was £36,000,000 in the summer and £37,500,000 in the winter, totaling £73,500,000. text: The 2021–22 Premier League marked the 30th season of the league since its founding in 1992 and the 123rd season of top-flight English football. The season began on 25 March 2021 and ended on 30 May 2022, with fixtures released on 16 June 2021. Manchester City defended their title for the second consecutive year, winning their sixth Premier League title and eighth English league title overall, making it their fourth title in the last five seasons. They were the defending champions, having won the previous season's title. The season featured full attendance after the restrictions of the COVID-19 pandemic, which had limited or halted matches in the final third of 2019–20 and the entire 2020–21 season. It also included a winter break with no matches scheduled between 23 January and 7 February 2022. The early title race was led by Liverpool, Manchester City, and Chelsea, who were within two points of each other by early December. Chelsea led briefly after a run of 14 unbeaten matches until a defeat to West Ham United gave City the advantage. City then won 12 consecutive games, including a victory over Chelsea, building a 13-point lead by January (though Liverpool had two games in hand due to COVID-19 postponements). Liverpool responded with a 10-game winning streak, including their games in hand, and a 2–3 home loss to Tottenham Hotspur in February reduced City's lead to one point before their match on 10 April. A 2–2 draw preserved City's narrow lead. On 7 October, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund acquired an 80% stake in Newcastle United for £300 million, ending Mike Ashley's 14-year ownership. An emergency meeting on 12 October involving the other 19 clubs expressed anger over the takeover, with Newcastle excluded from the meeting. On 18 November, clubs voted to tighten financial controls to limit Newcastle's spending. At the time of the takeover, Newcastle were in 19th place after failing to win any of their first seven games; Steve Bruce was dismissed and Eddie Howe appointed. Newcastle did not win until their 15th match, but after five January signings, they won 12 of their final 18 games to finish 11th. In December, multiple matches were postponed due to COVID-19 outbreaks, with clubs calling for a league shutdown; a meeting on 20 December led to fixtures being played over Christmas if safe, with clubs advised to play if they had 13 fit players plus a goalkeeper. On 2 March, Roman Abramovich announced plans to sell Chelsea, intending to donate all proceeds to Ukraine victims of the Russian invasion. Reports followed of interest from Hansjörg Wyss, Todd Boehly, Javed Afridi, and others. On 10 March, the UK government froze Abramovich's assets due to his ties with Vladimir Putin, halting Chelsea's ability to sell tickets, merchandise, or players, and negotiate contracts. A government licence allowed football operations, employee payments, and season-ticket access. For the first time in Premier League history, all title, Champions League, Europa League, Conference League qualifications, and relegation battles were decided on the final day. With a one-point lead over Liverpool, Manchester City needed to match or exceed Liverpool's result to secure back-to-back titles; Liverpool needed a win and hope City lost to Aston Villa, managed by Steven Gerrard. Liverpool fell behind Wolves early but equalised; Aston Villa took a 2–0 lead after 63 minutes via goals from Matty Cash and Philippe Coutinho. Manchester City scored three goals in under six minutes (Ilkay Gundogan and Rodri as substitutes) to take the lead. Liverpool responded with late goals from Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson to win 3–1, but the result was irrelevant as City won 3–2 against Villa to claim their fourth title in five seasons. The season is remembered for the high quality of play by Manchester City and Liverpool, resulting in a fierce title race similar to the 2018–19 season, but also for VAR issues in its third season in England, including a high intervention threshold that led to few decisions, such as the failure to award a penalty in the Everton–Manchester City match due to a handball by Rodri, which impacted the title race. Norwich City, promoted from the Championship, were relegated with four games to spare after a 10th loss in 12 matches, recording the worst goal difference since Derby County in 2007–08. Watford, also promoted, were the second team to be relegated after a defeat to Crystal Palace. The final relegation spot was contested by Everton, Burnley, and Leeds United, all of whom struggled in the final months. Everton won only three games between October and April, but victories over Manchester United, Chelsea, and Leicester City meant a 3–2 win over Crystal Palace in their final home game secured safety; Dominic Calvert-Lewin's 85th-minute goal led to fans storming the pitch. Fans again invaded the pitch at full time after avoiding relegation since 1951, extending their top-flight status to 69 years. Burnley and Leeds were level on 35 points, with Burnley having a better goal difference. Burnley fell behind 2–0 to Newcastle, while Raphinha scored a penalty to put Leeds ahead against Brentford in the 54th minute. A 78th-minute equaliser from Brentford and a Maxwel Cornet goal gave Burnley hope, but Jack Harrison's added-time goal confirmed Leeds' safety and relegated Burnley after six consecutive seasons in the Premier League. Chelsea secured a top-four finish for the fourth consecutive season, leaving only Tottenham and Arsenal in contention for the Champions League spot. Arsenal were in 4th with three games left, but losses to Tottenham in the North London derby and to Newcastle in their final away game, combined with Tottenham's win over Burnley, saw them fall behind. Spurs needed only a point against already relegated Norwich to qualify for the first time in three years and won 5–0, with Son Heung-min scoring two goals to share the Golden Boot with Mohamed Salah. Arsenal failed to qualify for the Champions League for the sixth season despite a 5–1 win over Everton. Manchester United had a difficult season, culminating in the sacking of Ole Gunnar Solskjær on 21 November 2021 after a 4–1 loss to Watford; Ralf Rangnick took over as interim manager. The club finished 6th with a zero goal difference and the worst points total in the Premier League era at 58, losing on the final day. They qualified for the Europa League, but not back-to-back spots, as West Ham's 3–1 defeat at Brighton meant they settled for the Europa Conference League. Brentford manager Thomas Frank had a strong first season, aided by the January signing of Christian Eriksen, winning seven of their last 11 games, including a 4–1 win over Chelsea. The team finished 13th, 11 points above the relegation zone and never spent a week in the bottom half. Brighton had their best top-flight season under Graham Potter, finishing ninth with 51 points despite a poor home record; their 4–0 win over Manchester United was their biggest top-flight victory. Twenty teams competed: the top 17 from the previous season and three promoted from the Championship—Norwich City, Watford, and Brentford. These replaced Fulham, West Bromwich Albion, and Sheffield United, all of whom were relegated after brief top-flight spells. Brentford's return marked their first season in the Premier League after a 74-year absence. Four players scored four goals: one for the home team, one for the away team.
