text: 2-XL is an educational toy robot marketed from 1978 to 1981 by the Mego Corporation and from 1992 to 1995 by Tiger Electronics. It was the first "smart-toy" to exhibit rudimentary intelligence, memory, gameplay, and responsiveness, and was given a personality that kept children engaged through verbal interactions, jokes, and funny sayings. The toy was invented and patented by Michael J. Freeman, Ph.D., who also voiced the robot using a synthesizer to create a high-pitched robot-like sound, shaping its personality. First introduced in 1978 by Mego, a US-based toy company in New York City, 2-XL became a commercial success and was sold in multiple countries with tapes translated into seven foreign languages. It used 8-track tapes that presented multiple-choice questions, with users selecting answers via buttons that changed the tape's path, enabling interactive gameplay. The robot could respond verbally based on user input, and its personality was highlighted by lines such as "Perhaps your brain went on strike! You are Wrong" or "Nice try but (whispering) you are wrong, but go ahead, I will be a nice little toy robot and give you a second chance now." If correct, it praised the user with phrases like "You must be a genius. Good work" or "Nice answer, football is correct." The original 2-XL had a brown plastic body with white facial features, two red light bulbs for eyes that flashed during operation, four red buttons for answering questions, and a volume/power knob. It played up to two hours of content covering sports, the Guinness Book of World Records, the metric system, general knowledge, and jokes. A 1980 revision featured brighter red eyes that responded to voice, a glossier plastic finish, and a rounder speaker. A school-specific version included earphone jacks, curriculum tapes, and a teacher's manual. In 1992, Tiger Electronics re-introduced 2-XL with cassette tapes that were twice as long as the original 8-track tapes and offered better sound quality, using all four tracks of a cassette to create interactive audio responses. Freeman again recorded the voice in a professional studio, and the new version included a light-up circular mouth and a headphone jack, allowing it to run on batteries. The cassette version used the same interactive logic as the original, leveraging the four-track structure to provide different audio outputs based on button presses. This concept was inspired by the Talk 'n Play system and earlier home cassette recorders. New tapes featured popular characters and media such as Spider-Man, X-Men, Star Trek: The Next Generation, Power Rangers, Jurassic Park, Superman, and Batman, allowing users to make choices that influenced story outcomes, similar to Choose Your Own Adventure books. The second version was available from 1992 to 1996, with about 45 tapes released, sold internationally including in Japan, Germany, Hungary, Italy, France, the UK, Ireland, Canada, and Brazil (distributed by Playtronic), and translated into many languages—though not recorded by Freeman. The original version included a program called "The World of 2-XL" with each unit, while other programs were sold separately. One final Mego tape, "Trilex," was a board game with a pyramid-shaped board and four colored slots aligned with the robot’s buttons, enabling users to drop checkers that would press the corresponding track buttons, aiming to form lines or triangles of three checkers of the same color, simulating a game-playing AI. Secondary products under the 2-XL name included laptop bags, earphones, and lunch boxes. Both versions won numerous awards, including FamilyFun’s 1992 best toy award, Right Start Magazine’s 1993 Europe’s best toy for ages 3–5, and Playthings magazine’s 75th anniversary cover naming 2-XL one of the top ten toys of all time. The Tiger 2-XL also won the 1992 Walt Disney Company Best Learning Toy award. The toy's success also inspired a game show, Pick Your Brain, and it served as a spokesrobot for basketball player Michael Jordan and his foundation in 1992 and 1993, appearing in several public service announcements with him. The name "2-XL" is a pun on "to excel."

It was discovered on 9 April 1861 by American astronomer Horace Tuttle at the Harvard College Observatory in Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States. The asteroid is named after Maia from Greek mythology, who is one of the Seven Sisters of the Pleiades and the mother of Hermes (Mercury), daughter of Atlas and Pleione. Maja belongs to the main belt's background population and orbits the Sun at a distance of 2.2–3.1 AU, completing one orbit every 4 years and 4 months (1,571 days) with a semi-major axis of 2.65 AU. Its orbit has an eccentricity of 0.17 and an inclination of 3° relative to the ecliptic. The observation arc for Maja begins at the Harvard Observatory, one night after its discovery. In the Tholen classification, Maja is a carbonaceous C-type asteroid, while in the SMASS classification, it is categorized as a "hydrated" carbonaceous subtype (Ch). Rotational lightcurves of Maja have been studied since 1988; analysis of a high-quality lightcurve by French amateur astronomers Maurice Audejean and Jérôme Caron from February 2011 yielded a rotation period of 9.73509 hours and a brightness amplitude of 0.25 magnitude (U=3). A modeled lightcurve from 2016, based on photometric data, confirmed a sidereal period of 9.73570 hours and identified two spin axes at (49.0°, −70.0°) and (225.0°, −68.0°) in ecliptic coordinates. Infrared surveys by IRAS, Akari, and NEOWISE indicate that Maja has a diameter between 62.87 and 82.28 kilometers and a surface albedo between 0.03 and 0.0759. The Collaborative Asteroid Lightcurve Link uses IRAS data, adopting an albedo of 0.0618 and a diameter of 71.82 kilometers based on an absolute magnitude of 9.36. The naming was proposed by Harvard's former president, J. Quincy, and officially cited in Paul Herget's *The Names of the Minor Planets* in 1955 (H 10). The asteroids 130 Elektra, 233 Asterope, and 1051 Merope were also named after the Seven Sisters, raising a minor concern in 1861 by George Phillips Bond, the observatory director, because these names were already used for some of the brightest stars in the Pleiades constellation in Taurus. As of now, no spacecraft has visited Maja. Although a flyby of Maja was initially planned for March 1997 during the Cassini–Huygens mission's departure from the inner solar system, delays in the launch—moved from April 1996 to October 1997—eliminated this possibility. text: Aabria Iyengar (née Lipscomb; born May 11, 1985) is an American web series actress known primarily for tabletop role-playing game anthologies, streams, and podcasts. She returned to Dimension 20 as the gamemaster for Burrow's End in 2023 and for the second season of Misfits and Magic in 2024, the first Side Quest campaign to receive a sequel season. In 2022, she appeared as gamemaster on Dimension 20: A Court of Fey & Flowers and joined the cast of the Vampire: The Masquerade web series NY by Night, playing as Margot "Fuego" Walker. Iyengar first played Dungeons & Dragons in 2015 or 2016 when invited to her now husband's board game group and was given a cleric character sheet to play. text: Aaron Leo Brody (August 23, 1930 – July 26, 2021) was an American food scientist known for developing innovations in food processing and packaging. He created the first frozen fish sticks in the 1950s and, while working at Mars, Incorporated, introduced Starburst to the United States. Brody was born in Boston, Massachusetts, as the elder of two children to Nathan Brozozek and Lillian Gorman, Jewish immigrants from Poland; his father’s name was Americanized to Brody upon entry through Ellis Island. He attended Solomon-Lewenburgh Junior High School and then Boston English School in 1947. Brody entered the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in 1947, earning a B.S. in Food Technology in 1951. He worked as an illustrator for the MIT school newspaper, primarily using pen on paper to depict sports figures. He was drafted into the Korean War and served from 1952 to 1954 at Fort Pickett in Blackstone, Virginia, where he reported on wounded soldiers returning from the war as a newspaper correspondent. After his military service, he pursued a graduate degree in the Food Packaging Department at MIT, earning a Ph.D. in 1957 under Bernard E. Proctor, a prominent food scientist involved in early food irradiation research and the chair of the MIT Food Technology Department. His work, "Masticatory Properties of Foods by the Strain Gage Denture Tenderometer," was featured in Life magazine on October 29, 1956, with a full-page illustration of the machine chewing mozzarella cheese; the device is on display at the MIT Museum and enabled food manufacturers to control product qualities for process design. Brody later earned an M.B.A. from Northeastern University in 1970. While still in school, he began working at the Birdseye Fisheries Lab Division of General Foods in 1951, contributing to the development of the first frozen precooked foods, including fish sticks. As a graduate student, he worked part-time at Raytheon Manufacturing Company, where he helped develop the first microwave oven, enabling microwave cooking, heating, and browning of foods. After completing his graduate studies, he joined the Whirlpool Corporation in Benton Harbor, Michigan, where he led the development of modified atmosphere packaging (MAP), invented an odor control system for refrigerators, a thermoelectric refrigerator/freezer, the Total Environmental Control “Tectrol” controlled atmosphere process for food preservation, a progenitor of MAP for fresh-cut vegetables, and radiation pasteurization of foods. He also patented an apparatus and method for storing perishable animal and plant materials, as well as non-food materials. At Mars, Inc.’s M&M Candies Division, Brody developed commercial confectionery products including Starburst and Pop Rocks; his team adapted the British candy Opal Fruits into M&M Fruit Chewies, which were later renamed Starburst due to the connotation of M&M’s with chocolate. At Mead Packaging, he invented the Crosscheck Aseptic Packaging System for high-acid fluid foods like juices and sauces, receiving patents US4,152,464, US4,391,080, and US4,409,775. At Container Corporation of America, he led the development of the Versaform insert injection molding system and served as Marketing Development Manager, his final corporate role. By the mid-1980s, Brody transitioned into independent consulting and teaching, offering courses in food packaging and product development and marketing at The University of Georgia, MBA strategic marketing and product development at Saint Joseph's University, and packaging courses at Michigan State University. He authored numerous articles and ten textbooks on food packaging, food technology, marketing, and packaging, including The Encyclopedia of Packaging Technology, which covers packaging technologies across industries from food to automobiles, soft drinks to pharmaceuticals, and Modified Atmosphere Packaging for Fresh-Cut Fruits and Vegetables, which details modern MAP technologies for fresh-cut fruits. Brody married Carolyn Goldstein on April 11, 1953, and remained married until her death in April 2021; they had three children. He died on July 26, 2021, from congestive heart failure. In 1964, he received the Industrial Achievement Award from the Institute of Food Technologists and the Leadership Award from the Packaging Institute. He was named Packaging Man of the Year in 1985 by the National Association of Packaging, Handling, and Logistics Engineers. In 1988, the Food Packaging Division of the Institute of Food Technologists awarded him the Riester-Davis Award for Lifetime Achievement in Food Packaging, the highest industry honor in the field. In 1994, he was the first recipient of the Institute of Food Technologists' Industrial Scientist Award for technical contributions to the food industry. In 1995, he was inducted into the Packaging Hall of Fame. In 2000, he received the Nicholas Appert Award from the Institute of Food Technologists for his lifetime contributions. The Michigan State School of Packaging established the Annual Aaron Brody Distinguished Lecture in Food Packaging as an endowment created by family and friends in recognition of his lifelong achievements. In 2015, the Food Packaging Division of the Institute of Food Technologists renamed the Riester-Davis Award to the Riester-Davis-Brody Award in his honor. Brody was quoted in The New York Times and featured on National Public Radio and CNN. One of his NPR interviews, titled "The Weird, Underappreciated World Of Plastic Packaging," explained that plastic packaging has become an integral part of the food system, and on CNN, he described how new plastics could prevent soft drinks from falling flat.

text: The Abasto Shopping is one of the largest shopping mall centers in Buenos Aires, Argentina. Originally, it functioned as the central wholesale fruit and vegetable market, known as the "Mercado de Abasto," from 1893 to 1984. Since 1999, it has operated as a shopping mall. It is also renowned for being the area where tango singer Carlos Gardel, known as "El Morocho del Abasto" ("the dark-haired guy from Abasto"), lived for most of his life. Today, although located within the Balvanera neighbourhood, the surrounding area is often referred to as Abasto. The shopping center is accessible via the adjacent underground station Carlos Gardel on Line B of the metro (subte). By the end of the 19th century, Buenos Aires was expanding rapidly due to European migration, and following the demolition of the Mercado Modelo near Plaza Lorea, the Devoto brothers, who had acquired land in the Balvanera neighbourhood in 1875, proposed building a supply market. The land was situated near the Sarmiento railway and halfway between La Boca and Olivos, two key zones for fruit and vegetable production. The town hall approved the proposal on November 29, 1888, and the Deliberating Council sanctioned it on January 8, 1889, authorizing the construction of the Mercado Central de Abasto ("Central Supply Market") on a 25,000 m² plot bounded by Corrientes Avenue, Lavalle, Anchorena, and Laprida streets. The municipality permitted the market to sell fruit, vegetables, and other foodstuffs but prohibited meat sales. The former marketeers of Mercado Modelo formed the Sociedad Anónima Mercado de Abasto Proveedor ("Market Supply Provider Anonymous Society") in 1889, which purchased the land and the building rights from the Devoto brothers. Construction began after mayor Francisco Seeber approved the sale, with the first section opening on April 1, 1893, covering 1,300 m². Ten years later, a refrigerated storage facility and an ice factory were established to meet hygiene standards. As population and consumer demand grew, a parking area for horses and vehicles was needed, and in 1928, an annex for retail sales was built between Guardia Vieja, Lavalle, Gallo, and Bustamante streets. Continued demand led to overcrowding, prompting architects José Luis Delpini, Viktor Sulčič, and Raúl Bes to design a new market on the same site. Work began on December 28, 1931, with foundations and was completed in 1934. The new Mercado de Abasto covered 44,000 m² (473,612 sq ft), included railway access, and had underground parking. In 1939, the sale of meat and fish was permitted. On October 14, 1984, the central market was relocated to the present Mercado Central outside Buenos Aires, and the original Abasto market was closed and abandoned. A redevelopment project for a shopping mall was proposed in the mid-1990s. In 1996, the building was sold to "Inversiones y Representaciones Sociedad Anónima" (IRSA), which restored the facade and remodeled the interior. The Abasto Shopping Centre opened in 1999 and currently features many locally known brands such as Akiabara, Cuesta Blanca, and Sarkany, along with a limited number of foreign brands including Adidas, Lacoste, and Nike.

text: Abdul Bari (1892–1947) was an Indian freedom activist, academic, and social reformer who aimed to promote social reform in Indian society by educating people and awakening them to the need for change. He envisioned a free India free from slavery, social inequality, and communal disharmony and actively participated in the freedom movement, for which he was killed. He opposed the Two-nation theory. Born on 21 January 1884 to Md Qurban Ali as the eldest of four children, he was born in Kansua but resided in Koilwar and was a descendant of Malik Ibrahim Baya, a 14th-century sufi saint and warrior. He enrolled at the T. K. Ghosh Academy in Patna, completed his matriculation there, and later earned a Master of Arts degree from Patna University in 1918. In 1937, he signed his first historical agreement with the TISCO (now Tata Steel) management. He served as president of the Bihar Pradesh Congress Committee from 1946 until his death on 28 March 1947. He was killed by three men during an altercation at Bari Path in Khusrupur, Bihar Province, while returning from Dhanbad to Patna. Mahatma Gandhi described him as "living like a fakir in the service of his countrymen," while Congress President J. B. Kripalani called his death a loss of "India's bravest and most selfless soldier of freedom," emphasizing his complete absence of communal bias and his identity as an Indian dedicated to serving the working classes. On the first anniversary of his death, Rajendra Prasad remembered his contributions in a message dated 22 March 1948, published in Mazdur Avaz. Abdul Bari was married to Zulaikha Begum of Koilwar and had two sons—Salahuddin Bari and Shahabuddin Bari—and three daughters—Tahira, Hamida, and Saeeda. The Government of Bihar honored him by naming Bari Path and Abdul Bari Bridge. On March 20, 2021, and March 28, 2024, the Tata Workers Union, led by Sanjiv Kumar Chowdhary, president of the TWU, paid tribute to Abdul Bari on his death anniversary.

text: Abu Baker Asvat (/ɑsfat/) (23 February 1943 – 27 January 1989), also known as Abu Asvat or Abu, was a South African medical doctor who practised in Soweto during the 1970s and 1980s. Born in Fietas into a Gujarati Indian family, his father was a migrant shopkeeper, and he had two brothers. After attending local high school, Asvat studied medicine in Karachi, Pakistan, where he was involved in student politics, founded a student organisation affiliated with the Pan Africanist Congress of Azania (PAC), and hosted its cadres en route to China. He married Zorah in 1977 and had three children. Upon returning to South Africa, he worked at Johannesburg’s Coronation Hospital (now Rahima Moosa Mother and Child Hospital), but was fired after confronting a white pharmaceutical representative who refused to engage with black doctors. He took over a small surgery in Soweto from his brother, establishing a thriving practice that treated over 100 patients daily, often on a pro bono basis. During the 1976 Soweto Uprising, he treated children shot by police, and his surgery was protected by residents of a nearby squatter camp. He opened a creche and soup kitchen for informal settlement residents and was known as "the people's doctor" in Soweto. Asvat promoted the educational methods of Brazilian radical educator Paolo Freire and was drawn to the Black Consciousness movement, particularly Steve Biko’s concept of blackness. He served as a key link between Lenasia and Soweto, breaking racial and social taboos, and was beaten and threatened by a Special Branch policeman in 1978. He received the first annual human rights award from The Indicator, a Lenasia-based newspaper, where he advocated for social mingling and immediate action against apartheid injustices. Asvat was a keen cricketer and initially supported Ali Bacher’s "Normal Cricket" initiative allowing black teams to play at white grounds, but became disillusioned when racial segregation persisted. He co-founded the Transvaal Cricket Board (TCB), which rejected "multi-racial" approaches and instead promoted a "non-racial" vision, organizing successful boycotts and growing the TCB league under his leadership. He voluntarily stepped down as TCB leader in 1981 but remained active as a cricketer, playing for The Crescents and organizing a junior league in the late 1980s. In 1982, Azapo launched the Community Health Awareness Project (Chap), which involved Asvat and others travelling across South Africa on weekends with medically equipped caravans, treating between 150 and 500 patients and delivering health lectures to groups of up to 6,000 people. In 1984, he compiled a 20-page manual on basic healthcare, distributed in English, Sotho, Northern Sotho, and Zulu, and worked with the Black Allied Mining and Construction Workers Union to expose hazardous asbestos mining conditions. He and associates visited the Vaal Triangle in 1984 during unrest to treat victims and document injuries from apartheid security forces. By the mid-1980s, Asvat was frequently quoted in major newspapers and became a prominent voice in the anti-apartheid movement on health issues, criticizing the government’s handling of the emerging AIDS epidemic in 1988 and maintaining a regular health column in The Sowetan. In 1984, he hired Albertina Sisulu, a co-president of the United Democratic Front and wife of imprisoned ANC leader Walter Sisulu, as his nurse. Despite banning orders, Sisulu was employed, paid during detention, and allowed to visit her husband at Robben Island. Despite political differences between the UDF and Azapo, which led to violence, Sisulu and Asvat continued working together, treating casualties from both sides. Asvat advocated for Soweto squatters, rushing to assist those whose shacks were threatened by the Soweto Town Council and West Rand Administration Board, often arranging emergency shelter in Lenasia or feeding displaced persons in his home. He was elected president of the People’s Education Committee (PEC) in Lenasia, despite his Black Consciousness views differing from the pro-ANC stance of the group, which aimed to enable black youth education after the 1976 riots and campaigned for African children to attend segregated Indian schools, achieving success by 1990 when 15% of Lenasia students came from African areas. During the 1986 State of Emergency, unknown forces attempted to fire-bomb his home, and eight months later, he survived an attempted stabbing at his surgery, slightly wounded in the face, with Albertina Sisulu raising the alarm. His wife was routinely harassed by Special Branch police. In 1988, a gunman pulled a weapon on Asvat but fled when a patient entered the room. The authorities planned to develop the squatter camp where his practice was located in Soweto’s "Chicken Farm" area, but Asvat refused to move unless alternative accommodations were provided. He and Sisulu continued working despite power cuts, eventually relocating to Rockville, where they remained harassed by the Security Police. On 27 January 1989, two men arrived at Asvat’s surgery, claiming to need treatment; once admitted by Sisulu, they drew a firearm and shot him twice, killing him. Sisulu sat beside him as he died, later telling his relatives that "My son died in my hands." In the days before his death, Asvat became unusually fearful, drove home on a flat tyre and told his wife he believed an unspecified 'they' were trying to set him up, and made two attempts to see his lawyers the next morning. Investigations identified Zakhele Mbatha and Thulani Dlamini as suspects, who were sentenced to death for robbery (the sentences were commuted after the abolition of the death penalty), though no money was taken, and the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) found the police negligent in assigning a robbery motive and failing to thoroughly investigate the attack. Rumours quickly emerged linking Asvat’s murder to Winnie Mandela, as they had first met during one of his rural clinics in Brandfort, where she was banished. Asvat provided medical care for her, and she regularly dined with the family and attended parties. After Asvat’s murder, Winnie Mandela claimed he was killed because he could corroborate baseless allegations that Methodist minister Paul Verryn had molested Stompie Seipei. Media reports circulated that Asvat had examined the boy and insisted he be taken to hospital, making his death part of a cover-up. In 2018, Fred Bridgland’s biography of Winnie Mandela argued she was behind the murder. The allegations stemmed from Kenny Kgase, one of four boys taken from Verryn’s manse and brought to Winnie Mandela’s Diepkloof house by her Mandela United Football Club, who escaped and reported seeing Stompie and being assaulted. Thabiso Mono, another boy, stated Winnie Mandela accused him and others of allowing Verryn to sleep with them and accused Stompie of being a police informant, and claimed he was beaten by Winnie and the United Football Club guards. Winnie ordered Katiza Cebekhulu to file a police report accusing Verryn, requiring a medical certificate from a doctor. Cebekhulu stated that Winnie shouted, “If you don’t cooperate, I’ll deal with you,” and left without Asvat providing the certificate, which angered her. Years later, Cebekhulu was ordered to show two youths, Mbatha and Dlamini, the location of Asvat’s clinic. At the TRC, Cebekhulu testified to a "volcanic row" between Mandela and Asvat after Asvat refused to support her false allegations. The hearings were adjourned due to claims of intimidation by Winnie Mandela. Mbatha and Dlamini testified that Winnie Mandela paid them R20,000 (equivalent to $8,000) and provided them with a gun to kill Asvat, and both claimed they were intimidated before testifying. Mbatha claimed he immediately implicated Mandela but was tortured into changing his statement to robbery. Dlamini’s 1989 confession implicated Winnie Mandela, but it was not presented to the court, with police justifying suppression by saying it was "at odds" with their investigation. Mbatha’s lawyers accused a group of men in combat fatigues linked to Winnie Mandela of intimidating his family during a TRC hearing. Winnie Mandela’s lawyer exposed inconsistencies in the testimonies. When Albertina Sisulu testified, she failed to confirm an appointment card placing Winnie Mandela at the surgery on the morning of the killing, claiming to have forgotten the details, and when questioned about not wanting to be remembered as having implicated a comrade, she denied it. Thabiso Mono stated he saw Winnie Mandela assaulting the boys with fists and sjamboks. During her own testimony, Madikizela-Mandela denied the allegations. The TRC’s final report stated it could not verify Winnie Mandela’s involvement, criticized the police for quickly concluding the motive was robbery and for failing to investigate the connection between Cebekhulu and Dlamini’s accounts, and deemed Mbatha and Dlamini’s testimonies not credible. In January 2018, prior to Winnie Mandela’s death, ANC MP Mandla Mandela, Nelson Mandela’s grandson by Evelyn Mase, called for a probe into Winnie Mandela’s role in the Asvat and Seipei murders. Asvat was buried the day after his death in accordance with Muslim rites at Avalon Cemetery. Thousands of people, both African and Indian, attended the funeral, with marchers toyi-toyied and singing struggle songs. Apartheid police attempting to seize Azapo banners were driven off by Lenasia residents, and many women were present. The section of the R554 road linking Soweto to Lenasia was renamed Abu Baker Asvat Drive by the post-apartheid government. A junior cricket tournament was instituted in his memory in 2002. In 2021, he was awarded the Order of Luthuli in Silver by President Cyril Ramaphosa.

President Thomas Jefferson advocated for the law, calling for its enactment in his 1806 State of the Union Address, and had supported the idea since the 1770s. The law built upon earlier efforts, including the Slave Trade Act of 1794, which prohibited American ships from participating in the international slave trade, and the 1800 Act, which banned U.S. citizens from investing in or working on slave-trading ships. The 1807 law went further by criminalizing the importation of slaves from abroad, even on foreign vessels. It did not affect the domestic slave trade, which grew in importance after the end of imported slaves, and some smuggling continued. The law applied only to importation and exportation of enslaved people, not internal trade between states. Article 1, Section 9 of the Constitution had protected states' participation in the Atlantic slave trade for twenty years, and this provision could not be altered by constitutional amendment, meaning federal prohibition could only begin on January 1, 1808. While all Thirteen Colonies had banned the international slave trade during the American Revolution, some states later reopened it: North Carolina banned imports in 1794 and strengthened the ban in 1795; Georgia allowed the trade until 1798; and South Carolina reopened the trade in December 1803, importing 39,075 enslaved people between 1804 and 1808. By 1807, only South Carolina allowed the Atlantic slave trade. The Migration or Importation of such Persons as any of the States now existing shall think proper to admit, shall not be prohibited by the Congress prior to the Year one thousand eight hundred and eight, but a tax or duty may be imposed on such Importation, not exceeding ten dollars for each Person. Historians estimate that up to 50,000 enslaved people were illegally imported after 1808, mostly through Spanish Florida and Texas, and South Carolina Governor Henry Middleton estimated 13,000 smuggled African slaves arrived annually in 1819. The 1808 law spurred demand for fast vessels, with records indicating seven slavers were regularly fitted out in New York as late as 1859 and many more in major ports. In 1820, slave trading became a capital offense, with 74 cases prosecuted between 1837 and 1860, though few captains were convicted and only Nathaniel Gordon, hanged in 1862, was executed. After 1808, many Americans continued the slave trade by transporting Africans to Cuba, with nearly one-third of all slave ships between 1808 and 1860 owned by American merchants or built and outfitted in American ports, and it is possible U.S. citizens transported twice as many Africans to Cuba and Brazil as to U.S. ports. The U.S. Navy delayed anti-slaving patrols, only gaining authority in 1820, and enforcement was sporadic and ineffective; U.S. ships falsely flew the American flag to evade British patrols, and the first U.S. warship sent to intercept slavers was the USS Cyane, which arrested 11 American slavers in 1820–1821. No further patrols occurred until 1842, when they were limited by political pressure from slave-owning states. The Atlantic slave trade was not fully ended until the U.S. Civil War, when American-built and -managed ships were barred from operating. In the South, the Fire-Eaters—pro-slavery extremists—called for repealing the 1807 law and legalizing the international slave trade, viewing it as a way to assert the morality of slavery, drive down slave prices, balance Northern immigration, and maintain Southern congressional representation. They believed that if slavery was morally acceptable, then the slave trade must be too, a view that alarmed even pro-slavery figures like former President John Tyler, who condemned the proposal. As cotton prices rose in the 1850s, demand for enslaved labor increased, leading to calls to reopen the trade to meet demand or lower prices. While some Southerners opposed the idea, the general sentiment supported reopening the trade as a logical extension of pro-slavery ideology. Conventions of Southern planters repeatedly urged the re-opening, but such efforts failed in Congress, and state attempts to allow the importation of "apprentices" from Africa were unsuccessful. text: Adrienne Camille Nelson (born 1967) is an American lawyer and jurist serving as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Oregon since 2023. She previously served as a justice of the Oregon Supreme Court from 2018 to 2023 and as a judge on the Multnomah County Circuit Court from 2006 to 2018. Nelson was born in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1967, and grew up in southwestern Arkansas. She graduated from Gurdon High School in Gurdon, Arkansas, in 1985. Her mother successfully sued her school district to allow Nelson to be valedictorian after the school initially named a white student with a lower GPA to that position. Nelson graduated from the University of Arkansas in 1990 with a Bachelor of Arts, summa cum laude, in English literature and criminal justice. She then attended the University of Texas School of Law, graduating in 1993 with a Juris Doctor. Nelson moved to Portland, Oregon, in 1993 to be closer to her mother, who had previously relocated to the state. She worked as a contract analyst for an insurance company for two years, then served as an attorney in private practice in Portland as a public defender with Multnomah Defenders Inc, a non-profit public interest law firm, from 1996 to 1999, and for the law firm Bennett, Hartman, Morris & Kaplan LLP from 1999 to 2004. She was a senior attorney in Student Legal and Mediation Services for Portland State University from 2004 to 2006 and served as an adjunct professor at Lewis & Clark Law School from 2002 to 2005. Nelson has been a member of the American Bar Association House of Delegates and the ABA Commission on Disability Rights. She received the Oregon Women Lawyers (OWLs) Judge Mercedes Deiz Award in 2003 and the Oregon State Bar President's Public Service Award in 2007. She has also served as president of the Multnomah Bar Foundation and president of the Oregon State Bar Foundation Board. In 2021, a school in Happy Valley, Oregon was named after Nelson. Governor Ted Kulongoski appointed Nelson as a judge on the Multnomah County Circuit Court in February 2006, to replace Sidney Galton, and she was re-elected to a new six-year term in 2012. Governor Kate Brown appointed Nelson to the Oregon Supreme Court in January 2018, to replace justice Jack Landau, who retired on December 31, 2017. Nelson's term on the Supreme Court ended in January 2019, but she was elected to a full six-year term in November 2018. Nelson is the first African-American to serve on the Oregon Supreme Court or on any state appellate court in Oregon. On July 14, 2022, President Joe Biden nominated Nelson to serve as a United States district judge of the United States District Court for the District of Oregon, to fill the seat vacated by Judge Michael W. Mosman, who assumed senior status on December 27, 2021. On October 12, 2022, a hearing on her nomination was held before the Senate Judiciary Committee. On December 1, 2022, her nomination was reported out of committee by a 12–10 vote. On January 3, 2023, her nomination was returned to the President under Rule XXXI, Paragraph 6 of the United States Senate; she was renominated later the same day. On February 2, 2023, her nomination was reported out of committee by an 11–9 vote. On February 14, 2023, the Senate invoked cloture on her nomination by a 53–44 vote. On February 15, 2023, she was confirmed by a 52–46 vote. She received her judicial commission on February 23, 2023. She is the first African-American woman to serve on the United States District Court for the District of Oregon. text: After the Deluge, also known as The Forty-First Day, is a Symbolist oil painting by English artist George Frederic Watts, first exhibited in an incomplete form as The Sun at St Jude's Church in Whitechapel in 1886 and completed in 1891. The painting depicts a scene from the story of Noah's Flood, showing Noah opening the window of his Ark to see that after forty days of rain the floodwaters have not yet subsided but the rain has stopped. Watts, who was born in 1817 to a London musical instrument manufacturer, developed a lifelong obsession with death following the deaths of his two brothers in 1823 and his mother in 1826. He was apprenticed as a sculptor at age 10 and by his mid-teens earned a living as a portrait painter; he joined the Royal Academy of Arts at 18, though he disliked its methods and attended intermittently. From 1837, he became fully dedicated to painting, and after traveling to Italy in 1843 for four years, he returned to London suffering from melancholia and painted many gloomy works. His skills were widely recognized, and in 1856 he focused on portrait painting, which was highly regarded, leading to his election to the Royal Academy in 1867—the highest honor available to an artist at the time—though he soon became disillusioned with its culture. From 1870, he gained fame as a painter of allegorical and mythical subjects, becoming one of the world’s most respected artists. In 1881, he added a glass-roofed gallery to his home at Little Holland House, which opened to the public and boosted his visibility. Despite his father’s strict evangelical Christianity and his personal dislike of organized religion, Watts had a deep knowledge of the Bible and frequently painted Noah and the Flood, seeing modern society’s prioritization of wealth over moral values as a decline akin to the biblical cleansing of a degenerate world. He believed this societal shift, which he described as "the hypocritical veiling of the daily sacrifice made to this deity," was leading to societal collapse. The painting illustrates the moment when sunlight first becomes visible after 40 days of rain, with a bright sunburst breaking through clouds, a highly stylized seascape where light rays project beyond the canvas. This composition echoes J. M. W. Turner’s 1843 painting Light and Colour (Goethe's Theory) – The Morning after the Deluge – Moses Writing the Book of Genesis, which features a circle of light but includes recognizable human figures, unlike Watts’s abstract approach. Watts’s interest in the sun as a divine symbol stemmed from his acquaintance with Max Müller, who promoted solar theories of mythology. His widow, Mary Seton Watts, wrote that Watts deliberately avoided depicting the Creator directly, stating that he wanted viewers to imagine the Creator’s hand moving through light and heat to re-create, emphasizing the power of light rather than painting a portrait of the sun. Although he had previously painted an orange sun above a flat sea in The Genius of Greek Poetry (1878), which evoked pantheism, After the Deluge was explicitly intended as a monotheistic image, reflecting the magnificence and redemptive mercy of a single, all-powerful God. The completed painting was first exhibited at the New Gallery in 1891, and accompanied by an explanatory note stating: "A transcendent power of light and heat bursts forth to re-create; darkness is chased away; the waters, obedient to the higher law, already disperse into vapoury mists and pass from the face of the earth." Between 1902 and 1906, it was exhibited across the United Kingdom in Cork, Edinburgh, Manchester, Dublin, and at Little Holland House, and in 1904 it was transferred to the newly opened Watts Gallery in Compton, Surrey, shortly before Watts’s death that year. Although Watts did not include After the Deluge in his 1886 donation of his 23 most significant non-portrait works to the nation, it was greatly admired by fellow artists and has been cited as an influence on painters such as Maurice Chabas, Giuseppe Pellizza da Volpedo, and Edvard Munch. Despite its omission from the national collection, it remains in the Watts Gallery’s collection and is recognized as a landscape stripped of materialism, offering a poetic, sublimated vision of nature.

text: Ako Adjei was appointed a member of the Gold Coast cabinet on 28 July 1954 by Prime Minister Dr. Kwame Nkrumah, serving as Minister of Trade and Labour. This appointment was partly due to his status as a middle-class intellectual and professional, a move seen as a strategy to attract such individuals to the CPP. As Minister of Trade and Labour, he oversaw the Agricultural Produce Marketing Board, the Cocoa Marketing Board, the Industrial Development Corporation, Trade Unions, and Cooperatives. On 29 February 1956, he was appointed Minister for Interior and Justice, a position previously held by Archie Casely-Hayford; he was also re-elected in the 1956 Gold Coast legislative election to represent the Accra East district. Following Ghana's independence on 6 March 1957, Ako Adjei remained in the Ministry of Interior and Justice, which was split in August 1957 into separate ministries, with Ako Adjei becoming Minister of Justice. It was rumored that Nkrumah made this change because Ako Adjei, though Ga, was considered "too gentlemanly" to manage the Ga-Adangbe Shifimo Kpee, a tribal organization active in Accra. Supporters believed he was better suited to handle judicial matters as a trained lawyer, and as Minister of Justice, he managed the Land Boundaries Settlement Commission, financial and ministerial affairs related to the Supreme Court, local courts, and customary law, and foreign processes. In 1958, he was moved to the Ministry of Labour and Cooperatives, where he helped establish labor structures that continue to exist and led Ghanaian delegations to the United Nations. In February 1959, he replaced Nathaniel Azarco Welbeck as Resident Minister of Guinea and was appointed Minister of External Affairs in April of the same year, holding both positions until September 1959 when he was relieved of his duties in Guinea and replaced by J. H. Allassani. On 8 April 1961, Nkrumah announced the removal of African Affairs from the Ministry of External Affairs and appointed Imoru Egala as Minister of State for African Affairs, a position without a successor. Ako Adjei returned to Ghana to argue for a more coordinated foreign policy, believing African unity would fail without integration of African relations under his ministry, but his efforts were unsuccessful. In May 1961, the portfolio was renamed Minister of Foreign Affairs, making Ako Adjei Ghana’s first Minister of Foreign Affairs in the first republic. He played a key role in shaping Ghana’s foreign policy during the Cold War, presenting a sober image of Ghana at international forums and advocating for a Union of African States, an Africa Customs Union, an Africa Free Trade Zone, and an Africa Development Fund—proposals later adopted by the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) and the Africa Union (AU). He announced a complete boycott of South African goods, ships, and airlines, allowing entry only to those who opposed apartheid. Ako Adjei remained Minister of Foreign Affairs until August 1962 when he was charged with treason in connection with the Kulungugu bomb attack on 1 August 1962, a failed assassination attempt on President Nkrumah. He, along with Tawia Adamafio and Hugh Horatio Cofie Crabbe, were accused of plotting the assassination. The Supreme Court acquitted them, citing circumstantial and fraudulent evidence, with the basis of the accusation centered on internal CPP dissensions. A member of Parliament, F. E. Techie Menson, described their actions during the incident as isolating themselves from the President and riding in separate vehicles. The three judges who acquitted them—Justice Sir Kobina Arku Korsah, Justice Edward Akufo-Addo, and Justice Kofi Adumua Bossman—were forced to resign, and two other judges, William Bedford Van Lare and Robert Samuel Blay, were dismissed for protesting. Nkrumah then appointed a 12-man jury headed by Justice Julius Sarkodee-Addo, which found the three guilty based on the testimony of a fetish priest. Ako Adjei and the others were sentenced to death, later commuted to life imprisonment and then to 20 years by a presidential address on 26 March 1965. Ako Adjei stated he was innocent and that Adamafio and Cofie Crabbe were also innocent, recounting that he accompanied Nkrumah to a meeting with Upper Volta’s President Maurice Yameogo on 31 July 1962, and that during the return journey, a grenade was thrown at the President after he stopped to receive a bouquet from a boy at Kulungugu, killing the boy and injuring the President. He was arrested on 29 August 1962, during a reception for a visitor, and remained in detention for four years. Ako Adjei, along with his colleagues, was released by the National Liberation Council after the 24 February 1966 military coup that overthrew Nkrumah. He was released from Nsawam Medium Security Prison on 6 September 1966. After his release, he completely forswore politics, dedicating himself to his family and legal practice, reorganizing his chambers, Teianshi Chambers, and resuming private legal work. In 1978, he was appointed to a constitutional drafting commission by the Supreme Military Council for the Third Republic. The last time he was seen in a high-profile gathering was during a senior citizens event organized by former President Rawlings, though his relatives denied interviews due to his health. Ako Adjei was the last surviving member of the Big Six and died on 14 January 2002 at the age of 85 at Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital, survived by his wife and four children. His death drew tributes from leaders including President John Agyekum Kufour, who declared a state burial, stating that the nation owes him gratitude for advancing democratic rule and that the era of the Big Six had ended but their legacy remains. President Nana Akufo-Addo noted that the death marked the end of the founding fathers’ era and that their vision for free democratic rule now prevails. Jake Obetsebi-Lamptey emphasized that the chapter of the Big Six has not been erased and that their experiences are valuable for future generations. On the day of burial, all flags flew at half-mast; the state funeral was held at the state house, attended by politicians, ministers, diplomats, chiefs, relatives, and sympathizers. Wreaths were laid by President Kufour, Minister Hackman Owusu-Agyeman, President of the Ghana Bar Association Paul Adu-Gyamfi, and a family member. Joseph Henry Mensah read the government tribute, stating that Ako Adjei was a key figure in articulating African unity and bridging the CPP and UGCC, and lamenting that Ghana lost a gem whose wisdom could have been fully utilized. A private burial followed at the Holy Church of God, Okoman, Dome, in Accra. Ako Adjei was married to Theodosia Ako Adjei (née Kote-Amon), with whom he had four daughters. He was a Christian and a member of the Presbyterian Church of Ghana, believing that God controls all affairs and that individuals should serve Him as tools. The Ako Adjei Interchange in Accra (formerly Sankara Interchange) and Ako-Adjei Park in Osu, Accra, are named in his honor. He once said, "Ghana is our country. We have nowhere to go. This is where God has placed us and the earlier we realized this the better for all of us."

text: Ako Adjei (17 June 1916 – 14 January 2002) was a Ghanaian statesman, politician, lawyer, and journalist. He was a founding member of the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC) and one of the six leaders detained during Ghana's struggle for independence from Britain, a group known as The Big Six. Adjei became a member of parliament as a Convention People's Party (CPP) candidate in 1954 and held ministerial offices until 1962, when he was wrongfully detained as Minister for Foreign Affairs following the Kulungugu bomb attack. Born in Adjeikrom, a small farming community in the Akyem Abuakwa area of the Eastern Region of Ghana (then the Gold Coast), Adjei’s father was Samuel Adjei, a farmer and trader, and his mother was Johanna Okaile Adjei, both from La near Accra. He had many siblings but was the youngest of his father’s children. His early education began at the Busoso Railway Primary School, where he walked 14 miles each day, followed by studies at the La Presbyterian Junior and Senior Schools. In March 1933, he won a scholarship to Christ Church Grammar School, but returned to the La Presbyterian Senior School after a month due to disliking the environment. He then entered the Accra Academy in April 1933, where he walked four miles to school and passed the Junior Cambridge examination in 1934. In December 1936, he passed the Cambridge Senior School Leaving Certificate Examination, one of only two students exempted from the London Matriculation Examination Board. While at the Accra Academy, he developed an interest in journalism and wrote for the African Morning Post, a newspaper owned by Nnamdi Azikiwe. Azikiwe arranged for him to study at Lincoln University, Pennsylvania, where he lived at Houston Hall and played football. He shared a room with K. A. B. Jones-Quartey and was adjacent to Kwame Nkrumah’s room, with whom he formed a close relationship. They frequently held discussions about African decolonization, including with Ozuomba Mbadiwe, Nwafor Orizu, and Ikechukwu Ikejiani. After one and a half years, he won a Phelps-Stokes Fund scholarship to attend Hampton Institute, then transferred to Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, earning a master’s degree in June 1943. He later became a lecturer at Fisk University through Dr. Edwin W. Smith, who invited him to assist in establishing the African Studies Department. To pursue a law career, Adjei moved to the United Kingdom, enrolling at the Inner Temple in May 1944. His father leased a family house in Accra to a Lebanese merchant for £10 per year for 50 years, with 30 years’ rent paid in advance, though the deal was completed after his father’s death and signed by Adjei and his brothers. In Britain, he became active in colonial politics and joined the West African Students Union (WASU), becoming its president. Upon Nkrumah’s arrival in London in 1945, Adjei hosted him at his home until he found accommodation and introduced him to WASU members, including Kankam Boadu, Joe Appiah, and Kojo Botsio. Together, they organized the Fifth Pan-African Congress in Manchester in 1945, which was attended by W. E. B. Du Bois, Hastings Banda, and Jomo Kenyatta and is regarded as a turning point in the independence struggle. Adjei enrolled at the London School of Economics and Political Science for an M.Sc. degree while studying law at the Inner Temple, though his dissertation on "The Dynamics of Social Change" was not completed due to time constraints. He passed all bar examinations and was called to the Bar at the Inner Temple in January 1947. Returning to the Gold Coast in May 1947, he enrolled at the Ghana bar and initially intended to launch a chain of newspapers to promote self-rule, but due to financial constraints, he joined Adumoa-Bossman and Co. chambers as a legal practitioner. He met J. B. Danquah, who was discussing the formation of a national political movement, and within four days joined a meeting of the UGCC Planning Committee. He became a member of the committee and, on 4 August 1947, one of the leading members when the UGCC was inaugurated at Saltpond. On 22 August 1947, the Accra branch was inaugurated, with Edward Akufo-Addo as president and Emmanuel Obetsebi-Lamptey and J. Quist-Therson as vice-presidents. As the movement grew, the leaders decided to convert it into a political party and needed a full-time secretary. J. B. Danquah recommended Ako Adjei, but he declined to focus on his newspaper and legal practice, instead suggesting Kwame Nkrumah, who was then running the West African National Secretariat (WANS) in London. Adjei recommended Nkrumah because he had observed his organizational skills and had been assured by Nkrumah that he would return to London after gaining experience in Ghana. Adjei wrote to Nkrumah and sent him £100, provided by George Alfred Grant, the UGCC’s founder and financier, for his trip to the Gold Coast. Upon Nkrumah’s arrival in December 1947, Adjei introduced him to key UGCC members, including G. A. Grant, J. B. Danquah, and R. S. Blay. As general-secretary, Nkrumah began expanding the UGCC’s reach and focused on the plight of ex-servicemen, who had not received their emoluments after World War II. The UGCC lawyers helped draft a petition to the governor, which was presented on 24 February 1948, coinciding with the Nii Kwabena Bonnie III-led boycott campaign and resulting in the 1948 Accra Riots. As a result, Ako Adjei and other UGCC leaders, including J. B. Danquah, Emmanuel Obetsebi-Lamptey, Edward Akufo-Addo, William Ofori Atta, and Kwame Nkrumah, were arrested and blamed by the British government for the unrest, with Adjei detained at Navrongo. The release of the Big Six led to a split between Nkrumah and the UGCC, with Nkrumah forming the Convention People's Party (CPP) in 1949. Ako Adjei remained with the UGCC and later criticized Nkrumah in his newspapers, the African National Times and the Star of Ghana. In the 1951 Gold Coast legislative election, he stood for the UGCC in the Accra Central Municipal Electoral District, polling 1,451 votes compared to Nkrumah’s 20,780 and Emmanuel Obetsebi-Lamptey’s 1,630. After the UGCC’s poor performance, he joined efforts to merge opposition parties and became Secretary of the Ghana Congress Party (GCP) in May 1952. He later refused to attend meetings due to criticism over introducing Nkrumah to dismantle the UGCC. In March 1953, under pressure from E. C. Quaye, Sonny Provençal, and Paul Tagoe, he joined the CPP and delivered his first speech at a major rally in Accra. In the 1954 Gold Coast legislative election, he ran for the CPP in Accra East, polling 11,660 votes against Nai Tete’s 768, Kwamla Armah-Kwarteng’s 471, and Nii Kwabena Bonnie III’s 317, and entered parliament on 15 June 1954. On 28 July 1954, he was appointed Minister of Trade and Labour by Prime Minister Kwame Nkrumah, a move intended to include middle-class professionals in the CPP. As Minister of Trade and Labour, he oversaw the Agricultural Produce Marketing Board, the Cocoa Marketing Board, the Industrial Development Corporation, Trade Unions, and Cooperatives. On 29 February 1956, he was appointed Minister for Interior and Justice, a position previously held by Archie Casely-Hayford, and was re-elected in the 1956 Gold Coast legislative election to represent Accra East. Following Ghana’s independence on 6 March 1957, major cabinet appointments were made by Prime Minister Dr. Kwame Nkrumah. After his release in 1966, Ako Adjei lived in relative obscurity, focusing on his family and legal career. In 1992, he published a biography of George Grant. In 1997, he was awarded the Order of the Star of Ghana, the highest national honor in Ghana, for his contributions to the independence struggle. He died after a short illness in 2002.

text: Sir Alec John Jeffreys, CH FRS MAE (born 9 January 1950), is a British geneticist renowned for developing techniques for genetic fingerprinting and DNA profiling, which are now used worldwide in forensic science to assist police detective work and to resolve paternity and immigration disputes. He is professor of genetics at the University of Leicester and became an honorary freeman of the City of Leicester on 26 November 1992. In 1994, he was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for services to genetics. Born into a middle-class family in Oxford, Jeffreys spent his first six years there before moving to Luton, Bedfordshire in 1956. He attributes his curiosity and inventiveness to his father and paternal grandfather, who held patents. At age eight, his father gave him a chemistry set, which he enhanced with extra chemicals, including a small bottle of sulphuric acid; an accidental splash caused a burn that left a permanent scar on his chin (now under his beard). His father also bought him a Victorian-era brass microscope, which he used to examine biological specimens. At about 12, he made a small dissecting kit, including a scalpel crafted from a flattened pin, to dissect a bumblebee, and later a deceased cat he found on the road while doing his paper round; dissecting the cat caused a foul smell when he ruptured its intestines. Jeffreys attended Luton Grammar School and Luton Sixth Form College, winning a scholarship to study at the University of Oxford’s Merton College, where he graduated in 1971 with first-class honours in biochemistry. He completed his Doctor of Philosophy degree on the mitochondria of cultured mammalian cells in the genetics laboratory. After his doctorate, he worked as a research fellow at the University of Amsterdam before joining the University of Leicester in 1977, where in 1984 he discovered a method of showing variations between individuals' DNA, inventing and developing genetic fingerprinting. He had a "eureka moment" in his lab on 10 September 1984 after observing an X-ray film of a DNA experiment that unexpectedly showed both similarities and differences between family members' DNA, realizing the potential of DNA fingerprinting to identify individuals. The method is now used in forensic science, paternity testing, and immigration disputes, and can also be applied to non-human species. Before commercialization in 1987, his laboratory was the only center in the world conducting DNA fingerprinting and received global inquiries. In 1985, his method was first used in a disputed immigration case to confirm the identity of a British boy from Ghana, whose DNA proved close relation to the family, bringing relief to the mother. DNA fingerprinting was first used in a police forensic case to identify the killer of Lynda Mann and Dawn Ashworth, murdered in 1983 and 1986 respectively in Narborough, Leicestershire; Colin Pitchfork was identified and convicted after DNA matches from his semen samples, and Richard Buckland, initially a suspect, was exonerated. The case is detailed in Joseph Wambaugh's 1989 book The Blooding and featured in Episode 4 of the 1996 American TV series Medical Detectives, with a further mini-series released in 2015 titled Code of a Killer. In 1992, Jeffreys' methods were used by German prosecutors to confirm the identity of Josef Mengele, who died in 1979, by comparing DNA from a femur bone of his exhumed skeleton with DNA from his mother and son, similar to paternity testing. DNA profiling, based on typing individual highly variable minisatellites in the human genome, was developed by Jeffreys and his team in 1985, with the term "DNA fingerprinting" retained for the initial test that types many minisatellites simultaneously. By focusing on a few highly variable minisatellites, DNA profiling became more sensitive, reproducible, and suitable for computer databases, becoming the standard forensic DNA system globally. The development of DNA amplification via the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) enabled automation, increased sensitivity, and the use of alternative marker systems. The most commonly used markers are now variable microsatellites, or short tandem repeats (STRs), which Jeffreys first exploited in 1990 in the Mengele case. STR profiling was refined by Peter Gill’s team at the Forensic Science Service in the 1990s, leading to the launch of the UK National DNA Database (NDNAD) in 1995. With automated and sophisticated equipment, modern DNA profiling can process hundreds of samples daily. The current NDNAD system uses sixteen microsatellites plus a sex determination marker, providing a discrimination power of one in over a billion. Under British law, anyone arrested in England, Wales, or Northern Ireland has their DNA profile taken and stored in the database, regardless of conviction (different rules apply in Scotland). As of 2020, the national database contained DNA information from about 5.6 million people. Jeffreys has opposed the current use of DNA profiling with government access to the database and has proposed a database of all people's DNA, with access controlled by an independent third party. His former doctoral students include Turi King. Jeffreys met his future wife, Sue Miles, in a youth club in central Luton before becoming a university student and married her on 28 August 1971. He has one brother and one sister and two daughters, born in 1979 and 1983.

Thelema, Crowley's belief system, has been described by scholars as a religion, a new religious movement, and a "magico-religious doctrine," with The Book of the Law (composed in 1904) serving as its central text, though the system fully developed in the years after 1904. In his autobiography, Crowley stated his purpose was to "bring oriental wisdom to Europe and to restore paganism in a purer form," though the meaning of "paganism" remained unclear. He also wrote in the 4th Book of Magick about a great pagan Umbral fleet ruled by Ottovius that would be passed to the great Spartan, a detail whose esoteric nature was unclear. His thought was influenced by diverse sources, including eastern religious traditions like Hindu yoga and Buddhism, scientific naturalism, and Western esotericism such as ceremonial magic, alchemy, astrology, Rosicrucianism, Kabbalah, and the Tarot. He was deeply influenced by the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, though he expanded upon their teachings with his own interpretations. Crowley incorporated concepts from South Asian traditions like yoga and Tantra into Thelema, believing in a fundamental resemblance between Western and Eastern spiritual systems. Historian Alex Owen noted that Crowley followed the "modus operandi" of the Decadent movement throughout his life. Crowley believed the twentieth century marked the beginning of the Aeon of Horus, a new era in which humans would take greater control of their destiny, following the Aeon of Osiris (dominated by paternalistic religions like Christianity, Islam, and Buddhism) and the Aeon of Isis (maternalistic and goddess-centered). He considered Thelema to be the proper religion of the Aeon of Horus and saw himself as its prophet. Thelema centers on the idea that each person has a True Will that should be discovered and pursued, in harmony with the Cosmic Will. This process, referred to as "the Great Work" or the attainment of the "knowledge and conversation of the Holy Guardian Angel," was achieved through the Abramelin operation, a ceremonial magic ritual from a 17th-century grimoire. The moral code "Do What Thou Wilt" is regarded by Thelemites as the religion's ethical law, though historian Marco Pasi noted it was not anarchistic or libertarian, as Crowley viewed individuals as part of a larger societal organism. Crowley believed in the objective existence of magic, which he spelled as "Magick," an archaic form of the word. In Magick in Theory and Practice, he defined Magick as "the Science and Art of causing change to occur in conformity with Will." He told his disciple Karl Germer that "Magick is getting into communication with individuals who exist on a higher plane than ours. Mysticism is the raising of oneself to their level." He saw Magick as a third way between religion and science, giving The Equinox the subtitle "The Method of Science; the Aim of Religion." He expressed positive views toward science and the scientific method, urging magicians to keep detailed records of their experiments, stating, "The more scientific the record is, the better." His understanding of magic was influenced by James Frazer, particularly the idea that magic preceded science in cultural evolution, though unlike Frazer, Crowley did not see magic as a relic to be eradicated, but rather as a force to be adapted to the new age of science. In his alternative framework, old systems of magic declined so that science and magic could synthesize into magick, which would accept both the supernatural and an experimental method. Crowley adopted a broad definition of magick that included almost all forms of technology, using an instrumentalist view of magic, science, and technology. To Crowley, the greatest aim of the magician was to merge with a higher power connected to the wellsprings of the universe, though he never consistently defined that power—sometimes as God, the One, a goddess, or one's own Holy Guardian Angel or higher self—and ultimately accepted that the nature of divinity remained a mystery. As a result, he wrote at times like an atheist, at times like a monotheist, and at other times like a polytheist. Sexuality played a central role in Crowley's ideas about magick and practice, and is described as central to Thelema. He outlined three forms of sex magick—autoerotic, homosexual, and heterosexual—and argued such acts could focus a magician's will on specific goals like financial gain or creative success. For Crowley, sex was a sacrament, with the consumption of sexual fluids interpreted as a Eucharist, often manifested through the Cakes of Light—a biscuit containing menstrual blood or a mixture of semen and vaginal fluids. The Gnostic Mass is the central religious ceremony in Thelema. Crowley's theological beliefs were inconsistent; historian Ronald Hutton noted that some writings suggest atheism, others polytheism, and others mystical monotheism. Based on The Book of the Law, Crowley described a pantheon of three deities from ancient Egypt: Nuit, Hadit, and Ra-Hoor-Khuit, and in 1928 stated all true deities derived from this trinity. Jason Josephson Storm argued that Crowley synthesized Christian theology and Neopaganism, drawing on 19th-century works like Frazer's Golden Bough, while remaining critical of institutional Christianity. Crowley did not consider himself a Satanist nor did he worship Satan, rejecting the Christian worldview in which Satan exists. He used Satanic imagery, such as describing himself as "the Beast 666" and referring to the Whore of Babylon, and sent "Antichristmas cards" to friends. In some writings, he identified Aiwass as Satan and called him "Our Lord God the Devil." Scholar Gordon Djurdjevic stated that Crowley was "emphatically not" a Satanist, "if for no other reason than simply because he did not identify himself as such." Crowley expressed strong anti-Christian sentiment, stating he hated Christianity "as Socialists hate soap," likely stemming from his experiences with the Plymouth Brethren. He was influenced by the King James Bible, especially the Book of Revelation, and was accused of advocating human sacrifice due to a passage in Book 4 stating that "a male child of perfect innocence and high intelligence is the most satisfactory victim" and that he had sacrificed about 150 annually—a tongue-in-cheek reference to ejaculation, not understood by critics. Crowley considered himself one of the outstanding figures of his time. Hutton described him as a self-indulgent, flamboyant young man who deliberately flouted social and religious norms, shielded from public outrage by his inherited wealth. Hutton also noted his "unappeasable desire" to control organizations and his "tendency to quarrel savagely" with challengers. Biographer Martin Booth described Crowley as "self-confident, brash, eccentric, egotistic, highly intelligent, arrogant, witty, wealthy, and, when it suited him, cruel." Richard B. Spence noted he was "capable of immense physical and emotional cruelty." Biographer Lawrence Sutin described him as showing "courage, skill, dauntless energy, and remarkable focus of will" alongside "blind arrogance, petty fits of bile, [and] contempt for the abilities of his fellow men." Thelemite Lon Milo DuQuette noted that Crowley "was by no means perfect" and "often alienated those who loved him dearest." Crowley enjoyed being outrageous and flouting conventional morality, with John Symonds noting he was "in revolt against the moral and religious values of his time." His political thought was studied by Marco Pasi, who found that socio-political concerns were subordinate to metaphysical and spiritual ones. He was neither on the left nor right but is best categorized as a "conservative revolutionary," despite not being affiliated with the German movement of the same name. Pasi noted Crowley's fascination with Nazism and Marxism–Leninism due to their anti-Christian stance and revolutionary potential, seeing in them the possibility of destroying old religious traditions and creating a void for Thelema to fill. He described democracy as an "imbecile and nauseating cult of weakness" and cited The Book of the Law stating "there is the master and there is the slave; the noble and the serf; the 'lone wolf' and the herd," influenced by Social Darwinism and Friedrich Nietzsche. Although he had contempt for most of the British aristocracy, he regarded himself as an aristocrat and styled himself as Laird Boleskine, once describing his ideology as "aristocratic communism." Crowley was bisexual but preferred women, with relationships with men being fewer and mostly early in life. He was particularly attracted to "exotic women," and stated he fell in love multiple times; Kaczynski noted that when he loved, he did so with his whole being, though the passion was typically short-lived. Even in later life, he attracted young bohemian women due to his charisma. He applied the term "Scarlet Woman" to female lovers he believed played an important role in his magical work. During homosexual acts, he usually played the passive role, which Booth believed appealed to his masochistic side. A recurring theme in his writings is that spiritual enlightenment arises through transgressing socio-sexual norms. Crowley advocated complete sexual freedom for both men and women, arguing that homosexual and bisexual people should not suppress their orientation, stating that a person "must not be ashamed or afraid of being homosexual if he happens to be so at heart; he must not attempt to violate his own true nature because of public opinion, or medieval morality, or religious prejudice which would wish he were otherwise." On other issues, he adopted a more conservative stance, opposing abortion on moral grounds, believing no woman following her True Will would desire one. Biographer Lawrence Sutin stated that "blatant bigotry is a persistent minor element in Crowley's writings." He described Crowley as a "spoiled scion of a wealthy Victorian family" who embodied many of the worst John Bull racial and social prejudices of his time, noting the contradiction between societal racism and fascination with people of color. Crowley insulted his close Jewish friend Victor Neuburg with antisemitic slurs and held mixed opinions about Jewish people as a group, praising their "sublime" poetry and qualities like imagination, romance, loyalty, probity, and humanity, while also claiming centuries of persecution led some to exhibit "avarice, servility, falseness, cunning and the rest." He praised the Chinese for exhibiting "spiritual superiority" over the English and Muslims for showing "manliness, straightforwardness, subtlety, and self-respect." Critics and adherents of Thelema have accused Crowley of sexism. Booth described him as exhibiting "general misogyny," which the biographer attributed to a bad relationship with his mother. Sutin noted that Crowley largely accepted the Victorian notion of women as secondary in intellect and sensibility. Scholar Manon Hedenborg White noted that some of Crowley's statements are "undoubtedly misogynist by contemporary standards," though characterized his attitude as complex and multi-faceted. His views on women varied dramatically in his writings. He described women as "moral inferiors" who needed to be treated with "firmness, kindness and justice," while also arguing that Thelema was essential to women's emancipation. Biographers Richard B. Spence and Tobias Churton have suggested that Crowley was a spy for British secret services, claiming he joined the Golden Dawn under their direction to monitor Mathers, who was a Carlist. Spence suggested the conflict between Mathers and the London lodge was part of an intelligence operation to undermine Mathers' authority. He proposed that Crowley's trip to Mexico was to explore Mexican oil prospects for British intelligence and that his trip to China was part of a British scheme to monitor the opium trade. Churton suggested that Crowley traveled to Moscow at the orders of British intelligence to spy on revolutionary elements. Spence and Sutin both wrote that Crowley's pro-German work in the United States during World War I was a cover for being a double agent for Britain, citing his hyperbolic articles in The Fatherland to make the German lobby appear ridiculous to Americans. Spence also wrote that Crowley encouraged the German Navy to destroy the Lusitania, informing them it would keep the US out of the war, while in reality hoping it would bring the US into the war on Britain's side. Today, Crowley is regarded as a source of inspiration by many seeking spiritual enlightenment or magical practice. While his books sold poorly and his disciples were few during his lifetime, his important works are now constantly in print, and the number of self-identified "thelemites" worldwide is several thousand. His influence on magically oriented new religious movements has been deep and pervasive; understanding aspects of Anglo-Saxon neo-paganism and contemporary satanism requires knowledge of Crowley's doctrines. In poetry, alpinism, and painting, he may have been a minor figure, but in the context of occultism, he has played and continues to play a major role. Crowley remains an influential figure among occultists and in popular culture, particularly in Britain and other parts of the world. In 2002, a BBC poll ranked him 73rd in a list of the 100 Greatest Britons. Richard Cavendish wrote that "In native talent, penetrating intelligence and determination, Aleister Crowley was the best-equipped magician to emerge since the seventeenth century." Scholar Egil Asprem described him as "one of the most well-known figures in modern occultism."
