text: After undertaking a ritual, he proclaimed himself "Master Therion" and wrote several short stories based on James George Frazer's The Golden Bough and a literary criticism work, The Gospel According to Bernard Shaw. In December, he moved to New Orleans, his favorite U.S. city, before spending February 1917 with evangelical Christian relatives in Titusville, Florida. Returning to New York City, he moved in with artist and A∴A∴ member Leon Engers Kennedy in May, learning of his mother's death. After the collapse of The Fatherland, Crowley continued his association with Viereck, who appointed him contributing editor of the arts journal The International, where he promoted Thelema, though the journal soon ceased publication. He then moved to the studio apartment of Roddie Minor, who became his partner and Scarlet Woman; through their rituals, which Crowley called "The Amalantrah Workings," he believed they were contacted by a preternatural entity named Lam, a relationship that ended soon after. In 1918, Crowley went on a magical retreat on Esopus Island in upstate New York, where he began an adaptation of the Tao Te Ching, painted Thelemic slogans on riverside cliffs, and later claimed to experience past life memories of being Ge Xuan, Pope Alexander VI, Alessandro Cagliostro, and Éliphas Lévi. Back in New York City, he moved to Greenwich Village, where he took Leah Hirsig as his lover and next Scarlet Woman. He took up painting as a hobby, exhibiting at the Greenwich Village Liberal Club and attracting attention from The Evening World. With financial support from sympathetic Freemasons, Crowley revived The Equinox with the first issue of volume III, known as The Blue Equinox. He spent mid-1919 on a climbing holiday in Montauk, New York, before returning to London in December. Now destitute and back in London, Crowley faced attacks from the tabloid John Bull, which labeled him a traitorous "scum" for his work with the German war effort; though friends urged him to sue, he declined. When suffering from asthma, a doctor prescribed heroin, to which he soon became addicted. In January 1920, he moved to Paris, renting a house in Fontainebleau with Leah Hirsig; they were soon joined in a ménage à trois by Ninette Shumway and Leah's newborn daughter Anne "Poupée" Leah. Crowley had plans to form a Thelemite community called the Abbey of Thelema, inspired by the Abbaye de Thélème in François Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel. After consulting the I Ching, he chose Cefalù in Sicily as the location and began renting the old Villa Santa Barbara on 2 April. Moving to the commune with Hirsig, Shumway, and their children Hansi, Howard, and Poupée, Crowley described the situation as "perfectly happy ... my idea of heaven." They wore robes, performed rituals to the sun god Ra at set times, and occasionally conducted the Gnostic Mass; the rest of the day they followed their own interests. Crowley continued widespread correspondences, painted, wrote a commentary on The Book of the Law, and revised the third part of Book 4. He offered a libertine education for the children, allowing them to play all day and witness acts of sex magic. He occasionally traveled to Palermo to visit rent boys and buy supplies, including drugs; his heroin addiction dominated his life and cocaine eroded his nasal cavity. There was no cleaning rota, and wild dogs and cats wandered throughout the building, making it unsanitary. Poupée died in October 1920, and Ninette gave birth to a daughter, Astarte Lulu Panthea, shortly after. New followers continued to arrive at the Abbey, including film star Jane Wolfe, who arrived in July 1920, was initiated into the A∴A∴, and became Crowley's secretary; Cecil Frederick Russell, who disliked same-sex sexual magic and left after a year; and Frank Bennett, an Australian Thelemite who spent several months at the Abbey. In February 1922, Crowley returned to Paris for a retreat in an unsuccessful attempt to quit heroin. He then went to London to seek money, where he published articles in The English Review criticizing the Dangerous Drugs Act 1920 and wrote a novel, The Diary of a Drug Fiend, completed in July; the book received mixed reviews and was lambasted by the Sunday Express, which called for its burning and prevented further reprints. A young Thelemite, Raoul Loveday, moved to the Abbey with his wife Betty May; while Loveday was devoted to Crowley, May detested him and life at the commune, claiming Loveday was made to drink the blood of a sacrificed cat and required self-cutting with razors each time using the pronoun "I"; Loveday drank from a polluted stream, developed a liver infection, and died in February 1923. Returning to London, May told the press about her experience. John Bull proclaimed Crowley "the wickedest man in the world" and "a man we'd like to hang," and although Crowley considered many accusations slanderous, he could not afford legal fees to sue, so the attacks continued, spreading across Europe and North America. The Fascist government of Benito Mussolini learned of Crowley's activities and issued a deportation notice in April 1923, forcing him to leave Italy; without Crowley, the Abbey closed. Crowley and Hirsig went to Tunis, where, suffering from poor health, he unsuccessfully tried again to quit heroin and began writing his "autohagiography," The Confessions of Aleister Crowley. They were joined by Norman Mudd, who became Crowley's public relations consultant. Employing a local boy, Mohammad ben Brahim, as his servant, Crowley went with him on a retreat to Nefta, where they performed sex magic together. In January 1924, Crowley traveled to Nice, France, where he met Frank Harris, underwent a series of nasal operations, and visited the Institute for the Harmonious Development of Man, developing a positive opinion of its founder George Gurdjieff. Destitute, he took on a wealthy student, Alexander Zu Zolar, and later another American follower, Dorothy Olsen. Crowley took Olsen to Tunisia for a magical retreat in Nefta, where he also wrote To Man (1924), a declaration of his status as a prophet entrusted with bringing Thelema to humanity. After spending the winter in Paris, in early 1925 Crowley and Olsen returned to Tunis, where he wrote The Heart of the Master (1938) as an account of a vision from a trance. In March, Olsen became pregnant, and Hirsig was called to care for her; she miscarried, after which Crowley took Olsen back to France. Hirsig later distanced herself from Crowley, who then denounced her. According to Crowley, Reuss named him head of O.T.O. upon his death, but this was challenged by Heinrich Tränker, who called the Hohenleuben Conference in Thuringia, Germany, which Crowley attended; prominent members like Karl Germer and Martha Küntzel supported Crowley's leadership, while Albin Grau, Oskar Hopfer, and Henri Birven backed Tränker, resulting in a split in O.T.O. Moving to Paris, where he broke with Olsen in 1926, Crowley had numerous lovers over the following years with whom he experimented in sex magic. Throughout, he was plagued by poor health due to heroin and cocaine addictions. In 1928, Crowley met Israel Regardie, a young Englishman who embraced Thelema and became his secretary for three years; that year, he also met Gerald Yorke, who began organizing Crowley's finances but never became a Thelemite; he also befriended journalist Tom Driberg, who did not accept Thelema. It was in this period that Crowley published Magick in Theory and Practice, which received little attention at the time. In December 1928, he met the Nicaraguan Maria Teresa Sanchez (Maria Teresa Ferrari de Miramar). Crowley was deported from France by authorities who disliked his reputation and feared he was a German agent. To allow her to join him in Britain, he married Sanchez in August 1929. Now based in London, Mandrake Press agreed to publish his autobiography in a limited six-volume set, also publishing his novel Moonchild and the short story collection The Stratagem. Mandrake went into liquidation in November 1930, before the full set of The Confessions could be published. Mandrake's owner, P. R. Stephensen, wrote The Legend of Aleister Crowley, an analysis of media coverage surrounding him. In April 1930, Crowley moved to Berlin, where he took Hanni Jaegar as his magical partner; the relationship was troubled. In September, he went to Lisbon, Portugal, to meet poet Fernando Pessoa, where he decided to fake his own death, doing so with Pessoa's help at the Boca do Inferno rock formation. He then returned to Berlin, where he reappeared three weeks later at the opening of his art exhibition at the Gallery Neumann-Nierendorf. Crowley's paintings aligned with the fashion for German Expressionism; few sold, but press reports were largely favorable. In August 1931, he took Bertha Busch as his new lover; their relationship was violent and involved frequent physical assaults. He continued to have affairs with both men and women in the city and met notable figures such as Aldous Huxley and Alfred Adler. In January 1932, he took the communist Gerald Hamilton as a lodger, through whom he was introduced to figures in the Berlin far left; it is possible he was operating as a spy for British intelligence, monitoring the communist movement. Crowley left Busch and returned to London, where he took Pearl Brooksmith as his new Scarlet Woman. Undergoing further nasal surgery, in 1932 he was invited as guest of honor at Foyles' Literary Luncheon and by Harry Price to speak at the National Laboratory of Psychical Research. In need of money, he launched court cases against those he believed had libelled him; some were successful. He gained publicity in a lawsuit against Constable and Co for publishing Nina Hamnett's Laughing Torso (1932), which he alleged libeled him by calling his occult practices black magic, but lost the case. The case worsened his financial situation, and in February 1935 he was declared bankrupt. During the hearing, it was revealed that Crowley was spending three times his income for several years. Crowley developed a friendship with Deidre Patricia Doherty, who offered to bear his child, born in May 1937; named Randall Gair, Crowley nicknamed him Aleister Atatürk. He died in a car accident in 2002 at age 65. Crowley continued to socialize with friends, holding curry parties where he cooked particularly spicy food. In 1936, he published his first book in six years, The Equinox of the Gods, which contained a facsimile of The Book of the Law and was considered volume III, number 3 of The Equinox periodical; the work sold well and received a second print run. In 1937, he gave a series of public lectures on yoga in Soho. Crowley was now living largely off contributions from O.T.O.'s Agape Lodge in California, led by rocket scientist Jack Parsons. He was intrigued by the rise of Nazism in Germany and, influenced by his friend Martha Küntzel, believed Adolf Hitler might convert to Thelema; when the Nazis abolished the German O.T.O. and imprisoned Germer, who fled to the U.S., Crowley then criticized Hitler as a black magician. When the Second World War broke out, Crowley wrote to the Naval Intelligence Division offering his services, but they declined. He associated with various figures in Britain's intelligence community, including Dennis Wheatley, Roald Dahl, Ian Fleming, and Maxwell Knight, and wrote that he originated the "V for Victory" sign first used by the BBC; this has never been proven. In 1940, his asthma worsened and, with German-produced medication unavailable, he returned to using heroin, becoming addicted again. As the Blitz hit London, Crowley relocated to Torquay, where he was briefly hospitalized with asthma and entertained himself with visits to the local chess club. Tiring of Torquay, he returned to London, where he was visited by American Thelemite Grady McMurtry, to whom Crowley awarded the title of "Hymenaeus Alpha." He stipulated that Germer would be his immediate successor, but McMurty should succeed Germer after Germer's death. With O.T.O. initiate Lady Frieda Harris, Crowley developed plans to produce a tarot card set, designed by him and painted by Harris, accompanied by a book, The Book of Thoth, published in a limited edition by Chiswick Press in 1944. To aid the war effort, he wrote a proclamation on the rights of humanity, "Liber OZ," and a poem for the liberation of France, La Gauloise. Crowley's final publication during his lifetime was a book of poetry, Olla: An Anthology of Sixty Years of Song. Another project, Aleister Explains Everything, was posthumously published as Magick Without Tears. In April 1944, Crowley briefly moved to Aston Clinton in Buckinghamshire, where he was visited by poet Nancy Cunard, before relocating to Hastings in Sussex, where he took up residence at the Netherwood boarding house. He took a young man named Kenneth Grant as his secretary, paying him in magical teaching rather than wages. He was also introduced to John Symonds, whom he appointed as his literary executor; Symonds held little regard for Crowley and later published unfavorable biographies. Corresponding with illusionist Arnold Crowther, it was through him that Crowley was introduced to Gerald Gardner, the future founder of Gardnerian Wicca; they became friends, and Crowley authorized Gardner to revive Britain's ailing O.T.O. Another visitor was Eliza Marian Butler, who interviewed Crowley for her book The Myth of the Magus. Other friends and family also visited him, including Doherty and Crowley's son Aleister Atatürk. On 1 December 1947, Crowley died at Netherwood of chronic bronchitis aggravated by pleurisy and myocardial degeneration, aged 72. His funeral was held at Woodvale Crematorium, Brighton on 5 December; about a dozen people attended, and Louis Wilkinson read excerpts from the Gnostic Mass, The Book of the Law, and "Hymn to Pan." The funeral generated press controversy and was labeled a Black Mass by tabloids. Crowley's body was cremated; his ashes were sent to Karl Germer in the U.S., who buried them in his garden in Hampton, New Jersey. Crowley's belief system, Thelema, has been described by scholars as a religion, more specifically as a new religious movement and as a "magico-religious doctrine." Although The Book of the Law, composed in 1904, is its central text, Thelema developed as a complete system in the years after 1904. In his autobiography, Crowley wrote that his purpose in life was to "bring oriental wisdom to Europe and to restore paganism in a purer form," though what he meant by "paganism" was unclear.

text: Crowley's influence spans several thousands of people worldwide and has been deeply and pervasively embedded in magically oriented new religious movements, making it difficult to understand aspects of Anglo-Saxon neo-paganism and contemporary satanism without a solid grasp of his doctrines. While he may have been a minor figure in poetry, alpinism, and painting, within the context of occultism, he has played and continues to play a major role. He remains a significant figure among occultists and in popular culture, especially in Britain, but also globally; in 2002, a BBC poll ranked him 73rd in a list of the 100 Greatest Britons. Richard Cavendish described Crowley as the best-equipped magician since the seventeenth century in terms of native talent, penetrating intelligence, and determination. Egil Asprem called him one of the most well-known figures in modern occultism, while Wouter Hanegraaff viewed him as an extreme representation of "the dark side of the occult" and the most notorious occultist magician of the twentieth century. John Moore regarded Crowley as a "Modern Master" compared to figures like George Gurdjieff, P. D. Ouspensky, Rudolf Steiner, and Helena Blavatsky, and described him as a "living embodiment" of Oswald Spengler's "Faustian Man." Biographer Tobias Churton saw Crowley as a pioneer of consciousness research, Hutton noted his important role in the modern Western response to Oriental spiritual traditions, and Sutin acknowledged his distinct original contributions to the study of yoga in the West. After his death, Thelema continued to develop; in 1969, the O.T.O. was reactivated in California under Grady Louis McMurtry, and in 1985, its title was unsuccessfully challenged in court by the Society Ordo Templi Orientis, led by Marcelo Ramos Motta. Kenneth Anger, an American filmmaker, was influenced by Crowley's writings from a young age. In the UK, Kenneth Grant promoted Typhonian Thelema through the Typhonian O.T.O., later renamed the Typhonian Order. Amado Crowley claimed to be Crowley's son and argued that Thelema was a false religion created to conceal Crowley's true teachings, a claim refuted by academic investigation. Djurdjevic stated that Crowley's influence on twentieth-century and contemporary esotericism has been enormous. Gerald Gardner, the founder of Gardnerian Wicca, used much of Crowley's published material in composing the Gardnerian ritual liturgy, and Rosaleen Norton was also heavily influenced by Crowley. Crowley became a dominant figure in the modern Pagan community. L. Ron Hubbard, founder of Scientology, engaged with Thelema in the early 1940s through Jack Parsons, and it has been argued that Crowley's ideas influenced some of Hubbard's work. Asbjørn Dyrendel, James R. Lewis, and Jesper Petersen noted that despite not being a Satanist, Crowley embodies the pre-Satanist esoteric discourse on Satan and Satanism through his lifestyle and philosophy, with his "image and ought" becoming an important influence on religious Satanism, notably affecting figures like Anton LaVey and Michael Aquino. Following his time in Cefalù, various "literary Crowleys" emerged in fiction: Shelley Arabin in John Buchan's 1926 novel The Dancing Floor, Damien Mocata in Dennis Wheatley's The Devil Rides Out, characters in Dion Fortune's The Secrets of Doctor Taverner (1926) and The Winged Bull (1935), and Dr. Trelawney in Anthony Powell's A Dance to the Music of Time. Crowley appeared on the cover art of The Beatles' 1967 album Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, and his motto "Do What Thou Wilt" was inscribed on the vinyl of Led Zeppelin's 1970 album Led Zeppelin III. Jimmy Page, co-founder of Led Zeppelin, bought Boleskine in 1971, part of the band's film The Song Remains the Same was filmed there, and he sold it in 1992. David Bowie referenced Crowley and his works in songs such as After All, "Quicksand" (1971), Station To Station, and it has been suggested that the lyrics of his 1983 hit "Let's Dance" substantially paraphrase Crowley's 1923 poem "Lyric of Love to Leah." Ozzy Osbourne and lyricist Bob Daisley wrote a song titled "Mr. Crowley" in 1980. A prophetic quote from Crowley's Magick in Theory and Practice (1911) was used as the opening introduction to the video game Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain (1996). Crowley began to receive scholarly attention from academics in the late 1990s.

text: On 8 April, Crowley heard a disembodied voice identifying itself as Aiwass, the messenger of Horus or Hoor-Paar-Kraat, and recorded everything the voice told him over the next three days, titling the work Liber AL vel Legis or The Book of the Law. The book declared that humanity was entering a new Aeon, with Crowley as its prophet, and introduced the supreme moral law "Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law," urging people to live in tune with their Will. This text and its philosophy became the foundation of Thelema. Crowley initially doubted the book's significance and often resented it, ignoring its commands, such as taking the Stele of Revealing from the museum, fortifying his island, and translating the book into all languages. Instead, he sent typescripts to known occultists, stored the manuscript, and neglected it. Returning to Boleskine, Crowley believed Mathers was using magic against him, leading to a breakdown in their relationship. On 28 July 1905, Rose gave birth to their first daughter, Lilith, and Crowley wrote the pornographic Snowdrops from a Curate's Garden to entertain his recovering wife. He founded a publishing company, the Society for the Propagation of Religious Truth, parodying the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, and published works like Crowley's Collected Works, edited by Ivor Back. His poetry received strong reviews but did not sell well; to gain publicity, he offered a £100 reward for the best essay on his work, won by J. F. C. Fuller, whose 1907 essay, The Star in the West, praised his poetry as among the greatest ever written. Crowley planned to climb Kanchenjunga in Nepal, the world's most treacherous mountain, but the expedition, involving Jacot-Guillarmod, Charles Adolphe Reymond, Alexis Pache, and Alcesti C. Rigo de Righi, was marred by conflict, with the others mutinying against his leadership as nightfall approached, resulting in the deaths of Pache and several porters, for which Crowley was widely blamed. In Moharbhanj, Crowley participated in big-game hunting and wrote The Scented Garden, a homoerotic work, before meeting Rose and Lilith in Calcutta and being forced to leave India after non-lethally shooting two men who attempted to mug him. He briefly visited Bennett in Burma, then toured southern China with his family, hiring porters and a nanny, smoking opium throughout the journey from Tengyueh to Yungchang, Tali, Yunnanfu, and Hanoi, and daily reciting the "Bornless Ritual" to invoke his Holy Guardian Angel. While Rose and Lilith returned to Europe, Crowley went to Shanghai to meet Elaine Simpson, who was fascinated by The Book of the Law; together they performed rituals to contact Aiwass. He then sailed to Japan and Canada before going to New York City, where he unsuccessfully sought support for a second Kanchenjunga expedition. Upon returning to Britain, he learned that his daughter Lilith had died of typhoid in Rangoon, which he later blamed on Rose's increasing alcoholism; under emotional distress, his health deteriorated, and he underwent several surgical operations. He began short-lived romances with actress Vera "Lola" Neville and author Ada Leverson; Lola Zaza was born in 1906, either in late summer, September, or the following winter, and contracted bronchitis and nearly died. With George Cecil Jones, Crowley continued performing the Abramelin rituals at the Ashdown Park Hotel in Coulsdon, Surrey, believing he attained samadhi or union with the Godhead, a turning point in his life. Using heavy amounts of hashish, he wrote "The Psychology of Hashish" (1909), championing the drug as a tool for mysticism. He claimed to have been contacted again by Aiwass in late October and November 1907, who dictated two additional texts, "Liber VII" and "Liber Cordis Cincti Serpente," later classified in Thelema's Holy Books. During the last two months of 1907, he wrote more Thelemic Holy Books, including "Liber LXVI," "Liber Arcanorum," "Liber Porta Lucis, Sub Figura X," "Liber Tau," "Liber Trigrammaton," and "Liber DCCCXIII vel Ararita," all received from a preternatural source. In June 1909, when the manuscript of The Book of the Law was rediscovered at Boleskine, he concluded that Thelema represented objective truth. His inheritance was dwindling; he was hired by George Montagu Bennett, the Earl of Tankerville, to protect him from witchcraft, recognizing Bennett's paranoia stemmed from cocaine addiction, and took him on holiday to France and Morocco. In 1907, he began taking paying students in occult and magical practice. Born to a wealthy family in Royal Leamington Spa, Warwickshire, England, on 12 October 1875, Crowley was the son of Edward Crowley (1829–1887), an engineer who retired from a brewing business, and Emily Bertha Bishop (1848–1917), who came from a Devonshire-Somerset family and described her son as "the Beast," a name he embraced. The couple married in November 1874 at London's Kensington Registry Office and were evangelical Christians; Crowley's father converted to the Exclusive Brethren, a fundamentalist Christian group, and read a Bible passage to his wife and son daily after breakfast. After the death of their baby daughter in 1880, the family moved to Redhill, Surrey. At age 8, Crowley attended H. T. Habershon's evangelical Christian boarding school in Hastings and later Ebor preparatory school in Cambridge, run by Reverend Henry d'Arcy Champney, whom Crowley viewed as a sadist. In 1887, when Crowley was eleven, his father died of tongue cancer, an event he described as a turning point in his life and maintained an admiration for, calling him "my hero and my friend." Inheriting a third of his father's wealth, he began misbehaving at school and was punished harshly by Champney; his family removed him after he developed albuminuria. He then attended Malvern College and Tonbridge School, both of which he despised and left after a few terms. He became increasingly skeptical of Christianity, pointing out Biblical inconsistencies, and engaged in behaviors contrary to Christian morality, including smoking, masturbation, and having sex with prostitutes from whom he contracted gonorrhea. Sent to live with a Brethren tutor in Eastbourne, he took chemistry courses at Eastbourne College and developed interests in chess, poetry, and mountain climbing. In 1894, he climbed Beachy Head and visited the Alps, joining the Scottish Mountaineering Club. The following year, he climbed the Eiger, Trift, Jungfrau, Mönch, and Wetterhorn. He adopted the name Aleister over Edward, believing it fulfilled the ideal of a dactyl followed by a spondee, as in "Jeremy Taylor," and noted that Aleister is the Gaelic form of Alexander. In March 1896, while on holiday in Stockholm, Crowley had his first significant mystical experience, which several biographers, including Lawrence Sutin, Richard Kaczynski, and Tobias Churton, believe resulted from his first same-sex sexual experience, enabling him to recognize his bisexuality. At Cambridge, he maintained a vigorous sex life with women, mostly prostitutes, from one of whom he contracted syphilis, and eventually participated in same-sex activities despite their illegality. In October 1897, he met Herbert Charles Pollitt, president of the Cambridge University Footlights Dramatic Club, with whom he entered into a relationship; they broke apart because Pollitt did not share Crowley's growing interest in Western esotericism, a relationship Crowley regretted for years. In 1897, Crowley traveled to Saint Petersburg, Russia, intending to learn Russian for a future diplomatic career, but a brief illness in October 1897 triggered reflections on mortality and the futility of human endeavor, leading him to abandon diplomacy in favor of the occult. In March 1898, he obtained A. E. Waite's The Book of Black Magic and of Pacts and Karl von Eckartshausen's The Cloud upon the Sanctuary, furthering his occult interests. That same year, Leonard Smithers published 100 copies of Crowley's poem Aceldama: A Place to Bury Strangers In, which was not a success. He also published a string of other poems, including White Stains, a Decadent collection of erotic poetry printed abroad to avoid British prohibition. In July 1898, he left Cambridge without a degree, despite a "first class" showing in his 1897 exams and consistent "second class honours" results prior to that. In August 1898, he was in Zermatt, Switzerland, where he met chemist Julian L. Baker, with whom he discussed alchemy. Back in London, Baker introduced Crowley to George Cecil Jones, Baker's brother-in-law and a fellow member of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, founded in 1888. On 18 November 1898, Crowley was initiated into the Outer Order of the Golden Dawn at the Isis-Urania Temple in London's Mark Masons Hall by Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers, taking the magical motto and name "Frater Perdurabo," which he interpreted as "Brother I shall endure to the end." He moved into a luxury flat at 67–69 Chancery Lane and invited Allan Bennett, a senior Golden Dawn member, to live with him as his personal magical tutor. Bennett taught Crowley ceremonial magic and the ritual use of drugs, and together they performed Goetia rituals until Bennett left for South Asia to study Buddhism. In November 1899, Crowley purchased Boleskine House in Foyers on the shore of Loch Ness in Scotland, describing himself as the "Laird of Boleskine" and wearing traditional highland dress even in London. He continued writing poetry, publishing Jezebel and Other Tragic Poems, Tales of Archais, Songs of the Spirit, Appeal to the American Republic, and Jephthah in 1898–99; most received mixed reviews, though Jephthah was a critical success. Crowley progressed through the lower grades of the Golden Dawn and was ready for the inner Second Order, but was unpopular due to his bisexuality and libertine lifestyle, developing feuds with members including W. B. Yeats. When the London lodge refused to initiate him into the Second Order, he visited Mathers in Paris, who personally admitted him into the Adeptus Minor Grade. A schism had developed between Mathers and the London members, who were dissatisfied with his autocratic rule. Acting under Mathers' orders, Crowley, with the help of his mistress and fellow initiate Elaine Simpson, attempted to seize the Vault of the Adepts at 36 Blythe Road in West Kensington from the London lodge members. In court, the judge ruled in favor of the London lodge, as they had paid for the space's rent, leaving both Crowley and Mathers isolated from the group. In 1900, Crowley traveled to Mexico via the United States, settling in Mexico City and beginning a relationship with a local woman. He developed a love for the country, continued experimenting with ceremonial magic using John Dee's Enochian invocations, and later claimed to have been initiated into Freemasonry. He wrote a play based on Richard Wagner's opera Tannhäuser and a series of poems published as Oracles (1905). Eckenstein joined him in 1900, and together they climbed several mountains, including Iztaccihuatl, Popocatepetl, and Colima, which they had to abandon due to a volcanic eruption. Leaving Mexico, he went to San Francisco before sailing for Hawaii aboard the Nippon Maru, where he had a brief affair with a married woman named Mary Alice Rogers, whom he later wrote about in a series of poems published as Alice: An Adultery (1903). Briefly stopping in Japan and Hong Kong, Crowley reached Ceylon, where he met Allan Bennett, who was studying Shaivism. The pair spent time in Kandy before Bennett decided to become a Buddhist monk in the Theravada tradition and traveled to Burma. Crowley then toured India, devoting himself to the Hindu practice of Rāja yoga, believing he achieved the spiritual state of dhyana, and studied at the Meenakshi Temple in Madura. He also wrote poetry published as The Sword of Song (1904) and contracted malaria, recuperating in Calcutta and Rangoon. In 1902, he was joined in India by Eckenstein and several other mountaineers: Guy Knowles, H. Pfannl, V. Wesseley, and Jules Jacot-Guillarmod. Together, the Eckenstein-Crowley expedition attempted K2, which was never climbed, reaching an altitude of 20,000 feet (6,100 m) before turning back due to illness, including influenza, malaria, and snow blindness. In November 1902, he socialized with painter Gerald Kelly in Paris and became a fixture of the Parisian arts scene. While there, he wrote poems on sculptor Auguste Rodin, later published as Rodin in Rime (1907). W. Somerset Maugham, after briefly meeting Crowley, used him as a model for the character of Oliver Haddo in his novel The Magician (1908). He returned to Boleskine in April 1903 and, in August, married Gerald Kelly's sister Rose Edith Kelly in a "marriage of convenience" to prevent her from entering an arranged marriage; the marriage appalled the Kelly family and damaged his friendship with Gerald. On a honeymoon to Paris, Cairo, and then Ceylon, Crowley fell in love with Rose and wrote a series of love poems, published as Rosa Mundi and other Love Songs (1906), as well as authoring the religious satire Why Jesus Wept (1904). In February 1904, Crowley and Rose arrived in Cairo, where they pretended to be a prince and princess and rented an apartment in which Crowley set up a temple room to invoke ancient Egyptian deities while studying Islamic mysticism and Arabic. Rose regularly became delirious and informed him "they are waiting for you." On 18 March, she explained that "they" were the god Horus, and on 20 March proclaimed that "the Equinox of the Gods has come." She led him to a nearby museum, where she showed him a seventh-century BCE mortuary stele known as the Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu; Crowley believed the exhibit's number, 666, was significant as the "Number of the Beast" in Christian belief and later called it the "Stele of Revealing." According to Crowley's later account, on 8 April he heard a disembodied voice identifying itself as Aiwass, the messenger of Horus or Hoor-Paar-Kraat. He wrote down everything the voice told him over the next three days and titled it Liber AL vel Legis or The Book of the Law. The book proclaimed that humanity was entering a new Aeon and that Crowley would serve as its prophet, stating that a supreme moral law was "Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the Law," and that people should live in tune with their True Will. This book and its philosophy became the cornerstone of Thelema. Crowley said he was unsure what to do with The Book of the Law and often resented it, ignoring its commands, including taking the Stele of Revealing from the museum, fortifying his own island, and translating the book into all the world's languages. According to his account, he instead sent typescripts of the work to several occult groups.

text: Alexander Henderson Manning (11 May 1819 – 20 October 1903) was a Canadian contractor, businessman, and the 20th Mayor of Toronto, serving a single term in 1873 and a second in 1885. Born in Dublin, Ireland, on 11 May 1819, he was educated there and immigrated to Toronto in 1834. Four years later, he lived in Ohio before returning to Toronto after two years. He worked as a builder and was a partner in a sawmill business. He worked on the construction of several projects, including the Welland Canal, the Library of Parliament, and the Toronto Normal and Model School. In the 1850s, he invested in real estate in Toronto. In the 1860s, he demanded overtime payments for road construction in Grey County, which was used to politically attack him for seeking excessive public funds. From 1870 to 1874, he worked on masonry and brickwork for the Canadian Library of Parliament. He was also an investor in the Toronto Street Railway and constructed railways in Vermont, Pennsylvania, New York, and other parts of Canada. Manning was unsuccessful in his first election as alderman for St. Lawrence Ward in 1855 but was elected in 1856 and reelected in 1857. He was not an alderman in the following council term but returned in 1867 and was reelected annually until 1873. He nominated himself for mayor in 1872 but was not selected by the city council; in 1873, he nominated himself again and was elected. During his first term, he advocated for a commissioner to oversee public projects and helped establish a system to assess and collect taxes. The city controversially purchased privately owned waterworks, which divided city council and the public. In 1874, he ran in the mayoral election that returned to popular vote but lost due to public allegations of misconduct in the waterworks tendering process. He won his first government contract to build the Welland Canal and Cornwall Canal. His 1879 contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway was criticized for being awarded due to his influence in the Conservative Party. A royal commission found the price was not rigged but noted irregularities in the awarding process, which damaged his ability to secure further contracts and led to his company going bankrupt in 1883. Manning ran for mayor in 1879 and came in third; he declined the nomination in 1881, but in 1884, over 5,000 citizens signed a petition for him to run. As an independent candidate, he focused on his prior experience as mayor, promising financial restraint and clean water. His opponent, John Jacob Withrow, criticized tax assessments on Manning’s income and businesses, and Manning responded by reading his assessor reports and defending the reductions he received. He won the mayoral race with support from Conservative voters. As mayor, he maintained low tax rates and was an effective city administrator. He advocated for a better sanitation system, though his reputation was hampered by associations with dishonest individuals. He also supported the creation of the Home for Incurables and called for the formation of the Toronto Volunteers Reception Committee to prepare for the return of troops from the North-West Rebellion, and formed a committee to build a monument to those who fought for the government in the rebellion, which was erected in 1895. Initially believing he would be unchallenged in his reelection, he faced a growing civic reform movement that produced candidate William Holmes Howland, a temperance advocate who highlighted Manning’s presidency of the Toronto Brewing and Malting Company. Manning supported the Daily Mail in its dispute with the Toronto Typographical Union, leading the union to campaign against him. He lost his reelection bid in 1885. Manning was active in several Toronto social organizations, including the Irish Protestant Benevolent Society, the St. Patrick's Society, and the National Club. He was an investor in the Grand Opera House and purchased it when it went bankrupt in 1876. In 1884, he hired E. J. Lennox to design the Manning Arcade and funded the construction of Old City Hall. He was a member of the Toronto Board of Trade, a director of the Traders Bank of Canada and the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and president of the Toronto Dry Dock and Shipbuilding Company and the North American Land Company Limited. He married Adeline Augusta Whittemore on 6 February 1850; she died in 1861, and he married Susan Celina Smith on 1 August 1861. They had two sons and two daughters. Manning died in Toronto on 20 October 1903 and was buried at St. James Cemetery in a tomb he built for his family. At the time of his death, he was the largest individual taxpayer in Toronto.

text: Alexei Alexeyevich Abrikosov (Russian: Алексе́й Алексе́евич Абрико́сов; June 25, 1928 – March 29, 2017[4][5]) was a Soviet, Russian, and American[6] theoretical physicist known primarily for his work in condensed matter physics. He shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics with Vitaly Ginzburg and Anthony James Leggett for theories explaining how matter behaves at extremely low temperatures.[6][7][8] Born in Moscow, Russian SFSR, Soviet Union, on June 25, 1928, to physicians Aleksey Abrikosov and Fani (née Wulf), Abrikosov was of Jewish descent.[9] After graduating from high school in 1943, he studied energy technology and earned a degree from Moscow State University in 1948. From 1948 to 1965, he worked at the Institute for Physical Problems of the USSR Academy of Sciences, where he received his Ph.D. in 1951 for his work on the theory of thermal diffusion in plasmas and his Doctor of Physical and Mathematical Sciences degree in 1955 for research on quantum electrodynamics at high energies. He moved to the United States in 1991 and resided there until his death in Palo Alto, California, in 2017 at the age of 88.[19] During his time in the U.S., he was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2000 and became a foreign member of the Royal Society in 2001.[3][10] From 1965 to 1988, he worked at the Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics (USSR Academy of Sciences) and remained a professor at Moscow State University since 1965. He also held tenure at the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology from 1972 to 1976 and at the Moscow Institute of Steel and Alloys from 1976 to 1991. He served as a full member of the USSR Academy of Sciences from 1987 to 1991 and became a full member of the Russian Academy of Sciences in 1991. In 1952 and 1957, Abrikosov published work explaining how magnetic flux can penetrate certain superconductors, leading to the classification of these materials as type-II superconductors, with the resulting pattern of magnetic flux lines known as the Abrikosov vortex lattice.[11] Together with Lev Gor'kov and Igor Dzyaloshinskii, he authored a foundational textbook on theoretical solid-state physics used for decades to train physicists. From 1991 until his retirement, he worked at Argonne National Laboratory in Illinois, where he was an Argonne Distinguished Scientist in the Condensed Matter Theory Group. At the time of receiving the Nobel Prize, his research focused on the origins of magnetoresistance—the property of some materials to change their electrical resistance under a magnetic field.[12][13][14][15][16] He received the Lenin Prize in 1966, the Fritz London Memorial Prize in 1972, the USSR State Prize in 1982, and the Landau Prize from the Russian Academy of Sciences in 1989. In 1991, he was awarded the Sony Corporation's John Bardeen Award and became a Foreign Honorary Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. He was also a member of the Royal Academy of London, a fellow of the American Physical Society, and a recipient of the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics. His father, Alexey Ivanovich Abrikosov (1875–1955), was a physician, and his mother, Fania Davidovna Woolf (1895–1965), was also a physician; through his father, he was the nephew of the Catholic nun Anna Abrikosova (1882–1936). His sister, Maria Alekseevna Abrikósova (1929–1998), was also a physician. He married Svetlana Yuriyevna Bunkova and had three children.[6][3]

text: Alfred Carlton Gilbert (February 15, 1884 – January 24, 1961) was an American inventor, athlete, magician, toy maker, and businessman. As the founder of the A. C. Gilbert Company, he is known for inventing the Erector Set and American Flyer Trains. Born in Salem, Oregon, Gilbert attended the Tualatin Academy and Pacific University in Forest Grove, Oregon, where he was a member of the Gamma Sigma Fraternity. He left Pacific after 1902 and transferred to Yale University, financing his education through work as a magician and earning a degree in medicine. His thesis was titled The Genito-Urinary Phenomena of Athletes. An accomplished athlete, he broke the world record for consecutive chin-ups (39) in 1900 and the distance record for the running long dive in 1902. He invented the pole vault box and set two world records in the pole vault, including a record of 12′ 3″ (3.66 meters) at the Spring meet of the Irish American Athletic Club at Celtic Park, New York, in 1906. At the 1908 Summer Olympics, he tied for gold with Edward Cook, setting an Olympic record. Choosing not to pursue medicine, Gilbert founded Mysto Manufacturing in 1907 with his friend John Petrie, which later became the A. C. Gilbert Company. He developed the Erector Set in 1913, inspired by steel construction girders used on the New York, New Haven & Hartford Railroad; the set was preceded by Frank Hornby’s Meccano, which Hornby patented as "Mechanics Made Easy" in 1901. In 1918, during World War I, when the Council of National Defense considered banning toy production, Gilbert successfully argued against it, earning the nickname "The man who saved Christmas." He had previously contributed to the war effort by becoming one of the Four Minute Men who gave lectures to encourage war bond purchases. By 1935, the company had sold more than 30 million Erector Sets. He expanded the product line to include chemistry sets, microscope sets, and other educational toys, amassing over 150 patents over 50 years. In 1938, he acquired the rights to the American Flyer toy train line from W. O. Coleman and moved production from Chicago to New Haven. He adopted a 3/16 scale for the trains while retaining the three-rail O-gauge track associated with Lionel. After World War II, O-gauge track was replaced with two-rail S-gauge track. Gilbert was praised for his commitment to scale realism, making American Flyer trains appear more authentic. He is credited with originating employee benefits such as free medical and legal advice and maternity leave. In 1915, he founded the Toy Manufacturers of America trade association and served as its first president. Frustrated that invention was not taught in schools, in 1941 he opened the Gilbert Hall of Science in New York City, which promoted science interest and sold his products. In 1950–1951, he marketed the Gilbert U-238 Atomic Energy Laboratory, which included radioactive ore samples of autunite, carnotite, torbernite, and uraninite. In 1908, he married Mary Thompson, whom he met at Pacific University; they had three children: two girls and a boy. In the 1930s, they lived at Maraldene in Hamden, Connecticut, which included kennels where Gilbert bred German Shepherds, one of which won the Max von Stephanitz award. He also owned a 600-acre estate called Paradise, used for hunting and housing big-game trophies, and served as a venue for entertaining clients and guests at the Yale Bowl. Upon retiring in 1954, he transferred the company to his son. That same year, he published his autobiography, The Man Who Lives in Paradise. After his death in 1961, the family sold the remaining shares of the A. C. Gilbert Company to Jack Wrather, which went out of business in 1967, though the Erector trademark continued to be used. A museum in Salem, Oregon, named A. C. Gilbert's Discovery Village, honors him and includes historic structures such as the house of his uncle Andrew T. Gilbert, opening in 1989. The television movie The Man Who Saved Christmas, released on December 15, 2002, dramatizes Christmas during 1917–1918 in the context of World War I and features Jason Alexander as Gilbert; the film takes several historical liberties. Pacific University in Forest Grove, Oregon, opened a residential hall named after Gilbert in 2009.

text: Alma S. Woolley (October 3, 1931, New York City – December 17, 2005, Baltimore) was an American nurse, nurse educator, nursing historian, and author. She led several schools of nursing and authored numerous books and articles on nursing education, the history of nursing education, and nurses. Woolley grew up during the Depression in the Bronx, New York City: her father died after being hit by a truck on his way to a public hospital; her maternal grandmother, who worked in a sweatshop, made all her clothes; her widowed mother worked as a stenographer for GM; and at age twelve, Woolley admired the smart gray uniforms with red trimming of the Cadet Nurse Corps during World War II, leading to her selection to attend the elite all-girls Hunter College High School, which she commuted to by public transport one hour each way. At Hunter, she won the all-city Latin Poetry Contest in 1949 and graduated second in her class, then attended Queens College and Cornell University's School of Nursing, earning a bachelor's degree in 1954. She joined the Visiting Nurse Service of New York, married, and worked at hospitals including Mary Immaculate Hospital in Jamaica, Queens, and later at Philadelphia General Hospital and Jefferson Medical College after moving to Philadelphia with her husband, Arthur E. Woolley. She became a nursing instructor at the University of Pennsylvania, enrolled in their graduate program, and earned an M.S. in medical-surgical nursing in 1965, an achievement that led to her early article in The American Journal of Nursing, "My Lamp Is Refueled," explaining how and why she maintained her professional engagement while raising four small children. In 1969, after moving to New Jersey with her husband and children, Woolley became an instructor at Atlantic Community College and was soon offered the task of creating a B.S. degree program in nursing for The Richard Stockton College of New Jersey, which opened in 1971. The original program she designed was for registered nurses, R.N.'s, without a university degree, to complete a Bachelor of Science in nursing. Woolley advocated for the transition of nursing education from non-university-trained R.N.'s to 4-year B.S.N. programs or their equivalents and published several pieces demonstrating the benefits of university-based nursing programs. In 1980, she earned a doctorate in nursing education from the University of Pennsylvania. In 1981, she was appointed Director of the School of Nursing at Illinois Wesleyan University and the Caroline F. Rupert Professor of Nursing; in 1986, she left Wesleyan to become Dean of Georgetown University School of Nursing and Health Studies. In 1989, she received the Distinguished Alumnus Award from the Cornell School of Nursing Alumni Association. She stepped down as dean of Georgetown's School of Nursing in 1992 and returned to teaching and writing, retiring as professor emeritus of nursing in 1996 and becoming a visiting professor at both the University of Maryland School of Nursing in Baltimore, Md, and the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences. She wrote or contributed to biographies of nurses including Maude Francis Essig, who served with American combat troops in World War I, and Virginia Matthews Dunbar, an early advocate of university curricula for nurses. Reflecting her belief that "the history of nursing education is an important lacuna in general histories of nursing" and that "as part of public history in the United States, nursing education can cite many accomplishments in the realm of health care policy," Woolley also published histories of nursing schools, including "Nuns and Guns" and Learning, Faith and Caring. Before her death in 2005, she was working on oral histories of women who, like her, had been recently admitted as members to the once all-male Cosmos Club of Washington, D.C.

text: The site contains a sub-circular enclosure within concentric ditches, with ramparts constructed from earth and stone excavated from the hillfort itself. It also includes remains of a Romano-British settlement and at least five hut circles within the hillfort’s interior. Three unenclosed huts on the north-west flanks, defined by a curving out bank, represent the earliest remains and may date back to the Bronze Age. There were four possible phases of development for the earthwork defences during the Iron Age: the first phase involved a univallate stone-walled enclosure, followed by the construction of ramparts and ditches forming a bivallate hillfort (phase 2), while phases 3 and 4 led to Castle Hill becoming a multivallate hillfort. Several trackways near Castle Hill may date from the prehistoric or Romano-British periods, and there is evidence of agricultural activity from the Bronze Age, Iron Age, and Romano-British times. A prehistoric cord rig was found on the north-west of the hilltop, and prehistoric or Romano-British ploughing has created lynchets on the north-east side. Medieval cultivation extended from Alnham village and ceased at a boundary bank on the south-east face of the hill. The most significant 20th-century structure in Alnham is the War Memorial Hall, built in 1920 to reflect the impact of World War I on small rural communities; it is a stone-built village hall with a stone incision above the porch door, and no names are inscribed because there were no village deaths during the war. Alnham is an isolated rural community, with the nearest main road being the A697, approximately 7.5 miles (12 km) away. The village lies on a north-south local road from Prendwick to Scrainwood, and from a junction near the centre, another road heads northwest from Alnham, past Castle Hill, for about 5 kilometres (3.1 mi) to Ewartly Shank, where it ends. In the mid-to-late 19th century, plans existed for a Northumberland Central Railway line to pass through Alnham, positioned to the east of Pennylaws Cottage, but the project was never constructed.

text: Alnham is a hamlet and civil parish in Northumberland, England, located about 14 miles (23 km) west of Alnwick and approximately 6 miles (10 km) from the Scottish border, situated on the south side of a small tributary of the River Alnham. The village lies on uneven ground, sloping from south to north, at the foot of the southern outliers of the Cheviot Hills, with the River Alnham flowing eastward through it from its source in the Cheviot Hills to the coast. The village's layout is influenced by the river. The 2011 Census estimated the population at around 245. Evidence of human occupation in Alnham and its surroundings dates back to prehistoric times, with a cup-marked stone found at Alnham Northfield indicating Neolithic habitation. Bronze Age occupation is evident through a rare bronze spearhead found at High Bleakhope, possibly indicating elite presence, and the spearhead may have been placed as an offering to a deity due to the site's remote and elevated position. Numerous cairns and unenclosed settlements are found in the surrounding area, and two Iron Age palisaded enclosures have been discovered on High Knowes. Castle Hill, a Cheviot multivallate hillfort, is an Iron Age site located to the west of Alnham, standing at 289 metres (948 ft) above Ordnance Datum, with a sub-circular enclosure and ramparts made of earth and stone, and at least five hut circles within it. Three unenclosed huts on the north-west flanks may date from the Bronze Age. The site shows at least four phases of development, beginning with a univallate stone-walled enclosure, followed by bivallate and then multivallate forms. There is also evidence of Romano-British settlement and agricultural activity, including prehistoric cord rig. The name "Alnham" comes from Old English hām (homestead) and the Celtic river-name Aln or Alaunos, meaning "homestead on the River Aln," with recorded variations including Alneham (1331), Elnam (1509), Ayneham (1557), and Ailnham (1663); it has also been historically known as "Yeldom" and in the Magna Britannia of 1724 as "Yarwell." Alnham was part of the Barony of Alnwick held by the Vesci family from the early 12th century until 1310, when it was sold to Henry de Percy, 1st Baron Percy, and has remained in the Percy family since. The Church of St Michael and All Angels, a Grade I listed building and part of the Diocese of Newcastle, was first recorded in an 1184 charter when William de Vesci granted it to Alnwick Abbey; it was later restored in the 13th century and again in 1664 and 1953. The church was damaged during Anglo-Scottish border conflicts and was in a ruinous state by the mid-1800s, with a detailed 1862 description noting damp, mildewed walls, rotting windows, and fungi. F. R. Wilson restored the church in 1870, and Gustav Adolph Renwick carried out further work in 1953. A medieval cross base, 2 feet (61 cm) high and Grade II listed, is located about 20 yards (18 m) south of the church. Tower House, also Grade II listed, was first recorded in 1541 as a "lytle toure" and served as the vicarage; it collapsed in 1651 and remained uninhabitable until 1844, when it was rebuilt with new battlements, turrets, and a residential wing. It is now a private residence. The medieval settlement at Alnham is a scheduled monument located south of St Michaels Church, consisting of earthworks, a toft, two houses, a small hill, and a group of three houses and an enclosure, likely originally larger and centered on the Church. Alnham Castle, a scheduled monument, includes the remains of a medieval tower house with a rectangular plan measuring 22 metres (72 ft) by 18 metres (59 ft) and up to 2 metres (6.6 ft) high, first mentioned in 1405 as one of Harry Hotspur's strongholds, and situated on a low ridge with a triangular annex to the east and south and a well-defined lynchet bank to the north, likely representing a garden and meadow. The former farmhouses of Alnham Castle, known as Castle Farm, are now the Pennywells—two Grade II listed cottages from the early 18th century—along with a Grade II listed garden wall and adjacent farm buildings (byres, stable, and shelter sheds built between 1830 and 1840), all of which have separate Grade II listings. Alnham has historically been affected by Anglo-Scottish border conflicts, with Scottish raids during Henry VIII's reign described in letters from the Earl of Northumberland in October and November 1532, and the tower reportedly in bad condition by 1541. A 1615 survey noted the village's vulnerability due to its location between the two realms. Alnham was a significant agricultural centre in the early 17th century, with Robert Norton's 1619 map showing four large common fields, 70 acres of arable land, and 168 acres of "Alnham oxe pasture." From the 18th century, the village declined due to land leasing policies that consolidated holdings, with the number of cottages dropping from five in Seymour's Survey of c. 1756 to two farms and three cottages by 1776. Alnham Common was first recorded in 1702 and divided in 1776. The 19th century saw Alnham consist of three farms, a church, a vicarage, a Church of England school (built in 1870), and six cottages, with farming remaining the primary economic activity. The population in 1801 was 233 and declined to 205 by 1891, with the 1831 census showing 45 male residents over 20 as labourers or servants, 8 as employers or professionals, and 15 as "middling sorts." In the 20th century, the only new building was the War Memorial Hall, erected in 1921, and the population gradually declined due to mechanisation and reduced farming incomes. Alnham is part of the North Core Strategy Delivery Area of Northumberland, one of the least populated areas in England with 26 residents per square km compared to the county average of 63. In 2001, the parish of Whittingham and Alnham had a total usual population of 505, and in 2011, Alnham Parish had an estimated population of 245. 20.4% of residents were aged 0–15 and 10.2% were aged 65+, with 100% identifying as white; 68.6% were Christian, and 81.3% of those aged 16–74 were economically active, primarily in agriculture, forestry, and fishing (25.7%). Alnham is part of the Berwick-upon-Tweed Parliament constituency, represented since May 2015 by Anne-Marie Trevelyan (Conservative), previously held by Alan Beith (Liberal Democrats), and is part of the Rothbury Ward, represented by Steven Christopher Bridgett (Independent). At the parish council level, Alnham is part of Whittingham Parish Council, which includes the former parishes of Alnham, Callaly, and Whittingham. There are seven listed structures in Alnham, including the Church, Tower House, the medieval settlement, and Alnham Castle.

text: The American Dialect Society (ADS), established in 1889, is a learned society dedicated to the study of the English language in North America, and of other languages or dialects of other languages influencing it or influenced by it. The Society publishes the academic journal American Speech. Founded as part of an effort to create a comprehensive American dialect dictionary, the ADS was established in 1889 by a group of American philologists when Joseph Wright began editing the English Dialect Dictionary, with the goal of producing a similar work for the United States. Its original constitution from 1890 defined its objective as "the investigation of the spoken English of the United States and Canada," a mission that has remained essentially unchanged, only expanded in 1991 to include "the English language in North America, together with other languages or dialects of other languages influencing it or influenced by it." Members of the Society, which has never had more than a few hundred active members, include linguists, lexicographers, etymologists, grammarians, historians, researchers, writers, authors, editors, professors, university students, and independent scholars. The Society's activities include a mailing list that primarily focuses on American English but also covers other linguistic topics. Members began collecting material, much of which was published in the journal Dialect Notes, but significant progress toward compiling a nationwide dictionary was not made until Frederic G. Cassidy was appointed Chief Editor in 1963. The first volume of the Dictionary of American Regional English, covering the letters A-C, was published in 1985. The Society's other major project is the Linguistic Atlas of the United States and Canada. Since 1991, the ADS has designated one or more words or terms as the word of the year, with the New York Times noting that the Society "probably started" the "word-of-the-year ritual." The "Gesellschaft für deutsche Sprache" (GfdS) has selected a word of the year since 1977. The Society also holds special votes each year to select words in various categories, such as "most original," "most unnecessary," "most outrageous," or "most likely to succeed." Several words chosen by the ADS appear on Merriam-Webster's Words of the Year lists.

text: Amrita Sher-Gil (30 January 1913 – 5 December 1941) was a Hungarian–Indian painter recognized as "one of the greatest avant-garde women artists of the early 20th century" and a pioneer in modern Indian art. She began painting from an early age, receiving formal art lessons at eight and painting servants in her household as a child, an experience that later influenced her return to India. Born Dalma-Amrita on 30 January 1913 at 4 Szilágyi Dezső square, Budapest, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire, she was the daughter of Umrao Singh Sher-Gil Majithia, a Punjabi Indian Jat Sikh aristocrat and scholar in Sanskrit and Persian, and Marie Antoinette Gottesman, a Hungarian-Jewish opera singer from an affluent bourgeois family. Her parents first met in 1912 in Lahore, and her mother came to India as a companion to Princess Bamba Sutherland, granddaughter of Maharaja Ranjit Singh. Sher-Gil was the elder of two daughters; her younger sister was Indira Sundaram (née Sher-Gil, born March 1914), mother of artist Vivan Sundaram. The family remained in Budapest until after the First World War. She was the niece of Indologist Ervin Baktay, who noticed her artistic talent during a 1926 visit to Shimla and advocated for her to pursue art, guiding her through critiques and academic training. In 1921, the family moved to Summer Hill, Shimla, India, where Sher-Gil began studying piano and violin and, by age nine, performed in concerts and plays at the Gaiety Theatre. She was expelled from her Catholic school, Convent of Jesus and Mary, for declaring herself an atheist. In 1924, after meeting an Italian sculptor in Shimla, her mother moved to Florence, where Sher-Gil enrolled at Santa Annunziata, exposing her to Italian masters, though she returned to India shortly after. At sixteen, she traveled to Europe with her mother to train in Paris, first at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière under Pierre Vaillent and Lucien Simon (where she met Boris Taslitzky) and later at the École des Beaux-Arts (1930–1934). She drew inspiration from Paul Cézanne, Paul Gauguin, and Amedeo Modigliani, and her work in Paris showed a maturity rarely seen in a 16-year-old. In 1931, she was briefly engaged to Yusuf Ali Khan, with rumors of an affair with her first cousin and later husband Viktor Egan; her letters reveal same-sex affairs. Her early works displayed Post-Impressionist influences, and her 1932 oil painting *Young Girls* marked a breakthrough, earning her a gold medal and election as an Associate of the Grand Salon in Paris in 1933—making her the youngest ever member and the only Asian to receive this honor. Her Paris period included self-portraits, nude studies, still lifes, and portraits of friends. One of her professors noted that her rich color palette suggested she was not at home in Europe, and that her true artistic atmosphere lay in the East. In 1933, she began feeling a strong longing to return to India, which she did at the end of 1934. In May 1935, she met English journalist Malcolm Muggeridge, with whom she had a brief intense affair and painted a portrait now held by the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi. By September 1935, she saw him off for England. In 1936, at the behest of art collector and critic Karl Khandalavala, she traveled to India to explore her Indian roots, where she was deeply influenced by Mughal and Pahari schools of painting and the Ajanta cave paintings. In 1937, she toured South India and produced her South Indian trilogy—*Bride's Toilet*, *Brahmacharis*, and *South Indian Villagers Going to Market*—reflecting her passion for color and empathy for impoverished subjects. She declared, "I can only paint in India. Europe belongs to Picasso, Matisse, Braque.... India belongs only to me," marking a shift in her artistic mission to depict Indian life. Her work during this phase, including *Village Scene*, *In the Ladies' Enclosure*, and *Siesta*, showed influences from miniature and Pahari schools. Though acclaimed by critics like Karl Khandalavala and Charles Fabri as the greatest painter of the century, her paintings found few buyers; the Nawab Salar Jung of Hyderabad returned them, and the Maharaja of Mysore chose Raja Ravi Varma's works. A Congress sympathizer, Sher-Gil was drawn to the poor and distressed, and her depictions of Indian villagers and women reflect their conditions. She admired Gandhi’s philosophy and lifestyle, and Nehru was charmed by her beauty and talent; he visited her at Saraya in October 1940 and attended her 1937 exhibition in New Delhi. Though she exchanged letters with Nehru, her parents burned them when she was away marrying in Budapest. In September 1941, Sher-Gil and Viktor Egan moved to Lahore, where she lived and painted at 23 Ganga Ram Mansions, The Mall. She was known for her affairs with both men and women, and painted several of her female lovers; *Two Women* is believed to depict her and her lover Marie Louise. Her later works include *Tahitian* (1937), *Red Brick House* (1938), *Hill Scene* (1938), and *The Bride* (1940); her last work was left unfinished just before her death. In 1941, at age 28, she became seriously ill just days before her first major solo show in Lahore, slipping into a coma and dying around midnight on 5 December 1941. The cause of death remains unknown; a failed abortion and subsequent peritonitis have been suggested, and her mother accused her husband Egan of murdering her. The day after her death, Britain declared war on Hungary, and Egan was interned as an enemy alien. Sher-Gil was cremated on 7 December 1941 in Lahore. Her art has influenced generations of Indian artists, including Sayed Haider Raza and Arpita Singh, and her depictions of women have made her a beacon for women globally. The Government of India has declared her works National Art Treasures, with most housed in the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi and some at the Lahore Museum. A postage stamp featuring her painting *Hill Women* was released in 1978 by India Post, and Amrita Shergil Marg is a road in Lutyens' Delhi named after her. Her work proved to Western societies that Indians could create fine art, and when sold in India, the government mandates that the art remain in the country—fewer than ten of her works have been sold globally. In 2006, *Village Scene* sold for ₹6.9 crores at an auction in New Delhi, the highest price ever paid for an Indian painting at the time. The Indian cultural centre in Budapest is named the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre. Contemporary artists have recreated her works. The 1969 documentary *Amrita Sher-Gil*, directed by Bhagwan Das Garga and produced by India’s Films Division, won the National Film Award for Best Non-Feature Film. In 1993, she inspired the Urdu play *Tumhari Amrita*. UNESCO designated 2013, the 100th anniversary of her birth, as the International Year of Amrita Sher-Gil. Her work is a key theme in the novel *Faking It* by Amrita Chowdhury. Aurora Zogoiby, a character in Salman Rushdie’s *The Moor’s Last Sigh* (1995), was inspired by Sher-Gil. Claire Kohda references Sher-Gil and her painting *The Three Girls* in her 2022 novel *Woman, Eating*, where the protagonist, Lydia, identifies with the subjects and speculates they were vampires. Sher-Gil was sometimes called India’s Frida Kahlo due to her revolutionary blending of Western and traditional art forms. On 30 January 2016, Google celebrated her 103rd birthday with a Doodle. In 2018, *The New York Times* published a belated obituary. That year, at a Sotheby’s auction in Mumbai, *The Little Girl in Blue* (a 1934 portrait of her cousin Babit, aged eight) sold for a record-breaking 18.69 crores. In 2021, *Portrait of Denyse* (1932, featuring Parisian art critic Denyse Proutaux) was auctioned by Christie’s with an estimated value of $1.8–2.8 million; Proutaux appeared in other Sher-Gil paintings, including *Young Girls* and *Denise Proutaux*, both exhibited in the "Amrita Shergil: The Passionate Quest" show at the National Gallery of Modern Art in New Delhi. On 18 September 2023, her 1937 painting *The Story Teller* fetched $7.4 million (Rs 61.8 crore) at a SaffronArt auction, setting a record for the highest price achieved by an Indian artist—just 10 days after Syed Haider Raza’s *Gestation* sold for ₹51.7 crore at Pundole.

He left Ambikapur, now in Chhattisgarh, at a young age to join Kashi Vidyapeeth in Varanasi, where he studied under Acharya Narendra Dev and Acharya JB Kriplani, both prominent freedom fighters. His grandfather, Pandit Lal Bihari Sharma, was the official tutor of Raja Bahadur Raghunath Saran Singh Deo, Maharaja of Sarguja (1879–1917), who was the great-grandfather of Madaneswar Saran Singh Deo, who later became Chief Secretary of Madhya Pradesh. Pandit Lal Bihari Sharma owned extensive landed property in Ambikapur, Sarguja, which his only son and heir, Anant Maral, abandoned when he joined Kashi Vidyapeeth and the freedom movement at a young age and never returned to claim it after Independence. During the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–1932), when the British suppressed the press, Anant Maral went underground and published the Congress Bulletin and Congress Samachar from Allahabad. He wrote the articles by hand, cut stencils to print copies, and distributed them by foot across villages to spread the Congress message. He also served as Youth League secretary in Varanasi. After earning the Shastri degree, he moved to Lahore, where he briefly worked as a college professor before becoming editor of Hindi Milap, a leading newspaper, gaining significant popularity in literary circles. In 1945, he published a well-researched treatise on the Bhakti Movement titled "Ram Bhakti Shakha" in Lahore (now in Pakistan), which was adopted as a textbook for MA Hindi Literature by Punjab University during the pre-Independence era, with preface by renowned Hindi scholar and former All India Radio director Udayshankar Bhatt. In 1942, during the Quit India Movement, he was arrested and imprisoned at Patna Camp Jail, where Sitaram Kesri, later Congress President, was also a cellmate. Upon Independence, he relocated from Lahore to Delhi and joined the Publications Division of the Government of India as editor of Ajkal, the most circulated and popular Hindi magazine of the time, which became a launching pad for many future poets. At the Publications Division, he played a key role in compiling and editing Mahatma Gandhi's Prayer Speeches, which were recorded earlier by All India Radio, and these were published as "Bhaiyon aur Behnon" (Brothers and Sisters). In 1949, Anant Maral Shastri was appointed Director of Information and Publicity in Madhya Bharat, a position he retained after the state reorganisation in 1956, serving until 1971. During his tenure, the Tansen Samaroh in Gwalior—honoring Miyan Tansen, one of Akbar’s nine gems—and the Kalidas Samaroh in Ujjain, celebrating the great Sanskrit poet and dramatist Kalidas, reached their peak of glory. India’s first President, Dr. Rajendra Prasad, inaugurated the first Akhil Bharatiya Kalidas Samaroh (National Kalidas Festival) in 1958, with Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru as chief guest at the second, during which Nehru was presented with Kalidasa’s epic Raghuvansh, translated from Sanskrit to Hindi by Anant Maral Shastri. This initiative was taken by Union Minister for Information and Broadcasting BV Keskar (1952–1962), who transformed the Tansen Samaroh into a national music festival. For nearly two decades, Anant Maral also led the Madhya Pradesh Shasan Sahitya Parishad and Kala Parishad (State Councils for Literature and Arts). Major events such as the Tagore Centenary, Alauddin Khan Centenary, and the 1960s celebration at Khandwa honoring the legendary Hindi poet Makhanlal Chaturvedi marked significant highlights in the state’s cultural history and remain sources of pride for Madhya Pradesh.

text: Anantnag district is an administrative district in the Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, located in the disputed Kashmir region and one of ten districts comprising the Kashmir Valley. Its headquarters is the city of Anantnag. As of the 2011 census, it was the third most populous district in Jammu and Kashmir (out of 22), following Jammu and Srinagar. The district includes six tehsils—Anantnag, Bijbehara, Dooru, Kokernag, Pahalgam, and Shangus—and is divided into seven blocks: Breng, Shangus, Achabal, Dachnipora, Qazigund, Khoveripora, and Shahabad. It covers a total area of 3,574 square kilometres (1,380 sq mi) and is bordered by Kargil and Kishtwar to the east, Doda and Ramban to the south, Ganderbal to the north, and Kulgam, Srinagar, Pulwama, and Shopian to the west. Anantnag has a moderate climate (Köppen classification), characterized by cool springs and autumns, mild summers, and cold winters, influenced by the Karakoram to the east and the Pirpanjal range to the south. The hilly eastern areas are cooler than the flat northern regions. Summer is mild with high humidity and cool nights, and precipitation occurs throughout the year, with July being the hottest month (mean max 32°C, mean min 6°C) and December–January the coldest (mean max 0°C, mean min −15°C). The record high is 33°C and the record low is −18°C. On 5–6 January 2012, heavy snowfall and low temperatures led to a state of emergency, with school closures on 6 and 7 January. Over recent years, there has been an increase in relative humidity and annual precipitation, likely due to commercial afforestation projects that expanded parks and green cover, making suburban areas more lush than the central region. The district shares the typical climate of the Kashmir Valley, as described by Pandit Kulan or Kalhana, who noted the mild sunshine, saffron, iced water, and grapes, and compared it to places like Peshawar, Baghdad, Damascus, Fez, and South Carolina, though it does not match any single climate. Sir Walter Lawrence observed that every hundred feet of elevation brings a new climate and vegetation phase. Anantnag has seven assembly constituencies: Anantnag, Anantnag West, Dooru, Kokernag, Shangus-Anantnag East, Bijbehara, and Pahalgam, and one Lok Sabha constituency. The current Member of Parliament for Anantnag-Rajouri is Mian Altaf Ahmed Larvi of the JKNC, and the District Development Commissioner (DDC) is Yousuf Gorsi of the JKNC, part of the PAGD. According to the 2011 census, the district had a population of 1,078,692, roughly equivalent to the nation of Cyprus or the U.S. state of Rhode Island, ranking 425th in India (out of 640). The population density is 375 inhabitants per square kilometre (970/sq mi), with a 37.48% growth rate between 2001 and 2011. The sex ratio is 927 females per 1,000 males (varying by religion), and the literacy rate is 64.32%. About 26.23% of the population lives in urban areas, with Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes constituting 0.17% and 10.75% of the population, respectively. Anantnag city, with a population of 108,505, is the largest city in the district, and the Anantnag Urban Agglomeration has a population of 158,785. Kashmiri is the predominant language, spoken by 85.10% of the population, followed by Gujari at 11.46% and Pahari at 1.21%. The nearest airport is Sheikh ul-Alam International Airport in Srinagar, 60 kilometres from Anantnag, and there is an Indian Air Force airbase in Awantipora. The district is well-connected by rail, with the Jammu–Baramulla line passing through it and numerous railway stations. It is also well-connected by roads, including NH 44, NH 244, and NH 501, which run through the district alongside other intra-district roads.

text: Andrea Carol Arpaci-Dusseau (also published as Andrea Dusseau) is an American computer scientist specializing in operating systems, file systems, data storage, distributed computing, and computer science education. She is a professor of computer sciences at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Along with her husband, Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau, she co-authored the free 2018 textbook "Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces" (OSTEP), which is downloaded millions of times annually and is used at hundreds of institutions worldwide. Arpaci-Dusseau earned her bachelor's degree in computer engineering from Carnegie Mellon University, graduating in 1991, and completed her Ph.D. in computer science at the University of California, Berkeley in 1998; her dissertation, "Implicit Coscheduling: Coordinated Scheduling with Implicit Information in Distributed Systems," was supervised by David Culler. After conducting postdoctoral research at Stanford University, she joined the University of Wisconsin–Madison faculty as an assistant professor in 2000 and became a full professor in 2009. She primarily teaches undergraduate and graduate-level operating systems courses. Arpaci-Dusseau is married to Remzi Arpaci-Dusseau, who is also a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison and an expert in data storage; the two are frequent collaborators. In 2018, Arpaci-Dusseau and her husband received the SIGOPS Mark Weiser Award "for outstanding leadership, innovation, and impact in storage and computer systems research." She was named an ACM Fellow in 2020 "for contributions to storage and computer systems."
