text: Emory Andrew Tate III, born on 1 December 1986 at the Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington, D.C., is an American and British social media personality, businessman, and former professional kickboxer who gained notoriety for promoting controversial positions within the manosphere. He has been described as the "king of toxic masculinity," has called himself a misogynist, and is politically categorized as both right-wing and far-right. As of June 2025, he has 10.7 million followers on Twitter and was the third-most googled person in 2023. He is multiracial, with an African American father, Emory Tate (1958–2015), a chess international master, and a White English mother, Eileen Tate, who worked as a catering assistant. He has a younger brother, Tristan, and a younger sister, Janine. Raised in Chicago, Illinois, and Goshen, Indiana, he moved to Luton in Bedfordshire, England, in 1997 after his parents divorced, living on Marsh Farm, which he described as the "worst area of the worst town." He was educated at Halyard High School and Luton Sixth Form College. Tate began practising boxing and martial arts in 2005 and worked in television advertising. From 2005, he began his kickboxing career in England, winning several titles, including the English ISKA Full Contact Cruiserweight Championship in 2009 and the International Kickboxing Federation Full Contact Cruiserweight British Title, and earned the nickname "King Cobra." In 2011, he won his first ISKA full contact world title in a rematch against Jean-Luc Benoît via knockout at 81.5 kg. He competed in the Enfusion 3: Trial of the Gladiators tournament in 2011 and 2012, winning a semi-final match but losing in the final. In 2013, he won his second ISKA world title in the Light Cruiserweight division. He held the Enfusion 90 kg world title in 2014 and became a four-time kickboxing world champion, retiring in 2014 due to eye injuries sustained during his career, which required surgical repair and led to a permanent retirement by age 30. In 2020, he returned to kickboxing, winning knockouts over Miralem Ahmeti, Iulian Strugariu, and Cosmin Lingurar in Romania, before retiring again with a 76–9–1 record. His brother Tristan, who also competed in kickboxing, retired early with a 43–9 record due to a shoulder injury. In 2016, Tate appeared on Big Brother's 17th series as a member of "The Others," but was removed after six days due to an ongoing police investigation into him for rape, which was later dropped. In December 2022, Tate and his brother were arrested in Romania with two women, and in June 2023, all four were charged with rape, human trafficking, and forming an organised crime group to sexually exploit women. Accusers reportedly went into hiding after a campaign of online harassment, and the Tate brothers filed a $5 million defamation lawsuit. In March 2024, British police obtained an arrest warrant for the brothers. In July 2024, a civil case in the UK was brought against the brothers and a third person for alleged tax evasion. In August 2024, Romanian police raided four properties owned by Tate and expanded the investigation to include trafficking minors, sex with a minor, money laundering, and attempting to influence witnesses. Tate and his brother have denied all charges. text: Three of Andrew and Tristan Tate’s Twitter accounts have been suspended at different times. In 2021, an account created by Tate to evade a prior ban was verified by Twitter, contrary to its policies, and was later permanently banned, with Twitter stating the verification occurred in error. In August 2022, after an online campaign to deplatform him, Tate was permanently banned from Facebook and Instagram, losing 4.7 million followers from the latter; Meta cited violations of its policy on "dangerous organizations and individuals." TikTok removed his account after determining it violated policies on content that attacks, threatens, incites violence against, or dehumanises an individual or group, with videos featuring Tate’s name as a hashtag receiving over 13 billion views. YouTube suspended his channel, which had 760,000 subscribers, citing multiple violations, including hate speech and COVID-19 misinformation, and Tate later deleted his Twitch channel, which had 50,000 subscribers. In November 2022, after Elon Musk acquired Twitter, Tate’s Twitter account was reinstated. Tate responded by stating that while most of his comments were taken out of context, he took responsibility for how they were received. Jake Paul denounced Tate’s sexism but called the bans censorship. Tate’s content continues to circulate on Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok via fan accounts. After the bans, Tate moved to alt-tech platforms Gettr and Rumble, causing Rumble to briefly become the most downloaded app on the Apple App Store. In 2025, Tate stated he launched the BRUV (Britain Restoring Underlying Values) Party as part of his plan to become prime minister, with the party’s website declaring it a "war to reclaim Britain" to defend borders, crush crime, purge corruption, and restore national pride. The party launch was widely ridiculed, with one user calling its manifesto a "mix of North Korea and homoeroticism" and another calling it the "very worst idea in the history of British politics"; some speculated it was a PR stunt, but Tate dismissed it, stating he was "100% serious" and would run in the next election. The party’s Twitter handle was suspended but was restored after Tate made a complaint to Elon Musk. In 2017, Tate and his brother moved from the UK to Romania, where they run multiple businesses; Tate cited a preference for countries where corruption is accessible and claimed he would face fewer rape charges there, noting that Romanian police require "evidence" or "CCTV proof" for rape reports, unlike the Western world during the #MeToo movement. He reportedly has several children in Romania whom he visits occasionally. Tate was raised Christian but later became an atheist; by early 2022, he identified as Christian again, tithing £16,000 monthly to the Romanian Orthodox Church. After a viral video of him praying at a mosque in Dubai in October 2022, he announced on Gettr that he had converted to Islam; scholars such as Mufti Menk have commended the decision, calling him a "very sincere brother." In March 2023, during incarceration in Romania, Tate’s legal team reported a "dark spot on his lung, most likely a tumor" following a Dubai medical consultation, sparking online rumors about lung cancer; Tate denied having cancer on Twitter. In June 2025, it was revealed Tate received Vanuatu citizenship through the country’s citizenship by investment scheme in December 2022; a Vanuatu government spokesperson stated they were "definitely looking into" revoking his citizenship. Tate was first arrested in Britain in July 2015 after two women accused him of rape and assault, and was arrested again in December 2015; in 2019, the Crown Prosecution Service declined to file charges. Canadian alt-right activist Lauren Southern wrote in her 2025 memoir that she met Tate in Romania in 2018; she described being taken from a nightclub to her hotel room, kissing him briefly, and then being strangled unconscious after resisting his advances, stating she would prefer not to share the rest. In April 2022, the US embassy received a report that an American citizen was being held against her will in a property owned by the Tate brothers in Pipera, Romania; Romanian police raided the home and a nearby webcam studio, discovering four women, two of whom (the American and a Romanian woman) claimed they were held against their will, triggering an investigation by DIICOT into human trafficking and rape. In December, the Tates and two women were arrested; all four were suspected of human trafficking and forming an organised crime group, with one suspected of rape; Romanian authorities seized 29 assets, including cars, properties, watches, and money, totaling nearly US$4 million. In June 2023, DIICOT upgraded the charges to "human trafficking in continued form," a more serious charge, with seven victims identified; the four accused were indicted on charges of rape, human trafficking, and forming an organised crime group to sexually exploit women; they deny all charges and remain under investigation for money laundering and trafficking of minors. In the same month, the Tate brothers filed a defamation lawsuit against one accuser, their parents, and two others in Palm Beach County, Florida, seeking $5 million in damages, claiming the five conspired to falsely accuse them. In January 2024, the Romanian criminal case was heard in the preliminary chamber, and three months later, the Bucharest Tribunal ruled that the case met legal criteria. That month, US District Judge Robin L. Rosenberg dismissed another defamation lawsuit by the Tates against a former US Marine who reported them to the US Embassy and military officials. In March 2024, Westminster Magistrates' Court issued a European arrest warrant against Andrew and Tristan Tate, based on allegations of sexual aggression from 2012 to 2015; the brothers categorically reject all charges. In July, Devon and Cornwall Police began civil proceedings against Tate, Tristan, and a third person for tax evasion with their online businesses; two months later, three women involved in the British investigation and a fourth British woman filed a civil case against Tate. In August 2024, Romanian police expanded their investigation to include trafficking minors, sex with a minor, money laundering, and attempting to influence witnesses; prosecutors said the new investigation involves 35 alleged victims, including a woman who was a minor at the time; the Tate brothers, among six detained, denied all allegations. In December 2024, the Westminster Magistrates' Court ruled in favor of Devon and Cornwall Police, allowing them to seize £2.8 million in unpaid taxes from the Tate brothers’ online businesses. In February 2025, Alison Hernandez, Police and Crime Commissioner for Devon and Cornwall, announced the force received around £1.2 million, which she intended to support victims of violence against women and girls. In the US, following pressure from the Trump administration on Romanian authorities to lift travel restrictions, Tate left Romania by private jet and arrived in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, where he became the subject of a statewide criminal investigation. In March 2025, Florida’s Attorney General, James Uthmeier, initiated a criminal investigation into Tate upon his arrival. Tate’s ex-girlfriend, Brianna Stern, accused him of choking and beating her at The Beverly Hills Hotel on 10 March, claiming she was later diagnosed with post-concussion syndrome; she filed a lawsuit against him for physical and sexual abuse. text: Andrew Chi-Chih Yao (Chinese: 姚期智; pinyin: Yáo Qīzhì; born December 24, 1946) is a Chinese computer scientist, theoretical physicist, and computational theorist. He is currently a professor and the dean of the Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences (IIIS) at Tsinghua University. Yao used the minimax theorem to prove what is now known as Yao's principle. Born in Shanghai (then part of the Republic of China) on December 24, 1946, Yao was raised in Hong Kong and then Taiwan after his parents moved there. He attended Taipei Municipal Chien Kuo High School, graduated from National Taiwan University with a Bachelor of Science (B.S.) in physics in 1967, and pursued graduate studies in the United States at Harvard University, where he earned a Master of Arts (M.A.) in physics in 1969 and a Ph.D. in theoretical physics in 1972; his doctoral thesis, titled "Internal Symmetries and Positivity," was completed under Nobel Prize laureate Sheldon Glashow. In 1975, after only two years of study, Yao completed a second Ph.D. in computer science from the University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign as a National Science Foundation fellow, with his dissertation "A Study of Concrete Computational Complexity" supervised by Taiwanese computer scientist Chung Laung Liu. He served as an assistant professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (1975–1976), assistant professor at Stanford University (1976–1981), and professor at the University of California, Berkeley (1981–1982). From 1982 to 1986, he was a full professor at Stanford University. In 1986, he became the William and Edna Macaleer Professor of Engineering and Applied Science at Princeton University, a position he held from 1986 to 2004, during which he continued research on algorithms and complexity. In 2004, he became a professor at the Center for Advanced Study, Tsinghua University (CASTU) and the director of the Institute for Theoretical Computer Science (ITCS) at Tsinghua University in Beijing. Since 2010, he has served as the dean of IIIS at Tsinghua University and initiated the Conference on Innovations in Theoretical Computer Science (ITCS). He is also the Distinguished Professor-at-Large in the Chinese University of Hong Kong. Yao was a naturalized U.S. citizen and worked in the U.S. for many years; in 2015, he renounced his U.S. citizenship and became an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences alongside Yang Chen-Ning. He received the Knuth Prize in 1996, the Turing Award in 2000—recognized for his fundamental contributions to the theory of computation, including complexity-based theory in pseudorandom number generation, cryptography, and communication complexity—and the Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technology in 2021. In 2022, he was listed on the Asian Scientist 100. In May 2024, Yao joined Yoshua Bengio, Geoffrey Hinton, and others in publishing an expert consensus paper warning about the extreme risks posed by AI, stating that AI safety research is lagging and calling for "proactive, adaptive governance mechanisms" for policymakers ahead of the AI Seoul Summit. Yao is a member of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences, a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, the American Association for the Advancement of Science, and the Association for Computing Machinery, and an academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. His wife, Frances Yao, is also a theoretical computer scientist.

His leadership contributed to winning Manager of the Year at the London Football Awards on 29 February 2024, following an unbeaten run in their first ten games. However, a 4–2 loss to Liverpool on 5 May marked the club's first four-game league losing streak in 20 years, and despite the poor form, Tottenham finished fifth, qualifying for the 2024–25 UEFA Europa League after a year-long absence from European football. Prior to the 2024–25 season, Postecoglou stated in an interview that he usually wins things in his second year, though after a 1–0 loss to Arsenal on 15 September, he clarified, "I'll correct myself – I don't usually win things, I always win things in my second year. text: Angelos Postecoglou (/ˈændʒ ˌpɒstəˈkɒɡluː/ ANJ POS-tə-KOG-loo; born 27 August 1965) is a soccer manager and former player who was most recently the head coach of Premier League club Nottingham Forest. Born in Nea Filadelfeia, a suburb of Athens, Greece, Postecoglou was born to a family that migrated from the Alaşehir district of Manisa during the 1923 population exchange between Turkey and Greece. After his father, Dimitris ("Jim"), lost his business following the 1967 Greek military coup, the family moved to Australia in 1970 when Postecoglou was five years old. He grew up in Melbourne, Victoria, and at age 10, his parents changed his surname to "Postekos" due to a trend among Greeks to shorten names at the time, though he legally retains Postecoglou. Postecoglou began playing for South Melbourne Hellas at age nine and played 193 games in the National Soccer League from 1984 to 1993, contributing to their 1984 and 1990–91 titles, the latter as captain in a penalty shootout win over Melbourne Croatia. He was coached by Hungarian Ferenc Puskás, whose 4–3–3 formation with rigid full-backs and attacking wingers influenced Postecoglou’s own coaching style, though he later used attacking full-backs in an inverted position. A knee injury ended his NSL career at age 27. He was named starting left back in South Melbourne's team of the century in 2000 and played four senior international games for Australia between 1986 and 1988, including a debut on 3 August 1986 against Czechoslovakia and appearances in both legs of the 1988 Trans-Tasman Cup, which Australia won 4–1 on aggregate. He also represented Australia at youth level in 1985. After retiring, Postecoglou served as an assistant coach at South Melbourne under Jim Pyrgolios and Frank Arok, becoming head coach in 1996 after Arok’s firing. He led South Melbourne to consecutive National Soccer League titles in 1997–98 and 1998–99, and won the 1999 Oceania Club Championship, qualifying for the 2000 FIFA Club World Championship. He stepped down from South Melbourne in 2000 to become coach of Australia’s youth teams, where he helped identify and develop players, though he was replaced in February 2007 after Australia failed to qualify for the 2007 FIFA U-20 World Cup. He worked as a football pundit for Fox Sports and as an elite consultant to Football Federation Victoria. Postecoglou coached Panachaiki in the Greek third division and Whittlesea Zebras in Melbourne while running coaching clinics. On 16 October 2009, he was appointed head coach of Brisbane Roar, replacing Frank Farina. He released several players and acquired others, including Tommy Oar, Michael Zullo, and Adam Sarota, who moved to Utrecht, and striker Sergio van Dijk to Adelaide United. The 4–0 win against Adelaide United in round 13 was widely praised. Postecoglou led the Roar to the Premiership and Championship in the 2010–11 season, winning the Grand Final 4–2 on penalties against Central Coast Mariners in front of 52,168 people at Lang Park, going on a 36-game unbeaten run and losing only one game all season. He signed a two-year extension until the 2013–14 season on 18 March 2011. In the 2011–12 season, Brisbane Roar became the first team to win back-to-back A-League championships, and Postecoglou became the most successful Australian domestic football coach with four national titles. He announced his resignation as head coach of Brisbane Roar on 24 April 2012 after two-and-a-half years. On 26 April 2012, he signed a three-year contract with Melbourne Victory as head coach. His first game was a 2–1 loss to Melbourne Heart, and his first win came against Adelaide United in Round 4. The following year, Melbourne Victory reached the A-League Preliminary Final after beating Perth Glory 2–1 in an Elimination Final. Postecoglou was appointed head coach of the Australia national team on 23 October 2013, replacing Holger Osieck, tasked with regenerating a team seen as overly reliant on the 2006 Golden Generation. In his first match, a friendly against Costa Rica, Australia won 1–0 thanks to a goal from Tim Cahill. For the 2014 FIFA World Cup, Australia was drawn in Group B with Spain, the Netherlands, and Chile, losing to Chile 3–1 and the Netherlands 3–2, and finishing with a 3–0 loss to Spain, but their competitive performances led to belief in a new Golden Generation. In 2015, Australia won the AFC Asian Cup by defeating Kuwait 4–1 and Oman 4–0, beating China 2–0 in the quarter-final and the United Arab Emirates 2–0 in the semi-final, and winning the final 2–1 after extra time against South Korea. On 22 November 2017, two weeks after qualifying for the 2018 FIFA World Cup, Postecoglou announced his resignation as Socceroos coach. On 19 December 2017, he was appointed head coach of Yokohama F. Marinos, beginning after the 2017 Japanese Emperor's Cup. His first domestic game ended in a 1–1 draw against Cerezo Osaka. After a difficult start, he guided the club to the J-League Cup final and a 12th-place finish in the league. He extended his contract with Yokohama after receiving interest from the Greece national team. In 2019, he won the J1 League with Yokohama F. Marinos, securing their first title in 15 years. On 10 June 2021, Postecoglou became head coach of Scottish Premiership club Celtic, signing a 12-month rolling contract, making him the first Australian manager to coach a major European club. Celtic had just lost their league title to Rangers for the first time in a decade and had not hired English manager Eddie Howe. His first game was a 1–1 draw against FC Midtjylland in a UEFA Champions League qualifier, followed by a 2–1 loss in the second leg, leading to elimination. He lost his first league game 2–1 away to Heart of Midlothian on 31 July. On 19 December 2021, Celtic won the Scottish League Cup after defeating Hibernian 2–1 at Hampden Park. On 2 February 2022, a 3–0 win over Rangers put Celtic at the top of the league for the first time in the season, ending a 13-game unbeaten start for opposing manager Giovanni van Bronckhorst. The league title was sealed on 11 May with a 1–1 draw at Dundee United. Postecoglou won the Scottish League Cup a second time in February 2023 after beating Rangers 2–1 in the final. Celtic ended the 2022–23 season with a record eighth domestic treble after winning the Scottish Cup at Hampden Park against Inverness Caledonian Thistle on 3 June. He was named a candidate for The Best FIFA Football Coach after winning the domestic treble. On 6 June 2023, Postecoglou was appointed head coach of Tottenham Hotspur, starting 1 July on a four-year contract, becoming both the first Australian and first Greek to manage in the Premier League. After an unbeaten start to the 2023–24 season with two wins and a draw in his first three matches, he won the Premier League Manager of the Month award for August, becoming the first manager since David Wagner to win it in his first month. On 24 September, he became the first Tottenham manager to earn points from Arsenal away at the Emirates Stadium in four years, after a 2–2 draw. After continuing the unbeaten streak for a second month, he won the September Manager of the Month award, becoming the first ever manager to win it in each of his first two months. On 1 October, he guided Spurs to their first victory against Liverpool in five years, winning 2–1 at home. On 23 October, he achieved his seventh victory in his ninth league game with a 2–0 win over Fulham. He broke the record for most points earned by a Premier League manager in their first nine games, accumulating 23 points and surpassing Guus Hiddink’s 22 from Chelsea in the 2008–09 season. Postecoglou led Tottenham to three consecutive wins and the league's top spot in October, winning Manager of the Month for a third consecutive time, becoming the first manager to win the award for the first three months of a single season. On 6 November, he suffered his first defeat as Tottenham manager in a 4–1 home loss to Chelsea, during which his side was reduced to nine men after a straight red card to Cristian Romero and a second yellow card to Destiny Udogie. The loss began a five-game winless streak, during which the club drew one match and lost the rest, dropping from first to fifth. Leading Tottenham to an unbeaten run in their first ten games contributed to Postecoglou winning Manager of the Year honours at the London Football Awards on 29 February 2024. However, Tottenham was unable to recapture their strong season start.

text: Anna Stepanovna Politkovskaya (née Mazepa; 30 August 1958 – 7 October 2006) was a Russian investigative journalist known for her reporting on political and social events in Russia, particularly the Second Chechen War (1999–2005). Born in New York City in 1958, she was the daughter of Ukrainian Soviet diplomats Stepan Fedorovich Mazepa (1927–2006) from Kostobobriv and Raisa Aleksandrovna (née Novikova; 1929–2021) from Kerch in Crimea. Her father, ethnically Ukrainian, attended a Ukrainian-language school in Chernihiv before the 1941 Nazi invasion and met her mother at a Russian-language night school in Kerch after the war. By 1952, her father was studying in Moscow, where he married her mother, and later became a founding member of the Special Committee against Apartheid in 1962, serving as its secretary until 1974. Her parents bought an apartment in central Moscow in 1962, where she mostly grew up, attending a music school and training in figure skating, and frequently visiting the Krupskaya Library. She graduated from Moscow State University's school of journalism in 1980 with a thesis on the poetry of Marina Tsvetaeva, under the supervision of Yasen Zasurskii, a close friend of the Mazepas. She married fellow student Alexander Politkovsky in 1978, and by 1981 they had two children, Ilya and Vera. Her initial journalistic work began with a brief internship in the mailroom at Izvestia in 1982, and she later worked as a reporter and editor for the Aeroflot emergencies and accidents section at Vozdushnyi transport, gaining access to travel across Russia. She also worked with the creative union Eskart and the St Petersburg publishing house Paritet. After her husband's declining influence following the 1993 Russian constitutional crisis, her career took off; from 1994 to 1999, she served as assistant chief editor of Obshchaya Gazeta, and from June 1999 to 2006, she wrote columns for the investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta. She published several award-winning books about Chechnya, life in Russia, and Russia under Vladimir Putin, including Putin's Russia (2004). Her reporting from Chechnya established her national and international reputation, and she frequently visited hospitals and refugee camps to interview victims of the conflict. She documented alleged abuses by Russian military forces, Chechen rebels, and the Russian-backed administration led by Akhmad and Ramzan Kadyrov, including the brutalization of civilians and the systematic torture, abduction, and murder of individuals. In 1999, she helped evacuate elderly residents from a bombed ethnically-mixed home in Grozny. In 2001, she was detained in Khattuni, Chechnya, where she was interrogated, beaten, and subjected to a mock execution using a BM-21 Grad rocket launcher, after which she was poisoned with tea. In September 2004, while attempting to fly to Beslan to mediate during the school hostage crisis, she fell violently ill and lost consciousness after drinking tea provided by an Aeroflot flight attendant, leading to her being taken off the flight and requiring medical treatment in Moscow. She was a U.S. citizen with a U.S. passport but never relinquished her Russian citizenship. She received numerous international awards for her work and used these platforms to urge Western governments to be more vigilant about Putin's policies after the September 11 attacks. In her book Putin's Russia, she accused the FSB of suppressing civil liberties to establish a Soviet-style dictatorship, admitting that society's apathy had enabled the rise of authoritarianism and warning that without information, Russia was hurtling back into a Soviet abyss. She concluded her essay "Am I Afraid?" with the statement that "If anybody thinks they can take comfort from the 'optimistic' forecast, let them do so. It is certainly the easier way, but it is the death sentence for our grandchildren." In May 2007, Random House posthumously published A Russian Diary, containing extracts from her notebook and writings from December 2003 to August 2005, covering the decline of Russian parliamentary democracy, the Beslan crisis, and the "winter and summer of discontent." The book was edited without her input due to her murder on 7 October 2006, the 54th birthday of Vladimir Putin. She was murdered in the elevator of her apartment block in Moscow on that day, an assassination that drew international attention. In 2014, five men were sentenced to prison for the murder, but it remains unclear who ordered or paid for the contract killing. Politkovskaya received death threats, including threats of rape and a mock execution, and claimed that Kremlin officials only spoke to her in secret, outside public view. She also stated that she was targeted for her work, and that people sometimes paid with their lives for speaking out. In 2001, she fled to Vienna after receiving threats related to a police officer, Sergey Lapin, whom she had exposed for torture and disappearances; Lapin was later convicted in 2005. A former fellow officer of Lapin was among the suspects in her murder, with the motive possibly being revenge for her role in Lapin's conviction. The European Court of Human Rights found the Russian Federation responsible for the forced disappearance of Khadzhi-Murat Yandiyev in 2006, and Colonel-General Alexander Baranov, mentioned by Politkovskaya as ordering the detention of militants in pits, was filmed giving orders to execute Yandiyev.

text: Anna Politkovskaya, an investigative journalist for Moscow's liberal newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was assassinated on 7 October 2006, Putin's birthday, in the lift of her apartment block in central Moscow. She had been shot twice in the chest, once in the shoulder, and once in the head at close range. The murder sparked widespread international reaction. Before her burial on 10 October 2006 at Troyekurovskoye Cemetery, over one thousand mourners paid their respects; no high-ranking Russian officials attended. She was buried near her father, who had died shortly before her. In 2001, she fled to Vienna after receiving email threats from a police officer, Corporal Sergey Lapin, whom she had accused of atrocities in Chechnya; Lapin was later convicted in 2005 for torture and disappearance of a Chechen civilian, a case she exposed in her article "Disappearing People." A former fellow officer of Lapin was among the suspects in her murder, with revenge being a suspected motive. In 2004, Politkovskaya had a conversation with Ramzan Kadyrov, then Prime Minister of Chechnya, who reportedly said, "You're an enemy. To be shot," and one of his assistants suggested she should have been shot in Moscow. On the day of her murder, she had planned to publish a lengthy story on torture by Chechen security detachments known as Kadyrovites. She had described Kadyrov as the "Chechen Stalin of our days" in her final interview. In May 2007, a posthumous collection of her articles, With Good Reason, was published by Novaya Gazeta at the Gorbachev Foundation, shortly after Vera's daughter was named Anna in her honor. In 2008, ten men were detained on suspicion of involvement in her murder; four were brought before the Moscow District Military Court. Three were charged with aiding the killer, who was allegedly the brother of two suspects; there was insufficient evidence to charge an FSB colonel, though he was suspected of organizing the murder and stood trial for another offense. The case was held before a jury, a rare occurrence in Russia, and was open to the press and public. On 25 November 2008, Murad Musayev, a lawyer for the defendants, stated that case notes suggested a Russian politician (not named) had ordered her death. On 5 December 2008, Sergei Sokolov, a senior Novaya Gazeta editor, testified that Dzhabrail Makhmudov was an FSB agent and that his uncle, Lom-Ali Gaitukayev, also worked for the FSB and was serving a 12-year sentence for an attempted murder. After the three men were acquitted in February 2009, Politkovskaya’s children, Vera and Ilya, along with their lawyers and Sokolov, criticized the trial. Andrew McIntosh, a Council of Europe official, condemned the lack of progress in the investigation, calling it a "blatant failure" and urging a relaunch of the probe, citing similar cases like the killings of Georgy Gongadze and Paul Klebnikov. On 19 January 2009, Stanislav Markelov, a lawyer who had investigated abuses documented by Politkovskaya, was assassinated in Moscow; journalist Anastasia Baburova died from injuries while trying to intervene. On 15 July 2009, Natalia Estemirova, a board member of Memorial and a key colleague of Politkovskaya in Chechnya, was abducted in Grozny and found dead in Ingushetia. In August 2009, the Supreme Court upheld the prosecution's objection to the acquittals and ordered a new trial. In August 2011, Russian prosecutors claimed to be close to solving the murder after detaining Dmitry Pavliuchenkov, a former policeman, alleged to be the principal organizer. In December 2012, Pavliuchenkov was found guilty and sentenced to 11 years in a high-security penal colony. In May 2014, five men were convicted of her murder, including three previously acquitted defendants; in June 2014, Lom-Ali Gaitukayev and Rustam Makhmudov received life sentences, though it remained unclear who ordered or paid for the killing. In September 2016, Vladimir Markin, an official of the Investigative Committee, included Politkovskaya’s killing in a list of the Most Dramatic Crimes in 21st century Russia and claimed it had been solved. Her colleagues at Novaya Gazeta protested that without identifying the instigator or sponsor, the case was not closed. On 7 October 2016, Novaya Gazeta released a video in which staff members repeatedly stated, "The sponsor of Anna's murder has not been found." Deputy chief editor Sergei Sokolov published a critical summary of the investigation, describing its false turns and shortcomings, and noted that after the 2014 convictions, the investigative team was reduced to one person who retired within a year, replaced by a lower-ranking investigator. He referenced the 2000 killing of Igor Domnikov, which was later solved, as evidence that perpetrators could be identified. The Intercept published a top-secret document from Edward Snowden showing that on 5 December 2005, the Russian Federal Intelligence Services (likely FSB) launched a cyberattack on Politkovskaya’s webmail account using malicious software not available in the public domain; it was unclear if this attack was linked to her death. Politkovskaya was described as brave, bold, and beautiful, and her fearless reporting on state abuses made her a lonely but powerful voice. A biographical film, initially titled Anna and later renamed Words of War, began production in 2022 with Maxine Peake, Jason Isaacs, and Ciaran Hinds, and had a limited release on 2 May 2025. The 2007–2008 academic year at the College of Europe was named in her honor. The international human rights organization RAW in WAR, founded in 2006 by Mariana Katzarova, established the annual Anna Politkovskaya Award to recognize a woman human rights defender in a conflict zone who stands up for victims at great personal risk. The award was first given on the first anniversary of her murder to Natalia Estemirova, who was abducted and killed in 2009. There is also a "Journalism-prize Anna Politkovskaja" awarded annually in Ferrara, Italy, by the magazine L'internationale and the comune of Ferrara.

text: Anne Legendre Armstrong (December 27, 1927 – July 30, 2008) was a United States diplomat and politician who made history as the first woman to serve as Counselor to the President and as United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom. She held these positions under the administrations of Richard Nixon, Gerald Ford, and Jimmy Carter. Armstrong was born on December 27, 1927, in New Orleans, Louisiana, and graduated from Vassar College in 1949. She married Tobin Armstrong, a cattle rancher from Texas, in 1950. From 1966 to 1968, she served as vice chairman of the Texas Republican Party, and from 1971 to 1973, she was co-chairman of the Republican National Committee. She delivered the keynote address at the 1972 Republican National Convention, becoming the first woman from either major party to do so. On December 16, 1972, at a White House Christmas dinner, she praised both "Jesus Christ, the Prince of Peace" and President Nixon, who had ordered the Christmas Bombing of North Vietnam, in the same breath. Nixon appointed her Counselor to the President on December 19, 1972, a role she held from January 19, 1973, to November 1974 under President Ford. During her time as Counselor, she founded the first Office of Women's Programs in the White House, which preceded the current White House Council on Women and Girls. Fluent in Spanish, she served as Nixon’s liaison to Hispanic Americans and was a member of a Cabinet committee on opportunities for Spanish-speaking people. From 1976 to 1977, she was the first woman to serve as United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom. At the 1976 Republican National Convention in Kansas City, Missouri, there was a draft effort to nominate her as vice presidential candidate with President Gerald Ford, but Senator Robert Dole was selected instead. In 1978, she supported George W. Bush in his successful primary challenge to Jim Reese in Texas's 19th congressional district. Armstrong was a strong advocate for the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA), stating in 1971 that it had become a symbol of meaning for many and would resolve numerous legal questions. In 1987, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from President Ronald Reagan. In 1989, she was awarded the Golden Plate Award by the American Academy of Achievement. She also received an honorary Doctor of Laws from St. Mary's University in 1978. Armstrong died of cancer in 2008 and is buried at Oakwood Cemetery in Austin, Texas.

text: Anne Morgan, Baroness Hunsdon (c. 1529 – 19 January 1607), was an English official born around 1529 at Arkestone, Herefordshire, the daughter of Sir Thomas Morgan and Anne Elizabeth Whitney, daughter of Sir James Whitney and Blanche Milbourne. The Morgan family was of Welsh origin. On 21 May 1545, she married Henry Carey, son of Sir William Carey and Mary Boleyn, the elder sister of Queen consort Anne Boleyn; due to Carey's mother having been a mistress of King Henry VIII, some, including John Hales, vicar of Isleworth, speculated that Carey was the King's illegitimate son. Henry Carey was created Baron Hunsdon on 13 January 1559, after which Anne was styled Baroness Hunsdon. Following her elevation, she served Queen Elizabeth I as a Lady of the Privy Chamber, who was also her husband's first cousin and held the couple in high favour. Carey was appointed Captain of the Gentlemen-at-Arms, serving as the Queen's personal bodyguard. A painting by an unknown artist commemorates a visit by the Queen to Anne and Carey at Hunsdon House in Hertfordshire in September 1571; Anne is believed to be depicted among the Queen's Ladies in the royal procession as the foremost lady dressed in white. Anne's portrait, painted by a follower of George Gower, is displayed at Hatfield House. The couple had thirteen children, two of whom died in infancy. Henry Carey had several illegitimate children, including Valentine Carey; one of his mistresses was Emilia Bassano, believed by some, including A. L. Rowse, to have been the inspiration for William Shakespeare's sonnet The Dark Lady, due to her black hair and dark complexion; her son Henry, born in 1592, may have been fathered by her, although she was 63 at the time of the child's birth. Upon Henry Carey's death on 23 July 1596, he left his family in debt; Queen Elizabeth I paid for his funeral expenses, gave Anne a gift of £400, and provided her with an annual pension of £200 from the Exchequer. Anne used part of the funds to erect a monument to her husband in Westminster Abbey. On 14 December 1595, seven months before Carey's death, Queen Elizabeth appointed Anne as Keeper of Somerset House, a royal residence where the Queen had lived before her accession; Anne held this post for life, having previously held it in 1574 with her husband. Anne died on 19 January 1607 and was buried in Westminster Abbey; her will, dated 10 January 1607, was proved on 22 January.

text: Annie Jump Cannon (December 11, 1863 – April 13, 1941) was an American astronomer whose cataloging work was essential to the development of modern stellar classification. Alongside Edward C. Pickering, she developed the Harvard Classification Scheme, the first systematic effort to classify stars based on temperature and spectral type. Cannon became nearly deaf after 1893 due to scarlet fever, which affected her social life and led her to focus intensely on her research. Born in Dover, Delaware, she was the eldest of three daughters of Wilson Cannon, a shipbuilder and state senator, and Mary Jump; her mother introduced her to astronomy and encouraged her to study mathematics, chemistry, and biology at Wellesley College. Using an old astronomy textbook, Cannon and her mother identified stars from their attic, and her mother also taught her household economics, which she applied to organize her research. At Wilmington Conference Academy and later Wellesley College, Cannon excelled in mathematics and became valedictorian, graduating with a physics degree in 1884. She developed skills in photography during a 1892 trip through Europe, and her photos and writings from Spain were published in a pamphlet titled "In the Footsteps of Columbus" for the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition. After her mother’s death in 1894, Cannon sought employment through her former instructor, Sarah Frances Whiting, who hired her as a junior physics teacher at Wellesley, allowing her to take graduate courses and learn spectroscopy. In 1894, she enrolled at Radcliffe College as a "special student" to access the Harvard College Observatory. In 1896, Pickering hired her as an assistant at the Observatory and she joined the Harvard Computers, a group of women tasked with completing the Henry Draper Catalogue, which aimed to map and classify every star to a photographic magnitude of about 9. Cannon used "Int" in her notes to denote brightness. By 1913, she could classify 200 stars per hour, classifying three stars per minute by spectral patterns and even identifying stars down to the ninth magnitude using a magnifying glass. Her work was highly accurate. Initially, disagreements arose over star classification, with Nettie Farrar leaving early, and conflicting approaches from Antonia Maury and Williamina Fleming; Cannon resolved this by applying a new system dividing stars into spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, M based on Balmer absorption lines, which later aligned with stellar temperature. In 1901, she published her first catalog of stellar spectra. Despite initial criticism for being outside traditional gender roles, Cannon gained respect through her "tidiness" and patience, and she helped men in the observatory gain recognition by facilitating international partnerships. In 1911, she became Curator of Astronomical Photographs at Harvard; in 1914, she was admitted as an honorary member of the Royal Astronomical Society; in 1921, she received an honorary doctorate in math and astronomy from Groningen University; in 1925, she became the first woman to receive an honorary doctorate of science from Oxford University. On May 9, 1922, the International Astronomical Union formally adopted her stellar classification system, which remains in use today with minor adjustments. In 1922, she spent six months in Arequipa, Peru, photographing southern hemisphere stars. In 1933, she represented professional women at the Chicago World's Fair (Century of Progress), and in 1935, she established the Annie J. Cannon Prize for distinguished contributions by women in astronomy. In 1938, she became the William C. Bond Astronomer at Harvard. Cecilia Payne collaborated with Cannon and used her data to demonstrate that stars are primarily composed of hydrogen and helium. Cannon’s career spanned over 40 years, ending with retirement in 1940, but she continued working actively in the observatory until shortly before her death. She classified approximately 350,000 stars in her lifetime, discovered 300 variable stars, five novas, and one spectroscopic binary, and compiled a bibliography of about 200,000 references. She died on April 13, 1941, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, at age 77, after being ill for over a month. The American Astronomical Society awards the Annie Jump Cannon Award annually to female astronomers for distinguished work in astronomy.

text: Anselm Kiefer, born on 8 March 1945 in Donaueschingen, Germany, the son of a German art teacher, grew up in a city heavily bombed at the end of World War II, experiencing the war's devastation firsthand. His family moved to Ottersdorf in 1951, and he attended public school in Rastatt, graduating in 1965. He initially studied pre-law and Romance languages at the University of Freiburg before switching to art, studying at art academies in Freiburg and Karlsruhe, where he studied under Peter Dreher, a realist and figurative painter. He received an art degree in 1969. In 1971, Kiefer moved to Hornbach (Walldürn) and established a studio, remaining in the Neckar-Odenwald-Kreis until 1992, during which time his work is known as The German Years. In 1992, he relocated to France, first to Barjac, and from 2008 lived primarily in Paris in the Marais district with his second wife, the Austrian photographer Renate Graf, and their two children; they divorced in 2014. Kiefer has lived and worked in France since 1992, and since 2008 has resided primarily in Paris. In 2018, he was awarded Austrian citizenship. His works incorporate materials such as straw, ash, clay, lead, and shellac, and he values a "spiritual connection" with these materials, extracting the spirit already within them through processes like acid baths and physical blows with sticks and axes. He is particularly drawn to lead for its alchemical properties, noting its colorful appearance during heating and melting, especially the gold-like hues associated with alchemists. Straw represents energy due to its gold color and heat when burned, with the resulting ash symbolizing new creation and transformation. Kiefer emphasizes a balance between order and chaos, stating that too much order makes a piece dead and too much chaos prevents coherence, and he believes his works lose their power if placed in inappropriate spaces. His early career included performances documented in photographs titled Occupations and Heroische Sinnbilder, in which he dressed in his father's Wehrmacht uniform and mimicked the Nazi salute in France, Switzerland, and Italy to provoke German reflection on the Third Reich's xenophobia. In 1969, he presented his first solo exhibition, "Besetzungen (Occupations)," at Galerie am Kaiserplatz in Karlsruhe. His paintings have grown increasingly large, incorporating lead, broken glass, and dried plants, resulting in encrusted surfaces and thick impasto. By 1970, while studying informally under Joseph Beuys at Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, his style resembled Georg Baselitz’s, using glass, straw, wood, and plant parts, creating temporary, fragile works that emphasized natural forms. He returned to his birthplace in 1971 and later incorporated German mythology and studied Kabbalah, including the works of Robert Fludd. He made extended journeys throughout Europe, the US, and the Middle East, which influenced his work. In the 1970s and early 1980s, he created works based on Richard Wagner’s Der Ring des Nibelungen, and in the early 1980s produced over thirty paintings referencing Paul Celan’s poem "Todesfuge" ("Death Fugue"). Between 1980 and 1983, he painted looming stone edifices referencing National Socialist architecture, particularly buildings by Albert Speer and Wilhelm Kreis; the grand plaza in To the Unknown Painter (1983) specifically refers to the outdoor courtyard of Hitler’s Chancellery in Berlin. Between 1984 and 1985, he made works on paper with manipulated black-and-white photographs of desolate landscapes with utility poles and power lines, such as Heavy Cloud (1985), in response to West Germany’s controversy over NATO’s nuclear missile stationing. By the mid-1980s, his themes expanded to include art and culture’s fate, occult symbolism, theology, and mysticism, focusing on societal trauma and renewal. His 1980s paintings became more physical, featuring unusual textures and materials. He incorporated ancient Hebrew and Egyptian history, as in Osiris and Isis (1985–87), and in the 1990s shifted to universal myths of existence and meaning. From 1995 to 2001, he produced a cycle of large cosmic paintings. One of his most unusual works is 20 Years of Solitude (1971–1991), a ceiling-high stack of hundreds of white-painted ledgers and handmade books strewn with dirt and dried vegetation, with pages stained by his semen; the title references his frequent masturbation during its creation. He shocked the art world in May 1993 at a dinner party in New York, where he and Renate Graf decorated a candlelit loft with white muslin, skinned animals on hooks, white sand, and waiters dressed as mimes, serving arcane white organ meats, which guests found unappetizing; performers including Johanna Constantine, Lavinia Coop, Armen Ra, and Flotilla DeBarge were hired, and Anohni sang for the guests. Since 2002, he has worked with concrete, creating towers for Pirelli warehouses in Milan, paintings of the sea and boats with leaden objects (2004–05), rune motif paintings (2004–06), and other sculptures. In 2003, he held his first solo show at Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac, Salzburg Villa Katz, titled Am Anfang, focusing on history and myths. In 2005, he held a second exhibition, Für Paul Celan, at the same gallery, focusing on books and Germanic mythology linked to Paul Celan’s poetry, featuring eleven canvas works, bound books, and five sculptures, including a monumental outdoor concrete and lead sculpture, lead books with bronze sunflowers, lead ships and wedges, and two lead books from The Secret Life of Plants. The exhibition toured to Paris and Galerie Yvon Lambert. In 2006, his exhibition Velimir Chlebnikov was shown in a studio near Barjac, then at White Cube in London, and finally at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum in Connecticut; it consists of 30 large (2 × 3 meters) paintings in two banks of 15, hung in a corrugated steel building mimicking the studio, referencing the Russian futurist Velimir Chlebnikov’s theories of a "language of the future" called "Zaum" and cataclysmic sea battles every 317 years, with toy-like, battered, rusted battleships hanging in paint and plaster waves, using black, white, gray, and rust colors. In 2007, he became the first artist since Georges Braque in 1970 to be commissioned to install a permanent work at the Louvre, Paris, and inaugurated the Monumenta exhibitions series at the Grand Palais, honoring Paul Celan and Ingeborg Bachmann. In 2009, he mounted two exhibitions at White Cube in London: Karfunkelfee, a series of forest diptychs and triptychs in glass vitrines filled with Moroccan thorns, referencing a term from German Romanticism by Ingeborg Bachmann, and The Fertile Crescent, a group of epic paintings inspired by a trip to India, linking Mesopotamian civilizations to post-WWII German ruins, with historian Simon Schama noting its meditation on the instability of built grandeur. In Morgenthau Plan (2012), a golden wheat field sculpture is enclosed in a five-meter-high steel cage. That year, he inaugurated a gallery space in Pantin, with the exhibition Die Ungeborenen, accompanied by a publication with a letter by Kiefer and essays by Alexander Kluge and Emmanuel Daydé. He continues to be represented by Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac and participates in group and solo exhibitions at their locations. In 1969, Kiefer began designing books; early examples are worked-over photographs, while recent ones consist of lead sheets layered with paint, minerals, or dried plant matter, such as the lead books on steel shelves symbolizing stored, discarded historical knowledge. The book Rhine (1981) comprises 25 woodcuts suggesting a journey along the Rhine River, with scenes of the unspoiled river interrupted by dark, swirling pages representing the sinking of the battleship Bismarck in 1941 during an Atlantic sortie codenamed Rhine Exercise. Kiefer’s first large studio was in the attic of his home in Hornbach, later moved to a factory in Buchen, and in 1988 he transformed a former brick factory in Höpfingen into an extensive artwork with installations and sculptures. In 1991, after twenty years in the Odenwald, he traveled to India, Mexico, Japan, Thailand, Indonesia, Australia, and the United States. In 1992, he established himself in Barjac, France, where he transformed his 35-hectare studio compound La Ribaute into a Gesamtkunstwerk—a derelict silk factory now housing an extensive system of glass buildings, archives, installations, storerooms, subterranean chambers, and corridors. Sophie Fiennes filmed the studio complex in Barjac for her documentary Over Your Cities Grass Will Grow (2010), which captured both the environment and the artist at work, with one critic noting that the project spans acres, featuring miles of corridors, large studio spaces, landscape paintings, sculptures, and serpentine excavated labyrinths resembling stalagmites or termite mounds, with no clear boundary between work and finished product.

text: Santa Anna made a major miscalculation by selling territory to the United States in the Gadsden Purchase, which involved land in northwest Mexico known as La Mesilla. This area was considered easier for building a transcontinental railway in the U.S., and the purchase money was intended to benefit Mexico’s empty treasury. However, Santa Anna sought immediate access to funds and negotiated with American bankers to receive cash upfront, with the bankers gaining rights to future revenue. The deal resulted in Mexico receiving only $250,000 against a credit of $650,000 going to the bankers, a sum James Gadsden believed was likely much higher. A group of liberal leaders, including Alvarez, Benito Juárez, and Ignacio Comonfort, overthrew Santa Anna under the Plan of Ayutla, leading to his exile in 1855. By the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, the United States paid Mexico $15 million for the land, known as the Mexican Cession. Santa Anna married twice: first in 1825 to Inés García, daughter of wealthy Spanish parents in Veracruz, with whom he had four children—María de Guadalupe, María del Carmen, Manuel, and Antonio López de Santa Anna y García. His family background was of modest means, but his creole lineage and the dowry from Inés allowed him to purchase his first hacienda, Manga de Clavo, in Veracruz. The first Spanish ambassador to Mexico, Fanny Calderón de la Barca, visited Inés at Manga de Clavo and noted the hospitality, including a breakfast where Inés offered her a cigar and others followed suit. Two months after Inés’ death in 1844, Santa Anna married 16-year-old María de los Dolores de Tosta; they rarely lived together, with De Tosta residing in Mexico City and Santa Anna traveling for political and military duties. They had no children, and biographer Will Fowler speculated the marriage was either platonic or that De Tosta was infertile. Several women claimed to have borne Santa Anna natural children; in his will, he acknowledged and provided for four—Paula, María de la Merced, Petra, and José López de Santa Anna—and biographers have identified three more: Pedro López de Santa Anna, Ángel and Augustina Rosa López de Santa Anna. From 1855 to 1874, Santa Anna lived in exile in Cuba, the United States, Colombia, and Saint Thomas, leaving Mexico due to his unpopularity after his defeat in 1848. During exile, he engaged in gambling and business ventures, and was a passionate fan of cockfighting, maintaining many roosters for competitions. In the 1850s, he traveled to New York City with a shipment of chicle, intending to sell it for carriage wheels, but failed to convince U.S. manufacturers of its usefulness in tires. Although he introduced chewing gum to the U.S., he did not profit from it. Thomas Adams, assigned to assist Santa Anna, experimented with chicle and, though his attempts to use it as rubber failed, helped found the chewing gum industry with a product called "chiclets." In 1865, Santa Anna tried to return to Mexico to serve during the French invasion, but was refused by Juárez. That year, a schooner owned by Gilbert Thompson, son-in-law of Daniel Tompkins, brought him to Staten Island, where he attempted to raise funds for an army to retake Mexico City. In 1874, Santa Anna returned to Mexico under a general amnesty issued by President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada, having become crippled and nearly blind from cataracts. He died at his home in Mexico City on 21 June 1876 at age 82 and was buried with full military honors in a glass coffin at Panteón del Tepeyac Cemetery. Santa Anna was highly controversial, with Will Fowler describing him as a liberal, Republican, army man, hero, revolutionary, and regional strongman, but never a politician, who presented himself as a mediator against party politics and was more willing to lead armies than govern. Historian Gates Brown considers Santa Anna one of history’s worst military leaders due to his errors in two wars that cost Mexico significant territory. During the Texas Revolution, Santa Anna attacked the Alamo after knowing the defenders would not be reinforced, despite having time to build a logistical base at San Antonio. He lost more men than the defenders, sacrificing a third of his force, and his subsequent executions at the Alamo and Goliad fueled rebellion. He also mistakenly believed General Houston would not attack with a smaller, tired force, contributing to his defeat at San Jacinto. In the Mexican-American War, Santa Anna marched newly recruited and inexperienced troops across 385 kilometers (239 miles) of desert in winter without resupplying, leading to heavy Mexican casualties at Buena Vista. At Cerro Gordo, he dismissed advice from officer Manuel Robles Pezuela to reinforce Atalaya hill, believing the terrain made it unnecessary; the U.S. attack and flanking maneuver destroyed Mexico’s chance to stop General Winfield Scott’s advance on Mexico City. Santa Anna became prominent in Tejano folk memory due to his role in the Texas Revolution and the Alamo. Texas educators, writers, and officials portrayed him as the central antagonist in Texas’ independence narrative, contributing to an exaggerated view of his personal influence and a symbolic representation of Mexican autocracy, rather than a complex figure navigating internal Mexican instability. Stephen Oleszek argues that Santa Anna’s rise as a Texas folk legend is tied to myth-making around the Alamo, where he was depicted as a symbol of despotism while Alamo defenders like William B. Travis and James Bowie were portrayed as heroes, reinforcing a hero-villain dichotomy to unify Anglo-Americans and justify the Texas Revolution. This narrative has been embedded in textbooks, media, and the slogan "Remember the Alamo!" More recent works, such as Santa Anna in Texas: A Mexican American Viewpoint, show that Mexican perspectives on Santa Anna were divided and often did not align with the villainous Texan narrative. text: Antonio de Padua María Severino López de Santa Anna y Pérez de Lebrón (21 February 1794 – 21 June 1876) was a Mexican general, politician, and caudillo who served as the 8th president of Mexico on multiple occasions between 1833 and 1855 and held the office of vice president from 1837 to 1839. He is widely regarded as a controversial and pivotal figure in 19th-century Mexican politics, often referred to as an "uncrowned monarch" and associated with the "Age of Santa Anna." Born in Xalapa, Veracruz, into a respected Spanish family, he was named after his father, licenciado Antonio López de Santa Anna y Pérez, a lawyer, and his mother, Manuela Pérez de Lebrón y Cortés. His family prospered in Veracruz, where the merchant class dominated politics; his paternal uncle, Ángel López de Santa Anna, was a public clerk who became disgruntled when barred from moving to Mexico City due to the Spanish crown’s preference for peninsular-born Spaniards. Santa Anna’s mother supported his military career over his father’s preference for commerce, and her relationship with the intendant of Veracruz secured his early military appointment. The family had seven children, including four sisters and two brothers, with Santa Anna being close to his sister Francisca and brother Manuel, who also joined the army. His origins in Veracruz gave him immunity from yellow fever, a significant advantage in military campaigns, and contributed to his rise as a provincial leader. He began his military career in 1810 at age 16 with the Fijo de Veracruz regiment, fought against insurgents during the Mexican War of Independence, and was wounded in 1811. He later served in Texas and earned recognition for bravery at the Battle of Medina. When Agustín de Iturbide switched sides in 1821 to support independence, Santa Anna joined him, was granted command of Veracruz, and later rebelled against Iturbide in 1822, claiming the dissolution of the Constituent Congress as justification. He then participated in the Plan of Casa Mata, which led to the end of the First Mexican Empire and the establishment of a republic. In 1823, he was sent to Yucatán, where he planned an invasion of Cuba but abandoned it when Spanish reinforcements arrived. After the 1828 election, when conservative Manuel Gómez Pedraza won, Santa Anna rebelled, nullified the results, and expelled Spanish nationals, leading to Gómez Pedraza’s resignation and the rise of Guerrero. In 1829, Santa Anna defeated a Spanish invasion at Tampico, earning the title "Victor of Tampico" and "Savior of the Patria," and styled himself the "Napoleon of the West." When Vice President Anastasio Bustamante overthrew Guerrero in 1829, Santa Anna seized Veracruz’s customs revenues and declared rebellion, forcing Bustamante’s cabinet to resign and leading to new elections in 1833. Santa Anna was elected president on 1 April 1833, but he was not interested in governing and is described as an "absentee president," with Vice President Valentín Gómez Farías managing day-to-day affairs. Gómez Farías implemented liberal reforms, including abolishing tithing, seizing church property, closing the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico, and secularizing Franciscan missions in Alta California. These actions provoked strong opposition from the church and army, leading to the Plan of Cuernavaca, which called for the repeal of the Ley del Caso, the removal of reform supporters, and the recognition of Santa Anna as the sole authority. As opposition grew, Santa Anna returned to the presidency, and Gómez Farías resigned, marking a shift from a federalist republic to a unitary central republic. Historians debate the number of his presidencies: Will Fowler cites six, the Texas State Historical Association claims five, Alexander Dawson and the University of Texas Libraries state eleven, though the latter notes he was only president for six years due to short terms. Santa Anna is viewed negatively in Mexican history, often ranked as "the principal inhabitant even today of Mexico's black pantheon of those who failed the nation," and considered one of the most unpopular and controversial Mexican presidents. After being overthrown and exiled in 1855 through the Plan of Ayutla, he faded from prominence during the Reform War, the Second French Intervention, and the establishment of the Second Mexican Empire. An elderly Santa Anna was allowed to return in 1874 by President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada and died in relative obscurity in 1876. He is best known in the United States for his roles in the Texas Revolution and the Mexican–American War, where his leadership prolonged the conflict and contributed to the Mexican Cession and the Gadsden Purchase in 1853. His intermittent rule from 1832 to 1853 saw the loss of Texas, military failures, and territorial concessions. Historian Alexander Dawson notes that Santa Anna switched sides between the Liberal and Conservative Parties, playing a key role in both discarding and restoring the liberal Constitution of 1824. He is remembered as a populist caudillo who used military power to dissolve Congress and referred to himself as "His Most Serene Highness."

text: Antonio Negri (/ˈnɛɡri/; Italian: [ˈneːɡri]; 1 August 1933 – 16 December 2023) was an Italian political philosopher renowned as one of the most prominent theorists of autonomism and co-author of the books *Empire* and *Multitude: War and Democracy in the Age of Empire* with Michael Hardt. Born in Padua, in the Veneto region of northeastern Italy, Negri’s father was a communist militant from Bologna in Emilia-Romagna, and although he died when Negri was two, his political engagement influenced Negri’s early exposure to Marxism; his mother was a teacher from Poggio Rusco in Lombardy. Negri began his activism in the 1950s with the Roman Catholic youth organization Gioventù Italiana di Azione Cattolica (GIAC), joined the Italian Socialist Party in 1956, and became a communist in 1955 while working at the Nahsonim kibbutz in central Israel, a Jewish communist community based on Zionist socialism. He earned a doctorate in philosophy in 1956 and was hired as a professor of dottrina dello Stato ("state doctrine"), a field akin to the philosophy of law, at the University of Padua, where he taught state and constitutional theory. In the early 1960s, he joined the editorial group of *Quaderni Rossi*, a journal that marked the intellectual revival of Marxism outside the Communist Party. In 1969, he co-founded the Potere Operaio (Worker Power) group with Oreste Scalzone and Franco Piperno, launching the operaismo (workerism) movement. On 16 March 1978, former Italian prime minister Aldo Moro was kidnapped in Rome by the Red Brigades (Brigate Rosse or BR), and nine days before his death, the BR called Moro’s family to inform them of his impending death—this call was later revealed to have been made by Valerio Morucci, not Negri. On 7 April 1979, Negri was arrested and charged with kidnapping, assassination, and insurrection, including leadership of the Red Brigades, masterminding the 1978 kidnapping and murder of Aldo Moro, and plotting to overthrow the government. While a leader of the BR testified that Negri had nothing to do with the group, charges such as "armed insurrection against the state" were dropped, but he was sentenced in absentia to 30 years in prison in 1984 after fleeing to France, with an additional four years for moral responsibility for political violence in the 1960s and 1970s, specifically for instigating the murder of Carlo Saronio and for "morally concurred" involvement in the murder of Andrea Lombardini during a failed bank robbery. Michel Foucault remarked, "Isn't he in jail simply for being an intellectual?" and French philosophers Félix Guattari and Gilles Deleuze signed *L'Appel des intellectuels français contre la répression en Italie* in 1977 in protest against Negri’s imprisonment. Italian President Francesco Cossiga described Negri as "a psychopath" who "poisoned the minds of an entire generation of Italy's youth." In 1983, while still in prison, Negri was elected to the Italian legislature as a member of the Radical Party, used parliamentary immunity to be freed, and fled to France with the help of Félix Guattari and Amnesty International, though his immunity was later revoked by the Chamber of Deputies. Protected by the Mitterrand doctrine, he taught at Paris VIII (Vincennes) and the Collège international de philosophie, alongside Jacques Derrida, Michel Foucault, and Gilles Deleuze. In 1997, after a plea-bargain that reduced his sentence from 30 to 13 years, he returned to Italy to serve the remainder of his sentence, during which time he wrote many of his most influential works. He was released in 2003 and lived in Venice and Paris with his partner, the French philosopher Judith Revel. He was the father of film director Anna Negri. Negri was a central theorist of autonomist Marxism and a prominent figure in libertarian socialism, communism, and Marxism. In *Empire*, co-authored with Michael Hardt, they ask how labor, with its life-affirming potential, has become a tool of capitalist discipline, exploitation, and domination, and they critique liberal and socialist notions of labor and institutional reform from a radical democratic perspective, challenging the state-form itself. They argue that the rise of "Empire" marks the end of national conflict, where the enemy is no longer ideological or national but is instead a criminal threatening the law, and is both "banalized" and "absolutized." Empire is constituted by a monarchy (the United States and G8, and institutions like NATO, IMF, WTO), an oligarchy (multinational corporations and nation-states), and a democracy (NGOs and the UN). The book asserts that resistance to Empire is only possible through negation—“the will to be against”—and that although Empire is total, economic inequality persists and the identity of the poor endures. *Multitude* picks up where *Empire* leaves off, analyzing war and its contradictions, and focusing on the multitude and democracy. It is presented as a reiteration from a new point of view in a more accessible style, remaining a philosophical work aimed at shaping a conceptual ground for democratic political processes rather than offering a concrete program. In 2009, Negri completed *Commonwealth*, the final book in a trilogy beginning with *Empire* and continuing with *Multitude* in 2004. In *Commonwealth*, the authors introduce the concept of "the republic of property," stating that property remains the foundation of every modern political constitution. Part two explores altermodernity, which involves breaking with the fixed dialectic between modern sovereignty and antimodern resistance, transforming tradition, identity, and resistance into new forms. They argue that communism is defined by the common, capitalism by the private, and socialism (identified with statism) by the public. Alex Callinicos notes that the "common" includes not only natural resources but also languages, social practices, and modes of sociality, which are both means and results of biopolitical production. David Harvey observes that Hardt and Negri seek an altermodernity outside the binary of modernity and anti-modernity, proposing a new form of communism that operates beyond the choice between capitalism and socialism, and that revolutionary thought must engage identity politics as the primary vehicle for struggle against the "republic of property." In May 2012, he self-published (with Michael Hardt) an electronic pamphlet titled *Declaration*, arguing that the Occupy and encampment movements explore new forms of democracy; the introduction was published at Jacobin under the title "Take Up the Baton." In October 2011, he and Hardt published an article in *Foreign Affairs* titled "The Encampment in Lower Manhattan Speaks to a Failure of Representation." In 2013, Negri published *Spinoza: Politics and Postmodernity*, a collection of essays on Spinoza and his contemporary relevance, translated by William McCuaig. In 2017, Negri and Michael Hardt published *Assembly*, which reflects on contemporary capitalism and social movements, drawing on concepts from their Empire trilogy such as the common, the multitude, and globalization. It introduces the concept of "assembly," inspired by Deleuze and Guattari’s "assemblage," as a way of understanding mass movements and constituent power. The book analyzes events since *Commonwealth* was published in 2009, including the rise of right-wing populism, Occupy Wall Street, automation, and the digital economy. It proposes that leadership in movements should serve specific, tactical, and short-term ends, while the multitude (or collective) articulates long-term goals to which leadership must submit. The book received generally positive reviews, with Kyle Perry arguing that advocates for a democratic world must embrace leadership, strategizing, and institution-building, and that new institutions should be "nonsovereign" and foster continuity and organization. Terence Renaud notes that while much of Hardt and Negri’s project may appear exhausted given the changed political terrain, they effectively highlight the internal challenges facing a resurgent left, such as sectarianism, heavy-handed leadership, and complacency, and insist on a self-critical, internally democratic left. Between 2016 and 2019, Negri published a three-volume collection of essays, translated and compiled into English. The first volume, *Marx and Foucault*, was published on 16 December 2016, in which he aims to show how the thinking of Marx and Foucault was synthesized into an original theoretical framework.

text: A total lunar eclipse occurred at the Moon’s descending node of orbit on Monday, April 24, 1967, with an umbral magnitude of 1.3356. This event took place when the Moon moved into Earth's shadow, causing it to be darkened, and specifically, the Moon's near side completely passed into Earth's umbral shadow, defining a total lunar eclipse. Unlike solar eclipses, which are visible only in a small region, a lunar eclipse can be observed from anywhere on the night side of Earth. A total lunar eclipse can last up to nearly two hours, whereas a total solar eclipse lasts only a few minutes at any given location due to the smaller size of the Moon's shadow. Occurring just 16 hours after perigee on April 23, 1967, at 20:00 UTC, the Moon’s apparent diameter was larger. This eclipse was the first in a tetrad, a series of four total lunar eclipses occurring consecutively, with the others on October 18, 1967; April 13, 1968; and October 6, 1968. The Surveyor 3 probe was active on the Moon during this eclipse. It was completely visible over northeast Asia, Australia, and much of the Pacific Ocean, rising over most of Asia and setting over North America and western and central South America. This eclipse is part of an eclipse season, which occurs roughly every six months and lasts about 35 days, repeating every 173 days; two or three eclipses typically happen during each season, with each eclipse separated by a fortnight. It is also part of a semester series, repeating approximately every 177 days and 4 hours at alternating nodes of the Moon’s orbit. The penumbral lunar eclipse on August 27, 1969, occurs in the next lunar year eclipse set. The Metonic cycle, repeating nearly every 19 years, aligns the Earth's shadow with the same calendar date and background stars. This eclipse belongs to Saros series 121, which repeats every 18 years, 11 days, and contains 82 events, beginning with a penumbral lunar eclipse on October 6, 1047, and ending with a penumbral eclipse on March 18, 2508. The series includes partial eclipses from May 10, 1408 to July 3, 1498; total eclipses from July 13, 1516 to May 26, 2021; and a second set of partial eclipses from June 6, 2039 to August 11, 2147. The longest duration of totality occurred in member 43 on October 18, 1660, lasting 100 minutes and 29 seconds. All eclipses in this Saros series occur at the Moon’s descending node. Eclipses are tabulated in three columns, with every third eclipse in the same column being one exeligmos apart, meaning they cast shadows over similar parts of Earth. This eclipse is part of a tritos cycle, repeating at alternating nodes every 135 synodic months (≈ 3986.63 days, or 11 years minus 1 month), with irregular appearances due to lack of synchronization with the anomalistic month, though groupings of three tritos cycles (≈ 33 years minus 3 months) show similar eclipses. It is also part of the long period inex cycle, repeating at alternating nodes every 358 synodic months (≈ 10,571.95 days, or 29 years minus 20 days), with irregular appearances due to lack of synchronization with the anomalistic month, but groupings of three inex cycles (≈ 87 years minus 2 months) show similar eclipses. A lunar eclipse is typically preceded and followed by solar eclipses by 9 years and 5.5 days (a half saros), and this lunar eclipse is related to two annular solar eclipses of Solar Saros 128.
