text: Arch Linux is an open source, rolling release Linux distribution that is kept up-to-date by regularly updating its individual software components. It provides monthly "snapshots" used as installation media and is intentionally minimal, requiring users to configure the system manually during installation to include only the software they need. The distribution uses Pacman, a package manager specifically developed for Arch Linux, to install, remove, and update software packages, with support for automatic dependency resolution. Pacman manages binary packages with a .pkg.tar.zst extension (zstd compression) or .pkg.tar.xz, and packages are compiled for the x86-64 architecture. All official packages are obtained from the Arch Linux package tree. The Arch User Repository (AUR) is a community-driven repository that hosts PKGBUILD scripts for software not included in the official repositories or alternative versions of existing packages; these scripts are built using the Arch build system (ABS) via the makepkg command and are not binary packages. AUR packages can be built manually or installed using AUR helper tools, though Arch developers emphasize that automatic downloading and execution of PKGBUILDs is not included in official repositories due to security risks, such as a malware incident on 19 July 2025 involving a modified Firefox build that was a remote access trojan (RAT). The AUR allows users to contribute PKGBUILDs, with those receiving 10 or more votes or over 1% usage from pkgstats eligible for promotion to the extra repository. The official repositories include core, extra, community, and testing, with community merged into extra in May 2023 and the unstable repository discontinued in July 2008; core-staging and extra-staging are used for rebuilds but are discouraged for use. The distribution does not schedule releases or provide traditional versions, instead relying on a rolling release model where packages are frequently updated, allowing systems to stay current. Manual interventions are occasionally required, as noted in the news section. Arch Linux's design emphasizes simplicity and transparency, avoiding complex abstractions and instead promoting direct user interaction through clean, well-documented configuration files, which has earned it a reputation as a distribution for advanced users who prefer the command line. The current logo was designed by Thayer Williams in 2007. Installation can be done manually via the Arch Wiki or automatically using the default 'archinstall' script introduced in April 2021, or through the 'pacstrap' utility. The distribution supports x86-64 processors and originally only targeted IA-32 CPUs, with the first x86-64 ISO released in April 2006. i686 support ended with the February 2017 ISO, making it unsupported in November 2017, and the community derivative Arch Linux 32 continues support for 32-bit hardware. The migration to systemd as the default init system began in August 2012 and became standard in October 2012, replacing the earlier SysV-style init. Until Pacman version 4.0.0, package signing was not supported, and packages were not verified for authenticity; however, package signing became mandatory for new builds in November 2011 and fully enabled by default in March 2012. The Arch build system enables source compilation and allows users to create custom PKGBUILD scripts to build packages compatible with Pacman. Arch Linux includes both libre and nonfree software, with the default kernel containing proprietary blobs, meaning it is not endorsed by the GNU project; the linux-libre kernel can be installed via the AUR or Parabola's repositories. The distribution is working toward making all official packages reproducible, allowing verification of package integrity across different environments. Arch Linux has a comprehensive community-run documentation site, the ArchWiki. The project was initiated in March 2002 by Judd Vinet, who chose the name for its meaning of "the principal," as in "arch-enemy," and stepped down in October 2007, transferring leadership to Aaron Griffin. Griffin stepped down in February 2020 after a voting period, transferring control to Levente Polyak, with a new two-year term added for the Project Leader position. In March 2021, developers considered porting packages to x86_64-v3 (Intel Haswell-era processors), and in February 2022, debug packages were introduced. In late 2021, Pacman 6.0 was released with support for parallel downloads. On 14 August 2025, the Arch User Repository, forums, and website were hit by a distributed denial-of-service attack, causing temporary unavailability and severely slowing or blocking AUR downloads. SteamOS 3.0, used in the Steam Deck, is based on Arch Linux. CachyOS is a gaming-focused distribution based on Arch Linux. Projects like PacBSD and Arch Hurd are adapting Arch Linux tools to other kernels, and the Arch Linux ARM project aims to port the distribution to ARM devices like the Raspberry Pi. Arch Linux has received reviews from OSNews, LWN.net, Tux Machines, and DistroWatch Weekly, with Greg Kroah-Hartman praising its performance and community feedback. In a 2023 DistroWatch poll, 17% of respondents used Arch and 30% used an Arch derivative, and as of 2025, Arch holds the third-highest average rating (9.18) on DistroWatch, behind only Artix Linux and BigLinux, both Arch derivatives.

text: Arthur William Bacot (28 April 1866 – 12 April 1922) was an entomologist at the Lister Institute of Preventive Medicine. Born in North London, he was the third son and fourth child of Edmund Alexander Bacot and Harriet. Bacot was a poor attender at school, leaving at the age of sixteen in 1882, and subsequently worked as an office worker in the City of London. He had no formal scientific training beyond membership in the London Natural History Society. A dedicated butterfly collector, he authored over fifty papers on British lepidoptera between 1893 and 1909. In 1908, he began researching morphological and genetic topics, conducting breeding experiments with the geometrid moth Acidalia virginaria (binomial name Scopula modicaria), which he presented to the London Hospital Medical School. Professor Greenwood of the Advisory Committee for Plague Investigation sought someone to study the breeding habits of the rat flea and its transmission of the plague virus; Bacot was asked to undertake this research in his spare time with a small fee and all expenses covered. The project succeeded, leading to his appointment at the Lister Institute. In 1914, during the First World War, he traveled to Sierra Leone in British West Africa to study Yellow Fever. By autumn 1917, concerns arose about the reduced efficiency of the British Expeditionary Force in France due to trench fever; Bacot, alongside Joseph Arkwright, investigated the disease's cause and prevention, identifying the link between lice and both typhus and trench fever. Bacot contracted trench fever himself while in Warsaw. In 1922, he went to Cairo with Arkwright at the request of the Egyptian Government to study typhus; both contracted the disease from lice. Arkwright survived after a prolonged illness, while Bacot died at the age of 55.

text: The Asia–Europe Meeting (ASEM) is a political dialogue forum designed to strengthen relations and promote various forms of cooperation between its partners. This is supported by biennial meetings of Heads of State and Government, alternating between Asia and Europe, and biennial meetings of Foreign Ministers, along with other Ministerial Meetings and political, economic, and socio-cultural events at various levels. doc_name: Assassination of Juvénal Habyarimana and Cyprien Ntaryamira
text: On the evening of 6 April 1994, the aircraft carrying Rwandan president Juvénal Habyarimana and Burundian president Cyprien Ntaryamira, both Hutu, was shot down with surface-to-air missiles as it prepared to land in Kigali, Rwanda; both were killed. The assassination triggered the Rwandan genocide, one of the bloodiest events of the late 20th century. Responsibility for the attack is disputed, with most theories pointing to either the Tutsi rebel Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF) or government-aligned Hutu Power followers opposed to negotiations with the RPF. The Rwandan Civil War began in 1990 when the RPF, dominated by the Tutsi ethnic group, invaded northern Rwanda from Uganda. Most of the RPF fighters were refugees or sons of refugees who had fled ethnic purges by the Hutu government during the Rwandan revolution. The attempt to overthrow the government failed, though the RPF maintained control of a border region. As the war reached a stalemate, peace negotiations began in May 1992, resulting in the signing of the Arusha Accords in August 1993 to establish a power-sharing government. The war radicalized internal opposition, with the RPF's show of force strengthening support for the "Hutu Power" ideology, which portrayed the RPF as an alien force intent on reinstating the Tutsi monarchy and enslaving the Hutus. The Coalition for the Defense of the Republic (CDR) embraced these racist principles, known as the Hutu Ten Commandments, and led to the collapse of the first Habyarimana government in July 1993 when Prime Minister Dismas Nsengiyaremye criticized the president for delaying a peace agreement. Habyarimana dismissed Nsengiyaremye and appointed Agathe Uwilingiyimana, who was seen as less sympathetic to the RPF, in his place. The main opposition parties split into factions: one committed to Hutu Power and another, labeled "moderate," seeking a negotiated settlement. Uwilingiyimana was unable to form a coalition, making ratification of the Arusha Accords impossible. The CDR, which openly called for ethnic cleansing of the Tutsi, was entirely unrepresented in the Accords. The security situation worsened throughout 1993, with armed Hutu militias attacking Tutsis and high-ranking Hutu Power figures considering how to turn the security forces to genocide. In February 1994, Roméo Dallaire, head of the United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda (UNAMIR), warned his superiors that political discussions were running out of time due to the risk of catastrophic consequences. In early April 1994, the United Nations Security Council faced a dispute between the United States and non-permanent members over UNAMIR. Despite a classified February Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) analysis predicting half a million deaths if the Arusha process failed, the U.S. sought to reduce its international commitments following the Somalia debacle and lobbied to end the mission. A compromise extending UNAMIR's mandate for three more months was reached on the evening of 5 April. Habyarimana was traveling regionally: on 4 April he flew to Zaire to meet with President Mobutu Sese Seko, and on 6 April to Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, for a one-day summit convened by Tanzanian President Ali Hassan Mwinyi. For the return trip, Habyarimana offered to take Tanzania's Ambassador to Rwanda, Saleh Tambwe, with him, then extended the offer to President Ntaryamira, who accepted, preferring Habyarimana's faster Dassault Falcon 50 to his own transport. Several Burundian ministers joined the flight, and as a result, Tambwe was not brought on board. According to interim Prime Minister Jean Kambanda's testimony to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), Mobutu had warned Habyarimana not to go to Dar es Salaam on 6 April, claiming the warning came from a senior official at the Élysée Palace in Paris. Mobutu linked this warning to the suicide of François de Grossouvre, a senior official working for President François Mitterrand, who died by suicide on 7 April after learning about the downing of the Falcon. Shortly before 8:20 pm local time (18:20 UTC), the presidential jet circled Kigali International Airport once before final approach in clear skies. A weekly flight by a Belgian C-130 Hercules carrying UNAMIR troops returning from leave had been scheduled to land before the presidential jet but was waved off to give the president priority. A surface-to-air missile struck one of the wings of the Dassault Falcon, followed by a second missile hitting its tail. The plane erupted into flames mid-air and crashed into the garden of the presidential palace, exploding on impact. The plane carried three French crew members and nine passengers. The attack was witnessed by numerous people. One of two Belgian officers in Kanombe saw and heard the first missile climb into the sky, saw a red flash, and heard the aircraft engine stop, followed by another missile. He immediately called Major de Saint-Quentin, who advised him to protect his Belgian comrades. Another Belgian officer in an unused airport control tower saw the lights of an approaching aircraft, a light rising from the ground, and the aircraft lights going out, followed by a second light rising from the same place and the plane turning into a falling ball of fire. He immediately radioed his company commander, who confirmed with the operational control tower that the plane was the presidential aircraft. A Rwandan soldier in Camp Kanombe recalled that the president's engine sound was different from other planes; he saw a projectile, a ball of flame, and the plane go down. As the leader of the bloc, he told soldiers to get up and said, "Kinani has been shot down," though they initially denied it. He then put on his uniform and heard the bugle sound. A Rwandan officer cadet at the airport, listening to Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines, heard the announcer state the presidential jet was coming in to land, then the broadcast abruptly switched to classical music. All twelve aboard the Falcon were killed. The French aircraft crew were: The crash caused chaos on the ground. Presidential Guards, who had been waiting to escort the president home, threatened people with their weapons. Twenty Belgian peacekeepers stationed along the airport perimeter were surrounded and some disarmed. The airport was closed, and the circling Belgian Hercules was diverted to Nairobi. In Camp Kanombe, the bugle call immediately after the crash was interpreted as a sign that the RPF had attacked the camp. Soldiers rushed to their armories, and the para-commando brigade Commandos de recherche et d'action en profondeur assembled on the parade ground at around 9:00 pm, while other units gathered elsewhere. At least one witness reported gunfire in Kanombe about an hour after the crash, and munitions explosions were initially reported. The senior officer for the Kigali operational zone called the Ministry of Defence; Defence Minister Augustin Bizimana was out of the country, and the officer who took the call failed to reach Colonel Théoneste Bagosora, who was at a reception with UNAMIR's Bangladeshi officers. The news of the crash, initially reported as an explosion of UNAMIR's ammunition dump, was relayed to UNAMIR Force Commander Dallaire, who ordered Kigali sector commander Luc Marchal to send a patrol to the crash site. Numerous people called UNAMIR for information, including Prime Minister Agathe Uwilingiyimana and Lando Ndasingwa. Uwilingiyimana informed Dallaire she was trying to gather her cabinet but many ministers were afraid to leave their families. She reported that all hardline ministers had disappeared. Dallaire asked her to confirm it was the president's plane, and called UNAMIR political head Jacques-Roger Booh-Booh. Uwilingiyimana confirmed it was the president's jet and that he was presumed on board. She also requested UNAMIR assistance in regaining control of the political situation, as she was legally next in line of succession, though some moderate ministers had already fled. At 9:18 pm, Presidential Guards, described as "nervous and dangerous," established a roadblock near the Hotel Méridien. Several other roadblocks had been set up in advance for Habyarimana's arrival. A patrol of UNAMIR Belgian soldiers sent to investigate the crash site was stopped at a Presidential Guards roadblock at 9:35 pm, disarmed, and sent to the airport. The para-commando brigade was ordered to collect bodies from the crash site, and UN peacekeepers were prevented from accessing it. Akingeneye was quickly recovered, but most corpses were damaged beyond immediate recognition. Habyarimana was identified lying in a flowerbed at about 21:30 on 6 April, while Ntaryamira was recognized at about 03:00 on 7 April. One Rwandan advisor was identified after his wife told the search party about his clothing. The last to be identified were the French aircrew, discovered at dawn outside the palace gardens. The bodies were taken into the Presidential Palace living room. Plans were initially made to take them to the hospital, but renewed conflict made this difficult, so the two presidents' bodies were stored in a freezer at a nearby army barracks. Two French soldiers arrived at the crash site and asked to be given the flight data recorder once it was recovered. The whereabouts of the flight data recorder were later unknown. The French military contacted Dallaire and offered to investigate the crash, which he refused immediately. A Rwandan colonel who called the army command about 40 minutes after the crash was told there was no confirmation that the president was dead. About half an hour later, at roughly 9:30, the situation remained confused, though it appeared clear the presidential aircraft had exploded and had likely been hit by a missile. News arrived that Major-General Déogratias Nsabimana, the army chief of staff, had been on the plane. Officers realized they needed to appoint a new chief of staff and began a meeting to decide who should take the role. Col. Bagosora joined them soon afterward. At about 10:00 pm, Ephrem Rwabalinda, the government liaison officer to UNAMIR, called Dallaire to inform him that a crisis committee was about to meet. After informing his superiors in New York, Dallaire went to attend the meeting, where he found Bagosora in charge. Observers feared that President Ntaryamira's death would lead to widespread violence in Burundi, as had occurred when his predecessor, Melchior Ndadaye, was assassinated in October 1993. However, unlike in Rwanda, the situation in Burundi remained peaceful. The Burundian government declared the plane crash an accident, and President of the National Assembly Sylvestre Ntibantunganya made a television broadcast, flanked by the minister of defence and the army chief of staff, appealing for calm. Several hundred Tutsis marched through the capital to celebrate the deaths of the presidents. Diplomats reported that most Burundians believed the assassination targeted Habyarimana, not Ntaryamira. On 16 April, a requiem mass was held for Ntaryamira at the Regina Mundi Cathedral in Bujumbura, attended by thousands, and he and his two ministers were buried in a state funeral. Ntibantunganya succeeded Ntaryamira as President of Burundi and believed Ntaryamira's death was "by the facts of circumstance" and that he was not targeted. In response to the assassination, President Mwinyi declared three days of national mourning in Tanzania and sent messages of condolence to the Rwandan and Burundian governments and the families of the deceased presidents. He wrote in his memoirs that the Tanzanian government was "shocked" by the downing of the plane. A group of about 70 Rwandans and Burundians at the New Mwanza Hotel celebrated the assassination, leading Prime Minister John Malecela to order their arrest. This action was countermanded by the attorney general, who stated their actions were not illegal. A mourning period was also established in Zaire. President of the UN Security Council Colin Keating appealed for peace in Rwanda and Burundi and sent condolences to the families of the late presidents. Following the 6 April assassination, Juvenal Habyarimana's remains were obtained by President Mobutu of Zaire and stored in a private mausoleum in Gbadolite, Zaire (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo). Mobutu promised Habyarimana's family that his body would eventually be given a proper burial in Rwanda. On 12 May 1997, as Laurent-Désiré Kabila's ADFL rebels advanced on Gbadolite, Mobutu had the remains flown by cargo plane to Kinshasa, where they waited on the tarmac of N'djili Airport for three days. On 16 May, the day before Mobutu fled Zaire, Habyarimana's remains were cremated under the supervision of an Indian Hindu leader. The Hindu leader's presence reflected the need to cremate the body and Mobutu's insistence on a religious ceremony rather than Habyarimana's own religion. Two prominent investigations, internationally recognized, have identified the Kanombe barracks as the likely source of the missile. In 2010, the "Mutsinzi Report," carried out by Rwandan officials in collaboration with British ballistics experts from the Royal Military Academy, identified a small area including a portion of the airport, the Kanombe camp, and a small area near the presidential residence as the launch site. In January 2012, a French report was made public with similar findings. Despite these reports, some have continued to cast doubt on the conclusion. French Judge Jean-Louis Bruguière led a 2004 inquiry that accused the RPF of shooting down the plane from Masaka Hill, but it was found to be based on the testimonies of witnesses not regarded as credible. A 1994 Belgian inquiry concluded that the missile was fired from Masaka Hill, but stated it would have been virtually impossible for a rebel soldier to reach Masaka carrying missiles. The base was controlled by FAR forces, including the Presidential Guard and the para-commando battalion, and the Anti-Aircraft Battalion (LAA) were also based there. This report was widely reported to exonerate the RPF, although according to Filip Reyntjens, it did not actually do so. While initial suspicion fell on Hutu extremists who carried out the subsequent genocide, several reports since 2000 have stated that the attack was carried out by the RPF on the orders of Paul Kagame, who later became president of Rwanda. All such evidence is heavily disputed, and many academics and the United Nations have refrained from issuing a definitive finding. Mark Doyle, a BBC News correspondent who reported from Kigali during the 1994 genocide, noted in 2006 that the identities of the assassins "could turn out to be one of the great mysteries of the late 20th century." A now-declassified US Department of State intelligence report from 7 April 1994 reports an unidentified source telling the US ambassador in Rwanda that "rogue Hutu elements of the military—possibly the elite presidential guard—were responsible for shooting down the plane." This conclusion was supported by other U.S. agencies, including the Defense Intelligence Agency.

text: The assassination of Rwandan President Juvénal Habyarimana and Burundian President Cyprien Ntaryamira on 6 April 1994, which triggered the Rwandan genocide, remains widely debated. Although initial suspicion focused on Hutu extremists, including figures like Colonel Théoneste Bagosora, several reports since 2000 have alleged that the RPF carried out the attack at the orders of Paul Kagame, who later became Rwanda’s president. These claims are heavily disputed, with no definitive conclusion from the United Nations or major academic institutions. A declassified U.S. Department of State report from 7 April 1994 cited an unidentified source stating that rogue Hutu military elements—possibly the elite presidential guard—were responsible, a view supported by the Defense Intelligence Agency, which reported on 9 May that the crash was an assassination by Hutu military hardliners. Philip Gourevitch, in his 1998 book, highlighted the lack of positive identification of the assassins, with Bagosora being a key suspect due to his close ties to Habyarimana and his statements about preparing an "apocalypse." The Belgian Senate’s 1997 report found insufficient information to determine specifics, while the 1998 French National Assembly report proposed two theories: Hutu extremists acting due to fears of RPF advances, or the RPF acting due to stalled Arusha Accords negotiations; it offered no definitive conclusion. The Organisation of African Unity’s 2000 report avoided assigning responsibility. In January 2000, Louise Arbour, chief prosecutor of the ICTR, terminated an investigation into the shootdown after three Tutsi informants accused Kagame and the RPF of being part of an "elite strike team," with one whistleblower, Jean-Pierre Mugabe, making a declaration in April 2000. A three-page memorandum by investigator Michael Hourigan was sent to the ICTR, and Hourigan stated he was "astounded" when Arbour reversed her position, claiming the investigation was outside her mandate; this was supported by Jim Lyons, a former FBI agent, who believed Arbour acted under orders, though Luc Reydams’ investigation concluded the decision was based on practical and legal assessments, not orders. Arbour later stated it was her personal decision, noting that the plane crash did not clearly constitute a war crime or crime against humanity under the law, and that the focus should have been on RPF actions during the genocide period. In 1998, French magistrate Jean-Louis Bruguière opened an investigation on behalf of the French crew families, concluding the attack was ordered by Kagame and issuing arrest warrants against nine of his aides in 2006; Rwanda responded by severing diplomatic ties. Bruguière’s key witness, Abdul Ruzibiza, a former RPF lieutenant, claimed involvement in the downing using SA-16 missiles and published his testimony in 2004 and a book in 2005, asserting Kagame’s responsibility; however, in November 2008 he retracted his claims, stating they were due to personal security concerns, and later claimed he did not personally participate but knew someone who did. Critics, including Linda Melvern and Colette Braeckman, questioned the reliability of Bruguière’s evidence, with Braeckman suggesting French military involvement. Kagame responded in a 2007 BBC interview by offering cooperation with an impartial, neutral inquiry, though the BBC doubted such a judge would accept the task. Paul Rusesabagina, known for his role in Hotel Rwanda, supported the theory that Kagame and the RPF were responsible, arguing it defied logic that the UN Security Council did not investigate, as it had after Rafic Hariri’s 2005 assassination. In February 2008, Spanish judge Fernando Andreu issued an 182-page indictment and international arrest warrants against 40 high-ranking RPF officials, charging them with crimes from 1990 to 2002, including the plane shootdown, based partly on universal jurisdiction. Kagame also ordered a Rwandan commission to investigate French involvement in the genocide, which issued its report in November 2007 and stated it would await Kagame’s validation. In January 2010, Rwanda released the Mutsinzi Report, which implicates Hutu Power proponents in the attack; Philip Gourevitch noted that France and Rwanda reestablished diplomatic relations shortly after Rwanda’s admission to the Commonwealth, and that the report had been shared with France prior to that, implying France’s acceptance of its findings. Ntaryamira’s death is commemorated annually in Burundi on 6 April, though it has been overshadowed by Habyarimana’s death and the subsequent genocide.

text: The attorney general of Guatemala (fiscal general de la República de Guatemala) serves as the chief public prosecutor and head of the Ministerio Público (Department of Justice). Under article 251 of the Constitution of Guatemala, the attorney general is appointed by the president from a group of six candidates who must be lawyers and possess the same qualifications as the magistrates of the Supreme Court. These candidates are nominated by a commission composed of the chief justice of the Supreme Court, the deans of the law schools at the country's universities, and both the chairman of the bar association and the chairman of its honor tribunal. The attorney general serves a four-year term and enjoys the same immunity as the magistrates of the Supreme Court. The president may remove the attorney general only if there is a justified reason, as specified in article 14 of the Organic Law of the Ministerio Público, which states that removal is permitted only in cases of conviction of the attorney general for committing a crime while carrying out their duties.

text: The Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002, informally known as the Iraq Resolution, was a joint resolution passed by the United States Congress in October 2002 as Public Law No. 107-243, authorizing the use of the United States Armed Forces against Saddam Hussein's Ba'athist Iraqi government in what would become Operation Iraqi Freedom. The resolution cited several justifications for military action, including support and encouragement of diplomatic efforts by President George W. Bush to strictly enforce through the U.N. Security Council all relevant Security Council resolutions regarding Iraq and to obtain prompt and decisive action to ensure Iraq abandoned its strategy of delay, evasion, and noncompliance and promptly complied with all such resolutions. It authorized President Bush to use U.S. Armed Forces "as he determines to be necessary and appropriate" to defend national security against the continuing threat from Iraq and to enforce all relevant U.N. Security Council Resolutions on Iraq. President Bush sought congressional authorization shortly after his September 12, 2002 statement before the U.N. General Assembly requesting swift Security Council action. Among the legislative proposals introduced in response, S.J.Res. 45 (Senators Daschle and Lott), H.J.Res. 114 (Rep. Hastert and Rep. Gephardt), and S.J.Res. 46 (Sen. Lieberman) were based on or modified from the White House proposal, while H.J.Res. 110 (Rep. Hastings) was a separate proposal never considered on the floor. Ultimately, the Hastert–Gephardt proposal became the focus of congressional action. Introduced on October 2, 2002, H.J.Res. 114 passed the House on October 10, 2002, by a vote of 296–133, and the Senate on October 11, 2002, by a vote of 77–23, and was signed into law as Pub. L. 107–243 on October 16, 2002. The resolution was supported by a list of senators including Baucus, Bayh, Biden, Breaux, Cantwell, Carnahan, Carper, Cleland, Clinton, Daschle, Dodd, Dorgan, Edwards, Feinstein, Harkin, Hollings, Johnson, Kerry, Kohl, Landrieu, Lieberman, Lincoln, Miller, Nelson (FL and NE), Reid, Rockefeller, Schumer, and Torricelli, as well as Akaka, Bingaman, Boxer, Byrd, Conrad, Corzine, Dayton, Durbin, Feingold, Graham, Inouye, Kennedy, Leahy, Levin, Mikulski, Murray, Reed, Sarbanes, Stabenow, Wellstone, and Wyden. In 2003, the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit refused to review the legality of the invasion, citing a lack of ripeness, and a three-judge panel dismissed the case, stating the judiciary cannot intervene absent a fully developed conflict between the President and Congress or if Congress granted the President "absolute discretion" to declare war. Similar judicial review efforts have been dismissed on various justiciability grounds. United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan stated in 2004 that the invasion was illegal and not in conformity with the UN Charter. Debate over the legality under international law centers on ambiguous language in U.N. Resolution 1441 (2002), which declared Iraq was in "material breach" of the cease-fire under U.N. Resolution 687 (1991), requiring cooperation with weapons inspectors. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties allows a party to invoke a "material breach" to suspend a multilateral treaty, and the U.S. and U.K. argue that this right enabled them to suspend the cease-fire under Resolution 687 and continue hostilities under the authority of U.N. Resolution 678 (1990), which originally authorized force after Iraq invaded Kuwait—this argument was previously used in Operation Desert Fox in 1998. They also assert that while Resolution 1441 required the Security Council to assess inspector reports, it did not require agreement on action, and if Iraq was found to have breached the resolution, no member state was constrained from acting to defend itself. The U.S. government further claimed the right to pre-emptive self-defense against terrorism fostered by Iraq. It remains unclear whether any party other than the Security Council can determine Iraq's breach of Resolution 1441, as U.N. members argue interpretation and enforcement of resolutions is not the responsibility of a single member. Other nations have maintained that a second resolution was required to initiate hostilities. On June 17, 2021, the House of Representatives voted to repeal the 2002 resolution by a vote of 268–161, with 219 Democrats and 49 Republicans supporting repeal and 160 Republicans and 1 Democrat opposing it. In July 2021, Senators Christopher Murphy, Mike Lee, and Bernie Sanders introduced S.2391, the National Security Powers Act of 2021, to repeal previous war authorizations and establish new procedures, but a Senator placed a quasi-anonymous hold on it in committee, preventing advancement; its House companion, H.R.5410, did not include repeal language and was similarly held in committee. On March 16, 2023, Senators Tim Kaine and Todd Young introduced S.316 to repeal the 1991 and 2002 AUMFs, which passed the Senate 68–27, but its House companion, H.R.932, was quasi-anonymously held by a Representative in the House Committee on Foreign Affairs since February 9, 2023. On July 13, 2023, Kaine and Young introduced S.Amdt.427 to S.2226, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, to repeal the 1991 and 2002 AUMFs, but failed to propose it on the floor in time, so when the bill passed the Senate, the amendment was not acted upon and was excluded by law. Both AUMFs were ultimately repealed when President Donald Trump signed the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 on December 18, 2025.

text: Arthur Wallis Myers CBE (24 July 1878 – 17 June 1939) was an English tennis correspondent, editor, author, and player, recognized as one of the leading tennis journalists of the first half of the 20th century. He was the son of the Rev. John Brown Myers, secretary of the Baptist Missionary Society, and Agnes Traphena (née Nutter), and attended the Watford Endowed School and The Leys School in Cambridge. In 1900, he married Lilian Gentry, daughter of Captain George Gentry of Maldon, Essex; the couple had seven children, with the youngest, Prue, writing a tribute to her father titled A. Wallis Myers: A Testament to Tennis. Myers was an active amateur tennis player, primarily competing in doubles. In April 1906, he won the doubles title with New Zealander Anthony Wilding at the Championships of Barcelona. He also won the Monte Carlo doubles championship in 1910 and 1921. In mixed doubles, he competed at Monte Carlo in 1909 and reached the semi-finals at the 1914 World Hard Court Championships with Phyllis Satterthwaite. In 1923, he partnered with Molla Bjurstedt Mallory at the Monte Carlo tournament and also won the doubles title at the South of France Championships. He served as captain of British tennis teams on tour in Europe, South Africa, and India. Myers began editing the Ayers Lawn Tennis Almanack in 1908 and became the lawn tennis correspondent for The Daily Telegraph the following year, a position he held until his death in 1939. He also served as lawn tennis editor of The Field and authored several books on tennis, including a biography of four-time Wimbledon champion Anthony Wilding, who died in the First World War. During the war, Myers worked in the Ministry of Information. In 1924, he founded the International Lawn Tennis Club of Great Britain with Lord Balfour, former Prime Minister and later a Member of the Cabinet, as its first President. Myers was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 1920 New Year Honours, dated 30 March 1920, for his work at the Ministry of Information. He was appointed Chevalier (Knight) of the Legion of Honour by French President Paul Doumer on 29 April 1932 for his service to the game of tennis.

text: Axitinib, marketed under the brand name Inlyta, is a small molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor developed by Pfizer. It has demonstrated significant inhibition of breast cancer growth in animal xenograft models and has shown partial responses in clinical trials for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and other tumor types. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved axitinib for the treatment of RCC after it demonstrated a modest increase in progression-free survival, although fatal adverse effects have been reported. Approval for RCC was granted by the FDA in January 2012, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) in September 2012, the UK Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) in September 2012, and the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) in July 2012. A Phase II trial indicated good response when axitinib was combined with gemcitabine for advanced pancreatic cancer, but Pfizer halted a Phase III trial on 30 January 2009 due to lack of improved survival compared to gemcitabine alone. A 2010 Phase III trial for previously treated metastatic RCC showed significantly extended progression-free survival compared to sorafenib, leading the Oncologic Drugs Advisory Committee (ODAC) to unanimously recommend FDA approval in December 2011 for axitinib as second-line treatment for advanced RCC. Axitinib has also been studied in combination with the ALK1 inhibitor dalantercept. A 2015 study showed that axitinib effectively inhibits the BCR-ABL1[T315I] mutated gene, common in drug-resistant chronic myeloid leukemia and adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia, representing one of the first instances of a new indication for an existing drug discovered through screening patient cells. Common side effects include diarrhea, hypertension, fatigue, decreased appetite, nausea, dysphonia, hand-foot syndrome, weight loss, vomiting, asthenia, and constipation, occurring in more than 20% of patients. Coadministration with strong CYP3A4/CYP3A5 inhibitors or inducers should be avoided due to potential increases or decreases in axitinib plasma exposure. Its primary mechanism of action involves inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 1–3, c-KIT, and PDGFR, thereby suppressing angiogenesis in tumors; it may also induce autophagy, similar to sorafenib. Axitinib has been shown to bind to the BCR-ABL fusion protein in a conformation distinct from VEGF binding, specifically inhibiting the drug-resistant T315I mutant isoform. In July 2024, the European Medicines Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use adopted a positive opinion recommending marketing authorization for Axitinib Accord, developed by Accord Healthcare S.L.U., for the treatment of adults with RCC. Pfizer reported US$1.036 billion in revenue for Inlyta in 2023. In the European Union, axitinib is sold under the brand name Inlyta.

She returned to South Africa in June 1990 and participated in the negotiations to end apartheid, serving as secretary-general of the ANC Women's League from 1991 to 1993. In 1995, she was appointed chair of the ANC's parliamentary caucus and a member of the Presidential Panel on the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. In May 1996, she became Deputy Speaker, succeeding Bhadra Ranchod, and was re-elected to that office in June 1999. In April 2004, she was elected Speaker of the National Assembly unopposed, with Gwen Mahlangu as deputy. During her term, she faced criticism over the Travelgate scandal and the use of parliamentary travel vouchers, and in January 2006, she chartered a jet costing R471,900 to attend the inauguration of Ellen Johnson Sirleaf in Liberia. In December 2007, she won election as ANC national chairperson with 61% of the vote, defeating Joel Netshitenzhe, and served in that role until December 2017. On 25 September 2008, she was appointed Deputy President following the resignation of Thabo Mbeki, though she did not become President, as Kgalema Motlanthe was appointed to that role. In May 2009, she was re-elected to the National Assembly but declined to be sworn in, leading to her stepping back from Parliament. She returned in May 2014 as Speaker, defeating Nosimo Balindlela in a vote of 260 to 88, and faced a no-confidence motion in September 2014 that was rejected 234 to 0 after opposition parties walked out. She has faced accusations of bias toward the ANC and being a puppet of President Zuma, and in March 2016, the Constitutional Court ruled that the National Assembly under her leadership breached the Constitution by failing to implement the Public Protector's Nkandla report. In April 2016, she identified herself as a presidential contender, but endorsed Cyril Ramaphosa at the ANC's 54th National Conference in December 2017, after being disappointed that Jacob Zuma did not support her campaign. She did not run for re-election as national chairperson and was not re-elected to the National Executive Committee at the 2017 conference, though she remained a member until 2022. In May 2019, she was re-elected to her parliamentary seat but was subsequently removed from the party list, and the ANC announced Thandi Modise would succeed her as Speaker. text: Balendra Shah, commonly known as Balen, was born on 27 April 1990 in Naradevi, Kathmandu, to a Maithili Madhesi family; his parents are Late Ram Narayan Shah, an Ayurvedic practitioner, and Dhruvadevi Shah, who moved to Kathmandu from Mahottari District after his father’s posting at Naradevi Ayurvedic Hospital. Shah pursued his 10+2 education at V.S. Niketan Higher Secondary School and earned a bachelor’s degree (BE) in civil engineering from Himalayan Whitehouse International College, followed by a master’s degree (MTech) in structural engineering from Visvesvaraya Technological University (VTU) in Karnataka, India. He is currently pursuing a PhD in Civil Engineering at Kathmandu University, supported by a KU Researcher's Fellowship, with a research focus on "Conservation of Newa Heritage Structure to promote Tourism and Economy." From an early age, Shah showed interest in music and poetry, releasing his first single, Sadak Balak, in 2012 during his ninth grade, and gaining prominence in 2013 through his appearance on the YouTube battle rap series Raw Barz. In July 2022, he drew controversy for using a sacred crown in Nephopko Shreepech, a hip-hop reality show he judged. As mayor, Shah introduced live telecasts of municipal council meetings, initiated garbage disposal from 7 June 2022 through an agreement with the Ministry of Urban Development, and directed private companies to manage uncollected solid waste in August 2022. He also ordered the demolition of private properties above the Tukucha River to uncover it, leading to a writ petition and an interim court order halting the demolition. Shah requested the removal of unauthorized police sub-stations on sidewalks and clashed with the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal over the removal of unapproved construction materials at Tribhuvan International Airport, resulting in a legal dispute and a high court stay. His office issued a 7-day public notice to evict landless squatters on riverbanks, leading to clashes, injuries, and a subsequent complaint from the Home Ministry, which escalated tensions with the federal government, culminating in the suspension of garbage collection from Singha Durbar. Shah has faced criticism from Human Rights Watch and social activists for using disproportionate force against street vendors, with videos circulating of police chasing, beating, and confiscating vendor properties, which critics argue harms the urban poor. In September 2023, activist Iih stood for 199 hours outside Kathmandu City Hall, demanding vendor rights, supported by figures including Gagan Thapa, Kamal Thapa, and Surendra Pandey; Shah responded by citing existing laws and expressed concern over confiscated properties, leading to an agreement on temporary permits, return of goods, and an alternative plan. Shah is known for his confrontational style, including removing illegal buildings, uncovering the Tukucha River, and clearing street vendors. In 2023, he placed a map of Greater Nepal in his office—a symbolic act interpreted as a response to the “Akhanda Bharat” mural in India’s new Parliament building, which some in Nepal saw as depicting Nepali territory as part of undivided India. This action drew strong objections from India. He also temporarily banned the screening of Indian films after Adipurush included the line “Sita is the daughter of India,” a claim disputed in Nepal where Sita is traditionally believed to have been born in Janakpur; despite a court order to remove the ban, Shah initially refused, prompting a contempt of court petition before allowing screenings to resume. During the Gen-Z Protests, the Nepal Student Union filed a police complaint accusing Shah of inciting violence against heritage sites, though he denied the claims, stating city teams worked continuously to ensure safety. Shah is a supporter of the irredentist Greater Nepal theory, which claims territories beyond Nepal’s current borders, including areas now in Indian states, that were once under Nepalese control before the 1816 Treaty of Sugauli. He was elected mayor on 26 May 2022 with 38.6% of the votes, defeating Nepali Congress candidate Sirjana Shrestha and CPN (UML) candidate Keshav Sthapit by a margin of over 23,000 votes, becoming the first independent candidate to hold the office. He was sworn in on 30 May 2022 and served until his resignation on 18 January 2026. He is currently contesting in the upcoming general elections as a candidate for the Prime Minister of Nepal and joined the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) in late 2025. Shah is married to Sabina Kafle, a public health professional, and lives in Gairigaun, Tinkune. text: Bandipore, the headquarters of the Bandipore district in the Indian-administered union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, lies on the northern banks of Wular Lake, the second-largest freshwater lake in Asia and one of the largest in South Asia. The lake, formed due to tectonic activity and fed by the Jhelum River and streams Madhumati and Arin, varies in size seasonally from 30 to 189 square kilometres, though much of it has been drained due to willow plantations built in the 1950s. Wular is home to numerous migratory birds, but pollution from the Jhelum River—carrying waste from Srinagar and surrounding areas—has led to a pandemic growth of algae, threatening the lake’s ecosystem. Despite being the richest wetland in South Asia and the largest freshwater lake in Asia, no conservation measures have been implemented. Bandipore is situated on the banks of Wular and serves as a stepping stone to the higher reaches of Razdan, Gurez, and Tragbal. It is also adjacent to the Lolab Valley in Kupwara, just 30 kilometres away via Aloosa village, and upgrading this road would provide a lifeline to the Lolab valley. Historically, Bandipore was a key link between North India and Central Asia via the Silk Road, with a customs and immigration post at Pazalpora now functioning as a forest check-post, earning Bandipore the title of gateway to Central Asia. Strong cultural and trade links exist between Skardu, Gurez, and Bandipore. As per the 2011 Indian census, the district had a population of 37,081, with males constituting 54% and females 46%, and an average literacy rate of 66.53%—lower than the national average of 74%—with 75% of males and 55% of females literate, and 12% of the population under 6 years of age. The region is Muslim-majority, though prior to the early 1990s, Pandits lived in villages such as Ajar, Sonerwani, Kaloosa, Kharapora, Mantrigam, and Aragam, with some families in Ajar and Kaloosa not migrating. The Sharda Mandir at Kaloosa, featuring a rare, ancient tree known as Bran—believed to be several hundred years old—is a significant site. Villages like Chakreshipora, named after Chakerishwar, reflect the region’s Hindu heritage, and the famous Ziariat of Kausar Sahab Afghani is located near Chekreshipora. The Forest Training and Research Institute of Jammu and Kashmir, established in 1905 (originally founded in 1911), is located 3 km from the main town and is a premier body in forest conservation. The majority of the population speaks Kashmiri, with some speaking Gojri and Pahari; Tehsil Gurez and Tulail are Shina-speaking areas with a Shina majority, and there are a few Pashtun villages on the Line of Control. The Kishan Ganga Hydro Electric Power Project, located in Gurez Tehsil, is worth INR 15,000 crores and currently generates 330 MW of electricity for Jammu and Kashmir. A degree college, named after Hassan Khoyihami and established on a hilltop near Putushai village, approximately 6 km from the main market, began functioning in 2005 in the higher secondary school at Kaloosa. Nishat Park in Bandipore, constructed in 1954 under the supervision of then Prime Minister Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad, is modeled after the Nishat Garden in Srinagar and is located on the outskirts of the main market, offering a peaceful environment with beautiful flowers and trees. The town is well-connected by road via the Bandipora–Srinagar and Bandipora–Sopore roads but lacks railway connectivity; the nearest railway station is Sopore, 34 km away, and the nearest airport is Srinagar, 65 km away. Bandipore is known for trekking, mountaineering, and fishing, with Langmarg being a scenic meadow and Arin Nallah hosting exotic trout species. Mount Harmukh, located on the eastern side of the town, is a major attraction for mountaineers, with Sheera Sar (Lake of Spirits) serving as the base camp; commercial cabs operate up to Kudara, after which a 17-kilometre trek is required to reach the higher reaches. To the north lies Gurez, 86 kilometres away, accessible by commercial cabs in summer but closed in winter due to snowfall. The surrounding ranges—Sirandar, Kudara, Vewan, Mowa, and Tresangam—are inhabited by Gujjars and Bakarwals. A centuries-old shrine in Butho village, locally known as Ded Mouj and rumored to house the burial of Moses, is a myth and not historically verified. The Darul Uloom Raheemiyyah, the largest Islamic institution in Jammu and Kashmir, is headed by Moulana Mohammad Rahmatullah Mir Qasmi. Notable individuals associated with Bandipore include Qazi Ghulam Nabi Jan (Chairman Land Development Bank & social activist), Qazi Ghulam Ali Jan (Assistant Conservator Forest), Hassan Khoehami (historian), Siyad Kashmiri Abdul Samad Lone (retired headmaster and poet), Naeem Akhtar (politician), Raheem Lone and Khalil Lone (noted hunters documented in Roosevelt’s book *East of the Sun and West of the Moon*), Nizam Uddin Bhat (politician), Faisal Ali Dar (social activist), Prof. Manzoor Fazili (academician and writer), Prof. Mohd Amin Malik (academician and columnist), Dr. Maroof Shah (writer), Masood Samoon (IAS and writer), and Asgar Samoon (IAS).

text: Barack Hussein Obama II (born August 4, 1961) is an American politician who served as the 44th president of the United States from 2009 to 2017. A member of the Democratic Party, he was the first African American president. Obama previously served as a U.S. senator representing Illinois from 2005 to 2008 and as an Illinois state senator from 1997 to 2004. Born in Honolulu, Hawaii, at Kapiolani Medical Center for Women and Children, Obama is the only president born outside the contiguous 48 states. He was born to an 18-year-old American mother, Ann Dunham (1942–1995), of English, Welsh, German, Swiss, and Irish descent, and a 27-year-old Kenyan father, Barack Obama Sr. (1934–1982), a married Luo Kenyan from Nyang'oma Kogelo. His last name, Obama, was derived from his Luo descent. His parents met in 1960 in a Russian language class at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa, where his father was a foreign student on a scholarship, and married in Wailuku, Hawaii, on February 2, 1961, six months before Obama was born. In late August 1961, shortly after his birth, Obama and his mother moved to the University of Washington in Seattle, where they lived for a year. During that time, Obama Sr. completed his undergraduate degree in economics in Hawaii, graduating in June 1962, and later earned a Master of Arts in economics from Harvard University. The couple divorced in March 1964. Obama Sr. returned to Kenya in 1964, where he married for a third time and worked as the senior economic analyst in the Ministry of Finance; he visited his son in Hawaii only once, at Christmas 1971, before being killed in an automobile accident in 1982 when Obama was 21 years old. In 1963, Dunham met Lolo Soetoro, an Indonesian East–West Center graduate student in geography, who married her on Molokai on March 15, 1965. After two one-year extensions of his J-1 visa, Lolo returned to Indonesia in 1966, and his wife and stepson followed in 1967. The family initially lived in the Menteng Dalam neighborhood in the Tebet district of South Jakarta and later moved to a wealthier neighborhood in the Menteng district of Central Jakarta. When Obama was six, he and his mother moved to Indonesia to join his stepfather. From age six to ten, he was registered in school as "Barry" and attended local Indonesian-language schools, supplemented by English-language Calvert School homeschooling by his mother, and became fluent in Indonesian. During his time in Indonesia, his stepfather taught him to be resilient and gave him a hardheaded assessment of how the world works. In 1971, Obama returned to Honolulu to live with his maternal grandparents, Madelyn and Stanley Dunham. He attended Punahou School, a private college preparatory school, with a scholarship from fifth grade until graduating in 1979. In high school, he continued to use the nickname "Barry" until making a visit to Kenya in 1980. From 1972 to 1975, he lived with his mother and half-sister, Maya Soetoro, in Hawaii while she was a graduate student in anthropology at the University of Hawaii. When she and Maya returned to Indonesia in 1975, Obama stayed in Hawaii so she could begin anthropology field work. His mother spent most of the next two decades in Indonesia, divorced Lolo Soetoro in 1980, earned a PhD in 1992, and died in 1995 in Hawaii from ovarian and uterine cancer. Obama wrote that the opportunity Hawaii offered to experience a variety of cultures in a climate of mutual respect became an integral part of his worldview. He also used alcohol, marijuana, and cocaine during his teenage years to "push questions of who I was out of my mind" and was a member of the "Choom Gang," a self-named group of friends who smoked marijuana. After graduating from high school in 1979, Obama moved to Los Angeles to attend Occidental College on a full scholarship. In February 1981, he made his first public speech calling for Occidental to disinvest from South Africa. In mid-1981, he traveled to Indonesia to visit his mother and half-sister and visited the families of college friends in Pakistan. Later in 1981, he transferred to Columbia University in New York City as a junior, where he majored in political science with a specialty in international relations and English literature, lived off-campus on West 109th Street, graduated in 1983 with a Bachelor of Arts degree and a 3.7 GPA, and worked briefly at the Business International Corporation as a financial researcher and writer and as a project coordinator for the New York Public Interest Research Group. Two years after graduating from Columbia, Obama moved to Chicago and was hired as director of the Developing Communities Project, a faith-based community organization in Roseland, West Pullman, and Riverdale. He worked as a community organizer from June 1985 to May 1988, helping set up a job training program, a college preparatory tutoring program, and a tenants' rights organization in Altgeld Gardens, and also worked as a consultant and instructor for the Gamaliel Foundation. In mid-1988, he traveled to Europe for three weeks and then to Kenya for five weeks, meeting many of his paternal relatives for the first time. Despite being offered a full scholarship to Northwestern University School of Law, he enrolled at Harvard Law School in the fall of 1988, living in nearby Somerville, Massachusetts. He was selected as an editor of the Harvard Law Review at the end of his first year, became president of the journal in his second year, and served as a research assistant to constitutional scholar Laurence Tribe. During summers, he worked at law firms Sidley Austin (1989) and Hopkins & Sutter (1990). His election as the first black president of the Harvard Law Review gained national media attention and led to a publishing contract and advance for a book about race relations, which evolved into a personal memoir, published in mid-1995 as Dreams from My Father. He graduated from Harvard Law in 1991 with a Juris Doctor magna cum laude. In 1991, he accepted a two-year position as Visiting Law and Government Fellow at the University of Chicago Law School to work on his first book and then taught constitutional law at the University of Chicago Law School for twelve years, first as a lecturer from 1992 to 1996 and then as a senior lecturer from 1996 to 2004. From April to October 1992, he directed Illinois's Project Vote, a voter registration campaign that registered 150,000 of 400,000 unregistered African Americans, leading Crain's Chicago Business to name him to its 1993 list of "40 under Forty" powers to be. In a 2006 interview, Obama highlighted the diversity of his extended family, describing it as "like a little mini-United Nations," noting he has a half-sister, Maya Soetoro-Ng, and seven other half-siblings from his Kenyan father's family, six of whom live. His mother was survived by her Kansas-born mother, Madelyn Dunham, who died on November 2, 2008, two days before Obama's election to the presidency. Obama has roots in Ireland; he met his Irish cousins in Moneygall in May 2011. In Dreams from My Father, he ties his mother's family history to possible Native American ancestors and distant relatives of Jefferson Davis and shares distant ancestors in common with George W. Bush and Dick Cheney. Obama lived with anthropologist Sheila Miyoshi Jager while a community organizer in Chicago in the 1980s; he proposed to her twice, both times being turned down, and the relationship was not made public until May 2017. In June 1989, Obama met Michelle Robinson when employed at Sidley Austin; she joined him at social functions and declined his initial requests to date. They began dating later that summer, became engaged in 1991, and were married on October 3, 1992. After suffering a miscarriage, Michelle underwent in vitro fertilization to conceive their children. Their first daughter, Malia Ann, was born in 1998, followed by a second daughter, Natasha ("Sasha"), in 2001. The daughters attended the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools and, when they moved to Washington, D.C., in January 2009, began at the Sidwell Friends School. The Obamas had two Portuguese Water Dogs; the first, a male named Bo, was a gift from Senator Ted Kennedy, and in 2013 was joined by Sunny, a female. Bo died of cancer on May 8, 2021. Obama is a supporter of the Chicago White Sox and threw out the first pitch at the 2005 ALCS when a senator, and in 2009 at the All-Star Game while wearing a White Sox jacket. He is primarily a Chicago Bears football fan in the NFL, but as a child and adolescent was a fan of the Pittsburgh Steelers and rooted for them ahead of their victory in Super Bowl XLIII, 12 days after he took office as president. In 2011, Obama invited the 1985 Chicago Bears to the White House, the first visit since their 1986 Super Bowl win due to the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster. He plays basketball, a sport he participated in as a member of his high school's varsity team, and is left-handed. In 2005, the Obama family applied the proceeds of a book deal and moved from a Hyde Park, Chicago condominium to a $1.6 million house (equivalent to $2.6 million in 2024) in neighboring Kenwood, Chicago. The purchase of an adjacent lot and sale of part of it to Obama by the wife of developer, campaign donor, and friend Tony Rezko attracted media attention due to Rezko's subsequent indictment and conviction on political corruption charges unrelated to Obama. In December 2007, Money Magazine estimated Obama's net worth at $1.3 million (equivalent to $2 million in 2024), and their 2009 tax return showed a household income of $5.5 million—up from about $4.2 million in 2007 and $1.6 million in 2005—mostly from book sales.

text: On January 14, 2009, House Democratic leaders introduced a 1,017-page plan to overhaul the U.S. health care system, which President Obama wanted Congress to approve by the end of 2009. After public debate during the congressional summer recess of 2009, Obama delivered a speech to a joint session of Congress on September 9 to address concerns over the proposals. In March 2009, Obama lifted a ban on using federal funds for stem cell research. On November 7, 2009, a health care bill featuring the public option was passed in the House. On December 24, 2009, the Senate passed its own bill—without a public option—on a party-line vote of 60–39. On March 21, 2010, the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA, colloquially "Obamacare") passed in the House by a vote of 219 to 212, having previously passed the Senate in December. Obama signed the bill into law on March 23, 2010. ---

### 🌕 **Cause-and-Effect Diagram: The 1967 Total Lunar Eclipse and the Surveyor 3 Probe**

This diagram connects the astronomical event (the total lunar eclipse on April 24, 1967) to a real-world space mission (Surveyor 3), creating a meaningful, memorable narrative that enhances understanding through context and relevance.

---

#### 🔍 **Cause-and-Effect Diagram (Text-Based Flow)**

| **Cause** | **Effect** | **Explanation / Connection** |
|---------|----------|-------------------------------|
| **Total lunar eclipse occurred on April 24, 1967** | → Surveyor 3 probe was active on the Moon during this event | The Moon entered Earth’s umbral shadow, turning red (a "blood moon"). This event provided a unique, natural lighting condition on the lunar surface. |
| **Surveyor 3 was operating on the Moon’s surface** | → Scientists could observe and record the Moon’s behavior during the eclipse | The probe was functioning normally, collecting data such as temperature, radiation, and surface conditions. |
| **The Moon was in Earth’s umbral shadow** | → Surface temperatures dropped significantly | The absence of direct sunlight caused a measurable drop in surface temperature — a key data point for scientists studying lunar thermal properties. |
| **Eclipse lasted nearly 2 hours (up to 1.3356 umbral magnitude)** | → Extended period of darkness allowed for long-duration observations | Surveyor 3 could monitor how the lunar surface responded over time, including changes in thermal gradients and radiation levels. |
| **Eclipse occurred just after perigee (April 23, 1967)** | → Moon appeared larger, increasing the shadow’s size and duration | The larger apparent diameter meant the Moon passed through Earth’s shadow more completely and for a longer time, enhancing the observational window for Surveyor 3. |
| **Eclipse was part of a tetrad (4 total eclipses in a row)** | → Provided a recurring opportunity for scientific study | Scientists could compare data across multiple eclipses, improving understanding of lunar surface behavior under varying conditions. |

---

### 📌 Why This Strategy Works

- **Contextual Relevance**: Instead of just memorizing eclipse parameters, students connect the event to a real mission — making it more engaging and memorable.
- **Narrative Structure**: The cause-and-effect chain tells a story: *An eclipse happened → the Moon went dark → Surveyor 3 observed it → scientists learned something new.*
- **Cognitive Linking**: The brain remembers events better when they are tied to real-world applications or human actions (like a probe collecting data).
- **Interdisciplinary Learning**: Blends astronomy, physics (thermal science), and space exploration — showing how science is applied in practice.

---

### 💡 Example for Students (Simplified Version)

> "On April 24, 1967, the Moon went dark during a total lunar eclipse. At that moment, the **Surveyor 3 probe** was on the Moon’s surface. Scientists used this rare event to study how the Moon’s surface cools when it’s in Earth’s shadow. Because the Moon was larger and the eclipse lasted nearly two hours, Surveyor 3 had a perfect chance to collect data on temperature, radiation, and surface changes — all under natural conditions. This made the eclipse not just a sky event, but a scientific milestone."

---

### ✅ Final Takeaway

By linking the **astronomical phenomenon** (total lunar eclipse) to the **real-world mission** (Surveyor 3), we transform abstract facts into a vivid, human-centered story. This strategy turns passive reading into active learning — helping students remember not just *what* happened, but *why* it mattered.

> 🚀 **The Moon went dark — and a robot learned something important about it.**

In March 2009, Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner introduced the Public–Private Investment Program for Legacy Assets, which included provisions for buying up to $2 trillion in depreciated real estate assets. In March 2009, Obama intervened in the automotive industry by renewing loans for General Motors and Chrysler to continue operations while reorganizing, setting terms for both firms' bankruptcies, including the sale of Chrysler to Italian automaker Fiat and a reorganization of GM giving the U.S. government a temporary 60 percent equity stake. In June 2009, dissatisfied with the pace of economic stimulus, Obama called on his cabinet to accelerate investment. He signed the Car Allowance Rebate System, known as "Cash for Clunkers," which temporarily boosted the economy. The Bush and Obama administrations authorized spending and loan guarantees totaling about $11.5 trillion from the Federal Reserve and the Department of the Treasury, though only $3 trillion had been spent by the end of November 2009. On August 2, 2011, after a lengthy congressional debate, Obama signed the bipartisan Budget Control Act of 2011, which enforced limits on discretionary spending until 2021, established a procedure to increase the debt limit, created a Congressional Joint Select Committee on Deficit Reduction with a goal of achieving at least $1.5 trillion in budgetary savings over 10 years, and established automatic spending reductions of up to $1.2 trillion if the committee failed to achieve savings. The legislation prevented a U.S. government default on its obligations. By November 2012, the unemployment rate fell to 7.7 percent, decreasing to 6.7 percent in the last month of 2013, and continuing to decline to 6.3 percent in the first quarter of 2014. GDP growth returned in the third quarter of 2009 at 1.6 percent, increasing to 5.0 percent in the fourth quarter, followed by a 3.7 percent increase in the first quarter of 2010, with lesser gains later, and overall growth of 2.9 percent in 2010. The Congressional Budget Office and many economists credit Obama's stimulus plan for economic growth, with the CBO reporting that the stimulus increased employment by 1–2.1 million, though it conceded that it is impossible to determine how many of those jobs would have existed without the stimulus. text: Baron Blitzkrieg is a supervillain appearing in American comic books published by DC Comics. The character, also known as Baron Reiter and simply the Baron, was created by Gerry Conway and Don Heck and first appeared in World's Finest Comics #246 (September 1977). Originally a vicious German army officer during World War II, Baron Reiter was blinded and disfigured when a concentration camp prisoner threw a bottle in his face. German scientists experimented on him as a Nazi, restoring his sight but not his appearance. As a result, he gains superhuman strength, invulnerability, optical energy beams, and the ability to fly. Initially, he could manifest these abilities one at a time, but underwent training to use them together. His early appearances were primarily antagonistic encounters with Wonder Woman and Superman. He later became a frequent opponent of the All-Star Squadron, brainwashed Commander Steel, confronted Hourman resulting in Red Bee's death, conspired with Zyklon to use the Liberty Bell to destroy Philadelphia before being defeated by the original Liberty Belle, Johnny Quick, and Jay Garrick / Flash, tried to stay hidden in Jamaica, and served as a benefactor of Axis Amerika. The Baron leads Shadowspire and collaborates with Vandal Savage's Symbolix organization in experimental research on Damage and an assassination attempt that is foiled by Deathstroke. During the "Infinite Crisis" storyline, he joins the Secret Society of Super Villains and is killed by Superboy-Prime during the Battle of Metropolis. In the "Blackest Night" storyline, his corpse is entombed below the Hall of Justice and later revived as a Black Lantern. In a flashback from JSA (vol. 2), during the 1940s, he led Gudra the Valkyrie, Horned Owl, Zyklon, and Nazi soldiers in an attempt to steal the Spear of Destiny, which was thwarted by the Justice Society of America and the Blackhawks. He possesses enhanced strength, agility, and endurance, wears body armor that provides some protection from physical attacks, has heat vision, and the ability to fly, and can travel between Earth-2 and Earth-X. In the alternate Flashpoint timeline, he makes a minor appearance and is killed by Frankenstein.

text: Basanti Dulal Nag Chaudhuri (6 September 1917 – 25 June 2006) was an Indian nuclear scientist and academic who served as Scientific Advisor to the Ministry of Defence, Government of India, and played a pivotal role in India's nuclear program. He is recognized as one of the pioneers of nuclear physics in India. As Director General of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), he was instrumental in Pokhran-I (Smiling Buddha), India's first successful nuclear bomb test on 18 May 1974, which made India the sixth nation in the world to become a nuclear superpower, following the United States of America, Soviet Union (now Russia), England, France, and China. He also initiated the first feasibility studies on India's ballistic missile program. Born into a Bengali Hindu family in Narayanganj, Dhaka, Bengal Presidency, British India (present-day Bangladesh), his family relocated to West Bengal, India, following the partition of India in 1947 and the communal violence in East Bengal. His father became a professor of English at Banaras Hindu University (now IIT-BHU), Varanasi. Nagchaudhuri earned a Bachelor of Science degree from Banaras Hindu University and a Master's degree from Allahabad University. In Allahabad, he met lawyer Parmeshwar Narayan Haksar and renowned physicist Meghnad Saha, with whom he became close and joined his research group. In July 1938, when Saha moved to Rajabazar Science College, University of Calcutta, Nagchaudhuri followed. With Saha's support and funding from the Tatas, he moved to the University of California, Berkeley in 1938 to pursue a doctorate in Nuclear Physics, under Ernest Lawrence, completing it in 1941. After returning to India, he joined Saha's research group at Rajabazar Science College and, in 1949, became affiliated with the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics (SINP), later serving as its Director after Saha's retirement in 1952. His research focused on nuclear isomers, induced radioactivity, Cherenkov radiation, and nonthermal plasma. Before returning to India, he had arranged for the shipment of parts for a cyclotron magnet to Calcutta University, but the second consignment was sunk by the Japanese; the team, led by Saha and later Nagchaudhuri, built the remaining components, overcoming persistent issues with vacuum pumps and demountable oscillators. The cyclotron began functioning in 1954 after Emilio Segre's visit, and Nagchaudhuri is credited with building the first cyclotron in India. In 1953, he succeeded Meghnad Saha as Palit Professor of Physics at Calcutta University, holding the position until 1959. He was a visiting professor at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1961–62 and was nominated as a Lincoln Lecturer. Through his connections with B.C. Roy and P.N. Haksar, he was appointed Chairman of the Cabinet Committee on Science & Technology from 1969 to 1972 and served as Scientific Advisor to the Ministry of Defence during this period. He became a Member of the Planning Commission in 1970 and served as Scientific Advisor to the DRDO from 1970 to 1974. In October 1972, Prime Minister Indira Gandhi approved the Smiling Buddha test, and Nagchaudhuri was a member of the steering committee for its preparations. The explosive lenses for the test were fabricated in the DRDO laboratories under his leadership. In 1970, he was tasked by Indira Gandhi to prepare a classified feasibility study for long-range ballistic missiles, leading to the initiation of Project Valiant in 1972 to develop a liquid-fuelled intermediate-range ballistic missile and Project Devil at DRDL for short-range surface-to-air missiles. Both projects were terminated in 1974 due to internal conflicts and lack of progress but laid the groundwork for the Integrated Guided Missile Development Program in the early 1980s. In 1970–71, he chaired a committee on India's maritime security, recommending coastal patrols, a registry of offshore fishing vessels, and a force to intercept illegal vessels—recommendations that formed the basis of the Rustamji Committee in 1974, leading to the establishment of the Indian Coast Guard. From 1 July 1974 to 1 January 1979, he served as Vice Chancellor of Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU). From 1975 to 1977, he chaired the National Committee on Environmental Planning and Coordination. He also served on the Board of Governors of the Indian Institute of Technology, Delhi. Nagchaudhuri was a member of numerous Indian and international scientific councils, including the Scientific Council of the International Centre for Theoretical Physics from 1976 to 1984 and the Research Advisory Council of the National Physical Laboratory from 1980 to 1982, and served as a member and vice-chair of the Board of Governors of the East-West Center. He also served on the boards of Bharat Dynamics Limited, Bharat Electronics Limited, and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited. He maintained an active interest in Hindustani Classical Music and Bengali literature and culture. He was elected a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy in 1964, awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 1975, and received honorary doctorates from Andhra University and Kanpur University. He died of a cerebral infarction on 25 June 2006 and was survived by his wife, Dipali Nag, his son, and his family.
