text: Established to provide income, the dive operations at Bikini Atoll began in June 1996 when the Bikini Council authorized diving as a means of generating revenue for the islanders, both currently and upon their eventual return. The council hired dive guide Edward Maddison, who had lived on Bikini since 1985, and Fabio Amaral, a Brazilian citizen, as head divemaster and resort manager. The tours are limited to fewer than a dozen experienced divers per week, cost more than $5,000, and include detailed histories of the nuclear tests. The operation generated over $500,000 during the 2001 season from May to October. To accommodate the dive and fishing programs, the Bikini Council built air-conditioned rooms with private bathrooms and showers, verandas overlooking the lagoon, and a dining facility serving American-style meals and Marshallese dishes featuring fresh seafood. Only 12 visitors are hosted at a time, and all fruits and vegetables used in the operations are imported due to lingering contamination. In October 2010, a live-aboard, self-contained vessel successfully conducted dive operations, and in 2011, the local government licensed it as a provider of dive expeditions. The dive season runs from May to October, and visitors may still land on the island for brief stays. In early 2017, Master Liveaboards announced they would add Bikini Atoll to their list of destinations for technical divers using their vessel Truk Master, with trips beginning in May 2018 after receiving a license from the Bikini Council. In May 2021, due to pent-up demand from the COVID-19 pandemic, Master Liveaboards announced they would add an additional vessel to operate at Bikini Atoll starting in 2022. The lagoon, undisturbed for decades, has abundant sea life, including sharks, with visibility exceeding 100 feet (30 meters), making it one of the top 10 diving locations globally. Divers receive history lessons, including movies and briefings on the ships, their histories, and tours of the island and atoll. The USS Saratoga (CV-3), the second largest of only three accessible aircraft carriers, is among the ships available for diving. Sport fishing was also opened to visitors, as coral reefs have largely recovered after 50 years of absence of humans, attracting large fish such as 30 lb (14 kg) dogtooth tuna, 20 lb (9.1 kg) barracuda, and giant trevally up to 50 pounds (23 kg). The atoll is open to visitors aboard self-sufficient vessels with prior approval, requiring payment for a diver and two local government representatives to accompany them and verify that artifacts are not removed. Extensive research has confirmed low radiation levels, and the site is recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site on 3 August 2010 for its direct tangible evidence of nuclear tests, including sunken ships and the Bravo crater, equivalent to 7,000 times the force of the Hiroshima bomb. In 1998, the International Atomic Energy Agency conducted environmental testing to validate previous data on air absorption rates, soil, and food radionuclide concentrations, and recommended against permanent resettlement due to radiological conditions. However, a 2012 assessment by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory found cesium-137 levels were dropping faster than expected, with scientific director Terry Hamilton stating that conditions were improving at an accelerated rate and that with soil removal and potassium addition, the 15 millirem standard could be approached, making the island potentially habitable. Despite this, the islanders lack funding to remove topsoil and virtually none of the living islanders have ever lived on Bikini. As of 2013, about 4,880 descendants of the original Bikini people live on Kili and other Marshall Islands, with some having migrated to the United States. The island is currently inhabited by 4–6 caretakers and visited by a few scientists. In 1995, the council learned that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standard required reducing radiation levels to 15 millirems, substantially less than the U.S. Department of Energy standard of 100 millirems, which significantly increased cleanup costs and stalled the effort. In 1975, islanders who returned to Bikini Atoll learned it was unsafe and sued the United States for $900 billion, demanding a radiological study. The U.S. established the Hawaiian Trust Fund for the People of Bikini with $3 million, added $3 million when residents were removed in 1978, and created the Resettlement Trust Fund for the People of Bikini with $20 million in 1982, adding $90 million to cover cleanup, reconstruction, and resettlement. The Compact of Free Association, signed in 1983 and effective in 1986, was modified in 2004 and included Section 177 providing $75 million over 15 years for reparations. Payments began in 1987 with $2.4 million annually to the entire Bikini population and $2.6 million into the Bikini Claims Trust Fund, which is intended to exist in perpetuity and provide 5% annual payments. The U.S. also provided $150 million in compensation for damage from nuclear testing and displacement. In 2001, the Nuclear Claims Tribunal ruled against the U.S., awarding $278 million for loss of land use and $251,500,000 for atoll rehabilitation to restore Bikini to a safe and productive state. However, the U.S. Congress has failed to fund the settlement, and the only recourse is a petition to Congress. The Supreme Court denied the islanders' appeal to compel funding. By 2001, of the original 167 residents, 70 were still alive, and the population had grown to 2,800, mostly living on Kili, in Majuro, or in the United States. The Hawaiian Trust Fund was liquidated in December 2006. As of 31 March 2013, the Resettlement Trust Fund was valued at approximately $82 million and the Bikini Claims Trust Fund at approximately $60 million. In 2006, each trust member received about $500 annually, and in 2012, the trusts produced $6 to $8 million in annual investment income, paying less than $15,000 per family annually with little left for cleanup. In 2017, after lobbying by Bikini leaders, the Trump administration stated there would be no limits on withdrawals from the main fund and no further audits. Mayor Anderson Jibas used fund assets to purchase a plane, construction equipment, two cargo ships, an apartment complex in Majuro, and 283 acres of land in Hawaii. By March 2023, only $100,041 remained in the fund, which held $59 million in 2017. The council stopped paying its approximately 350 employees and ceased monthly subsistence payments to 6,800 members. By 2023, a state of emergency was declared on Kili, requiring Marshallese government intervention, and aid restored electricity after funds were depleted. text: Humans have inhabited Bikini Atoll for about 3,600 years, with archaeological findings dating back to between 1960 and 1650 BC, and other artifacts from 1000 BC to 1 BC and AD 400 to 1400, though these dates may be affected by non-stratigraphic samples and driftwood. In 1529, the Spanish ship La Florida, commanded by Álvaro de Saavedra, visited the atoll, which may have been Bikini or Enewetak, and the islanders fled after Saavedra fired his musket. Otto von Kotzebue was the first westerner to definitively see the atoll in 1816 and 1817, naming it Eschscholtz Atoll after the ship's naturalist. In 1834, three crew members of a trading schooner were killed at Bikini, leading to retaliation where 30 Marshallese hostages were killed by the Hawaiian brig Waverly. During the German colonial period from 1885, the atoll was used for copra oil production, with Bikini islanders recruited into the trade. The Marshall Islands, including Bikini, were captured by the Imperial Japanese Navy in 1914 and mandated to Japan in 1920, with local leaders managing affairs until World War II began. Japanese forces built a watchtower on Bikini to guard against American invasion, and after the American capture of Kwajalein in February 1944, only five Japanese soldiers remained, who chose suicide over capture. The Battle of Eniwetok followed. The U.S. conducted a series of 23 nuclear weapons tests at Bikini Atoll between 1946 and 1958 at seven sites, with a combined explosive yield of about 77 megatons, detonated on the reef, sea, air, and underwater. In February 1946, the U.S. asked the 167 Micronesian inhabitants to relocate temporarily for testing, with their leader, King Juda, agreeing to the request, stating "Everything is in God's hands." Nine of the eleven family heads chose Rongerik Atoll, which was one-sixth the size of Bikini and lacked sufficient water and food, and was considered haunted by traditional beliefs. The residents were transported to Rongerik on March 7, 1946, and left with only a few weeks of supplies, leading to starvation. In 1947, the U.S. convinced the United Nations to designate Micronesia as a Strategic Trust Territory, with the U.S. Navy initially managing it from Guam and later the Department of the Interior from Saipan, with a directive to promote economic advancement and protect land and resources. Despite this, residents on Rongerik were starving, and in January 1948, anthropologist Leonard Mason found the community suffering from malnutrition and poisoning from fish, with residents pleading for food. The Navy then moved them to Ujelang Atoll, which was later replaced by a move to Kwajalein Atoll in March 1948, where they lived in tents beside the airport runway. In June 1948, the Bikini community chose Kili Island, a small, uninhabited island of 0.36 square miles (0.93 km²) without a lagoon or coral reef, as a long-term home. In June, 184 residents moved to Kili, where they soon faced food shortages and difficulty fishing due to rough seas and lack of a protected lagoon, leading to starvation. In 1949, a 40-foot ship was donated to transport copra but was wrecked. The U.S. airdropped food, and residents relied on imported rice and canned goods. In 1955 and 1956, rough seas caused unloading problems, worsening food shortages, and some moved to Jaluit, where food was more available. A satellite community was established on Jaluit for some families, and homes on both Kili and Jaluit were damaged by typhoons in 1957 and 1958. In June 1968, President Lyndon B. Johnson promised return to Bikini to 540 family members, with the Atomic Energy Commission clearing debris and the U.S. Trust Territory rebuilding structures and replanting crops. However, regular air flights were ended, coconut trees were replanted in 1972, but coconut crabs were found to have high radioactivity and were unsafe to eat. The Bikini Council delayed return due to concerns. In 1972, three extended families, totaling about 100 people, returned despite risks. In 1973, scientists found some wells too radioactive and that pandanus and breadfruit were unsafe; urine samples showed low levels of plutonium-239 and 240. In May 1977, dangerously high levels of strontium-90 were found in well water, and in June, the Department of Energy stated that all living patterns on Bikini exceeded federal radiation guidelines for thirty-year doses. A later study found an 11-fold increase in caesium-137 body burdens, with a 75% increase described as "incredible." Women experienced miscarriages, stillbirths, and genetic abnormalities, and research found that coral soil, low in potassium, caused plants to absorb caesium-137 instead. The Trust Territory evacuated the residents again. In 1986, the islanders received $75 million in damages, and in 1988, $90 million for radiological cleanup. In 1987, elders traveled to Eneu Island to reestablish property lines, and construction began on a hotel, docks, roads, generators, desalinators, and power lines. The Bikini Atoll Divers was established to generate income. In 1995, it was discovered that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency required radiation levels to be reduced to 15 millirems, far below the Department of Energy’s 100 millirem standard, significantly increasing cleanup costs and halting efforts. As a result of military use and failed resettlement, the atoll is littered with abandoned concrete bunkers and heavy equipment. In September 1978, Trust Territory officials relocated the residents, and the radiological survey began after their removal and return to Kili. As of 2013, Kili Island, at 0.36 square miles (0.93 km²), supported about 600 residents living in cinderblock houses, who rely on a settlement trust fund and receive one to two boxes of frozen chicken and two to four 51-lb boxes of food annually. Of the original 167 residents, 25 lived on Bikini in 1946. The current resident population of the atoll is 4–6 caretakers, including Edward Maddison, who lived on Bikini Island from 1985 to 2020. His grandfather was one of the original residents relocated in 1946. He assisted the U.S. Department of Energy with soil monitoring, testing cleanup methods, mapping wrecks in the lagoon, and accompanying visitors on dives. He was the divemaster of Bikini Atoll Divers. Maddison died in Majuro, Marshall Islands, on March 29, 2020.

text: Bikini Atoll, known as Eschscholtz Atoll between the 19th century and 1946, is a coral reef in the Marshall Islands comprising 23 islands surrounding a 229.4-square-mile (594.1 km²) central lagoon, located at the northern end of the Ralik Chain, approximately 530 miles (850 km) northwest of Majuro. The atoll's English name derives from the German colonial name Bikini, transliterated from the Marshallese Pikinni, meaning "surface of coconuts," and was given when the atoll was part of German New Guinea. Humans have inhabited the atoll for about 3,600 years, with archaeological evidence dating artifacts to between 1960 and 1650 BC. The islanders traditionally cultivated plants such as coconut, pandanus, papaya, banana, arrowroot, taro, limes, breadfruit, and pumpkin, and relied on fishing using coconut husk line and sea shell hooks, employing over 25 methods. They were skilled boatbuilders and navigators, using two-hulled proas, and lived in a matrilineal society where land, passed through the mother, was the primary measure of wealth and social status. Each family belonged to a clan (Bwij) that owned land, with a chief (Iroij) overseeing land tenure, resource use, and disputes, supported by clan heads (Alap) and laborers (Dri-jerbal). The islanders were also known for their hospitality and traditional dress, with men wearing fringed skirts 25 to 30 inches long and women wearing woven pandanus and hibiscus mats belted around the waist, later adopting Christian missionary-influenced wau gowns. In 1914, Japan occupied the islands, establishing copra plantations where chiefs could retain up to $20,000 annually. During WWII, Japanese troops and American forces attacked the atoll, killing many soldiers. In 1946, the United States selected Bikini Atoll as a nuclear testing site, relocating 167 residents—comprising about 40 families—to Rongerik Atoll, which lacked sufficient food, leading to starvation by early 1948. They were then moved to Kwajalein Atoll for six months before settling on Kili Island, which is one-sixth the size of Bikini. In 1972, about 100 residents voluntarily returned to Bikini, but by May 1978, scientists found dangerously high levels of strontium-90 in well water and abnormally high caesium-137 in residents' bodies, prompting an evacuation in September 1978. The United States conducted 23 nuclear tests between 1946 and 1958 at seven sites on the atoll, including air, underwater, and surface detonations, with a combined yield of about 77 Mt, including the 15 Mt Castle Bravo test in 1954. These tests destroyed islands such as Bokonijien, Aerokojlol, and part of Namu, and caused extensive radioactive contamination. The U.S. used explosives to cut a channel and blow up coral heads to allow larger vessels access, resulting in irradiated coral and mud spreading across the lagoon. As of 2008, the atoll had recovered nearly 65% of its pre-contamination biodiversity, though 28 coral species are locally extinct. Radiation levels have decreased, allowing limited tourism and diving, but the atoll remains unfit for habitation due to persistent contamination, especially in food sources like plants and wildlife. The Bikini islanders are prohibited from returning home. A trust fund established to support the islanders' needs, paying about $550 annually per person as of 2013, was drained in the late 2010s: it stood at $71 million in 2016 with $4 million withdrawn, dropped to $4 million by 2020, and to $100,000 by 2023. This led to halted deliveries and unpaid salaries, triggering an emergency and government intervention. The population of descendants now numbers in the thousands, with 1,250 on Kili, 2,150 on Majuro (including 280 on Ejit), 350 on other Marshall Islands, and 850 in the United States, with 5,400 reported in 2016. The atoll's current resident population is only 4–6 caretakers, including Edward Maddison, who lived on Bikini from 1985 to 2020, worked with the U.S. Department of Energy on soil monitoring and cleanup, and served as divemaster for Bikini Atoll Divers, dying in Majuro on March 29, 2020. The atoll is now a World Heritage Site, recognized for its Cold War history and as a natural enclave, though it remains a symbol of nuclear impact and displacement.

text: William Franklin Graham Jr. (/ˈɡreɪəm/; November 7, 1918 – February 21, 2018) was an American evangelist, ordained Southern Baptist minister, and civil rights advocate whose broadcasts and world tours featuring live sermons became well known in the mid-to-late 20th century. Over a career spanning more than six decades, Graham rose to prominence as an evangelical Christian figure in the United States and abroad. According to a biographer, he was considered "among the most influential Christian leaders" of the 20th century. Beginning in the late 1940s and early 1950s, Graham became known for filling stadiums and other massive venues around the world where he preached live sermons, which were often broadcast via radio and television, with some continuing into the 21st century. He hosted his annual "crusades," evangelistic live-campaigns, from 1947 until his retirement in 2005, and hosted the radio show *Hour of Decision* from 1950 to 1954. He repudiated racial segregation, insisting on racial integration for all of his revivals and crusades as early as 1953, and later invited Martin Luther King Jr. to preach jointly at a revival in New York City in 1957. He helped shape the worldview of a large number of people from diverse backgrounds, leading them to find a relationship between the Bible and contemporary secular viewpoints. According to his website, Graham spoke to live audiences of at least 210 million people in more than 185 countries and territories through various meetings, including BMS World Mission and Global Mission events. Graham was close to U.S. presidents Dwight D. Eisenhower, Lyndon B. Johnson (one of his closest friends), and Richard Nixon. He was also a lifelong friend with Robert Schuller, another televangelist and founding pastor of the Crystal Cathedral, whom Graham encouraged to start his own television ministry. Graham was appreciated by mainline Protestant denominations, as he encouraged mainline Protestants converted to his evangelical message to remain within or return to their mainline churches. Despite early suspicions toward Catholicism common among evangelical Protestants, Graham eventually developed amicable ties with many American Catholic Church figures and later encouraged unity between Catholics and Protestants. Graham operated a variety of media and publishing outlets; according to his staff, more than 3.2 million people responded to the invitation at Billy Graham Crusades to "accept Jesus Christ as their personal savior." His lifetime audience, including radio and television broadcasts, likely surpassed billions of people. As a result of his crusades, Graham preached the gospel to more people, live and in-person, than anyone in the history of Christianity. He was on Gallup's list of most admired men and women a record 61 times. Grant Wacker wrote that by the mid-1960s, he had become the "Great Legitimator," saying: "By then his presence conferred status on presidents, acceptability on wars, shame on racial prejudice, desirability on decency, dishonor on indecency, and prestige on civic events." Graham was born on November 7, 1918, in the downstairs bedroom of a farmhouse near Charlotte, North Carolina. Of Scots-Irish descent, he was the eldest of four children born to Morrow (née Coffey) and dairy farmer William Franklin Graham Sr. He was raised on the family dairy farm with his two younger sisters Catherine Morrow and Jean and younger brother Melvin Thomas. When he was nine, the family moved about 75 yards (69 m) from their white frame house to a newly built red brick house. He was raised by his parents in the Associate Reformed Presbyterian Church. Graham attended the Sharon Grammar School and started reading books early, especially novels for boys like Tarzan, which inspired him to hang on trees and give the Tarzan yell; according to his father, this yelling led him to become a minister. Graham was 15 when Prohibition ended in December 1933, and his father forced him and his sister Catherine to drink beer until they became sick, creating a lifelong aversion to alcohol and drugs. Graham was turned down for membership in a local youth group for being "too worldly." Albert McMakin, who worked on the Graham farm, persuaded him to see evangelist Mordecai Ham. According to his autobiography, Graham was 16 when he was converted during a series of revival meetings that Ham led in Charlotte in 1934. After graduating from Sharon High School in May 1936, Graham attended Bob Jones College, where he found the coursework and rules too legalistic and was almost expelled, but Bob Jones Sr. warned him not to throw his life away, saying, "At best, all you could amount to would be a poor country Baptist preacher somewhere out in the sticks... You have a voice that pulls. God can use that voice of yours. He can use it mightily." In 1937, Graham transferred to the Florida Bible Institute in Temple Terrace, Florida. While still a student, he preached his first sermon at Bostwick Baptist Church near Palatka, Florida. In his autobiography, he wrote of receiving his calling on the 18th green of the Temple Terrace Golf and Country Club, adjacent to the institute's campus. Reverend Billy Graham Memorial Park was later established on the Hillsborough River, directly east of the 18th green and across from where Graham often paddled a canoe to a small island in the river, where he would practice preaching to the birds, alligators, and cypress stumps. In 1939, Graham was ordained by a group of Southern Baptist clergy at Peniel Baptist Church in Palatka, Florida. In 1940, he graduated with a Bachelor of Theology degree. Graham then enrolled at Wheaton College in Wheaton, Illinois, where he decided to accept the Bible as the infallible word of God. Henrietta Mears of the First Presbyterian Church of Hollywood in California helped him wrestle with this issue, which he settled at Forest Home Christian Camp (now called Forest Home Ministries) southeast of Big Bear Lake in southern California. While attending Wheaton, Graham was invited to preach one Sunday in 1941 at the United Gospel Tabernacle church. After that, the congregation repeatedly asked him to preach at their church and later asked him to become its pastor. After praying and seeking advice from his friend Dr. Edman, Graham became their church's pastor. In June 1943, Graham graduated from Wheaton College with a degree in anthropology. That same year, Robert Van Kampen, treasurer of the National Gideon Association, invited Graham to preach at Western Springs Baptist Church, and Graham accepted the opportunity on the spot. While there, his friend Torrey Johnson, pastor of the Midwest Bible Church in Chicago, told Graham that his radio program, *Songs in the Night*, was about to be canceled due to lack of funding. Consulting with members of his church in Western Springs, Graham decided to take over Johnson's program with financial support from his congregation. Launching the new radio program on January 2, 1944, still called *Songs in the Night*, Graham recruited the bass-baritone George Beverly Shea as his director of radio ministry. With World War II underway, Graham applied to become a chaplain in the U.S. Army. After being initially turned down for being underweight, he was awarded a commission as a Second Lieutenant but came down with a severe case of mumps in October 1944 before beginning chaplain training at Harvard Divinity School and was bedridden for six weeks. Due to his illness and the expectation that the war would end soon, he was discharged from the army. After a period of recuperation in Florida, he was hired as the first full-time evangelist of the new Youth for Christ (YFC), co-founded by Torrey Johnson and Canadian evangelist Charles Templeton. In his first year as a YFC evangelist, Graham spoke in 47 U.S. states. He traveled extensively as an evangelist in the United States and Europe in the immediate post-war era, making his first overseas trip in 1946. In 1948, in a Modesto, California hotel room, Graham and his evangelistic team established the Modesto Manifesto: a code of ethics for life and work to protect against accusations of financial, sexual, and power abuse. The code includes rules for collecting offerings in churches, working only with churches supportive of cooperative evangelism, using official crowd estimates at outdoor events, and a commitment to never be alone with a woman other than his wife (which became known as the "Billy Graham rule"). Graham was 29 when he became president of Northwestern Bible College in Minneapolis in 1948, making him the youngest president of a college or university in the country, and held the position for four years before resigning in 1952. While serving in this position, Charles Templeton urged him to apply to Princeton Theological Seminary for an advanced theological degree after he himself had done so, but Graham declined and continued as president. The first Billy Graham Crusade was held on September 13–21, 1947, at the Civic Auditorium in Grand Rapids, Michigan, and was attended by 6,000 people. He would preach the gospel and invite individuals to come forward (a practice begun by Dwight L. Moody); such people were called "inquirers" and were given the chance to speak one-on-one with a counselor to clarify questions and pray together. The inquirers were often given a copy of the Gospel of John or a Bible study booklet. He attracted national media coverage, especially in the conservative Hearst chain of newspapers, although Hearst and Graham never met. The crusade event ran for eight weeks—five weeks longer than originally planned. Graham became a national figure, with heavy coverage from the wire services and national magazines. Pianist Rudy Atwood, who played for the tent meetings, wrote that they "rocketed Billy Graham into national prominence, and resulted in the conversion of a number of show-business personalities." In 1953, Graham was offered a five-year, $1 million contract from NBC to appear on television opposite Arthur Godfrey, but he had prior commitments and turned down the offer to continue his live touring revivals. Graham held crusades in London that lasted 12 weeks, and a New York City crusade at Madison Square Garden in 1957, which ran nightly for 16 weeks. At a 1973 rally in Durban, South Africa—the first large mixed-race event in apartheid South Africa—Graham openly declared that "apartheid is a sin." In Moscow, Russia, in 1992, one-quarter of the 155,000 people in Graham's audience went forward at his call. During his crusades, he frequently used the altar call song, "Just As I Am." In 1995, during the Global Mission event, he preached a sermon at Estadio Hiram Bithorn in San Juan, Puerto Rico, that was transmitted by satellite to 185 countries and translated into 116 languages. By the time of his last crusade in 2005 in New York City, he had preached 417 live crusades, including 226 in the U.S. and 195 abroad. Graham spoke at InterVarsity Christian Fellowship's Urbana Student Missions Conference at least nine times—in 1948, 1957, 1961, 1964, 1976, 1979, 1981, 1984, and 1987. At each Urbana conference, he challenged the thousands of attendees to make a commitment to follow Jesus Christ for the rest of their lives. He often quoted a six-word phrase reportedly written in the Bible of William Whiting Borden, the son of a wealthy silver magnate: "No reserves, no retreat, no regrets." Borden had died in Egypt on his way to the mission field. Graham also held evangelistic meetings on several college campuses: at the University of Minnesota during InterVarsity's "Year of Evangelism" in 1950–51, a 4-day mission at Yale University in 1957, and a week-long series of meetings at the University of North Carolina's Carmichael Auditorium in September 1982. In 1955, he was invited by Cambridge University students to lead the mission at the university; the mission was arranged by the Cambridge Inter-Collegiate Christian Union, with London pastor-theologian John Stott serving as Graham's chief assistant. This invitation was greeted with much disapproval in the correspondence columns of *The Times*. In 1950, Graham founded the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association (BGEA) with its headquarters in Minneapolis. The association relocated to Charlotte, North Carolina, in 2003, and maintains a number of international offices, such as in Hong Kong, Tokyo, and Buenos Aires. BGEA ministries have included: In April 2013, the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association started "My Hope With Billy Graham," the largest outreach in its history. It encouraged church members to spread the gospel in small group meetings after showing a video message by Graham. "The idea is for Christians to follow the example of the disciple Matthew in the New Testament and spread the gospel in their own homes." "The Cross" video is the main program in the My Hope America series and was also broadcast the week of Graham's 95th birthday. Graham's early crusades were segregated, but he began adjusting his approach in the 1950s. During a 1953 rally in Chattanooga, Tennessee, Graham tore down the ropes that organizers had erected to segregate the audience into racial sections. In his memoirs, he recounted that he told two ushers to leave the barriers down "or you can go on and have the revival without me." During a sermon held at Vanderbilt University in Nashville on August 23, 1954, he warned a white audience, "Three-fifths of the world is not white. They are rising all over the world. We have been proud and thought we were better than any other race, any other people. Ladies and gentlemen, I want to tell you that we are going to stumble into hell because of our pride." In 1957, Graham's stance toward integration became more publicly visible when he allowed black ministers Thomas Kilgore and Gardner C. Taylor to serve as members of his New York Crusade's executive committee. He also invited Martin Luther King Jr., whom he first met during the Montgomery bus boycott in 1955, to join him in the pulpit at his 16-week revival in New York City, where 2.3 million gathered at Madison Square Garden, Yankee Stadium, and Times Square to hear them. Graham recalled in his autobiography that during this time, he and King developed a close friendship and that he was eventually one of the few people who referred to King as "Mike," a nickname which King asked only his closest friends to call him. Following King's assassination in 1968, Graham mourned that the U.S. had lost "a social leader and a prophet." In private, Graham advised King and other members of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC). Despite their friendship, tensions between Graham and King emerged in 1958, when the sponsoring committee of a crusade that took place in San Antonio, Texas, on July 25 arranged for Graham to be introduced by that state's segregationist governor, Price Daniel. On July 23, King sent a letter to Graham and informed him that allowing Daniel to speak at a crusade that occurred the night before the state's Democratic Primary "can well be interpreted as your endorsement of racial segregation and discrimination." Graham's advisor, Grady Wilson, replied to King that "even though we do not see eye to eye with him on every issue, we still love him in Christ." Though Graham's appearance with Daniel dashed King's hopes of holding joint crusades with Graham in the Deep South, the two remained friends; the next year King told a Canadian television audience that Graham had taken a "very strong stance against segregation." Graham and King would also come to differ on the Vietnam War. After King's "Beyond Vietnam" speech denouncing U.S. intervention in Vietnam, Graham castigated him and others for their criticism of U.S. foreign policy. By the middle of 1960, King and Graham traveled together to the Tenth Baptist World Congress of the Baptist World Alliance. In 1963, Graham posted bail for King to be released from jail during the Birmingham (Alabama) campaign, according to Michael Long, and the King Center acknowledged that Graham had bailed King out of jail during the Albany Movement.

## 🌍 **Chronological Timeline Map: The Story of Bikini Atoll**

---

### 📅 **Pre-Colonial Era (c. 3,600 years ago – 19th century)**

  - Archaeological evidence (charcoal, fish bones, shells) dated between 1960–1650 BC.  
  - Early inhabitants lived off traditional practices: cultivating plants, fishing, and navigating using proas (two-hulled boats).  
- **Traditional Society**:  
  - Matrilineal system: land passed through mothers.  
  - Clans (Bwij) owned land; chiefs (Iroij) controlled land tenure and disputes.  
  - Extended family networks; strong cultural values of hospitality and community.  
- **Lifestyle**:  
  - Cultivated coconuts, taro, pandanus, fish, and shellfish.  
  - Wore traditional clothing (fringed skirts, woven mats), with modesty influenced by Christian missionaries later.

---

### 📅 **19th Century – Pre-World War II**
- **1800s–1914**: Atoll known as *Eschscholtz Atoll* (German name).  
- **1914**: Japan occupies the Marshall Islands, including Bikini.  
  - Islanders work on copra plantations under Japanese rule.  
  - Chiefs receive up to $20,000/year; profits shared with workers.  
  - Cultural traditions of hospitality remain strong.

---

### 📅 **1946 – Forced Relocation Begins**
- **July 1946**: U.S. selects Bikini Atoll as a nuclear testing site.  
- **1946**: 167 residents (40 families) are **forcibly relocated** to **Rongerik Atoll**.  
  - Rongerik lacks food resources and cannot sustain the population.  
  - By early 1948, residents face **starvation** due to lack of food and fish.  
- **November 1948**: Evacuated to **Kwajalein Atoll** (temporary).  
- **1948–1950**: Move to **Kili Island** (a small island, 1/6th the size of Bikini).  
  - Kili becomes the long-term home for most islanders.  
  - Traditional land-based economy (taro, copra) declines due to displacement.

---

### 📅 **1954 – Castle Bravo Test & Radiation Crisis**
- **March 1954**: **Castle Bravo nuclear test** detonated at Bikini Atoll.  
  - Yield: **15 megatons** (largest U.S. test ever).  
  - Massive radioactive fallout spreads across the Marshall Islands.  
  - Fallout detected in well water and soil; **strontium-90 and caesium-137** levels rise dramatically.  
  - **HYSPLIT modeling** used to map fallout and assess contamination.  
- **Aftermath**:  
  - Radiation levels deemed unsafe for human habitation.  
  - Bikini Atoll is declared uninhabitable due to contamination.

---

### 📅 **1972 – First Return to Bikini**
- **1972**: About **100 residents voluntarily return** to Bikini.

In 1953, he became a member of the First Baptist Church Dallas, though he never lived in Texas; in 2008, he transferred his membership to the First Baptist Church of Spartanburg, South Carolina, approximately 1.5 hours from his home in Montreat, North Carolina. Graham died of natural causes on February 21, 2018, at his home in Montreat, North Carolina, at the age of 99. On February 28 and March 1, 2018, he became the fourth private citizen in U.S. history to lie in honor at the United States Capitol rotunda in Washington, D.C., making him the first religious leader to receive this honor; during the ceremony, Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell and Speaker of the House Paul Ryan referred to him as "America's pastor," and President Donald Trump called him "an ambassador for Christ"; televangelist Jim Bakker praised Graham as the greatest preacher since Jesus and stated that Graham visited him in prison. A private funeral service was held on March 2, 2018, and Graham was buried beside his wife in the Prayer Garden on the northeast side of the Billy Graham Library in Charlotte, North Carolina, at the foot of the cross-shaped brick walkway. His pine plywood casket, handcrafted in 2006 by convicted murderers at the Louisiana State Penitentiary, was topped with a wooden cross nailed to it by the prisoners. He is commemorated on the liturgical calendar of the Anglican Church in North America on February 21. On May 16, 2024, a bronze statue of Graham was unveiled in the U.S. Capitol by House Speaker Mike Johnson. Graham's "My Answer" advice column appeared in newspapers for more than 60 years as of 2017. He authored several books, many of which became bestsellers; in the 1970s, *The Jesus Generation* sold 200,000 copies in the first two weeks after publication; *Angels: God's Secret Agents* achieved sales of one million copies within 90 days of release; and *How to Be Born Again* made publishing history with its first printing of 800,000 copies.

text: During the 1964 United States presidential election, supporters of Republican nominee Barry Goldwater sent an estimated 2 million telegrams to Graham's hometown of Montreat, North Carolina, seeking his endorsement. Supportive of President Lyndon B. Johnson's domestic policies and wishing to preserve his friendship with the president, Graham resisted pressure to endorse Goldwater and remained neutral. Following Johnson's election victory, Graham's role as the main White House pastor was solidified; Johnson even considered making Graham a cabinet member and grooming him as his successor, though Graham insisted he had no political ambitions and wished to remain a preacher. Graham's biographer David Aikman acknowledged that the preacher was closer to Johnson than any other president he had ever known, and in February 2025, the BGEA stated that Graham was "probably closer to Johnson than to any other president." He spent the last night of Johnson's presidency in the White House and stayed for the first night of Nixon's. After Nixon's 1968 presidential campaign victory, Graham became an adviser, regularly visiting the White House and leading the president's private worship services. In a meeting with Golda Meir, Nixon offered Graham the ambassadorship to Israel, which he declined. In 1970, Nixon appeared at a Graham revival in East Tennessee, which drew one of the largest crowds in Tennessee of Vietnam War protesters; Nixon was the first president to give a speech from an evangelist's platform. Their friendship strained in 1973 when Graham rebuked Nixon for his post-Watergate behavior and the profanity heard on the Watergate tapes; they reconciled after Nixon's resignation. Graham officiated at one presidential burial and one presidential funeral: he presided over the graveside services of President Lyndon B. Johnson in 1973 and participated in eulogizing him; he officiated at the funeral of former First Lady Pat Nixon in 1993 and at the death and state funeral of Richard Nixon in 1994. During the Monica Lewinsky scandal, Graham asserted that he believed President Bill Clinton to be "a spiritual person." He was unable to attend the state funeral of Ronald Reagan on June 11, 2004, due to recovering from hip replacement surgery, a fact mentioned by George W. Bush in his eulogy. On April 25, 2010, President Barack Obama visited Graham at his home in Montreat, North Carolina, where they "had a private prayer." Graham had a friendly relationship with Queen Elizabeth II, first meeting in 1955 and preaching at Windsor Chapel the following year; their relationship may have stemmed from shared traditional views on Christian faith. Graham was outspoken against communism and supported American Cold War policies, including the Vietnam War; in a secret letter from April 15, 1969, made public twenty years later, Graham encouraged Nixon to bomb the dikes in North Vietnam if peace talks in Paris failed, stating the action would "destroy the economy of North Vietnam" and, by Nixon's estimate, would have killed a million people. In 1982, Graham preached in the Soviet Union and attended a wreath-laying ceremony honoring the war dead of World War II, when the Soviets were American allies against Nazism; he voiced fear of a second holocaust, not against Jews, but "a nuclear holocaust," and advised that "our greatest contribution to world peace is to live with Christ every day." In a 1999 speech, Graham discussed his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Il Sung, praising him as a "different kind of communist" and "one of the great fighters for freedom in his country against the Japanese," noting he had never met Kim Jong Il but had "exchanged gifts with him." During the Watergate affair, there were suggestions that Graham had expressed antisemitic opinions in private discussions with Nixon; he denied this, emphasizing his efforts to build bridges with the Jewish community. In 2002, declassified Nixon tapes confirmed that in a 1972 conversation with Nixon, Graham agreed that Jews controlled the American media, calling it a "stranglehold," and suggested that if Nixon was re-elected, they might be able to do something about it. When the tapes were made public, Graham apologized and said, "Although I have no memory of the occasion, I deeply regret comments I apparently made in an Oval Office conversation with President Nixon ... some 30 years ago. ... They do not reflect my views and I sincerely apologize for any offense caused by the remarks." According to Newsweek, the revelation was magnified due to Graham's longstanding support of Israel and his refusal to join calls for Jewish conversion. In 2009, more Nixon tapes were released, in which Graham is heard in a 1973 conversation with Nixon referring to a group of Jewish journalists as "the synagogue of Satan"; a Graham spokesman stated he has never been an antisemite and that the comparison, in line with the Book of Revelation, was directed at those claiming to be Jews but not holding traditional Jewish values. After a 1957 crusade in New York, some fundamentalist Protestant Christians criticized Graham for his ecumenism, even calling him "Antichrist." Graham expressed inclusivist views, stating in a 1997 interview with Robert Schuller that people without explicit faith in Jesus can be saved, as they are members of the body of Christ because they have been called by God, and that they may not know the name of Jesus but know in their hearts they need something they do not have and turn to the only light they have. Iain Murray, from a conservative Protestant perspective, argued that "Graham's concessions are sad words from one who once spoke on the basis of biblical certainties." In 1970, Graham stated that feminism was "an echo of our overall philosophy of permissiveness" and that women did not want to be "competitive juggernauts pitted against male chauvinists," asserting that the role of wife, mother, and homemaker was the destiny of "real womanhood" according to the Judeo-Christian ethic. These assertions, published in the Ladies' Home Journal, elicited protest letters and were offered as a rebuttal to the establishment of "The New Feminism" section following a sit-in protest at the Journal offices. Graham's daughter Bunny recounted that her father denied her and her sisters higher education, saying, "There was never an idea of a career for us"; she wanted to go to nursing school at Wheaton with a five-year program, but her father said no, with no explanation. She added, "He has forgotten that. Mother has not." Graham's daughter Anne is a Christian minister leading AnGeL Ministries. Graham talked his future wife, Ruth, into abandoning her ambition to evangelize in Tibet in favor of marrying him, stating that doing otherwise would be "to thwart God's obvious will." After agreeing to marry him, Graham cited the Bible for claiming authority over her, saying, "then I'll do the leading and you do the following." According to her obituary, Ruth was active in Christian ministry after marriage, often teaching Sunday School, and all three of Graham's daughters became Christian ministers. Graham regarded homosexuality as a sin and in 1974 described it as "a sinister form of perversion." In 1993, he said that AIDS might be a "judgment" from God, but two weeks later retracted the remark, saying, "I don't believe that, and I don't know why I said it." He opposed same-sex marriage, stating that "I believe the home and marriage is the foundation of our society and must be protected," and his obituary noted he did not want to discuss homosexuality as a political issue. Corky Siemaszko, writing for NBC News, noted that after the 1993 incident, Graham "largely steered clear of the subject." However, in a 1997 appearance on the May 2 episode of 20/20, Graham stated, "I think that the Bible teaches that homosexuality is a sin, but the Bible also teaches that pride is a sin, jealously is a sin, and hate is a sin, evil thoughts are a sin, and so I don't think that homosexuality should be chosen as the overwhelming sin that we are doing today." In 2012, Graham and his son Franklin publicly endorsed North Carolina Amendment 1, a measure to ban same-sex marriage in the state, and condemned President Obama's public support for same-sex marriage later that year. Graham was frequently honored by surveys, including "Greatest Living American," and consistently ranked among the most admired persons in the United States and the world, appearing most frequently on Gallup's list of most admired people. On the day of his death, Graham had been on Gallup's Top 10 "Most Admired Man" list 61 times and held the highest rank of any person since the list began in 1948. In 1967, he was the first Protestant to receive an honorary degree from Belmont Abbey College, a Roman Catholic school. In 1983, he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by U.S. President Ronald Reagan. Graham received the Big Brother of the Year Award for his work on behalf of children, was cited by the George Washington Carver Memorial Institute for contributions to race relations, received the Templeton Foundation Prize for Progress in Religion, and the Sylvanus Thayer Award for his commitment to "Duty, Honor, Country." The "Billy Graham Children's Health Center" in Asheville is named after and funded by Graham. In 1999, the Gospel Music Association inducted Graham into the Gospel Music Hall of Fame to recognize his contributions to Christian music artists such as Michael W. Smith, dc Talk, Amy Grant, Jars of Clay, and others who performed at the Billy Graham Crusades; he was the first non-musician inducted and helped revitalize interest in hymns and create new favorite songs. In 2000, former First Lady Nancy Reagan presented the Ronald Reagan Freedom Award to Graham. In 2001, Queen Elizabeth II awarded him an honorary knighthood, presented by Sir Christopher Meyer, British Ambassador to the U.S., at the British Embassy in Washington DC on December 6, 2001. A professorial chair is named after him at Samford University, the Billy Graham Professor of Evangelism and Church Growth. His alma mater, Wheaton College, has an archive of his papers at the Billy Graham Center. The Southern Baptist Theological Seminary has the Billy Graham School of Missions, Evangelism and Ministry. Graham received 20 honorary degrees and refused at least that many more. In San Francisco, California, the Bill Graham Civic Auditorium is sometimes erroneously called the "Billy Graham Civic Auditorium" and incorrectly considered to be named in his honor, but it is actually named after rock and roll promoter Bill Graham. On May 31, 2007, the $27 million Billy Graham Library was officially dedicated in Charlotte; former presidents Jimmy Carter, George H. W. Bush, and Bill Clinton appeared to celebrate with Graham. A highway in Charlotte bears Graham's name, as does I-240 near his home in Asheville. As Graham's final crusade approached in 2005, his friend Pat Boone created a song in honor of Graham, co-written and produced with David Pack and Billy Dean, digitally combining studio recordings of various artists into a "'We Are the World'-type" production titled "Thank You Billy Graham"; the song's video was introduced by Bono and included Faith Hill, MxPx, John Ford Coley, John Elefante, Mike Herrera, Michael McDonald, Jeffrey Osborne, LeAnn Rimes, Kenny Rogers, Connie Smith, Michael Tait, and other singers, with brief narration by Larry King; it was directed by Brian Lockwood as a tribute album. In 2013, the album My Hope: Songs Inspired by the Message and Mission of Billy Graham was recorded by Amy Grant, Kari Jobe, Newsboys, Matthew West, tobyMac, and other music artists with new songs to honor Graham during his My Hope America outreach and the publication of his book The Reason for My Hope: Salvation. text: Bhupinder "Bindy" Singh Johal (January 14, 1971 – December 20, 1998) was an Indo-Canadian gangster from Vancouver, British Columbia, known as a self-confessed drug kingpin with a reputation for outspokenness, disregard for authority, and a long-standing rivalry with Robbie Kandola and the Dosanjh Brothers, who led a rival Punjabi Mafia faction. Johal operated alongside international drug lord Ranjit Cheema and controlled his own faction within the Punjabi Mafia, a loosely affiliated criminal organization originating in British Columbia that became increasingly ethnocentric over time and remained active and notorious in Vancouver since the early 1990s. He was born in 1971 (some sources note 1972 or 1973) in Shankar Nakodar, Punjab, India, to a Jatt Sikh family, and immigrated to Vancouver at age four, being raised by his mother after his parents separated. He was considered a "problem child" by teachers, displayed temperamental behavior, lacked respect for authority, and suffered severe depression after his parents cut his hair following an armed assault in Canada linked to the assassination of Indira Gandhi. He was expelled from Sir Charles Tupper Secondary School and sentenced to 60 days in jail in 1989 after assaulting his vice-principal, a defense he made that was dismissed by the judge as "cold-blooded cynicism" due to lack of evidence of racism. After moving to Richmond, he enrolled at McNair Secondary School, where he smashed a car window with a baseball bat and was convicted of possessing a dangerous weapon. He dropped out of college after his first semester to begin a criminal career, joining the Hispanic gang Los Diablos, which later became the Punjabi Mafia. He built a reputation as a hit-man for Jimmy and Ron Dosanjh, later betraying and killing both of them—Jimmy in February 1994 and Ron in April 1994—after the latter had taken out a contract to kill Johal for over C$230,000. The Dosanjh brothers were killed by men loyal to Johal, with Ron being shot in his red pickup truck while waiting for a traffic light and dying instantly from multiple bullets to the face. Johal was charged with two counts of first-degree murder in connection with the Dosanjh killings, along with Sarbjit Gill, Rajinder "Big Raj" Benji, Michael Kim Budai, Sun News Lai, Preet "Peter" Sarbjit Gill, and Kim "Phil" Ho-Sik, with the Crown alleging that Peter Gill was the actual gunman. The trial, one of the most expensive in Canadian history due to required security, resulted in acquittals for all defendants, including Gill, who was later convicted of obstruction of justice and sentenced to six years in prison; Gillian Guess, an active juror, was sentenced to 18 months for obstruction of justice. The Crown appealed the acquittals, but Johal was killed before a new trial began. Johal earned approximately $500,000 to $900,000 per week through illegal activities such as murder for hire, debt collection, and drug dealing, and was affiliated with the Buttar brothers, known for brutal gangland slayings. He formed a hit squad called "The Elite," consisting of five Indo-Canadian hit men, responsible for 25 murders over five years. Johal had a legendary bad temper, was convicted in 1997 of aggravated assault for attacking two men in a bar with a broken beer bottle, and had convictions for obstruction of justice, possession of dangerous weapons, and aggravated assault. In 1996, Chinese-Canadian drug dealer Randy Chan was kidnapped by Roman Mann, one of Johal’s associates, due to dissatisfaction with the quality of cocaine sold; Johal negotiated Chan’s release in exchange for 5 kilograms of cocaine and $500,000 from the Lotus triads. Johal openly admitted his gangster status and threatened rivals in interviews, becoming a folk hero among young Indo-Canadians who admired his success, wealth, and defiance of societal expectations, with many citing him as an inspiration to join organized crime. His gang was responsible for several murders, including the killing of Amarjit Singh Dheil in January 1997, Gorinder Singh Khun Khun on October 21, 1997 (after Johal believed Khun Khun was involved in the murder of neighbor Greg Olson), and Vinuse News MacKenzie on July 1, 1998, to eliminate a romantic rival. On September 19, 1998, Derek Chand Shankar insulted Johal, prompting Johal to order his murder after Buttar drove Shankar to the Queensborough Bridge, where he was shot. On November 29, 1998, Johal punched Roman "Danny" Mann after Mann expressed a desire to leave the gang, and Mann was later found dead in an industrial lot with a single bullet through his head; Johal blamed the Hells Angels. On December 20, 1998, at 4:30 a.m., Johal was fatally shot in the back of the head at the Palladium nightclub in Vancouver and died four hours later at Vancouver General Hospital. No witnesses described the assailant. Four months prior to his death, at least three of Johal’s associates had been killed, according to Bal Buttar’s confessions. In 2004, Buttar claimed he ordered Johal’s assassination out of fear that Johal would kill him. Buttar was never convicted of Johal’s murder due to his quadriplegic condition. Kash Heed, commanding officer of the 3rd Police District in Vancouver, stated it was disappointing that someone as intelligent and bright as Johal would turn to crime, noting that young people who emulate gangsters like Bindy see the benefits of criminal life without understanding the dangers.

text: Birendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev (Nepali: श्री ५ महाराजाधिराज वीरेन्द्र वीर विक्रम शाह देव; 29 December 1945 – 1 June 2001) was King of Nepal from 1972 until his assassination in 2001. He was the second son of King Mahendra and became crown prince because Mahendra's first son, Rabindra Shah, was born out of wedlock to a Gurung woman, making him an "illegitimate child." Birendra was born at the Narayanhiti Royal Palace in Kathmandu and became crown prince upon his grandfather King Tribhuvan's death in 1955. He studied at St Joseph's School in Darjeeling and later at Eton College in the United Kingdom from 1959 to 1964, before returning to Nepal to travel to remote villages. He then studied at the University of Tokyo and political theory at Harvard University from 1967 to 1968. Birendra married Aishwarya Rajya Lakshmi Devi, his second cousin, on 27 February 1970; the wedding cost $9.5 million and was one of the most lavish Hindu nuptial ceremonies in history. He ascended the throne on 31 January 1972 at age 26, with his coronation delayed until 24 February 1975, when he was 29, due to mourning and religious inauspiciousness traditions. As an absolute monarch, he inherited the panchayat system, which banned political parties; prominent leaders of the Nepali Congress were frequently arrested. In the 1980s, liberal student-led groups demanded constitutional change, and in May 1980, a referendum was held offering a multi-party or panchayati system, with the party-less system winning 55% to 45%. Following this, Birendra restructured the country into five development regions and visited each annually until 1990. In April 1990, after pro-democracy riots, he lifted the ban on political parties and agreed to become a constitutional monarch, appointing a Constitution Recommendation Commission that presented a draft constitution on 10 September 1990. The draft was approved by Prime Minister Krishna Prasad Bhattarai and his cabinet, and on 9 November 1990, Birendra promulgated the new constitution, transforming Nepal into a constitutional monarchy with multiparty democracy. As a constitutional monarch, he gained popularity due to his democratic views and the inability of political parties to govern. However, he could not prevent the Nepalese Civil War, which lasted from 1996 to 2006. On 1 June 2001, Birendra and his family were massacred by his son, Crown Prince Dipendra, during a dinner at the Narayanhiti Palace; after shooting himself, Dipendra was declared king but failed to regain consciousness and died days later. Birendra's younger brother Gyanendra then became king. During his reign, Birendra maintained Nepal's independence despite influences from India, China, and the Soviet Union. His first trips as king were to India in October 1973 and China two months later. He prevented the breakup of Mustang from Nepal and Tibet, disarmed Khampas rebels in the north by offering land, money, and citizenship to those who surrendered arms and confiscating weapons, and prohibited movement toward Tibet for those who did not surrender. He blocked the use of the army to suppress the Maoist revolution, which would have worsened the situation. Birendra was a lover of nature and a strong supporter of conservation. He established the Rhino Patrol force in 1970, introduced National Park law, and gazetted Chitwan National Park in December 1970 with borders delineated the following year and established in 1973. In 1976, he established Royal Karnali Wildlife Reserve (later Royal Bardiya), added Babai River Valley in 1984, and proclaimed it a national park in 1988. The fourth protected area, Langtang National Park, was established in 1976 with a 1,710 km² area in Nuwakot, Rasuwa, and Sindhulpalchok. He also established Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve and Royal Shuklaphanta Wildlife Reserve in 1976, which were later enlarged and converted to national parks in the late 1980s. Rara National Park was established in 1976 to fulfill his father's dream of a pristine reserve with a 106 km² area in Mugu and Jumla, including Rara Lake. Sagarmatha National Park was established in 1976 with a 1,148 km² area in Solukhumbu. In 1984, Khaptad National Park (225 km²) was established in Bajhang, Bajura, Achham, and Doti, and Parsa Wildlife Reserve was established and later extended to a national park. Shey Phoksundo National Park, a trans-Himalayan park of 3,555 km² in Dolpa and Mugu, was also established in 1984. To preserve royal hunting traditions and prevent wildlife depletion, he established Dhorpatan Hunting Reserve in 1987. The King Mahendra Trust for Nature Conservation was established in 1990 with Gyanendra as chairman, and he declared the Annapurna Conservation Area. Under his efforts, Sagarmatha National Park (1979) and Chitwan National Park (1984) were inscribed in UNESCO World Heritage Sites, along with the Durbar squares of Kathmandu, Lalitpur, and Bhaktapur, and religious sites such as Swayambhunath, Boudhanath, Pashupatinath, and Changu Narayan in 1979. On 28 December 1975, a trolley bus system was established with Chinese aid. He followed his father by establishing industrial estates: Nepalgunj (1973), Pokhara (1974), Butwal (1976), Bhaktapur (1979), Dhankuta (1980), Birendranagar (1981), and Gajendranarayan (1986). Birendra is credited with devising the Melamchi water project to Kathmandu. Industries such as Gorakhali Tires, Udayapur Cement, Nepal Metal, and Nepal Pharmaceuticals were established during his reign. He was the patron of the Pashupati Area Development Trust. In April 1979, the Nepal Oriental Magnesite factory was established with joint investment from Nepal and Orissa Industries, India, at Lakuri Danda in Dolakha. In 1983, a Nepal-Pakistan Joint Economic Commission was established, bringing significant foreign investment. A 60 megawatt hydropower project at Kulekhani began operation in 1982 with aid from the World Bank, Kuwait, and Japan. TU Teaching Hospital was established in 1982 with support from Japan International Cooperation Agency. Nardevi Ayurvedic Hospital was established in 1974, and the Nepal Police Hospital was established on 27 Chaitra 2040 BS to provide free health services to police and their families. In 1976, he established Securities Exchange Center Ltd, which later evolved into the Nepal Stock Exchange. He also established Nepal Television in 1984, which launched its first channel in 1985 with French aid. By 1986, there were 2,054 industrial establishments employing about 125,000 workers. By 1990, television reach made video rental and satellite dishes common. The Lamosangu-Jiri road to Solukhumbu was commissioned in 1985 with Swiss aid. The government focused on agriculture, with nearly 90% of the population involved by 1990. Bhrikuti Pulp and Paper was established in 1985 with Chinese support. Corn production increased from 500,000 tons in 1961 to over 1 million tons in 1991. Lumbini Sugar Mills at Sunwal, Nawalparasi was built in 1982 with Chinese technical assistance. Gorakhali Rubber Industries led to rubber cultivation in Jhapa, Illam, and other eastern areas. text: The Black Widow pulsar (PSR B1957+20) is an eclipsing binary millisecond pulsar in the Milky Way, discovered in 1988 and located approximately 6,500 light-years (2,000 parsecs) from Earth. It rotates with a period of 1.6074 milliseconds and orbits a substellar companion, likely a brown dwarf or super-Jupiter, with a period of 9.2 hours and an eclipse duration of about 20 minutes. At the time of its discovery, it was the first known such pulsar. The prevailing theory suggests that the companion is being destroyed by the powerful outflows or winds of high-energy particles from the neutron star, leading to the name "black widow." Since then, similar systems have been identified, and as of February 2023, around 41 black widows are known. Observations have revealed a bow shock in H-alpha and a smaller shock in X-rays (detected by the Chandra X-ray Observatory), indicating a forward velocity of about one million kilometers per hour. In 2010, the neutron star's mass was estimated to be at least 1.66 M⊙ and possibly as high as 2.4 M⊙, with the latter value potentially surpassing PSR J0740+6620 as the most massive neutron star detected and approaching the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit. However, by January 2023, the upper mass limit was revised down to 1.8 M⊙. The pulsar's companion is believed to be a brown dwarf. Artist impressions of the Black Widow pulsar are available.

text: Blenheim Palace, designed with its principal and secondary rooms on the piano nobile, features an internal layout defined by court etiquette, with state apartments arranged along an axis of increasing importance and public use, culminating in the central saloon ("B"), which served as the communal state dining room. To either side of the saloon are suites of state apartments, decreasing in importance but increasing in privacy: the first room ("C") was intended as an audience chamber, the next ("L") as a private withdrawing room, and the next ("M") as the occupant's bedroom, the most private. A small room between the bedroom and the internal courtyard was designated as a dressing room, and this arrangement mirrors the layout on the east side of the saloon, where the Duke and Duchess had their own suites, with the bow room ("O") corresponding in importance to the saloon. The palace includes a 30-tonne marble bust of Louis XIV, positioned high above the south portico so that the defeated king is forced to look down on the parterre and spoils of his conqueror, a design intended to honor the Duke but never realized as he died before completion. The Duke was to have sat enthroned in the painted saloon, whose ceiling was originally to be painted by James Thornhill, depicting Marlborough kneeling to Britannia with a map of the Battle of Blenheim, but the Duchess objected to his overcharging, so the commission was given to Louis Laguerre. Laguerre's trompe l'œil painting features Peace as a woman holding back John Churchill, who holds a zigzag thunderbolt of war, with the walls showing nations at peace, and includes a self-portrait alongside Dean Jones, a chaplain disliked by the Duchess, and a depiction of French spies with large ears and eyes. The room also has four marble door-cases displaying the Duke's crest as a prince of the Holy Roman Empire, only one of which was carved by Gibbons; the others were copied by the Duchess's cheaper craftsmen. The long library (H), designed by Nicholas Hawksmoor in 183 ft (56 m), was intended as a picture gallery with saucer domes to be painted by Thornhill, but this was not done due to the Duchess's displeasure. The library is furnished with the Duke's war spoils and art collection, including a large statue of Queen Anne, whose base records their friendship. From the northern end of the library, which houses the largest pipe organ in private ownership in Europe, built in 1891 by Henry Willis & Sons at a cost of £3,669 and replacing a 1888 organ by Isaac Abbott, access leads to the raised colonnade and chapel. The chapel, designed with the Duke's gargantuan tomb and sarcophagus as the dominant feature, was altered by the Earl of Godolphin to place the high altar against the west wall, and was commissioned by the Duchess in 1730, designed by William Kent, with statues of the Duke and Duchess as Caesar and Caesarina. The tomb was completed after the dowager Duchess's death in 1744, when the Duke's coffin was returned from Westminster Abbey and both were interred together. Successive Dukes and their wives are also buried in the chapel vault, and other family members are interred in St. Martin's parish churchyard at Bladon. The palace is Grade I listed on the National Heritage List for England since August 1957, and its park, woodlands, and formal gardens are Grades I listed on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens and are a Site of Special Scientific Interest. The park features the River Glyme, which Vanbrugh envisioned being crossed by the "finest bridge in Europe," containing some 30-odd rooms, though it was later modified by Capability Brown, who flooded and submerged the lower stories of the bridge, creating a more harmonious English landscape garden. The bridge, originally seen as incongruous by Alexander Pope and Horace Walpole, was narrowed at its base and the three small canal-like streams were absorbed into a single river-like stretch. The great parterre, nearly half a mile long (800 m) and as wide as the south front, was grassed over by Brown, and the Great Court was re-paved by Duchêne in the early 20th century. The Column of Victory, 134 ft (41 m) high, terminates a great avenue of elms planted in the positions of Marlborough's troops at the Battle of Blenheim, and Vanbrugh had originally intended an obelisk to mark the site of the former royal manor and Henry II's trysts, which the 1st Duchess rejected as "very odd things." Following the 1st Duke's death in 1722, his daughter Henrietta succeeded him, an unusual succession requiring a special Act of Parliament, and after her death, the title passed to Charles Spencer, Earl of Sunderland, whose mother was the Duke's second daughter Anne. The 1st Duke, a soldier, was not wealthy and used his fortune to complete the palace; the Marlboroughs were not particularly rich compared to other ducal families. The 5th Duke (1766–1840) was a spendthrift who depleted the family's fortune, selling the Boccaccio for £875 and his own library in over 4000 lots, and upon his death in 1840, the family faced financial difficulties. By the 1870s, the Marlboroughs were in severe financial trouble, and in 1875 the 7th Duke sold the Marriage of Cupid and Psyche and the famed Marlborough gems for £10,000, which was insufficient. In 1880, the 7th Duke petitioned Parliament to break the entail on the palace under the Blenheim Settled Estates Act 1880, allowing the dispersal of assets. The Sunderland Library was sold in 1882 for nearly £60,000, including rare books like Horace's Epistles (1480) and Josephus's works (1648); Raphael's Ansidei Madonna sold for £70,000; Van Dyck's Equestrian Portrait of Charles I for £17,500; and the Rubens painting, given by Brussels in 1704, was sold for a record sum and is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. These sales failed to cover debts, and the maintenance of the palace remained unaffordable, worsened by the British agricultural depression. When the 9th Duke inherited in 1892, the land was generating dwindling income. Charles, 9th Duke of Marlborough (1871–1934), saved the palace and family by marrying the American railroad heiress Consuelo Vanderbilt in 1895 for $2.5 million (equivalent to $94.5 million today), in 50,000 shares of the Beech Creek Railway with a 4% dividend guarantee, plus £100,000 annual income each. The marriage was negotiated with her parents, who paid for it, and the bride was locked in her room until agreeing. The wedding was signed in the vestry of St. Thomas Episcopal Church, and on the return carriage, the Duke told Consuelo he loved another woman and would never return to America, as he "despised anything that was not British." The honeymoon began with the replacement of the Marlborough gems, and the Duke commissioned European tapestries, paintings, and furniture to restore the palace. He then undertook an exhaustive restoration and redecoration, including gilt boiseries in the west staterooms to imitate Versailles, undermining Vanbrugh's rivalry with Louis XIV, and moving the state and principal bedrooms upstairs.

text: Blenheim Palace, located in Woodstock, Oxfordshire, England, is the seat of the Dukes of Marlborough and one of the largest country houses in the country. Originally known as Blenheim Castle, it has been called Blenheim Palace since the 19th century. Built between 1705 and 1722, the palace was named after the 1704 Battle of Blenheim, a military victory achieved by the 1st Duke of Marlborough during the War of the Spanish Succession against the French and Bavarians. The land for the palace was granted by the Crown as a reward for these triumphs, with Parliament providing funds and the rent for the land set at one copy of the French royal flag annually, displayed in Windsor Castle. The palace was designed in the rare and short-lived English Baroque style by Sir John Vanbrugh, with assistance from Nicholas Hawksmoor, following the success of their earlier work on Castle Howard. The project faced significant financial difficulties, including the Crown cancelling support in 1712, leading to a three-year exile of the Marlboroughs on the Continent and a breakdown in relations with the Duchess, who criticized Vanbrugh for extravagance and impracticality. Despite initial funding, no exact sum was allocated by Parliament, and work halted after £220,000 had been spent and £45,000 owed. The Duke contributed £60,000 initially, and after his death in 1722, the Duchess, driven by ambition, completed the palace and its park, with Hawksmoor designing the Arch of Triumph and finishing key interior elements. The palace's design emphasizes grandeur over comfort, featuring massive stone structures, a severe Baroque style, and a strong visual axis that culminates in a procession celebrating the Duke’s military achievements. The palace includes a grand entrance with two approaches, a monumental East Gate that functions as a water tower, and a central axis leading to a painted saloon where the Duke was to be enthroned, with a 30-tonne marble bust of Louis XIV positioned above the south portico to symbolize his defeat. The palace is unique as a family home, mausoleum, and national monument and is the birthplace and ancestral home of Sir Winston Churchill. The estate, originally a royal deer park known as the Palace of Woodstock, had a long history, including being used to imprison Elizabeth I and later ruined during the Civil War. The 1st Duchess wanted the historic ruins demolished, while Vanbrugh advocated for preservation, and the ruins were ultimately removed. The palace was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. A parliamentary warrant from 1705 appointed Vanbrugh as architect but did not mention the Crown or Queen. The final completion date is unknown, but the Duchess was still negotiating costs as late as 1735 and noted in 1732 that the chapel was finished and more than half the tomb was ready. The palace's design, intended to be viewed from a distance, uses perspective and massed stone to create a pantheonesque effect, with statues of Britannia, chained French captives, and the English lion devouring the French cock, many by Grinling Gibbons, reinforcing its heroic and national character. The palace was completed after the Duke's death, and the entire structure, including its park, was finalized under the Duchess’s direction.

text: Stiven Mesa Londoño, born on 27 January 2000 in Itagüí, a suburb of Medellín, is a Colombian rapper, singer, and songwriter known professionally as Blessd. His parents separated when he was young, and he moved with his mother to Bogotá, where he described his adolescence as difficult due to communication issues with his stepfather and being far from his family. He spent time in a detention center for minors after a fight, which led him to change his path and return to Medellín, where he lived with his maternal grandparents. Before leaving school to pursue music, he studied at the Institución Educativa Pedro Estrada. Inspired by his uncle, a rapper who played songs and helped him practice freestyling, Blessd began performing as a hobby at age 15 and competed in rap battles in Bogotá. He worked with his father and grandparents selling fruits and vegetables at the Central Mayorista de Antioquia starting at 2:00 am to earn money for recording songs. Initially a rapper, he shared his songs via WhatsApp in Medellín; his producer Lil Jay encouraged him to explore Reggaeton and create romantic songs, leading to the viral success of "Una," which gained over three million YouTube views after being filmed with the help of Megastore Tienda. After "Una" went viral, Blessd performed in over 500 schools across Antioquia and left school to focus on music. He was signed by manager Dr. Velasquez to JM World Music. In October 2020, he released "Viernes Social" with Puerto Rican artists Alexis, Yomo, Amaro, and Xantos, which became number one on Colombian radio and had over one million plays in 24 hours. In November 2020, he released "Lejania" with Ryan Castro, which gained popularity in Medellín, Colombia, and Costa Rica. In January 2021, he released "Imposible," which led to a remix with Maluma, produced by Prodigiez and released in May 2021 after they met at Maluma’s home for the video shoot. In summer 2021, "Hace Tiempo" gained over 10 million YouTube views in one month and earned him a spot in YouTube’s Foundry Class of 2021. In August 2021, he released a remix of "Dos Problemas" featuring Javiielo, Big Soto, and Neutro Shorty. In late 2021, he released his first studio album, Hecho en Medellín, which includes the songs "Hace Tiempo," "Quien TV," and "Medallo," and completed tours in the United States (New Jersey, Massachusetts, Florida) and Europe (Madrid, Barcelona, Paris, Málaga, Bilbao), serving as an opening act for Karol G’s Bichota tour in Medellín and performing in Mexico City, Caracas, Venezuela, and Guayaquil, Ecuador. In January 2022, he was nominated for a Lo Nuestro Award in the "Artista Revelación Masculino" category and was highlighted by Billboard as one of 22 Latin artists to watch in 2022. In the same month, he released "Niña de Mis Sueños" and a "Quien TV" Remix with Ryan Castro, after a year-long hiatus due to label disagreements over the "Lejania" remix. On 14 February, MonitorLatino reported that "Quien TV" Remix became the most popular song in Colombia and "Niña de Mis Sueños" charted at number 6 on Billboard. Blessd is a Catholic who learned about religion from his grandmother and named himself Blessd due to his faith; he has tattoos of Jesus, The Virgin Mary, a cross on his neck, and the word "bendito" (blessed) on his fingers, and is often seen praying on his knees before performances. He is inspired by Arcángel, Akapellah, Diomedes Diaz, and Joe Arroyo. He previously dated Colombian influencer Nicole Rivera, known as La Suprema, who appears in the "Confia en Mi" video, and confirmed the end of their relationship on 15 March 2022 via Twitter. He is a fan of football, supporting his hometown club Atlético Nacional, which featured his logo on its kits, and also supports F.C. Barcelona. In October 2024, he became part-owner of the Danish football club Vendsyssel FF, and on 15 December 2024, released "Himno de la grandeza," a song expressing his love and respect for Atlético Nacional.

text: Boavita is a town and municipality located in the Colombian Department of Boyacá, within the Northern Boyacá Province subregion. Its urban center lies in the Eastern Ranges of the Colombian Andes at an elevation of 2,114 metres (6,936 ft), approximately 184 kilometres (114 mi) from Tunja, the department's capital. The municipality shares borders with Capitanejo, Santander, and the Nevado River to the north, San Mateo and La Uvita to the east, Tipacoque and Soatá to the west, and Susacón to the south. The name Boavita originates from the Chibcha language and does not mean "good life"; instead, it signifies "Point on the hill worshipping the Sun" or "Gate of the Sun." Before the Spanish conquest, the area was inhabited by a tribe known as the Guavitas, part of the Laches and Muisca groups, and was governed by a cacique who remained loyal to the Tundama of Tundama. Modern Boavita was officially founded on February 9, 1613, by Sr. Hugarte. The primary economic activities in the municipality are agriculture, livestock farming, and mining, with key agricultural products including dates, sugarcane, yuca, coffee, cotton, potatoes, maize, chick peas, beans, peas, wheat, and arracacha. Mining in the region involves carbon extraction. Boavita experiences a subtropical highland climate (Köppen classification: Cfb), characterized by moderate temperatures year-round. Its geographic coordinates are 6°20′N 72°35′W (6.333°N 72.583°W).
