text: Boliney, officially known as the Municipality of Boliney (Ilocano: Ili ti Boliney; Filipino: Bayan ng Boliney), is a municipality in the province of Abra, Philippines. According to the 2024 census, it has a population of 3,778 people. The municipality covers a land area of 216.92 square kilometres (83.75 sq mi), which constitutes 5.21% of Abra’s total area of 4,165.25 square kilometres (1,608.21 sq mi). It is bordered to the north by Sallapadan, Bucloc, and Daguioman, to the east by Tubo and the provinces of Kalinga and Mountain Province, and to the west by Luba and Manabo. Boliney is located 52.93 kilometres (32.89 mi) from the provincial capital Bangued and 422.00 kilometres (262.22 mi) from Manila. The municipality is politically subdivided into 8 barangays, each consisting of puroks and some having sitios. The population density is 17 inhabitants per square kilometre (44/sq mi). The residents are primarily of Cordillera sub-tribes, including the Masadiit of the Tingguian Tribes, Belwang of the Igorot, and Balatoc of the Kalinga tribe, with descendants of other Tinguian sub-tribes such as Binongan, Banao, Maeng, and Ammotan (now called Muyadan of Manabo) also present. The main livelihood of the people comes from rice terraces, though most rice lands were severely damaged or lost due to landslides, mud piles, and the killer quakes in 1990 and 1992; they now obtain most of their rice from Bangued and receive some from other mountain municipalities. Rehabilitation efforts for communal facilities such as roads, trails, irrigation systems, footbridges, and rice fields have been carried out by the Masadiit Farmers Cooperative Inc. (MFCI) with a fund of ₱2,903 million from the Presidential Management Staff, and by the Inter NGO Disaster Relief Services (INDRS) with C$292,516.00 and ₱7 million from Oxfam. Boliney is part of the lone congressional district of Abra and is governed by a mayor as its local chief executive and a municipal council as its legislative body, in accordance with the Local Government Code. The mayor, vice mayor, and councilors are elected directly by the people every three years. The municipality is situated 52.93 kilometres (32.89 mi) from Bangued and is accessible by road, which was completed in 1974; prior to that, access was only possible via a 24-kilometre (15 mi) mountain trail. After 1974, the road was extended by about 14 kilometres (8.7 mi) to reach Danac, the farthest barangay; the current road extends to the Poblacion, while the rest has been abandoned. The Boliney Schools District Office oversees all educational institutions within the municipality, managing and operating both public and private schools from primary to secondary levels.

text: Briana Collette Scurry, born on September 7, 1971, is an American retired soccer goalkeeper. She was the starting goalkeeper for the United States women's national soccer team at the 1995 World Cup (3rd place), 1996 Summer Olympics (gold medal), 1999 World Cup (champions), 2003 World Cup (3rd place), and the 2004 Summer Olympic Games (gold medal). She played in the semi-final and playoff for third place in the 2007 Women's World Cup (3rd place). Scurry was a founding member of the WUSA, playing three seasons as starting goalkeeper for the Atlanta Beat from 2001 to 2003. Her career total of 173 international appearances is the second most among female soccer goalkeepers and the fifteenth most of any American female player, as well as the thirty-second most among all women. Scurry was elected to the National Soccer Hall of Fame on August 3, 2017, becoming the first woman goalkeeper and the first black woman to receive the honor. She is openly gay and married Chryssa Zizos, CEO of Live Wire Strategic Communications, LLC, on June 1, 2018. In 2022, she released her best-selling memoir, *My Greatest Save*, and was the subject of the CBS feature-length documentary *The Only*, released that year. Scurry was born in Minneapolis, Minnesota, to parents Ernest and Robbie Scurry and is the youngest of nine children, with three brothers and five sisters. She played goalie for the Anoka High School Tornadoes for four years and was instrumental in their Minnesota State Championship win in 1989, which ended in a shootout victory. In high school, she ran track and played floor hockey and softball, but basketball was her first and deepest love. She was named Anoka High School's Athena Award winner, High School All American, and Minnesota's top female athlete. In 2010, she was inducted into the Minnesota State High School Hall of Fame, and in September 2011, she was named to the inaugural class of the Anoka High School Hall of Fame. Scurry attended the University of Massachusetts Amherst, completing her four-year collegiate career with 37 shutouts in 65 starts and a career record of 48–13–4 with a 0.56 goals-against-average. She split time in the net in 1992, starting 13 games and earning seven shutouts, and played three games as a forward that year. In 1993, she helped lead the UMass Minutewomen to a 17–3–3 record, to the semifinals of the NCAA Women's Soccer Championship, and titles in the Atlantic 10 Conference regular season and tournament. In her senior season, she started all 23 games, recorded 15 shutouts, and had a 0.48 goals-against-average, the third best in the nation. She was named National Goalkeeper of the Year in 1993 by the Missouri Athletic Club Sports Foundation and was a 1993 second-team All-American, All-Northeast Region, and All-New England first-team selection. Scurry was a founding player for the Atlanta Beat in the Women's United Soccer Association (WUSA), the world's first women's professional league, where she served as starting goalkeeper for the three seasons (2001–2003). She helped the Beat reach two WUSA Championship Games and was named Goalkeeper of the Year in 2003. On March 13, 2009, she was named to the preseason roster of the Washington Freedom in the inaugural season of Women's Professional Soccer (WPS), but suffered a season-ending concussion early in the 2010 season and announced her retirement on September 8, 2010. Scurry was a goalkeeper for the United States women's national soccer team from 1994 to 2008, earning 173 caps, starting 159 games, and finishing her international career with a record of 133–12–14 and 71 shutouts. Her first appearance for the US team was on March 16, 1994, against Portugal, during which she recorded her first shutout. In her first year, she earned seven shutouts in 12 starts. She was a member of the gold-medal-winning US Women's National Team at the 1996 Olympic Games in Atlanta, starting and playing every minute of the team's five matches, conceding only three goals. In the 1999 Women's World Cup, she played every minute, allowing only three goals and recording four shutouts, and saved one penalty during the shootout in the final against China, leading to the United States' victory. Following the World Cup, she announced her intention to play in the WNBA. She started for the US in the 2003 FIFA Women's World Cup and the 2004 Summer Olympic Games, played two matches in the 2007 FIFA Women's World Cup, and was the alternate goalkeeper on the 2008 Olympic Team. On June 23, 2008, coach Pia Sundhage announced that Scurry would not be on the Olympic team; her last match for the United States was on November 5, 2008, against the Korea Republic. While playing in the Women's Professional Soccer league in 2010, she suffered a traumatic brain injury when a player from the opposing team collided with her knee into her right temple, leaving her temporarily totally disabled and dealing with severe depression. To address her symptoms, she underwent occipital nerve surgery in 2013. Scurry has since rebuilt her life and become an advocate for increased concussion awareness and research, testifying before Congress twice. In 2011, she was appointed general manager of the WPS franchise magicJack. In February 2021, The Washington Post reported that Chelsea Clinton, Jenna Bush Hager, Dominique Dawes, and Scurry were part of an investment group investing in the Washington Spirit. Scurry served as part of the rotation of studio commentators for ESPN's telecasts of the 2011 FIFA Women's World Cup. Since 2021, she has served as a broadcast analyst for CBS soccer coverage, including serving as the lead desk analyst for the 2022 CONCACAF W Championship. On December 6, 2017, she was announced as the First Assistant Coach of the Washington Spirit and would serve as Technical Advisor for the Spirit Academy programs in Maryland and Virginia. Scurry appeared as a fictionalized version of herself in the 2000 film *Air Bud: World Pup* and was the subject of the 2022 Paramount Plus documentary *The Only*, directed by Anthony J. Cortese, which featured interviews with other USWNT players such as Mia Hamm, Brandi Chastain, Kristine Lilly, and Abby Wambach.

text: The Bright Star Catalogue, also known as the Yale Catalogue of Bright Stars, Yale Bright Star Catalogue, or YBS, is a star catalogue that includes all stars of stellar magnitude 6.5 or brighter, which corresponds to roughly every star visible to the naked eye from Earth. The catalog lists 9,110 objects, of which 9,095 are stars, 11 are novae or supernovae that were "bright stars" only at their peak, and four are non-stellar objects: the globular clusters 47 Tucanae (HR 95) and NGC 2808 (HR 3671), and the open clusters NGC 2281 (HR 2496) and Messier 67 (HR 3515). The catalogue has a fixed number of entries, but its data is maintained and continuously updated, with a comments section about the objects being steadily enhanced. The abbreviation for the catalog is BS or YBS, but all citations of stars in it use HR before the catalog number, a tribute to its predecessor, the Harvard Revised Photometry Catalogue, published in 1908. The earliest predecessor, titled Harvard Photometry, was published in 1884 by the Harvard College Observatory under Edward Charles Pickering and contained about 4,000 stars. Pickering then promoted a similar survey for the southern celestial hemisphere, conducted by Solon I. Bailey between 1889 and 1891, resulting in the publication of the Revised Harvard Photometry in 1908, which included stars down to magnitude 6.5 in both hemispheres, a work continued by John A. Parkhurst through the 1920s. The Yale Bright Star Catalogue was first published in 1930 by Yale astronomer Frank Schlesinger; although the number of entries remains fixed at 9,110, the data for listed objects is corrected and extended, and a comments section is appended. The 1991 edition was the fifth in sequence and introduced a significant expansion of the comments section, which grew to just over the size of the catalogue itself. This edition, along with earlier ones, was compiled and edited by Ellen Dorrit Hoffleit of Yale University. The Harvard Revised Photometry, based on visual observations, has been replaced by photo-electric measurements using band pass filters, most notably the UBV photometric system, which can differ substantially—up to 1.8 magnitudes—from the older system. As a result, many stars brighter than V=6.50 are not included in the YBSC, and hundreds of stars in the YBSC are fainter than V=6.50. In 1983, Dorrit Hoffleit, Michael Saladyga, and Peter Wlasuk published a Supplement adding 2,603 stars with V magnitudes brighter than 7.10 measured at that time. The YBS has one predecessor and five editions.

text: Busbie Castle was located in what is now Knockentiber (Scottish Gaelic: Cnoc an Tobair, hill of the well), a village in East Ayrshire, Parish of Kilmaurs, Scotland. Knockentiber lies 2 miles (3.2 km) WNW of Kilmarnock and 1/2 mile NE of Crosshouse. The castle overlooked the Carmel Glen and its Burn, which flows into the River Irvine, a mile or so to the south, after passing through the old Busbie Mill. Ainslie's map of 1822 labels the settlement as Bushby, while Armstrong's map of 1775 shows Busbie Castle in a ruinous state but still with its old woodland policies. The 1860s first edition of the Ordnance Survey (OS) indicates a pre-reformation chapel dedicated to the Virgin Mary was situated near the castle site. A small hamlet of thatched cottages was clustered nearby; in 1860, the OS shows 'Old Busbie' on the opposite side of the road from the castle. Over time, Busbie and Knockentiber grew together. The castle was a simple keep, approximately 50 feet (15 m) high and about 40 feet (12 m) long by 25 feet (7.6 m) wide. Its entrance was on the ground floor, leading to a wheel-stair to the first-floor hall in the north-west angle and to two cellars or stores on the ground floor. The first-floor hall featured a large fireplace and two window seats. Historical records from the Registrum Magni Sigilli in 1465 list "Terras de le Moite," and in 1539, "9 marcat. de Busby, viz., lie Mote, Knokintibber, et Hallethornis," and in 1541, "Terras de Moite, Knokintebir," and in 1571, "Terras de Moit," and in 1583, "20 solidatas terrarum antiqui extentus de Moit-Mowat cum earum mansione," and in 1599, "9 marcat. terrarum de Busbeyis (viz., lie Mote, Knockiutibber et Halythornis)." In 1691, the Laird of Busbie's dwelling had six hearths and seven other dwellings were associated with the castle and its lands. The castle was a ruin since at least the 1770s and was demolished in 1949 or 1952 due to safety concerns and lack of funds to consolidate it. H. Ritchie built Busbie House as a replacement. Busbie Estates and Collective Securities Limited owned significant land in the 1950s. MacIntosh in 1894 describes the castle as a "prominent object in an otherwise monotonous landscape," noting gun ports, arrow slits, and a sculptured cable winding fantastically around the walls. He claims the castle likely had three floors, was roofless and in decay, and dates it to the 14th century, possibly built by the Mowat family from Flintshire in the 12th century. A Robert de Montealt is recorded in Scotland during the time of King David I; later, several soldiers with that name led armies into Scotland. William Craufurd of Wallston married a daughter of Mowat of Busbie around 1400. Charles Mowat of Busbie is mentioned in 1534 for involvement in the murder of William Cunyngham of Craganis and his servant; he was tutor to Hugh, Earl of Eglinton in 1546 and fined £47 in 1571–2 for celebrating mass at Eglinton Castle. In 1547, Charles Mowat was involved in the murder of Lord Boyd, with Sir Neil Montgomerie of Lainshaw as the victim; he was required to remain in France until Sir Neil Montgomerie’s son allowed him to return. A brother of the Earl of Eglinton appeared in court for provoking John Mowatt, Laird of Busby, and his servant Andrew Stevenston in Stewarton. The Mowat involved in the Montgomerie murder was later killed by William and Harrie (Sic) Stewart, sons of Lord Ochiltree, in 1577. Alexander, the eldest son, did not inherit; instead, James, his younger brother, succeeded to the Busbie lands. James’s son, also named James, is the last Mowat to appear in public records. The name de Monhaud or de Monte Alto is recorded as being pronounced 'Mowat' by Dalrymple. James Ritchie of Craigton obtained the lands in 1763, succeeded by his son Henry in 1799, who also acquired the Cloncaird estate. William Wallace of Cairnhill (now Carnell), the nephew of Henry, next inherited the estate. General Sir James Wallace died in 1867 and passed the property to William Wallace of Busbie and Cloncaird. In 1661, Hugh, Earl of Eglinton inherited the lands of Busbie, Knockentiber, and Robertown, a family holding these lands as far back as 1638. The barony, formerly part of the Barony of Kilmaurs, extended from Kilmaurs south to the River Irvine. It had no manor house and was later held by the Eglinton family. Hugh Montgomerie, 1st Earl of Eglinton, received a charter on 3 February 1499 from James V for the £40 lands of old extent of Roberton in Cunninghame. These lands were part of the Lands and Barony of Ardrossan, which included parts of Kilmaurs, Knockentiber, Craig, Gatehead, Woodhills, Greenhill, Altonhill, Plann, Hayside, Thorntoun, Rash-hill Park, Milton, Windyedge, Fardelhill, Muirfields, and Corsehouse. The present Busbie farm appears on older maps, such as the 1860 OS, as a mill with a clear millrace or lade and a sluice. The water was drawn from the Carmel near a dwelling marked as Busbie Holm, rejoining the burn just beyond the mill. The exact date when the mill ceased operation is unclear. It is likely the mill was associated with the castle and the Lairds of Busbie. A Robertown mill is known to have existed, named after the barony.

text: Henry Franklin "Buster" Smith (August 24, 1904 – August 10, 1991), also known as Professor Smith, was an American jazz alto saxophonist and mentor to Charlie Parker. He played a key role in developing the Texas Sax Sound while working with Count Basie and Lester Young in the 1930s. Smith performed with several prominent band leaders, including Duke Ellington, Earl Hines, and vocalist Ella Fitzgerald. He recorded his only album as leader in 1959, titled *The Legendary Buster Smith*, released by Atlantic Records, which featured songs such as "Kansas City Riffs," "Buster's Tune," "E Flat Boogie," and Kurt Weill's "September Song." For the sessions, he enlisted his brother Boston Smith to play piano and included musicians from throughout his career. Despite intending to record a follow-up, Smith was injured in an auto accident in the 1960s, which ended his ability to play the saxophone. He then began playing bass guitar in Dallas and continued to participate in the local music scene, leading a dance music band until 1980 and performing in the Legendary Revelations in the mid-1980s. Smith was born and raised in Alsdorf, Texas, a small township near Telico in the outskirts of Dallas, where he attended school as a child. He earned the nickname "Buster" from his parents due to being born as an overweight child; he was the third of five boys with no sisters, and both of his older brothers died in childhood from measles. His early musical influences were his mother and father, who played guitar; at age four, he played the organ with his brother, Boston Smith, who played the piano. His grandfather later gave away the family organ, believing it would lead Buster toward a life of sin. In 1919, Smith picked cotton for a week to earn $3.50 to buy a clarinet. By age eighteen, he had learned to play several instruments. In 1922, his family moved to Dallas, where he joined the Voodie White Trio, playing alto saxophone and clarinet. In 1923, he began his professional music career playing alto saxophone with medicine shows, where he had to play loudly to attract customers—an experience that shaped his loud musical style. In 1925, Oran "Hot Lips" Page invited him to join the Oklahoma City Blue Devils, where he wrote much of the group's music, learning from banjo player Johnny Clark and writing lyrics with co-workers from the bank. The Blue Devils' lineup included Walter Page, Oran Page, Lester Young, Count Basie, Jimmy Rushing, and Emir "Bucket" Coleman. They toured the Kansas City area and the Midwest, playing jazz for a year and bringing all members into prominence. Basie and Page left the group, but Smith stayed briefly before leaving as well. After leaving, he and Basie formed the Buster Smith-Count Basie Band of Rhythm, where they developed a louder style of jazz. Smith achieved a louder sound by using a tenor saxophone reed in his alto saxophone, and Lester Young complemented this by using a baritone saxophone reed on his tenor saxophone, a combination later known as the Texas Sax Sound. Smith gained significant influence in the Texan music community and mentored Charlie Parker during the 1930s, forming a "father-son relationship" through mentorship. In 1941, Smith returned to Dallas and stopped touring, remaining active in the local music scene. He wrote for jazz and blues bands, performed frequently, and taught young Texan musicians such as Aaron "T-Bone" Walker and Red Garland. He also performed session work with artists including Pete Johnson's Boogie-Woogie Boys, Eddie Durham, Leo "Snub" Mosley, Bon and His Buddies, and the Don Redman Orchestra. Smith died in Dallas on August 10, 1991, from a heart attack.

text: The Bust of Charles I was a sculptural work created by the Italian artist Gianlorenzo Bernini, which one historian described as "setting the visual conventions for centuries... [establishing itself as] the official portrait of secular absolutism." The sculpture depicted King Charles I of England, who wrote to Bernini praising the artist's name as "exalted above those of all men of talent who have exercised your profession." Bernini never traveled to London to complete the bust; instead, he used a painted triple portrait of Charles I, created by the Flemish artist Anthony van Dyck, specifically for this purpose. Although Bernini never met Charles I in person, the bust was regarded as a success at the time, and Charles rewarded Bernini with jewelry valued at over 4,000 Roman scudi—more than 60 times the average yearly salary of a worker in Rome. Pope Urban VIII sent the bust to Charles's queen, Henrietta Maria, in 1637, in an effort to promote reconciliation between the Roman Catholic Church and the Church of England. The bust was presented in 1637 and was admired for its craftsmanship and resemblance to the king. Charles also gave Bernini a valuable diamond ring. Henrietta Maria commissioned a companion bust of herself, but the English Civil War prevented its completion. After the English Civil War, the bust was sold but was later recovered and added to the Royal Collection during the Restoration, only to be destroyed by a fire at Whitehall Palace in January 1698. Numerous copies of the bust exist in various forms, including engravings and bronze sculptures. For a period in the 19th and early 20th centuries, there was a belief in England and elsewhere that Bernini had also produced a bust of Oliver Cromwell, the victor over Charles I in the English Civil War; however, this attribution was refuted in 1922. Media related to the Bust of King Charles I (Bernini) is available at Wikimedia Commons.

text: Cabell Calloway III (December 25, 1907 – November 18, 1994) was an American jazz singer, songwriter, and bandleader who became a prominent figure in the swing era through his regular performances at the Cotton Club in Harlem. He gained acclaim for blending jazz and vaudeville, a career that spanned over 65 years. A master of energetic scat singing, Calloway led one of the most popular dance bands in the United States from the early 1930s to the late 1940s, featuring trumpeters Dizzy Gillespie, Jonah Jones, and Adolphus "Doc" Cheatham, saxophonists Ben Webster and Leon "Chu" Berry, guitarist Danny Barker, bassist Milt Hinton, and drummer Cozy Cole. He achieved several hit records in the 1930s and 1940s, becoming the first African-American musician to sell one million copies of a record, with his most famous song, "Minnie the Moocher," originally recorded in 1931. This song earned him the nickname "The Hi-de-ho Man" and was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999 and added to the Library of Congress' National Recording Registry in 2019. Calloway reached the Billboard charts in five consecutive decades (1930s–1970s). He made numerous stage, film, and television appearances, including roles in Stormy Weather (1943), Porgy and Bess (1953), The Cincinnati Kid (1965), and Hello Dolly! (1967), and experienced a career resurgence in the 1980s with his appearance in The Blues Brothers (1980). He was the first African-American to have a nationally syndicated radio program and received the National Medal of Arts from the U.S. Congress in 1993. He posthumously received the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2008. Born in Rochester, New York, on December 25, 1907, Calloway's father, Cabell Calloway Jr., graduated from Lincoln University of Pennsylvania in 1898, and his mother, Martha Eulalia Reed, was a Morgan State College graduate, teacher, and church organist who also worked as a lawyer and in real estate. The family moved to Baltimore, Maryland, in 1919, where Calloway grew up in the West Baltimore neighborhood of Druid Hill. He skipped school to earn money by selling newspapers, shining shoes, and cooling down horses at the Pimlico racetrack, where he developed an interest in racing and gambling. After being caught playing dice on the church steps, he was sent to Downingtown Industrial and Agricultural School in 1921. Upon returning to Baltimore, he resumed hustling and worked as a caterer while improving his education. He began private vocal lessons in 1922 and studied music throughout his schooling. Despite his parents' and teachers' disapproval of jazz, he began performing in nightclubs in Baltimore, with mentors including drummer Chick Webb and pianist Johnny Jones. He joined his high school basketball team and played professionally with the Baltimore Athenians in the Negro Professional Basketball League during his senior year, graduating from Frederick Douglass High School in 1925. He briefly attended law school in Chicago before leaving to pursue a singing career. In 1927, he joined his older sister, Blanche Calloway, on tour for the revue Plantation Days, whom he credited as his inspiration for entering show business. After the tour ended, he enrolled at Crane College in Chicago but refused an opportunity to play basketball for the Harlem Globetrotters to pursue singing. He performed at "Black and tan" clubs such as Chicago's Dreamland Café, Sunset Cafe, and Club Berlin, where he was an understudy for Adelaide Hall and met Louis Armstrong, who taught him scat singing. He left school to join the Alabamians band. In 1929, the band opened at the Savoy Ballroom and, after the Alabamians disbanded, Armstrong recommended Calloway to join the musical revue Connie's Hot Chocolates, where he established himself as a vocalist singing "Ain't Misbehavin'" by Fats Waller. When the Missourians asked him to front their band in 1930, they became known as Cab Calloway and His Orchestra. In 1931, the band was hired at the Cotton Club in Harlem to substitute for Duke Ellington, leading to a permanent position. The band performed twice a week for NBC radio broadcasts, and Calloway appeared on programs with Walter Winchell and Bing Crosby, becoming the first African American to have a nationally syndicated radio show. During the Great Depression, he earned $50,000 a year at age 23. In 1931, he recorded "Minnie the Moocher," the first single by an African American to sell a million copies. He performed the song and others, "St. James Infirmary Blues" and "The Old Man of the Mountain," in the Betty Boop cartoons Minnie the Moocher (1932), Snow-White (1933), and The Old Man of the Mountain (1933), providing voice-over and using rotoscoping to base the characters' movements on his dance steps. The success of "Minnie the Moocher" made him known as "The Hi-de-ho Man." He appeared in a series of short films for Paramount, where his and Ellington's groups were featured more than any other jazz orchestras of the era. In these films, he performed a gliding backstep dance move, described by some as a precursor to Michael Jackson's moonwalk, which he called "The Buzz" in later years. The 1933 film International House featured his song "Reefer Man," about a man who smokes marijuana. Fredi Washington was cast as his love interest in Cab Calloway's Hi-De-Ho (1934), and Lena Horne made her film debut as a dancer in Cab Calloway's Jitterbug Party (1935). In 1936, he made his first Hollywood feature film appearance opposite Al Jolson in The Singing Kid, singing several duets with Jolson and featuring Calloway's band and 22 Cotton Club dancers. Film critic Arthur Knight noted that the film reflected a shift in American culture through Calloway's rhythmic and melodic singing style. In 1938, he released Cab Calloway's Cat-ologue: A "Hepster's" Dictionary, the first dictionary published by an African American, which became the official reference book of the New York Public Library. A revised version was released in 1939 with Professor Cab Calloway's Swingformation Bureau, and the final edition, The New Cab Calloway's Hepsters Dictionary: Language of Jive, was published in 1944. Poet Lemn Sissay stated in a 2014 BBC documentary that Calloway was taking ownership of language for a people whose languages had been taken away. His band included notable musicians such as Ben Webster, Illinois Jacquet, Milt Hinton, Danny Barker, Doc Cheatham, Ed Swayze, Eddie Barefield, and Dizzy Gillespie. Calloway recalled that he expected precision in his musicians, as he built songs around scat or dance steps. The band formed baseball and basketball teams, playing each other and local semi-pro teams, and participated in charity games. In 1941, he fired Dizzy Gillespie after a fracas when Calloway was hit with spitballs; he wrongly accused Gillespie, who stabbed Calloway in the leg with a small knife. From 1941 to 1942, he hosted a weekly radio quiz show called The Cab Calloway Quizzicale, a parody of Kay Kyser's The College of Musical Knowledge. During World War II, he entertained U.S. troops before they departed overseas. The band recorded songs with social commentary, including "Doing the Reactionary," "The Führer's Got the Jitters," "The Great Lie," "We'll Gather Lilacs," and "My Lament for V Day." In 1943, he appeared in Stormy Weather, one of the first mainstream Hollywood films with a black cast, featuring Bill "Bojangles" Robinson, Lena Horne, the Nicholas Brothers, and Fats Waller. He hosted Horne's character Selina Rogers as she performed the title song in a big all-star revue for soldiers. In 1946, he published a humorous pseudo-gossip column called "Coastin' with Cab" for Song Hits magazine. In the late 1940s, poor financial decisions and gambling led to the breakup of his band. In 1956, his daughter Lael and he recorded "Little Child," an adaptation of "Little Boy and the Old Man," which charted on the Billboard Hot 100. In 1958, Lee Sherman was the choreographer for The Cotton Club Revue of 1958, which starred Calloway and featured tap dancing prodigies Maurice Hines and Gregory Hines. That year, he released the album Cotton Club Revue of 1958 on Gone Records, produced by George Goldner and conducted and arranged by Eddie Barefield. In 1958, he appeared in St. Louis Blues, the life story of W.C. Handy, featuring Nat King Cole and Eartha Kitt. The Cotton Club Revue of 1959 toured South America, visiting Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo, and also stopped in Uruguay and Argentina before returning to North America, including a Broadway run. He remained a household name through TV appearances and concerts in the U.S. and Europe, touring with the Harlem Globetrotters in 1961 and 1962 for halftime entertainment. In 1965, he appeared in The Cincinnati Kid with Steve McQueen, Ann-Margret, and Edward G. Robinson. He performed on The Ed Sullivan Show on March 19, 1967, with his daughter Chris Calloway. In 1967, he co-starred with Pearl Bailey as Horace Vandergelder in an all-black cast of Hello, Dolly! on Broadway, with Chris Calloway joining as Minnie Fay, reviving the show's business and leading to a rare RCA Victor cast recording. In 1973–74, he was featured in an unsuccessful Broadway revival of The Pajama Game with Hal Linden and Barbara McNair. His autobiography, Of Minnie the Moocher and Me, was published in 1976, including his complete Hepster's Dictionary as an appendix. In 1978, he released a disco version of "Minnie the Moocher" on RCA Victor that reached the Billboard R&B chart. He appeared in The Blues Brothers (1980), introducing him to a new generation. In 1985, he and his Orchestra performed at The Ritz London Hotel for a 60-minute BBC TV show, with Adelaide Hall, Doc Cheatham, Max Roach, and the Nicholas Brothers also appearing. A performance with the Cincinnati Pops Orchestra in August 1988, directed by Erich Kunzel, was recorded and featured a classic rendition of "Minnie the Moocher," 57 years after its original recording. In January 1990, he performed at the Meyerhoff Symphony Hall with the Baltimore Symphony. That year, he made a cameo in Janet Jackson's music video "Alright." He continued performing at jazz festivals, including the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival and Greenwood Jazz, and in 1992 embarked on a month-long tour of European jazz festivals. He was booked to headline "The Jazz Connection: The Jewish and African-American Relationship" at New York City's Avery Fisher Hall in 1993 but withdrew due to a fall at home. In January 1927, he had a daughter named Camay with Zelma Proctor. His daughter was one of the first African Americans to teach in a white school in Virginia. He married his first wife, Wenonah "Betty" Conacher, in July 1928; they adopted a daughter named Constance and divorced in 1949. He married Zulme "Nuffie" MacNeal on October 7, 1949. The family lived in Long Beach on the South Shore of Long Island, New York, bordering Lido Beach, and in the 1950s moved to Westchester County, New York, where he and Nuffie raised their daughters Chris Calloway (1945–2008), Cecilia "Lael" Eulalia Calloway, and Cabella Calloway (1952–2023). Calloway was an Episcopalian. In December 1945, he and friend Felix H. Payne Jr. were beaten by police officer William E. Todd in Kansas City, Missouri, after attempting to enter the whites-only Pla-Mor Ballroom to visit bandleader Lionel Hampton. They were hospitalized and charged with intoxication and resisting arrest, but the charges were dismissed. When Hampton learned of the incident, he refused to continue the concert. Todd claimed they refused to leave and struck him, but Calloway and Payne maintained they were sober; six civil rights organizations, including the NAACP, demanded Todd be fired, though he had already resigned after a pay cut. In 1952, Calloway was arrested in Leesburg, Virginia, on his way to a race track in Charles Town, West Virginia, charged with speeding and attempted bribery of a policeman. On June 12, 1994, Calloway suffered a stroke at his home in Westchester County, New York, and died five months later from pneumonia on November 18, 1994, at the age of 86, at a nursing home in Hockessin, Delaware. A memorial service was held.

text: Cab Calloway was arrested in Leesburg, Virginia in 1952 on his way to a race track in Charles Town, West Virginia, and charged with speeding and attempted bribery of a policeman. In 1946, six civil rights organizations, including the NAACP, demanded that Todd be fired, but he had already resigned after a pay cut. On June 12, 1994, Calloway suffered a stroke at his home in Westchester County, New York, and died five months later from pneumonia on November 18, 1994, at the age of 86, at a nursing home in Hockessin, Delaware. A memorial service was held at Cathedral of St. John the Divine. He was survived by his wife, who died in 2008, five daughters, and seven grandsons, and was buried at Ferncliff Cemetery in Hartsdale, New York. Music critics have noted his influence on later entertainers such as James Brown, Michael Jackson, Janet Jackson, and modern-day hip-hop performers. John Landis, who directed Calloway in The Blues Brothers, stated, "Cab Calloway is hip-hop." Timothy White wrote in Billboard (August 14, 1993): "No living pathfinder in American popular music or its jazz and rock 'n' roll capillaries is so frequently emulated yet so seldom acknowledged as Cabell 'Cab' Calloway. He arguably did more things first and better than any other band leader of his generation." In 1998, the Cab Calloway Orchestra, directed by Calloway's grandson Chris "CB" Calloway Brooks, was formed. In 2009, Big Bad Voodoo Daddy released an album titled How Big Can You Get?: The Music of Cab Calloway. In 2012, Calloway's legacy was celebrated in a PBS American Masters episode titled "Cab Calloway: Sketches." In 2019, plans were announced to demolish Calloway's boyhood home at 2216 Druid Hill Avenue in Baltimore, replacing it and the block with Cab Calloway Legends Park. Family members and the National Trust for Historic Preservation advocated for preservation due to its significance as an African-American cultural heritage site. Although the block is designated "historically significant" on the National Register of Historic Places, Baltimore City officials stated at a July 9, 2019 hearing that the Calloway house and adjacent properties have "extensive structural damage." The Commission on Historical and Architectural Preservation's executive director noted that properties in worse condition than the Calloway House have been restored with city tax credit support. Maryland Governor Larry Hogan urged the demolition be postponed to allow for preservation as a historic house museum, similar to the Louis Armstrong House in New York. text: Camilla Antoinette Clifford (29 June 1885 – 28 June 1971), known professionally as Camille Clifford, was a Belgian-born stage actress whose brief theatrical career was defined by her performance as "Miss New York" in the Henry W. Savage production of The Prince of Pilsen, a role in which she portrayed a "Gibson Girl"-like woman. Although her towering coiffure and hourglass figure embodied the Gibson Girl style, she only performed the role on stage and never modeled for any of Charles Dana Gibson's illustrations. Clifford was born on 29 June 1885 in Antwerp, Belgium, to Reynold Clifford and Matilda Ottersen, and was raised in Sweden, Norway, and Boston. On 31 August 1903, she made her stage debut as Mazie Manhattan, the New York Girl in "The Song of the Cities," in a Henry W. Savage production of The Prince of Pilsen at the Tremont Theatre in Boston. The role required her to walk across the stage in the style of Charles Dana Gibson's illustrations, leading to a misconception that she was a Gibson model—when in fact, she imitated his work, not the other way around. In early 1904, the Savage company signed a contract with George Musgrove and Frank McKee for a European tour, and to select an actress to join the new "London Company," a contest was held among those who had played Mazie Manhattan; Clifford won and the company departed in late April 1904. Clifford performed in the United States from 1902 and in England from 1904, returning to Boston on 3 July 1906. While typically playing walk-on, non-speaking roles, she gained fame for her beauty and, in the musical show The Catch of the Season, which opened at London's Vaudeville Theatre on 9 September 1904, she sang the song "Sylvia, the Gibson Girl." Her signature style included a long, elegant gown wrapped around a tightly corseted, eighteen-inch wasp waist. She retired from the stage after marrying Captain the Hon. Henry Lyndhurst Bruce (1881–1914), the eldest son and heir apparent of Henry Bruce, 2nd Baron Aberdare, in 1906; they had one child, Margaret, who died five days after birth. Her first husband was killed during the Great War in 1914, and his younger brother, Clarence, succeeded to the barony. In 1917, she married Captain John Meredyth Jones Evans; after the war, she left the stage permanently and later owned a stable of successful racehorses. Together, they were the parents of children, though the specific names are not provided. Her second husband died in 1957, and she died on 28 June 1971. Despite being known as "the quintessential Gibson Girl," she was not the only person to imitate the character on stage or screen. Photographs of her taken by Lizzie Caswall Smith in 1905 are frequently featured in historical fashion books and on websites to illustrate the Edwardian style.

text: An east–west route was proposed near Christie Street and Dupont Street, extending east to the Don Valley Parkway, with Highway 400 continuing south to the Gardiner Expressway. North of Spadina Road, the Spadina Expressway would have connected via an interchange, running from north of Highway 401 through the Cedarvale and Nordheimer ravines and Spadina Road, with only a partial section built and now known as Allen Road. The expressway would have continued east along a CN/CP railway corridor north of Dupont Street to Mount Pleasant Road, then cut through the Rosedale neighbourhood east of Mount Pleasant Road to connect with the Don Valley Parkway, with this section to be built through ravine parklands. The Crosstown expressway was rejected by Metro Council in December 1961 and later revived in May 1962 by Toronto Public Works Commissioner Douglas Ford, who proposed it alongside a one-way street plan for downtown to absorb Spadina Expressway traffic, eliminate the need for road widening, preserve residential areas, and encourage development; he also stated it would be folly to terminate the Spadina at anything other than a controlled-access expressway. Metro Planning Commissioner Murray Jones estimated 40,000 daily vehicles would move between Highway 400 and the Don Valley Parkway, and Metro Traffic Director Samuel Cass noted the plan would prevent heavy traffic from using residential streets in Rosedale and Moore Park. In 1964, Metro Planning Commissioner Eli Comay proposed extending Bay Street north of Davenport to connect with the Crosstown, criticizing the city for allowing an apartment development in the path of the extension; Toronto Controller William Dennison accused Comay of setting policy unilaterally, and the Toronto Board of Control rejected Comay and allowed the development to proceed. Metro Council twice instructed planners to cease work on the Crosstown, with Chairman William Allen joking that the only way to get it out of his mind was to leave the country. The Crosstown reappeared in the 1965 transportation plan and was approved by Metro Council, though the City of Toronto’s official plan had no such expressway and the Ontario Minister of Municipal Affairs rejected and rewrote that section to align with the Metro plan. The City of Toronto remained consistently opposed. Although land was acquired, the expressway was not built, though a short connecting road between the Don Valley Parkway and the Bayview Avenue Extension and Bloor Street would have likely been integrated. When the first section of the Don Valley Parkway opened from Bloor Street to Eglinton Avenue, it served as the southern terminus and remains an on/off ramp, with the unnamed roadway being a four-lane arterial with interchanges at either end, including the named 'Chester Hill' interchange. The East Metro Freeway was a proposed north–south expressway beginning at Highway 401 east of Morningside Avenue, following the Rouge River valley to Highway 407, with phase 2 extending beyond Highway 407 between the Ninth Line and York-Durham Line in Markham to Stouffville; it was a last priority for the province, with construction not planned until after the Scarborough Expressway was completed, and was not an extension of the Scarborough Expressway, as the latter’s western terminus would have been 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) west of the East Metro’s southern terminus. After the Spadina Expressway was cancelled, the Scarborough Expressway was put on hold and reviewed; with the Scarborough plan dropped, the East Metro route became less necessary and faced serious opposition from Rouge River naturalist groups, leading to its official removal from planning documents on June 1, 1994. Part of the Donald Cousens Parkway follows the East Metro Freeway route from 14th to 16th Avenue, though this arterial road now lies entirely within Markham, whereas the original Metro plan intended a terminus in Stouffville. Markham continues to seek a southern arterial connection to Highway 401, while Toronto has not rerouted Morningside Road to meet the Ninth Line at Steeles Avenue; instead, the current plan is to extend Morningside Avenue from McNicoll Avenue to Steeles Avenue just east of Tapscott Road using a private right of way and widen Steeles from just east of Markham Road to Ninth Line, with new traffic lights and a six-lane roadway to eliminate the bottleneck; a direct connection is not possible due to needing to cut across Cedar Brae Golf Club and build near the Rouge River. The Richview Expressway, named after the Richview Sideroad (now Eglinton Avenue through Etobicoke), was only partially completed due to low use and local opposition, resulting in a wide right-of-way from Black Creek Drive to Highway 427, which now includes high-speed flyover ramps at the Highway 401 and Highway 427 interchange originally intended for the Richview Expressway. The expressway was also known as the Hamilton Expressway because the original routing of Highway 403 (to Hamilton) was planned to terminate at the present site of the Highway 401 and Highway 427 interchange; had that routing been followed, the Richview would have been considered a municipal extension of Highway 403. However, the province realigned Highway 403 to turn north and meet Highway 401 at a new junction, also accommodating Highway 410 to Brampton, while widening Highway 401 between Highway 403 and Highway 427. A portion of the right-of-way between Highway 403 and the Richview Expressway was later used for Eastgate Parkway, which runs a short distance before curving north and terminating at Eglinton Avenue just west of Mississauga’s boundary with Etobicoke, while the rest of the corridor remained unbuilt. Lands allocated for the Richview Expressway were sold, with several apartment buildings now constructed on the old right-of-way. The corridor was revisited in the 2014 Toronto municipal election when John Tory’s SmartTrack plan proposed heavy rail, with challenger Olivia Chow highlighting the existing buildings; Tory was elected, but the heavy rail proposal was dropped in 2016 in favor of extending the Eglinton Crosstown LRT west to the city’s border with Mississauga. Although the expressway was never completed, plans included on/off ramps for the Scarborough Expressway (Gardiner Expressway Eastern Extension), which was intended to connect the Gardiner to Highway 401 at Toronto’s eastern boundary, with one segment built before public opposition halted the project. Traffic from the east would have gone directly downtown and served southeast Toronto; instead, such traffic now combines with northbound traffic on the Don Valley Parkway, where daily volumes exceed capacity, prompting ongoing proposals for new routes. The Scarborough Expressway was first conceived in the 1940s, with detailed planning beginning in 1967, and construction expected after the Spadina Expressway. Early plans had the route beside the CN route in southern Scarborough, later shifting to an eastern extension of the Gardiner along Lake Ontario’s base, following the Scarborough Bluffs, connecting to Highway 401 via Ontario Highway 2A, a short stub freeway part of the original 401 alignment. The 1967 proposal would have required demolishing 1,200 homes; after fierce opposition, the city redesigned the route in 1973, moving it entirely into the Lakeshore East CN/GO railway corridor from the Don Valley Parkway/Gardiner interchange, depressed in a deep ditch, reducing demolitions to 706 homes. This still did not satisfy east Toronto residents, who continued to oppose the plan, leading the city to shelve it in 1974. Property had been acquired by Metro Toronto, and some infrastructure, such as an overpass for roadway and railway tracks, was built, but opposition from residents, especially in eastern Toronto, caused the route to be severed from the Gardiner. The fiercest resistance came from eastern Toronto, leading to the deletion of the section beyond the Toronto/Scarborough boundary, which would have ended at Victoria Park Avenue and potentially flooded east-end neighbourhoods. Residents continued to oppose the plan and appeared before the Ontario Municipal Board each time Metro sought additional land. Metro and Scarborough continued to promote the expressway, renamed the "Scarborough Transportation Corridor," with parts of Eglinton Avenue East considered as a potential arterial to relieve Highway 401. Until the early 1990s, Metro and Scarborough maintained the plan, but by 1994 expressway development was no longer a priority. By 1996, Metro began planning to demolish the eastern end of the Gardiner Expressway, effectively ending the Scarborough Expressway/Scarborough Transportation Corridor. The intended connection between the Don River and Leslie Street was demolished in 2001, leaving only an offramp from the Gardiner to Carlaw Avenue, which was removed in 2021 to realign ramps between the Gardiner and the Don Valley Expressway. All that remains are concrete pillars from the elevated expressway to Leslie Street. Much of the land acquired across Scarborough remains vacant, with the City of Toronto conducting studies on its future use, including local streets, housing, and public parkland. Bridges along the CN/GO corridor were built with space for two lanes on either side of the railway, which are now empty and available for future rail upgrades. In the early 2000s, much of the land east of Manse Road in Scarborough was sold; the parcel between Kingston Road and Lawrence Avenue was developed into homes, as was a portion south of the railway and east of Poplar Road. A police station, Toronto Police 43 Division, was built on a parcel south of Lawrence Avenue.

text: The cancelled expressways in Toronto were a series of planned municipal expressways in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, that were only partially built or cancelled due to public opposition. Metropolitan Toronto's system of superhighways or freeways was intended to manage suburban growth and connect to the downtown core, in conjunction with the province's developing 400-Series Highways that would link to municipalities outside Metro. However, these expressways faced strong resistance from citizens in the downtown core, who opposed the demolition of homes and parklands, air pollution, noise, and the high cost of construction. The Spadina Expressway, planned since the 1940s, was cancelled in 1971 after only partial construction. Following its cancellation, other expressway plans, including a 'ring' around the central core, were abandoned. By the 1940s, urban development had extended beyond Toronto’s borders, and the city’s planning department recognized that population growth would require development of farmlands outside the city. In 1943, the City of Toronto Planning Board developed a plan for a nine-mile radius around Yonge Street and Queen Street, including a network of superhighways. With the creation of Metropolitan Toronto (Metro) in 1953, a new level of government was established with authority to build infrastructure such as highways, sewers, and public transit, while local governments handled land use planning. Metro planned to build an extensive network of highways that crisscrossed the city, with the province covering 50% of road project costs. Metro focused on roads serving the downtown core and connecting it to the suburbs, with key routes including the "Toronto-Barrie Highway" (Highway 400) on the north-west and the Queen Elizabeth Way on the southwest. The province was already planning Highway 400 in farmland areas, and Metro would extend these highways into the city. Construction began with the Lakeshore Expressway, which connected the QEW to the downtown core; the western section opened in 1958, continued eastward as an elevated highway to York Street in 1962, and reached the Don River by 1964. During construction, it was renamed the Gardiner Expressway after Fred Gardiner, the first chair of Metro and a major supporter. The Don Valley Parkway opened between Bloor Street and Eglinton Avenue in 1961 and expanded north and south to connect with Highway 401 in the north and the Gardiner in the south. These plans were part of a larger network first proposed in 1959 and fully developed by 1966 as the official plan. The inner ring included the Crosstown east-west along Davenport connecting to the Don Valley in the east and the Highway 400 extension to the west, the Highway 400 extension down Christie and Grace Streets from Davenport to the Gardiner near Fort York, and the Gardiner and Don Valley Expressways. The outer ring consisted of Highway 401 along the north, Highway 427 on the west, the Gardiner on the south, and the Scarborough Expressway to the east, connecting the Gardiner to Highway 401 in the far east. Other links included the Richview, a shorter at-grade expressway connecting the western end of the Crosstown at the Highway 400 extension to Highway 27 further west, eventually linking to the proposed Ontario Highway 403 and the Spadina Expressway, which ran north–south and connected the middle of Highway 401 to the downtown core, ending on Spadina Avenue near the University of Toronto. By 1962, the Spadina Expressway was approved and construction began in 1963 from Wilson Avenue to Lawrence Avenue. Initially, Metro approved only the Lawrence to Wilson section, but the province would not fund it unless the full route was approved, which it was. During construction, priority was given to access to the Yorkdale Shopping Centre, which opened in 1964, allowing drivers to travel from Lawrence Avenue north to Yorkdale via a paved section. The interchange with Highway 401 was completed later. In 1961, the Crosstown was cancelled by Metro Council, though carried forward by planning officials. Toronto and Metro proposed alternate routes for Highway 400, with Toronto favouring a route along railway lines. Metro developed its official transportation plan in 1964, evaluating three concepts: a road-oriented plan that included all expressways and omitted the Spadina subway, a transit-oriented plan that included Eglinton Avenue and Queen Street subways, extended the Spadina north to Vaughan, extended the Bloor-Danforth line east into Scarborough, and included express bus routes and commuter rail, and a mixed system that included all roads but omitted a Queen Street subway. The balanced plan, expected to be implemented by 1980, was estimated to cost $1 billion to construct, with the expressway component (Crosstown, Spadina, and Gardiner and Don Valley extensions) costing $210 million. The mixed system, though the most expensive, was approved by Metro Council in December 1966. The official plan included the Crosstown again, though it was not approved for construction. Toronto rejected the Crosstown, and the Ontario government revised the city’s official plan to allow for its possible construction. Construction of the Crosstown was not expected until the 1970s. After the Spadina south to Lawrence was completed, approval was given to proceed south to Eglinton, with the process of expropriating homes and parklands beginning, though without an interchange for the Crosstown. Construction plans became a point of growing protests in the late 1960s. The Gardiner and Don Valley Parkway had initially run through industrial areas, parkland, or unused areas, generating little public concern. As the Gardiner approached the downtown core, it began demolishing long-established neighbourhoods, and the planned expressways generally ran through well-settled areas. The Spadina Expressway passed through Forest Hill, The Annex, Harbord Village, Kensington Market, and Chinatown, while the Crosstown would have created a below-grade barrier on The Annex’s northern border and run beside Rosedale, displacing a forested ravine. Jane Jacobs, a new resident in The Annex who had previously blocked the Lower Manhattan Expressway in New York City, played a key role in opposing the Spadina Expressway. With David and Nadine Nowlan, she formed the "Stop Spadina And Save Our City" group, which became a major rallying point for anti-expressway sentiment. By the late 1960s, the Spadina Expressway had become a politically 'hot' topic. By 1969, construction had reached Eglinton Avenue (though paved only to Lawrence Avenue), less than half the planned route, and had already spent almost all of its $79 million budget. Metro Toronto had to return to the Ontario Municipal Board for additional loans, which were approved in a two-to-one decision. Stop Spadina appealed, and construction was halted pending the outcome. In 1971, Premier John Robarts retired and William Davis took office, who agreed to hear the appeal. On June 3, 1971, Davis stated in the Provincial Legislature: “If we are building a transportation system to serve the automobile, the Spadina Expressway would be a good place to start. But if we are building a transportation system to serve people, the Spadina Expressway is a good place to stop. It is our determination to opt for the latter.” Davis agreed to continue funding for the TTC subway line (now Line 1 Yonge–University) and later in 1972 agreed to complete the unfinished portion of the Spadina between Eglinton and Lawrence. The debate over continuing the Spadina further south from Eglinton continued throughout the 1970s. The cancellation of the Spadina Expressway marked the end of expressway construction in Toronto. Work on other expressways in the system was abandoned. Highway 400 initially stopped at Jane Street, where the province left it, and was later extended to Weston Road as Black Creek Drive, scaled down to a four-lane at-grade expressway instead of a six-lane freeway. The western terminus of the Richview forms the oversized interchange between Highways 401 and 427 and Eglinton Avenue near Pearson Airport. Highway 403 was built and now connects further west to Highway 401 at a major interchange that also connects to Highway 410. Both ends of the Scarborough Expressway were built: in the east as a large interchange that quickly turns into a smaller one with Kingston Road, and in the downtown core as a several-kilometre extension of the Gardiner past the Don Valley Parkway to Leslie Street. Lands acquired for the proposed Scarborough and Richview Expressways remained in municipal ownership for another twenty years and much of it remains in public ownership today, though future uses are undetermined. In 2001, the Gardiner East extension was demolished between the Don Valley Parkway and Leslie Street, and there were plans to remove the connection to the Don Valley Parkway, as of 2021 the connection is being realigned. In subsequent decades, the Peel and York Regions have expanded significantly in population and industrial development. An extensive highway network of Highways 403, 407, 410, 427, and 404 has developed in these suburbs and remains in the provincial inventory. Metro Toronto has not built any new expressways since the Spadina cancellation, with new expressways instead constructed by the province, some later transferred to municipal control. The province revised the Belfield Expressway route to terminate at Toronto International Airport instead of crossing Malton to Brampton, expropriated the right-of-way, and opened it as Highway 409. The segment of Highway 404 in Metro Toronto was originally intended as a northern extension of the Don Valley Parkway between Sheppard Avenue and Steeles Avenue, with the province continuing it into York Region, though the province ultimately assumed the entire project. Highway 400 initially stopped at Jane Street and was later extended to Weston Road as Black Creek Drive (scaled down to a four-lane at-grade expressway) and transferred from the province to Metro Toronto upon completion in 1982. Highway 2A and a section of QEW (east of Highway 427, re-designated as part of the Gardiner) were transferred to municipal control in 1997, drawing criticism from local politicians as a financial burden. As an alternative to road construction, the city and province have expanded TTC services and GO Transit commuter rail. Although TTC ridership declined in the 1980s and 1990s, it has recently reversed the trend, setting a new record in 2008, indicating growing demand for alternatives to private vehicles. Since expressways reached capacity in the 1970s, commuting has been handled by increased transit, with only 10% of commuters using the Gardiner Expressway to get downtown, according to 2006 figures. Highway advocates, such as political candidate Abel Van Wyk, argue that expressways are necessary to meet demand from suburban growth and automobile traffic between suburbs and the downtown core, and believe new expressways are needed to reduce congestion. Opposing groups, including residents of the core, oppose expansion due to air pollution, noise, and health effects that degrade urban living standards and hinder urban growth. Transit advocates argue that transit lines have higher capacity than expressways and represent better use of government resources. Cycling advocates promote cycling routes as alternatives for commuting and recreation. Special interest groups, such as the Citizens' Transportation Alliance of Greater Toronto, advocate for expressway construction, proposing a new expressway to the northwest (likely an expansion of Black Creek Drive) and one to the east through Scarborough along a hydro corridor or an expansion of Kingston Road, and supporting the filling in of 'missing links' in the arterial road grid. The Canadian Automobile Association published a 2004 plan including a new Scarborough Expressway over Lake Ontario, new expressways and arterial roads, and the Richview Expressway, which was quickly dismissed by Toronto City Council. The City of Toronto and the Government of Ontario focus instead on transit alternatives, aiming to reduce highway dependence through improvements to the current transit network as described in the Transit City plan. In April 2009, the province announced accelerated construction of several Transit City initiatives, including an east–west Eglinton Light Rail line connecting to the airport. Line 1 was extended north to Vaughan, and the Eglinton Crosstown LRT is under construction. It is proposed that Line 1 be extended north to Richmond Hill, Line 2 east to Scarborough City Centre, Line 5 west to Toronto Pearson International Airport, and a new Ontario Line serve the core and neighbourhoods in former North York and East York. Other plans debated during municipal elections included new toll highways or expansions of existing expressways via tolling, though toll highways have been seen as political poison and no politician has included them in any election campaign. The Crosstown Expressway was a planned east–west expressway through central Toronto. Although consistently opposed by Toronto City Council, it remained in the Metro Toronto plan until it was cancelled after the Spadina cancellation. In 1944, it was first proposed and included in the City of Toronto Official Plan in 1949 as the 'north-west arm' of the Don Valley Roadway system. The highway would have connected to Highway 400 at Old Weston Road and St. Clair Avenue, proceeded south-easterly between Davenport Road and Dupont Street, entered the Rosedale Ravine to connect with the main Don Valley roadway south of the Bloor Street Viaduct at the intersection of today’s Rosedale Valley Road and Bayview Avenue, and was estimated to cost $15 million as part of a $179 million development plan. As part of the 1959 Metropolitan Toronto plan, the expressway would have connected the Highway 400 extension along an east–west route near Christie Street and Dupont Street, east to the Don Valley Parkway, with Highway 400 continuing south to the Gardiner. North of Spadina Road, the Spadina Expressway would have connected via an interchange. The expressway would continue east along a CN/CP railway corridor north of Dupont Street to Mount Pleasant Road, then cut through Rosedale to connect with the Don Valley Parkway, with this section built through ravine parklands. The Crosstown was rejected by Metro Council in December 1961. Almost immediately, transportation officials lobbied Toronto and Metro to revive the project. In May 1962, Toronto Public Works Commissioner Douglas Ford proposed the construction of the Crosstown, along with an extensive one-way street plan for downtown Toronto, arguing it would absorb Spadina traffic and eliminate the need for road widening, preserve residential amenities, and encourage development. He stated that it would be folly to proceed otherwise.

text: The Canon EOS R50 is an entry-level APS-C mirrorless interchangeable-lens camera manufactured by Canon, announced on 27 February 2023 alongside the full-frame Canon EOS R8. It functions as an RF-mount replacement for Canon's discontinued EOS M50 Mark II and EOS 250D. Designed following the compact and lightweight principles of the EOS M50 Mark II and EOS 250D, the R50 incorporates the RF lens mount system and features from earlier EOS R series cameras, fitting the internal components of the EOS R10 into a more travel- and vlogging-friendly form factor. The camera features a 24.2-megapixel APS-C CMOS sensor, DIGIC X processor, Dual Pixel CMOS AF II focus system, and a 2.36-million-dot OLED electronic viewfinder, though physical controls have been simplified for beginner photographers. It lacks features such as a fully mechanical shutter, sensor self-cleaning, and in-body image stabilization, though in-lens stabilization is supported. The R50 includes a fully-articulating 1.62-million-dot LCD touchscreen, a built-in stereo microphone, a 3.5mm audio jack for external microphones, a UHS-I SD card slot, and built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth connectivity. It can shoot at 12 fps with a buffer of up to 42 JPEG images using the electronic first curtain shutter, or 15 fps with a buffer of up to 37 images using the electronic shutter, with shutter speeds ranging from 1/8000 seconds to 30 seconds. For video, it records up to 4K UHD resolution oversampled from the full sensor width at up to 29.97 fps and supports 1080p slow motion at up to 120 fps. The DIGIC X processor enables subject detection in multiple modes, up to 651 autofocus zones and 4503 autofocus points, and in-camera focus bracketing. Upon release, the EOS R50 received generally positive reviews; Engadget awarded it 87/100, calling it "a good balance between power and affordability," while Digital Photography Review gave it 84%, praising its photo and video quality and autofocus, though noting a lack of available RF-mount APS-C lenses. Some critics were more critical, with TechRadar and PCMag both giving it 3.5 stars and criticizing its ergonomics and limited physical controls, with PCMag noting the small size made it difficult to hold comfortably. On 26 March 2025, Canon introduced the EOS R50 V, a vlogging-focused variant that removes the built-in flash and electronic viewfinder but adds improved video recording capabilities, enhanced wired and wireless connectivity, and more video-oriented physical and digital controls, including the ability to shoot in Canon Log Clog3. Other Canon APS-C mirrorless cameras from the same period feature processors such as DIGIC 5/5+, DIGIC 6/6+, DIGIC 7, DIGIC 8, and DIGIC X; video capabilities including 1080p, 4K, 7K, and 8K; screen types such as flip (tilt), articulating, and touchscreen; body features like in-body image stabilization, multi-function hot shoe, and weather sealing; specialty models including astrophotography, Cinema EOS, and high-resolution cameras; and firmware add-ons like Magic Lantern Support.

text: The Cape Town Cycle Tour, formerly known as the Cape Argus Cycle Tour, is an annual cycle race held in Cape Town, South Africa, typically covering a distance of 109 km (68 mi). It is the first event outside Europe to be included in the Union Cycliste Internationale's Golden Bike Series. South Africa hosts three of the world's largest sporting events by number of entrants, with the Cape Town Cycle Tour, which can attract up to 35,000 cyclists, being the world's largest individually timed cycle race. The other two are the Comrades Marathon, the world's largest ultra-marathon running event, and the Midmar Mile, the world's largest open water swim. The Cycle Tour was the final leg of the Giro del Capo, a multi-stage race for professional and leading registered riders, which was last held in 2010. Traditionally staged on the second Sunday of March, the event has featured well-known competitors such as Miguel Indurain, Jan Ulrich, Matt Damon, Helen Zille, and Lance Armstrong. The race usually follows a scenic 109 km circular route starting at Grand Parade in Cape Town, traveling along Nelson Mandela Boulevard (N2), the M3 to Muizenberg, Main Road along the False Bay coast to Simon's Town and Smitswinkel Bay, then crossing the peninsula westward past the entrance to the Cape of Good Hope section of Table Mountain National Park (including Cape Point), heading north along the Atlantic coast through Scarborough, Kommetjie, Noordhoek, Chapman's Peak, Hout Bay over Suikerbossie Hill to Camps Bay, and ending near the Cape Town Stadium in Green Point. Between 2009 and 2010, and prior to 1999, the route varied in length between 104 km (65 mi) and 110 km (68 mi). The course records for conventional bicycles on the 110 km course over Chapman's Peak are documented. Penny Krohn holds the record for the most consecutive age group victories with 25. The fastest time ever recorded—also the highest average speed—was set in 1993 on the 105 km course by Wimpie van der Merwe in a fully faired recumbent, completing it in 02:16:40 at an average speed of 46.1 km/h. Japie Malan, at 92 years old during the 2012 Cycle Tour, is the oldest cyclist to complete the race within the seven-hour limit on a tandem, finishing in 05:49:00; he is also the oldest man (90 years old at the time) to complete the race on a single bicycle during the 2010 Cycle Tour, finishing in 06:48:52, and the oldest man to ride the Argus for the first time, which he did in 2004 at age 84. Mary Warner, at 80 years old during the 2006 tour, is the oldest woman to complete the race, finishing in 06:43:38. In 1978, Bill Mylrea and John Stegmann organized the Big Ride-In to advocate for cycle paths in South Africa, which drew hundreds of cyclists, including the Mayor of Cape Town at the time, and was first won by Lawrence Whittaker in September 1978. The original plan for the race was 140 km (87 mi), including a leg to Cape Point, but it was reduced to 104 km (65 mi) after being denied entry to the then Cape Point Nature Reserve; organizers convinced the initially reluctant Cape Argus, a local newspaper and sponsor, to allow the event to use its name. The event is now part of a week-long series of five cycling events that begin a week before the Cycle Tour and conclude with the main race. Between 2000 and 2003, the route was altered due to the closure of Chapman's Peak Drive, with a return via Ou Kaapse Weg and the Blue Route. The race has been halted three times due to extreme weather—twice when many competitors had already completed it, and once significantly shortened due to fire—and once cancelled. text: Carla Hall, born on May 12, 1964, is an American chef, television personality, and former model who was born and raised in Nashville, Tennessee. She graduated from Hillsboro High School and earned a degree in accounting from Howard University's Business School in 1986. After working as a Certified Public Accountant at Price Waterhouse in Tampa, Florida for two years, she left due to disliking the job. She then worked as a model on the runways of Paris, Milan, and London, during which time she decided to pursue a culinary career. Upon returning to the United States, she moved to Washington, D.C., where she started a lunch delivery service called the Lunch Bunch after her friend's coworkers expressed interest in her leftover sandwiches. After four years, she enrolled at L'Academie de Cuisine in Bethesda, Maryland, earning a Culinary Career Training certificate and later completing an externship at the Henley Park Hotel, where she was promoted to sous chef. By 1999, she became the executive chef at the Garden Cafe in the State Plaza Hotel and later served as executive chef at the Washington Club. In 2001, she founded Alchemy Caterers in Wheaton, Maryland, which she later renamed Alchemy by Carla Hall, and she remains in charge of the company. She authored the cookbook Cooking with Love: Comfort Food that Hugs You. Her big break came in 2008 when she competed on Top Chef: New York, where her crawfish gumbo earned her top-rated dish in the Thanksgiving challenge and Super Bowl XLIII tickets; she won two more challenges and was in the top for several others, impressing judges Jacques Pépin and Emeril Lagasse. She finished as runner-up to Hosea Rosenberg in the final challenge of the season. Hall gained popularity on the show for her personality and her call-and-response phrase "Hootie Hoo!", which she and her husband used to locate each other. She promoted the philosophy of "cooking with love," stating that cooking with care and calmness results in better food, and if one is not in a good mood, the only thing to make is a reservation. She participated in Top Chef: All-Stars, the eighth season, where she finished fifth overall and was awarded "Fan Favorite" by viewers, beating out Fabio Viviani. Since September 26, 2011, she has been one of the five co-hosts on The Chew, a one-hour ABC show centered on food from all angles that replaced All My Children, and remained a cohost until its cancellation in 2018. In 2014, she launched a Kickstarter campaign that raised $264,703 from 1,550 backers, exceeding her $250,000 goal, to open her restaurant Carla Hall's Southern Kitchen, which opened on June 17, 2016, in Brooklyn, New York, and closed in August 2017. She appeared on the May 3, 2009, cover of the Washington Post Magazine in a feature titled "Fit for Fame" about exercising while being famous. She portrayed a version of herself named "Spaghetti Scientist Carla Hall" in the BoJack Horseman episode "That Went Well," voiced Mpishi the harrier hawk in a season 2 episode of The Lion Guard titled "Ono and the Egg," and voiced the president in Season 1, Episode 5 of Butterbean's Café titled "A Grilled Cheese for the Big Cheese!" In 2016, she made a cameo in Fox's The Passion: New Orleans as a food truck operator. In 2018, she made a guest appearance on ABC's General Hospital as the Quartermaine family's cook. She has served as a judge on Food Network's Halloween Baking Championship and, in 2020, also hosted the season. She appeared as a judge on Season 7 of Food Network's Holiday Baking Championship as a replacement for Lorraine Pascal due to COVID-19 restrictions. In 2020, she judged the Channel 4 competition series Crazy Delicious, which took place on an edible set and was hosted by Jayde Adams alongside Heston Blumenthal and Niklas Ekstedt. As of 2020, she is featured in segments with Sesame Street characters Cookie Monster and Gonger in Snack Chat. In 2021, she appeared in Antiques Roadshow Celebrity Edition, episode 2, hosted Worst Cooks in America with Anne Burrell, and is a host and judge on Best Baker in America. In 2022, she was the headliner judge for the National Gingerbread House Competition. Hall lives in Washington, D.C. and married Matthew Lyons in 2006; she has a stepson named Noah.
