text: Christopher Nolan's use of practical, in-camera effects, miniatures, models, and shooting on celluloid film has been highly influential in early 21st century cinema. IndieWire noted in 2019 that Nolan "kept a viable alternate model of big-budget filmmaking alive," emphasizing that in an era where blockbuster filmmaking has become "a largely computer-generated art form," his approach remains significant. Due to his deep involvement in the technical and creative aspects of production, Stuart Joy described him as a "complete filmmaker" who "oversees all aspects of production while also managing cultural and industrial factors outside of the text." Nolan has produced some of the most influential and popular films of his time, with many regarded by critics as among the best of their respective decades. According to The Wall Street Journal, his ability to combine box-office success with artistic ambition has given him substantial industry clout. His films have earned more than $6 billion. Memento and The Dark Knight have been selected by the US Library of Congress for preservation in the National Film Registry for their cultural, historical, or aesthetic significance. These films, along with Inception, appeared in BBC's 100 Greatest Films of the 21st Century and The Hollywood Reporter's poll of best films ever made. In 2017, The Dark Knight, Inception, and Interstellar were included in Empire magazine's "The 100 Greatest Movies." In 2018, The Hollywood Reporter listed Nolan as one of the 100 most powerful people in entertainment, describing him as a "franchise unto himself." Parade ranked him number eight in its 2022 list of 75 Best Movie Directors of All Time. Five of his films were included in The New York Times 2025 list of The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century, and Memento, The Dark Knight, and Oppenheimer appeared in Rolling Stone's list of "The 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century." His work has been "intensely embraced, analysed and debated by ordinary film fans as by critics and film academics." Geoff Andrew of the British Film Institute called him a "persuasively inventive storyteller" and noted that his films are notable for their brilliant narrative ingenuity and adult engagement with complex philosophical questions rather than technical virtuosity. David Bordwell considers Nolan "one of the most accomplished living filmmakers," citing his ability to transform genre films into art and event films, along with his critical acclaim, box office success, and popularity. In 2008, Philip French named Nolan "the first major talent to emerge this century." Mark Kermode praised him for bringing the discipline and ethics of art-house filmmaking to Hollywood blockbusters, stating he proves profitability without appealing to the lowest common denominator. The Observer's Ryan Gilbey described Nolan as a "skillful, stylish storyteller" capable of merging Spielberg's spectacle with Roeg's or Resnais' intellectual depth. Mark Cousins applauded Nolan for embracing big ideas, noting that Hollywood filmmakers generally avoid such concepts—unlike Nolan. Scott Foundas of Variety called him "the premier big-canvas storyteller of his generation," while Justin Chang of the Los Angeles Times labeled him "the great proceduralist of 21st century blockbuster filmmaking, a lover of nuts-and-bolts minutiae." Nolan has been praised by contemporaries, with Kenneth Branagh calling his approach to large-scale filmmaking "unique in modern cinema" and stating he remains an artist and auteur, a heroic figure for audiences and behind-the-scenes professionals. Michael Mann credited Nolan with "inventing the post-heroic superhero" and highlighting his "singular vision." Nicolas Roeg noted that while "commercial art" is often self-negating, Nolan's work is deeply poetic despite being in the commercial arena. Martin Scorsese described Nolan as creating "beautifully made films on a big scale." Damien Chazelle praised Nolan for making seemingly impersonal projects like superhero epics and deep-space mind-benders feel deeply personal. Steven Spielberg referred to Nolan's Dark Knight series as an example of both art and blockbuster, and has described Memento and Inception as "masterworks." Denis Villeneuve expressed admiration for Nolan's ability to maintain his identity and create a distinct universe at scale, bringing intellectual concepts to the screen in a rare and impressive way. Nolan has been nominated for eight Academy Awards (winning two), eight British Academy Film Awards (winning two), and six Golden Globe Awards (winning one). From 2011 to 2014, he appeared on Forbes Celebrity 100 list based on income and popularity. In 2015, he was included in Time's 100 most influential people in the world. In 2006, he was named an Honorary Fellow of UCL; in 2017, he received an honorary doctorate in literature. In 2012, he became the youngest director to receive a hand-and-footprint ceremony at Grauman's Chinese Theatre in Los Angeles. In 2019, he was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire for services to film. In 2023, he received the Federation of American Scientists' Public Service Award for his depiction of scientists in Oppenheimer. In 2024, he was awarded the British Film Institute Fellowship for his "extraordinary achievements and enormous contribution to cinema" and the Honorary César award for "continually pushing the boundaries of storytelling." In March 2024, Nolan was made a knight bachelor for his contributions to film, and his wife Emma Thomas was honoured with a damehood.

text: Christopher Nolan's success with The Dark Knight led Warner Bros. to sign him to write, direct, and co-produce Inception (2010), an idea he had developed around nine years earlier. Described as a contemporary sci-fi action film set within the architecture of the mind, Inception starred a large ensemble led by Leonardo DiCaprio and became a critical and commercial success, grossing over $836 million worldwide. Film critic Mark Kermode named it the best film of 2010, calling it proof that cinema can be both blockbuster and art. Philosophy professor David Kyle Johnson praised it as a classic almost immediately, highlighting its exploration of philosophical themes like leap of faith and the allegory of the cave. The film earned nominations for eight Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Original Screenplay, and won in Best Cinematography, Best Sound Mixing, Best Sound Editing, and Best Visual Effects. Nolan also received a BAFTA and a Golden Globe nomination for Best Director. Around the release of The Dark Knight Rises (2012), Joseph Bevan of the British Film Institute noted that Nolan had transitioned from promising British indie director to master of intelligent escapism. After initial hesitation, Nolan agreed to direct the film, working with his brother and David S. Goyer to develop a story that would conclude the trilogy on a high note. The film received positive reviews, with Kenneth Turan calling it "potent, persuasive and hypnotic" and Christy Lemire describing it as "typically spectacular, ambitious" though criticizing its "overloaded" story and grimness. It became the thirteenth film to gross $1 billion and was followed by a tragic shooting at a midnight showing in Aurora, Colorado, where 12 people were killed and 58 injured; Nolan issued a statement expressing condolences for the victims. The Dark Knight trilogy inspired a trend in superhero films to adopt its gritty, realistic tone, with Ben Child of The Guardian calling the trilogy "thrilling totems of the genre for decades to come." During story discussions for The Dark Knight Rises, Goyer proposed Man of Steel (2013), which Nolan produced after being impressed by Zack Snyder’s work in 300 (2006) and Watchmen (2009), and hired Snyder to direct. The film, starring Henry Cavill as Clark Kent, received mixed reviews and grossed over $660 million against a $220 million budget. Nolan then directed, wrote, and produced Interstellar (2014), originally scripted by Jonathan Nolan and initially intended for Steven Spielberg. Based on scientific theories by Kip Thorne, the film follows astronauts traveling through a wormhole in search of a new home for humanity. In a 2014 discussion, Nolan expressed admiration for scientific objectivity, wishing it were applied broadly. Interstellar, starring Matthew McConaughey, Anne Hathaway, and Jessica Chastain, received positive reviews and grossed $773 million worldwide. A. O. Scott of The New York Times called it a "sweeping, futuristic adventure driven by grief, dread and regret," while documentary filmmaker Toni Myers praised its exploration of multi-generational storytelling. The film was lauded for its scientific accuracy, leading to two academic papers and a call from the American Journal of Physics for its inclusion in school science curricula. At the 87th Academy Awards, it won Best Visual Effects and received four other nominations. In 2014, Nolan and Emma Thomas served as executive producers on Transcendence, the directorial debut of cinematographer Wally Pfister. In the mid-2010s, Nolan supported film preservation through Syncopy’s joint venture with Zeitgeist Films to release Blu-ray editions of Zeitgeist’s films. He directed the documentary short Quay (2015) for the Brothers Quay’s animation films and initiated a theatrical tour showcasing their works. As an advocate for analogue film, Nolan and visual artist Tacita Dean hosted an informal summit on Reframing the Future of Film at the Getty Museum in March 2015, with follow-up events in London, Mexico City, and Mumbai. In April 2015, he joined the board of directors of The Film Foundation and was appointed, alongside Martin Scorsese, to the National Film Preservation Board by the Library of Congress as a DGA representative. He also serves on the Motion Picture & Television Fund Board of Governors. After serving as an executive producer on Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice (2016) and Justice League (2017), Nolan returned to directing with Dunkirk (2017), a film based on his original screenplay and co-produced with Thomas. Set during World War II in 1940, it follows the evacuation of Allied soldiers from Dunkirk, France, and is structured as a survival tale with minimal dialogue. Nolan waited to make it until he earned trust from a major studio to produce it as a British film with an American budget. Before filming, he sought advice from Spielberg, who advised him to prioritize research over imagination. The film, starring an ensemble cast, received widespread critical acclaim and grossed over $526 million worldwide, becoming the highest-grossing World War II film of all time. Mick LaSalle of the San Francisco Chronicle called it "one of the best war films ever made," and it earned Nolan his first Oscar nomination for Best Director. In 2018, Nolan supervised a new 70 mm print of Stanley Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), made from the original camera negative, and presented it at the 2018 Cannes Film Festival, where it was met with a standing ovation. In 2019, Nolan and Thomas received executive producer credits on The Doll's Breath, an animated short by the Quay brothers. His next film, Tenet (2020), described by Tom Shone as a "globe-spinning riff on all things Nolanesque," had been in development for over a decade and took more than five years to write. Delayed three times due to the COVID-19 pandemic, it was the first major Hollywood tent-pole to open in theatres after the shutdown. The film follows an unnamed protagonist (played by John David Washington) who travels through time to stop a world-threatening attack. It grossed $363 million worldwide on a $200 million budget, becoming Nolan’s first box-office underperformer. Critics found it polarizing, praising its ambition and technical aspects while criticizing its confusing narrative. Peter Bradshaw awarded it five stars, calling it a "cerebral cadenza" with "supercharged energy and imagination," while Leslie Felperin described it as "a chilly, cerebral film" that is "easy to admire but almost impossible to love." At the 93rd Academy Awards, it won Best Visual Effects and was nominated for Best Production Design. Following its release, Nolan joined the Advisory Board of the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers and served as an executive producer on Zack Snyder’s Justice League (2021), a director’s cut of the 2017 film. Nolan’s 12th film, Oppenheimer (2023), is a biopic based on J. Robert Oppenheimer and his role in developing the atomic bomb, marking his first R-rated film since Insomnia (2002) and his first feature not made for Warner Bros. Financed and distributed by Universal Pictures, it was made with a $100 million production budget and equal marketing budget, offering Nolan total creative control, 20% of first-dollar gross, a 100-day theatrical window, and a blackout period. The film received critical acclaim, with Matthew Jackson of The A.V. Club calling it a "masterpiece" and the best of Nolan’s career, and BBC Culture’s Caryn James describing it as "boldly imaginative and his most mature work yet," combining the action of The Dark Knight trilogy with the cerebral depth of Memento, Inception, and Tenet. It grossed over $975 million worldwide, becoming the third-highest-grossing film of 2023. Nolan won the Academy Awards for Best Director and Best Picture. In 2025, he was elected president of the Directors Guild of America, representing over 19,500 members. His next directorial effort, The Odyssey, an adaptation of Homer’s epic poem, is scheduled for release in July 2026 and follows Odysseus (played by Matt Damon) on his journey home after the Trojan War, including encounters with Polyphemus, the Sirens, and Circe, and his reunion with Penelope. With an estimated $250 million budget, it will be the most expensive film of his career and the first mainstream blockbuster shot entirely on IMAX film. Nolan is married to Emma Thomas, whom he met at University College London when he was 19; she has worked as a producer on all his films since 1997. The couple has four children and resides in Los Angeles. They were included in the Sunday Times Rich List of 2025 with an estimated net worth of £360 million. Nolan prefers to maintain mystery about his work, refusing to discuss his personal life and stating he does not want audiences to think of him while watching his films. He does not own a smartphone or email address, instead hand-delivering scripts to actors and having his wife manage outreach. His films are centered on metaphysical themes such as time, memory, and personal identity, featuring mathematically inspired ideas, unconventional narratives, materialistic perspectives, and evocative sound. Guillermo del Toro called him an "emotional mathematician," and Will Gompertz described him as an "art house auteur making intellectually ambitious blockbuster movies that can leave your pulse racing and your head spinning." Joseph Bevan wrote that his films allow arthouse audiences to enjoy superhero films and multiplex crowds to engage with complex plots. Nolan views himself as "an indie filmmaker working inside the studio system." Critics have noted that Nolan defies Hollywood norms by creating original, complex genre films that challenge studio expectations, yet his films consistently draw large audiences. In The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan, professional philosophers and writers analyzed his work, identifying themes of self-destruction, truth, and the nature of heroes and villains. Robbie B. H. Goh described Nolan as a "philosophical filmmaker" who integrates existentialism, morality, epistemology, and the distinction between appearance and reality into action and suspense-driven films, maintaining engagement while offering deeper reflection. David Bordwell described Nolan’s work as experiments with cinematic time using subjective viewpoints and crosscutting. His use of practical effects, miniatures, models, and shooting on celluloid has been influential in early 21st century cinema. IndieWire noted that Nolan kept a viable alternative to computer-generated filmmaking alive. Stuart Joy described him as a "complete filmmaker" who oversees all aspects of production and manages external cultural and industrial factors. Nolan has made some of the most influential and popular films of his time, with many regarded as among the best of their decades. According to The Wall Street Journal, his ability to combine box-office success with artistic ambition has given him significant industry clout. His films have earned over $6 billion. Memento and The Dark Knight have been selected by the National Film Registry.

text: Sir Christopher Edward Nolan, born on 30 July 1970 in Westminster, London, is a British and American filmmaker recognized as a leading figure of the 21st century. His films have generated over $6 billion worldwide, making him the seventh-highest-grossing film director. He has won two Academy Awards, a Golden Globe Award, and two British Academy Film Awards. Nolan was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 2019 and knighted in 2024 for his contributions to film. He developed an interest in filmmaking from a young age, beginning to make films at seven using his father's Super 8 camera and action figures, including a stop motion animation titled Space Wars. His uncle, who worked at NASA, sent him launch footage that he re-filmed and edited. From age 11, he aspired to be a professional filmmaker. He studied English literature at University College London, where he was president of the Film Society and co-screened feature films in 35mm with his future wife, Emma Thomas. After graduating in 1993, he worked as a script reader, camera operator, and director of corporate films. He directed, wrote, and edited the short film Larceny (1996), which premiered at the Cambridge Film Festival and is considered one of UCL's best shorts, and later made Doodlebug (1997). He and Thomas attempted to make a feature film titled Larry Mahoney, which they abandoned due to lack of industry support. His first feature film, Following (1998), which he wrote, directed, photographed, and edited, was made on a budget of around £3,000 with friends and used minimal equipment, and was well-received by critics who compared it to Hitchcock. It led to the creation of Memento (2000), a film developed from a short story by his brother Jonathan, which told the story in reverse and earned critical acclaim, including nominations for Best Screenplay and Best Director, and was listed as one of the best films of the 2000s. Memento earned Nolan two Independent Spirit Awards and led to the founding of Syncopy Inc. with Thomas in 2001. After Memento, he was recommended by Steven Soderbergh to Warner Bros. to direct Insomnia (2002), a remake of the 1997 Norwegian film, which received positive reviews and earned $113 million against a $46 million budget. Following Memento and Insomnia, Nolan established himself as an auteur. He was briefly attached to direct a Howard Hughes biopic and a Ruth Rendell novel adaptation before choosing to direct Batman Begins (2005), which revived the franchise and was praised for its psychological depth and realism. The film starred Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Gary Oldman, Morgan Freeman, and Liam Neeson and was the biggest project he had undertaken to that point. He then directed The Prestige (2006), an adaptation of a Christopher Priest novel co-written with his brother Jonathan, which received critical acclaim and two Academy Award nominations. The Dark Knight (2008), the sequel to Batman Begins, expanded on the noir quality of the first film and became one of the best superhero films ever made, earning over $1 billion worldwide and winning two Academy Awards: Best Sound Editing and a posthumous Best Supporting Actor award for Heath Ledger. The film's failure to receive a Best Picture nomination prompted the Academy to increase the number of nominees from five to ten, known as "The Dark Knight Rule." Nolan then directed Inception (2010), a film he had conceived around nine years earlier, which became a critical and commercial success, named the best film of 2010 by Mark Kermode and praised for its philosophical themes. The film grossed over $836 million worldwide and was nominated for eight Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Original Screenplay, winning Best Cinematography. After the release of Tenet (2020), Nolan parted ways with Warner Bros. Pictures and signed with Universal Pictures for Oppenheimer (2023), which won him Academy Awards for Best Director and Best Picture. Nolan's films are known for their metaphysical themes, exploration of epistemology, existentialism, ethics, time, memory, and personal identity, use of mathematically inspired imagery, unconventional narrative structures, practical special effects, experimental soundscapes, large-format film photography, and materialistic perspectives. He is a strong advocate for traditional film stock over digital cameras. He has co-written several films with his brother Jonathan and runs the production company Syncopy Inc. with his wife, Emma Thomas. Nolan and Thomas have maintained strong ties with University College London, with both receiving honorary fellowships and Nolan receiving an honorary doctorate in 2017.

In 2016, the second version, ARC++, was introduced, using Linux kernel features cgroups and namespaces to create isolated containers that can run Android apps, eliminating the need to recompile apps and enabling access to Google Play for ChromeOS devices. ARC++ was introduced with Android Marshmallow and upgraded to Android Nougat and Android Pie. ARCVM launched in 2021 with Android 11 and runs on Android 13 starting with ChromeOS 117, using virtual machines to enhance Android environment isolation for improved security and maintainability. In 2018, Google announced Linux on ChromeOS, known as Crostini, allowing desktop Linux applications; this feature was released to the stable channel with Chrome 69 in October 2018 as a beta option and officially released with Chrome 91. All Chromebooks made since 2018, and some earlier models, can run Linux apps, which can be installed and launched alongside other apps. Google maintains a list of devices launched before 2019 that support Linux apps. Since 2013, Linux applications have been run in ChromeOS via Crouton, a third-party script set for distributions like Ubuntu. In 2018, Google officially introduced Crostini, named as a pun on Crouton, which runs a virtual machine via crosvm, using Linux's KVM tool, with the Termina VM containing a Gentoo-based ChromeOS kernel and LXD containers. Linux apps run in isolated containers, not on the VM itself, with a default Debian container and support for installing programs via APT or .deb files, or granting access to files and USB devices. As of ChromeOS 121, Debian 12 (Bookworm) is the default container base image. ChromeOS is built on the Linux kernel, originally based on Ubuntu, changed to Gentoo in February 2010. ChromeOS includes the Chromium Shell ("crosh") with minimal functionality like ping at startup; in developer mode, a full-featured bash shell is accessible via VT-2 or the crosh command shell, with a root password required for full privileges, defaulting to "chronos" or "facepunch" initially, later set to empty. ChromeOS is partially developed under the open-source ChromiumOS project, with ChromeOS receiving only Google and partner support and automatic updates to the latest version. Early in the project, Google shared design goals for ChromeOS, including minimal screen space through a single tab strip, reduced window management, floating "panels" for secondary tasks, and split screens for viewing content side by side, leveraging HTML5 offline modes, background processing, and notifications. On April 10, 2012, ChromeOS offered a choice between a full-screen interface and overlapping, resizable windows via the Ash window manager and Aura graphics engine, including translucent tabs, torn tabs, and a mouse-enabled shortcut list. In 2016, ChromeOS included "Native CUPS Support" as an experimental feature, becoming stable in 2020, enabling most printers even without Google Cloud Print support. Google Cloud Print, which allowed any device to print to supported printers via a proxy installed on ChromeOS, was discontinued after December 31, 2020, and ceased operations on January 1, 2021. ChromeOS stores user files on remote servers, and handling local files offline may cause confusion about which application opens them, a problem noted by Matthew Papakipos as similar to issues in Windows. ChromeOS uses a three-channel release system: Stable, Beta, and Developer (Dev), with a fourth canary channel confirmed by entering the ChromeOS shell in developer mode and using the command update_engine_client -channel canary-channel -update, which requires a powerwash to return to other channels. In 2022, two new channels, LTC (Long-term support candidate) and LTS (Long-term support), were added, available only to Enterprise admins, with LTC providing three months of support before switching to LTS. ChromeOS features a hardened design with auto-updating, sandboxing, and a verified boot process that checks for system compromises, shipped with a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) and a physical switch under the battery to enable developer mode, which reverses security functions but increases flexibility. Full disk encryption is enabled by default, with the decryption password stored in the TPM, which can be updated manually via settings, resetting the device to factory defaults. The user's Google Account password is the default sign-in method, with additional authentication like PINs, passwords, fingerprint, facial recognition, or smart unlock (via a paired phone) to prevent unauthorized access. If multi-factor authentication (MFA) is enabled on the Google Account, users may be prompted during setup, with the device designated as "trusted" for subsequent logins, and MFA can be required for each sign-in using hardware tokens like YubiKeys. At its debut, ChromeOS was seen as a competitor to Microsoft Windows and its cloud-based applications, though engineering director Matthew Papakipos argued that ChromeOS is designed for netbooks with limited computational power, unable to run resource-intensive programs like Adobe Photoshop. Some observers, including Tony Bradley of PC World, claimed that existing operating systems like Windows or Linux-based netbooks already provided a web-centric experience similar to ChromeOS, questioning the need for a new system. In 2016, Chromebooks were the most popular computer in the US K–12 education market. In 2020, Chromebooks became the second most-popular end-user operating system, growing from 6.4% in 2019 to 10.8% in 2020, with most growth occurring at the expense of Windows, which fell from 85.4% in 2019 to 80.5% in 2021. Google's offer of multiple open-source operating systems, including Android and ChromeOS, drew criticism, with Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer accusing Google of indecision and Steven Levy noting the dissonance between the two systems at Google I/O 2011.

text: ChromeOS, a proprietary operating system developed by Google, is derived from the open-source ChromiumOS, which itself originates from Gentoo Linux, and uses the Google Chrome web browser as its primary user interface. Google announced the project in July 2009, initially describing it as a cloud-based operating system where applications and user data reside in the cloud, primarily running web applications. The operating system first shipped with Chromebooks in 2011 and has since been offered as an installable Linux distribution called ChromeOS Flex since 2020. ChromeOS supports progressive web applications, Android apps from Google Play, and Linux applications. In 2025, Google confirmed that ChromeOS will transition from the Linux kernel to the Android kernel, resulting in a merged development path with Android, formally announced at the Snapdragon Summit in September 2025 under the internal codename "Aluminium OS." The new operating system will be desktop-optimized, running the same Android software on both desktop and mobile devices, adapted for different screen sizes, and will support both ARM and x86 processors, with the x86 version expected to be the first mainline maintained x86 architecture version of Android. Jeff Nelson, a Google employee, created the concept of ChromeOS in 2006 as "Google OS," initially a Linux distribution focused on speed, and early versions used Firefox before switching to Chrome in 2007. To determine marketing needs, developers analyzed usage patterns from 200 Google employee machines and their own usage. Google required hardware partners to use solid-state drives for performance and reliability, noting that ChromeOS requires only one-sixtieth the drive space of Windows 7; in 2019, ChromeOS recovery images were still between 1 and 3 GB in size. On November 19, 2009, Google released the source code as the ChromiumOS project, and at a news conference, Sundar Pichai demonstrated an early version that booted in seven seconds and featured a desktop resembling Chrome with application tabs. Chris Kenyon of Canonical announced a contract to contribute engineering resources, and Canonical was an early engineering partner; initially, ChromiumOS could only be built on Ubuntu, but in February 2010, the team switched to Gentoo Linux due to its flexible package management system, and the build environment is no longer restricted to any distribution, though installation guides use Debian (and thus Ubuntu) apt syntax. In 2010, Google released the unbranded Cr-48 Chromebook in a pilot program, with retail hardware delayed until 2011. On May 11, 2011, Google announced two Chromebooks from Acer and Samsung at Google I/O; the Samsung model launched on June 15, 2011, and the Acer model in mid-July. In August 2011, Netflix announced official support for ChromeOS, and later that month, Citrix released a client for remote access to Windows applications. Dublin City University became the first European educational institution to provide Chromebooks to students in September 2011. By 2012, demand for Chromebooks grew, and Google introduced new devices from Samsung, including the first Chromebox, the Samsung Series 3, and a lower-priced Chromebook in October 2012 priced at $250, using an ARM processor from Samsung's Exynos line, with reduced memory and screen resolution; Acer followed with the C7 Chromebook at $199, using an Intel Celeron processor and a laptop hard disk to reduce cost. In April 2012, Google introduced the Aura window manager and a conventional taskbar, marking a shift from a single-browser interface to a more traditional desktop experience. Google Drive integration was added in ChromeOS version 20, released in July 2012, and Adobe Flash support was fully sandboxed by the end of 2012. Before 2013, Google did not manufacture its own ChromeOS devices, which were designed and marketed by third-party partners; this changed in February 2013 with the release of the Chromebook Pixel, which featured an Intel Core i5 processor, a 2,560×1,700 touchscreen, and a price competitive with business laptops. By the end of 2013, analysts were divided on ChromeOS's future, despite predictions of its demise since 2009, as device sales continued to grow. In mid-2014, Time magazine published a piece highlighting conflicting views on Chromebooks' success. Intel's announcement of Intel-based Chromebooks, Chromeboxes, and LG's Chromebase further fueled uncertainty. Seizing the opportunity from the end of Windows XP support, Google offered significant discounts in early 2014 to promote Chromebooks in businesses. ChromeOS devices outsold Apple Macs worldwide in 2020. Since July 2021, ChromeOS's embedded controller has been based on a Google-maintained fork of Zephyr, a real-time operating system. In March 2014, Google hosted a hacking contest called Pwnium, where two exploits were demonstrated and a third at Pwn2Own; all were patched within a week. Google Native Client has been available since 2010, but few apps existed initially; in June 2014, Google announced ChromeOS would sync with Android phones and run Android apps from Google Play, expanding app availability. Google also adopted Material Design, with a new default wallpaper introduced in 2014 and fully integrated in Chrome 117. Chrome Enterprise, launched in 2017, includes ChromeOS, Chrome Browser, and device management features for businesses, offering standard features like bookmark and extension syncing, cloud printing, multi-layered security, remote desktop, and automatic updates, and advanced features such as Active Directory integration, unified endpoint management, advanced security, device policies, guest access, kiosk mode, and app whitelisting/blacklisting. The education sector was an early adopter, and Chromebooks are widely used in classrooms, with cloud-based computing advantages gaining traction in financial services, healthcare, and retail. ICT managers cite benefits such as advanced security, simplified management, reduced operational costs, and secure file access across devices. Google's Grab and Go program allows businesses to provide employees access to fully charged Chromebooks for checkout and return. In February 2014, Google released Chromebox for Meetings, a kit for conference rooms with a Chromebox, camera, noise-cancelling microphone, speakers, and remote control, supporting Google Hangouts, Vidyo, and UberConference. Partners released various models, and in 2016, Google introduced an all-in-one Chromebase for smaller meeting rooms. Google targeted the consumer market with the Chromebook in 2011 and the Chromebook Pixel in 2013, and expanded into enterprise with the Pixelbook in 2017, with a second-generation model released in 2019. In 2021, several vendors offered all-in-one Chromebase devices. Google has partnered with OEMs including Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and Samsung; in August 2019, Dell launched the Latitude 5300 2-in-1 Chromebook Enterprise and Latitude 5400 Chromebook Enterprise, designed for security-conscious organizations and bundled with cloud-based support services. Other OEMs like Acer and HP also launched devices with Chrome Enterprise Upgrade. With a broader hardware range, ChromeOS became a viable option for enterprises avoiding migration to Windows 10 before Windows 7 support ended. Laptops running ChromeOS are known as Chromebooks; the first was the CR-48, released to testers in December 2010, with retail models following in May 2011. A desktop design, the Chromebox, was released by Samsung in May 2012, and a partnership with AOPEN led to the first commercial Chromebox in March 2015. In early 2014, LG introduced the first Chromebase, a monitor with built-in camera, microphone, and speakers. The Chromebit is an HDMI dongle that turns a TV or monitor into a personal computer; the first, an Asus model, shipped in November 2015 and reached end of life in November 2020. In March 2018, Acer launched the Chromebook Tab 10, a tablet with a screen size and resolution identical to the Apple iPad and a Wacom-branded stylus that does not require charging. ChromeOS supports multi-monitor setups via video-out ports, USB 3.0 Standard-A, or USB-C, with USB-C being preferred. On February 16, 2022, Google announced a development version of ChromeOS Flex, a distribution that can be installed on conventional PC hardware to replace Windows or macOS, similar to CloudReady, which Google acquired in 2020. ChromeOS automatic updates are available for 10 years for all Chromebooks manufactured in 2019 and onwards, covering the operating system, browser, and hardware; Google maintains a web page detailing the auto-update policy and end dates. Previously, the update period was 8 years, and shorter before that, though earlier models received updates for longer. Initially, ChromeOS was a thin client relying on servers for web applications and data; Google later encouraged developers to create packaged applications using HTML5, CSS, Adobe Shockwave, and JavaScript. In September 2014, Google launched App Runtime for Chrome (ARC), initially with four Android apps—Duolingo, Evernote, Sight Words, and Vine—and in 2016, ARC++ was introduced using Linux kernel features to run Android apps in isolated containers, enabling Google Play availability. ARC++ was introduced with Android Marshmallow and upgraded to Nougat and Pie. ARCVM launched in 2021 with Android 11 and runs on Android 13 starting with ChromeOS 117, using virtual machines to enhance Android environment isolation for security and maintainability. In 2018, Google announced Linux on ChromeOS (Crostini), allowing desktop Linux applications, which was released to the stable channel in October 2018 as a beta feature.

text: Cindy Sherman is a conceptual photographer whose work explores the construction of identity, gender, and social roles through self-portraiture. She often assumes multiple characters using costumes, makeup, and props to transform herself, challenging traditional representations of women in media and popular culture. Her early work, such as the Untitled Film Stills series, features cinematic references and portrays archetypal female figures, highlighting the influence of visual culture on individual identity. In later series, Sherman experimented with digital manipulation and grotesque imagery to question notions of beauty, fame, and social perception. Her artistic style is widely recognized for its critical approach to representation, blending realism with theatricality and making the viewer aware of the artificiality inherent in images. Sherman created the six-image series Cindy Sherman: Untitled (Balenciaga) in 2008, which were first shown publicly in 2010. In the same year, she collaborated with Anna Hu on a jewelry design. She returned to working with Teller on Marc Jacobs' Spring/Summer 2024 campaign. In the early 1990s, she worked with the Minneapolis band Babes in Toyland, providing photographs for the albums Fontanelle and Painkillers, creating a stage backdrop for live concerts, and acting in the promotional video for "Bruise Violet"; she also worked as a film director. Sherman moved from photography to film with her 1997 movie Office Killer, starring Jeanne Tripplehorn, Molly Ringwald, and Carol Kane, in which Dorine, played by Carol Kane, serves as a stand-in for Sherman, reflecting their shared interest in arranging bodies in diorama-like scenes. According to author Dahlia Schweitzer, Office Killer is a comedy, horror, melodrama, noir, feminist statement, and art piece, featuring artistically executed murder scenes reminiscent of her Untitled Horror series. The film grossed $37,446 and received poor reviews, described as "crude" and "laugh-free," with art critic Roberta Smith noting it lacks the artist's usual finesse and calling it a "fascinating if lumpish bit of Shermaniana," while Stephen Holden called it "sadly inept." Sherman had a cameo in John Waters' film Pecker and appeared in The Feature in 2008, starring her ex-husband Michel Auder, which won a New Vision Award. In 2009, Paul Hasegawa-Overacker and Tom Donahue completed a documentary, Guest of Cindy Sherman, about their relationship with Sherman, which she initially supported but later opposed. In the catalog essay by Philipp Kaiser for Sherman's 2016 exhibition at Metro Pictures Gallery, he noted six short films she made in college that preceded Office Killer, and included a conversation between Sherman and Sofia Coppola in which Sherman admitted she may star in an upcoming film project. Sherman's first solo show in New York was at The Kitchen in 1980, and her photographs were the first show at the newly opened Metro Pictures Gallery that year. "Untitled Film Stills" were first shown at Artists Space, where Sherman was a receptionist. Her first solo exhibitions in France were presented by Galerie Chantal Crousel in Paris. Sherman has participated in many international events, including SITE Santa Fe (2004), the Venice Biennale (1982, 1995), and five Whitney Biennials. Her work has been featured in solo exhibitions at the Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam (1982), Whitney Museum of American Art in New York (1987), Kunsthalle Basel (1991), Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, D.C. (1995), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (1998), Serpentine Gallery in London and the Scottish National Gallery of Modern Art (2003), and Martin-Gropius-Bau in Berlin (2007). Major retrospectives have been organized by the Museum Boymans-van Beuningen in Rotterdam (1996), the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles and the Museum of Modern Art in New York (1997), sponsored by Madonna, and Kunsthaus Bregenz, Austria, Louisiana Museum for Moderne Kunst, Denmark, and Jeu de Paume in Paris (2006–2007). In 2009, she was included in "The Pictures Generation, 1974–1984" at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. In 2012, the Museum of Modern Art mounted a show chronicling her work from the mid-1970s, including over 170 photographs, which traveled to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art and the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis. In 2013, she was invited to organize a show at the Venice Biennale. In 2016, after a sabbatical spent "coming to terms with health issues and getting older," Sherman produced and staged her first photo gallery in five years, the series "The Imitation of Life," named after a 1959 Douglas Sirk melodrama, which presents her in highly stylized glamour portraits inspired by old Hollywood divas such as Gloria Swanson, Mary Pickford, and Ruby Keeler. The series was exhibited at Metro Pictures Gallery in New York City and the Broad Museum in Los Angeles in 2016, and later at Spruth Magers in Berlin and the Wexner Center for the Arts in Columbus, Ohio in 2017. In 2019, the National Portrait Gallery in London organized a major retrospective of her work from the mid-1970s to the present. In 2024, at the Goulandris Museum of Cycladic Art in Athens, Sherman held her first exhibition in Greece, gathering over a hundred of her early works. In 2024, at Fotografiska Stockholm, she exhibited Tapestries, a series of tapestries based on her digitally altered Instagram selfies, marking her first major exploration of this medium. In her Imitation of Life series, Sherman poses in vintage costume and theatrical makeup as various ageing actress-like women. Scholar Douglas Crimp describes her work as a "hybrid of photography and performance art that reveals femininity to be an effect of representation." Sherman does not consider her work or herself to be feminist, stating "The work is what it is and hopefully it's seen as feminist work, or feminist-advised work, but I'm not going to go around espousing theoretical bullshit about feminist stuff." Many scholars emphasize the relationship between her work and the concept of the gaze, particularly Laura Mulvey's analysis of the male gaze in relation to her Untitled series, where she notes that "the accouterments of the feminine struggle to conform to a facade of desirability haunt Sherman's iconography," functioning as a parody of different voyeurisms. Others question whether this confrontation with the male gaze and the feminine struggle was intentional, and whether such intentionality is important in understanding the feminist standpoint of her photography. Sherman herself has expressed uncertainty about the Untitled series' relationship with the male gaze, stating in a 1991 interview with David Brittain that she did not analyze it at the time as a feminist issue, though now she has mixed feelings about the series being too reminiscent of original pin-up images. Her work is also analyzed through the lens of abjection, with scholars like Hal Foster and Laura Mulvey interpreting her use of the grotesque in projects like Vomit Pictures as de-fetishizing the female body. Scholar Michele Meager interprets Sherman as having been "crowned a resistant celebrity" to feminist theory. In 2010, Sherman's nearly six-foot-tall chromogenic color print Untitled#153 (1985), featuring her as a mud-caked corpse, was sold by Phillips de Pury & Company for $2.7 million, near the $3 million high estimate. In 2011, a print of Untitled#96 sold for $3.89 million at Christie's, making it the most expensive photograph at that time. Sherman was represented by Metro Pictures for 40 years and by Sprüth Magers before moving to Hauser & Wirth in 2021. In April 2023, Phillips NY auctioned Untitled #546 (2010), sized 159 cm x 359 cm, for $355,600, well above estimate. Sherman's work is credited as a major influence on contemporary portrait photographers, including Ryan Trecartin, and extends to artists in other mediums such as painter Lisa Yuskavage, visual artist Jillian Mayer, and performance artist Tracey Ullman. In April 2014, actor and artist James Franco exhibited a series of photographs at the Pace Gallery called New Film Stills, restaging twenty-nine images from Sherman's Untitled Film Stills, which received mainly negative reviews, calling the appropriations 'sophomoric,' 'sexist,' and 'embarrassingly clueless.' Sherman lived with artist Robert Longo from 1974 to 1980, who also included her in his 'Men in the Cities' series. She married director Michel Auder in 1984, making her stepmother to Auder's daughter Alexandra and her half-sister Gaby Hoffmann; they divorced in 1999. She was in a five-year relationship with Paul Hasegawa-Overacker, creator of the documentary Guest of Cindy Sherman, and from 2007 to 2011 had a relationship with artist David Byrne. Between 1991 and 2005, Sherman lived in a fifth-floor co-op loft at 84 Mercer Street in Manhattan's Soho neighborhood, which she later sold to actor Hank Azaria. She bought two floors in a 10-story condo building overlooking the Hudson River in West Soho and currently uses one as her apartment and the other as her studio and office. For many years, she spent her summers in the Catskill Mountains. In 2000, she purchased songwriter Marvin Hamlisch's 4,200-square-foot house on 0.4 acre in Sag Harbor for $1.5 million. She later acquired a 19th-century home on a ten-acre waterfront property on Accabonac Harbor in East Hampton, New York. Sherman has expressed contempt for social media platforms, calling them "so vulgar," yet maintains an active Instagram account featuring her selfies. She serves on the artistic advisory committee of the Stephen Petronio Company in New York City and on the Artists Committee of the Americans for the Arts. Along with David Byrne, she was a member of Portugal's Estoril Film Festival jury in 2009. In 2012, she joined Yoko Ono and nearly 150 other artists in founding Artists Against Fracking. In 2023, Sherman served on the jury that selected Sarah Lucas as the first winner of the New Museum's $400,000 Hostetler/Wrigley Sculpture Award. Ahead of the 2024 United States presidential election, she was one of 165 leading contemporary artists who contributed pieces to Artists for Kamala, an online sale with all proceeds going directly to Kamala Harris' campaign. Her works are held in various collections.

text: Cynthia Morris Sherman, born on January 19, 1954, in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, is an American artist known primarily for her photographic self-portraits, in which she portrays herself in diverse roles and imagined characters. She is the youngest of five children, born to Dorothy and Charles Sherman; her father worked as an engineer at Grumman Aircraft, and her mother taught reading to children with learning difficulties. Sherman has described her mother as good to a fault and her father as strict and cruel, and she was raised Episcopalian. In 1972, she enrolled at Buffalo State University, where she majored in painting but soon began exploring ideas that would define her work, dressing in various characters using thrift-store clothing. Frustrated by the limitations of painting, she switched to photography, recalling that "there was nothing more to say [through painting]" and that she could instead focus on an idea. She met Robert Longo at college, who encouraged her to document her "dolling up" process, which became the foundation of her Untitled Film Stills series. In 1974, she co-founded Hallwalls with Longo, Charles Clough, and Nancy Dwyer as an arts center for diverse artists. She was exposed to contemporary art at institutions such as the Albright-Knox Art Gallery, SUNY Buffalo campuses, Media Studies Buffalo, the Center for Exploratory and Perceptual Arts, and Artpark. She qualified for the ITF Junior Masters in October 2018, winning her first major title and becoming the junior world No. 1 the following week on 29 October 2018. Burel was selected as an alternate in the French Fed Cup team for the 2018 first-round match against Belgium. In September, she reached her first final on the ITF Circuit in Clermont-Ferrand, losing to Lesley Kerkhove. She was a wildcard entrant at the Australian Open, where she lost in the first round to Carla Suárez Navarro. In March, she received a wildcard into the Lyon Open but lost in the first round to Jil Teichmann. In September at Strasbourg, she defeated Kateryna Bondarenko before losing to Zhang Shuai in the second round. At the French Open, she entered as a wildcard, defeated Arantxa Rus in the first round and Kaja Juvan to reach the third round—becoming the youngest Frenchwoman since 18-year-old Alizé Cornet achieved the same in 2008—before losing to Zhang Shuai for the second consecutive tournament. She qualified for the Australian Open again, losing to Alison Van Uytvanck in the first round. Burel made her top 200 debut on 8 March 2021, rising 37 positions to world No. 181 after reaching the quarterfinals in Lyon. She qualified for Wimbledon, making her first main draw appearance at the grass-court Grand Slam, defeating Ellen Perez before losing in the second round to Kaja Juvan. Burel reached her first WTA Tour final at the Ladies Open Lausanne, losing to Tamara Zidanšek, and achieved her top 100 debut at world No. 98 on 19 July 2021. She made her WTA 1000 debut at the Canadian Open as a qualifier, losing to 13th seed Ons Jabeur in the first round. Burel reached a new career-high WTA singles ranking of No. 74 on 21 February 2022 and recorded her first WTA 1000 win at the Miami Open against qualifier Magdalena Fręch, though she lost to 28th seed Petra Kvitová in the second round. She qualified for the US Open, reaching the third round by defeating 25th seed Elena Rybakina and Alison Van Uytvanck, before losing to sixth seed Aryna Sabalenka. Burel qualified for the Australian Open again, defeating wildcard Talia Gibson in the first round, her first win at this major. In April, she qualified for the WTA 1000 Madrid Open, losing to Camila Osorio in the first round and then to 20th seed Barbora Krejčíková in the second round. She reached the final at the Ladies Open Lausanne, losing to Elisabetta Cocciaretto. Burel won her first WTA 125 title at the Open Angers Arena Loire in December, defeating compatriot Chloé Paquet in three sets. At the Australian Open, she reached the third round for the first time at this major, defeating Aleksandra Krunić and fifth seed Jessica Pegula, her first top-10 win, before losing to Océane Dodin, which led to a new career-high singles ranking of world No. 44, reaching the top 50 for the first time on 5 February 2024. At the Upper Austria Ladies Linz, she reached the quarterfinals, defeating Sinja Kraus and Kateřina Siniaková, before losing to third seed Donna Vekić. At the upgraded WTA 500 in Strasbourg, she reached the quarterfinals, defeating wildcard Karolina Plíšková and seventh seed and defending champion Elina Svitolina, her second career top-20 win, before losing to third seed Danielle Collins. Burel recorded a first-round win over Eva Lys at Wimbledon, losing her next match to qualifier Sonay Kartal. text: Clive John Derby-Lewis (22 January 1936 – 3 November 2016) was a South African politician who initially joined the National Party and later served in the Conservative Party after its split from the National Party in 1982 due to a softening of apartheid policies. He served as a town councillor for Bedfordview (1972–1977), Deputy Mayor (1973–1974), and Mayor (1974–1975), and was made a Freeman of the Johannesburg Mini-Council. He represented Edenvale, Gauteng, on the Transvaal Provincial Council (1972–1981), where he was the National Party spokesman for Education and Hospital Services, and served on various boards including hospitals, primary and high schools, and a school for physically challenged children. He was a founder member of the Conservative Party, serving on its General Council, Parliamentary Caucus, and Transvaal Party Council, including its Information and Financial Committee. After losing his seat in the 1989 election, he was appointed to the State President's Council, where he served on the Economic Affairs and Amenities Committees. He visited London twice as part of a Conservative Party delegation, including in June 1989, and joined the Western Goals Institute as an honorary Vice-President, participating in the 22nd World Anti-Communist League Conference in Brussels in July 1990. Derby-Lewis was known for racially inflammatory remarks, such as claiming in Parliament in 1989 that "If AIDS stops Black population growth it will be like Father Christmas" and remarking "What a pity" about a black man on a runway, which he later apologised for. He was described as a "right-wing extremist" by The Daily Telegraph and as a "rabid racist" by journalist John Carlin. In October 1993, he was convicted of conspiracy to murder Chris Hani, the leader of the South African Communist Party, and sentenced to death, a sentence later reduced to life imprisonment when capital punishment was abolished in 1995. He confessed to his role in the assassination during his amnesty application to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, stating it was encouraged or sanctioned by senior Conservative Party leaders and that he acted "in defence of my people, who were threatened with a Communist take-over," citing his Christian faith in the Afrikaanse Protestant Church as central to his actions. His amnesty application was denied in April 1999, and in 2000, the Cape High Court dismissed an appeal to overturn the decision. Derby-Lewis applied for parole in June 2010, citing his age over 70 and having served more than 15 years, and was denied medical parole in 2011, 2013, and 2015. His medical parole was granted on 29 May 2015 by a judge, and he was released in June 2015 after serving 22 years due to terminal lung cancer. He died from the disease on 3 November 2016. Born in Cape Town, Derby-Lewis had German and Scots ancestry and grew up in Kimberley, being educated at the then-Christian Brothers' College. He worked as a chartered accountant, served as an extraordinary minister of Holy Communion at Blessed Sacrament Church in Johannesburg before leaving the Catholic Church in the early 1980s, and later joined the Afrikaanse Protestantse Kerk, a staunch supporter of apartheid. He spent nineteen years as a volunteer in the South African Citizen Force and became the youngest ever commanding officer of the Witwatersrand Rifles Regiment, affiliated with the Cameronians, earning the John Chard Medal for meritorious service. He married Gaye Derby-Lewis, a former nun from Australia, in 1986, which was his second marriage, and had three children from his first marriage. He was the only member of the Conservative Party Parliamentary Caucus to have served in all four levels of government in South Africa. During his time in Parliament, he was opposed by the Progressive Federal Party, and in March 1988, opposition leader Harry Schwarz called him the "biggest racist in Parliament." He was also a member of the Standing Committees on Provincial Affairs of Natal and Trade and Commerce, and served as Chief Spokesman on Economic Affairs, Technology and Mineral Affairs when the Conservative Party became the Official Opposition. A list of senior ANC and South African Communist Party figures, allegedly developed by Arthur Kemp and including Nelson Mandela and Joe Slovo, was reportedly used in the planning of Hani's assassination. Derby-Lewis had abetted Janusz Waluś, a Polish immigrant, by delivering him the gun used in the assassination on 10 April 1993. text: Cléo Hamon, born on 25 November 2001 in Cormeilles-en-Parisis, France, is a French pair skater. With her former partner Denys Strekalin, she is a two-time French national champion (2020, 2021), a 2018 Volvo Open Cup champion, and has competed in the final segment at three World Junior Championships (2017–2019). Her brother, Axel, is a triathlete. Hamon began learning to skate in 2006 and competed in ladies' singles, winning silver in the advanced novice category at the Rooster Cup in April 2016 and placing 13th at the Golden Bear of Zagreb in October 2016. In the 2014–2015 season, she partnered with Xavier Vauclin and became the French national novice champions in March 2015. She also skated with Brice Panizzi. In August 2016, Hamon teamed up with Ukraine's Denys Strekalin to compete for France in pairs, coached by Mehdi Bouzzine in Courbevoie. They made their international debut in February 2017, placing seventh in junior pairs at the Bavarian Open, and finished fourteenth at the 2017 World Junior Championships in Taipei, Taiwan. In September 2017, they debuted on the ISU Junior Grand Prix (JGP) series, placing eighth in Riga, Latvia. In December, they won silver at the French Championships behind Lola Esbrat / Andrei Novoselov. At the 2018 World Junior Championships in Sofia, Bulgaria, they finished eleventh. Competing in the 2018 JGP series, they placed sixth in Linz, Austria, and fifth in Ostrava, Czech Republic. They won gold at the Volvo Open Cup in November 2018. At the 2019 World Junior Championships in Zagreb, Croatia, they finished ninth. After placing eighth at the 2019 JGP United States, they debuted on the senior Challenger series with a seventh-place finish at the 2019 CS Finlandia Trophy, placing tenth at the 2019 CS Warsaw Cup, and ninth at their first European Championships. Hamon/Strekalin won the French senior national title for the first time due to the absence of James/Cipres and finished the season at the 2020 World Junior Championships, placing fifth. They were scheduled to participate in the 2020 World Championships in Montreal, which would have been their senior World debut, but the event was canceled due to the COVID-19 pandemic. With the pandemic ongoing, they began the new season at the 2020 CS Nebelhorn Trophy, where only pairs training in Europe competed; they were fourth after the short program and, after the top-ranked Hase/Seegert withdrew, placed third in the free and won the bronze medal. They were scheduled to make their Grand Prix debut at the 2020 Internationaux de France, but the event was canceled due to the pandemic. In February, they won their second straight National title. Later that month, they placed fifth at the International Challenge Cup. On March 1, they were named to the team for the 2021 World Championships, where they placed twentieth in their World Championship debut. They finished the season at the 2021 World Team Trophy, where they finished fifth in both segments and Team France finished in fifth place overall. They began the season at the 2021 Lombardia Trophy, where they finished in fourth place. They were originally scheduled to compete at the Nebelhorn Trophy, where the final Olympics spots would be decided, but were later replaced by Coline Keriven / Noël-Antoine Pierre. It was later announced that Hamon would be taking a break from figure skating due to health issues from burnout, which was the reason for their replacement at the Nebelhorn Trophy. text: Youna Kang[4][5] (born 27 February 1990), known online as CodeMiko and alias The Technician, is a South Korean-American Twitch streamer and YouTuber. She is best known for her live streams on Twitch, where she interviews other streamers, content creators, and internet personalities as her virtual persona CodeMiko,[6] and for advancing interactivity in VTuber technology.[7] Kang created the CodeMiko persona using Unreal Engine, a motion capture suit from Xsens, motion capture gloves from Manus VR, and a facial tracking helmet from MOCAP Design.[a][b][7] The avatar consists of 36,000 polygons, modeled in Autodesk Maya and textured using Adobe Substance. Originally developed alone, the project is now managed by a team including an engineer, an artist / animator / rigger,[8] a publicist, a personal assistant, and a manager.[9] Kang now leads development efforts in broadcasting and idea generation, focusing on introducing new standards of interactivity with her audience.[8] CodeMiko's virtual environment is quasi-interactive, allowing viewers to influence the avatar and surroundings through live chat or donations.[7] Kang conceived the idea for CodeMiko while working at Nickelodeon.[8] After being laid off due to the COVID-19 pandemic,[9] she transitioned to full-time streaming.[8] Early earnings were around $300 per month, insufficient to cover rent,[8] and she incurred over $20,000 in debt to purchase the necessary equipment, including the Xsens Mo-cap suit,[10] which she has credited as pivotal to her success despite poor risk management.[10][9] Since the project's success, she can now afford a comfortable living.[9] Her streaming breakthrough occurred in 2021, following a viral tweet on Twitter[11] and going viral on r/LiveStreamFails on Reddit.[10] The CodeMiko avatar has an in-universe backstory as a video game character without a game, who always wanted to be in a mainstream video game but failed due to her 'Glitch'—a narrative arc similar to Vanellope von Schweetz from Wreck-It Ralph. She was forced into minor roles, like a bush in The Last of Us, mirroring the struggles of a Hollywood actress seeking any role in a film, and for her, any video game.[10] She eventually found her place in Kang’s Unreal Engine project, becoming a Twitch streamer and currently roaming various game worlds, including the world of dead memes and The Sims. The avatar is aware of the Technician and frequently breaks the fourth wall, both indirectly through cross-over interviews such as CodeMiko interviewing The Technician,[13] and directly via augmented reality.[14] The character's "glitchiness" is expressed through occasional transitions into her evil alter ego, "Glitch," who replaces her pink-haired avatar with a semi-transparent, Matrix-inspired digital rain avatar and speaks with a deeper, hoarser voice via a voice changer, often being profane and offensive. It was previously believed that CodeMiko was initially released under the name 'mikoglitch',[15] but in a VOD,[16] Youna clarified this was false and explained that 'mikoglitch' was created to circumvent a temporary shadow ban on her 'CodeMiko' channel. The interview format has been likened to the 1990s animated parody show Space Ghost Coast to Coast.[8] Kang described Glitch as "kind of stupid, unfiltered, and not afraid to say whatever is on her mind or what she sees."[8] In 2021, CodeMiko participated in PogChamps 3, placing last with four losses and zero wins, alongside streamer Myth,[17] and was coached by WGM Anna Rudolf[18] and Andrea Botez.[19] Kang developed "TOS PTSD" after unintentionally violating Twitch's terms of service, resulting in bans, leading to economic anxiety and seeking help from psychiatrist Alok Kanojia on stream.[8][20] She expressed concern about Twitch's proposed "Brand Safety Score" system, fearing her X-rated humor might make her content unsuitable for advertisers and threaten her income, though she later noted her concerns lessened due to brand sponsorships.[22][9] The project has received positive reception, with Kotaku calling CodeMiko "The Future Of Streaming"[8] and Designboom stating she is "Revolutionizing the digital space."[7] The Financial Times reported her content as signaling "The next frontier of digital entertainment",[12] and Quartz described her as "The talk show host of the future."[23] The Verge noted she is "reshaping the Twitch landscape in her image."[10] The project has also attracted interest from producers of sexually explicit content.[12]

text: The Codex Arundel (British Library Arundel MS 263) is a bound collection of pages of notes written by Leonardo da Vinci, primarily between 1480 and 1518, and spans a 40-year period from 1478 to 1518. It consists of 283 paper leaves of various sizes, most measuring around 22 cm × 16 cm, with only a few being blank; two folios, 100 and 101, were incorrectly numbered twice. The codex contains short treatises, notes, and drawings on diverse subjects such as mechanics and the flight of birds, reflecting Leonardo's practice of using a single folio sheet for each subject, arranged as a cohesive treatise across both sides of the pages. Later book binders cut these folios into individual pages and stacked them, disrupting the original structure and creating a seemingly random arrangement. The manuscript is similar in format to the Codex Leicester, which also compiles notes, diagrams, and sketches, and is recognized as second in importance to the Codex Atlanticus. Written in Italy during the late 15th and early 16th centuries, most of the pages date from 1480 to 1518. The manuscript was acquired in the early 17th century by Thomas Howard, 2nd Earl of Arundel (1585–1646), and later presented to the Royal Society in 1667 by his grandson, Henry Howard, 6th Duke of Norfolk (1628–1684). It was first catalogued in 1681 by William Perry as a scientific and mathematical notebook. In 1831, the British Museum purchased it along with 549 other Arundel manuscripts (half of Arundel's collection) from the Royal Society; it was catalogued by the British Museum in 1834 and remained in the British Library as MS Arundel 263 after the library separated from the British Museum in 1973. The most recent facsimile was published in 1998, and on 30 January 2007, it was digitized along with the Codex Leicester as part of the British Library's "Turning the Pages" project and made available in the 2.0 format, reuniting the two Leonardo notebooks online.

text: The Coppa Italia Serie C (Italian: Serie C Italian Cup), previously known as Coppa Italia Lega Pro, is a straight knockout competition featuring teams from Serie C in Italian football, first held in 1972. The tournament consists of six rounds and starts in August with the first set, involving 56 of the 60 participating teams. The remaining four teams, which also compete in the Coppa Italia, join the competition during the second set. All matches are played as single legs, except for the semi-finals and the final. In the event of a tie—whether after a single leg or on aggregate—extra time is played, and if necessary, a penalty shootout determines the winner. In addition to receiving the trophy, the winning team qualifies for the next edition of the Coppa Italia and for the third round of Serie C promotion play-offs. If the winning team's spot is not available, it is awarded to the runners-up, or, as a secondary option, to the 4th-placed team in the same group as the winners.

text: Cornelia Ann Parker CBE RA (born 14 July 1956) is an English visual artist renowned for her sculpture and installation art. Born in Cheshire, England, her early life, marked by a mentally fragile mother and a violent father, significantly influenced her work. Her German mother served as a nurse in the Luftwaffe during the Second World War, and her British grandfather fought in the Battle of the Somme during the First World War. Parker studied at the Gloucestershire College of Art and Design (1974–1975) and Wolverhampton Polytechnic (1975–1978), earning her MFA from Reading University in 1982. She received honorary doctorates from the University of Wolverhampton (2000), the University of Birmingham (2005), the University of Gloucestershire (2008), and the University of Manchester (2017). In 1997, she was shortlisted for the Turner Prize alongside Christine Borland, Angela Bulloch, and Gillian Wearing, who won. She served as Honorary Professor at the University of Manchester from 2015 to 2018 and as Visiting Fellow at Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford from 2016 to 2019, and was appointed Honorary Fellow at Trinity Hall, Cambridge in 2020. Her first solo museum exhibition was at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston in 2000; a survey exhibition followed at MCA Sydney in 2019, and a major retrospective opened at Tate Britain in May 2022. Parker has one daughter, Lily, with her former husband Jeff McMillan, and lives and works in London. She is best known for large-scale installations such as Cold Dark Matter: An Exploded View (1991), first shown at the Chisenhale Gallery in Bow, East London, where she had a garden shed blown up by the British Army and suspended its fragments, with a central light casting dramatic shadows on the walls; this inspired an orchestral composition by Joo Yeon Sir. In 1997, she exhibited Mass (Colder Darker Matter), suspending charred remains of a church struck by lightning in Texas; eight years later, she created Anti-Mass (2005) using charcoal from a black congregation church in Kentucky destroyed by arson. Hanging Fire (Suspected Arson) (1999) features charred remains of an actual suspected arson case. The Maybe (1995) at the Serpentine Gallery, London, was a performance piece conceived by Tilda Swinton, who lay apparently asleep in a vitrine; Parker collaborated to create an installation with glass cases containing relics such as Freud's couch pillow, Mrs. Simpson's ice skates, Charles Dickens' quill pen, and Queen Victoria's stocking; a version was later re-performed in Rome (1996) and MoMA, New York (2013). Avoided Object is an ongoing series developed in collaboration with institutions including the Royal Armouries, British Police Forces, Colt Firearms, and Madame Tussauds. Parker has intervened in historical artworks, such as exhibiting the backs of Turner paintings (Room for Margins, 1998) and wrapping Rodin's The Kiss with a mile of string (2003), titled The Distance (A Kiss With String Attached), as part of the 2003 Tate Triennial Days Like These; this piece was later re-staged at the Whitworth Art Gallery, Manchester (2015) and Tate Britain (2022). Subconscious of a Monument (2005) consists of dry soil fragments suspended from the ceiling, taken from beneath the Leaning Tower of Pisa to prevent collapse. These "avoided" objects have been transformed through burning, shooting, squashing, stretching, drawing, exploding, cutting, or being dropped from cliffs; Parker describes them as 'preempted' objects, like Embryo Firearms 1995, or non-objects such as cracks, creases, shadows, dust, or dirt, including The Negative of Whispers (1997), earplugs made from fluff gathered in the Whispering Gallery, St Paul's Cathedral. Another example is Pornographic Drawings (1997), made from ink derived from solvent dissolved from confiscated pornographic video tape by HM Customs and Excise. Parker states: "I resurrect things that have been killed off... My work is all about the potential of materials—even when it looks like they've lost all possibilities." In 2009, for Jupiter Artland, she created Nocturne: A Moon Landing, a firework display containing a lunar meteorite, making the moon "land on Jupiter"; the following year, she made Landscape with Gun and Tree, a nine-metre-tall cast iron and Corten steel shotgun leaning against a tree, inspired by Thomas Gainsborough's Mr and Mrs Andrews, using a facsimile of the gun owned by Robert Wilson, a founder of Jupiter Artland. For the 2011 Folkestone Triennial, she created The Folkestone Mermaid, a life-size, life-cast sculpture of Georgina Baker, a 38-year-old mother of two from Folkestone, celebrating womankind. To mark the 800th anniversary of Magna Carta, she created Magna Carta (An Embroidery) in 2015, a hand-embroidered version of the Wikipedia article on Magna Carta as it appeared on 15 June 2014, completed with embroiderers including members of the Embroiderers Guild, HM prisoners, Peers, MPs, judges, human rights lawyers, a US ambassador and his staff, and public figures such as Edward Snowden, Julian Assange, Jimmy Wales, Jarvis Cocker, and Doreen Lawrence. While the embroidery was on display at the British Library, Parker presented One More Time, a Terrace Wires commission for St Pancras International Station, London, co-presented by HS1 Ltd. and the Royal Academy of Arts. In 2016, she became the first female artist commissioned to create a new work for the Roof Garden of the Met in New York: Transitional Object (PsychoBarn), a scaled-down replica of the house from the 1960 Hitchcock film Psycho, constructed from a salvaged red barn. Parker curated the Found exhibition at The Foundling Museum in 2016, incorporating sixty-eight artists and contributing her own piece, A Little Drop of Gin, a limited-edition photogravure using a 1750s gin glass and droppings of gin, which earned her the Artist of the Year Apollo Award in 2016. She appeared in the BBC Four series What Do Artists Do All Day? (2013), the Brilliant Ideas series (May 2015), "Danger! Cornelia Parker" on BBC One (summer 2016), and Gaga for Dada (autumn 2016), and contributed to the BBC Four production Bricks! (21 September 2016). On 1 May 2017, she was chosen as the official election artist for the UK general election, the first woman to hold that role; she observed the campaign leading to the vote on 8 June and produced two films and 14 photographic works, previewed on BBC Newsnight on 2 February 2018 and made available online via the UK Parliament website prior to an exhibition in Westminster Hall. In 2017, she created a series of blackboard drawings with 5- to 10-year-old children from Torriano Primary School, asked to copy news headlines from UK and US newspapers, noting that at that age children have a barely formed view of the world and will be profoundly affected by political turmoil. In November 2019, she opened her first major retrospective in Australia at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney for the Tenth Sydney International Art Series. In May 2022, she exhibited 100 artworks at Tate Britain in her largest solo exhibition to date, including films such as Chomskian Abstract 2007, Made in Bethlehem 2012, War Machine 2015, American Gothic 2016, Left, Right & Centre 2017, Election Abstract 2018, Thatcher’s Finger 2018, and Flag 2022. Tabish Khan of Culture Whisper praised her work as accessible and playful yet intellectually rigorous. In May 2023, her photograph "Snap" was used as the cover artwork for Peter Gabriel's song "Four Kinds of Horses". In November 2024, her glass rendition of the chandelier from Van Eyck's The Arnolfini Portrait was suspended in the Procuratie Vecchie in St Mark's Square, Venice, as part of Murano Illumina il Mondo, the first time in living memory that artworks were displayed in the colonnade. In 2011, she curated Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain at the Whitechapel Gallery using works from the Government Art Collection arranged as a colour spectrum. For the 2014 Royal Academy Summer Exhibition, she curated the Black and White Room, featuring well-known artists she believed should become Royal Academicians. In 2016, during her Hogarth Fellowship at the Foundling Museum, she curated a group exhibition titled FOUND, presenting works from over sixty artists responding to the theme of "found". In 2010, she was elected to the Royal Academy of Arts and appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 2010 Birthday Honours. She received honorary doctorates in 2000, 2005, 2008, and 2017 from Wolverhampton, Birmingham, Gloucestershire, and Manchester respectively. She won the Artist of the Year Apollo Award in 2016, with shortlisted artists including Carmen Herrera, David Hockney, Ragnar Kjartansson, Jannis Kounellis, and Helen Marten. In politics, prior to the 2015 general election, she endorsed Caroline Lucas of the Green Party, and in 2024 she participated in a plea to end the Gaza genocide. She was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 2022 Birthday Honours for services to the arts.
