text: The series champion of Countdown receives the Richard Whiteley Memorial Trophy in memory of the show's original presenter. Runner-up prizes in the finals have increased over the years from a £100 book voucher to £250, then to £500, and finally to £1,000, with beginning in Series 68, the runner-up wins a laptop. The first episode of Countdown was repeated on 1 October 2007 on More4 and on 2 November 2007 on Channel 4 as part of Channel 4 at 25, a celebration of its 25th birthday. On 2 November 2007, Countdown aired a special 'birthday episode' to mark its 25th anniversary, featuring 2006 winner Conor Travers and 2002 winner Chris Wills as players, with VIP guests selecting the letters and numbers; guests included Gordon Brown, Amir Khan, and Richard Attenborough. A statement from the French TV network France Télévisions was read by Carol Vorderman to commend Channel 4 on Countdown's success. On 26 March 2010, Queen Elizabeth II congratulated Countdown for reaching 5,000 episodes, and on 5 September 2014, the programme received a Guinness World Record at the end of its 6,000th show for being the longest-running television programme of its kind during Series 71. Countdown has occupied a daytime broadcast slot since its inception in a 30-minute format, and since 2001, episodes last around 45 minutes including advertising breaks. During normal series, the winner of each game returns for the next day's show; a player who wins eight games is declared an "octochamp" and retires. At the end of each series, the eight best players—ranked first by number of wins and then by total score to break ties—are invited back for the series finals, where they compete in a knockout tournament seeded so that the first plays the eighth, the second plays the seventh, and so on. The winner of the knockout, culminating in the Grand Final, becomes the series champion. Each series lasts approximately six months with about 125 episodes. Approximately every four series, a Champion of Champions tournament occurs, inviting sixteen of the best players since the previous championship, selected by producer Damian Eadie, typically including series winners and other notable contestants. Series 33 was designated a "Supreme Championship," in which 56 of the best contestants from all prior series participated in a knockout tournament, with Series 10 champion Harvey Freeman declared Supreme Champion after defeating Allan Saldanha in the final. There are also occasional special episodes featuring past contestants in themed matches, such as David Acton and Kenneth Michie returning for a rematch of their Series 31 final, and brothers Sanjay and Sandeep Mazumder playing against each other on 20 December 2004. Since the shift to 45-minute episodes, the game is divided into three sections with advertising breaks. The first section includes two letters rounds and one numbers round; the second includes two letters rounds and one numbers round, followed by the Dictionary Corner anecdote, then two further letters rounds and one numbers round; the third section includes two letters rounds, Susie Dent's "Origins of Words" feature since September 2007, two further letters rounds, one numbers round, and a final "Conundrum" puzzle. Contestants swap control after every round, so each has five letters rounds and two numbers rounds. Since Series 46 in 2001, the host poses a "Teatime Teaser" at the end of the first two sections, giving a set of short words and a cryptic clue to a single word that can be anagrammed from them, with the solution revealed at the start of the next section; the anagram length has varied between seven and nine letters. The contestant in control chooses between two stacks of face-down letter tiles—one with vowels (A-E-I-O-U) and one with consonants—and the assistant reveals the top tile, repeating this nine times to form a nine-letter group with at least three vowels and four consonants. Contestants have 30 seconds to form the longest valid single word using the letters, with no letter used more than it appears; letter frequencies are weighted according to natural English usage, similar to Scrabble, and are periodically altered by producers. The two stacks are not replenished between rounds. Both contestants write down their words; after time runs out, the host asks for declared word lengths, starting with the contestant who chose the letters. If one has not written their word, they must state this; if both declare the same length, the one who chose the letters must give their word first to prevent cheating. If both state they have not written their words, the host allows a moment to do so, typically edited out. The contestant with the longer valid word scores one point per letter or 18 points if all nine are used. If the words are identical or of the same length, both score. If a contestant is visually impaired, Dictionary Corner verifies the word. Inaccurate declarations of word length result in zero points, even if the word is valid. Dictionary Corner reveals the longest and any unusual words formed from the letters at the end of each round. Most words in the Oxford Dictionary of English are valid, as are accepted forms not explicitly listed. Words not allowed include those that are not in the dictionary or not in accepted forms. The contestant in control selects six of 24 shuffled number tiles—two each of numbers 1 to 10 (small numbers) and four large numbers (25, 50, 75, 100)—and decides how many large numbers to use, after which the tiles are randomly drawn and placed on the board. A random three-digit target from 100 to 999 is generated by "CECIL" (Countdown's Electronic Calculator In Leeds). Contestants have 30 seconds to find a sequence of calculations using the numbers and basic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division), not using any number more than it appears, and only exact division is allowed; fractions and negative numbers are not permitted. Both contestants must declare their results, and if both declare the same result and have not written their calculations down, the one who made the selection goes first. The contestant whose result is closer to the target scores points: ten for exact match, seven for within one to five, five for within six to ten; no points if more than ten away, or if calculations are flawed, too slow, or not written down. Both score if they reach the same result or are equally close. If neither reaches the target exactly, the assistant attempts a solution. Some games have multiple exact solutions; for example, 7 × (75 + 50 + 2 – 8 – 3) = 812. Not all games are solvable, especially when six small numbers are chosen and the target is large. Selecting one large and five small numbers is the most common choice, though two large numbers offer the best chance of an exact solution; selections with zero or four large numbers are generally considered hardest. The 24 tiles are laid out in four rows, with the top row containing only the large numbers; the contestant may specify how many tiles to draw from each row or simply state how many large and small numbers to use, with the assistant drawing them randomly. Numbers are usually placed from right to left, starting with small ones, though sometimes in scrambled order. On rare occasions, the contestant makes no choice, and the assistant selects the tiles. Unlike the letters round, the number tiles are fully replenished after each numbers round. A special edition on 15 March 2010 for previous champions Kirk Bevins and Chris Davies used instead of the four large numbers, the numbers 12, 37, and two unrevealed numbers. In a further special broadcast on 16 August 2010 between Series 59 finalists Charlie Reams and Junaid Mubeen, the other two numbers were revealed as 62 and 87. The final round is the Countdown Conundrum, where contestants are shown a combination of two or three words totaling nine letters and must form a single word using all letters in 30 seconds, buzzing in to respond (a bell for the champion, a buzzer for the challenger). Each contestant is allowed only one guess; the first to answer correctly scores 10 points. If a contestant buzzes in and either responds incorrectly or fails to respond, they are frozen out and the remaining time is given to the opponent. If neither solves it, the presenter asks the audience if anyone knows the answer and chooses someone to call it out (this practice was temporarily stopped in 2009 due to camera angle issues after a studio change). The Conundrum is intended to have one solution, though on occasion more than one valid word is found (e.g., MISSATTEE can become ESTIMATES or STEAMIEST), and any such result is accepted. On rare occasions, the Conundrum is presented as a nine-letter word to be anagrammed into another (e.g., SMARTENED becoming TRADESMEN). If the contestants' scores are within ten points going into the Conundrum, it is called a "Crucial Countdown Conundrum"; since ten points are at stake, solving it will either win the game or force a tiebreaker. If scores are tied after the Conundrum, additional Conundrums are played until the tie is broken. There have been several instances with two Conundrums to decide the winner, but only a handful of episodes required three, and there have been rare cases requiring even more, though not all such episodes are included in the broadcast. The rules of Countdown are derived from Des chiffres et des lettres, with the main difference being round length—DCedL's number rounds are 45 seconds, Countdown's are 30 seconds. DCedL also features "duels" with short tasks like mental arithmetic, forming themed words, or spelling correctly. Other differences include a different scoring system (9 points for exact solution, 6 for closest in DCedL) and a different proportion of letters to numbers rounds (10 to 4 in Countdown, 8 to 4 in DCedL). The pilot episode had different rules: only eight letters were selected per letters round; if two contestants offered a word of the same length or equally close solution in a numbers game, only the contestant who selected the round received points; five points were awarded for an exact numbers solution, three for within five, and one point for the closer solution regardless of distance. The style and colour scheme of the set have changed many times, and the show moved to Manchester after over 25 years in Leeds, but the clock has always been the centrepiece, and the clock music composed by Alan Hawkshaw remains a well-recognized feature. Executive producer John Meade commissioned Hawkshaw to revise the music for extra intensity at the start of Series 31 in January 1996, but after hundreds of viewer complaints, the original tune was reinstated after just 12 shows. The original set, known as the Pastel set, was used from 1982 until Series 17 in early 1989. A brown wooden set was introduced in Series 18 in July 1989 but remained in use for less than two years. Series 22 in July 1991 introduced the familiar "Wings" set in red, used until 1995. Series 31 in January 1996 changed the colour scheme to purple, then to tangerine at the end of 1999 with updated score and CECIL displays. In January 2003, the set was updated to a pink and purple striped theme with the letters and numbers boards on separate islands. In January 2009, a new numerical blue theme was introduced with the boards on opposite sides of a single display stand. New modern displays for scores and numbers came in January 2013, and a slight redesign occurred in July 2017 while retaining the blue background used up to the most recent series. The original clock was used until September 2013, when it was replaced. Until the end of Series 21, if contestants had equal scores after the first conundrum, the match was declared a draw and both returned for the next show. A significant format change occurred in September 2001, when the show expanded from nine rounds and 30 minutes to the current fifteen rounds and 45 minutes. The older format was split into two halves, each with three letters and one numbers game, plus a conundrum at the end of the second half. Under the old format, Grand Finals were extended to fourteen rounds, but now all shows use the fifteen-round format. The rules regarding valid words have changed over time; American spelling was allowed until 2002, and more unspecified inflections were assumed valid. In September 2007, Susie Dent began the "Origin of Words" feature, which follows the eighth letters round, partway through the third section of each episode; it was omitted during her maternity leave and reinstated upon her return. When the 15-round format was first introduced in September 2001, the round composition differed from today's: each of the first two sections had four letters rounds and one numbers round, and the third section had three letters rounds, one numbers round, and the conundrum. This created an imbalance, with one contestant making letters rounds six times and choosing numbers only once, while the other made letters five times and numbers twice. Dictionary Corner's guest spot was immediately before the first advertising break, and Susie Dent's Origin of Words spot preceded the second numbers game before the second break. The change to the current format was implemented on 25 March 2013, three weeks into the second section of Series 68, to comply with Channel 4's decision to increase advertising and alter its timing, reducing the actual show length from 36 to 35 minutes. Since its debut in 1982, Countdown has had more than 8,600 televised episodes and 92 complete series, and there have been sixteen Champion of Champions tournaments, the most recent in January 2023. Several of the programme's most successful contestants have received national media coverage; teenager Julian Fell set a record score of 146 in December 2002. In 2006, 14-year-old Conor Travers became the youngest series champion in the show's history, and 11-year-old Kai Laddiman became the youngest octochamp in 20 years. Conor Travers went on to win the 30th Anniversary edition.

text: Countdown is a British game show featuring word and mathematical tasks that began airing on 2 November 1982 and is broadcast on Channel 4. It was the first programme to be broadcast on Channel 4 and has aired 92 series since its debut, with over 8,000 episodes, making it one of Britain's longest-running game shows. The original French version, Des chiffres et des lettres (Numbers & Letters), ran on French television from 1965 until 2024. Each episode features two contestants competing in three game types: a ten-letter round where they attempt to form the longest word from nine randomly selected letters, a four numbers round in which they use arithmetic to reach a random target from six numbers, and a conundrum, a buzzer round to solve a nine-letter anagram. During series heats, the winning contestant returns the next day until they either lose or retire with eight wins as an undefeated "Octochamp"; the best eight contestants are invited to the series finals, decided in knockout format. Contestants of exceptional skill have received national media coverage, and the show is widely recognised and parodied in British culture. Produced by Yorkshire Television, Countdown was recorded at The Leeds Studios for 27 years before moving to Granada Studios in 2009 and then to Dock10 in Greater Manchester in 2013 following the development of MediaCityUK. Richard Whiteley presented the show for 23 years until his death on 26 June 2005; after his death, Des Lynam presented from October 2005 to December 2006, Des O'Connor from January 2007 to December 2008, Jeff Stelling from January 2009 to December 2011, and Nick Hewer from January 2012 until his retirement in June 2021, with Colin Murray standing in for him during part of the COVID-19 pandemic. Anne Robinson presented from June 2021 to July 2022, after which Murray returned on 14 July as a stand-in host. On 25 July 2022, Les Dennis guest hosted from 4 to 15 August, followed by Jenny Eclair from 16 to 19 August after Murray tested positive for COVID-19. Guest hosts including Floella Benjamin, Richard Coles, Trevor McDonald (for a second time), and Moira Stuart hosted one week each during the show's 40th anniversary celebrations in 2022. Murray was named the permanent host in January 2023. In the early years, the show had multiple assistant presenters: Carol Vorderman, hired for Series 1 as "vital statistician," alternated with Dr Linda Barrett until Barrett left after Series 2; letters were initially placed by Cathy Hytner, then by Karen Loughlin in Series 14 (1987) and Lucy Summers in Series 17 (early 1989); numbers were handled by Beverley Isherwood, later taken over by Hytner mid-Series 3. From Series 18 (July 1989) onwards, Vorderman permanently handled both letters and numbers. After 26 years, she left in December 2008 (alongside O'Connor) and was replaced by Rachel Riley, who has held the role since January 2009. Dr Anne-Marie Imafidon stood in for Riley from December 2021 to March 2022, and Dr Tom Crawford, an Oxford and Cambridge lecturer, stood in for Riley for three weeks in early 2025, making his first appearance on 24 February as the show's first-ever male arithmetician. Susie Dent first appeared in June 1992 as a rotating lexicographer and became a recurring member in 2003; since 2005 she has been the sole lexicographer and has been credited as a co-presenter since January 2015, appearing in "Dictionary Corner" with a weekly celebrity guest. Notable past lexicographers who appeared in more than 100 episodes include Catherine Clarke, Damian Eadie, Alison Heard, Mark Nyman, Richard Samson, Julia Swannell, Della Thompson, Freda Thornton, and Yvonne Warburton. The show originated from the French format Des chiffres et des lettres, created by Armand Jammot, which debuted in September 1965 under the name Le Mot Le Plus Long (The Longest Word) before adding numbers in January 1972. Belgian record executive Marcel Stellman brought the format to Britain, proposing it to several networks. Yorkshire Television purchased the concept in 1981 and produced two non-televised pilot episodes under the title Calendar Countdown, aired in Yorkshire between April and June 1982. Richard Whiteley, who hosted the spin-off, earned the nickname "Twice Nightly Whiteley" due to his daily appearances on both Calendar and the spin-off. He was assisted by Cathy Hytner and Denise McFarland-Cruickshanks for letters and numbers, Robina Sharp for selecting numbers and operating a fruit machine for the target, and Angela Garbut as the vital statistician; Ted Moult, who appeared in the pilot episodes and throughout the regional series, was the first Dictionary Corner guest and only appeared in the first seven episodes. After an additional, unbroadcast pilot episode with a refined format, the show was bought by Channel 4, which launched in November 1982. The show was renamed Countdown, expanded its hosting team, and was initially commissioned for four times a week for seven weeks, but due to its success, it has continued to be recommissioned as of 2024. A proposed spin-off, Junior Countdown, hosted by Gyles Brandreth and Ted Moult, was abandoned after a flawed pilot. Countdown was the first programme broadcast by Channel 4 on 2 November 1982, with Whiteley opening with the line: "As the countdown to a brand new channel ends, a brand new Countdown begins." Production staff recruited additional hostesses through national newspaper ads, with clear emphasis on mathematical skill for number experts; Beverley Isherwood and Linda Barrett were hired to handle number and letter tile selection, and a lexicographer was required for Dictionary Corner to verify words and provide entertainment. The lexicographer role was traditionally filled by an Oxford University Press member or production staff member, with past guests including Nigel Rees, Jo Brand, Martin Jarvis, Richard Digance, Geoffrey Durham, Ken Bruce, Magnus Magnusson, Pam Ayres, Paul Zenon, Jenny Eclair, Al Murray, John Sergeant, and Gyles Brandreth. Over time, the additional hostesses were dropped, retaining Vorderman primarily for tile selection and calculation verification. The role of lexicographer rotated among over thirty individuals until January 2005, when Susie Dent was permanently appointed after her 1992 debut. On 26 June 2005, Richard Whiteley died after a failed heart operation; the episode scheduled for that day was postponed as a mark of respect, with no episode aired, and the remaining episodes were broadcast after his death, preceded by a tribute from Carol Vorderman. The show went into hiatus from 1 July to determine its next steps, with no repeats aired. In October 2005, Des Lynam took over as main presenter, having previously participated in Celebrity Countdown in April 1998; his tenure ended in December 2006 due to a demanding schedule, with viewers reacting angrily to a proposed move from Leeds to Worthing. In January 2007, Des O'Connor took over; during his tenure, Susie Dent went on maternity leave in 2007–2008, with Alison Heard temporarily replacing her until 6 February 2008. By July 2008, both O'Connor and Vorderman announced they would leave at the end of that year after Series 59; O'Connor left to focus on other projects, and Vorderman left after rejecting a 33% salary decrease and being offered a 90% cut, with her agent stating the show could survive without her. Media reports suggested Rory Bremner or Alexander Armstrong as possible successors, but both declined. Several prominent women, including Anthea Turner, Ulrika Jonsson, and Myleene Klass, were considered, but Channel 4 selected an unknown male or female arithmetician with "charm and charisma." When Lynam became presenter, the show drew an average of 1.7 million viewers daily, around half a million more than in Whiteley's final years; the Series 54 final on 26 May 2006 attracted 2.5 million viewers. Daily viewership had previously ranged from 3 to 4 million in its 16:15 slot, and a drop in viewership after scheduling changes led Labour MP Jonathan Shaw to propose returning the show to a later time. The show has since moved to 14:10 as of 2025. In November 2008, Jeff Stelling was confirmed as host, and Rachel Riley was confirmed as Vorderman's replacement. Stelling left in December 2011 due to football commitments with Sky Sports, and Nick Hewer was announced as his replacement, taking over on 9 January 2012. During the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic, Colin Murray filled in for Hewer during his isolation. Des O'Connor died on 14 November 2020 after a fall at home; the episode aired two days later was dedicated to his memory. On 7 December 2020, Hewer announced he would step down at the end of Series 83 in summer 2021, calling it a "privilege and a pleasure." On 15 February 2021, Anne Robinson, who first appeared in Dictionary Corner in 1987, was announced as Hewer's successor, beginning Series 84. Hewer's final episode aired on 25 June 2021. On 28 June 2021, Robinson became the show's first female host in its 39-year history. In May 2022, it was announced she would leave after one year, with Murray taking over for most of Series 86; she recorded 265 episodes, equivalent to two full series and the first three weeks of Series 86. The show quickly gained cult status in British television and maintains that image today, with its audience primarily consisting of students, homemakers, and pensioners due to its "teatime" broadcast slot and inclusive format. It has been one of Channel 4's most-watched programmes for over twenty years but has never won a major television award. Each episode awards the winner of the reigning champion (or the championship when two new contestants compete) a teapot styled to resemble the clock used in each round, introduced in December 1998 and custom-made, obtainable only by winning. Defeated contestants and retiring undefeated champions receive Countdown-themed merchandise. Initially, the series winner received a leather-bound copy of the twenty-volume Oxford English Dictionary, worth over £4,000; David Acton (Series 31 winner) opted for a CD-ROM version due to veganism and donated the price difference to charity. Between 2011 and 2021, the prize included ordinary hardback twenty-one-volume dictionaries, a laptop, and a lifetime subscription to Oxford Online (replaced by a MacBook Pro from Series 68); the physical dictionaries were discontinued after Series 83 as obsolete. Since Series 54 in 2006, the series champion also receives the Richard Whiteley Memorial Trophy. Runner-up prizes in finals increased from a £100 book voucher to £250, then £500, then £1,000, and from Series 68, the runner-up wins a laptop. The first episode was repeated on 1 October 2007 on More4 and on 2 November 2007 on Channel 4 as part of Channel 4 at 25, a 25th-anniversary celebration. On 2 November 2007, the show celebrated its 25th anniversary with a special 'birthday episode' featuring 2006 winner Conor Travers and 2002 winner Chris Wills; VIP guests selected the letters and numbers. Guests included Gordon Brown, Amir Khan, and Richard Attenborough. A statement from France Télévisions was read by Carol Vorderman to commend Channel 4 on the success of Countdown.

It is an erect, mostly glabrous shrub that grows to a height of 30 cm (10 in), with pinnate leaves measuring 10–30 mm (0.4–1 in) long and having between three and seven leaflets on a petiole 1–11 mm (0.039–0.433 in) long; the leaflets are 5–15 mm (0.20–0.59 in) long. text: Darwin is the core Unix-like operating system underlying macOS, iOS, watchOS, tvOS, iPadOS, audioOS, visionOS, and bridgeOS. It was initially released as an independent open-source operating system by Apple in 2000 and is composed of code derived from NeXTSTEP, FreeBSD, and other BSD operating systems, Mach, and other free software projects, as well as code developed by Apple. Darwin's unofficial mascot is Hexley the Platypus. It is mostly POSIX-compatible but has never been certified as compliant with any version of POSIX; however, starting with Leopard, macOS has been certified as compatible with the Single UNIX Specification version 3 (SUSv3). The heritage of Darwin traces back to Unix derivatives enhanced by NeXTSTEP (later known as OPENSTEP, from version 4.0 onward), first released in 1989. After Apple acquired NeXT in 1996, it announced it would base its next operating system on OPENSTEP, which evolved into Rhapsody in 1997, Mac OS X Server 1.0 in 1999, Mac OS X Public Beta in 2000, and Mac OS X 10.0 in 2001. In 1999, Apple announced the release of the Mach 2.5 microkernel, BSD Unix 4.4 OS, and Apache Web server components of Mac OS X Server. At that time, interim CEO Steve Jobs referenced British naturalist Charles Darwin by saying "because it's about evolution." In 2000, the core operating system components of Mac OS X were released as open-source software under the Apple Public Source License (APSL) as Darwin, while higher-level components like Cocoa and Carbon frameworks remained closed-source. Up to Darwin 8.0.1, released in April 2005, Apple provided a binary installer (as an ISO image) after each major Mac OS X release to allow installation of Darwin as a standalone operating system on PowerPC and Intel x86 systems; minor updates were distributed as separate packages. Darwin is now only available as source code, and as of January 2023, Apple no longer mentions Darwin by name on its Open Source website, publishing only an incomplete collection of open-source projects related to macOS and iOS. The kernel of Darwin is XNU, a hybrid kernel using Open Software Foundation Mach Kernel (OSFMK) 7.3 from the OSF, elements of FreeBSD (including the process model, network stack, and virtual file system), and an object-oriented device driver API called IOKit, providing the flexibility of a microkernel and the performance of a monolithic kernel. The last bootable full release of Darwin supported 32-bit and 64-bit Apple PowerPC systems and 32-bit Intel PCs. Darwin currently supports the 64-bit x86-64 variant of Intel x86 processors in Intel-based Macs and 64-bit ARM processors in the iPhone 5S and later, the 6th generation iPod Touch, the 5th generation iPad and later, the iPad Air family, the iPad Mini 2 and later, the iPad Pro family, the fourth generation and later Apple TVs, the HomePod family, and Macs with Apple silicon such as the 2020 Apple M1 Macs, as well as the Raspberry Pi 3B. An open-source port of the XNU kernel exists for Intel and AMD x86 platforms not officially supported by Apple, though it has not been updated since 2009, and another exists for ARM platforms, though it has not been updated since 2016. Older versions supported some or all of 32-bit PowerPC, 64-bit PowerPC, 32-bit x86, and 32-bit ARM. Darwin supports the POSIX API through its BSD lineage (largely FreeBSD userland), enabling many programs written for other UNIX-like systems to be compiled without source code changes. Darwin does not include key macOS components such as the Carbon and Cocoa APIs or the Quartz Compositor and Aqua user interface, so it cannot run Mac applications, though it does support lesser-known macOS features like mDNSResponder (a core component of Bonjour) and launchd (an advanced service management framework). In July 2003, Apple released Darwin under version 2.0 of the APSL, which the Free Software Foundation (FSF) qualifies as a free software license. The APSL is similar to AGPL and is incompatible with the GNU General Public License. Earlier versions of the APSL did not meet the FSF's definition of free software, though they met the Open Source Definition. A table of major Darwin releases with their dates and corresponding derivative operating system releases is provided, noting that OS releases may have been issued on different dates. The version jump from Darwin 1.4.1 to 5.1 with the release of Mac OS X v10.1.1 was designed to align Darwin with the Mac OS X version and build numbering system, inherited from NeXTSTEP. In macOS build numbering, each version has a unique beginning build number identifying the whole version (e.g., Mac OS X v10.0 started with build numbers beginning at 4, v10.1 began at 5). Build dates for Darwin versions are not publicly available; the command `uname -r` shows the Darwin version number (e.g., "20.3.0"), and `uname -v` shows the XNU build version string including the Darwin version number. The command `sw_vers` displays the corresponding ProductName ("macOS"), ProductVersion ("11.2.3"), and BuildVersion ("20D91"). Due to Darwin's free software nature, various projects have aimed to modify the system or use its components. Among these, DarwinBSD, OpenDarwin, and PureDarwin are considered "alternative Darwin distributions" akin to Linux distributions. OpenDarwin was a community-led operating system based on Darwin, founded in April 2002 by Apple and the Internet Systems Consortium, aiming to foster collaboration between Apple developers and the free software community. Apple benefited from incorporating OpenDarwin improvements into Darwin releases, and the community gained control over its own operating system for use in distributions like GNU-Darwin. On July 25, 2006, the OpenDarwin team announced the project's shutdown, citing that it had "become a mere hosting facility for Mac OS X related projects" and that efforts to create a standalone Darwin OS had failed. Contributing factors included the unavailability of sources, limited interaction with Apple, difficulty building and tracking sources, and lack of community interest. The last stable release was version 7.2.1, released on July 16, 2004. PureDarwin is a project to create a bootable operating system image from Apple's released Darwin source code. Since the closure of OpenDarwin and the release of bootable images from Darwin 8.x, creating a full operating system has become increasingly difficult due to many components becoming closed source. In 2015, PureDarwin released a preview based on Darwin 9 with an X11 GUI, followed by a command-line-only 17.4 Beta based on Darwin 17 in 2019. Other projects are categorized as "Darwin distributions" or alternative derivatives. Some projects re-implement parts of macOS APIs above the level of Darwin, but are not considered Darwin derivatives beyond the extent that such programs are derived from operating system application programming interfaces and constraints.

text: David Peter Robbins (12 August 1942 in Brooklyn – 4 September 2003 in Princeton) was an American mathematician. He is best known for introducing alternating sign matrices and for his work on generalizations of Heron's formula related to the area of polygons, leading to the naming of Robbins pentagons—cyclic pentagons with integer side lengths and areas—after him. Robbins grew up in Manhattan and attended the Fieldston School. He studied at Harvard, where his undergraduate advisor was Andrew Gleason, and later pursued graduate studies at MIT. After teaching at Fieldston during a hiatus, he completed his Ph.D. in 1970. He taught at MIT, Phillips Exeter Academy, Hamilton College, and Washington and Lee University. In 1980, he moved to Princeton, New Jersey, where he worked at the Institute for Defense Analyses Center for Communications Research until his death from pancreatic cancer. A symposium in his honor was held in June 2003, and the proceedings were published as a special issue of Advances in Applied Mathematics. In 2005, the Mathematical Association of America established the David P. Robbins Prize, awarded every three years to one or more researchers in algebra, combinatorics, or discrete mathematics; the first recipient in 2008 was Neil Sloane for his work on the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences. The American Mathematical Society also has a prize named after him, the David P. Robbins Prize (AMS), with the first winners being Samuel P. Ferguson and Thomas C. Hales for their work on the Kepler conjecture.

text: Davyd Whaley (December 6, 1967 – October 15, 2014) was an American abstract painter recognized for incorporating Jungian themes related to the subconscious in his artwork. Born in Bristol, Tennessee, in 1967, Whaley lived and worked in Los Angeles. He served as a United States Navy veteran for four years and had a twenty-year career as an electrical engineer before transitioning to painting. In 2004, he met television director Norman Buckley, with whom he married as soon as legally permitted in 2008, remaining married until Whaley's death on October 15, 2014, in Los Angeles. Whaley was primarily self-taught but studied painting at the Art Students League of New York from 2008 to 2011, working under mentors Ronnie Landfield and Larry Poons. His style is characterized by brilliant colors and a focus on Jungian themes, reflecting his interest in dream analysis and the subconscious. His paintings appeared on various television shows, including CSI: Crime Scene Investigation, Californication, and Pretty Little Liars. He relocated his studio from his home to the Santa Fe Art Colony in downtown Los Angeles. In 2016, the Davyd Whaley Foundation was established by his husband, Norman Buckley, to honor Whaley's legacy of service by awarding grants to artists. Whaley was a philanthropist who taught art to underprivileged individuals, counseled grieving families in hospitals, and taught terminally-ill and war-scarred children to paint. He was honored as Volunteer of the Year by the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors in 2012. His core goals—making art, purchasing art by others, helping people whenever possible, and growing in consciousness—formed the foundation's mission. A monograph of his work was published in 2016, featuring an essay titled "A Hero's Journey" by Peter Clothier.

text: Daya Ram Thapar (6 April 1894 – 15 December 1965) was an Indian Army medical officer and Director-General of the Indian Armed Forces Medical Services. Born into a prominent Punjabi family in Lahore, he received his early education there, including studies at Government College Lahore. He entered the University of Edinburgh in 1911 for medical studies, graduating with a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (M.B.Ch.B.) in 1916. He later obtained a diploma in tropical medicine and hygiene (DTM&H) from London and an M.D. from Edinburgh in 1930, with a thesis on ascariasis. While a student at Edinburgh, he organized the Scottish Wing of the Indian Volunteers' Ambulance Corps in 1914 following the outbreak of war, recruiting 120 Indian students to serve as dressers and interpreters. He was commissioned as a temporary lieutenant in the Indian Medical Service (IMS) on 25 March 1918, promoted to temporary captain on 25 March 1919, received a regular commission as a lieutenant on 14 March 1920, and was promoted to substantive captain on 25 March 1921. He was promoted to major on 25 September 1929, appointed staff captain (medical) on 1 July 1936, and promoted to lieutenant-colonel on 25 September 1937. On 14 October 1937, he was posted to Peshawar as second-in-command of a hospital and became the officiating Officer Commanding on 3 May 1938. He was posted to Rawalpindi on 15 June 1939 as Officer in Command of No. 1 Battalion Indian Hospital Corps. Assigned as Officer Commanding Indian Hospital Corps at Kirkee on 22 October 1942, he was promoted to acting colonel on 5 November 1942 and to temporary colonel on 5 May 1943 while serving as Commandant, Indian Army Medical Corps (IAMC) HQ at Pune. He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Indian Empire (CIE) in the 1946 Birthday Honours and had previously received an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1942 New Year Honours. His final appointment prior to Indian independence was as deputy director of Medical Services, Medical Department. He was promoted to substantive colonel on 1 October 1946 (with seniority from 25 September 1940). Following Indian independence in 1947, he was promoted to major general on 3 September. On 1 January 1951, he was promoted to lieutenant general and appointed Director-General of the Armed Forces Medical Services, with an ex-officio appointment as a member of the Medical Council of India. He retired in 1954 and served as Colonel Commandant of the Army Medical Corps until April 1956. He died in New Delhi in December 1965. Thapar was the son of Dewan Bahadur Kunj Behari Thapar OBE; his younger brother was General Pran Nath Thapar, the future Chief of Staff of the Indian Army. He was the father of journalist Romesh Thapar and the noted author and historian Romila Thapar.

text: Well casing acted as a flow conduit, possibly intersecting a naturally occurring fault, and then escaping at the surface some distance from the wellhead. If the substance released was oil from the subsurface, it could indicate an indefinite release of oil. The oil slick was comparable in size to naturally occurring oil seeps and was not large enough to pose an immediate threat to wildlife. The fundamental strategies for addressing the spill were containment, dispersal, and removal. In summer 2010, approximately 47,000 people and 7,000 vessels were involved in the response. By 3 October 2012, federal response costs reached $850 million, mostly reimbursed by BP. As of January 2013, 935 personnel were still involved, and by that time, cleanup had cost BP over $14 billion. It was estimated with plus-or-minus 10% uncertainty that 4.9 million barrels (780,000 m³) of oil was released from the well; 4.1 million barrels (650,000 m³) went into the Gulf. A report by the Department of the Interior and NOAA stated that "75% [of oil] has been cleaned up by Man or Mother Nature"; however, only about 25% of released oil was collected or removed, while about 75% remained in the environment in one form or another. In 2012, Markus Huettel, a benthic ecologist at Florida State University, maintained that while much of BP's oil was degraded or evaporated, at least 60% remains unaccounted for. In May 2010, a local native set up a network for people to volunteer in cleaning up beaches, offering boat use through the Vessels of Opportunity program; however, only a third of registered boats participated, leading to disappointment and prompting the formation of The Florida Key Environmental Coalition, which gained significant influence in the clean-up efforts. Containment booms stretching over 4,200,000 ft (1,300 km) were deployed, either to corral oil or protect ecologically sensitive areas like marshes, mangroves, shrimp/crab/oyster ranches; booms extend 18–48 in (0.46–1.22 m) above and below the water surface and were effective only in calm, slow-moving waters. Including one-time use sorbent booms, a total of 13,300,000 ft (4,100 km) of booms were deployed. Booms were criticized for washing up on shore, allowing oil to escape above or below, and being ineffective in waves over three to four feet (90–120 cm). The Louisiana barrier island plan was developed to protect Louisiana's coast but was criticized for expense and poor results, with critics alleging it was politically motivated with little scientific input. The EPA expressed concern that booms threatened wildlife. A group called Matter of Trust campaigned to encourage hair salons, dog groomers, and sheep farmers to donate hair, fur, and wool clippings stuffed in pantyhose or tights to contain oil near shores, a technique from the Exxon Valdez disaster. The spill was notable for the volume of Corexit oil dispersant used and for experimental application methods. Altogether, 1.84×10⁶ US gal (7,000 m³) of dispersants were used; 771,000 US gal (2,920 m³) were released at the wellhead. Subsea injection, never previously tried, was used due to the spill's unprecedented nature, with BP, USCG, and EPA jointly deciding on it. Over 400 sorties were flown to release the product. Although dispersant use was described as "the most effective and fast moving tool for minimizing shoreline impact," the approach continues to be investigated. A 2011 analysis by Earthjustice and Toxipedia showed the dispersant contained cancer-causing agents, hazardous toxins, and endocrine-disrupting chemicals. Environmental scientists expressed concerns that dispersants increased toxicity to sea turtles and bluefin tuna, especially when applied at the source, as they are carried by currents through the Gulf. According to BP and federal officials, dispersant use stopped after the cap was in place; however, marine toxicologist Riki Ott wrote in an open letter to the EPA that Corexit use continued after that date, and a GAP investigation stated that "a majority of GAP witnesses cited indications that Corexit was used after [July 2010]." A NALCO manual obtained by GAP stated that Corexit 9527 is an "eye and skin irritant" and may cause hemolysis, kidney or liver injury, central nervous system effects, nausea, vomiting, anesthetic or narcotic effects, advising not to get it in eyes, on skin, or on clothing, and to wear protective clothing. For Corexit 9500, the manual advised the same precautions and to avoid breathing vapor. According to FOIA requests, neither protective gear nor the manual were distributed to Gulf cleanup workers. Corexit EC9500A and EC9527A were the principal variants. These formulations are neither the least toxic nor the most effective among EPA-approved dispersants, but BP chose them because they were available the week of the rig explosion. On 19 May, the EPA gave BP 24 hours to choose less toxic alternatives from the National Contingency Plan Product Schedule and begin applying them within 72 hours of approval or provide a detailed reason why no approved products met the standards. On 20 May, BP determined that none of the alternative products met all three criteria of availability, non-toxicity, and effectiveness. On 24 May, EPA Administrator Lisa P. Jackson ordered EPA to evaluate alternatives and ordered BP to reduce dispersant use by 75%. BP reduced Corexit use from 25,689 to 23,250 US gal (97,240 to 88,010 L) per day, a 9% decline. On 2 August 2010, the EPA stated that dispersants did no more harm to the environment than the oil and that they stopped a large amount of oil from reaching the coast by breaking it down faster. However, some independent scientists and EPA experts continue to voice concerns. Underwater injection of Corexit into the leak may have created oil plumes discovered below the surface. Because the dispersants were applied at depth, much of the oil never rose to the surface. One plume was 22 mi (35 km) long, more than 1 mi (1,600 m) wide, and 650 ft (200 m) deep. Experts were most concerned about the slow breakdown of oil in cold, 40°F (4°C) water at depths of 3,000 ft (900 m). In late 2012, a study from Georgia Tech and Universidad Autonoma de Aguascalientes in Environmental Pollution reported that Corexit used during the BP oil spill increased the toxicity of the oil by 52 times. The scientists concluded that "mixing oil with dispersant increased toxicity to ecosystems" and made the Gulf oil spill worse. The three basic approaches for removing oil from water were combustion, offshore filtration, and collection for later processing. USCG reported recovering 33,000,000 US gal (120,000 m³) of tainted water, including 5,000,000 US gal (19,000 m³) of oil. BP reported recovering or flaring 826,800 bbl (131,450 m³). It is calculated that about 5% of leaked oil was burned at the surface and 3% was skimmed. On the most demanding day, 47,849 people were assigned and over 6,000 marine vessels, 82 helicopters, and 20 fixed-wing aircraft were involved. From April to mid-July 2010, 411 controlled in-situ fires remediated approximately 265,000 bbl (11.1 million US gal; 42,100 m³). The fires released small amounts of toxins, including cancer-causing dioxins. According to EPA's report, the released amount is not enough to pose an added cancer risk to workers and coastal residents, while a second research team concluded only a small added risk. Oil was collected using skimmers; in total, 2,063 various skimmers were used. For offshore, more than 60 open-water skimmers were deployed, including 12 purpose-built vehicles. EPA regulations prohibited skimmers that left more than 15 parts per million (ppm) of oil in the water. Many large-scale skimmers exceeded the limit. Due to Corexit use, the oil was too dispersed to collect, according to a spokesperson for shipowner TMT. In mid-June 2010, BP ordered 32 machines that separate oil and water, each capable of extracting up to 2,000 bbl/d (320 m³/d). After one week of testing, BP began proceeding, and by 28 June, had removed 890,000 bbl (141,000 m³). After the well was capped, shore cleanup became the main task. Two main types of affected coast were sandy beaches and marshes. On beaches, techniques included sifting sand, removing tar balls, and digging out tar mats manually or mechanically. For marshes, techniques such as vacuum and pumping, low-pressure flush, vegetation cutting, and bioremediation were used. Dispersants are said to facilitate microbial digestion of oil, but conflicting results have been reported. Mixing dispersants with oil at the wellhead would keep some oil below the surface, allowing microbes to digest it before it reached the surface. Risks included increased microbial activity reducing subsea oxygen levels, threatening fish and other animals. Several studies suggest microbes successfully consumed part of the oil. By mid-September, other research claimed microbes mainly digested natural gas rather than oil. David L. Valentine, a professor of microbial geochemistry at UC Santa Barbara, said the capability of microbes to break down the leaked oil had been greatly exaggerated. However, biogeochemist Chris Reddy said natural microorganisms were a major reason the oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico was not far worse. Genetically modified Alcanivorax borkumensis was added to waters to speed digestion. The delivery method of microbes to oil patches was proposed by the Russian Research and Development Institute of Ecology and the Sustainable Use of Natural Resources. On 18 May 2010, BP was designated the lead "Responsible Party" under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, granting operational authority to coordinate the response. The first video images were released on 12 May, and further images were released by members of Congress who had access through BP. During the spill response, at the request of the Coast Guard, the FAA implemented a 900 sq mi (2,300 km²) temporary flight restriction zone over the operations area to prevent civilian air traffic from interfering with response aircraft. All flights in the area were prohibited except those authorized by air traffic control, routine flights supporting offshore oil operations, federal, state, local, and military flights supporting response, and air ambulance and law enforcement operations. Exceptions were granted on a case-by-case basis based on safety, operational requirements, weather, and traffic volume. No flights, except those conducting aerial chemical dispersing operations or for landing and takeoff, were allowed below 1,000 m (3,300 ft). Despite restrictions, there were 800 to 1,000 flights per day. Local and federal authorities, citing BP's authority, denied press access to document the spill from the air, boats, or on the ground, blocking access to public areas. In some cases, photographers were granted access only with BP officials escorting them on BP-contracted boats and aircraft. In one example, the U.S. Coast Guard stopped Jean-Michel Cousteau's boat and allowed it to proceed only after being assured no journalists were on board. In another, a CBS News crew was denied access to oil-covered beaches and told, "This is BP's rules, not ours." Some members of Congress criticized the restrictions on journalist access. The FAA denied that BP employees or contractors made decisions on flights or access, stating those decisions were made by the FAA and Coast Guard. The FAA acknowledged that media access was limited to hired planes or helicopters, arranged through the Coast Guard. The Coast Guard and BP denied having a policy of restricting journalists, noting that media had been embedded with authorities since the beginning, with over 400 embeds aboard boats and aircraft, and that they wanted to provide access while maintaining safety. On 15 April 2014, BP announced that coastal cleanup was substantially complete, while the U.S. Coast Guard continued using physical barriers such as floating booms to prevent further spread. Skimmer boats removed a majority of the oil and sorbents absorbed any remnant oil like a sponge. Although the method did not remove oil completely, chemicals called dispersants were used to hasten oil degradation to prevent further damage to marine habitats below the surface. For the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, cleanup workers used 1,400,000 US gal (5,300,000 L; 1,200,000 imp gal) of various chemical dispersants. The state of Louisiana received funding from BP to conduct regular testing of fish, shellfish, water, and sand. Initial testing regularly showed detectable levels of dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, a chemical used in cleanup. Testing over 2019 reported by GulfSource.org showed no results for the pollutants tested. Due to the Deepwater Horizon spill, marine life was suffering, with thousands of animals visibly covered in oil. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, working with the Smithsonian's National Zoological Park, rescued animals to assist in cleanup, although many animals were found dead. The spill area hosts 8,332 species, including more than 1,270 fish, 604 polychaetes, 218 birds, 1,456 mollusks, 1,503 crustaceans, 4 sea turtles, and 29 marine mammals. Between May and June 2010, the spill waters contained 40 times more polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.

text: The Deepwater Horizon oil spill began on 20 April 2010 off the coast of the United States in the Gulf of Mexico, at the BP-operated Macondo Prospect in Mississippi Canyon Block 253, approximately 41 mi (66 km) off the Louisiana coast. The disaster started when high-pressure methane gas expanded into the marine riser and ignited at approximately 7:45 p.m. CDT, causing an explosion that engulfed the Deepwater Horizon drilling rig, resulting in the deaths of eleven crew members who were never found, and the rescue of ninety-four others, seventeen of whom were injured. The rig sank on 22 April 2010. An oil slick was discovered the same day, and oil flowed for 87 days. The United States federal government estimated the total discharge at 4.9 million barrels (210,000,000 US gal; 780,000 m³), with a plus-or-minus 10% uncertainty, making it the largest marine oil spill in petroleum industry history and 8 to 31 percent larger than the Ixtoc I spill. BP initially estimated a flow rate of 1,000 to 5,000 barrels per day, but the Flow Rate Technical Group estimated an initial rate of 62,000 bbl/d (9,900 m³/d). The spill directly affected 70,000 sq mi (180,000 km²) of ocean, comparable to the area of Oklahoma, with oil washing up on 125 mi (201 km) of Louisiana’s coast and along the Mississippi, Florida, and Alabama coastlines by early June 2010. Oil reached Gulf Park Estates in Mississippi in late June, Grand Isle and Lake Pontchartrain in July, and a new wave of oil coated 16 mi (26 km) of Louisiana coastline in September. By October, weathered oil reached Texas. As of July 2011, about 491 mi (790 km) of coastline in Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida were contaminated, with a total of 1,074 mi (1,728 km) oiled since the spill began. By December 2012, 339 mi (546 km) of coastline remained subject to evaluation and cleanup. The spill affected marine and wildlife habitats, fishing, and tourism industries, with oil found as far as the Florida Panhandle and Tampa Bay, where dispersant-treated oil was embedded in sand. In April 2013, dolphins and other marine life continued to die in record numbers, with infant dolphins dying at six times the normal rate. Studies in 2014 found that tuna and amberjack exposed to the oil developed heart and organ deformities, and cardiotoxicity was widespread in exposed animal life. Investigations attributed the explosion to defective cement on the well, primarily blaming BP, but also Transocean and Halliburton, with a White House commission concluding the spill resulted from "systemic" root causes and warning of recurrence without reform. In November 2012, BP pleaded guilty to 11 counts of manslaughter, two misdemeanors, and a felony count of lying to Congress, agreed to four years of government monitoring, and was temporarily banned from new U.S. government contracts, paying $4.525 billion in fines and other payments. As of 2018, cleanup costs, charges, and penalties exceeded $65 billion. In September 2014, a U.S. District Court judge ruled BP was primarily responsible due to gross negligence and reckless conduct. In April 2016, BP agreed to pay $20.8 billion in fines, the largest environmental damage settlement in U.S. history. The Deepwater Horizon was a 10-year-old semi-submersible drilling rig built by Hyundai Heavy Industries, owned by Transocean, and operated under the Marshallese flag, chartered to BP from March 2008 to September 2013. It was drilling a deep exploratory well 18,360 ft (5,600 m) below sea level in approximately 5,100 ft (1,600 m) of water. BP held a 65% share of the Macondo Prospect, with 25% owned by Anadarko Petroleum and 10% by MOEX Offshore 2007, a unit of Mitsui. BP attempted to cap the well using remotely operated vehicles, a containment dome, and a "top kill" method, all of which failed. A riser insertion tube and stopper were used to divert oil, collecting 924,000 US gal (22,000 bbl; 3,500 m³) before being removed. A second containment system was connected to the blowout preventer on 16 June 2010, and a better-fitting cap ("Top Hat Number 10") was installed on 10 July. A final device with a larger chamber and manual valve was secured on 15 July 2010, sealing the well. Relief wells were drilled starting in May 2010, with the first test oil and mud pumped on 3 August 2010, and cement pumped into the well on 4 August 2010. The failed blowout preventer was removed on 3 September 2010, and a replacement was installed. Cement pumping began on 16 September 2010, and the well was declared sealed on 19 September 2010. Despite this, reports in early 2012 indicated the well site was still leaking. Oil slicks were reported in March 2011, August 2011, March 2012, October 2012, and January 2013, with chemical analysis confirming the oil originated from the Macondo well. The U.S. Coast Guard initially claimed the oil was too dispersed to recover, but later warned BP and Transocean of financial liability. A white, milky substance was observed seeping from the wreckage, which BP and the U.S. Coast Guard stated was not oil and not harmful. In October 2012, BP reported plugging a leak from a failed containment dome. In December 2012, a U.S. Coast Guard subsea survey found no oil from the wells or wreckage, though the source of the oil sheen remained unknown. Scientists suggested the sheen could be residual oil or formation oil escaping through a subsurface fault, potentially indicating an indefinite release. The fundamental strategies were containment, dispersal, and removal, with approximately 47,000 people and 7,000 vessels involved in summer 2010. By 3 October 2012, federal response costs reached $850 million, mostly reimbursed by BP. By January 2013, 935 personnel remained involved, and cleanup had cost BP over $14 billion. The total estimated volume of leaked oil was 4.9 million barrels (780,000 m³), with BP arguing that government figures did not account for over 810,000 bbl (34 million US gal; 129,000 m³) of oil collected or burned before reaching the Gulf. The spill also released thousands of tons of hydrocarbon gases into the atmosphere. Researchers found deep plumes of dissolved oil and gas remained confined to the northern Gulf, with long-lasting impacts on dissolved oxygen. Estimates suggested up to 75% of the oil remained below the surface, with over 100×10⁶ US gal (2.4 million barrels) remaining in the Gulf. In 2013, over 4,600,000 lb (2,100 t) of oily material was removed from Louisiana’s coast, and tar balls continued to wash up on Alabama and Florida Panhandle beaches. Cleanup patrols were reduced to an as-needed basis, and scientists at the Gulf of Mexico Oil Spill and Ecosystem Science Conference suggested up to one-third of the oil may have mixed with deep ocean sediments, risking damage to ecosystems and fisheries. A 2013 study found a dispersant-treated oil plume had reached 80 mi (130 km) off the Tampa Bay region, with possible fish lesions.

---

### 🔗 Preservation Milestones & Associated Technological/Cultural Shifts

---

#### 📅 **1681: First Cataloguing by William Perry**
- **Milestone**: The Codex Arundel was first catalogued in 1681 as a scientific and mathematical notebook.
- **Technological/Cultural Shift**:  
  → **The rise of early scientific cataloging and institutional librarianship**  
  This reflects the emergence of **systematic classification systems** in the 17th century, driven by the **Scientific Revolution**. The development of libraries as organized repositories of knowledge (e.g., the Royal Society’s growing collection) required standardized cataloging practices.  
  → This was a shift from **personal or scattered collections** to **institutionalized knowledge management**, laying the foundation for modern archival science.  
  🔍 *Technological context*: While no digital tools existed, the use of **manual indexing, classification, and descriptive metadata** marked a foundational step in preserving intellectual heritage.

---

#### 📅 **1834: Cataloguing by the British Museum**
- **Milestone**: The manuscript was catalogued by the British Museum in 1834.
- **Technological/Cultural Shift**:  
  → **The institutionalization of national museums and the expansion of public access to cultural heritage**  
  This period saw the rise of **national museums** (like the British Museum) as centers of public education and scientific inquiry.  
  → The cataloguing process reflected the **standardization of museum practices**, including **systematic numbering (MS Arundel 263)** and **classification by subject and provenance**.  
  🔍 *Technological context*: Use of **paper-based, handwritten catalogues** with standardized formats—early forms of **metadata management**. This was a critical step in making rare manuscripts accessible to scholars, even if only through physical access.

---

#### 📅 **1998: Most recent facsimile publication**
- **Milestone**: A facsimile edition of the Codex Arundel was published in 1998.
- **Technological/Cultural Shift**:  
  → **The rise of facsimile publishing and high-resolution reproduction technology**  
  This era saw the development of **photographic reproduction techniques**, **offset printing**, and **digital scanning** that allowed for accurate, high-fidelity copies of fragile manuscripts.  
  → Facsimiles enabled **wider scholarly access** without risking damage to the original.  
  🔍 *Technological context*: The use of **photography and print technology** to preserve and disseminate fragile documents. This was a key step in **democratizing access** to rare texts, especially for those without physical access to the British Museum.

---

#### 📅 **2007: Digitization and inclusion in "Turning the Pages" project**
- **Milestone**: The Codex Arundel was digitized and made available online in the 2.0 format as part of the British Library’s "Turning the Pages" project on 30 January 2007.
- **Technological/Cultural Shift**:  
  → **The digital revolution in cultural heritage preservation and access**  
  This marks a **paradigm shift** from physical access to **interactive, user-friendly digital platforms**.  
  → The "Turning the Pages" project leveraged **digital imaging, touch-screen interfaces, and responsive web design** to allow users to "turn the pages" of manuscripts like a physical book—enhancing engagement and accessibility.  
  🔍 *Technological context*:  
  - High-resolution **digital scanning**  
  - **Interactive web platforms** with zoom, annotation, and navigation  
  - **Open-access digital libraries** as part of a global movement to preserve and share cultural heritage  
  → This reflects the **cultural shift toward digital inclusion**, where knowledge is no longer confined to physical institutions but is available globally, instantly, and affordably.

text: By 26 May 2010, over 130 lawsuits had been filed against BP, Transocean, Cameron International Corporation, or Halliburton Energy Services relating to the spill, with observers expecting these to be consolidated into one multidistrict litigation. On 21 April 2011, BP filed $40 billion in lawsuits against Transocean, Halliburton, and Cameron, alleging failed safety systems and irresponsible contractor behavior, including that Halliburton improperly used modeling software to assess safe drilling conditions; the firms denied the claims. On 2 March 2012, BP and plaintiffs agreed to settle roughly 100,000 claims involving individuals and businesses affected by the spill. On 13 August 2012, BP requested U.S. District Judge Carl Barbier to approve the settlement, asserting its actions did not constitute gross negligence or willful misconduct. On 13 January 2013, Judge Barbier approved a medical-benefits portion of BP’s proposed $7.8 billion partial settlement, covering individuals who lived for at least 60 days along oil-impacted shores or participated in cleanup and can document specific health conditions caused by oil or dispersants, as well as those injured during cleanup. BP also committed $105 million over five years for a Gulf Coast health outreach program and medical exams. A plaintiff group stated the deal had no specific cap, and BP maintained $9.5 billion in assets set aside in a trust to pay claims, with the settlement not increasing the $37.2 billion originally budgeted for spill-related expenses; BP initially expected to spend $7.8 billion, raising its projection to $9.2 billion by October 2013, citing it could be "significantly higher." On 31 August 2012, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) filed papers in federal court in New Orleans blaming BP for the Gulf oil spill, describing it as an example of "gross negligence and willful misconduct," calling some of BP’s arguments "plainly misleading" and stating the court should disregard BP’s claim that the Gulf region was "undergoing a robust recovery"; BP rejected the charges, asserting it was not grossly negligent and looking forward to presenting evidence at trial in January. The DOJ also charged Transocean, the rig owner and operator, with gross negligence. On 14 November 2012, BP and the DOJ reached a settlement: BP paid $4.5 billion in fines and other payments, the largest of its kind in U.S. history, and was temporarily banned from new federal contracts due to "lack of business integrity"; the plea was accepted by Judge Sarah Vance on 31 January 2013. The settlement included $2.394 billion to the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation, $1.15 billion to the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, $350 million to the National Academy of Sciences for oil spill prevention and response research, $100 million to the North America Wetland Conservation Fund, $6 million to General Treasury, and $525 million to the Securities and Exchange Commission. Oil sector analysts at Canaccord Genuity noted the settlement would only be a partial resolution of the many claims against BP. On 3 January 2013, the DOJ announced that Transocean Deepwater Inc. agreed to plead guilty to violating the Clean Water Act and pay a total of $1.4 billion in civil and criminal fines and penalties: $800 million to the Gulf Coast restoration Trust Fund, $300 million to the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, $150 million to the National Wild Turkey Federation, and $150 million to the National Academy of Sciences; MOEX Offshore 2007 agreed to pay $45 million to the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, $25 million to five Gulf states, and $20 million to supplemental environmental projects. On 25 July 2013, Halliburton pleaded guilty to destroying critical evidence after the spill and agreed to pay the maximum allowable fine of $200,000 and serve three years of probation. In January 2014, a panel of the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected BP’s effort to limit payments to what it called "fictitious" and "absurd" claims in the settlement fund, ruling that BP had not explained how the court could identify claimants without cognizable injury and calling BP’s position "nonsensical"; the Supreme Court later refused to hear BP’s appeal after victims, claimants, and Gulf coast chambers of commerce objected to BP’s attempt to renege on the settlement. In September 2014, Halliburton settled a large percentage of legal claims against it by paying $1.1 billion into a trust in three installments over two years. BP and its partners—Transocean and Halliburton—went on trial on 25 February 2013 in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Louisiana in New Orleans to determine payouts and fines under the Clean Water Act and the Natural Resources Damage Assessment, with plaintiffs including the U.S. Justice Department, Gulf states, and private individuals; tens of billions of dollars in liability and fines were at stake. A finding of gross negligence would result in a four-fold increase in BP’s Clean Water Act fines and liability for punitive damages in private claims. The trial’s first phase assessed liability and whether BP, Transocean, Halliburton, and others acted with gross negligence and willful misconduct; the second phase in September 2013 focused on the oil flow rate, and the third phase in 2014 on damages. Plaintiffs’ lawyers attributed the explosion to mishandling of a rig safety test, inadequate staff training, poor equipment maintenance, and substandard cement. The Wall Street Journal reported the U.S. government and Gulf Coast states had prepared a $16 billion settlement offer to BP, though it was unclear if it was officially proposed or accepted. On 4 September 2014, U.S. District Judge Carl Barbier ruled BP guilty of gross negligence and willful misconduct, describing its actions as "reckless," and found Transocean’s and Halliburton’s actions to be "negligent." He assigned 67% of the blame to BP, 30% to Transocean, and 3% to Halliburton. Fines would be proportioned to the degree of negligence, based on the number of barrels spilled, with Clean Water Act fines potentially up to $4,300 per barrel at the judge’s discretion. The number of barrels spilled was disputed: BP argued 2.5 million barrels over 87 days, while the court asserted 4.2 million barrels. BP strongly disagreed with the ruling and filed an immediate appeal. Barbier ruled BP acted with "conscious disregard of known risks," rejected BP’s assertion of equal responsibility among parties, and stated BP employees took risks leading to the largest environmental disaster in U.S. history, with key decisions driven by a desire to save time and money rather than ensuring well security. BP strongly disputed the ruling and filed an immediate appeal. On 2 July 2015, BP, the U.S. Justice Department, and five Gulf states announced a record $18.7 billion settlement. To date, BP’s total costs for clean-up, environmental and economic damages, and penalties have reached $54 billion. In addition to private lawsuits and civil actions, the federal government charged multiple companies and five individuals with federal crimes. In the November 2012 resolution of federal charges against BP, the company pleaded guilty to 11 felony counts related to the deaths of 11 workers and paid a $4 billion fine; Transocean pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor as part of its $1.4 billion fine. In April 2012, the DOJ filed the first criminal charge against Kurt Mix, a BP engineer, for obstructing justice by deleting messages showing BP knew the flow rate was three times higher than claimed and that the "Top Kill" method was unlikely to succeed; three more BP employees were charged in November 2012: site managers Donald Vidrine and Robert Kaluza were charged with manslaughter for negligent supervision of safety tests and failure to alert onshore engineers of drilling problems, and David Rainey, BP’s former vice-president for Gulf exploration, was charged with obstructing Congress by misrepresenting the oil flow rate; Anthony Badalamenti, a Halliburton manager, was charged with instructing two employees to delete data related to Halliburton’s cementing job. None of the individual charges resulted in prison time, and no upper-level executives were charged. Anthony Badalamenti was sentenced to one year probation, Donald Vidrine paid a $50,000 fine and received 10 months probation, Kurt Mix received six months’ probation, and David Rainey and Robert Kaluza were acquitted.

### 🔗 **Cause-and-Effect Chain for Factional Splits**

#### 🔹 **Split 1: From VS to KF (1970–1973)**

KF became the leading revolutionary force in Aarhus, Aalborg, and Odense. |

> ✅ **Key Insight**: This split was driven by a **principled ideological divergence** — a desire for revolutionary purity and worker-centered struggle, rejecting what they saw as soft or reformist elements in VS.

---

#### 🔹 **Split 2: From KF to KF-p (1975–1977)**

| **Cause** | **Effect** |
|---------|----------|
| **Internal factional conflict within KF** in 1975, particularly among university-based activists in Aarhus. | A group known as the **"Coffee Club" (Kaffeklubben)** emerged, advocating for strategic renewal and reform within KF. |

> ✅ **Key Insight**: This split reflected a **struggle between ideological purity (Leninism)** and **pragmatic adaptation (renewal)**. KF-p’s formation shows that even within a new organization, internal divisions can lead to further fragmentation.

| **KF → KF-p** | Internal ideological conflict; Coffee Club’s reformist proposals; tension over Leninist orthodoxy | Formation of KF-p (1977); 6% of delegates leave; KF-p emphasizes October Revolution; denied entry to VS |

text: The Deepwater Horizon spill caused widespread environmental and health impacts. The state of Louisiana received funding from BP to conduct regular testing of fish, shellfish, water, and sand, though initial tests detected dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate, a cleanup chemical, and later testing over 2019 by GulfSource.org reported no results. Marine life suffered significantly, with thousands of animals visibly covered in oil, and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, in collaboration with the Smithsonian's National Zoological Park, rescued animals while many were found dead. The spill area hosts 8,332 species, including over 1,270 fish, 604 polychaetes, 218 birds, 1,456 mollusks, 1,503 crustaceans, 4 sea turtles, and 29 marine mammals. Between May and June 2010, spill waters contained 40 times more polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) than before the spill, with PAHs most concentrated near the Louisiana Coast and levels increasing 2–3 fold off Alabama, Mississippi, and Florida. PAHs are carcinogenic and pose health risks to humans and marine life, and they can harm marine species directly while microbes used to break down oil may reduce oxygen levels. The oil contained approximately 40% methane by weight, compared to about 5% in typical oil deposits, which can suffocate marine life and create "dead zones." A 2014 study funded by NOAA, Stanford University, and the Monterey Bay Aquarium and published in Science found that oil toxins caused irregular heartbeats and cardiac arrest, with PAH cardiotoxicity potentially affecting many species. Another peer-reviewed study from 2014, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, found that tuna and amberjack exposed to spill oil developed fatal or life-shortening heart and organ deformities, with scientists suggesting these effects could apply to other large predator fish and humans due to similar developing hearts. BP claimed the oil concentrations in the study were rarely seen in the Gulf, but The New York Times reported this contradicted the study. The oil dispersant Corexit, previously used only on the surface, was released underwater in unprecedented amounts to make oil more biodegradable, emulsifying it into tiny droplets that remained suspended in water and on the sea floor. The oil and dispersant mixture entered the food chain via zooplankton, with signs of the mix found under the shells of blue crab larvae, and insect populations in coastal marshes were significantly impacted. Petroleum compounds and Corexit were found in migratory bird eggs as far as Minnesota. Dispersant and PAHs were believed to cause "disturbing numbers" of mutated fish, including 50% of shrimp lacking eyes and eye sockets, and fish with sores and lesions were first noted by fishermen in November 2010; prior to the spill, about 0.1% of Gulf fish had lesions, but estimates rose to 20% and later 50%. In October 2013, Al Jazeera reported the Gulf ecosystem was "in crisis" due to declining seafood catches, deformities, and lesions. Researchers J. Christopher Haney, Harold Geiger, and Jeffrey Short concluded that over one million coastal birds died directly from the spill, supported by National Audubon Society observations of bird mortality after the acute phase. In July 2010, the spill was reported to be having a "devastating" effect on marine life, with damage to the ocean floor endangering the Louisiana pancake batfish, whose range is entirely within the spill area. A definitive link between the spill and the death of a Gulf coral community was found in March 2012. NOAA has recognized a cetacean Unusual Mortality Event (UME) since before the spill and is investigating possible connections to the spill, with potential criminal charges if a link is established; only 2% of killed mammal carcasses have been recovered. In the first birthing season after the spill, dead baby dolphins were found at about 10 times the normal number along Mississippi and Alabama shorelines. A NOAA/BP study found nearly half the bottlenose dolphins tested in mid-2011 in Barataria Bay were in "guarded or worse" condition, including 17% not expected to survive. BP denies the disease conditions are related to the spill, stating dolphin deaths began before the spill. By 2013, over 650 dolphins had been stranded, a four-fold increase over the historical average. The National Wildlife Federation reports that sea turtle strandings, mostly of endangered Kemp's ridley sea turtles, increased from an average of 100 per year before the spill to roughly 500 since the spill. NWF senior scientist Doug Inkley noted the marine death rates were unprecedented and occurring high in the food chain, suggesting "something amiss" with the Gulf ecosystem. In December 2013, a study in Environmental Science & Technology found half of 32 dolphins captured near southeastern Louisiana were seriously ill or dying. BP called the report "inconclusive" regarding spill causation. Tar balls continued to wash up along the Gulf coast in 2012 and were still found in Mississippi and Louisiana coasts in 2013, along with oil sheens in marshes and severe coastal erosion due to tree and marsh grass death. In 2013, former NASA physicist Bonny Schumaker noted a "dearth of marine life" within 30 to 50 miles of the well after multiple flights since May 2010. In 2013, researchers found oil on the seafloor was not degrading and observed a "dirty blizzard" where oily particles clumped around sediments and fell to the ocean floor, potentially having long-term effects as oil could remain in the food chain for generations.
