text: Dollywood is a theme park jointly owned by Herschend and Dolly Parton through her entertainment company, Dolly Parton Productions, and is located in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, within the Knoxville metropolitan area near the gateway to The Great Smoky Mountains. It hosts nearly 3 million guests annually from mid-March to the Christmas holidays and is the largest ticketed tourist attraction in Tennessee, having won several international awards. In addition to thrill rides, the park features traditional Smoky Mountain crafts, food, and music, hosting concerts and musical events each year, including performances by Dolly Parton and her family as well as national and local acts. The park is part of a 150-acre (61 ha) Dollywood amusement destination that includes the 35-acre (14 ha) Dollywood's Splash Country water park, the 20-acre (8.1 ha) Dollywood's DreamMore Resort and Spa, and the 5-acre (2.0 ha) Dolly Parton's Stampede Dinner Attraction. Originally opened on June 10, 1961, as "Rebel Railroad" by the Robbins brothers from Blowing Rock, North Carolina, the park was themed around the centennial of the Civil War, featuring a steam train, general store, blacksmith shop, and saloon, with riders protected by Confederates from attacks by Union soldiers, train robbers, and Native Americans. It was modeled after their earlier park, Tweetsie Railroad. In 1964, it was renamed "Goldrush Junction" with a wild west theme similar to Tweetsie Railroad. In 1970, Art Modell, owner of the Cleveland Browns, purchased the park and added an outdoor theater and the Robert F. Thomas Chapel. In 1975, the name changed to "Goldrush," and in 1976, Jack and Pete Herschend, owners of Silver Dollar City, bought the park, which continued operating as Goldrush that year. In 1977, the Herschends renamed it "Silver Dollar City Tennessee" to make it a sister park to their original Silver Dollar City in Branson, Missouri, spending about $1 million on upgrades and adding two new steam locomotives, #70 and #71, and the remains of engine #72 from the White Pass & Yukon Route Railroad. In 1986, Dolly Parton, who grew up in the area, acquired an interest in the park and it reopened on May 3, 1986, as "Dollywood." Parton stated she became involved to bring jobs to her home region after achieving success in her career. The park employs approximately 4,000 people, making it the largest employer in the community. From 1986 to 2010, the park doubled in size to 150 acres (61 ha). On November 16, 2010, Dollywood earned the Liseberg Applause Award, which Dolly Parton accepted at the IAAPA Attractions Expo 2010 in Orlando. The 1986 reopening included the Rivertown Junction area with Smoky Mountain River Rampage, Back Porch Theater, Aunt Granny's Dixie Fixins' Restaurant, Dolly's Tennessee Mountain Home, and "Rags to Riches: The Dolly Parton Story" museum; the "The Butter Churn" ride was removed, and attendance doubled to over a million guests. In 1987, the Daydream Ridge area opened with the Mountain Slidewinder, Mountain Dan's Burger House, Sweet Dreams Candy Shop, The Rainbow Factory, and Critter Creek Playground; engine #70 was restored. In 1988, the 1,739-seat Celebrity Theater opened with the "Showcase of Stars" concert series. Five new children's rides were added to Fun Country, including a Zamperla Balloon Race. The Dollywood Foundation was established to provide books and school supplies to children in Sevier County. In 1989, Thunder Express, a steel mine train coaster, was built adjacent to Blazing Fury and relocated from Six Flags Over Mid-America; the 1989 season was the last for the National Mountain Music Festival. In 1990, a 1924 Dentzel Carousel was relocated to near the train depot, replacing the Silver Dollar Saloon; a 600-seat Gaslight Theater opened nearby. The Smoky Mountain Christmas Festival premiered in November, extending the operating season into December. In 1991, Eagle Mountain Sanctuary, an outdoor aviary, and the Wings of America Theater with the Birds of Prey show and the 300-seat Valley Theater were added. In 1992, the Showstreet area opened with the Showstreet Palace Theater, The Butterfly Emporium, The Backstage Restaurant, The Spotlight Bakery, Friendship Gardens, and WDLY-FM, a working radio station; the main entrance moved from Rivertown Junction to Showstreet; the Barnwood Theater became Imagination Station. Attendance topped 2 million for the first time in 1992. In 1993, Fun Country was renovated into The Country Fair with the Wonder Wheel (60 ft tall), Twist and Shout, and Tennessee Twister; the Balloon Race ride was relocated to Daydream Ridge. "Sunset Musicfest" debuted in 1994; the Gaslight Theater became the Heartsong Theater. In 1995, the Jukebox Junction 1950s "Main Street" area opened with Rockin' Roadway, The Pines Theater, Red's Diner, and Cas Walker's Music Store; Sunset Musicfest did not return. In 1996, the Dollywood Boulevard area opened with Thunder Road, Silver Screen Café, and Centerstage gift shop. In 1997, "U Pick Nick" aired in the Celebrity Theater; the Flooded Mine dark ride was closed and demolished in October; Silver Screen Café became DJ Platters. In 1998, Daredevil Falls, billed as "The Highest and Fastest Waterfall Ride in America" with a 62 ft (19 m) drop, opened in the former Flooded Mine location. Thunder Express was closed in September and sold to Magic Springs Theme Park in Arkansas; the antique carousel was removed and replaced with a new Chance Rides carousel. In 1999, the Tennessee Tornado steel looping coaster opened in the former Thunder Express area; the Southern Gospel Museum and Hall of Fame opened; the Balloon Race ride was removed. In 2000, Daydream Ridge was renovated into Dreamland Forest, a children's mountain-themed interactive play area. The Festival of Nations premiered in April 2001. In 2001, Dolly's Splash Country, a 25-acre (100,000 m²) water park, opened adjacent to Dollywood's parking lot. In 2002, Dollywood Boulevard was redeveloped into Adventures in Imagination; Smoky Mountain Wilderness Adventure replaced Thunder Road; a new Dolly museum, Chasing Rainbows, opened in the former DJ Platters building. In 2003, KidsFest premiered and Imagination Station became Celebration Hall; the "Showcase of Stars" concert series ended. In 2004, Thunderhead Gap opened with the Thunderhead wooden roller coaster; the Country Fair Falls log flume was demolished in November; most Country Fair rides, including the Swingamajig, Tennessee Twister, The Convoy, and The Barnstormer, were removed to make room for new rides in 2005, which included Dizzy Disk, Amazing Flying Elephants, Lemon Twist, Shooting Star, Sky Rider, VeggieTales Sideshow Spin, Waltzing Swinger, Piggy Parade, Busy Bees, and Lucky Ducky; the National Southern Gospel & Harvest Celebration debuted. In 2006, the Timber Tower ride, along with Lil' Loggers Landing, Beaver Creek, Beaver Creek Boat Float, and Lumberjack Lifts, opened in a new area adjacent to Thunderhead; the Barbeque & Bluegrass festival premiered. In 2007, Mystery Mine, a Gerstlauer Eurofighter coaster with two vertical lift hills, dark ride elements, fire effects, a 95-degree 85-foot (26 m) drop, a heartline roll, and a dive loop, opened using an abandoned mine shaft theme; the ride cost $17 million ($25.8 million in 2024 dollars). In 2008, River Battle, an interactive water raft ride, opened in Wilderness Pass, connecting Timber Canyon and Craftsman's Valley; "Thunder Road" returned to Imagination Cinema; Della's Lye Soap shop moved to Wilderness Pass; a new exhibit for the Wings of America show birds was relocated; the Polar Express 4-D Experience was shown during Smoky Mountain Christmas. In 2009, new shows "Imaginé" by Le Grand Cirque and "Sha-Kon-O-Hey! Land of Blue Smoke," featuring music by Dolly Parton and the story of the last family in the Smoky Mountains, were introduced; "Imaginé" headlined Festival of Nations; "Thunder Road" was renamed "White Lightning" and then replaced by Journey to the Center of the Earth: 4-D Adventure; a multi-line zipline attraction, SkyZip (owned by Skyline Eco-Adventures of Maui, Hawaii), opened as the first multi-line zip line tour in a theme park. In 2010, Adventure Mountain opened in Wilderness Pass at a cost of $5 million, featuring three adventure courses—Geyser Gorge, Black Bear Cliff, and Rocky Top—with 100 rope features, swinging beams, suspension bridges, flying islands, and floating stairs, ranging from a few inches to over 26 feet (7.9 m) in height; it included a scaled-down play area, Camp Teachittoomee; the park also brought back "Sha-Kon-O-Hey! We’ll now walk through the document **through this lens**, extracting and organizing the most important facts in a way that leverages this framework.

## 🔍 Step-by-Step Breakdown Using the XNU Triad

---

### 🟦 1. **Mach – The Microkernel Flexibility Layer**

**What it does**:  
Provides the foundation of a *microkernel* — minimal core services (like task scheduling, inter-process communication, and memory management), running in kernel space with strong isolation.

**From the document**:
- XNU uses **Open Software Foundation Mach Kernel (OSFMK) 7.3**.
- This gives Darwin the **flexibility of a microkernel** — allowing modular design and efficient message-passing between components.
- The Mach component enables **separation of concerns**, such as running user-space services (like network or security daemons) safely outside the main kernel.

🧠 *Memory Hook*:  
> "Mach = Microkernel = Flexibility"  
> Think: *Mach is the brain’s nervous system — it sends signals, but doesn’t do the heavy lifting.*

---

### 🟨 2. **FreeBSD – The Networking & Process Powerhouse**

**What it does**:  
Provides the **process model, virtual file system (VFS), and network stack** — essential for Unix-like behavior and compatibility.

**From the document**:
- XNU integrates **elements of FreeBSD**, including:
  - Process model (how processes are created, scheduled, and managed)
  - Network stack (handles TCP/IP, sockets, routing)
  - Virtual file system (VFS) — allows consistent access to files, devices, and network resources
- This makes Darwin **POSIX-compatible**, so many Unix/Linux programs can run without modification.
- The BSD lineage ensures strong compatibility with Unix standards and tools.

🧠 *Memory Hook*:  
> "FreeBSD = Networking & Process Model = POSIX Power"  
> Think: *FreeBSD is the engine — it powers the system, handles traffic, and runs processes smoothly.*

---

### 🟥 3. **IOKit – The Device Driver Backbone**

**What it does**:  
An **object-oriented device driver API** that allows dynamic, safe, and modular device management — especially critical for modern hardware (like GPUs, Wi-Fi, cameras).

**From the document**:
- IOKit is the **object-oriented device driver API** used in Darwin.
- It enables Apple to support a wide range of hardware (e.g., iPhone 5S, iPad Pro, Apple Silicon) with flexible, maintainable drivers.
- Unlike older driver models, IOKit supports **dynamic loading**, **memory mapping**, and **event-driven communication** with hardware.

🧠 *Memory Hook*:  
> "IOKit = Device Drivers = Hardware Bridge"  
> Think: *IOKit is the hands — it connects the system to every piece of hardware.*

---

## 🔄 How the Triad Works Together (The Hybrid Design)

> **Hybrid Kernel = Flexibility + Performance**

| Component | Role | Benefit |
|--------|------|--------|
| **Mach** | Core communication & isolation | Enables modularity and safety |
| **FreeBSD** | Process & network management | Ensures performance and POSIX compliance |
| **IOKit** | Hardware interaction | Supports diverse, modern devices |

✅ **Result**:  
Darwin combines:
- The **flexibility** of a microkernel (Mach)  
- The **performance** of a monolithic kernel (FreeBSD + IOKit)  
→ A powerful, scalable, and secure foundation for macOS, iOS, and other Apple OSes.

- **Mach** = The nervous system (sends signals between parts)
- **FreeBSD** = The engine (handles power, processes, and movement)
- **IOKit** = The steering wheel and sensors (connects to real-world roads and devices)

Donjuan Triumphant made his racecourse debut on 20 June 2015 at Redcar, finishing second by a head to Receding Waves, and sustained narrow defeats at Ayr, Carlisle, and Haydock before winning his first race at Ayr two weeks later by three and a quarter lengths with apprentice jockey Jack Garritty. He then won the Listed Rockingham Stakes at York on 10 October by one and a half lengths from Dhamaan and the Group 2 Critérium de Maisons-Laffitte in France on 11 October by five and a half lengths after taking the lead 200 metres from the finish. text: Donald Andrew McClurkin Jr. (born November 9, 1959) is an American gospel singer and minister who has won three Grammy Awards, ten Stellar Awards, two BET Awards, two Soul Train Awards, one Dove Award, and one NAACP Image Award. He is one of the top-selling gospel artists, having sold over 13 million albums. Variety referred to him as a "Reigning King of Urban Gospel." McClurkin was born in Copiague, New York. At age eight, his two-year-old brother was killed by a speeding driver, causing family turmoil. He later experienced childhood sexual abuse from his great uncle and his great uncle's son. Two of his sisters struggled with substance abuse, prompting McClurkin to find solace in church and through an aunt who sang background vocals with gospel musician Andraé Crouch. By adolescence, he formed the McClurkin Singers and later the New York Restoration Choir, releasing recordings as early as 1975. He released three albums with the choir before launching a solo career. In 1989, he was hired as an associate minister at Marvin Winans' Perfecting Church in Detroit, Michigan, serving as an assistant for over a decade. In 1991, McClurkin was diagnosed with leukemia after experiencing sharp pain, swelling, and internal bleeding; at age 31, he chose to follow his own advice to "believe that God will save you" and practice what he preached. In 2001, he was ordained and sent by Marvin Winans to establish Perfecting Faith Church in Freeport, New York, where he serves as senior pastor. A friendship with a Warner Alliance executive led to his signing with the label for his 1996 self-titled album, produced by Bill Maxwell, Mark Kibble of Take 6, Cedric and Victor Caldwell, and Andraé Crouch. The album, featuring the popular song "Stand," went gold after being praised by Oprah Winfrey. At the 48th Annual Grammy Awards, he won Best Traditional Soul Gospel Album for "Psalms, Hymns & Spiritual Songs." McClurkin is best known for his hit songs "Stand" and "We Fall Down," which were played extensively on Gospel and Urban radio. His three solo albums have topped the Billboard Charts. Following the success of his near double platinum album "Live in London and More," he released "Psalms, Hymns and Spiritual Songs" in 2005 and "We All Are One: Live In Detroit" in 2009, both of which topped Billboard charts across genres. The album debuted at No. 45 on the Billboard 200 and No. 4 on the Gospel Billboard charts. His 2016 album "The Journey" debuted at number one on the Billboard Top Gospel Albums chart, marking his seventh solo release and including live performances of classics like "Speak to My Heart," "Great Is Your Mercy," "Stand," and "That’s What I Believe." His last recorded album, "A Different Song," was released in 2019 and debuted at No. 2 on the Gospel Billboard charts. McClurkin includes a language medley—Japanese, Russian, Spanish, and Dutch—in most live performances due to his love for sharing gospel music globally. Tom Versen and Tony Sisti of T&T Creative signed him to a radio syndication deal with Dial Global Local and syndicator Gary Bernstein, providing a mobile recording studio based in his church for on-the-road broadcasts. text: Donald Clarence Simpson (October 29, 1943 – January 19, 1996) was an American film producer, screenwriter, and actor renowned for his work on major blockbuster films of the 1980s and 1990s. He began his career in the 1970s at Warner Bros. and Paramount Pictures, where he worked in marketing exploitation films, including Woodstock and A Clockwork Orange, and co-wrote and had a small role in the 1976 film Cannonball. In 1975, he was interviewed for a position at Paramount by his friend Steve Tisch, who declined the offer, and was later named vice-president of production in 1977 and president in 1981. He was fired in 1982 after passing out during a studio meeting due to drug use and was known for managing eight productions simultaneously and frequently throwing tantrums during filming. He formed a professional partnership with Jerry Bruckheimer, producing successful films such as Flashdance (1983), Beverly Hills Cop (1984), Top Gun (1986), Beverly Hills Cop II (1987), and The Rock (1996), the latter released posthumously. The duo earned Producers of the Year honors from the National Association of Theatre Owners in 1985 and 1988 and launched their own production company affiliated with Paramount in 1985. In 1990, they signed a five-year $300 million deal with Paramount, which ended after Days of Thunder (1990) underperformed at the box office despite a $60 million budget and grossing $158 million, with both parties blaming each other for the results. They later signed with Disney, with The Ref (1994) being a financial failure, but returned to success with Dangerous Minds, Crimson Tide, and Bad Boys in 1995. Simpson never married; he took Scientology classes in the 1970s but quit after spending $25,000 with no personal gains, and during Days of Thunder, he expelled Scientology leader David Miscavige after refusing to pay for a costly sound device. Known for his brash personality, Simpson made controversial remarks, such as criticizing Steven Spielberg and David Lynch, and claimed his primary duty as a producer was to make money. He worked out daily with equipment provided by Arnold Schwarzenegger and frequented Canyon Ranch for workouts and tanning. Though he claimed never to have had plastic surgery, reports indicate he underwent ten procedures between 1988 and 1994, including a penis-enlargement surgery, which led to infections and reversals. Simpson was infamous for his extravagant lifestyle, often describing making movies as the best thing after eating and having sex, and was a central figure in Hollywood's cocaine-party scene, hosting lavish all-night parties and being known for S&M preferences. He used cocaine since the 1970s, increasing his use over time, and was known for erratic behavior and excessive spending. In a 1994 interview, he claimed to have stopped using drugs and only had a food addiction, but screenwriter James Toback stated his drug use never ceased, prompting David Geffen and Jeffrey Katzenberg to intervene. Simpson refused traditional rehab and instead worked with doctor Stephen Ammerman, who developed a "dangerously unorthodox" detox program involving medications like morphine to manage withdrawal. Ammerman died in August 1995 at Simpson’s home from an accidental overdose of cocaine, Valium, venlafaxine, and morphine. Frustrated by Simpson’s drug use and declining performance, Bruckheimer ended their partnership in December 1995, agreeing to complete The Rock, which was dedicated to Simpson’s memory. Simpson died on January 19, 1996, in the bathroom of his Bel Air, Los Angeles, home, initially attributed to natural causes; an autopsy revealed he died of heart failure from combined drug intoxication, with 21 different drugs detected in his system, including antidepressants, stimulants, sedatives, and tranquilizers. Investigations revealed he obtained prescription drugs from 15 doctors, with 2,200 pills found in his bedroom closet, and his monthly prescription expenses totaled over $60,000. A 1998 book by Charles Fleming described him as "a supercharged simple-minded creature, an Aesop's fable on crystal meth." After his death, his brother Lary Simpson established a production banner to develop projects originated by Don Simpson, which continued until Lary’s death on January 25, 2023, at age 77. Simpson is credited as a producer on all films unless otherwise noted.

text: Doris Salcedo, born in 1958 in Bogotá, Colombia, is a visual artist and sculptor whose work is deeply rooted in her experiences of political violence and personal loss in Colombia. Her art uses common materials such as wooden furniture, clothing, concrete, grass, and rose petals to give form to pain, trauma, and the profound emptiness left by disappearance—experiences shaped by the disappearance of family members during Colombia’s civil conflict. Salcedo earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts from Jorge Tadeo Lozano University in 1980 and a Master of Fine Arts from New York University in 1984, after which she returned to Bogotá to teach at the Universidad Nacional de Colombia. She is married to Azriel Bibliowicz, a Colombian novelist and sociologist who studies the Jewish experience in Colombia, and they live and work in Bogotá. Her installations often address memory, forgetting, and the political dimensions of history. Works such as Unland: The Orphan's Tunic (1997) and the La Casa Viuda series from the early 1990s transform everyday objects like chairs and tables into memorials for victims of Colombia’s civil war. In Unland, a table made from two destroyed tables joined by a whitish veil of fabric—presumably an orphan’s tunic—contains hundreds of human hairs as thread, with Huyssen describing it as a “memory sculpture” where the table becomes a metaphor for the body of an orphaned community. Salcedo emphasizes that her art involves a process of metamorphosis, where materials charged with personal and historical meaning are reconfigured to evoke emotional and psychological resonance. In her 2002 work Noviembre 6 y 7, she spent 53 hours placing wooden chairs against the façade of the Palace of Justice in Bogotá, re-inhabiting the space of a violent siege. In 2003, for the 8th Istanbul Biennial, she created an installation of 1,550 wooden chairs stacked between two buildings, which she described as a “topography of war” representing mass graves and the shared experience of violence, not a specific event. In 2005, at Castello di Rivoli, she extended the gallery’s vaulted ceiling to evoke incarceration and entombment in her work Abyss. In 2007, she created Shibboleth for the Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, a 167-metre-long crack in the floor that symbolized borders, segregation, racial hatred, and the experience of marginalized people, particularly in post-colonial societies. The crack, which began as a thin line and widened into a chasm, was designed to represent the fractures in modernity and colonialism, with Salcedo stating that the history of racism runs parallel to the history of modernity. The crack was later mended, but a sliver remained. In 2013, she created Flor de Piel, a tapestry of thousands of preserved, hand-sewn red rose petals measuring 340 cm x 500 cm, intended as a shroud for a nurse tortured to death in Colombia’s war, which was acquired by the Harvard Art Museums in 2014. Plegaria Muda, a series of two coffin-sized tables with grass growing between them, translates to “silent prayer” and reflects on gang violence and mass grave sites in Colombia. Since 1988, Salcedo has interviewed families of people “disappeared” by military forces during Colombia’s civil war and has visited abandoned villages, murder sites, and mass graves, maintaining extensive files on concentration camps, both historical and contemporary. She has consistently focused on political violence, stating that “violence defines the evils of our society.” In a 2008 interview, she noted the historical recurrence of concentration camps, from Spain’s use in Cuba in 1896 to the British in South Africa, the Germans in West Africa, and the U.S. prison system, where minor offenses like marijuana possession lead to long-term incarceration, resulting in a socially excluded underclass—what she calls “socially dead”—who are denied civil rights and participation in life. She has exhibited internationally in events such as Carnegie International (1995), XXIV São Paulo Biennial (1998), Documenta XI (2002), and the 8th Istanbul Biennial (2003), and has had solo exhibitions at The New Museum of Contemporary Art (1998), San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (1999 and 2005), Tate Britain (1999), Tate Modern (2007), and the Harvard Art Museums (2016–17). Her installation “Plegaria Muda” traveled to museums across Europe and South America from 2010 to 2013, including MUAC (Mexico), Moderna Museet (Malmö), CAM Gulbenkian (Lisbon), MAXXI (Rome), Pinacoteca São Paulo (2012), Museum of Contemporary Art (Chicago, 2015), and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum (2015). In Atrabiliarios, she uses pairs and singles of women’s shoes, encased in translucent animal skin with medical sutures, to evoke the memory of those who have disappeared, highlighting the survivors’ uncertainty, longing, and mourning. Salcedo’s work consistently explores the intersection of personal and collective memory, the trauma of political violence, and the enduring presence of loss and resistance.

Author Tom Wolfe wrote about Downey in his article "The Hair Boys," which described Harvey's Drive-in and the distinctive fashions worn by the hair boys, claiming Harvey's was one of the world's great unacknowledged centers of fashion. text: Downey is a city in southeastern Los Angeles County, California, United States, located 13 miles (21 kilometers) southeast of Downtown Los Angeles and considered part of the Gateway Cities. It is the birthplace of the Apollo space program and Taco Bell and is home to the world's oldest operating McDonald's restaurant, the Speedee McDonald's Store, which opened in 1953 at the southwest corner of Florence Avenue and Lakewood Boulevard. The store was damaged in the 1994 Northridge Earthquake and reopened in 1996 with a museum and gift shop. As of the 2020 census, the city had a total population of 114,355, with a population density of 9,215.5 inhabitants per square mile (3,558.1/km²). The city covers a total area of 12.6 square miles (33 km²), of which 12.4 square miles (32 km²) is land and 0.2 square miles (0.52 km²) is water. The racial makeup was 23.4% White, 3.7% African American, 2.1% Native American, 6.7% Asian, 0.3% Pacific Islander, 40.0% from other races, and 23.9% from two or more races, with 75.1% of the population identifying as Hispanic or Latino of any race. The city is adjacent to South Gate and Bell Gardens to the west and northwest, Pico Rivera to the northeast, Santa Fe Springs and Norwalk to the east, and Paramount and Bellflower to the south. According to the Köppen Climate Classification system, Downey has a semi-arid climate (BSk). Mission San Gabriel Arcángel was initially founded on September 8, 1771, near Tongva settlements on a bluff overlooking the Rio Hondo, near the modern intersection of San Gabriel Blvd and Lincoln Avenue, and was later relocated to its present site in San Gabriel after five years due to flooding. In 1784, Governor Pedro Fages granted former soldier Manuel Nieto (1734–1804) a land concession of 300,000 acres (120,000 hectares) stretching from the Santa Ana River to the Old San Gabriel River (now the Rio Hondo and Los Angeles River) and from the mission highway (approximately Whittier Boulevard) to the ocean, though the acreage was later reduced due to encroachment on Mission San Gabriel lands. The land, known as Rancho Los Nietos, passed to Manuel Nieto’s four children after his death and was partitioned in 1833 by Mexican Governor José Figueroa; the northwestern portion, including the Downey-Norwalk area, was granted as Rancho Santa Gertrudes to Josefa Cota, widow of Antonio Nieto, covering approximately 21,000 acres (8,500 hectares) and containing the old Nietos homestead, a center of social life east of the pueblo of Los Angeles. Dairy was a major industry, with the Central Milk Agency marketing milk for "seven hundred dairymen whose dairy herds range from thirty to two thousand head" valued at over $1,000,000 per month. Some settlers came from Ireland, and the city was founded and named for John Gately Downey, the former and youngest governor of California, born in Ireland, who supported Republican Lincoln during the Civil War and pioneered modern subdivision development between the Rio Hondo and San Gabriel River around 1865. He believed oranges would flourish in Southern California and imported several varieties, leading to oranges becoming one of the state’s biggest cash crops. Two small settlements—College Settlement and Gallatin—were established along the Rio Hondo River, with Gallatin building a school known as the "Little Red Gallatin School House" in the late 1860s, later expanded to a two-story building in 1871 and moved to its present site in 1893. By 1883, College Settlement, Gallatin, and Downey joined, and with Governor Downey’s efforts, the Southern Pacific Railroad was convinced to route through and stop in Downey, making the depot area the new center of activity and forming a larger Downey. Farmers grew grain, corn, castor beans, and fruit, and by 1935 Downey was characterized as an "orange-grove town." Downey was incorporated in 1956 and adopted a charter form of government in 1964. After World War II, suburban homes and factories replaced farms. During World War II, Vultee Aircraft was Downey’s largest employer, producing 15% of all American military aircraft by 1941 and pioneering the use of women in manufacturing and the first powered assembly line for airplanes. After WWII, the plant was idle from 1945 to 1948 before being occupied by North American Aviation, which later became North American Rockwell, then Rockwell International, and eventually Boeing. In 1961, the facility was transferred to NASA and became the birthplace of the Apollo Space Program and the Space Shuttle, producing and testing many of the 20th century’s greatest aviation, missile, and space endeavors. The Rockwell plant closed in 1999, and the site was demolished and replaced by the Columbia Memorial Space Center, Downey Landing shopping center, Promenade at Downey shopping center (formerly Downey Studios), a Kaiser Permanente hospital, and a city recreation fields park. In the 1960s, Downey Records gained notoriety with recordings such as The Chantays' "Pipeline," and later, the local music scene led to the founding of The Blasters and Dark Angel. Rancho Los Amigos National Rehabilitation Center, the main public rehabilitation hospital for Los Angeles County, is located in Downey and is renowned worldwide for its innovations in spinal cord injury and post-polio syndrome care. Downey was featured in the 2008 film Pineapple Express, with many buildings along Florence Avenue appearing in a driving sequence. In 2010, the population was 111,772 with a density of 8,893.3 inhabitants per square mile (3,433.7/km²), and the median household income was $60,939, with 11.8% of the population below the poverty line. In 2023, the median household income was estimated at $87,400 and the per capita income at $37,122, with 7.0% of families and 9.1% of the population below the poverty line. In 2022, the Greater Los Angeles Homeless Count reported 218 homeless individuals in Downey, with approximately 30–40 homeless residents in the area. Crime reports from 2008 show a drop in robberies, aggravated assaults, and petty thefts, but auto thefts reached a 10-year high with 1,231 vehicles reported stolen, along with 252 robberies, 172 aggravated assaults, 24 rapes, 711 burglaries, and 2,038 larceny/thefts. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, gang activity increased, and although it persists in the southern area today, the city formed GOOD (Gangs Out Of Downey) to engage youth aged 10–20 in anti-gang programs, including sports, after-school care, scholarship programs, and counseling, maintaining a partnership with the Downey Police Department. In 2017, Downey was recognized as L.A. County's "Most Business-Friendly City" by the Los Angeles County Economic Development Corporation. The city is in California's 30th senatorial district, represented by Democrat Bob Archuleta, and the 64th Assembly district, represented by Democrat Blanca Pacheco, and in the 42nd congressional district, represented by Democrat Robert Garcia. Author Tom Wolfe wrote about Downey in his 1968 book "The Pump House Gang," including an article titled "The Hair Boys" about Harvey's Drive-in and the fashion of the hair boys, with a drawing of one appearing in "In Our Time." In 1955, a global news story emerged when truck driver George Di Peso at 7739 Alderdale Street tried to drown a gopher by placing a hose into its hole, only to find the hose being slowly pulled down, which was reported worldwide in a July 3, 1955, Los Angeles Times article titled "Tokyo Awaits Arrival of Downey Hose."

text: Dragnet is an American crime drama television series starring Jack Webb and Harry Morgan that aired for four seasons, from January 12, 1967, to April 16, 1970. To distinguish it from the earlier 1950s Dragnet series, the ending year of each season was included in the on-screen title, beginning as Dragnet 1967 and concluding as Dragnet 1970. The series aired every Thursday from 9:30 to 10:00 pm (ET) and was directed by Jack Webb. All four seasons have been released on DVD; Season 1 ("Dragnet 1967") was released by Universal Studios Home Entertainment, while Seasons 2 ("1968"), 3 ("1969"), and 4 ("1970") were released by Shout! Factory. This was the second television series in the Dragnet media franchise, which includes film, television, books, and comics, and it holds the distinction of being one of the first examples of a discontinued American TV series being revived years later with some original cast members. Actors who played multiple roles during the series include Don Ross, Olan Soule, Marco Lopez, Herb Vigran, Clark Howat, Art Balinger, Alfred Shelly, Art Gilmore, Ralph Moody, Virginia Gregg, Ed Deemer, Howard Culver, Bert Holland, Don Stewart, Bobby Troup, Len Wayland, William Boyett, Stacy Harris, Stuart Nisbet, Kent McCord, Robert Brubaker, Harry Bartell, Jill Banner, Robert Patten, Sidney Clute, Anthony Eisley, Virginia Vincent, Don Dubbins, James McEachin, Peggy Webber, Jack Sheldon, and Vic Perrin. Each episode typically begins with stock footage of Los Angeles followed by Sgt. Joe Friday’s introduction, "This is the city," after which he specifies the day and time and describes the watch or shift he and Gannon are working. Friday, usually the lead investigator, and Gannon investigate each case, with Friday maintaining a polite but terse, clipped, and rigid manner of questioning witnesses or suspects, often responding to irrelevant details with, "Ma’am (Sir), we just want to get the facts." At the end of each episode, the legal fate of the arrested suspects is revealed. Friday and Gannon are rarely shown outside their professional relationship; Gannon occasionally mentions his wife, Eileen, and family, and sometimes encourages Friday, who is single, to have a social life. In a rare departure from the crime drama, the 1968 episode "Homicide: DR-06" shows Friday inviting the Gannons to his apartment for a steak dinner, only to have the evening repeatedly interrupted by other tenants seeking his assistance. In 1965, Jack Webb was approached by Universal Pictures to produce a Dragnet television movie for NBC; NBC programming director Mort Werner was impressed and decided to develop Dragnet into a weekly series. Webb was initially more interested in continuing the franchise with TV movies but ultimately agreed. The movie, which had a working title of Dragnet 1966, was released on January 27, 1969 (midway through the third season) on The NBC Monday Movie under the promotional title World Premiere: Dragnet, and is commonly referred to as Dragnet 1966 to distinguish it from other franchise works. It is included as an extra in the Dragnet 1968 DVD set. All episodes of the series were directed by Jack Webb. In one episode, Friday and Gannon investigate a bank robbery committed by a man and a woman; tracking their car leads them to a woman who matches the suspect’s description, initially lies to them, and is already on probation, leading the detectives to believe they have a suspect—until additional reports reveal other women being forced to rob banks in the same way. Though the first woman is cleared, the spree continues until one victim fights back. Sergeant Carl Maxwell, a fellow detective, goes AWOL after a case he worked on is dismissed; Friday and Gannon are given three days to find him before he is terminated from the LAPD. When they locate him drinking at a resort, he rants about the stresses of policing and claims he is a minority for being a cop, but a speech from Friday convinces him to return. Friday and Gannon also investigate an officer accused of police brutality following a drunk driving arrest; officers Pete Malloy (Martin Milner) and Jim Reed (Kent McCord), the main characters of Adam-12, appear as witnesses. In another episode, 17-year-old Hal Rustin (Michael Burns) is a car thief whose mother, Eunice Rustin (Peggy Webber), is unable to stop him. He is given a tour of jail to illustrate the consequences of crime, but it fails, and he later kills someone with a shotgun. Note: Harry Morgan had a bloody nose the night before filming.

text: Dua Lipa co-wrote her songs with her co-writers and cites Kylie Minogue, Pink, Nelly Furtado, Jamiroquai, Prince, Kendrick Lamar, and Chance the Rapper as musical influences. In a 2018 GQ interview, she stated that her idea of pop includes P!nk, Christina Aguilera, Destiny's Child, and Nelly Furtado. Her second studio album, Future Nostalgia (2020), was inspired by artists she listened to during her teens, such as Gwen Stefani, Madonna, Moloko, Blondie, and Outkast. Early in her career, her stage presence drew criticism, exemplified by a YouTube comment on her "New Rules" BRIT Awards performance that became an internet meme, which she credited as motivation to improve. A study by the Office for National Statistics found that the number of people born with the name "Dua" in England and Wales rose from 63 in 2017 to 126 in 2019, the year she earned her first UK number-one with "New Rules." In May 2018, she was named one of British Vogue’s 25 most influential British women of 2018 at age 22, with the review calling "New Rules" an "anthem of female empowerment" and describing her as a "culture definer." Lyndsey Havens of Billboard credited her with leading the revival of disco in 2020 through "Don't Start Now" (2019), and she was dubbed "the Future of Pop" due to the success of Future Nostalgia. She inspired French photographer Hugo Comte’s first photo-book and was included in Time’s 100 Next list by Kylie Minogue, who called her a "shining star." Mark Sutherland and Jem Aswad of Variety rated her one of the most impactful women in global entertainment. Wax figures of Dua Lipa are displayed at Madame Tussauds in major cities worldwide. She has won seven Brit Awards from nineteen nominations, three Grammy Awards from ten, two MTV Video Music Awards from twenty-three, two MTV Europe Music Awards from sixteen, two American Music Awards from seven, three iHeartRadio Music Awards from nineteen, nine Spotify 1 billion streams plaques, and one Bambi Award. She holds two Guinness World Records: in 2020 for most tickets sold for a livestreamed concert by a solo female artist, and in 2021 for most monthly listeners on Spotify for a female artist, though she did not surpass Ariana Grande’s prior peak. In 2024, she won the Top Dance/Electronic Song award at the Billboard Music Awards for "Houdini," which topped the Hot Dance/Electronic Songs chart for 17 weeks. Time included her in its 2024 Time 100 list of the world’s most influential people, and Billboard ranked her number 25 on its 2025 "Top 100 Women Artists of the 21st Century" list. Lipa identifies as a feminist and has spoken out against sexism in the music industry and advocated for social equality in the LGBT community. On 12 February 2018, she raised a rainbow flag during a performance of "Be the One" at the Hollywood Palladium as part of The Self-Titled tour. At the 2018 Brit Awards red carpet, she wore a white rose dress in support of the Time's Up movement and stated in her acceptance speech her delight at women being present and winning awards, clarifying that her feminism is about equal opportunities, not misandry. In September 2018, some fans were removed from a Shanghai concert for waving rainbow flags, despite homosexuality being decriminalized in China in 1997; Lipa expressed pride and gratitude for their visibility. In November 2018, she criticized Brexit, stating that no refugee leaves without having to, based on her personal experience. In June 2019, she publicly supported Sudan’s democratic transition by sharing a "Stand with Sudan" image, rejecting the Khartoum massacre as an act of "brutal murder and rape" and a violation of freedom and human rights. In December 2019, she endorsed the Labour Party led by Jeremy Corbyn, calling the election "the most important in a generation" and describing Boris Johnson’s victory as a "total disaster." She participated in a Global Feminism short film directed by Annie Lennox’s The Circle, released ahead of International Women’s Day to raise awareness of misogyny, rape, and violence against women. In April 2019, she called for a boycott of the Sultan of Brunei’s hotel interests after Brunei’s penal code introduced death penalties for homosexuality. At a Billboard Women in Music event, she used her Powerhouse Award speech to highlight ongoing gender inequality, criticized the lack of diversity in the Billboard Hot 100, and encouraged young girls to be "powerhouses of the future." Lipa was the headliner party host for the 2020 Sydney Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras parade and performed several songs. In July 2020, she signed an open letter to the UK government, delivered to then Minister for Women and Equalities Liz Truss, requesting the banning of conversion therapy. She supports universal health care, noting that in the UK, the National Health Service is considered a right. In June 2020, she criticized the Israel Defense Forces’ treatment of Palestinians and referred to "fake Jews" and "fake Christians" in the Israeli government and U.S. midwest, claiming they created Hamas to justify occupation and oppression. An Im Tirtzu petition with over three thousand signatories demanded that Lipa’s songs be banned from Israeli Army Radio and Galgalatz due to what they called antisemitism and conspiracy theories; the radio responded that it does not boycott artists. In July 2020, she supported the "Let the Music Play" campaign, sending an open letter to Culture Secretary Oliver Dowden urging government support for the UK live music industry’s economic losses during the pandemic. On 18 July 2020, she posted explaining "why Kosovo is not and will never be Serbia," urging a petition for Apple to map Kosovo as an independent state. The next day, she shared an irredentist map of Greater Albania, which is commonly associated with extreme Albanian nationalism, leading to accusations of ethnic nationalism and fascism; she later stated the post was misinterpreted and that she rejects ethnic separatism. In August 2020, she urged her followers to vote against Donald Trump. After supporting Bernie Sanders in the 2020 Democratic primaries, she expressed support for Joe Biden during a virtual event for Albanian Americans, arguing Kosovars owed support to Biden for opposing the NATO bombing of Yugoslavia. In January 2021, she called on Kosovo citizens to vote in the 2021 parliamentary election. In May 2021, she criticized The New York Times for an advertisement that labeled her and others as antisemitic. In July 2021, through her Sunny Hill Foundation, she joined Tirana’s "Adopt a Kindergarten" initiative to rebuild a kindergarten damaged in the 2019 Albania earthquake; the project was completed in October 2021 and named "Sunny Hill Kindergarten." She has raised awareness of the Taliban’s 2021 takeover of Afghanistan through social media and her lifestyle newsletter Service95. In August 2022, she was named an Honorary Ambassador of Kosovo by President Vjosa Osmani, stating it was an honor to represent her country and supporting Kosovans’ right to visa liberalization, freedom to travel, and to dream big. On 13 November 2022, she denied reports of performing at the 2022 FIFA World Cup opening ceremony, criticizing Qatar’s human rights record. In October 2023, she signed an open letter with 185 other artists for the "Artists4Ceasefire" campaign, urging President Biden to push for a ceasefire and humanitarian corridor in Gaza. She and her father, Dukagjin, co-founded the Sunny Hill Foundation in 2016 to help people in Kosovo facing financial hardship. In August 2018, she organized the Sunny Hill Festival to raise funds, receiving the Pristina Key from then-Mayor Shpend Ahmeti, the first time the award was given. In 2019, she hosted the festival again with Miley Cyrus as a performer. In mid-November 2018, she participated in UNICEF’s "Go Blue" campaign on World Children’s Day, re-recording "Be the One" with the word "red" changed to "blue" to promote children’s rights. In December 2018, she performed at a benefit concert for Ellie Goulding’s "Streets of London" event at Wembley Arena, which funds homeless support and raises awareness. In April 2019, she became a UNICEF supporter during a visit to a refugee camp in Beirut, Lebanon, including Bourj el-Barajneh, where she visited Syrian and Palestinian youth lacking adequate health and education. She later supported a campaign with her management to raise £100,000 for charities like The Black Dog and CALM. Lipa called attention to the high suicide rates among women in the arts, stating they are nearly 70% higher than the global average and described mental health as the "issue of our generation." Following the 2019 Albania earthquake, on 26 November 2019, she asked fans to donate and co-released a limited edition "Pray for Albania" t-shirt line with Albanian designers, with all proceeds going to victims. At the end of May 2020, she participated in a digital event "Dream with Us" to raise funds for COVID-19 relief. She contributed a cover of "Times Like These" to BBC Radio 1’s Live Lounge on 23 April 2020 as part of a charity supergroup, Live Lounge Allstars, with profits going to Children in Need, Comic Relief, and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund.   - It defines the Deputy Speaker’s role as the **presiding officer** of the National Assembly when the Speaker is absent or incapacitated.  
  - If both Speaker and Deputy Speaker are unable to serve, a **temporary appointee** is designated to act as Speaker.

---

1. **Deputy Speaker’s Duties**  
   - Presides over sessions of the National Assembly when the Speaker is absent.  
   - Maintains order and decorum during debates.  
   - Ensures fair and impartial conduct of proceedings.  
   - May cast a vote only in case of a tie (as per constitutional rules).  
   - Acts as a key figure in legislative process and parliamentary governance.

2. **Succession Rules**  
   - **Primary Succession**: Deputy Speaker → Speaker (when Speaker is absent or unable to serve).  
   - **Secondary Succession**: If both Speaker and Deputy Speaker are unable to serve → A temporary Speaker is appointed by the National Assembly.  
   - This ensures **continuity of legislative function** and prevents paralysis in governance.

   - Elected by the National Assembly on **1 March 2024**.

text: Dua Lipa (/ˈduːə ˈliːpə/ ⓘ DOO-ə LEE-pə; born 22 August 1995) is an English singer and songwriter with seven Brit Awards and three Grammy Awards. Born in London, England, she is the eldest child of Kosovo Albanian parents Anesa (née Rexha) and Dukagjin Lipa from Pristina, FR Yugoslavia (present-day Kosovo), and has a sister, Rina, and a brother, Gjin. The name Dua, suggested by her grandmother, means "love" in Albanian, and her maternal grandmother is of Bosniak descent; both of her grandfathers were historians, with her father's ancestry traced to Peja, Kosovo. Musically influenced by her father, the lead singer and guitarist of the Kosovan rock band Oda, who played music at home including works by David Bowie, Bob Dylan, Radiohead, Sting, the Police, and Stereophonics, Lipa began singing at age five. She attended Fitzjohn's Primary School, where she took cello lessons and was initially told she could not sing in the choir; at nine, she began weekend singing lessons at the Sylvia Young Theatre School. After Kosovo declared independence in 2008, she moved to Pristina, where she attended Mileniumi i Tretë School and considered a music career. At 15, she returned to London alone and shared a flat with a family friend, attending Parliament Hill School to pass her A-Levels and later re-entering Sylvia Young Theatre School part-time. She uploaded songs to SoundCloud and YouTube, covering tracks like "If I Ain't Got You" and "Beautiful." In 2013, she modelled with Topshop, signed with Tap Management (directed by Ben Mawson and Ed Millett), and was introduced to Mawson by her lawyer, who discouraged her from signing another publishing deal. Mawson and Millett offered her a monthly salary to leave her job as a waitress in a cocktail bar to focus on music; during a session, she co-wrote "Hotter than Hell," which led to her signing a record deal with Warner Bros. Records in 2014. In August 2015, she released her first single, "New Love," produced by Emile Haynie and Andrew Wyatt; her second single, "Be the One," reached number one in Belgium, Poland, and Slovakia, charted in the top ten in over eleven European territories, and became an airplay success in Australia and New Zealand. In November 2015, she was named on the BBC Sound of... 2016 long list. Her first tour in the UK and Europe began in January 2016 and concluded in early December 2016. On 18 February 2016, she released "Last Dance," followed by "Hotter than Hell" on 6 May, which peaked at number 15 in the UK; on 26 August, "Blow Your Mind (Mwah)" was released, peaking at number 30 in the UK and becoming her first entry on the US Billboard Hot 100, debuting at number 72, while topping the Billboard Dance Club Songs chart and reaching number 23 on the Billboard Mainstream Top 40 chart. In November 2016, she was featured on Sean Paul's single "No Lie," which reached number ten in the UK and became a top-ten hit in ten countries six years after its release, becoming Sean Paul's most-streamed song as of December 2022, with the music video surpassing 1 billion views on YouTube by April 2022. A documentary about her, See in Blue, was commissioned by The Fader in January 2017. That month, she won the EBBA Public Choice Award and released "Scared to Be Lonely" with Martin Garrix, which reached number 14 in the UK. In May 2017, she performed at the anniversary of Indonesian television channel SCTV and won the award for Young and Promising International Artist at the SCTV Music Awards. Her debut album, Dua Lipa, was released on 2 June 2017; its sixth single, "New Rules," released the following month, became her first number one in the UK, the first by a female solo artist to reach the top since Adele's "Hello" in 2015, and charted in the top ten in Australia (number two), the US (number six), and Canada (number seven). As of 2024, the music video for "New Rules" has streamed over three billion views on YouTube. In June 2017, she performed at the Glastonbury Festival, in July at the We The Fest in Jakarta, and on BBC's Later... with Jools Holland in October. In December 2017, she was named the most streamed woman of 2017 in the UK by Spotify. In 2017, she had four singles reach the UK top 10: "Be the One," "New Rules," "No Lie," and "Bridge over Troubled Water," a charity single for the families of the victims of the Grenfell Tower fire. text: Dulcie Evonne September (20 August 1935 – 29 March 1988) was a South African anti-apartheid political activist who was assassinated in Paris, France, in 1988. The second eldest daughter of Jakobus and Susan September, she grew up in Gleemore, a suburb of Cape Town. While in Cape Town, she developed a strong awareness of apartheid’s injustices and became deeply involved in political activism, advocating for national liberation, democracy, and social justice. She began her primary education at Klipfontein Methodist Mission and later attended Athlone High School, where she experienced firsthand the segregation enforced by Bantu education laws, which became central to her political beliefs. Several of her teachers at Athlone High School were active in civic and political organizations, which helped shape her political consciousness. Though her formal schooling ended halfway through Standard Eight (Grade 10), she continued her education through night classes and passed her Standard Eight exams in 1952. In 1954, she enrolled at the Wesley Training School in Salt River to become a teacher and completed her Teacher’s Diploma in 1955 at Battswood Training College. She began teaching at City Mission School in Maitland and later at Bridgetown East Primary School in Athlone in 1956. In 1957, she joined the Cape Peninsula Students' Union (CPSU), affiliated with the Unity Movement of South Africa, where she met political allies such as Dr. Kenneth Abrahams, Ottilie Abrahams, Neville Alexander, Marcus Solomon, and Fikile Bam. She was also a member of the Athlone branch of the Teacher's League of South Africa (TLSA). After growing frustrated with TLSA, she joined the African Peoples' Democratic Union of Southern Africa (APDUSA) in 1960 and was elected to its finance committee. The APDUSA soon split due to internal conflict, and under the leadership of Dr. Kenneth Abrahams and Neville Alexander—both suspended in 1962—September and others formed the unofficial Caucus to resolve divisions. After the Sharpeville massacre, she and other activists adopted a militant stance. Under Neville Alexander’s direction, she co-founded the Yu Chi Chan Club (YCCC) in July 1962, inspired by the Chinese Communist Revolution and named after Chinese guerilla warfare, which was disbanded by the end of that year and replaced by the National Liberation Front (NLF) in January 1963. On 12 July 1963, security police raided both her and Neville Alexander’s homes, and when NLF materials were found, September was detained on 7 October 1963 and imprisoned without trial at Roeland Street Prison. She was charged under the Criminal Procedure Act for "conspiracy to commit acts of sabotage and incite acts of politically motivated violence," and after months of court proceedings, judgment was delivered on 15 April 1964. She was sentenced to five years in prison, during which she endured severe physical and psychological abuse. Along with Elizabeth van der Heyden, Doris van der Hayden, and Dorothy Alexander, she was transferred to Kroonstad, a facility for political prisoners, after authorities discovered they were radicalizing illiterate female prisoners. In March 1965, the Bloemfontein Appeal Court dismissed their appeals. She was released in April 1969 under a strict five-year banning order imposed by the Pretoria regime. The restrictions, under the Suppression of Communism Act of 1950, prohibited her from social gatherings, political activities, and teaching in South Africa, imposed a curfew, restricted her movement to “Bantu areas,” banned communication with other banned individuals, and limited visitors to medical personnel and her father—later changed to her sister and brother-in-law. In 1973, as her banning order neared expiration, she applied for a permanent departure permit after securing a position at Madeley College of Education in Staffordshire. She left South Africa on 19 December 1973. In London, she joined the Anti-Apartheid Movement, participated in rallies at South Africa House in Trafalgar Square, and later joined the International Defence and Aid Fund for Southern Africa. In 1976, she joined the African National Congress (ANC) and worked in the ANC Women's League, where she gained recognition for her work on women’s issues and helped welcome newly exiled South Africans. In 1979, during the International Year of the Child (IYC), she was elected chairperson of the IYC Committee of the ANC Women's Section in London. As an ANC representative, she attended conferences in Finland, Canada, and France and worked with the United Nations (UN), non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and the Women’s International Democratic Federation (WIDF) to promote children’s and women’s rights. In 1981, she was called to work full-time in the Regional Preparatory Committee (RPC) at ANC headquarters in Lusaka, where she was elected chairperson. By the end of 1983, she was appointed ANC Chief Representative in France, Switzerland, and Luxembourg, and underwent short military training in the Soviet Union. In this role, she campaigned for economic sanctions against the South African government. Between October 1986 and September 1987, she was involved in the Albertini Affair, an anti-apartheid campaign that ended with embarrassment for both South African and French governments, during which she campaigned for the release of Pierre Andre Albertini, a French national imprisoned by South Africa, and petitioned French President Francois Mitterrand to deny South Africa’s new ambassador, Hennie Geldenhuys, until Albertini was freed. By 1987, she had become a significant threat to the South African government, leading strong anti-apartheid campaigns in France, Switzerland, and Luxembourg and building strong alliances with anti-apartheid groups and left-wing politicians. On the morning of 29 March 1988, she was shot five times with a silenced .22 caliber rifle outside the ANC’s Paris office at 28, Rue des Petites-Écuries as she was opening the office after collecting mail. She was 52 years old. Her death sparked a strong public reaction in Paris, with more than 20,000 people gathering to mourn. The case remains unsolved, with speculation that South African hitmen were involved, possibly with French secret service collaboration. The French government concluded there was insufficient evidence to arrest suspects and closed the case after ten years. Before her assassination, she had been investigating illegal arms trafficking between France and South Africa. According to the Truth Commission Files, the motive may have been linked to her knowledge of illegal arms deals and possible nuclear collaboration between the French government and South African Armscor. Upon discovering this, she reportedly said she “feared for her life.” During her investigation, she reported her concerns to ANC superiors, who dismissed her. Some of her friends allege she reported being followed and threatened and requested protection from French authorities, which was denied. Charles Pasqua, the interior minister, denied these claims, stating she never made such a request. However, sources claim the French had intelligence that South Africa planned to kill her by December 1987, though this is officially denied. On the day after her murder, Alfred Nzo, secretary-general of the ANC, stated: "If ever there was a soft target, Dulcie September was one." Jean-Michel Jarre composed a song titled "September" for his 1988 Revolutions album, dedicated to her, which was performed at his Destination Docklands concert in October 1988 and included in the album recording Jarre Live (1989). Conceptual artist Hans Haacke created a 1989 installation titled "One Day, The Lions of Dulcie September Will Spout Water in Jubilation," modifying a defunct fountain in front of the Grande halle de la Villette in Paris as part of the Magiciens de la terre exhibition. Her short story "A Split Society – Fast Sounds on the Horizon" was included in the 1992 anthology Daughters of Africa, edited by Margaret Busby. The solo play Cold Case: Revisiting Dulcie September, written by Basil Appollis and Sylvia Vollenhoven, pays tribute to her and was performed at a French cultural festival in Paris, winning the inaugural Adelaide Tambo Award for Human Rights in the Arts. A book about her murder, Dulcie: Een Vrouw Die Haar Mond Moest Houden by Evelyn Groenink, was published in the Netherlands in 2001. A podcast titled They Killed Dulcie by Open Secrets and Sound Africa was released in March 2019. The 2021 documentary Murder in Paris, directed by Enver Samuel and edited by Nikki Comninos, explores her life and assassination. An online awareness campaign and petition for justice were launched using the hashtags “#justicefordulcie” and “#mercidulcie.” A 300-page graphic novel, Dulcie from Cape Town to Paris, published by Benoît Collombat and Grégory Mardon, revisits her murder investigation 30 years after her death. A square in the 10th arrondissement of Paris is named after her, officially inaugurated on 31 March 1998, with the inscription “Dulcie September Square: Representative of the African National Congress: Assassinated in Paris on 29 March 1988.” A street in Cléon, near Rouen, is named after her, as is a place in Nantes and a primary school in Évry-sur-Seine, as well as a middle school (collège) in Arcueil, near Paris. In August 2010, the first Dulcie September Memorial Lecture took place at the University of the Western Cape’s Centre for Humanities Research, and the Dulcie September Fellowship Awards in the Humanities and Social Sciences were launched, featuring speakers including Barbara Masekela and Margaret Busby. In October 2011, Staffordshire University Students' Union renamed their boardroom the "September Room" and erected a plaque in her memory. She was a former student of Madeley College of Education, one of the founding colleges of North Staffordshire Polytechnic. In 2013, the Athlone Civic Centre was renamed the Dulcie September Civic Centre. text: Edward Maurice Charles Marsan OBE (born 9 June 1968) is an English actor who won the London Film Critics Circle Award and the National Society of Film Critics Award for Best Supporting Actor for his performance in the film Happy-Go-Lucky (2008). He was born in the Stepney district of London to a working-class family; his father was a lorry driver and his mother was a school dinner lady and teaching assistant. He was raised in Bethnal Green and attended Raine's Foundation School. He left school at 16 and initially worked as a printer before starting his career in theatre. Marsan trained at the Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts, graduating in 1991, and later studied under Sam Kogan at the Kogan Academy of Dramatic Arts, now known as The School of the Science of Acting, of which he is now a patron. His first year at drama school was funded by Mr Benny, a bookmaker who ran a menswear shop where Marsan worked; he received scholarships for the remainder of the course. It took many attempts for Marsan to secure a place at drama school. His first television appearance was in 1992 as a "yob" in the London Weekend Television series The Piglet Files. One of his more significant early television roles was in the mid-1990s BBC sitcom Game On, where he played an escaped convict who was an old flame of Mandy's. He went on to appear in Casualty, The Bill, Grass, Kavanagh QC, Grange Hill, Silent Witness, Ultimate Force, Southcliffe, and more. He also voiced the Manticore in the Merlin episode "Love in the Time of Dragons". In 2011, he starred alongside Olivia Colman and Peter Mullan in the British drama film Tyrannosaur. In 2013, he began portraying Terry Donovan, the brother to the lead character in seven series and 82 episodes of Showtime's drama series Ray Donovan, and also played Ludwig Guttmann in the television film The Best of Men. In May 2015, he appeared as the practical magician Gilbert Norrell in the BBC period drama Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell. His film roles include the main villain in the 2008 superhero film Hancock alongside Will Smith, as Inspector Lestrade in Guy Ritchie's Sherlock Holmes, and other films such as Sixty Six, Gangs of New York, 21 Grams, The Illusionist, V for Vendetta, Gangster No. 1, Miami Vice, Mission: Impossible III, I Want Candy, Vera Drake, Happy-Go-Lucky, Filth, Tyrannosaur, and Heartless. In 2021, he played anti-Fascist activist Soly Malinovsky in the television adaptation of the novel Ridley Road. In 2022, he portrayed the real-life John Darwin in ITV's drama series The Thief, His Wife and the Canoe. In 2024, he appeared as Mitch Winehouse, father of Amy Winehouse, in the biopic Back to Black. Marsan married make-up artist Janine Schneider in 2002; they have four children. He is a humanist and was appointed a patron of Humanists UK in 2015. In 2015, he criticized the lack of representation of working-class people in the arts on BBC Radio 5 Live, stating that too much drama is written from "the white, privileged, middle class perspective". In 2024, he was interviewed on HARDtalk in an episode entitled "Do the arts neglect working-class people?". Marsan was appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 2025 New Year Honours for service to drama.

text: Eduardo Le Monnier (born Edouard Stanislas Louis Le Monnier; 30 September 1873 in Paris – 14 February 1931 in Buenos Aires) was a French architect known for his work in Brazil, Uruguay, and primarily in Argentina.[1][2][3] He studied at the National School of Decorative Arts in Paris and moved to Brazil in 1894, where he worked on projects such as the General Carneiro station in Belo Horizonte and served as a professor at the School of Fine Arts in Curitiba. He arrived in Buenos Aires on 1 November 1896, where he developed most of his projects and concrete works. One of his first works there was the bakery La Burdalesa (Paraná nº 861/9, year 1898, already demolished). In 1901, he revalidated his diploma at the University of Buenos Aires and joined the Central Society of Architects (SCA). In 1902, he completed the Artistic Ironworks Motteau, featuring a remarkable Art Nouveau style (Avenida Juan de Garay no. 1272, demolished), followed by the headquarters of the mutual savings society La Bola de Nieve in Buenos Aires and in Rosario, province of Santa Fe (Cordoba and Laprida streets, year 1906). He won the Municipal Prize for the Best Facade in 1903 for the residence he built for Bartolomé Ginocchio on Lima Street No. 1642. Two years later, in 1905, he received the third prize for the façade of Felix Egusquiza's residence on Libertad Street No. 1394, and in 1907 he presided over the SCA. Due to these recognitions, several aristocratic families hired him to build large residences in the Barrio Norte; the most notable is the Fernández Anchorena Palace, now housing the Apostolic Nunciature, located at Avenida Alvear 1637, constructed between 1907 and 1909. Another residence, smaller but equally opulent, was built on Avenida de los Incas 3260 and still stands today. In the second half of the 1920s, up to the crisis of 1929, there was a significant rise in financial institutions in Argentina, which established large parent companies in downtown Buenos Aires, becoming the financial city that persists today. Le Monnier designed the headquarters of the Uruguayan Argentine Bank (Avenida Roque Sáenz Peña nº 501, year 1928) and the adjacent buildings of the Bencich brothers, owners of a construction company (Edificio Bencich, Av. Roque Sáenz Peña 615 and Edificio Miguel Bencich, Av. Roque Sáenz Peña nº 614/6). He also taught at the National Academy of Visual Arts and Architecture. He died in Buenos Aires on 14 February 1931, at the age of 58.[citation needed]

text: Edward William McBride (ca 1791 – September 3, 1834) was a businessman and political figure in Upper Canada. Born in Newark (Niagara-on-the-Lake) around 1791, he was the son of a United Empire Loyalist. He served in the local militia during the War of 1812. He worked as assistant to King's Printer John Cameron and assumed the role when Cameron became ill in April 1815, continuing until February 1816, several months after Cameron's death. After that, he operated an inn at Niagara. In 1824, he was elected to the Legislative Assembly of Upper Canada for the town of Niagara as a Reformer. He supported government funding for the Welland Canal and defended those who supported Robert Gourlay. For a time, he co-published the Niagara Herald, a newspaper owned by John Crooks, alongside Bartemas Ferguson. As a freemason, he was accused of being associated with the kidnapping and presumed murder of Captain William Morgan, who is said to have revealed secrets of the order. Although McBride denied these accusations, this contributed to his defeat in the 1828 election. He died in Niagara in 1834.

text: Eger Vaughan Murphree (November 3, 1898 – October 29, 1962) was an American chemist best known for co-inventing the process of fluid catalytic cracking. Born in Bayonne, New Jersey, he moved to Kentucky as a child and graduated from Kentucky University with degrees in chemistry and mathematics in 1920, earning a master's degree in chemistry in 1921. He played college football as a tackle for Kentucky and served as captain of the 1920 Kentucky Wildcats football team. After teaching physics and math and coaching football for one year at Paris High School in Paris, Illinois, Murphree worked several years at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology as a staff assistant and research associate in the Chemical Engineering Department. In 1930, he joined Standard Oil of New Jersey. During the Second World War, he was a member of the committee that organized the Manhattan Project and was recognized as a leader in synthetic toluene, butadiene and hydrocarbon synthesis, fluid catalytic cracking, fluid hydroforming, and fluid coking. He participated in the early Manhattan Project as a member of the S-1 Section, served as head of the centrifuge project (which was later abandoned), and was the overall engineer for the Manhattan Project in June 1942. He described Deputy District Engineer Kenneth Nichols as "more like the industrial engineers I was accustomed to dealing with—stable, conservative, thorough and precise." He was scheduled to be on the Lewis Committee reviewing the project in November 1942 but was ill; he (along with James Conant) opposed the committee’s recommendation to build only a small electromagnetic plant, and a full-size plant was constructed. In the 1950s, he served in the Defense Department on missile scheduling and coordinating the programs of the three military services, a role previously held by Nichols. From 1947 to 1962, he served as Vice President of research and engineering at Standard Oil of New Jersey, the company later known as Exxon. He received the Perkin Medal in 1950 and the Industrial Research Institute (IRI) Medal in 1953. The E. V. Murphree Award in Industrial and Engineering Chemistry, awarded annually by the American Chemical Society, is named in his honor. Murphree died on October 29, 1962, at Overlook Hospital in Summit, New Jersey, from coronary thrombosis. He was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 1999.
