text: EGOT is an acronym for the Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony Awards, designating individuals who have won all four of the major performing art awards in the United States. These awards recognize outstanding achievements in television, audio recording/music, film, and theatre, respectively, and achieving the EGOT has been referred to as the "grand slam" of American show business. Including those with honorary or special awards, 27 people have achieved this status, with only Robert Lopez having won all four awards twice. The term was coined by actor Philip Michael Thomas in late 1984 while starring in Miami Vice, when he expressed a desire to achieve the EGOT within five years. The acronym gained wider recognition after a 2009 episode of 30 Rock introduced EGOT status as a recurring plotline. There is debate over whether only the Primetime Emmy Award should count, as some—including Thomas—consider other Emmy categories subordinate to the Primetime honor. Starting in 2016, the Daytime Emmy Awards had a category for Outstanding Musical Performance in a Daytime Program, which was removed after the 2019 ceremony because three of the four winners were Broadway ensembles, including five individuals (Cynthia Erivo, Rachel Bay Jones, Katrina Lenk, Ben Platt, and Ari'el Stachel) who already had Tony and Grammy awards and only needed an Oscar to complete their EGOT. In 2023, TheaterMania writer Zachary Stewart criticized the practice of "selling" producer credits for shows favored to win a Tony as a "shortcut" to EGOT status, distinguishing between producers who do the actual work and those who merely finance it, often late in the award season. American composer Richard Rodgers (1902–1979) received his fourth distinct award in 1962, with 10 competitive awards between 1946 and 1979; he was the first person to win all four and primarily a composer. Helen Hayes (1900–1993) received her fourth distinct award in 1977, with six competitive awards between 1932 and 1980; she was the first woman and first performer to achieve the EGOT, and the first to win the Triple Crown of Acting, with a 45-year interval between her first and fourth award—the longest among EGOT winners. Rita Moreno (born 1931) received her fourth distinct award in 1977, with five awards between 1961 and 1978; she was the first Latina and the first to win a Grammy as her second award, and became a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2015 and a Peabody Award winner in 2019; she is the second EGOT recipient and the first Hispanic actress to win the Triple Crown of Acting. John Gielgud (1904–2000) received his fourth distinct award in 1991, with five competitive awards between 1948 and 1991; he was the first to win a Tony as his first award, won his Emmy at age 87, and became the oldest winner, the first male performer, the first LGBTQ winner, and the first non-American. Audrey Hepburn (1929–1993) received her fourth distinct award posthumously in 1994, with four competitive awards between 1954 and 1994; she was the fifth person to complete the feat and the first to do so posthumously, and the first to win two awards in consecutive shows (the 1994 Grammys followed her 1993 posthumous Emmy), and is the only EGOT winner to not win multiple awards in any of the four fields. Marvin Hamlisch (1944–2012) received his fourth distinct award in 1995, with 12 competitive awards between 1974 and 2001; he had the most Oscars of any EGOT winner (three, all in the same year), won "General Field" Grammys in 1974 (Song of the Year and Best New Artist), and was the first EGOT winner to have won both an Oscar and a Grammy for the same work ("The Way We Were"). Jonathan Tunick (born 1938) received his fourth distinct award in 1997, with five awards between 1977 and 2024; he was the first EGOT winner to win an Emmy as his second award and the first to win the Tony as his fourth award. Mel Brooks (born 1926) received his fourth distinct award in June 2001, with 11 awards between 1968 and 2002; he was the first to win the Emmy as his first award and the first to win his Oscar for screenwriting; he is the only person to have won the Triple Crown of Writing, with an Oscar, Emmy, and Tony in writing categories. Brooks is one of only two people to have two awards of each type, though one of his Oscars was honorary; when he appeared on the January 30, 2015 episode of Real Time with Bill Maher, he called himself an EGOTAK, noting he had also received awards from the American Film Institute and Kennedy Center. Mike Nichols (1931–2014) received his fourth distinct award in November 2001, with 15 awards between 1961 and 2012; he was the first to win the Grammy as his first award, the first to win multiple awards for directing (an Oscar, several Tonys, and two Emmys), and has the longest timespan of awards among EGOT winners at 51 years; he is one of only two people (the other being Bob Fosse) to achieve the Triple Crown of Directing. Whoopi Goldberg (born 1955) received her fourth distinct award in 2002, with five competitive awards between 1985 and 2009; she is the first African American winner, the first to win the Oscar as her second award, and the third person after Audrey Hepburn (1954) and Marvin Hamlisch (1974) to win two qualifying awards in the same year (her Tony and first competitive Emmy in 2002). Scott Rudin (born 1958) received his fourth distinct award in 2012, with 21 awards between 1984 and 2021, tying with Alan Menken for the most competitive EGOT awards; he is the only EGOT winner who is solely a producer and did not win any of his four awards for a creative endeavor (singing, writing, acting). Robert Lopez (born 1975) received his fourth distinct award in 2014, with 12 awards between 2004 and 2022; he is the first Filipino and Asian to achieve the EGOT, the youngest winner (39 years, 8 days) to receive all four awards in competitive categories, and at the time the fastest to complete his qualifying run (9 years, 8 months), with a subsequent shortest interval of 7 years, 8 months (June 27, 2010 to March 4, 2018) until 2024 when Benj Pasek and Justin Paul surpassed it. Lopez is the first person to win each EGOT award twice; as of 2025, he is one Oscar away from becoming the first triple EGOT winner; he is currently the only winner to have two of each EGOT award in competitive categories, as Mel Brooks' second Oscar in 2023 was honorary; his first two Emmys were Daytime Emmys, followed by a Primetime Emmy in 2021 for WandaVision; he is the only EGOT recipient to follow a Daytime Emmy win with a subsequent Primetime Emmy win. Lopez received his Grammy for The Book of Mormon in collaboration with Scott Rudin, making them the first pair of EGOT winners to co-win the same award; he is also the first person to have won the Oscar last, sharing it with his wife Kristen Anderson-Lopez in 2014 and again in 2018; as of 2024, Kristen Anderson-Lopez lacks only a Tony to achieve EGOT status in her own right. Andrew Lloyd Webber (born 1948) received his fourth distinct award in 2018, with 12 competitive awards between 1980 and 2025; on September 9, 2018, he, John Legend, and Tim Rice simultaneously became EGOTs after being awarded the Primetime Emmy for Outstanding Variety Special (Live) for Jesus Christ Superstar Live in Concert. Tim Rice (born 1944) received his fourth distinct award in 2018, with 12 awards between 1980 and 2018, sharing all awards with Elton John, John Legend, Andrew Lloyd Webber, and Alan Menken; on September 9, 2018, he, Lloyd Webber, and Legend became EGOTs via the same Emmy. John Legend (born 1978) received his fourth distinct award in 2018, with 21 awards between 2006 and 2025; he has the most Grammy Awards (12) of any competitive EGOT recipient, is the first African American man to achieve EGOT status, and the first person to receive the four awards in four consecutive years; he is the first EGOT recipient to have won both a competitive Primetime and Daytime Emmy, matched by Robert Lopez in 2021; on September 9, 2018, he, Andrew Lloyd Webber, and Tim Rice became EGOTs via the same Emmy. Alan Menken (born 1949) received his fourth distinct award in 2020, with 21 competitive awards between 1990 and 2020, tying with Scott Rudin for the most competitive EGOT awards; if his special Emmy is counted, he becomes the fully competing EGOT with the most overall awards; if EGOT status is recognized without regard to non-competitive awards, Quincy Jones holds the record with 30 fully competitive awards, including 29 Grammys; Menken has the most Oscar wins (8) by an EGOT. Jennifer Hudson (born 1981) received her fourth distinct award in 2022, with five competitive awards between 2007 and 2022, making her the youngest competitive female EGOT to date. Viola Davis (born 1965) received her fourth distinct award in 2023, with five competitive awards between 2001 and 2023, becoming the eighteenth person to competitively win each of the four awards; she acknowledged her new EGOT status while accepting her 2023 Grammy; she is the third EGOT recipient and the first African American actress to win the Triple Crown of Acting. Elton John (born 1947) received his fourth distinct award in 2024, with nine competitive awards between 1987 and 2024, becoming the nineteenth person to competitively win each of the four awards. Benj Pasek (born 1985) received his fourth distinct award in 2024, with seven competitive awards between 2017 and 2025, becoming the twentieth person to competitively win each of the four awards; he and Justin Paul set a new record for achieving EGOT status in the fastest time (7 years, 7 months); Pasek shares all seven of his competitive award wins with his writing partner Justin Paul. Justin Paul (born 1985) received his fourth distinct award in 2024, with seven competitive awards between 2017 and 2025, becoming the twenty-first person to competitively win each of the four awards; he and Benj Pasek set a new record for achieving EGOT status in the fastest time (7 years, 7 months); Paul shares all seven of his competitive award wins with his writing partner Benj Pasek. Six additional artists have received all four awards, though one was for an honorary or similar non-competitive distinction: Barbra Streisand lacks a competitive Tony; Liza Minnelli lacks a competitive Grammy; and Harry Belafonte, James Earl Jones, Quincy Jones, and Frank Marshall lack a competitive Oscar. Barbra Streisand (born 1942) received her fourth distinct award in 1970, with 18 awards between 1963 and 2001, three of which were non-competitive; at age 28, she obtained her fourth award with a special Tony, making her the youngest special EGOT winner; with only six years between her first award (1964 Grammy) and her 1970 Tony, she held the record for the fastest special EGOT until 2023 when Frank Marshall achieved it in four years. Streisand is the only EGOT to win an Oscar in both music and acting, and the only winner to have three competitive awards for debut performances (first studio album, first feature film, first television special); she also has the Peabody Award, AFI Life Achievement Award, Kennedy Center Honor, Cecil B. DeMille Award, National Medal of Arts, American Society of Cinematographers Board of Governors Award, and Presidential Medal of Freedom. Liza Minnelli (born 1946) received her fourth distinct award in 1990, with seven awards between 1965 and 2009, two of which were special. James Earl Jones (1931–2024) received his fourth distinct award in 2011, with eight awards between 1969 and 2017, two of which were special. text: Between 1954 and 2014, American singer, activist, and actor Harry Belafonte (1927–2023) received a total of six awards, including a Grammy Hall of Fame Award and the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award, with two of those being special awards. He received his fourth distinct award in 2014. American record producer, musician, songwriter, composer, arranger, and film and television producer Quincy Jones (1933–2024) received his fourth distinct award in 2016. Between 1964 and 2024, Jones received a total of 33 awards—the highest number among any EGOT winner—comprising 28 Grammys, one Tony, one Emmy, a special Grammy Legend Award, and two special Oscars (the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award and the Academy Honorary Award). His final qualifying award was a fully competitive 2016 Tony for The Color Purple. American film producer and director Frank Marshall (born 1946) received his fourth distinct award in 2023. Between 2019 and 2023, Marshall received a total of four awards and is the only EGOT winner to have won a Sports Emmy Award and to have received the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. With just four years between his first award (a 2019 honorary Oscar), a long format TV sports documentary, and competitive Grammy and Tony music awards, Marshall completed his EGOT collection in the shortest time of any person to achieve this status. As of July 2025, 74 living people are one award away from achieving (competitive) EGOT status. Additionally, 12 living individuals are one award away from achieving EGOT status, including those who have won at least one non-competitive award. As of 2024, 16 out of the 21 EGOT winners were American nationals, while the remaining five—John Gielgud, Audrey Hepburn, Elton John, Andrew Lloyd Webber, and Tim Rice—were British. There are conflicting definitions for the PEGOT: some define it as including the Peabody Award, others as the Pulitzer Prize. As of 2024, Mel Brooks, Rita Moreno, Mike Nichols, and Barbra Streisand have achieved PEGOT status via Peabody wins, while Marvin Hamlisch and Richard Rodgers have achieved it via Pulitzer wins. The REGOT includes a Razzie Award; Alan Menken has a REGOT due to his Razzie win (with Jack Feldman) for Worst Original Song for "High Times, Hard Times" from Newsies, and Liza Minnelli has a REGOT if her non-competitive Grammy Legend Award is counted. Lady Gaga reordered the acronym as EGORT after hosting Saturday Night Live and joking about her win for Worst Screen Combo (with Joaquin Phoenix) from Joker: Folie à Deux. Publications such as Vulture have listed the REGOT as including an induction into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame; Elton John is the only person with such a REGOT, though Harry Belafonte and Quincy Jones would be included if non-competitive awards are counted. In 2018, Leah Collins of CBC Arts proposed a Canadian equivalent of the EGOT—comprising the Canadian Screen Awards (and predecessors Gemini and Genie Awards), the Juno Awards, and the Dora Mavor Moore Awards—referred to by Toronto-based game show Trivia Club as the "Two-Can-Ju-Do," with no individual having won in all four categories. In 2019, Caitlin Welsh of Nova Entertainment proposed the "LAHA" as an Australian equivalent—Logie Awards, ARIA Music Awards, Helpmann Awards, and AACTA Awards—with no winners of all four awards identified, though Noni Hazlehurst has received nominations in all four.

text: During the 2014–15 season, Eintracht Frankfurt's Alexander Meier was the league's top scorer, but the team struggled in 2015–16, finishing 16th and surviving only through a relegation playoff, where they defeated 1. FC Nürnberg 2–1 on aggregate. Niko Kovač was appointed coach in March 2016, and in his first full season, the team survived comfortably and reached the 2017 DFB-Pokal final, losing to Borussia Dortmund. In 2017–18, Eintracht reached their second consecutive DFB-Pokal final, winning 3–1 against heavy favourites Bayern Munich—Kovač had already agreed to join Bayern from the next season—and he was replaced by Adi Hütter. In 2018–19, Luka Jović, Ante Rebić, and Sébastien Haller formed an attacking trio that scored 41 league goals and 16 Europa League goals, earning the nickname "the Buffalo Herd," and Eintracht won all six group games in the Europa League against Lazio, Apollon Limassol, Marseille, Shakhtar Donetsk, Inter Milan, and Benfica, drawing both legs 1–1 in the semi-finals against Chelsea before losing on penalties at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea won the tournament, and Eintracht missed Champions League qualification after dropping from 4th to 7th. After Jović, Rebić, and Haller left in summer 2019, the team regressed in 2019–20 and failed to qualify for Europe, but returned to the Europa League with a 5th-place finish in 2020–21, after which Adi Hütter left for Borussia Mönchengladbach. In the 2021–22 Europa League, Eintracht topped their group, stunned Barcelona in the quarter-finals with a 3–0 lead at Camp Nou and won 3–2, with approximately 30,000 Frankfurt fans in attendance, and beat West Ham home and away in the semi-finals to reach their first European final since 1980. In the final at Seville's Ramón Sánchez Pizjuán Stadium, Frankfurt beat Rangers 5–4 on penalties after a 1–1 draw in extra-time, with Rafael Santos Borré scoring Eintracht's goal and the winning penalty; goalkeeper Kevin Trapp was named man of the match after making a crucial late save from Ryan Kent and saving Aaron Ramsey's penalty. Eintracht won the competition unbeaten, qualifying for the 2022–23 UEFA Champions League, their first appearance since 1960; they finished second in their group and advanced to the knockout stages, but lost in the round of 16 to S.S.C. Napoli. In the 2022–23 DFB-Pokal, the team reached the final on 3 June 2023, losing 2–0 to RB Leipzig, and a 7th-place finish secured qualification for the UEFA Europa Conference League. Since November 2024, the executive board consists of Axel Hellmann (CEO), Markus Krösche (head of sports), Julien Zamberk (head of finances), and Philipp Reschke (head of fan relations, merchandising and HR). The club crest originates from the coat of arms of Frankfurt, referencing the 13th-century one-headed Imperial Eagle, and evolved with little change until 1980, when a stylized black and white eagle was adopted; in 1999, during its centenary, the club re-adopted a more traditional eagle crest. Since 2005, Eintracht has had a living mascot, a golden eagle named Attila from the Hanau Zoo, who has been present at over 200 games. The official club colours—red, black, and white—come from the founding clubs Frankfurter FC Viktoria (red and white) and Frankfurter FC Kickers (black and white); red and white are from the city coat of arms, and black and white from Prussia. After the merger, both sets of colours were adopted, and since Kickers Offenbach wear red and white, Eintracht avoids that kit, preferring black and red or black and white; in the 2023–2024 season, the home kit is black and red. In the 2021–22 Europa League, Eintracht played an unbeaten campaign with an all-white kit, earning the nickname "la bestia blanca" (the white beast), a play on "la bestia negra" (the black beast), after knocking out Barcelona. The club is nicknamed "Die Adler" (The Eagles), derived from the logo, and supporters also use "SGE," from the old name Sportgemeinde Eintracht (Frankfurt), meaning "Sports Community Harmony." The nickname "Launische Diva" (Moody Diva) was common in the early 1990s when Eintracht defeated top teams but lost to weaker ones. "Schlappekicker" (Slipper Kickers) dates back to the 1920s, when J. & C. A. Schneider, a local slipper manufacturer, was a major backer. Green denotes the highest level of German football; yellow the second. The club's initial games from 1899 to 1906 were played on the former Hundswiese field, near Hessischer Rundfunk; in 1906, they established Victoriaplatz by Eschersheimer Landstraße, purchasing stands for 350 marks in 1908; from 1912, they moved to Roseggerstraße in Dornbusch, then to the former Riederwaldstadion in 1920 after merging with Frankfurter Turngemeinde von 1861. The stadium was inaugurated as Waldstadion in 1925 with the German championship final between FSV Frankfurt and 1. FC Nürnberg; it was renovated for the 2006 FIFA World Cup and has a maximum capacity of 59,500 for Bundesliga fixtures as of 2025. Though officially called Deutsche Bank Park, fans typically refer to it as Waldstadion. Eintracht Frankfurt U21 is the reserve team, previously known as U23 to emphasize its role as a youth-pro to professional link; the club dissolved the team after the 2013–14 season in the Regionalliga Süd. On 14 February 2022, the club applied to re-admit the reserves to the Hessenliga for the 2022–23 season, and in their first season back, Frankfurt II won the Hessenliga and was promoted to the Regionalliga Südwest, where they now play. The main rival is Kickers Offenbach, across the Main River, with the two clubs having played in the 1959 German championship final, which Eintracht won. Eintracht also has regional rivalries with Darmstadt 98 (Hesse derby) and with 1. FSV Mainz 05 and 1. FC Kaiserslautern in Rhineland-Palatinate. The original rival was FSV Frankfurt, with a fierce early rivalry that faded after World War II due to Eintracht's dominance and lack of contact; today, fan relations are generally friendly. In the 2011–12 season, Eintracht played FSV in a league match for the first time in nearly 50 years—the last being on 27 January 1962 in the Oberliga Süd—first on 21 August 2011 at Eintracht's stadium (due to FSV's Bornheimer Hang holding fewer than 11,000), which ended 4–0, and again on 18 February 2012, which ended 6–1. A friendship between Eintracht fan clubs and Oldham Athletic supporters has lasted over 30 years, with small sections visiting each other's grounds at least once a season. Eintracht also has an international friendship with Atalanta supporters. The sports club Eintracht Frankfurt e.V. has nineteen sections, including athletics, where Betty Heidler (2007 hammer throw world champion) and Olympians Andrea Bunjes, Ariane Friedrich, Kamghe Gaba, and Kathrin Klaas were members; the rugby union section reached the German championship final twice, in 1940 and 1965. Within football, the club directly manages only the youth system and the reserve team; professional footballers are managed by Eintracht Frankfurt Fußball-AG, a subsidiary of the parent club.

text: Eintracht Frankfurt e.V., based in Frankfurt, Hesse, is a German professional sports club founded on 8 March 1899. Its football club, established as Frankfurter Fußball-Club Victoria von 1899 and Frankfurter Fußball-Club Kickers von 1899, merged in May 1911 to form Frankfurter Fußball Verein (Kickers-Victoria), which later joined the gymnastics club Frankfurter Turngemeinde von 1861 in 1920 to create TuS Eintracht Frankfurt von 1861. The name "Eintracht" means 'harmony' or 'concord' and is equivalent to 'United' in English. In 1927, due to pressure from nationalistic gymnastics authorities, the football and gymnastics sections separated. The club has spent a total of 56 seasons in the top division of German football, making it the seventh longest continuously participating club in the Bundesliga. Eintracht is currently in the Bundesliga, the top tier of the German football league system, and has won the German championship once, the DFB-Pokal five times, the UEFA Europa League twice, and finished as runners-up in the European Cup once. It was one of the founding members of the Bundesliga in 1963 and played in the top division for 33 consecutive seasons, finishing in the top half of the table in most of those years. The club has 155,000 members, making it the fourth largest football club in Germany. Since 1925, the club has played at the Waldstadion, currently known as Deutsche Bank Park due to sponsorship. Eintracht has won or drawn more than three-quarters of their games and finished in the top half of the table in most seasons, despite having the highest number of losses in the league (657). With an average attendance of 47,942 since 2013, the club ranks eighth among the 36 Bundesliga and 2. Bundesliga teams for attendance. Charly Körbel, who made 602 appearances in the Bundesliga, spent his entire senior career as a defender with the club. The primary rival is Kickers Offenbach, though the two have only played two league matches in the last 40 years. In 2024, Eintracht Frankfurt has nearly 14,000 active athletes across over 50 sports, making it the largest multi-sports club in the world with a professional football team. The club won its first German championship in 1959, defeating rivals Kickers Offenbach 5–3 after extra time in front of 75,000 fans at Berlin's Olympiastadion. This victory earned them a place in the 1959–60 European Cup, where they defeated BSC Young Boys and Wiener Sport-Club to reach the semi-finals, winning 6–1 at home and 12–4 on aggregate against Rangers, who gave them a guard of honour. They lost 7–3 to Real Madrid in the final at Hampden Park, a match remembered for a hat-trick by Alfredo Di Stéfano and four goals by Ferenc Puskás. After 1959, Eintracht finished as runners-up in 1961 and 1962 in the Oberliga, missing the final both times. From 1973 to 1981, the club achieved its most successful period in the Bundesliga era, winning three DFB-Pokals and the UEFA Cup. The first DFB-Pokal title came in 1973–74, defeating Hamburger SV 3–1, with the final delayed until August 1974 due to the 1974 FIFA World Cup. They won again in 1975, beating MSV Duisburg 1–0, and reached the semi-finals of the European Cup Winners' Cup in 1975–76. Under coach Gyula Lóránt, Eintracht went unbeaten in the second half of the 1976–77 season, finishing fourth, only two points behind champions Borussia Mönchengladbach. Lóránt left for Bayern Munich, and Dettmar Cramer took over before being replaced by Otto Knefler, who left due to health issues. In January 1979, Friedel Rausch became head coach, and Cha Bum-kun joined in July, becoming the first Korean to play in Europe, scoring 12 goals in his debut season. text: El Anatsui, born on 4 February 1944 in Anyako, in the Volta Region of Ghana, is a Ghanaian sculptor who has spent much of his career in Nigeria. He gained international recognition for his "bottle-top installations," which consist of thousands of aluminum pieces collected from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire to form metallic, cloth-like wall sculptures. Though the materials appear stiff and sturdy, they are actually flexible, which aids in installation. Anatsui was included in the 2023 Time 100 list of the world's most influential people, with art historian Okeke-Agulu noting that his work transforms ordinary materials like printer’s plates or liquor-bottle caps into magnificent, globally displayed compositions. The youngest of his father’s 32 children, Anatsui lost his mother and was raised by his uncle; his first artistic experience was drawing letters on a chalkboard, which his school headmaster encouraged, and he viewed the forms as images rather than letters. He earned a B.A. in 1968 and a postgraduate diploma in Art Education in 1969, both from the College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST) in Kumasi. Influenced by artists like Oku Ampofo, Vincent Akwete Kofi, and Kofi Antubam, who rejected foreign influences in favor of indigenous art, Anatsui taught at Winneba Specialist Training College (now University of Education) after graduating and later moved to the University of Nigeria, Nsukka in 1975, becoming a senior lecturer in 1982, head of the Fine and Applied Arts department and full professor of sculpture in 1996, a role he held until 2011. He is affiliated with the Nsukka group and has built a global reputation while living and working in Nsukka. Anatsui noted that his education emphasized Western art, lacking focus on African culture, prompting him to visit the National Cultural Centre in Kumasi, where he encountered Adinkra, a system of signs and symbols, which introduced him to abstract art. In the 1970s, he worked in wood, carving trays and creating wall panels with Adinkra symbols and designs using hot rods, chain saws, gouges, flame, or paint. In the late 1970s, he began working in clay, exploring themes of fragility and transformation, particularly in broken pots that he saw as acquiring spiritual uses for ancestors and deities. He later explored food-related materials such as mortars and bottle tops. Much of his work uses found materials, emphasizing their history of use and the human hand’s imprint; he believes used objects carry energy from those who touched them, grounding his art in culture and environment. Bottle caps are especially favored because they resemble cloth, allowing both sculptural and painterly interpretations, and they reflect political and sociological contexts through brand names and colors. He sees the transformation of these materials—removed from their functional roles—as a way to generate reflection, thought, or wonder. Themes in his work include the destruction and reconstitution of materials as a metaphor for Africa’s colonial and post-colonial history, traditional West African textile motifs, and resistance to Western misinterpretations of African history. The concept of Sankofa ("go back and retrieve") is central to his practice, representing a return to African cultural roots as a path to self-discovery. His career began in Nsukka and expanded to Enugu, Lagos, and internationally. In 1990, he had his first major group show at the Studio Museum in Harlem and was featured in the exhibition "Contemporary African Artists: Changing Traditions," which ran for five years. He has exhibited globally, including at the Brooklyn Museum (2013), Clark Art Institute (2011), Rice University Art Gallery (2010), Metropolitan Museum of Art (2008–09), National Museum of African Art (Smithsonian, 2008), Fowler Museum (UCLA, 2007), Venice Biennale (1990 and 2007), Hayward Gallery (2005), Liverpool Biennial (2002), and the Arab Museum of Modern Art (2019) and Kunstmuseum Bern (2020). In 1995, he held his first solo exhibition outside Africa in London, where he demonstrated African art in non-traditional, conceptually rich ways. In 2005, he appeared in the permanent collection at the de Young Museum in San Francisco and had his first display of metal sheets at Skoto Gallery in New York, which popularized his bottle-cap works. In 2006 and 2007, he was invited to the Venice Biennale, where he created two hanging metal tapestries displayed at Palazzo Fortuny, including Dusasa, which featured golds, reds, and blacks and created a gentle, unique aesthetic. Art curator Robert Storr described the series as exalting and distinct from postwar European art. Anatsui began referring to his metal works as "hangings" rather than "cloths" during this period. A 2010 retrospective, "When I Last Wrote to You About Africa," opened at the Royal Ontario Museum and toured the U.S. for three years. A major exhibition, "Gravity & Grace: Monumental Works by El Anatsui," premiered at the Brooklyn Museum in 2013 and traveled to the Des Moines Art Center (2013–14) and the Bass Museum of Art (2014). A career-spanning survey, "Triumphant Scale," organized by Okwui Enwezor and Chika Okeke-Agulu, opened in March 2019 at Haus der Kunst in Munich and traveled to the Arab Museum of Modern Art (Doha) and Kunstmuseum Bern (2020). In 2023, Anatsui was selected for the Hyundai Commission at Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, where his work "Behind the Red Moon," made from thousands of metal bottle tops and fragments, addresses the transatlantic slave trade and will be on view through April 14, 2024. He was elected to the International Society for Education through Art (InSEA) world council in 1992, a founding member and fellow of the Forum for African Arts in 2000, and a member of the International Selection Committee for the Dakar Biennale in 2000. He was a fellow at the Civitella Ranieri Foundation in 2001. Anatsui won an honorable mention at the First Ghana National Art Competition in 1968 and was named Best Student of the Year at KNUST in 1969. In 1983, he received a commission for two large terrazzo-surfaced cement sculptures on the Nsukka campus. In 1984, he was invited to the Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste residency in Cuxhaven, West Germany. In 1990, he received an honorable mention at the 44th Venice Biennale and was included in the documentary Nigerian Art-Kindred Spirits. In 2015, he was awarded the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale, and in 2017, he received the Praemium Imperiale, becoming the first Ghanaian to win this international art prize.

text: Dame Elisabeth Joy Murdoch, Lady Murdoch AC DBE (née Greene; 8 February 1909 – 5 December 2012), was an Australian philanthropist and matriarch of the Murdoch family. She married Sir Keith Murdoch in 1928, 23 years his junior, and inherited the bulk of his fortune upon his death in 1952. She was the mother of Rupert Murdoch, international media proprietor, and had other children: Janet Calvert-Jones AO (born 1939), Anne Kantor AO (1937–2022), and Helen Handbury AO (1929–2004). Born in Melbourne on 8 February 1909, she was the youngest of three daughters of Marie Grace de Lancey (née Forth) and Rupert Greene; her grandfather, William Henry Greene, was an Irish railway engineer who emigrated to Australia and married Fanny, the fourth of George Govett’s 10 daughters. Her mother’s ancestors were Scottish and English, with one maternal great-grandfather, Frederick Forth, serving as a lieutenant governor in the West Indies. She was educated at St Catherine's School in Toorak and Clyde School in Woodend. Before marriage, she volunteered with the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. She joined the management committee of the Royal Children's Hospital in 1933, serving as its president from 1954 to 1965, and was designated to succeed her predecessor Ella Latham; she oversaw the hospital’s relocation from Carlton to a new campus in Parkville. In 1961, she was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire, Civil Division (CBE) for her work at the hospital, and in 1963, a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire, Civil Division (DBE) for her role in building the new children's hospital. In 1989, she received a Companion of the Order of Australia, Civil Division (AC) for community services, and in 2001, the Centenary Medal for philanthropic contributions to the Australian arts. She was a Life Governor of the Royal Women's Hospital, patron of the Murdoch Children's Research Institute and the Australian American Association (Victoria), a founding member of the EW Tipping Foundation and the Deafness Foundation of Victoria, and the first woman on the council of trustees of the National Gallery of Victoria. She was also a founding member of the Victorian Tapestry Workshop and a member of the Patrons Council of the Epilepsy Foundation of Victoria. Her garden, "Cruden Farm" at Langwarrin, designed by Edna Walling, is one of Australia’s finest landscape gardens and is open to the public. In 1983, she was awarded an honorary Doctorate of Laws by the University of Melbourne and became a fellow of Trinity College, Melbourne in 2000. A portrait of her by Christopher Pyett, adapted by Normana Wight and woven by Merrill Dumbrell, was commissioned for the National Portrait Gallery in 2000. In 2001, she was inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women and a rose, Treloars, was named after her. A Tasmanian Boronia species, Boronia elisabethiae, was named in her honour following donations to the Royal Botanic Gardens in Melbourne. In 2002, she received recognition from the French government for funding an Auguste Rodin exhibition in Melbourne. In 2003, she joined Philanthropy Australia as a life member and was awarded the key to the City of Melbourne. In 2004, Langwarrin Secondary College was renamed Elisabeth Murdoch College. In 2005, at age 96, she received the Victorian of the Year award. In 2009, the main performance venue of the Melbourne Recital Centre was named in her honour, and she was elected an Honorary Fellow of the Australian Academy of the Humanities. In 2010, Geelong Grammar School named a new girls' boarding house after her. In January 2007, at age 97 years and 11 months, she surpassed Dame Alice Chisholm as Australia’s longest-lived dame. She was also a patron of the Australian Family Association. She died in her sleep at Cruden Farm, Langwarrin, Victoria, on 5 December 2012, at the age of 103. At the time of her death, she had 77 living descendants.

In 1994, she was elected to the first post-apartheid South African Parliament at the age of 79 and served for five years until June 1999, becoming South Africa's longest-serving parliamentarian. Her autobiography, Call Me Woman (1985), won the CNA Literary Award, making her the first black writer to receive South Africa's leading literary prize. Born Nnoseng Ellen Serasengwe in Thaba 'Nchu, Orange Free State, she came from an educated, politically active family. Her maternal grandfather, Jeremaiah Makgothi, was taken to the Cape in circa 1875 to attend the Lovedale Institute, where he qualified as a teacher, worked as a court interpreter, and served as a Methodist lay preacher; he was the only layman to work with Robert Moffat on the translation of the Bible into Setswana. Both Makgothi and her father, Philip S. Mefare, were politically active—Makgothi was secretary of the Orange Free State branch of the South African Native National Congress, and Mefare was a member of its successor, the African National Congress. Kuzwayo began her schooling at a school built by Makgothi on his farm in Thabapatchoa, about 12 miles from Tweespruit, and attended Adams College, Amanzimtoti, before completing a teacher training course at Lovedale College in Fort Hare, graduating at age 22. She married Ernest Moloto in her late twenties, had two sons, and after enduring abuse, fled to Johannesburg. She had a part as a shebeen queen alongside Sidney Poitier in the 1951 film Cry, the Beloved Country. After her first marriage ended, she married Godfrey Kuzwayo in 1950. She taught in the Transvaal until 1952, when she gave up teaching due to the introduction of the Bantu Education Act, 1953, which limited black education opportunities. She then trained as a social worker from 1953 to 1955. After the 1976 Soweto uprising, she was the only woman on a committee of 10 tasked with organizing civic affairs in Soweto, and was detained for five months in 1977–78 under the Prevention of Terrorism Act; she later recounted her arrest in her 1996 testimony to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. She also served as president of the Black Consumer Union of South Africa and the Maggie Magaba Trust. In 1979, she was named Woman of the Year by The Star, and was nominated again in 1984. In 1987, she received an honorary doctorate of Laws from the University of the Witwatersrand, becoming the first black woman to receive such an honor from the university, and also received honorary doctorates from the University of Natal and the University of Port Elizabeth. She was awarded the Order of Meritorious Service by Nelson Mandela in 1999. With director Betty Wolpert, she co-produced the documentary films Awake from Mourning (1982) and Tsiamelo –– A Place of Goodness (1983), based on the story of her family's land dispossession. Kuzwayo died in Johannesburg at the age of 91 from complications of diabetes, survived by her sons Bobo and Justice Moloto, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren. A South African marine research ship, the Ellen Khuzwayo, was named after her and launched in 2007.

text: Elsie Tu's worldview was shaped by her father's influence, leading her in her youth to believe that "I could at least be good and useful in life"; her father died when she was in China. She married William Elliott, who was eight years her junior, and worked with the Plymouth Brethren missionary group in 1946. In 1947, she traveled to China with her husband, but grew increasingly disillusioned with his fundamentalism and their church, describing the period as "the lowest point in [her] life" and considering suicide. The couple separated during an abortive trip back to England, and she returned to Hong Kong alone, later divorcing him in 1964. In Hong Kong, she met her second husband, Andrew Tu Hsueh-kwei, who had come from Inner Mongolia in the 1950s. They became working partners at the Mu Kuang English School, with Andrew teaching Chinese and Elliott teaching all other Form 1 subjects; despite cultural and language differences, Elsie found Andrew's ideas brought her back to her father's values. In 1985, 30 years after meeting, they married when Elsie was 71 and Andrew was 63, remaining married until Andrew died in 2001. Andrew was also a social activist and leader of the Chinese Alliance for Commemoration of the Sino-Japanese War Victims, which demands justice, reparations, and apologies for victims of the Second Sino-Japanese War. Tu authored two volumes of autobiography and other works; Colonial Hong Kong in the Eyes of Elsie Tu was published in 2003, and Shouting at the Mountain: A Hong Kong Story of Love and Commitment, co-written with Andrew Tu, was completed after his death in 2001 and published in 2005. She also completed the publication of her husband's autobiography of his childhood in Inner Mongolia, Camel Bells in the Windy Desert. In the 1960s, Tu was recognized as a champion fighting for the underprivileged and against corruption; Chief Executive Leung Chun-ying praised her "passion and devotion to Hong Kong and her tremendous contributions to social reform and development" after her death, and Chief Secretary Carrie Lam recalled meeting her during her university days, describing her as an exemplary champion of social justice who commanded respect. Founding chairman of the Democratic Party Martin Lee praised her as a pioneer in fighting for democracy, and other democrats such as Lau Chin-shek, Lee Wing-tat, Fred Li Wah-ming, and Frederick Fung acknowledged that their involvement in social activism was inspired or assisted by Elsie Tu. Tu received numerous honours, including the Ramon Magsaysay Award for Government Service in 1975, a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in 1977 for her anti-corruption work, and the Grand Bauhinia Medal (GBM) in 1997 as one of the first recipients of the highest honour in the SAR award system. She also received honorary degrees: an honorary doctoral degree in Social Science from the University of Hong Kong in 1988, honorary doctoral degrees in Laws from the Hong Kong Polytechnic University and in Social Science from the Open Learning Institute of Hong Kong in 1994, and honorary doctoral degrees in Civil Law from both Armstrong College (later Newcastle University) and Durham University in 1996.

text: Elsie Tu CBE GBM (née Hume; Chinese: 杜葉錫恩; 2 June 1913 – 8 December 2015), formerly known as Elsie Elliott, was a British-born Hong Kong social activist who served as an elected member of the Urban Council of Hong Kong from 1963 to 1995 and a member of the Legislative Council of Hong Kong from 1988 to 1995. Born on 2 June 1913 in Newcastle upon Tyne, England, into a working-class family of John and Florence Hume, she was the second of four children. After attending Benwell Secondary Girls' School and Heaton Secondary School, she studied at Armstrong College, graduating in 1937 with a Bachelor of Arts. From 1937 to 1947, she worked as a schoolteacher in Halifax, where she volunteered in Civil Defence during the Second World War. She converted to Christianity in 1932 during her university years. In 1946, she married William Elliott and moved to China in 1947 as a missionary with the Christian Missions in Many Lands, stationed in Yifeng. After the Chinese Communist Party took power in 1949 and expelled foreign missionaries from mainland China, she relocated to Hong Kong, living in an illegal apartment in the Wong Tai Sin squatter community known as Kai Tak New Village, where she observed corruption involving triad protection money. Disillusioned with her husband's rigid Protestant faith and the Plymouth Brethren's refusal to engage in social issues, she left the church in 1955 and divorced him in 1964. She lived briefly in a kitchen in a Kowloon Walled City tenement and founded Mu Kuang English School in 1954 in an old army tent near Kai Tak, starting with 30 pupils; she remained principal until 2000. The school now serves 1,300 children in low-income families on Kung Lok Road in Kwun Tong. She met Andrew Tu Hsueh-kwei at the school, who became her husband 30 years later. Elliott was shocked by the injustices in Hong Kong, including child labour and poor working conditions, and wrote to The Guardian, prompting UK Parliament debate and eventually leading to labour reforms. She became politically active, winning her first Urban Council seat in 1963, and later served as vice-chairman from 1986 until her defeat in 1995, consistently receiving the highest votes. She was also the spokeswoman for the United Nations Association of Hong Kong, advocating for self-government. In 1966, she opposed a proposed 5-cent to 25-cent increase in Star Ferry fares, collecting over 20,000 signatories and flying to London to protest, which led to a hunger strike by So Sau-chung and eventually the Kowloon riots. She faced accusations of inciting the riots, dubbed the "Elliott riot," and was subjected to official inquiries. She campaigned against triad protection money and police corruption, reporting minibus rackets and corruption to various officials, including Governor Murray MacLehose and ICAC Director G. A. Harknett, and helped Mak Pui-yuen, who was victimised for reporting corruption. Her activism contributed to the establishment of the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) in 1974. In 1979, she co-founded the Association for the Promotion of Public Justice (APPJ) with Andrew Tu, which later established a Filipino Overseas Workers Group. She advocated for gay rights, urging decriminalisation as in the UK in 1967, though the government cited local opposition; homosexuality was decriminalised in Hong Kong in 1991. In 1980, after John MacLennan, a police inspector, was shot in his home during an investigation into homosexuality, she suggested he was persecuted for knowing too much and corresponded with MacLehose and other officials, leading to a Commission of Inquiry. In 1980, she was found under surveillance by the Standing Committee on Pressure Groups (SCOPG), but she remained unbothered, stating she had done nothing wrong. She was appointed to the HKSAR Basic Law Consultative Committee in 1985 and, when the Urban Council became an electoral college in 1985, she was elected to the Legislative Council in 1988, serving until 1995, during which she chaired the House Committee from 1991 to 1995 and remained the most popular legislator. In the lead-up to the 1997 handover, she supported a gradual pace of democratisation preferred by the Chinese government, opposing Governor Chris Patten's electoral reforms and criticising him as a hypocrite. In the March 1995 Urban Council election, she lost to Szeto Wah by 2,397 votes, and in the September 1995 Legislative Council election, she lost again in Kowloon East to Szeto Wah, supported by the pro-Beijing Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong (DAB). She was appointed to the Beijing-controlled Provisional Legislative Council from December 1996 to June 1998, serving on the Selection Committee responsible for electing the first Chief Executive. After the Provisional Legislative Council was dissolved in 1998, her political career ended. She stepped away from active politics but continued to comment on social issues and write critical articles. In 2002, she supported the enactment of the anti-subversion law under Basic Law Article 23, and in 2003, she publicly endorsed Regina Ip, who promoted the law, during the 1 July Protest with over 500,000 demonstrators. In 2013, she criticised widening income inequality and expressed sympathy for dock workers striking against billionaire Li Ka-shing's Hutchison Whampoa, marking her 100th birthday in June 2013. The Mu Kuang alumni established the Elsie Tu Education Fund in her honour. She died on 8 December 2015 at the age of 102 from pneumonia-related complications at Kwun Tong United Christian Hospital. All three former Chief Executives—Tung Chee-hwa, Donald Tsang, and Leung Chun-ying—were pallbearers at her funeral on 20 December, and her ashes were buried with those of her husband, Andrew Tu, at the Cape Collinson Crematorium in Chai Wan. Her father, John Hume, a grocer's assistant who fought in the First World War and was gassed, profoundly influenced her conscience and world-view, instilling in her a hatred of war and compassion for people, as well as a left-leaning perspective on religion, Marxism, and workers' rights. She married William Elliott, eight years her junior, and described the period as the lowest point in her life, eventually divorcing him in 1964. She later married Andrew Tu Hsueh-kwei, who came to Hong Kong from Inner Mongolia in the 1950s, and they worked together at Mu Kuang English School, with Andrew teaching Chinese and Elliott teaching other Form 1 subjects. She believed Andrew's ideas reminded her of her father's values.

text: The Embraer EMB 110 Bandeirante, meaning "pioneer," is a Brazilian twin-turboprop light transport aircraft designed by Embraer for both military and civil use. It was designed by French engineer Max Holste in accordance with specifications issued by the Brazilian Ministry of Aeronautics in 1965, aiming to create a general-purpose aircraft with low operational costs and high reliability for civilian and military operations. The aircraft was to have turboprop engines, a low-mounted wing, and sufficient capacity for eight personnel, based on a study of Brazilian commercial air traffic and existing airport infrastructure. This specification, known as IPD-6504, significantly influenced the aircraft's design. Early development predated the founding of Embraer, which was established in August 1969; construction of the prototype was supervised by Brazilian aeronautical engineer Ozires Silva, who also played a key role in founding the company. The first prototype, designated YC-95, made its maiden flight on 26 October 1968 from São José dos Campos Airport, piloted by José Mariotto Ferreira and accompanied by flight engineer Michel Cury, landing after approximately 50 minutes. Prior to this, 110,000 project hours were logged, producing 12,000 manufacturing drawings and 22,000 hours of structural and aerodynamic calculations, with an estimated 282,000 hours spent on manufacturing and tooling. The prototype was officially presented four days later, with a repeat of the maiden flight. The positive results led to the approval of production in mid-1969, with Embraer assuming responsibility on 2 January 1970. Two additional prototypes, designated EMB 100, flew on 19 October 1969 and 29 June 1970, respectively; however, due to shifting market conditions, the EMB 100 was quickly redesigned into the EMB 110 Bandeirante, which featured greater capacity and technological improvements. In May 1970, the Brazilian Air Force (FAB) placed an initial order for 80 production aircraft. The Bandeirante received its Brazilian airworthiness certificate in late 1972 and entered service with the Brazilian airline Transbrasil on 16 April 1973. A typical configuration seats between 15 and 21 passengers and is flown by two pilots; the EMB 110P1A/41 model has a length of 15.1 metres (50 ft), a height of 4.92 metres (16.1 ft), and a wingspan of 15.33 metres (50.3 ft). It has a maximum cruising speed of 411 km/h (222 kn), an economical cruising speed of 341 km/h (184 kn), achieving a range of 1,964 km (1,060 nmi) with 45 minutes of reserve fuel, and a service ceiling of 21,500 feet (6,600 m). During the 1970s, Embraer developed the EMB 120 Brasilia, an enlarged derivative with a pressurized cabin, greater speed, and capacity for up to 30 passengers, leading to the decision to halt further EMB 110 development and focus on the EMB 120. Between 1968 and 1990, Embraer produced a total of 494 aircraft in various configurations for diverse roles. The passenger model first flew on 9 August 1972 and entered commercial service on 16 April 1973 with Transbrasil. Ryanair operated a 15-seat EMB 110 starting on 8 July 1985, continuing until 1989. By October 2018, about 150 EMB 110s were still in service with airlines, air taxis, government entities, and air forces worldwide. Production ended in 1990, with the EMB 110 being superseded by the EMB 120 Brasilia. Deliveries to the Brazilian Air Force began in February 1973, with the first delivery on 9 February 1973. Two EMB 111A Patrulha maritime patrol aircraft were leased to the Argentine Navy during the Falklands War as a stop-gap between the retirement of the last Lockheed SP-2H Neptune and the introduction of modified Lockheed L-188 Electras. On 15 December 2010, the Brazilian Air Force flew its first upgraded EMB 110, designated C/P-95, equipped with modern avionics from Israeli firm Elbit Systems' Brazilian subsidiary, Aeroeletronica; at that time, the FAB had 96 active EMB 110s, which reduced to 48 by 2017. In 2020, 39 Bandeirantes were still in airline service with 15 operators: 31 in North/South America, 1 in Africa, and 7 in Asia Pacific & Middle East.

text: The emerald ash borer (Agrilus planipennis), a green buprestid beetle native to temperate northeastern Asia—including Russia, Mongolia, northern China, Japan, and Korea—is native to that region where it typically occurs at low densities and does not cause significant damage to ash trees (Fraxinus spp.). Females lay eggs in bark crevices, flakes, or cracks, and the eggs, measuring 0.6 to 1.0 mm in diameter and initially white, turn reddish-brown if fertile, hatch about two weeks later, and the larvae chew through the bark to feed on the phloem, cambium, and outer xylem, creating long serpentine galleries. The larvae go through four instars, with fully mature fourth-instar larvae being 26 to 32 mm long; they excavate J-shaped chambers in the sapwood or outer bark in the fall, where they develop into pupae and emerge as adults the following spring. Adults are bright metallic green, about 8.5 mm long and 1.6 mm wide, with darker green elytra that may have copper hues, and a small spine at the tip of the abdomen; they have serrate antennae beginning at the fourth segment. Adults emerge after 400–500 degree-days above 10 °C (50 °F), peaking at around 1,000 degree-days, feed on ash leaves for one week before mating, and males locate females by visual cues, dropping directly onto them to mate, with mating lasting up to 50 minutes and females mating with multiple males. A typical female lives about six weeks and lays 40–70 eggs, with longer-lived females laying up to 200. Larvae can overwinter in their galleries and may require an additional summer of feeding before overwintering again, with a two-year life cycle more common in cool climates like European Russia. The beetle is invasive in North America, where it was first identified in Canton, Michigan in 2002 (though possibly present since the late 1980s), likely introduced via shipping materials such as packing crates, and has a core population in Michigan and surrounding states and provinces, spreading to Ontario, northern Louisiana, Nebraska, New Brunswick, Colorado, and the Pacific Northwest (Oregon), with a population found in Moscow, Russia in 2003, spreading westward at up to 40 km (25 mi) per year and expected to reach central Europe between 2031 and 2036. It has spread to far eastern Ukraine from Russia and is not recorded in the European Union as of 2019. In North America, it primarily infests green ash (F. pennsylvanica), black ash (F. nigra), white ash (F. americana), and blue ash (F. quadrangulata), with blue ash showing higher resistance due to high tannin content in its leaves, a trait absent in most American ash species except blue ash. In Europe, F. excelsior is the main host, moderately resistant to infestation. The beetle can also infest non-ash species such as white fringe tree and Olea europaea (in lab settings), though it is unclear if these trees were healthy when infested. Ash trees in pure stands or in landscaping are more vulnerable due to environmental stresses like compacted soil, pollution, road salt, and urban heat, and because most landscaping ashes come from a few cultivars with low genetic diversity. Damage occurs as larval feeding disrupts nutrient and water transport, effectively girdling the tree and killing it; stressed trees may regenerate via stump sprouting or produce higher seed crops. Without natural suppressors like resistant trees, predators, or parasitoid wasps present in its native range, populations grow rapidly and all ash trees in an area are expected to die within 10 years. Every North American ash species is susceptible, though some Asian ash species like F. baroniana, F. chinensis, F. floribunda, F. mandshurica, and F. platypoda are resistant. In North America, the beetle has killed tens of millions of ash trees and threatens to kill most of the 8.7 billion ash trees, eliminating nearly all ash trees in the National Capital Region in nine years, reducing the density from 17–18 per hectare to 5–6 per hectare and transforming ash-dominated swamplands into shrublands, impacting wildlife. The loss of ash affects soil nutrients, increases invasive plants, and alters species that depend on ash. Control efforts include monitoring via visual surveys and traps using purple or green colors or volatile pheromones, girdling trees as trap trees, and quarantines restricting transport of ash firewood or live plants without inspection or treatment. Infested trees are often removed in urban areas, with replacements using non-ash species like maple, oak, or linden, and in rural areas, trees may be harvested for lumber or firewood under quarantine. Insecticides such as azadirachtin, imidacloprid, emamectin benzoate, and dinotefuran are used, with dinotefuran and imidacloprid being systemic and effective for one to three years; treatments are typically applied via direct injection or soil drench and are mainly used in urban areas with high-value trees, though not feasible for large forested areas. Insecticide use does not stop damage progression. The U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service ended all EAB quarantine activities on 14 December 2020 due to ineffectiveness, shifting focus to biological controls. Government agencies in the U.S. and Canada use the native parasitoid wasp Cerceris fumipennis for biological surveillance—volunteers catch the wasps as they return with beetles, indicating infestation—without significantly reducing beetle populations. The native range of the emerald ash borer in Asia was surveyed for parasitoid species that target the beetle without attacking other insects, in hopes they could suppress populations when introduced.

text: An emoticon, a portmanteau of "emotion" and "icon," is a pictorial representation of a facial expression using characters such as punctuation marks, numbers, and letters to convey a person's feelings, mood, or reaction without detailed description. ASCII emoticons have roots dating back hundreds of years, with early examples including Robert Herrick’s 1648 poem "Tumble me down, and I will sit Upon my ruins, (smiling yet:)"—though experts question whether the colon was intentionally used to represent a smile. In the 17th century, punctuation like colons and semicolons were often placed within parentheses, as seen in Richard Baxter’s 1653 work with 14 instances of ":)". Typographical art using punctuation to express emotions appeared in newspapers as early as 1881, and in 1912, Ambrose Bierce proposed a bracket "‿" to represent a smiling face, while in 1936, Alan Gregg suggested using brackets and other punctuation to depict various moods. A 1953 New York Herald Tribune article used a dash and right bracket to represent a tongue in cheek, and MAD magazine in 1962 featured typewriter-generated artwork with emoticon-like elements. In the 1970s, a student at the University of Illinois developed pictograms resembling smiling faces on the PLATO IV system, likely in 1972, which Mary Kalantzis and Bill Cope consider the first emoticons. In 1982, computer scientist Scott Fahlman proposed the use of ASCII symbols, specifically the smiley :-) and frown :-(, on the Carnegie Mellon University bulletin board system to convey humor or sarcasm, and this protocol became widely adopted. The emoticon spread to ARPANET and Usenet, with other suggestions including * and &, and the smiley became integral to digital communication. In 1996, The Smiley Company, founded by Nicolas Loufrani and his father Franklin, launched The Smiley Dictionary, cataloging over 500 ASCII emoticons, which removed the hyphen to create :) instead of :-), influencing modern usage. Loufrani later created graphical representations of emoticons, registered in the U.S. Copyright Office in 1997 and released as GIFs in 1998, and developed a set of 640 icons published in 2001 and 2002. These portrait emoticons, which include hand gestures like white gloves, became the foundation for modern emojis. In 2007, Google began petitioning the Unicode Technical Committee (UTC) to standardize emojis, leading to a 2009 proposal with 625 new emoji characters, including many emoticon-style designs. The Smiley Company auctioned an NFT of 42 original graphical emoticons in 2022, with proceeds going to its non-profit arm. Emoticons and emojis are often confused, but most commonly used emojis are emoticons representing emotions. In 2024, the BBC reported that two of the top three emojis were portrait emoticons. Scott Fahlman auctioned his original 1982 emoticons as NFTs in 2021, selling for $237,500. In Western usage, emoticons typically have eyes on the left, followed by a nose and mouth, with the two-character version :) being very popular. Variants include :( for sadness, :(( for extreme sadness, :'( for weeping, :"> for a blush, ;) for a wink, :D for a grin, :P for a tongue-out expression, and :-> for a smug look. The combination <3 represents a heart, </3 a broken heart, :O shock, :/ melancholy, and :| neutrality. Crinkled eyes in XD or XDDDD suggest amusement. The equal sign = is used for eyes as in =), and the hyphen is often omitted. Younger users increasingly use :) without a hyphen, a shift linguists interpret as a form of covert prestige. In some countries, keyboard layouts influence emoticon use: Scandinavia uses =), and in Cyrillic-using regions, the right parenthesis ) is used as a smiley, with multiple parentheses indicating greater happiness. The shrug emoticon ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ uses the Japanese katakana character ツ. Kaomoji, popularized in Japan on ASCII NET in 1986, are distinct from the Scott Fahlman movement and evolved into forms like owo, uwu, and TwT, especially in anime and furry communities. Users of 2channel developed emoticons using scripts like Kannada, such as ಠ_ಠ for disapproval and ಥ for a tearing eye, which spread to 4chan and other Western sites. In South Korea, emoticons use Hangul letters, with consonants like ㅅ, ㅁ, or ㅂ for the mouth/nose and ㅇ, ㅎ, or ㅍ for eyes, and vowels like ㅜ and ㅠ for crying, as in ㅜㅜ. Semicolons and carets are common, with -;/ indicating sweating. The character 囧 (U+56E7), meaning "patterned window," was used as an emoticon as early as January 20, 2005, and can be combined with Orz, such as 囧rz. Other variants include 崮, 莔, 商, and 囧興.

text: The English Ladies' Football Association (ELFA) was established in 1921 in response to the Football Association (FA)’s ban on women's football, with its founding meeting held in Liverpool on 10 December 1921, attended by representatives from about 30 women's teams. The ELFA was formed to support women footballers, popularise the game among women, and assist charity, and initially included a league of 57 amateur teams. Leonard Bridgett, manager and coach of Stoke Ladies, was elected as its first president. W. Henley was appointed as Secretary of the Association's pro team and helped organise a subsequent meeting in Blackburn on 17 December, where 57 clubs attended and many others expressed interest. The ELFA approved changes to rules to accommodate women players, including adjustments to pitch sizes and ball usage. On 7 January 1922, a meeting in Manchester approved the ball and pitch dimensions and saw the presentation of a cup for the Ladies' English Cup Competition. The ELFA also arranged a representative team for a match against Grimsby and District Ladies on 21 January. On 18 February 1922, a council meeting in Birmingham removed the Northern Union’s ground ban for ELFA-affiliated clubs and organised the draw for the first round of the ELFA Cup competition. The competition saw 23 clubs participate, with matches held on 18 March 1922 (first round), 22 April 1922 (second round), 20 May 1922 (third round), and a semi-final. The ELFA Cup was won by Stoke Ladies, who defeated Doncaster and Bentley Ladies 3–1 on 24 June 1922. The ELFA folded within a year, and women continued playing in local parks and dog-tracks without support from the FA, lacking money, infrastructure, coaches, or pitches—restrictions that persisted for fifty years until 1971. Women's football had existed before World War I but gained momentum during the war when women, especially in munitions factories, took on male roles and played football during breaks, leading to the formation of organised teams for war charity fundraising. The Munitionettes' Cup was established in August 1917, with Blyth Spartans as the first winners. After the war, factories closed and women were pressured to return to traditional roles, and football was deemed unladylike and dangerous by medical experts. On 5 December 1921, the FA formally cited concerns about football's unsuitability for women and requested clubs to refuse use of their grounds for women's matches. Despite its short lifespan, the ELFA laid the foundation for the revival of women's football. Preston Ladies competed in the British Ladies' Football World Championship at least twice in the 1930s, winning in 1937 by a 5–1 score and losing in 1939 to Edinburgh Ladies 5–2. A successor, the Women's Football Association (WFA), was formed in 1969, promoting a national England team and a premier league, though it remained voluntary with limited resources and often rescheduled or cancelled matches. In the 1970s, international recommendations and the Sex Discrimination Act of 1975 (with a clause exempting sports) helped advance the cause, but the FA only lifted its ban on women's football in 1992. In March 2018, the National Football Museum opened an extension to its permanent gallery dedicated to women's football, including the English Ladies Football Association Winner's Medal awarded to Lilian Bridgett of Stoke Ladies in 1922.

text: A solar equinox occurs when the Sun appears directly above the equator, rising due east and setting due west, happening twice annually around 20 March and 23 September. This event is also defined as the moment when Earth's equatorial plane passes through the center of the Sun's disk and when Earth's rotation axis is perpendicular to the Sun-Earth line, with no tilt toward or away from the Sun. Modern definitions use the Sun's ecliptic longitude, with equinoxes occurring when the apparent geocentric longitude is 0° and 180°. The term derives from Latin *aequinoctium*, meaning "equal night," as daytime and nighttime are approximately equal globally, though not exactly due to the Sun's angular size, atmospheric refraction, and rapid changes in day length near the equinoxes. A properly aligned sundial shows 12 hours of daylight. In the Northern Hemisphere, the March equinox is known as the vernal or spring equinox and marks the start of spring in many cultures, including the Assyrian, Hindu, and Persian calendars, while the September equinox is the autumnal or fall equinox marking the beginning of autumn; in the Southern Hemisphere, these names are reversed. The March equinox is called the northward equinox, as the Sun's declination crosses the celestial equator northward, and the September equinox is the southward equinox, with the declination crossing southward. Equinoxes alternate with solstices, and leap years cause slight variations in dates. Daylight increases most rapidly at the vernal equinox and decreases most rapidly at the autumnal equinox. The solar terminator is perpendicular to the equator, resulting in equal illumination of both hemispheres. For about four days, both the North and South Poles experience daylight; for example, in 2021, sunrise on the North Pole occurred on 18 March 07:09 UTC and sunset on the South Pole on 22 March 13:08 UTC, while sunrise on the South Pole was on 20 September 16:08 UTC and sunset on the North Pole on 24 September 22:30 UTC. The subsolar point is on the equator during equinoxes, crossing northward at March and southward at September. Julius Caesar set 25 March as the spring equinox in the Julian calendar in 45 BC, but due to a 11.3-minute annual drift, by 300 AD it had shifted to about 21 March and by the 1580s to 11 March. Pope Gregory XIII introduced the Gregorian calendar to correct this, reducing leap years from every 100 years to 97 every 400 years, maintaining the vernal equinox near 21 March. Despite this, a residual variation of ±27 hours remains. The dates of equinoxes shift over the 400-year Gregorian cycle; in the 21st century, the earliest March equinox was 19 March 2096 and the latest 21 March 2003, while the earliest September equinox was 21 September 2096 and the latest 23 September 2003 (Universal Time). On equinox, the Sun's center spends roughly equal time above and below the horizon, making day and night about equal, though sunrise and sunset are defined as when the Sun's upper limb is level with the horizon, resulting in days being about 14 minutes longer than nights at the equator and longer near the poles. The real equality of day and night occurs only at latitudes far from the equator, with seasonal differences of at least 7 minutes, and happens a few days before the spring equinox and after the fall equinox in mid-latitudes. The equilux—the date when day and night are exactly equal—is a neologism from the 1980s, gaining recognition in the 21st century, and is rare due to rapid day length changes, with mid-latitude equilux occurring a few days before spring and after fall equinoxes. The March to September interval is about 186 days, and September to March is about 179 days, making the polar day at the North Pole about 7 days longer than at the South Pole. Mirror-image conjugate auroras have been observed during equinoxes. Equinoxes are sometimes considered the start of spring and autumn, with traditional harvest festivals celebrated on these dates. In Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan, and Central Asia, Nowruz, the Persian New Year, is celebrated on the northern hemisphere's spring equinox. Religious architecture, such as Angkor Wat in Cambodia, is often aligned with equinox events. Catholic churches have traditionally oriented their buildings to the equinox, following Charles Borromeo's recommendations. Around equinoxes, geostationary satellites experience temporary disruptions due to the Sun being directly behind them, causing solar noise that degrades or disrupts signals, lasting from minutes to an hour, with larger antennas experiencing shorter outages. Satellites also face power issues during equinoxes because they pass through Earth's shadow, relying on batteries for longer durations than at other times. Equinoxes occur on any planet with a tilted axis; Saturn's equinox, when its rings are edge-on to the Sun, happens every 14.7 years and was most recently on 6 May 2025, with minimal sunlight and more planetshine than solar light. Mars's most recent equinoxes were on 12 January 2024 (northern autumn) and 26 December 2022 (northern spring).

Oja is a Fellow of the International Association for Pattern Recognition and the IEEE, and a member of the Finnish Academy of Sciences. He served as chairman of the European Neural Network Society from 2000 to 2005 and as chairman of the Academy of Finland’s Research Council for Natural Sciences and Engineering from 2007 to 2012. In 2019, he was awarded the Frank Rosenblatt Award for his contributions to artificial intelligence research. text: The Evangelical Lutheran Church in Tanzania (ELCT; Swahili: Kanisa la Kiinjili la Kilutheri Tanzania) is the federation of Lutheran churches in Tanzania and one of the largest Lutheran denominations globally, with over 6 million members, representing 13% of the Tanzanian population. It is the second largest Lutheran church in the world and the largest in East Africa. The church is led by a presiding bishop and twenty-eight diocesan bishops, representing 28 dioceses, with its head office located in Mbeya since 1967. It is affiliated with the All Africa Conference of Churches (AACC), the Christian Council of Tanzania, the Global Confessional and Missional Lutheran Forum, and the Lutheran World Federation. The ELCT offers worship, Christian education, and a range of social services, including disaster response, healthcare, and AIDS education and relief. The first Lutheran missionaries arrived in German East Africa in 1887 when the Evangelical Missionary Society for East Africa (EMS), based in Berlin, Germany, established a station at Kigamboni, Dar es Salaam. A second group of German missionaries entered via South Africa and settled in the Southern Highlands. Missions from Germany continued throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries despite interruptions from the Hehe Wars (1891), the Maji Maji Uprising (1905–1907), World War I, and World War II. In 1938, seven Lutheran churches formed the Federation of Lutheran Churches in Tanganyika, which later merged into the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Tanzania. In 1964, Johannes Lilje, presiding bishop of the United Evangelical Lutheran Church of Germany, consecrated Stefano Moshi, elected as the first president of the new church body and a proponent of episcopacy, as the first presiding bishop of the ELCT. The church's seat is in Arusha and is primarily financed through collections, donations, and project grants from churches in the Global North. The ELCT is led by a presiding bishop, or "Mkuu," elected to four-year terms from among the bishops, and 24 bishops who oversee local dioceses; the current presiding bishop is Alex Malasusa. The church employs 1,360 ordained pastors (28 overseas), 3,000 lay evangelists, and 300 community officers (2014 figures). Women are not ordained in all dioceses, though the national church began ordaining women as of 1990; ordination remains a sensitive issue, with local dioceses making independent decisions. The ELCT is one of the fastest-growing churches globally, with an annual increase of approximately 8% in baptized members. Social services are central to its mission and include departments focused on disaster response, healthcare, and AIDS education and relief. The ELCT comprises regional dioceses in Kenya, South Sudan, Tanzania, Indonesia, Mongolia, Germany, Norway, Sweden, and Peru. Lutheranism is rooted in the theology of Martin Luther, with official confessional writings in the Book of Concord. The ELCT accepts the unaltered Augsburg Confession as a true witness to the Gospel and does not adhere to biblical inerrancy, instead supporting scholarly methods of biblical analysis, aligning with moderate Protestant traditions. Like other Lutheran bodies, the ELCT recognizes two sacraments: Communion (Eucharist) and Holy Baptism (including infant baptism); Confession and absolution is often included but is considered a return to the forgiveness of baptism, so strictly speaking, only two sacraments exist. The ELCT holds to the Lutheran doctrine of sacramental union, affirming that Christ's body and blood are truly present "in, with and under" the bread and wine, with all communicants receiving both bread and wine and the actual body and blood of Christ. This is sometimes referred to as consubstantiation, though Lutherans reject a philosophical explanation, viewing the presence as a mystery rather than a philosophical concept. This belief is more aligned with Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions than with most Protestant views, which often doubt or deny the actual presence of Christ's body and blood in communion. In August 2013, the ELCT established a relationship with the North American Lutheran Church through a "Memorandum of Understanding," paving the way for full communion between the two churches.
