text: Evi Nemeth (born June 7, 1940 – missing-at-sea June or July 2013) was an engineer, author, and teacher renowned for her expertise in computer system administration and networks. She was the lead author of the "bibles" of system administration: UNIX System Administration Handbook (1989, 1995, 2000), Linux Administration Handbook (2002, 2006), and UNIX and Linux System Administration Handbook (2010, 2017). Known in technology circles as the matriarch of system administration, she earned her bachelor's degree in mathematics from Penn State in 1961 and her PhD in mathematics from the University of Waterloo, Ontario in 1971. She taught at Florida Atlantic University and the State University of New York at Utica (SUNY Tech) before joining the computer science department at the University of Colorado Boulder (CU-Boulder) in 1980, where she served as manager of the college's computing facility from 1982 to 1986. She also held visiting Associate Professor positions at Dartmouth College in 1990 and UC San Diego in 1998, while on sabbatical from CU-Boulder. At CU-Boulder, she was well known for her undergraduate systems administration program, which enabled students to gain in-depth knowledge and skills in Unix system administration. Together with Steve Wozniak, she established the Woz scholarship program at CU-Boulder to fund inquisitive undergraduates. Nemeth was also recognized for her ability to inspire and teach young people, mentoring numerous middle- and high-school students—known as "the munchkins"—and talented young undergraduates, who worked with her to support computing at the university and attended national meetings where they installed networks and broadcast sessions on the Internet via the multicast backbone. She coached the university's student programming teams in the ACM International Collegiate Programming Contest. From 1998 to 2006, she worked with the Cooperative Association for Internet Data Analysis (CAIDA) at the University of California, San Diego, on Internet measurement and visualization projects. Outside the United States, she contributed to bringing Internet technology to the developing world through programs of the Internet Society and the United Nations Development Programme. A network guru T-shirt from the 1980s, featuring OSI Model layers with an added "financial" Layer 8 and a "political" Layer 9, was credited to her. During the Summer 1994 USENIX conference in Boston, she coordinated the production of a commemorative deck of playing cards celebrating the 25th anniversary of UNIX. After retiring, she sailed her 40-foot sailboat Wonderland around the world, including a circuit of the Atlantic, through the Panama Canal, and across the Pacific to New Zealand. In late May 2013, she traveled with six others aboard the vintage yacht Niña across the Tasman Sea en route to Australia from New Zealand. On June 4, the last message sent by Nemeth from Niña was received, as the Tasman Sea had 65 mile-per-hour winds and swell height reaching 26 feet; a natural disaster (e.g., a rogue wave) may have caused the boat’s disappearance. On July 5, New Zealand authorities officially ended the search for the Niña, though relatives of the crew continued to search.

text: M. Fathima Beevi (30 April 1927 – 23 November 2023) was an Indian judge who served as a justice of the Supreme Court of India. Appointed to the apex court in 1989, she became the first female judge of the Supreme Court of India and the first Muslim woman to be appointed to any of the higher judiciaries in the country. She retired from the Supreme Court on 29 April 1992. After her retirement, she served as a member of the National Human Rights Commission and later as the Governor of Tamil Nadu from 25 January 1997 to 2001. In 2023, she was honoured with the Kerala Prabha Award, the second-highest honour given by the Government of Kerala, and posthumously awarded the Padma Bhushan in the 2024 honours list. Born on 30 April 1927 in Pathanamthitta, then part of the Kingdom of Travancore (now in Kerala), she was the daughter of Annaveettil Meer Sahib and Khadeeja Beevi, belonging to the Rowther family. She attended Town School and Catholicate High School in Pathanamthitta, earned a BSc in chemistry from Women's College, Thiruvananthapuram, and obtained her LL.B. from Government Law College, Thiruvananthapuram. Enrolled as an Advocate on 14 November 1950, she topped the Bar Council exam that year and began her career in the lower judiciary in Kerala, becoming Munsiff in May 1958, Sub-ordinate Judge in 1968, Chief Judicial Magistrate in 1972, and District & Sessions Judge in 1974. In January 1980, she was appointed Judicial Member of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, and elevated to the High Court as a Judge on 4 August 1983. She became a permanent Judge of the High Court on 14 May 1984 and retired from the High Court on 29 April 1989. As Governor of Tamil Nadu, she rejected mercy petitions filed by four condemned prisoners in the Rajiv Gandhi assassination case, invoking her power under Article 161 of the Constitution. She faced controversy for giving a clean chit to the law and order situation in Tamil Nadu, prompting the Central government to request her resignation. She resigned under controversial circumstances after accepting Jayalalithaa's assembly majority following the May 2001 elections and over the arrest of former Chief Minister M. Karunanidhi, who had previously advocated for her appointment. Jayalalithaa defended her decision, stating that as a former Supreme Court judge and legal expert, she did not require instruction on law or the Constitution, and her decision was not justiciable. Despite not being eligible to contest an election under constitutional provisions, Fathima Beevi administered the oath of office to J. Jayalalitha as Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu on 14 May 2001, based on the majority party's election of her as their leader. Several Public Interest Litigations were filed in the Supreme Court challenging the validity of her appointment, and she justified her action by citing the majority party's election of Jayalalithaa. The Supreme Court later overturned her appointment, ruling that a Governor cannot appoint a non-member of the legislature as Chief Minister, as such an action would be contrary to the Constitution and laws. During her tenure as Governor, she also served as Chancellor of Madras University, where her withholding of approval for the establishment of a new department for contemporary Tamil literature reportedly led to the Vice-Chancellor, P.T. Manoharan, resigning. She had previously served as Chairman of the Kerala Commission for Backward Classes (1993) and member of the National Human Rights Commission (1993), and received the Hon. D. Litt. and Mahila Shiromani Award in 1990, as well as the Bharat Jyoti Award. There were discussions among left parties about her potential nomination as President of India, during which the NDA Government proposed Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam. Fathima Beevi passed away on 23 November 2023 at the age of 96.

text: Fazal Elahi Chaudhry (1 January 1904 – 2 June 1982) was a Pakistani barrister, politician, and statesman who served as the fifth president of Pakistan from 1973 until his resignation in September 1978, following the 1977 coup d'état that overthrew Zulfikar Ali Bhutto's government and established martial law under Zia-ul-Haq. He was the first legislatively-elected president in Pakistan's history and served as a constitutional figurehead under the 1973 constitution, which shifted executive power to the prime minister. Born in Marala, Kharian Tehsil of Gujrat District, Punjab, into an influential Punjabi Muslim Gujjar family, Chaudhry received his early education in Kharian, then attended Aligarh Muslim University in 1920, earning his LLB in civil law in 1924. He later returned to Punjab, studied at the University of the Punjab, obtaining a master's degree in political science in 1925 and an advanced LLM in Law and Justice in 1927. After establishing a law firm in Lahore, he began practising civil law and returned to Gujrat. In 1930, he was elected unopposed to the Gujrat District Board. He joined the All-India Muslim League in 1942, became president of the Punjab Muslim League for Gujrat District in 1945, and participated in the 1946 Indian provincial elections on the Muslim League ticket. After Pakistan's independence in 1947, he was appointed parliamentary secretary and later served as education and health minister in Liaquat Ali Khan's cabinet. He represented Pakistan at the United Nations in 1952 and was elected to the West Punjab Assembly in 1951. In 1956, he was elected to the West Pakistan Assembly and served as its first Speaker from 20 May 1956 to 7 October 1958. He joined the Convention Muslim League and was elected deputy speaker of the National Assembly in 1965, serving until 1969 when Yahya Khan declared martial law. In 1970, he was elected to the National Assembly on the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) ticket and later became its speaker in 1972. Under the 1973 constitution, Chaudhry contested the presidential election against Khan Amirzadah Khan of the National Awami Party (Wali), winning with an absolute electoral college majority of 139 votes to Khan's 45, and was sworn in on 14 August 1973, becoming the first ethnic Punjabi president. He succeeded Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who became prime minister. As a figurehead, the presidency had become ceremonial, with executive authority vested in the prime minister. After the 1977 coup d'état, Bhutto's government and all provincial governments were overthrown by Zia-ul-Haq, who assumed the role of chief martial law administrator; Chaudhry continued as president but had no influence over governmental, military, or national affairs. Due to contentious relations with the Zia-led military regime, he resigned on 16 September 1978, handing over the presidency to Zia-ul-Haq. Chaudhry remained a respected legislator and politician throughout his career and died of a heart ailment on 2 June 1982 in Lahore at the age of 78.

text: The Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) is a U.S. federal law that established the foundational system for pesticide regulation to protect applicators, consumers, and the environment. It is administered and regulated by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and appropriate state environmental agencies. FIFRA has been amended several times, with a major revision in 1972 through the Federal Environmental Pesticide Control Act (FEPCA), which expanded EPA's authority by shifting the burden of proof to chemical manufacturers, enforcing compliance against banned and unregistered products, and establishing a regulatory framework to address gaps in the original law. The Federal Insecticide Act of 1910 was the first pesticide law, ensuring quality by protecting farmers and consumers from fraudulent or adulterated products, though it did not address environmental or health risks. During World War II, increased wartime research led to a surge in pesticide use, with synthetic organic insecticide usage rising from 100 million pounds in 1945 to over 300 million pounds by 1950, contributing to post-war food surpluses due to reduced pest damage. The 1947 Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act addressed shortcomings of the 1910 law, assigning initial regulation to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which was later transferred to the EPA in 1972 with a shift in focus to human health and environmental protection. The 1972 FEPCA amendment required the EPA to evaluate potential risks to humans, the environment, and wildlife and take action when risks outweighed benefits. In 1988, Congress mandated the reregistration of many pesticides registered before 1984, and in 1996, the Food Quality Protection Act (FQPA) required older pesticides to pose no unreasonable risk to infants, children, or sensitive individuals with "reasonable certainty," and established a 15-year review cycle for all pesticides. In 2012, the Pesticide Registration Improvement Extension Act amended the registration process. As of May 2007, there are 28 listed restricted pesticides, and any area where they are used is considered a restricted area. Pesticides must undergo 120 safety and effectiveness tests; only 1 in 139,000 passes, and the law explicitly forbids certain substances and uses, unlike other pesticide laws that only impose costs. FIFRA establishes regulations requiring that pesticides not cause unreasonable adverse effects on human health or the environment, defined as risks that are unreasonable considering social, economic, and environmental costs, or dietary risks violating food standards under Section 408 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA). Applicants must provide scientific data from over 100 tests under EPA guidelines. The EPA sets tolerance levels for pesticide residues on or in food/feed, establishing a "reasonable certainty of no harm," and may exempt certain residues if they meet FDCA standards. Registered pesticides must conform to approved uses and labeling. Most older pesticides were required to be reregistered under 1972, 1988, and 1996 amendments to meet current safety, labeling, and risk standards. Reregistration fees for food/feed active ingredients are $50,000 (initial) and $100,000–$150,000 (final), with non-food use fees at $50,000–$100,000; annual maintenance fees are $425 per product up to fifty, with a maximum of $20,000 per company, and $100 per product over fifty, capped at $35,000. Fees may be reduced or waived for small businesses, public health, or minor use pesticides, and failure to pay results in cancellation. Adjuvants—chemicals added to enhance efficacy or alter physical properties—are regulated by the EPA, with over 200 registered pesticides recommending their use; the EPA sets tolerance levels for adjuvants but does not require registration. Devices used to trap or kill pests (excluding standalone application equipment) and pesticide intermediates used in manufacturing are regulated but not required to be registered under FIFRA, though intermediates may be regulated under the Toxic Substances Control Act of 1976. Under FIFRA, no individual may sell, use, or distribute a pesticide not registered with the EPA, except in limited cases, and all pesticides must have a label with detailed safe use instructions. Pesticides are classified as "general use" (available to the public) or "restricted use" (requiring certified applicator credentials). While the EPA primarily enforces FIFRA, state agencies have enforcement authority under Sections 23, 24, 26, and 27, though EPA authority supersedes state authority and can be rescinded if states fail to ensure safe enforcement. Section 9 authorizes inspections of pesticides in storage, Section 13 allows the EPA to issue Stop Sale, Use, or Removal Orders (SSURO) and seize violative pesticides, Section 15 provides indemnity for suspended or cancelled registrations, and Section 16 allows judicial review. Section 14 imposes civil penalties, with commercial applicators, wholesalers, dealers, and retailers facing fines of up to $5,000 per offense, private applicators receiving warnings for first offenses and fines up to $1,000 for subsequent violations. Violations are treated as misdemeanors with fines and/or imprisonment: private applicators face up to $1,000 and 30 days, commercial applicators up to $25,000 and one year, and manufacturers up to $50,000 and one year. The EPA must continuously monitor registered pesticides and require registrants to report new adverse effects and conduct ongoing studies. If new evidence of harm is found, the EPA may conduct a special review and amend or cancel the registration. The Endangered Species Act requires the EPA to consider impacts on endangered species and habitats when registering pesticides, ensuring they do not harm listed species or their habitats, with labels providing guidance through bulletins. The EPA implements usage limitations and monitoring to protect endangered species while minimizing disruption to pesticide users.

doc_name: Fencing at the 1908 Summer Olympics – Men's sabre
text: The men's sabre was one of four fencing events at the 1908 Summer Olympics programme and marked its fourth appearance, making it the only fencing event held at every Summer Olympics. The top two positions in the individual event were claimed by Hungarian fencers: Jenő Fuchs won gold and Béla Zulawszky took silver, while bronze was awarded to Bohemian Vilém Goppold von Lobsdorf. A total of 76 competitors from 11 nations participated, with each nation allowed to enter up to 12 fencers. This was the fourth time the event was held, and Georges de la Falaise of France, the 1900 gold medalist, returned after skipping the 1904 Games. Belgium, Bohemia, Great Britain, the Netherlands, and South Africa each made their debut in the men's sabre, while Austria made its third appearance, having missed only the 1904 Games. The competition consisted of four rounds, with each pool conducting a round-robin format to three touches. European sabre rules at the time used a full-body target area, unlike the above-the-waist target used in the 1904 Games, which later became standard post-World War I. Barrages were used to determine advancement when necessary. The first round featured pool sizes ranging from 4 to 8 fencers, with the three fencers who lost the fewest bouts advancing; a three-way tie for two spots led to the elimination of the British fencer. Renaud lost both playoff matches, allowing Grade and Jack to advance, while Lichtenfels suffered two losses in the playoff. The fifth pool had only four fencers, resulting in only one elimination—Langevin. Petri defeated van Tomme in the playoff for third place after losing to the Belgian in the main pool, and Badman defeated van Minden in the playoff for third place. The tenth pool, the largest at twice the size of the fifth, had eight fencers, with five eliminated; von Lobsdorf defeated all seven of his opponents to win first place, with no match between Sarzano and Stohr. Chapuis was eliminated in the three-way playoff for second and third. The final pool included seven fencers. Eight second-round pools were held, ranging from 4 to 5 fencers. Notley won two playoff matches to secure second place in his pool and advance. Doorman, who had lost to Petri in the main pool, defeated the German in the playoff for second place. Two semifinals, each with eight fencers, were held, with the top four from each advancing to the final. Four fencers tied at 5-2 records and all advanced to the final; Ceccherini withdrew after his first four bouts, resulting in walkover wins for Tóth, van der Voodt, and Doorman. Fuchs and von Lobsdorf did not finish within the time limit and were both recorded as losers. The gold medal playoff was won by Fuchs, who secured victory with a one-touch bout decided by a parry and riposte to his fellow Hungarian's head.

text: Fleabag is a British comedy-drama television series created and written by Phoebe Waller-Bridge, adapted from her 2013 Edinburgh Festival Fringe one-woman play of the same name, which won a Fringe First Award. The series was produced by Two Brothers Pictures for BBC Three and co-produced with Amazon Studios. Waller-Bridge stars as Fleabag, a free-spirited but angry and confused young woman living in London, while Sian Clifford co-stars as her sister Claire, and Andrew Scott joins in the second season; most main characters are unnamed, including Waller-Bridge and Scott. The protagonist frequently breaks the fourth wall, delivering exposition, internal monologues, and commentary to the audience. The show premiered on 21 July 2016 and concluded its second and final series on 8 April 2019. It received widespread critical acclaim for its writing, acting, and the unique personality of the title character, with many critics and viewers calling it one of the greatest comedy and television series of all time. Waller-Bridge won the British Academy Television Award for Best Female Comedy Performance for the first series, and the second series earned her Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Comedy Series, Outstanding Lead Actress, and Outstanding Writing for a Comedy Series; additional acting nominations were given to Clifford, Olivia Colman, Fiona Shaw, and Kristin Scott Thomas. The series also won the Golden Globe Awards for Best Television Series and Best Actress for Waller-Bridge, with a nomination for Scott. The initial concept for Fleabag came from a challenge by a friend to create a 10-minute sketch for a stand-up storytelling night. BBC Three originally broadcast the show, with a repeat run on BBC Two from 21 August to 25 September 2016; the second series aired simultaneously on BBC One and BBC Three, with BBC Three only offering it online. The show was picked up by Amazon Prime Video and premiered in the United States on 16 September 2016, with Series 2 released on 17 May 2019; it is also available on IFC in the US and Net5 in the Netherlands. A French remake titled Mouche (meaning 'fly') was produced by Jeanne Herry and aired on 3 June 2019 on Canal+, set in Paris with Camille Cottin in the lead role. Filming took place in and around London, primarily in North West and Central areas, with key locations including Dartmouth Park, Southampton Road, Laurier Road, Croftdown Road, Highgate Road, York Rise, Twickenham, Hampton Hill, Highgate, Tufnell Park, Belsize Park, Maida Vale, Kentish Town, Parliament Hill Fields, Southwark, Bloomsbury, Soho, Stanmore, Lincoln's Inn Fields, and Finsbury Square. Specific sets include Bold Café & Restaurant in Dartmouth Park as Fleabag's Guinea Pig Café, Cambridge Park Road in Twickenham for Dad and Godmother's house, the British Museum's Lecture Theatre in Russell Square for the feminist lecture, Kensal Green Cemetery for the daily jog, Hedsor House in Maidenhead for the silent retreat, Smith & Wollensky in Covent Garden for the family dinner party, St. Andrew's in Kingsbury for Hot Priest's church, the Tate Modern in Bankside for Godmother's sexhibition, Heron Tower in Bishopsgate for Claire's penthouse office, St Dunstan and All Saints Church in Stepney for the funeral, and 137 – Taylor and Taylor in Shoreditch for the hair salon. Filming for the first series began in late April 2016 and aired from 21 July to 25 August 2016; filming for the second series started in late August 2018 and aired from 4 March to 8 April 2019. Isobel Waller-Bridge, Phoebe's sister, composed the music for both series. Both series received 100% approval ratings on Rotten Tomatoes, with the first averaging 8.5/10 based on 42 reviews and the second 9.3/10 based on 99 reviews; Metacritic awarded the first series a score of 88 out of 100 and the second 96 out of 100, both indicating universal acclaim. Critics such as Emily Nussbaum of The New Yorker described the first series as a "precision black-humour mechanism, a warped and affecting fable about one single woman's existence," Maureen Ryan of Variety called it "scathingly funny" and noted it reveals itself as a tragedy, Hank Stuever of The Washington Post described it as a "funny, highly profane but surprisingly poignant dramedy," Mike Hale of The New York Times praised its "restless, almost feral energy and its slap-in-the-face attitude," and Mary McNamara of the Los Angeles Times commended its unpredictability and "clear eye for truth that often becomes, like all good comedy, quite devastating." The second series received unanimous acclaim and was considered a cultural phenomenon, with Serena Davies of The Daily Telegraph calling it "a near-perfect work of art," Mary Elizabeth Williams of Salon praising it as a "brilliant swan song," Alan Sepinwall of Rolling Stone calling it a "tragicomic masterpiece reaching new heights," James Poniewozik of The New York Times noting it feels "immediately confident, if inevitably less groundbreaking" but continues to push its form, and Hannah Jane Parkinson of The Guardian describing the conclusion as "the most electrifying, devastating TV in years," stating that many who did not watch or appreciate the first series were converted. Fleabag was ranked second-highest among shows of the 2010s by Metacritic's decade-end list and has since been recognized by multiple publications as one of the greatest television series of all time. Former U.S. President Barack Obama named the second season among his favorite films and television series of 2019, including it in his annual list on Twitter on 29 December 2019 with the addendum: "and a quick list of TV shows that I considered as powerful as movies: Fleabag: Season 2, Unbelievable, and Watchmen."

text: Florence Ann Farmer (24 January 1873 – 26 June 1958) was a pioneering woman in politics in Stoke on Trent, Staffordshire, England, becoming the first female councillor on the county borough council and later the first female Lord Mayor of the city in 1931–32. She was one of the children of George and Mary Farmer, born in Longton, Staffordshire, and her father, George, was an active Liberal local politician who served as secretary of the local party, a Justice of the Peace, and mayor of Longton from 1895 to 1896. After leaving school, Farmer trained as a teacher and served as headmistress of Uttoxeter Road Girls School in Longton from 1895 to 1906. She resigned from teaching to co-found the Phoenix Steam Laundry company with her brother George, and after his death in 1917, continued the business with his widow, Maude, until 1927 when Maude retired, leaving Florence in charge. Farmer was a founding member of the National Federation of Launderers and became the first woman to sit on its national executive committee. Women could only be elected to the local board of guardians since the Local Government Act 1894, and it was not until 1907 that women were allowed to serve on borough councils under the Qualification of Women (County and Borough Councils) Act 1907. Initially a Liberal, Farmer shifted to socialism and joined the Labour Party after the end of the First World War. In 1915, she was elected to the County Borough of Stoke on Trent board of guardians, and in November 1919, she became the first woman elected to the Stoke-on-Trent Council, winning unopposed for No. 23 ward (Longton). She served on various committees, including the watch committee, where she proposed the appointment of women constables; although initially defeated, the proposal was later accepted, leading to the first women constables in Stoke being appointed in 1921. Appointed a Justice of the Peace in 1920, she became the first woman to be made an Alderman of the City of Stoke-on-Trent in 1928. She chaired the local Labour Party branch from 1929 to 1931. When Lady Cynthia Mosley, the MP for Stoke-on-Trent, resigned from the Labour Party in 1931 to join her husband Oswald Mosley’s New Party, Farmer was nominated as the Labour candidate but was not selected; the nomination went to Ellis Smith. In October 1931, she was unanimously chosen to be Lord Mayor of Stoke-on-Trent for 1932–33, becoming the first woman to hold the office and only the fourth woman in England to serve as a Lord Mayor. At her investiture in November 1931, she wore the same mayoral chains that her father had worn as mayor of Longton in 1895. Farmer remained on the city council until 1945 and was granted the Freedom of the City in 1946. She never married and died in June 1958 at the age of 85.

text: Fort Oglethorpe is a city primarily located in Catoosa County with some areas extending into Walker County in the U.S. state of Georgia. As of the 2020 census, the city had a population of 10,423, with 3,994 households and 2,240 families. The city covers a total area of 13.9 square miles (36.0 km²), all of which is land, and is situated at 34°56′44″N 85°14′44″W (34.94556°N 85.24556°W). It lies 9 miles (14 km) south of Chattanooga, Tennessee, via U.S. Route 27, which continues 18 miles (29 km) south to LaFayette, Georgia. The Chickamauga and Chattanooga National Military Park occupies the southern two-thirds of the city. The city is part of the Chattanooga, Tennessee–Georgia Metropolitan Statistical Area. Fort Oglethorpe was established on land originally owned by William Hamilton Hargrave and his wife Amelia Cecilia Strange-Hargrave, a Confederate soldier and landowner, near the Chickamauga National Battlefield. The U.S. Army established a cavalry post at the site in 1902, later naming it Fort Oglethorpe after James Oglethorpe, founder of the Colony of Georgia. During and after World War I (1917–1920), the fort served as a detention camp for civilian internees and prisoners of war. During World War II, it functioned as a war-time induction and processing center and again housed prisoners of war, and also served as a major training center for the Women's Army Corps. The post land was declared surplus in 1947 and returned to civilian use, leading to the incorporation of the town in 1949. As of the 2000 U.S. census, the population was 6,940, with 2,873 households and 1,881 families, and a population density of 532.6 inhabitants per square mile (205.6/km²). The racial makeup was 93.14% White, 2.38% African American, 0.19% Native American, 2.07% Asian, 0.03% Pacific Islander, 0.56% from other races, and 1.63% from two or more races, with 1.41% identifying as Hispanic or Latino. Household data showed 29.3% had children under 18, 47.0% were married couples, 15.0% had a female householder with no husband, and 34.5% were non-families; 30.6% were made up of individuals, and 13.3% had someone 65 or older living alone. The average household size was 2.29, and average family size was 2.86. The age distribution included 22.8% under 18, 9.5% aged 18–24, 26.3% aged 25–44, 21.8% aged 45–64, and 19.6% aged 65 or older, with a median age of 38. For every 100 females, there were 82.2 males, and for every 100 females aged 18 and over, there were 76.9 males. The median household income was $32,095, median family income was $40,643, male median income was $28,160, and female median income was $21,141. The per capita income was $16,288, with 11.5% of families and 17.4% of the population below the poverty line, including 30.8% of those under 18 and 11.3% of those 65 or older. As of circa 2024, 9,013 residents lived in Catoosa County and 250 lived in Walker County. The portion in Catoosa County is within the Catoosa County School District, which includes Lakeview–Fort Oglethorpe High School, while the Walker County portion is within the Walker County School District.

text: Fox has maintained several long-running game shows, making them the longest-running in the network’s history. The supernatural mystery series Fringe debuted in 2008 with moderate ratings but received critical acclaim during its first season on Tuesdays, eventually developing a large loyal fanbase that made it a cult favorite. Glee premiered in 2009 with average ratings when its pilot aired as a lead-out program for the eighth-season finale of American Idol, but earned positive reviews from critics. The show’s cast has been acknowledged by Barack Obama and Oprah Winfrey, who have each asked them to perform live at national events. In the early 2010s, Fox achieved its first live-action comedy successes in years with the new comedies Raising Hope and New Girl. The second season of Glee reached its highest ratings during the 2010–11 season, peaking during its Super Bowl XLV lead-out episode in February 2011, which was the most expensive post-Super Bowl episode ever produced on U.S. television. Glee consistently attracted worldwide media attention and built a large, loyal international fanbase. Fox’s live telecast of Super Bowl XLV in 2014 helped it become the first U.S. television network to earn an average single-night prime time audience of at least 100 million viewers. American Idol lost its position as the top-rated prime-time program during the 2011–12 finale, falling to second behind NBC Sunday Night Football, ending its eight-year streak as the top-rated prime-time broadcast network series in American television history, which included dominance in both the Adults 18–49 demographic and total viewership. Idol remained in the Nielsen Top 10 from 2003 to 2013 and was the highest-rated non-sports prime-time program and reality series in the U.S. from 2003 to 2012, marking the longest Nielsen ratings streaks for any Fox program in those categories. The 2012 season finale of American Idol marked the end of the 25th anniversary of the Fox network, during which it won the 18–49 demographic for the eighth consecutive season, the longest such streak according to Nielsen records (still standing as of 2026). However, Fox experienced a significant viewership decline during the 2012–13 season, with American Idol and Glee suffering steep ratings drops, and the network falling to third in total viewership (a 22% decrease) and second in the 18–49 demographic (a position it held as of 2014). This decline continued into the 2013–14 season, when Fox placed fourth among major networks in total viewership for the first time since 2001. On January 13, 2014, Fox announced it would abandon the traditional pilot season concept and instead directly pick up shows to series. The network achieved renewed ratings success with its February 2014 broadcast of Super Bowl XLVIII, which became the second most-watched television broadcast by average in U.S. history, and the lead-out programs New Girl and Brooklyn Nine-Nine. In May 2014, Kevin Reilly resigned as chairman of Fox Entertainment. On July 15, 2014, 21st Century Fox announced a merger of the network and 20th Century Fox Television into the newly created Fox Television Group, with Dana Walden and Gary Newman appointed as co-chairpersons. The 2014–15 season saw the series finale of Glee and the debut of new dramas Gotham and Empire. Empire’s ratings increased week-to-week throughout its first season, becoming the network’s first successful American Idol lead-out since House and the first American television program to consistently increase its episode-to-episode viewership during its first five weeks since ABC’s Roseanne in 1992. Empire ended its first season as the first American television show to increase its episodic viewership consistently throughout a single season and as Fox’s fourth program (and first since the 2013 finale of American Idol) to enter the Nielsen Top 10 by the end of the 2014–15 season. The 2015–16 season marked a notable turnaround for Fox, as it jumped ahead of ABC to third place in nationwide ratings (in both overall viewership and the 18–49 demographic) and achieved several firsts. This improvement was driven by the transfer of the Miss Universe and Miss USA pageants from NBC, as well as the return of The X-Files after its 2002 season end and the live musical special Grease: Live, which became the first live American television musical special of the 21st century to be broadcast in front of a live studio audience and the first live musical special aired by a non-Big Three network on primetime. By 2016, Empire and The X-Files ranked in the Nielsen Top 10 for the season, marking the first season since the 2007–2008 American Idol-House tandem that Fox had two programs in the Top 10 without American Idol or any other Fox reality show. The same year, American Idol concluded its original run on Fox after fifteen seasons, ending an era of one of the most successful shows in American television history. In February 2017, Fox broadcast Super Bowl LI, which attracted an average of 111.3 million viewers—ranking among the top five most-watched Super Bowl games and the second-highest audience in network history behind Super Bowl XLVIII. In March 2017, Rob Wade was named Fox’s new president of alternative entertainment and specials, having previously worked as a showrunner for Dancing with the Stars, head of entertainment for BBC Worldwide, and executive producer of America’s Got Talent and The X Factor. On July 27, 2018, 21st Century Fox shareholders agreed to sell most of its key assets—including 20th Century Fox and FX Networks—to The Walt Disney Company for $71.3 billion, following a spin-off of certain businesses. The sale did not include the Fox Broadcasting Company, television stations, or the Fox Sports, Fox News, and Fox Business cable channels, which were to be maintained under a new entity tentatively called "New Fox." Because Disney already owns ABC, the acquisition would have violated the FCC’s rules against merging any of the four major broadcast networks. As a result of the Disney/Fox deal and the December 4, 2019, merger of CBS and Viacom, Fox became the only major American broadcast network without a film studio. After the deal, Fox emphasized sports programming in its upfronts, including acquiring the NFL’s Thursday Night Football package and the rights to the FIFA World Cup. On June 27, 2018, WWE announced that SmackDown would move to Fox on Friday nights beginning October 4, 2019, under a five-year contract valued at $205 million per year. Fox also increased its non-scripted output, announcing The Masked Singer (based on the South Korean format King of Mask Singer), Mental Samurai, and Spin the Wheel for the 2018–19 season. In August 2018, Fox Television Group CEO Dana Walden stated the network planned to commission more series from independent studios not co-owned with the Big Three, citing limited opportunities due to vertical integration, and noted that top programs like The Big Bang Theory and This Is Us were distributed by third parties. Fox also planned to acquire new pitches directly from writers and offer them to outside producers, while gradually reducing scripted programming development from 20th Television, though The Simpsons would remain. Following the sale, Dana Walden became chairwoman of Disney Television Studios and ABC Entertainment. Charlie Collier succeeded Gary Newman as chairman and CEO of Fox on November 1, 2018, with Newman temporarily remaining in a transitional role. In early 2019, The Masked Singer premiered to Fox’s highest ratings for a non-scripted premiere without an NFL lead-in since 2011 and recorded the largest-ever Nielsen ratings gain for a non-scripted series after three days of delayed viewership. On January 30, 2019, Fox ordered a second season, with the first-season finale drawing an average audience of 11.5 million viewers. The next day, the "New Fox" entity, officially named Fox Corporation, began trading on March 19, 2019. At its 2019–20 upfronts, Fox announced 10 new scripted series, with three (Almost Family, Bless the Harts, and Prodigal Son) for the fall, and the second and third seasons of The Masked Singer scheduled for October 2019 and February 2020 (with the latter premiering after Super Bowl LIV). Fox also established Fox Alternative Entertainment, led by Rob Wade, for investments in non-scripted formats, with its first production being the second season of The Masked Singer. Thursday Night Football finished as the second highest-rated series of the 2018–19 season in the key demographic, behind only Sunday Night Football, while The Masked Singer tied for third with The Big Bang Theory and This Is Us. In the 2019–20 season, Thursday Night Football and The Masked Singer again finished as the second and third highest-rated programs in the key demographic, and Fox finished the season as the highest-rated network among viewers 18–49 (with CBS leading in overall viewers). Fox repeated this victory in the 2020–21 season but was narrowly beaten by NBC in the 2021–22 season by a tenth of a ratings share. In October 2022, Collier stepped down to join Roku, with Rob Wade promoted to president and CEO of Fox Entertainment. That season, Fox lost Thursday Night Football to Amazon Prime Video. In May 2023, Fox dropped its procedural drama 9-1-1 after six seasons, which had been the network’s scripted tentpole since 2018. As a 20th Television production, ABC picked up the series for a seventh season. Its spin-off, 9-1-1: Lone Star, remained on Fox and was renewed for a fifth season. In September 2024, it was announced that 9-1-1: Lone Star would conclude after its fifth season, becoming the last 20th Television-produced drama to air on the network. Fox also lost SmackDown to USA Network in September 2024, and began a strategy of regular sports programming on Friday nights, starting with a package of primetime college football games, leveraging its contract extension with the Big Ten Conference, which included options to carry Friday-night games after the addition of west coast teams. On April 2, 2025, Fox and 20th Television Animation announced a four-season, 15-episode renewal for The Simpsons, Bob’s Burgers, Family Guy, and American Dad!, marking the return of the latter to the network after an 11-year run on TBS from October 2014 to March 2025. As of 2015, Fox provides 17 hours of regularly scheduled network programming each week, including fifteen hours of prime time programming from Monday through Saturday (8:00 to 10:00 p.m. Eastern and Pacific) and Sunday (7:00 to 10:00 p.m.), and one hour of late night programming on Saturdays (11:00 p.m. to 12:00 a.m.), which is currently a repeat of primetime series. The network also airs a Sunday morning political discussion show, Fox News Sunday with Shannon Bream (9:00 a.m. to 10:00 a.m. Eastern and Pacific), its only regular national news program. Sports programming is typically aired on weekends, mostly between 11:00 a.m. and 11:30 p.m. ET, with the Saturday and Friday prime time blocks (starting in 2024) mainly scheduled for sports, and encores airing when no sports are scheduled. Except for The Critic, The PJs, and Futurama, which were cancelled in 1995, 2000, and 2003, Fox typically airs a Sunday night lineup of original adult animation sitcoms, all produced or co-produced by 20th Television. This block, known as Animation Domination from May 1, 2005, to September 14, 2014, was rebranded as Sunday Funday in 2014 after the reintroduction of live-action comedy series, though animated series remain a key part of the schedule. The first shows in the Animation Domination lineup were American Dad! (which moved to TBS in October 2014 and returned in early 2026), Family Guy (which returned after a three-year cancellation), The Simpsons (the longest-running cartoon on Fox, predating the lineup by 16 years), and King of the Hill (which predated the lineup by eight years). After King of the Hill’s cancellation, Family Guy’s spinoff The Cleveland Show aired from 2009 to 2013, and Bob’s Burgers began in 2011. Current animated shows in the lineup include The Simpsons, Family Guy, Bob’s Burgers, Krapopolis, Grimsburg, Universal Basic Guys, and American Dad! returning in early 2026. Other shows include Sit Down, Shut Up, Allen Gregory, Napoleon Dynamite, Bordertown, Bless the Harts, Duncanville, The Great North, Housebroken, and the live-action/animated hybrid Son of Zorn. An extension called Animation Domination High-Def launched on Saturday late nights in July 2013, marking the return of first-run programming in that slot since the 2010 cancellation of The Wanda Sykes Show. Due to low ratings, Fox announced on April 17, 2014, that it would discontinue the block, with the planned end on June 28, 2014, though it continued airing in encore form until the start of the 2016–17 season, when the hour returned to encores of comedies or reality series.

text: Fox Broadcasting Company, LLC, stylized in all caps as FOX, is an American commercial broadcast television network and the flagship property of Fox Corporation, operated through Fox Entertainment. Launched by News Corporation on October 9, 1986, it emerged as a competitor to the Big Three networks—American Broadcasting Company (ABC), Columbia Broadcasting System (CBS), and National Broadcasting Company (NBC). Fox became the most successful attempt at a fourth television network, achieving the highest-rated free-to-air position in the 18–49 demographic from 2004 to 2012 and again from 2020 to 2021, and was the most-watched American television network in total viewership during the 2007–08 season. It is a member of the North American Broadcasters Association and the National Association of Broadcasters. Unlike other major networks, Fox does not operate its own news division and instead relies on Fox News, Fox Business Network, and Fox Weather for news programming. Fox and its affiliated companies operate entertainment channels internationally, though programming differs from the American network. In Canada, most viewers have access to at least one American-based Fox affiliate via over-the-air or pay television, but Fox's NFL broadcasts and most prime time programming are subject to simultaneous substitution rules imposed by the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) to protect domestic network rights. Fox is headquartered at 1211 Avenue of the Americas in Midtown Manhattan, New York City, with additional offices at the Fox Network Center in Los Angeles and the Fox Media Center in Tempe, Arizona. 20th Century Fox (now 20th Century Studios) began television production as early as 1948 under TCF Television Productions until 1958, producing syndicated programs. After the DuMont Television Network closed in August 1956 due to financial difficulties, the NTA Film Network was launched as a fourth network, with 20th Century Fox producing content for it, though the film network failed after a few years. 20th Century Fox continued producing content for the Big Three networks, including Perry Mason, Batman, and M*A*S*H. While running Paramount Pictures, Barry Diller attempted to create a fourth network with the Paramount Television Service in 1977, which was canceled before broadcasting. Diller later joined 20th Century Fox. In March 1985, News Corporation paid $255 million for a 50% interest in TCF Holdings, the parent of 20th Century Fox. In May 1985, News Corporation paid $2.55 billion to acquire six major U.S. independent stations—WNEW-TV in New York, WTTG in Washington, D.C., KTTV in Los Angeles, KRIV-TV in Houston, WFLD-TV in Chicago, and KRLD-TV in Dallas—from Metromedia. WCVB-TV in Boston was part of the original deal but was spun off to Hearst Broadcasting. Two years later, News Corporation acquired WXNE-TV in Boston and changed its call letters to WFXT. Radio personality Clarke Ingram suggested that Fox is a revival or linear descendant of DuMont, as Metromedia was formed from DuMont’s remaining stations, WNEW-TV and WTTG, and DuMont’s original operations in Manhattan became the Fox Television Center. In 1985, 20th Century Fox announced plans to form a fourth network using its studios and the Metromedia stations for production and distribution. Organizational plans were delayed until regulatory hurdles were cleared. In December 1985, Rupert Murdoch paid $325 million to acquire the remaining equity in TCF Holdings from Marvin Davis. The Metromedia station acquisition was approved by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in March 1986, with WNEW-TV and KRLD-TV changing call letters to WNYW and KDAF, respectively. These six stations, reaching 22% of U.S. households, formed the Fox Television Stations group. All original owned-and-operated stations (except KDAF, which was sold to Renaissance Broadcasting in 1995 and became a WB affiliate) remain part of Fox today. Fox initially affiliated with the top-rated independent station in each market, but in some cases, such as Denver, Phoenix, and St. Louis, it affiliated with a second-tier independent station when a more established one declined. Due to these factors, Fox was forced to affiliate with UHF stations in most markets, similar to DuMont’s experience. Barry Diller, then head of Fox Inc., is credited with creating the network, with the New York Times noting in October 1986 that his "current obsession" was creating a network to compete with NBC, CBS, and ABC. The network officially debuted with a soft launch at 11:00 p.m. Eastern and Pacific Time on Thursday, October 9, 1986, featuring a late-night talk show, The Late Show, hosted by Joan Rivers. The show quickly declined in ratings and was discontinued by early 1987 after Rivers and her husband Edgar Rosenberg left due to creative disagreements. The program then used guest hosts, and some affiliates, such as WCGV-TV in Milwaukee and WDRB-TV in Louisville, signed on under the condition they would not carry The Late Show. Before its April 5, 1987 launch, Fox rebranded from FBC to "Fox" under original President Garth Ancier, with ad man Jay Chiat suggesting the use of the "Fox" heritage and "searchlight" iconography to link the network to 20th Century Fox. Several station groups, including Media Central and Pappas Telecasting, initially avoided Fox but later joined. On April 5, 1987, Fox held its "grand opening" by expanding into prime time, premiering Married... with Children and The Tracey Ullman Show on Sunday nights. Both shows were rebroadcast at 7:00 and 7:30 p.m. Eastern/Pacific to allow viewers to sample programming without missing major network programs. Over the next several weeks, Fox added new shows, including 21 Jump Street, Mr. President, and Duet, completing its Sunday schedule. On July 11, 1987, the network launched its Saturday night lineup with the two-hour pilot of Werewolf, followed by The New Adventures of Beans Baxter, Karen's Song, and Down and Out in Beverly Hills, which were canceled by the start of the 1987–88 season and replaced by Second Chance and Women in Prison, both canceled by mid-1988. Fox had planned to cancel The Late Show and develop The Wilton North Report, but after a ratings resurgence under guest host Arsenio Hall, the network could not reach a deal with Hall to return as host and instead revived The Late Show in early 1988. The show then used guest hosts and eventually selected Ross Shafer as permanent host, only to be canceled by October 1988, while Hall signed a deal with Paramount Television to develop The Arsenio Hall Show. Fox aired the 39th Primetime Emmy Awards and the next five editions. Although Married... with Children and The Tracey Ullman Show had modest success, several affiliates, including KMSP-TV in Minneapolis and KPTV in Portland, Oregon, disaffiliated in 1988 due to weak programming, citing that the network’s offerings harmed their syndicated programming. At the start of the 1989–90 season, Fox added a third night of programming on Mondays. The season marked a turnaround, with the debut of The Simpsons, an animated series that originated as shorts on The Tracey Ullman Show. Ranked a three-way tie for 29th in the Nielsen ratings, it became a breakout hit and the first Fox series to break into the Top 30. As of 2025, The Simpsons is the longest-running American sitcom, the longest-running American animated program, and the longest-running American scripted primetime television series. In 1989, Fox introduced the documentary series Cops and the crime-focused magazine program America's Most Wanted, which debuted as a half-hour series on Sundays before expanding to an hour and moving to Fridays in the 1990–91 season. These series became staples on the network for over two decades and formed the nucleus of Fox’s Saturday night schedule starting in the 1994–95 season. Married... with Children, which centered on a dysfunctional lower-middle-class family, saw a significant increase in viewer interest after Michigan homemaker Terry Rakolta began a boycott in 1989 over risqué humor and sexual content. The show became Fox’s longest-running live-action sitcom, airing for 11 seasons. Fox survived where DuMont and other fourth-network attempts had failed because it operated just under the FCC’s legal threshold for a network, allowing it to generate revenue without adhering to the Financial Interest and Syndication Rules that applied to the Big Three. DuMont faced regulatory barriers, including a ban on acquiring additional stations and tighter FCC ownership limits, which restricted its growth. In contrast, Murdoch was willing to invest heavily in programming and talent. DuMont operated on a shoestring budget and could not retain programs or stars. Most later startup networks, such as UPN and The WB, followed Fox’s model. DuMont operated during a time when the FCC did not require television manufacturers to include UHF capability, so viewers had to buy expensive converters to access UHF stations, which had poor signal quality compared to VHF stations. By the time Fox launched, cable allowed UHF stations to compete equally with VHF stations. Fox was not initially considered a major competitor to the Big Three, as it targeted a younger demographic—adults aged 18 to 34—with edgier content, while the Big Three focused on older audiences. Until the early 1990s, most Fox stations were formatted as independent stations, airing first-run or acquired programming, and during prime time, either syndicated shows or movies. Few stations carried local newscasts, especially in early years, with only a few in larger markets retaining long-standing newscasts, and those were limited to one newscast per day. On September 6, 1990, Fox reached an agreement with TCI, the nation’s largest cable company, to establish a cable-only national feed, Foxnet, for markets without over-the-air affiliates. Foxnet launched on June 6, 1991, bringing Fox programming to smaller markets and reaching 1.3 million subscribers by 1992. text: Fox's prime time programming schedule differs from the "Big Three" networks (ABC, CBS, and NBC) by airing only two hours on Monday through Saturday evenings and three hours on Sundays, compared to the three hours from 8:00 to 11:00 p.m. on weekdays and four hours from 7:00 to 11:00 p.m. on Sundays (Eastern and Pacific Time) for the older networks. This schedule, known as "common prime," includes the 10:00 p.m. (Eastern/Pacific) or 9:00 p.m. (Central/Mountain) hour, which is programmed exclusively by ABC, CBS, and NBC. Fox traditionally avoids programming the 10:00 p.m. hour, allowing local affiliates to air local newscasts during that time, though exceptions occur for special film presentations that exceed a two-hour timeslot, live sports overruns, or primetime entertainment following NFL playoff games. Fox did schedule programming in the 10:00 p.m. hour on Sundays from September 1989 to September 1993, but never added programming at that hour on other nights. The original reason for the reduced prime time hours was to avoid FCC requirements that would have classified Fox as a network and imposed associated regulations, though these rules have since been relaxed. Unlike the "Big Three," Fox does not air national morning or evening newscasts or any network daytime programming (such as soap operas, game shows, or talk shows), and instead relies on its owned-and-operated stations and affiliates to produce or distribute syndicated daytime content, including programs like Divorce Court and The Wendy Williams Show, distributed by corporate sister 20th Television. Fox also does not carry children's programming on Saturday mornings or late-night programming on Monday through Friday nights, with local affiliates producing their own content or airing syndicated programs. Due to irregular sports scheduling, many Fox stations fill weekend afternoons with syndicated programming, infomercials, and movies. Fox produces two versions of program promotions: one with standard airtimes based on time zones and another with "clean" end tags allowing stations to insert local airtime and station information via graphical and verbal continuity. This practice, different from ABC, NBC, and CBS, which only allow station logo insertions, was later adopted by The WB, UPN, The CW, and MyNetworkTV. A third promo version is used for cable network advertising, featuring "check local listings" in the end tag. Fox is the only broadcast network that currently airs adult animated comedies, beginning with The Simpsons in 1989, followed by King of the Hill (1997, until 2009, with a return to Hulu in 2025), Family Guy (cancelled twice, revived by Adult Swim in reruns, returned by Fox in 2005 due to home video sales), Futurama (1999, until 2003, picked up by Adult Swim, then Comedy Central from 2008–2013, returned to Hulu in 2023), American Dad! (2005, until 2014, picked up by TBS until March 2025, returned the next year), The Cleveland Show (2009, until 2013), Bob's Burgers (2011), The Great North (2021, until 2025), Krapopolis (2023), and Grimsburg and Universal Basic Guys (2024). Other adult animated shows like The Critic, The PJs, Sit Down, Shut Up, Allen Gregory, Napoleon Dynamite, Bordertown, Son of Zorn (Fox's only live-action/animated hybrid sitcom), Bless the Harts, Duncanville, and Housebroken were short-lived and unsuccessful. While ABC, CBS, and NBC have attempted to replicate Fox's success with adult animated shows, none have succeeded. Within Fox's station group, locally produced news varies significantly compared to ABC, NBC, and CBS, which typically offer at least 4½ hours of local newscasts on weekdays and one hour on weekends. Most Fox stations run a late-evening newscast at 10:00 p.m. (Eastern/Pacific) or 9:00 p.m. (Central/Mountain), lasting 30 minutes to one hour, due to the network not programming that hour. Several charter stations, such as WNYW in New York City, which launched its 10:00 p.m. newscast in March 1967, already aired prime time newscasts before Fox's launch. Most Fox stations also offer a weekday morning newscast from 7:00 a.m., one to three hours long, as a local alternative to national morning news. Fox has fewer stations with independent news operations than the "Big Three"; as of October 2015, 70 of its 236 stations (including all 18 owned-and-operated stations) had in-house news departments, compared to roughly 5/8–7/8 of stations on the other networks. KVVU (channel 5) in Las Vegas has the highest weekly news programming hours among Fox stations at 78½ hours. Many Fox stations use a newscast-intensive schedule similar to ABC, NBC, or CBS affiliates, including midday or early-evening newscasts, often extended by half-hour to compete with national evening newscasts. Some stations, especially those not owned by Fox Television Stations or formerly owned by Tribune Broadcasting, air early-evening newscasts only Monday through Friday due to weekend sports overruns. WSVN in Miami was the first Fox station to adopt this format, moving its late newscast from 11:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. and expanding it to one hour in 1989, and increasing its weekday morning newscast by two hours. This format was later adopted by former major network stations that switched to Fox between 1994 and 1996. Many upstart news departments begin with only a prime time newscast before adding more over time. In smaller to mid-sized markets outside the top 50 Nielsen-designated markets, local Fox newscasts are often outsourced to NBC, ABC, or CBS affiliates due to lack of funds, studio space, or legal duopolies or management agreements. ### 🔹 **BEFORE: The Context – Why the ELFA Was Needed**

Before the ELFA existed, women’s football had already been playing in informal, grassroots settings, especially during and after **World War I**.

  - "Unladylike"
  - "Dangerous to women’s health"
- **FA’s ban (5 December 1921)**: The Football Association officially banned women’s football, demanding clubs stop using their grounds for women’s matches.

➡️ **Key takeaway**: The ELFA was born out of **social pressure, gender norms, and institutional exclusion**. Women’s football had a strong grassroots base, but it was suddenly suppressed—making the ELFA a necessary, defiant response.

When Fox launched on October 9, 1986, as the Fox Broadcasting Company, it used a logo with three squares containing "FBC" similar to the UK’s BBC logo from 1997–present, with the network name in a rectangle below, mostly matching the color of ITV’s 1998–2004 logo, used primarily in the opening of The Late Show with Joan Rivers. On April 5, 1987, a more familiar logo based on 20th Century Fox’s design was introduced, featuring "FOX" with searchlights and a double-pane platform; Fox O&Os used a variant from 1987 to 1989 with an "O" and searchlight in negative space intersecting the "X" and panes; until the mid-1990s, some affiliates using CGI or local production houses emulated this design. In September 1993, the logo was modernized with a current proprietary logotype, angle changed (removing tilt), and the "O" gained a trademark pillar-like bowl, becoming a key element in advertising; the 1987 logo remained in print ads through 1993–94. Starting with this logo, Fox displayed an on-screen bug in the lower right corner (initially for one minute per segment, later throughout the program, then reverting after the 2009 digital transition). The "O" was later redesigned with the pillar, replacing the searchlight motif. A 1995–96 logo removed searchlights but kept two lower panes and added a third pane above the wordmark; a 1996 variant excluded the panes and restored searchlights behind the "F" and "X." The current logo, introduced in 1999, removed searchlights entirely and used only a wordmark. Despite this, searchlights remained part of 21st Century Fox branding, appearing in Fox News Channel’s logo and in the universal station logo introduced in 2006 by Fox O&Os (retained by seven former O&Os sold to Local TV in 2008 and spread to Tribune Broadcasting affiliates, modified in 2012 to feature one searchlight); the 1996–99 searchlight logo is still used by a few affiliates; searchlights were also in FX’s logo until 2008. The screen bug was used from 1999 to 2014; when the network upgraded to HD, the watermark remained in the 480i format. Until March 14, 2016, the network did not display the on-screen bug, only the hashtag without the Fox bug on some affiliates. For the 2019–20 season, Fox implemented branding by Trollbäck + Company, slightly thickening the logo and incorporating animations of its shapes into advertising and on-air elements, including an animation of abstract shapes morphing into the main Fox logo. Controversy arose in 2002 and 2003 over profanity by Cher and Nicole Richie during live broadcasts of the Billboard Music Awards on Fox affiliates in the Eastern and Central Time Zones, despite five-second audio delays; the indecent content was edited out in time zones west of the Mountain Time Zone. The Parents Television Council condemned both incidents as among the worst on television from 2001 to 2004 and filed tens of thousands of complaints with the FCC. Fox representatives’ apology was labeled a "sham" by PTC president L. Brent Bozell III, who argued the network could have easily used audio delays to remove the language. In 2004, Fox announced extending live delays to five minutes to allow easier editing of obscenities. In June 2007, the U.S. Second Circuit Court of Appeals ruled in Federal Communications Commission v. Fox Television Stations that the FCC could not fine broadcasters for fleeting expletives, such as during the Billboard Awards; the FCC later appealed the decision. The U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari and oral arguments began on November 4, 2008. The Parents Television Council has also criticized many popular Fox shows for perceived indecent content, including Family Guy, The Simpsons, American Dad!, Futurama, Cops, Hell's Kitchen, 24, House, Married... with Children, Bones, Arrested Development, Prison Break, 'Til Death, Malcolm in the Middle, The O.C., and That '70s Show, and has filed complaints with the FCC regarding such content.

text: François de Malherbe (1555–16 October 1628) was a French poet, critic, and translator. Born in Le Locheur (near Caen, Normandie), he came from a family of standing, though its noble lineage did not meet the heraldic standards for pre-16th century nobility. He was the eldest son of François de Malherbe, a conseiller du roi in Caen’s magistracy. Malherbe received an elaborate education in Caen, Paris, Heidelberg, and Basel. At twenty-one, he entered the household of Henri d'Angoulême, the illegitimate son of Henry II and governor of Provence, serving as secretary and marrying there in 1581. According to Tallemant des Réaux, his early verses were of poor quality. After Henri d'Angoulême died during Malherbe’s visit to Provence, he had no steady employment, though he earned a significant sum from Henry III through servile verses, which he later libelled. For many years, he lived between Provence and Normandy, with little known about this period. His work *Larmes de Saint Pierre*, imitated from Luigi Tansillo, was published in 1587. In 1600, he composed an ode of welcome for Maria de' Medici, marking the first of his notable poems. It took several years for his fortunes to improve; he was introduced to Henry IV by Cardinal Du Perron, though the king initially showed little interest, eventually summoning him to court and providing him with support, though the promised pension was not paid until after Henry IV’s reign. His father died in 1606, and Malherbe inherited his estate. From then on, he lived at court, maintaining a close correspondence with his wife, though seeing her only twice in twenty years. In old age, he suffered a major tragedy when his son, Marc Antoine, died in a duel against Paul de Fortia de Piles. Malherbe suspected foul play and used his influence to have de Fortia and Jean Baptiste de Covet brought to justice; he died before the case was resolved, reportedly from disease contracted during the siege of La Rochelle, where he had gone to petition the king. He died in Paris on 16 October 1628, at the age of seventy-three, just 15 months after his son’s death. The football team from Caen, France, Stade Malherbe de Caen, founded in 1913, is named after him. Malherbe had a significant and lasting impact on French literature, particularly in establishing the poetic rules of "Classicism" that would dominate for nearly two centuries until the Romantic era. His emphasis on technical perfection, simplicity, and vocabulary purity offered a corrective to the excesses of Pierre de Ronsard and La Pléiade, though Boileau-Despréaux’s praise in "Enfin Malherbe vint" is limited by his lack of knowledge of earlier French poetry. Malherbe’s personal character, marked by a bludgeon-like wit, was not amiable, as noted by his contemporary and rival Mathurin Régnier, who opposed him not only for his loyalty to Ronsard but also due to Malherbe’s discourtesy toward Régnier’s uncle, Philippe Desportes, whom Malherbe had initially plagiarized. While his poetic output is limited and often frigid, his best-known works include the *Consolation a Duperier* (featuring the line “Et, rose, elle a vécu ce que vivent les roses”), his odes to Marie de' Medici and Louis XIII. His prose is more extensive and highly refined, including translations of Livy and Seneca and numerous well-written letters, many addressed to Peiresc, as well as a detailed and critical commentary on Desportes. His most important disciples were François Maynard and Racan; Claude Favre de Vaugelas is credited with purifying French diction around the same time. Two of his poems were set to music by Maurice Jaubert. The primary biographical sources are Racan’s *Vie de Malherbe* and Tallemant des Réaux’s *Historiette*. The standard edition of his works is *Oeuvres poétiques*, edited by René Fromilhague and Raymond Lebègue (1968), while Antoine Adam’s popular collection *Poésies* is based on the Pléiade edition (1982). Key secondary sources include G. Brunot’s *La Doctrine de Malherbe* (1891), René Fromilhague’s *Malherbe: Technique et création poétique* (1954), David Lee Rubin’s *High Hidden Order* (1972) and its appendix in *The Knot of Artifice* (1981), and Claude K. Abraham’s *Enfin Malherbe* (1971), which focuses on Malherbe’s prosody.

text: Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón (Spanish pronunciation: [ˈfɾiða ˈkalo]; 6 July 1907 – 13 July 1954) was a Mexican painter renowned for her portraits, self-portraits, and works inspired by nature and Mexican artifacts. Influenced by the country’s popular culture, she used a naïve folk art style to explore themes of identity, postcolonialism, gender, class, and race in Mexican society. Her paintings often had strong autobiographical elements and blended realism with fantasy. Associated with the post-revolutionary Mexicayotl movement, Kahlo has also been described as a surrealist or magical realist and is known for depicting her chronic pain. Her 1940 self-portrait, The Dream (The Bed), holds the record as the most expensive work by a female artist ever auctioned, selling for $54.7 million. Born to a German father and a mestiza mother of Purépecha descent, Kahlo lived most of her life at La Casa Azul in Coyoacán, now the Frida Kahlo Museum. Though disabled by polio as a child, she was a promising medical student until a severe bus accident at 18 caused lifelong pain and medical issues. During recovery, she returned to art, initially considering a career as a medical illustrator. Her mother provided her with a specially-made easel and oil paints from her father, and a mirror was placed above the easel so she could see herself. Painting became a means to explore identity and existence, as she stated, "I paint myself because I am often alone and I am the subject I know best," and later, "to begin again, painting things just as [she] saw them with [her] own eyes and nothing more." Most of her early works were portraits of herself, her sisters, and schoolfriends, drawing inspiration from Renaissance artists like Botticelli and Bronzino and avant-garde movements such as Neue Sachlichkeit and Cubism. After moving to Cuernavaca in 1929 with Diego Rivera, she adopted a folk art style influenced by Adolfo Best Maugard’s treatise, incorporating elements from pre-Columbian and colonial Mexican art. In San Francisco in 1930, she met American artists like Edward Weston and Nickolas Muray, developed her folk art style, and created works such as Frieda and Diego Rivera (1931) and The Portrait of Luther Burbank (1931). Though she publicly presented herself as Rivera’s spouse, her work was included in the Sixth Annual Exhibition of the San Francisco Society of Women Artists. In Detroit, she faced health issues from a failed pregnancy and explored new techniques like etching and frescos, emphasizing themes of terror, suffering, wounds, and pain, and created retablo-style works such as Henry Ford Hospital (1932), My Birth (1932), and Self-Portrait on the Border of Mexico and the United States (1932). Despite no exhibitions in Detroit, she gave an interview to the Detroit News, titled "Wife of the Master Mural Painter Gleefully Dabbles in Works of Art." After returning to Mexico City in 1934, she made few paintings due to health issues, but in 1937 and 1938, following her divorce and reconciliation with Rivera, she produced more works than in all previous years, including My Nurse and I (1937), Memory, the Heart (1937), Four Inhabitants of Mexico (1938), and What the Water Gave Me (1938). The National Autonomous University of Mexico exhibited her work in early 1938, and she made her first significant sale in 1938 when Edward G. Robinson bought four paintings for $200 each. André Breton, impressed by her work, called it "a ribbon around a bomb," arranged her first solo exhibition at Julien Levy Gallery in New York in 1938, and later invited her to Paris in 1939. In New York, her colorful Mexican dress caused a sensation, and the exhibition, attended by Georgia O'Keeffe and Clare Boothe Luce, received positive press despite condescending reviews; she sold half of the 25 paintings. She received commissions from A. Conger Goodyear and Clare Boothe Luce. In Paris, despite Breton’s invitation, her paintings were not cleared by customs and the gallery refused to show most of them, considering them too shocking, and they were displayed alongside photographs, pre-Columbian sculptures, and Mexican market items. The exhibition opened in March 1939, received less attention due to the looming Second World War, and made a financial loss, leading her to cancel a planned London exhibition. However, the Louvre purchased The Frame, making her the first Mexican artist in their collection. She was warmly received by artists like Pablo Picasso and Joan Miró and by the fashion world, with Elsa Schiaparelli designing a dress inspired by her and Vogue Paris featuring her. Kahlo remained critical of the Surrealists, calling them "this bunch of coocoo lunatics and very stupid surrealists." In the United States, her work continued to gain attention, being featured at the Institute of Contemporary Art in Boston in 1941 and in two high-profile exhibitions in New York in 1942: the Twentieth-Century Portraits exhibition at MoMA and the Surrealists' First Papers of Surrealism exhibition. In 1943, she was included in the Mexican Art Today exhibition at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and Women Artists at Peggy Guggenheim's The Art of This Century gallery. In Mexico, she became a founding member of the Seminario de Cultura Mexicana in 1942, participated in exhibitions at the Benjamin Franklin Library in 1943 and 1944, and was invited to "Salon de la Flor." She also taught at the Escuela Nacional de Pintura, Escultura y Grabado ("La Esmeralda") starting in 1943, encouraging informal, non-hierarchical teaching and a focus on Mexican folk culture and street subjects. When her health prevented commuting, she held classes at La Casa Azul, and four students—Fanny Rabel, Arturo García Bustos, Guillermo Monroy, and Arturo Estrada—became devoted followers, known as "Los Fridos." She secured three mural commissions for herself and her students. Kahlo struggled to earn a living from her art until the mid to late 1940s, refusing to adapt her style, and received two government commissions in the early 1940s—one not completed and one rejected. However, she had regular private clients, such as engineer Eduardo Morillo Safa, who ordered over thirty family portraits. Her financial situation improved with a 5000-peso national prize for Moses (1945) in 1946 and the purchase of The Two Fridas by the Museo de Arte Moderno in 1947. By the mid-1940s, her paintings were featured in most group exhibitions in Mexico, and she could sell whatever she painted, sometimes incomplete works. As her health declined, she underwent a failed spinal surgery and painted works like Broken Column (1944), Moses (1945), Without Hope (1945), Tree of Hope, Stand Fast (1946), and The Wounded Deer (1946), reflecting her physical state. In her final years, she was mostly confined to La Casa Azul, painting still lifes of fruit and flowers with political symbols such as flags or doves. She expressed concern about expressing her political convictions, stating, "I have a great restlessness about my paintings... I must struggle with all my strength to ensure that the little positive my health allows me to do also benefits the Revolution, the only real reason to live." Her painting style became more intense, with brasher colors and faster brushstrokes. Photographer Lola Alvarez Bravo staged her first solo exhibition in Mexico at Galería Arte Contemporaneo in April 1953, despite her doctors’ bed rest orders; she arrived in an ambulance and was carried to the gallery, where she stayed for the event. The exhibition was a major cultural event and received global media attention. In 1954, Kahlo was hospitalized in April and May, then resumed painting after a one-year break, creating political works such as Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick (c. 1954), Frida and Stalin (c. 1954), and the still-life Viva La Vida (1954). Estimates vary on the total number of paintings she produced, ranging from fewer than 150 to around 200.
