text: Frida Kahlo, who lived in Mexico City, underwent a new bone graft surgery on her spine at Hospital ABC, which led to a difficult infection requiring multiple follow-up surgeries. After discharge, she was largely confined to La Casa Azul, using a wheelchair and crutches for mobility. During her final years, she remained active in political causes, rejoining the Mexican Communist Party in 1948 and campaigning for peace, including collecting signatures for the Stockholm Appeal. In August 1953, her right leg was amputated at the knee due to gangrene, leading to severe depression and anxiety, with her reliance on painkillers increasing significantly. When Diego Rivera began another affair, she attempted suicide by overdose. In her diary from February 1954, she wrote, "They amputated my leg six months ago, they have given me centuries of torture and at moments I almost lost my reason. I keep on wanting to kill myself. Diego is what keeps me from it, through my vain idea that he would miss me... But never in my life have I suffered more. I will wait a while." In her last days, she was mostly bedridden with bronchopneumonia but made a public appearance on 2 July 1954, participating with Rivera in a demonstration against the CIA invasion of Guatemala. She anticipated her death, speaking about it to visitors and drawing skeletons and angels in her diary, with the last drawing being a black angel interpreted by biographer Hayden Herrera as the Angel of Death. Her final words were "Espero Alegre la Salida – y Espero no Volver jamás" ("I joyfully await the exit – and I hope never to return – Frida"). The demonstration worsened her illness, and on the night of 12 July 1954, she developed a high fever and extreme pain. At approximately 6 a.m. on 13 July 1954, her nurse found her dead in bed; she was 47 years old. The official cause of death was pulmonary embolism, though no autopsy was performed. Herrera has argued that Kahlo committed suicide, and the nurse reported that Kahlo had taken eleven painkillers that night, exceeding her prescribed maximum of seven. That evening, she had also given Rivera a wedding anniversary gift over a month in advance. On the evening of 13 July, Kahlo's body was taken to the Palacio de Bellas Artes, where it lay in state under a Communist flag. The following day, it was carried to the Panteón Civil de Dolores for an informal funeral attended by friends and family, with hundreds of admirers outside. In accordance with her wishes, she was cremated in a spectacular manner, with legend stating that mourners saw her hair catch fire, her corpse sit up, and her face form a final seductive grin. Rivera, who described her death as "the most tragic day of my life," died in 1957. Kahlo's ashes are displayed in a pre-Columbian urn at La Casa Azul, which opened as a museum in 1958. In the twenty-first century, Frida has become both a commercial icon and a symbol for various groups, including feminists, the LGBTQ community, and Chicanos, with the term "Fridamania" coined to describe her widespread appeal. The Tate Modern considers her "one of the most significant artists of the twentieth century," and art historian Elizabeth Bakewell calls her "one of Mexico's most important twentieth-century figures." Her reputation as an artist developed late in life and grew posthumously, as during her lifetime she was primarily known as Diego Rivera’s wife and an eccentric in the international cultural elite. Recognition increased in the late 1970s due to feminist scholars challenging the exclusion of female and non-Western artists from art history and the Chicano Movement elevating her as an icon. The first two books about Kahlo were published in Mexico in 1976 and 1977 by Teresa del Conde and Raquel Tibol, and in 1977, The Tree of Hope Stands Firm (1944) became the first Kahlo painting sold in an auction, netting $19,000 at Sotheby's. The first two retrospectives of her work were held in 1978, one at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in Mexico City and another at the Museum of Contemporary Art in Chicago. A joint retrospective of her paintings and Tina Modotti’s photographs at the Whitechapel Gallery in London, curated by Peter Wollen and Laura Mulvey, opened in May 1982 and traveled to Sweden, Germany, the United States, and Mexico. The 1983 publication of Hayden Herrera’s biography Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo became an international bestseller. By 1984, Mexico declared her works part of national cultural heritage, prohibiting their export. As a result, her paintings rarely appear in international auctions, and comprehensive retrospectives are rare. Nevertheless, her works have broken records for Latin American art: in 1990, Diego and I was auctioned for $1,430,000, making her the first Latin American artist to exceed one million dollars; in 2006, Roots (1943) sold for $5.6 million; and in 2016, Two Nudes in a Forest (1939) sold for $8 million. Her popularity has led to the term "Fridamania," and she is considered "one of the most instantly recognizable artists," with her image used as frequently as those of Che Guevara or Bob Marley. Her life and art have inspired a wide range of merchandise and fashion. A biopic, Julie Taymor’s Frida, released in 2002, starred Salma Hayek (who co-produced it), grossed $56 million worldwide, and earned six Academy Award nominations, winning for Best Makeup and Best Original Score. The 2017 Disney-Pixar film Coco features a fictionalized Kahlo as a supporting character, voiced by Natalia Cordova-Buckley. Her appeal stems from a fascination with her painful and tragic life story, and she is seen as a symbol of non-conformity and a "cultural minority," simultaneously a victim and a survivor. Scholars note that her popularity is tied to the sharing of pain as a means of finding dignity and hope in modern society. Kirk Varnedoe stated that Kahlo resonates with contemporary sensibilities due to her self-obsession, creation of a personal world, and constant redefinition of identity—qualities shared by artists like Cindy Sherman and Kiki Smith and popular figures like Madonna. However, critics argue that her life has been mythologized, with dramatic elements overshadowing her art and reducing her works to literal depictions of her biography. Stephanie Mencimer notes that Kahlo has been embraced as a symbol for every politically correct cause and that, like a game of telephone, her story has been distorted, omitting uncomfortable details that reveal her complexity and flaws. This elevation of her life over her art diminishes understanding of her historical significance and obscures deeper truths in her work. Critics also warn that by sanitizing her biography, her image is set up for eventual decline, as is typical of women artists. Baddeley compares interest in Kahlo to that in Vincent van Gogh, noting that while Van Gogh is associated with his paintings, Kahlo is recognized through an image of herself—an observation on how male and female artists are perceived. Peter Wollen draws a parallel between Kahlo’s cult following and that of Sylvia Plath, whose complex art has been overshadowed by a simplified focus on her life. Kahlo’s legacy is commemorated through La Casa Azul, opened in 1958 and visited by about 25,000 people monthly, and Casa Roja (Museo Casa Kahlo), which focuses on her family. In 1985, Mexico City dedicated Parque Frida Kahlo in Coyoacán, featuring a bronze statue. In 2001, she became the first Hispanic woman honored with a U.S. postage stamp, and in 2012, she was inducted into the Legacy Walk in Chicago. In 2007 and 2010, commemorations were held on the centenary of her birth and the birthyear she attested to, including the Bank of Mexico releasing a $500-peso note featuring her painting Love's Embrace of the Universe, Earth, (Mexico), I, Diego, and Mr. Xólotl (1949) on the reverse and Diego Rivera on the front. A major retrospective at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in 2007 attracted approximately 75,000 visitors. Her influence extends to various artistic fields: Paul Leduc released a biopic in 1984, and she is the protagonist of novels by Barbara Mujica (2001), Slavenka Drakulic (2008), and Barbara Kingsolver (2009). James Newton released an album titled Suite for Frida Kahlo in 1994, Michael Marra wrote a song titled "Frida Kahlo's Visit to the Taybridge Bar," and in 2017, Monica Brown and John Parra published a children's book, Frida Kahlo and her Animalitos. In 1996 and 2005, the Mexican Cultural Institute in Washington, DC hosted "Homage to Frida Kahlo" exhibitions showcasing global artists’ works inspired by her. Notable artists such as Marina Abramovic, Alana Archer, Gabriela Gonzalez Dellosso, Yasumasa Morimura, Cris Melo, and Rupert Garcia have used or appropriated her imagery. Kahlo has also been the subject of stage performances, including Annabelle Lopez Ochoa’s one-act ballet Broken Wings (2016), with Tamara Rojo as the lead, and a full-length version, Frida, premiered in 2020 by Dutch National Ballet with Maia Makhateli as Kahlo. Three operas have been composed about her: Robert Xavier Rodriguez’s Frida (1991), Kalevi Aho’s Frida y Diego (2014), and Gabriela Lena Frank’s El último sueño de Frida y Diego (2022). She is the main character in plays such as Dolores C. Sendler’s Goodbye, My Friduchita (1999), Robert Lepage and Sophie Faucher’s La Casa Azul (2002), Humberto Robles’ Frida Kahlo: Viva la vida! (2009), and Rita Ortez Provost’s Tree of Hope (2014). In 2018, Mattel released seventeen new Barbie dolls for International Women’s Day, including one of Kahlo, which drew criticism for its slim waist and missing unibrow. In 2014, she was honored in the Rainbow Honor Walk in San Francisco’s Castro neighborhood. In 2018, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors unanimously renamed Phelan Avenue to Frida Kahlo Way, which is located near City College of San Francisco and Archbishop Riordan High School. In 2019, Rafael Blanco painted a temporary mural titled “Frida Kahlo” that won third place at the Reno Mural Festival. Also in 2019, Frida’s “Fantasmones Siniestros” (“Sinister Ghosts”) was burned to ashes, publicizing an Ethereum NFT. Time created 89 covers to celebrate women of the year from 1920 onward, selecting Kahlo for 1938. In 2022, as part of a collaboration with Centre Pompidou, Swatch released a watch based on The Frame.

text: A German school due to her father's wishes; she was soon expelled for disobedience and sent to a vocational teachers' school, where her stay was brief because she was sexually abused by a female teacher. In 1922, Kahlo was accepted into the elite National Preparatory School, where she studied natural sciences with the goal of becoming a physician. The school had only recently begun admitting women, with just 35 girls out of 2,000 students. She performed well academically, was a voracious reader, and became deeply immersed in Mexican culture, political activism, and social justice. The school promoted indigenismo, a movement that emphasized Mexico's Indigenous heritage and rejected European colonial superiority. Nine of her schoolmates, with whom she formed an informal group called the "Cachuchas," became leading figures in the Mexican intellectual elite; they were rebellious, staged pranks and plays, and debated philosophy and Russian classics. To conceal her age and to declare herself a "daughter of the revolution," she claimed to have been born on 7 July 1910, the start of the Mexican Revolution, a date she maintained throughout her life. She fell in love with Alejandro Gomez Arias, the group's leader and her first love; her parents disapproved. Due to political instability and violence, they were often separated and exchanged passionate love letters. On 17 September 1925, Kahlo and Arias were on their way home from school when they got off a bus to retrieve an umbrella Kahlo had left behind, then boarded a second crowded bus. The driver attempted to pass an oncoming electric streetcar, which crashed into the wooden bus, dragging it a few feet. Several passengers were killed; Arias suffered minor injuries, but Frida was impaled by an iron handrail through her pelvis. She later described the injury as "the way a sword pierces a bull," and the handrail was removed by Arias and others, causing her immense pain. Kahlo suffered multiple injuries: a fractured pelvic bone, punctured abdomen and uterus, a broken spine in three places, eleven fractures in her right leg, a crushed and dislocated right foot, a broken collarbone, and a dislocated shoulder. She spent a month in hospital and two months recovering at home before returning to work. X-rays revealed that the accident had displaced three vertebrae, and she was required to wear a plaster corset for the better part of three months, confining her to bed rest. The accident ended her dreams of becoming a physician and caused her lifelong pain and illness; her friend Andrés Henestrosa stated that Kahlo "lived dying." By late 1927, her bed rest ended, and she began socializing with her former schoolfriends, who were now university students and involved in student politics. She joined the Mexican Communist Party (PCM) and met political activists and artists such as Julio Antonio Mella and photographer Tina Modotti. At one of Modotti's parties in June 1928, Kahlo was introduced to Diego Rivera. They had met briefly in 1922 when he was painting a mural at her school. Shortly after their 1928 introduction, Kahlo asked Rivera to judge whether her paintings showed enough talent for her to pursue a career as an artist. Rivera recalled being impressed by her work, stating it demonstrated "an unusual energy of expression, precise delineation of character, and true severity... They had a fundamental plastic honesty, and an artistic personality of their own... It was obvious to me that this girl was an authentic artist." Kahlo soon began a relationship with Rivera, who was 21 years her senior and had two common-law wives. They were married in a civil ceremony at the town hall of Coyoacán on 21 August 1929. Her mother opposed the marriage, referring to it as a "marriage between an elephant and a dove," a comment based on Rivera's size and Kahlo's fragility; her father approved, as Rivera was wealthy and could support Kahlo, who could not work and required expensive medical treatment. The wedding was reported by Mexican and international press, and the couple became the subject of constant media attention, referred to simply as "Diego and Frida." In late 1929, Kahlo and Rivera moved to Cuernavaca in Morelos, where Rivera had been commissioned to paint murals for the Palace of Cortés. Around the same time, she resigned from the PCM in support of Rivera, who had been expelled shortly before the marriage for supporting the leftist opposition within the Third International. During the civil war in Morelos, life in Cuernavaca deepened Kahlo's sense of Mexican identity and history. Like many other Mexican women artists and intellectuals, she began wearing traditional Indigenous Mexican peasant clothing to emphasize her mestiza ancestry: long colorful skirts, huipils, rebozos, elaborate headdresses, and jewelry. She especially favored the dress of women from the matriarchal society of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, which represented an authentic Indigenous Mexican cultural heritage in post-revolutionary Mexico. The Tehuana outfit allowed her to express her feminist and anti-colonialist ideals. After Rivera completed the commission in late 1930, he and Kahlo moved to San Francisco, where he painted murals for the Luncheon Club of the San Francisco Stock Exchange and the California School of Fine Arts. Kahlo and Rivera returned to Mexico for the summer of 1931 and traveled to New York in the fall for the opening of Rivera's retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). In April 1932, they headed to Detroit, where Rivera had been commissioned to paint murals for the Detroit Institute of Arts. By this time, Kahlo had become bolder in her interactions with the press, impressing journalists with her fluency in English and stating on her arrival that she was the greater artist of the two. "Of course he [Rivera] does well for a little boy, but it is I who am the big artist," she said in an interview with the Detroit News in February 1933. The year in Detroit was difficult for Kahlo. Although she enjoyed San Francisco and New York, she disliked aspects of American society, which she viewed as colonialist, and found most Americans "boring." She disliked socializing with capitalists such as Henry and Edsel Ford and was angered that many Detroit hotels refused to accept Jewish guests. Kahlo had previously undergone an abortion in her marriage to Rivera and was deeply ambivalent about having a child. After the failed abortion, she reluctantly agreed to continue the pregnancy, but miscarried in July, which caused a serious hemorrhage requiring two weeks in the hospital. In May, Rivera was fired from the Rockefeller Center project and hired to paint a mural for the New Workers School. Although Rivera wanted to stay in the U.S., Kahlo was homesick, and they returned to Mexico soon after the mural's unveiling in December 1933. Back in Mexico City, Kahlo and Rivera moved into a new house in the wealthy neighborhood of San Ángel, commissioned by Juan O'Gorman, a student of Le Corbusier. The house consisted of two sections joined by a bridge; Kahlo's was painted blue and Rivera's pink and white. The bohemian residence became a key meeting place for artists and political activists from Mexico and abroad. Kahlo experienced further health problems—undergoing an appendectomy, two abortions, and the amputation of gangrenous toes—and her marriage to Rivera became strained. He was unhappy to be back in Mexico and blamed Kahlo for their return. Although he had been unfaithful before, he now began an affair with her younger sister Cristina, which deeply hurt Kahlo. After discovering the affair in early 1935, she moved to an apartment in central Mexico City and considered divorcing him. She also had an affair with American artist Isamu Noguchi. Kahlo was reconciled with Rivera and Cristina later in 1935 and moved back to San Ángel. She became a loving aunt to Cristina's children, Isolda and Antonio. Despite the reconciliation, both Rivera and Kahlo continued their infidelities. In 1936, she resumed her political activities, joining the Fourth International and becoming a founding member of a solidarity committee to aid Republicans in the Spanish Civil War. She and Rivera successfully petitioned the Mexican government to grant asylum to Leon Trotsky and offered La Casa Azul as a residence for him and his wife Natalia Sedova. The couple lived there from January 1937 until April 1939, during which time Kahlo and Trotsky became good friends and had a brief affair. According to their friends, the divorce was mainly due to their mutual infidelities. They were granted a divorce in November 1939, but remained friendly; she continued to manage his finances and correspondence. Following her separation from Rivera, Kahlo moved back to La Casa Azul and, determined to earn her own living, began another productive period as an artist, inspired by her experiences abroad. Encouraged by growing recognition, she moved from using small tin sheets since 1932 to large canvases, which were easier to exhibit. She adopted a more sophisticated technique, limited graphic details, and began producing more quarter-length portraits, which were easier to sell. She painted several of her most famous works during this period, including The Two Fridas (1939), Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair (1940), The Wounded Table (1940), and Self-Portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird (1940). Three exhibitions featured her work in 1940: the fourth International Surrealist Exhibition in Mexico City, the Golden Gate International Exposition in San Francisco, and Twenty Centuries of Mexican Art at MoMA in New York. On 21 August 1940, Trotsky was assassinated in Coyoacán, where he had continued to live after leaving La Casa Azul. Kahlo was briefly suspected of involvement, as she knew the murderer, and was arrested and held for two days with her sister Cristina. The following month, Kahlo traveled to San Francisco for medical treatment for back pain and a fungal infection on her hand. Her continuously fragile health had declined since her divorce and worsened due to heavy alcohol consumption. Rivera was also in San Francisco after fleeing Mexico City following Trotsky's murder and accepted a commission. Although Kahlo had a relationship with art dealer Heinz Berggruen during her visit, she and Rivera were reconciled. They remarried in a simple civil ceremony on 8 December 1940. Kahlo and Rivera returned to Mexico soon after. The union was less turbulent than before for its first five years. Both were more independent; while La Casa Azul was their primary residence, Rivera retained the San Ángel house as his studio and second apartment. Both continued having extramarital affairs; Kahlo had affairs with both men and women, with evidence suggesting her male lovers were more important to her than her female lovers. Despite medical treatment in San Francisco, Kahlo's health problems persisted throughout the 1940s. Due to spinal issues, she wore twenty-eight separate supportive corsets, ranging from steel and leather to plaster, between 1940 and 1954. She experienced leg pain, a chronic hand infection, and was treated for syphilis. The death of her father in April 1941 plunged her into depression. Her ill health increasingly confined her to La Casa Azul, which became the center of her world. She enjoyed caring for the house and garden and was accompanied by friends, servants, and pets, including spider monkeys, Xoloitzcuintlis, and parrots. While gaining recognition in her home country, her health continued to decline. By the mid-1940s, her back had worsened to the point that she could no longer sit or stand continuously. In June 1945, she traveled to New York for an operation that fused a bone graft and steel support to her spine to straighten it. The operation was a failure. According to biographer Hayden Herrera, Kahlo sabotaged her recovery by not resting as required and by once physically reopening her wounds in a fit of anger. Her paintings from this period, such as The Broken Column (1944), Without Hope (1945), Tree of Hope, Stand Fast (1946), and The Wounded Deer (1946), reflect her declining health. In 1950, Kahlo spent most of the year in Hospital ABC in Mexico City, where she underwent a new spine bone graft surgery. The surgery caused a difficult infection and required several follow-up procedures. After discharge, she was mostly confined to La Casa Azul, using a wheelchair and crutches to move. During these final years, Kahlo dedicated her time to political causes as her health allowed. She had rejoined the Mexican Communist Party in 1948 and campaigned for peace, such as by collecting signatures for the Stockholm Appeal. Kahlo's right leg was amputated at the knee due to gangrene in August 1953. She became severely depressed and anxious, and her dependence on painkillers escalated. When Rivera began another affair, she attempted suicide by overdose. She wrote in her diary in February 1954, "They amputated my leg six months ago, they have given me centuries of torture and at moments I almost lost my reason. I keep on wanting to kill myself. Diego is what keeps me from it, through my vain idea that."

text: In 1953, despite her doctors prescribing bed rest, Frida Kahlo ordered her four-poster bed to be moved to the gallery for the opening of a major exhibition, which was a significant cultural event in Mexico and received international media attention. She arrived in an ambulance, was carried on a stretcher to the bed, and remained there throughout the event. That same year, the Tate Gallery in London held an exhibition on Mexican art that included five of her paintings. In 1954, Kahlo was hospitalized in April and May, after which she resumed painting following a one-year break. Her final works include the political paintings Marxism Will Give Health to the Sick (c. 1954) and Frida and Stalin (c. 1954), as well as the still-life Viva La Vida (1954). Estimates of her total output range from fewer than 150 to around 200 paintings. Her early works from the mid-1920s show influence from Renaissance masters and European avant-garde artists like Amedeo Modigliani, while by the end of the decade, she drew inspiration from Mexican folk art, particularly its themes of fantasy, naivety, and fascination with violence and death. Her style blended reality with surreal elements and frequently depicted pain and death. André Breton, a key early supporter, claimed her as a Surrealist, stating she developed her style without knowing the movement’s ideological foundations, and described her work as situated at the intersection of political and artistic lines. Bertram D. Wolfe called her a "sort of 'naïve' Surrealism," though Kahlo herself detested Surrealism, viewing it as bourgeois art. Some art historians, like Andrea Kettenmann, see her as a symbolist focused on inner experience, while Emma Dexter argues her work aligns more with magical realism or New Objectivity due to its roots in Aztec mythology and Mexican culture rather than Surrealism. Influenced by Mexicanidad, a romantic nationalism emerging after the revolution, Kahlo aimed to paint for the Mexican people and rejected the idea of formal art education, instead cultivating an image of being self-taught and naive. While muralists dominated the Mexican art scene in the 1920s, Kahlo focused on small-scale self-portraits, especially inspired by votive paintings or retablos—religious images made by amateurs to thank saints for surviving calamities—whose format emphasized figures over realistic backgrounds. She owned approximately 2,000 retablos, displayed in La Casa Azul, and used their narrative potential to explore allegory and iconography. Her self-portraits often mimicked colonial-era bust-length portraits but subverted them by portraying her as less attractive, reflecting shifting societal values in the 1930s as Mexicans moved away from socialism toward individualism. Her mask-like faces were linked to Indigenous and Catholic depictions of goddesses and saints. She was influenced by Mexican folk artists Hermenegildo Bustos and José Guadalupe Posada, as well as European artists Hieronymus Bosch and Pieter Bruegel the Elder, and poet Rosario Castellanos, whose works addressed female suffering and patriarchal structures. Root imagery in her paintings symbolizes personal growth, entrapment, and the influence of the past on the present; in My Grandparents and I, a young Kahlo holds a ribbon from an ancient tree bearing her ancestors’ portraits, with her left foot as a tree trunk, reflecting her view of humanity’s unity with the earth and Mexico. Trees represent hope, strength, and intergenerational continuity, while hair symbolizes growth and the feminine; in Self-Portrait with Cropped Hair, she wears a man’s suit and shorn hair, holding scissors menacingly near her genitals, interpreted as a threat to Rivera or a projection of her anger toward patriarchal values and machismo. Kahlo’s lifelong suffering from a youth bus accident led to frequent hospitalizations and surgeries, often performed by quacks, and her medical-themed paintings frequently depict bleeding and open wounds, especially in childbirth and miscarriage, reflecting guilt over living at the expense of others. Her paintings, though personal, are ambiguous and raise questions about Mexican society, particularly gender, race, and class. Historian Liza Bakewell notes Kahlo recognized the contradictions of being Mexican—modern yet pre-Columbian, young yet old, anti-Catholic yet Catholic, Western yet New World, independent yet colonized, mestizo yet not Spanish or Indian—and used pre-Columbian and Christian symbols, including monkeys, skeletons, skulls, blood, and hearts, often tied to Aztec myths like Coatlicue, Quetzalcoatl, and Xolotl. She also frequently depicted La Llorona and La Malinche, figures associated with suffering and misfortune, such as in Henry Ford Hospital (1932), where she painted herself weeping with an exposed heart, traditionally seen as a depiction of grief but now interpreted as a commentary on the taboo of remaining childless in Mexican society. Kahlo often portrayed her body in various states—wounded, as a child, or in different clothing like the Tehuana dress, a man’s suit, or a European gown—using it as a metaphor to explore societal roles. Her depictions of the female body, especially during miscarriages or childbirth and cross-dressing, position the viewer as a voyeur, making it difficult to avoid a conscious response. According to Nancy Cooey, Kahlo made herself into the central figure of her own mythology as a woman, a Mexican, and a suffering person, expressing spiritual resistance and sexuality. Nancy Deffebach notes she created a subject who was female, Mexican, modern, and powerful, diverging from traditional gender roles. Until the late 1980s, her work was often seen as less political and more naïve than that of male muralists. Art historian Joan Borsa criticizes that critical reception has frequently ignored or downplayed the politics in her exploration of personal history, including sexuality, marginality, cultural identity, female subjectivity, and power. Magdalena Carmen Frida Kahlo y Calderón was born on 6 July 1907 in Coyoacán, near Mexico City. While she claimed to have been born at La Casa Azul, the official registry lists the birth at her maternal grandmother’s home. Her parents were photographer Guillermo Kahlo (1871–1941) and Matilde Calderón y González (1876–1932), who were 36 and 30 when she was born. Guillermo, originally from Germany, moved to Mexico in 1891 after an accident ended his university studies. Kahlo claimed her father was Jewish, but genealogists in 2006 found he was Lutheran. Matilde was born in Oaxaca to an Indigenous father and a Spanish mother. The couple had daughters Matilde (c. 1898–1951), Adriana (c. 1902–1968), and Cristina (c. 1908–1964), and two half-sisters, María Luisa and Margarita, raised in a convent. Kahlo described her childhood as "very, very sad," with both parents often ill and their marriage lacking love. Her relationship with her mother was tense; she described her as kind, active, intelligent, but also calculating, cruel, and fanatically religious. Her father’s photography business declined during the Mexican Revolution due to the loss of government commissions and reduced private clients. At age six, Kahlo contracted polio, which caused her right leg to grow shorter and thinner, leading to isolation and bullying. This experience made her reclusive but also close to her father, who shared her experience of disability. He taught her literature, nature, philosophy, sports, and photography, and encouraged her to pursue strength despite societal norms. Due to polio, she began school later and attended kindergarten and primary school in Coyoacán, then was homeschooled for grades five and six. Her sister Cristina went to a convent school, while Kahlo was enrolled in a German school due to her father’s wishes; she was expelled for disobedience and sent to a vocational teachers’ school, where she was sexually abused by a female teacher. In 1922, she was accepted into the elite National Preparatory School, where she studied natural sciences with the goal of becoming a physician. The school had only 35 female students out of 2,000, and she excelled academically, becoming deeply committed to Mexican culture, political activism, and social justice. The school promoted indigenismo, emphasizing Indigenous heritage and rejecting European superiority. Nine of her classmates, with whom she formed the informal group known as the "Cachuchas," became prominent figures in the Mexican intellectual elite.

text: Friedrich Wilhelm Ernst Paulus (23 September 1890 – 1 February 1957) was a German Generalfeldmarschall during World War II, best known for the surrender of the German 6th Army during the Battle of Stalingrad (July 1942 to February 1943). The battle ended in disaster for the Wehrmacht, with Soviet forces encircling the Germans within Stalingrad, resulting in the death or capture of most of the 265,000-strong 6th Army, their Axis allies, and collaborators. Paulus had fought in World War I in France and the Balkans, rising to captain by the war's end. After the armistice, he served in the Reichswehr as a brigade adjutant and was selected among 4,000 officers allowed to serve in the limited defensive army. He joined the 13th Infantry Regiment at Stuttgart and held various staff positions from 1921 to 1933, including guest lectures in Moscow during the 1920s as part of military cooperation between the Weimar Republic and the Soviet Union. In 1934–35, he briefly commanded a motorized battalion; in October 1935, he became chief of staff at Panzer Troop Command, overseeing the training of the Panzerwaffe. In February 1938, he was appointed chief of staff to General Heinz Guderian’s XVI Army Corps, where Guderian praised his intelligence and diligence but expressed doubts about his decisiveness and command experience. Paulus remained in that role until May 1939, when he was promoted to major general and became chief of staff for the German Tenth Army, which later became the Sixth Army. He saw action in the invasions of Poland and the Low Countries and was promoted to lieutenant general in August 1940. In November 1941, after Field Marshal Walter von Reichenau, his patron, was reassigned, Paulus was promoted to General der Panzertruppe and appointed commander of the Sixth Army, taking command on 20 January 1942, six days after Reichenau’s death. Paulus led the drive on Stalingrad, where his troops engaged in over three months of brutal urban warfare. In November 1942, during Operation Uranus, the Soviet Red Army launched a massive counter-offensive that surrounded the 6th Army. Paulus refused to request evacuation and followed Hitler’s orders to hold Stalingrad at all costs. Operation Winter Storm, a relief effort by Army Group Don under Field Marshal Erich von Manstein, was launched in December, but Paulus was not given permission to break out, and Manstein’s forces failed to reach Stalingrad due to Soviet offensives elsewhere. Kurt Zeitzler eventually convinced Hitler to allow a breakout, provided Paulus continued to hold Stalingrad—an impossible task. For two months, Paulus and his forces fought on, but the lack of food, ammunition, and deteriorating conditions gradually weakened the defense. On 7 January 1943, General Konstantin Rokossovsky offered surrender terms, including normal rations, medical care, and retention of badges and uniforms. Paulus requested permission from Hitler to surrender, but the High Command rejected the request, stating that holding out helped the entire front. On 25 January, after the Soviets overran the last airstrip, Paulus again requested permission, emphasizing that his men were without food or ammunition, with 18,000 wounded, and that collapse was inevitable. Hitler rejected the request once more and ordered Paulus to hold Stalingrad to the death. On 30 January, Paulus informed Hitler that his forces were only hours from collapse. Hitler responded by promoting Paulus to field marshal, noting there was no precedent of a German field marshal being captured alive, implying Paulus must commit suicide. text: "Full Leather Jacket" is the 21st episode of the HBO original series The Sopranos and the eighth episode of the show's second season. It was written by Robin Green and Mitchell Burgess, directed by Allen Coulter, and originally aired on March 5, 2000. Meadow hopes to attend Berkeley, but her parents, Tony and Carmela, want to prevent it. Their neighbor, Jean Cusamano, has a sister, Joan O'Connell, who is a distinguished alumna of Georgetown University. Carmela persuades Jean to ask Joan to write a letter of recommendation for Meadow. Joan declines, but Carmela visits her, offers her a ricotta pie, and insists, "I want you to write that letter." Jean informs Carmela that the letter has been written, and Carmela requests a copy. Silvio and Paulie pressure Richie to build a wheelchair ramp for Beansie's house as partial reparation for crippling him. Richie refuses scornfully, but when he learns the request comes from Tony, he sends his nephew Vito Spatafore and his construction workers to fully adapt Beansie's house. Richie owns a leather jacket he obtained years ago from the feared mobster Rocco DiMeo. He gives it to Tony, who accepts it reluctantly but politely. Richie values the jacket and the act of giving it to Tony deeply. He is deeply offended when he sees it being worn by the husband of the Sopranos' maid. Adriana, embarrassed by Christopher in a restaurant, leaves him and returns to her mother's. Christopher goes to her, proposes marriage, and presents her with a ring. She says she loves him and the ring. In bed, he tells her, "I'm back on track, rededicating myself"—to her and to Tony. Matt and Sean continue working with Christopher, breaking into safes. After enduring various slights and snubs from members of the DiMeo family, they feel they are making no progress and decide to take drastic action. They ambush Christopher as he leaves a diner, believing this will earn them favor with Richie. Christopher is shot three times and left unconscious; Sean is killed. Matt flees and asks for Richie's protection; Richie, furious, chases him away. As Christopher lies comatose in the hospital, Tony asks, "How could this happen?" The episode's title is a play on the 1987 film Full Metal Jacket, whose title refers to full metal jacket bullets. Here, it alludes to the leather jacket that Richie gave to Tony. Additionally, after Christopher is shot, the camera pans the sidewalk showing the metal cartridge casings expelled from the weapons. Thematically, Matt and Sean ambushing Christopher to prove themselves to Richie reflects the killing of the Vietnamese sniper by Joker in the film Full Metal Jacket, which—on one level—can be seen as a reluctant act by Joker to prove himself to Animal Mother and the others. Richie is shown as being abusive of others around him in a manner similar to how Animal Mother abuses the other Lusthog Squad marines, who still rely on him for their safety. More generally, this episode is connected to the film referenced in its title through the theme of "loss of innocence." text: Gael García Bernal (Spanish: [ɡaˈel ɣaɾˈsi.a βeɾˈnal]; born 30 November 1978) is a Mexican actor and filmmaker known for his roles in films such as Amores perros (2000), Y tu mamá también (2001), Bad Education (2004), The Motorcycle Diaries (2004), Babel (2006), Coco (2017), Old (2021), Cassandro (2023), and Magellan (2025). On television, he played music conductor Rodrigo De Souza in the series Mozart in the Jungle (2014–2018) and starred as the titular character in the Disney+ special Werewolf by Night (2022). He was nominated for a BAFTA Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role in 2005 for his portrayal of young Che Guevara in The Motorcycle Diaries and won his first Golden Globe Award for Best Actor – Television Series Musical or Comedy in 2016 for Mozart in the Jungle. He co-founded the production company Canana Films with fellow actor Diego Luna in Mexico City. In 2016, Time magazine included him in its annual Time 100 list of the most influential people, and in 2020, The New York Times ranked him No. 25 in its list of the 25 Greatest Actors of the 21st Century. Born in Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico, he is the son of Patricia Bernal, an actress and former model, and José Ángel García, an actor and director; his stepfather is Sergio Yazbek, whom his mother married when he was young. He began acting at age one and spent much of his teen years in telenovelas. García Bernal and Diego Luna were friends from childhood in Mexico City. At age fourteen, he taught indigenous people in Mexico to read, often working with the Huichol people; at fifteen, he participated in peaceful demonstrations supporting the Zapatista uprising of 1994. He studied philosophy at UNAM but took a sabbatical during a student strike to travel in Europe, later becoming the first Mexican accepted to study at the Central School of Speech and Drama in London and attending the European Graduate School for a master's in media and communication. After gaining success in telenovelas, Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu offered him a role in his debut feature, Amores perros (2000), which won critical acclaim and was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. His next role was in Alfonso Cuarón's Y tu mamá también (2001), which achieved crossover success in the U.S. and became the second-highest grossing Spanish-language film there. The following year, he portrayed Che Guevara in the 2002 TV miniseries Fidel and Father Amaro in the box-office record-breaking El crimen del Padre Amaro (2002). He reprised Che Guevara in The Motorcycle Diaries (2004), which broke the box office record set by Y tu mamá también three years earlier and earned him a BAFTA nomination in 2005. He also performed in theatre, including a 2005 production of Bodas de Sangre by Federico García Lorca at the Almeida Theatre in London. He has worked with acclaimed directors such as González Iñárritu, Pedro Almodóvar, Walter Salles, Alfonso Cuarón, Michel Gondry, and Iciar Bollaín, and has taken on English-language roles, including in Gondry's The Science of Sleep and The King, which received positive reviews. In 2007, he directed his first feature film, Déficit. He starred in the 2008 film Blindness, an adaptation of José Saramago's Nobel Prize-winning novel, where characters have no names or histories; director Fernando Meirelles noted that García Bernal focused on what his character wanted rather than their past. He again collaborated with Diego Luna in Rudo y Cursi, directed by Carlos Cuarón. The duo owns Canana Films, which recently partnered with Golden Phoenix Productions to produce television documentaries on the unsolved murders of over 300 women in Ciudad Juárez. In May 2010, he made a cameo as himself playing Cristiano Ronaldo in the Nike advertisement Write the Future. In 2010, he co-directed with Marc Siver four short films titled "Los Invisibles" for Amnesty International, focusing on Central American migrants in Mexico, their journey, risks, hopes, and contributions to Mexico, the U.S., and the world; he directed the films, conducted interviews, and narrated them. He starred in Even the Rain (2010), Spain's official entry for the 2011 Academy Awards. He narrated Human Planet for Hispanic audiences, which premiered on Discovery en Español on 25 April 2011 and aired on Discovery Channel in Latin America on 12 May. In 2014, he appeared in the American Spanish-language comedy film Casa de mi padre, opposite Will Ferrell, where he played a feared drug lord, marking his third collaboration with Diego Luna. He was also set to star in film adaptations of José Agustín's Ciudades Desiertas and Jon Stewart's directorial biopic Rosewater, in which he portrayed Maziar Bahari to critical acclaim, and was scheduled to appear in the 20th Century Fox reboot Zorro film Zorro Reborn, with a script by Glen Gers, Lee Shipman, and Brian McGeevy. In April 2014, he joined the main competition jury at the 2014 Cannes Film Festival. In June 2014, he began production on the dramatic comedy Zoom, directed by Pedro Morelli. In 2014, he was cast as Rodrigo de Souza in the Amazon Studios series Mozart in the Jungle, a role that earned him a Golden Globe in 2016. In 2016, he starred in two films submitted for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film: Desierto (Mexico) and Neruda (Chile). In 2017, he was named a member of the U.S. Dramatic Jury at the 2017 Sundance Film Festival and provided the voice of Héctor, a trickster protagonist, in the Pixar film Coco. He founded The Ambulante Documentary Film Festival, which brings documentary films to underserved areas, and helped create the Amnesty International series Los Invisibles; for this work, he received the Washington Office on Latin America's Human Rights Award in 2011. In October 2019, he and Diego Luna joined the Creative Advisory Board for EXILE Content alongside Adam Grant. In 2021, he starred in the M. Night Shyamalan thriller Old. In November 2021, he was cast in the Disney+ special Werewolf by Night by Marvel Studios. In 2024, he starred with Diego Luna in the Hulu original miniseries La Máquina. In 2025, he played Ferdinand Magellan in the historical drama Magellan, directed by Lav Diaz; the film is an international co-production between the Philippines, Spain, Portugal, Taiwan, and France and premiered at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival, being announced as the Philippines' official submission for Best International Feature Film at the 98th Academy Awards. García Bernal met Argentine actress Dolores Fonzi on the set of Private Lives in 2001; their son was born on 8 January 2009 in Madrid, Spain, and their daughter on 4 April 2011 in Buenos Aires, Argentina. He divides his time between Buenos Aires and Mexico City. He has been in a relationship with Mexican journalist Fernanda Aragonés since 2019 and had a child with her on 30 September 2021. He describes himself as "culturally Catholic but spiritually agnostic." He has received awards including the Ariel Award, BAFTA Awards, Cannes Film Festival recognition, Golden Globe Awards, and Goya Awards.

text: Gallium is a chemical element with the symbol Ga and atomic number 31. It was discovered by the French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran in Paris, France, in 1875. Elemental gallium is a soft, silvery metal at standard temperature and pressure, and in its liquid state, it appears silvery white. When sufficient force is applied, solid gallium fractures conchoidally. Its melting point is 29.7646 °C (85.5763 °F; 302.9146 K), which is just above room temperature and approximately equal to average summer daytime temperatures in Earth's mid-latitudes. This melting point is used as a temperature reference point in the International Temperature Scale of 1990 (ITS-90) established by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM), and the triple point of gallium, 302.9166 K (29.7666 °C, 85.5799 °F), is preferred by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Gallium melts in a person's hands at normal human body temperature of 37.0 °C (98.6 °F) and has a strong tendency to supercool below its melting point; Ga nanoparticles can remain liquid below 90 K, and seeding with a crystal helps initiate freezing. Gallium is one of four non-radioactive metals (with caesium, rubidium, and mercury) that are liquid at or near room temperature; unlike mercury, it is neither highly reactive nor highly toxic and can be used in metal-in-glass high-temperature thermometers. It has one of the largest liquid ranges for a metal and a low vapor pressure at high temperatures. Its boiling point is 2676 K, nearly nine times higher than its melting point on the absolute scale, the greatest ratio between melting point and boiling point of any element. Liquid gallium wets glass and skin, as well as most other materials (except quartz, graphite, gallium(III) oxide, and PTFE), making it mechanically difficult to handle. Gallium's volume expands by 3.10% when it changes from liquid to solid, requiring care when storing it in containers that may rupture. It shares the higher-density liquid state with water, silicon, germanium, bismuth, and plutonium. Gallium does not occur as a free element in nature but is found in trace amounts as gallium(III) compounds in zinc ores like sphalerite and in bauxite. It is obtained by smelting and is a silvery blue metal that fractures conchoidally like glass. Gallium does not crystallize in simple crystal structures; its stable phase under normal conditions is orthorhombic with 8 atoms per conventional unit cell, where each atom has one nearest neighbor at 244 pm, and the remaining six neighbors are spaced at 27, 30, and 39 pm, grouped in pairs. The bonding between nearest neighbors is covalent, forming Ga₂ dimers, which explains its low melting point compared to aluminum and indium. This structure is similar to iodine and results from interactions between gallium's single 4p electrons, farther from the nucleus than the 4s electrons and the [Ar]3d¹⁰ core. In the liquid state, gallium exhibits a complex low-coordinated structure where each atom is surrounded by 10 others, rather than the 11–12 typical of most liquid metals. The physical properties of gallium are highly anisotropic, with significant differences between linear and volume thermal expansion coefficients, especially near the melting point, where the coefficient of thermal expansion increases by several hundred percent upon melting. Gallium has 30 known isotopes, ranging from mass number 60 to 89; only two are stable and occur naturally: gallium-69 (60.1% abundance) and gallium-71 (39.9% abundance). All other isotopes are radioactive; gallium-67 has the longest half-life at 3.2617 days. Isotopes lighter than gallium-69 decay via beta plus decay or electron capture to zinc isotopes, while those heavier than gallium-71 decay via beta minus decay to germanium isotopes; gallium-70 can decay to either zinc-70 or germanium-70. Gallium-67 and gallium-68 (half-life 67.84 minutes) are used in nuclear medicine imaging. Gallium primarily exists in the +3 oxidation state, with the +1 state found in some compounds, such as GaCl₂, which contains both gallium(I) and gallium(III) and can be formulated as GaIGaIIICl₄; the monochloride is unstable above 0 °C and disproportionates into elemental gallium and gallium(III) chloride. True gallium(II) compounds include GaS (formulated as Ga₂⁴⁺(S²⁻)₂) and Ga₂Cl₄(C₄H₈O₂)₂. Strong acids dissolve gallium, forming gallium(III) salts such as Ga(NO₃)₃, and aqueous solutions contain the hydrated ion [Ga(H₂O)₆]³⁺. Gallium(III) hydroxide, Ga(OH)₃, can be precipitated from gallium(III) solutions by adding ammonia and dehydrated at 100 °C to form gallium oxide hydroxide, GaO(OH). Alkaline hydroxide solutions dissolve gallium, forming gallate salts containing the Ga(OH)₄⁻ anion; gallium hydroxide, which is amphoteric, also dissolves in alkali to form gallate salts. Gallium reacts with chalcogens at high temperatures; at room temperature, it is unreactive with air and water due to a protective oxide layer, but at higher temperatures, it reacts with oxygen to form gallium(III) oxide, Ga₂O₃. Reducing Ga₂O₃ with elemental gallium at 500–700 °C yields dark brown gallium(I) oxide, Ga₂O, a strong reducing agent capable of reducing H₂SO₄ to H₂S, which disproportionates back to gallium and Ga₂O₃ at 800 °C. Gallium(III) sulfide, Ga₂S₃, has three crystal modifications and can be formed by reacting gallium with H₂S at 950 °C or Ga(OH)₃ at 747 °C. Reacting alkali metal carbonates and Ga₂O₃ with H₂S produces thiogallates containing the [Ga₂S₄]²⁻ anion, which decompose in strong acids to release H₂S; HgGa₂S₄ is used as a phosphor. Gallium also forms lower oxidation state sulfides, such as gallium(II) sulfide and green gallium(I) sulfide, produced by heating gallium(II) sulfide to 1000 °C under nitrogen. The binary chalcogenides Ga₂Se₃ and Ga₂Te₃ have the zincblende structure and are semiconductors but are easily hydrolyzed and have limited utility. Gallium reacts with ammonia at 1050 °C to form gallium nitride (GaN), and forms binary compounds with phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony: gallium phosphide (GaP), gallium arsenide (GaAs), and gallium antimonide (GaSb), all with the same structure as ZnS and important semiconducting properties. These compounds are synthesized by direct reaction of gallium with elemental phosphorus, arsenic, or antimony, or by reacting Ga₂O with phosphorus at low temperatures; GaP also exhibits higher electrical conductivity than GaN. Gallium forms ternary nitrides, such as examples with lithium and phosphorus or arsenic (e.g., Li₃GaP₂ and Li₃GaAs₂), which are easily hydrolyzed by dilute acids and water. Gallium(III) oxide reacts with fluorinating agents like HF or F₂ to form gallium(III) fluoride, GaF₃, an ionic compound insoluble in water but soluble in hydrofluoric acid, forming GaF₃·3H₂O; dehydration of this adduct forms GaF₂OH·nH₂O, and the adduct reacts with ammonia to form GaF₃·3NH₃, which can be heated to form anhydrous GaF₃. Gallium trichloride is formed by reacting gallium metal with chlorine gas and exists as dimeric molecules, Ga₂Cl₆, with a melting point of 78 °C; similar dimers exist with bromine and iodine. Like other group 13 trihalides, gallium(III) halides are Lewis acids, reacting with alkali metal halides to form salts with GaX⁻₄ anions and with alkyl halides to form carbocations and GaX⁻₄. When heated, gallium(III) halides react with elemental gallium to form gallium(I) halides; for example, GaCl₃ reacts with Ga to form GaCl. At lower temperatures, the equilibrium shifts back, and GaCl disproportionates into elemental gallium and GaCl₃. GaCl can also be produced by reacting gallium with HCl at 950 °C, yielding a red solid. Gallium(I) compounds are stabilized by forming adducts with Lewis acids; so-called "gallium(II) halides," GaX₂, are actually adducts with the structure Ga⁺[GaX₄]⁻. Gallium forms a hydride, GaH₃ (gallane), produced by reacting lithium gallium hydride (LiGaH₄) with gallium(III) chloride at −30 °C. In the presence of dimethyl ether, gallane polymerizes to (GaH₃)ₙ; without solvent, it forms dimer Ga₂H₆ (digallane), a gas with a structure similar to diborane, unlike α-AlH₃ where aluminum has a coordination number of 6. Gallane is unstable above −10 °C and decomposes into elemental gallium and hydrogen. Organogallium compounds are less reactive than organoaluminum compounds but more reactive than organothallium compounds; alkylgalliums are monomeric, and Lewis acidity decreases in the order Al > Ga > In, so organogallium compounds do not form bridged dimers. They form stable peroxides and are liquids at room temperature with low melting points, being mobile and flammable. Triphenylgallium is monomeric in solution but forms chain structures in crystals due to weak Ga···C interactions. Gallium trichloride is a common starting reagent for organogallium compound synthesis, such as in carbogallation reactions, and reacts with lithium cyclopentadienide in diethyl ether to form the trigonal planar gallium cyclopentadienyl complex GaC.

text: Organoindium compounds are less reactive than organoaluminium compounds but more reactive than organothallium compounds. Alkylgallium compounds are monomeric, and Lewis acidity decreases in the order Al > Ga > In, meaning organogallium compounds do not form bridged dimers like organoaluminium compounds. Organogallium compounds are less reactive than organoaluminium compounds and do form stable peroxides. These alkylgalliums are liquids at room temperature with low melting points, are mobile, and are flammable. Triphenylgallium is monomeric in solution but forms chain structures in crystals due to weak Ga···C interactions. Gallium trichloride is a common starting reagent for forming organogallium compounds, such as in carbogallation reactions; it reacts with lithium cyclopentadienide in diethyl ether to form the trigonal planar gallium cyclopentadienyl complex GaCp3. Gallium(I) forms complexes with arene ligands like hexamethylbenzene, which is bulky enough to give a half-sandwich structure [Ga(η6-C6Me6)]+, while less bulky ligands such as mesitylene allow two ligands to bind in a bent sandwich structure. Benzene, being even less bulky, allows dimer formation, as in [Ga(η6-C6H6)2][GaCl4]·3C6H6. In 1871, Dmitri Mendeleev predicted the existence of gallium, naming it "eka-aluminium" and accurately forecasting its density, melting point, oxide character, and bonding in chloride. He predicted eka-aluminium would be discovered by spectroscope, would dissolve slowly in acids and alkalis, not react with air, that M2O3 would dissolve in acids to form MX3 salts, that eka-aluminium salts would form basic salts, that eka-aluminium sulfate would form alums, and that anhydrous MCl3 would be more volatile than ZnCl2—all of which were later confirmed. Gallium was discovered in 1875 by French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran using spectroscopy from a sample of sphalerite, and he later obtained the free metal by electrolysis of its hydroxide in potassium hydroxide solution. He named the element "gallia" from Latin Gallia, meaning Gaul, his native region, and it was later speculated (though denied by Lecoq in 1877) that he named it after himself due to "le coq" (rooster) and "gallus" (rooster). De Boisbaudran initially measured gallium's density as 4.7 g/cm³, which did not match Mendeleev's prediction; Mendeleev suggested a remeasurement, which yielded the correct value of 5.9 g/cm³, exactly as predicted. From 1875 until the semiconductor era, gallium's primary uses were high-temperature thermometry and metal alloys with unusual stability or low melting points, some of which are liquid at room temperature. The development of gallium arsenide as a direct bandgap semiconductor in the 1960s marked the most significant stage in gallium's applications. In the late 1960s, the electronics industry began using gallium commercially for light-emitting diodes, photovoltaics, and semiconductors, while the metals industry used it to reduce alloy melting points. First blue gallium nitride LEDs were developed in 1971–1973 but were weak; only in the early 1990s did Shuji Nakamura combine GaN with indium gallium nitride to develop modern blue LEDs, now the basis of ubiquitous white LEDs, commercialized by Nichia in 1993. Nakamura and two other Japanese scientists received a Nobel Prize in Physics in 2014 for this work. Global gallium production slowly increased from several tens of tons per year in the 1970s to about 100 t/yr by 2010 and rapidly accelerated, reaching approximately 450 t/yr by 2024. Gallium does not exist as a free element in Earth's crust; high-content minerals like gallite (CuGaS2) are too rare to serve as primary sources. Its crustal abundance is approximately 16.9 ppm, making it the 34th most abundant element, comparable to lead, cobalt, and niobium. Unlike these elements, gallium does not form its own ore deposits with concentrations above 0.1 wt.% and occurs at trace levels in zinc ores (~50 ppm) and slightly higher in aluminum ores, extracted as a by-product. This lack of enrichment is due to gallium's geochemical behavior. The USGS estimates over 1 million tons of gallium is contained in known bauxite and zinc ore reserves. Some coal flue dusts contain small amounts of gallium, typically less than 1% by weight, but these are not extractable without mining the host materials. Gallium is produced exclusively as a by-product during processing of bauxite and sulfidic zinc ores (mainly sphalerite), with minor amounts from coal. During the Bayer process, gallium accumulates in sodium hydroxide liquor and is extracted via methods such as ion-exchange resins; at a typical feed concentration of 50 ppm, about 15% of the gallium is extractable. The remainder goes to red mud and aluminum hydroxide streams. Gallium is removed from the resin in solution and then electrolyzed to produce gallium metal. For semiconductor use, it is further purified by zone melting or the Czochralski process, achieving purities of 99.9999% routinely and commercially. Gallium production is constrained by the annual extraction of bauxite, sulfidic zinc ores, and coal. Supply potential is defined as economically extractable amounts under current market conditions and includes at least 2,100 t/yr from bauxite, 85 t/yr from sulfidic zinc ores, and potentially 590 t/yr from coal—significantly exceeding current production of 375 t in 2016. The average price for low-grade gallium was $120 per kg in 2016 and $135–140 per kg in 2017. In 2017, world low-grade gallium production was about 315 tons, a 15% decrease from 2016. China, Japan, South Korea, Russia, and Ukraine were leading producers, while Germany ceased primary production in 2016. High-purity gallium production was about 180 tons in 2017, mostly from China, Japan, Slovakia, the UK, and the U.S. The 2017 annual production capacity was estimated at 730 tons for low-grade and 320 tons for refined gallium. China produced about 250 tons of low-grade gallium in 2016 and 300 tons in 2017, accounting for more than half of global LED production. As of July 2023, China produced between 80% and 95% of global gallium output. As of August 2023, China produced 80% of the world's gallium and 60% of germanium, and began restricting exports of both, key materials in the semiconductor industry, amid a "chip war" with the U.S. In 2024, China produced 98% of the world’s low-purity gallium (USGS). Semiconductor applications dominate commercial demand, accounting for 98% of total use, with 44% used in light fixtures and 36% in integrated circuits, and smaller shares in photovoltaics and magnets. Extremely high-purity gallium (>99.9999%) is commercially available for semiconductors. In 2007, gallium arsenide and gallium nitride in electronic components accounted for about 98% of U.S. gallium consumption, with 66% used in integrated circuits (mostly GaAs) for ultra-high-speed logic chips and MESFETs in cell phones, and 20% in optoelectronics. Worldwide, gallium arsenide makes up 95% of annual gallium consumption, valued at $7.5 billion in 2016, with 53% from cell phones, 27% from wireless communications, and the rest from automotive, consumer, fiber-optic, and military applications. The rise in GaAs consumption is linked to 3G and 4G smartphones, which use up to 10 times more GaAs than older models. Gallium arsenide and gallium nitride are used in optoelectronic devices with a market share of $15.3 billion in 2015 and $18.5 billion in 2016. Aluminium gallium arsenide is used in high-power infrared laser diodes, while gallium nitride and indium gallium nitride are used in blue and violet optoelectronic devices, such as laser diodes and LEDs. For example, gallium nitride 405 nm diode lasers are used as violet light sources in higher-density Blu-ray Disc drives. Other major applications of gallium nitride include cable television, wireless infrastructure, power electronics, and satellites. The GaN radio frequency device market was estimated at $370 million in 2016 and $420 million in 2016. Multijunction photovoltaic cells for satellite power use molecular-beam or metalorganic vapour-phase epitaxy of gallium arsenide, indium gallium phosphide, or indium gallium arsenide; the Mars Exploration Rovers and several satellites use triple-junction gallium arsenide on germanium cells. Gallium is also a component in photovoltaic compounds like copper indium gallium selenium sulfide (Cu(In,Ga)(Se,S)2), used in solar panels as a cost-efficient alternative to crystalline silicon. Gallium readily alloys with most metals and is used in low-melting alloys. The nearly eutectic alloy of gallium, indium, and tin is a room-temperature liquid used in medical thermometers, known as Galinstan (with "-stan" referring to tin), having a melting point of −19 °C (−2.2 °F). This alloy is used to cool computer chips and as a thermal paste replacement in high-performance computing. Gallium alloys have been evaluated as substitutes for mercury dental amalgams but have not gained wide acceptance. Liquid gallium-indium alloys have been found to precipitate gaseous CO2 into solid carbon and are being researched for carbon capture and removal. Due to high surface tension and deformability, gallium-based liquid metals can be used to create actuators by controlling surface tension, with potential applications in artificial muscle for robotic actuation. Plutonium in nuclear weapon pits is stabilized in the δ phase and made machinable by alloying with gallium. Although gallium has no biological function, gallium ions behave like iron(III) in the body and are used in pharmaceuticals and radiopharmaceuticals. Interest in gallium's anticancer properties arose when 67Ga(III) citrate localized to tumor sites in animals. Clinical trials show gallium nitrate has antineoplastic activity against non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and urothelial cancers. New gallium-ligand complexes such as tris(8-quinolinolato)gallium(III) (KP46) and gallium maltolate are under development. Gallium nitrate (brand name Ganite) is used intravenously to treat hypercalcemia from bone tumor metastasis by interfering with osteoclast function. Gallium maltolate, an oral, highly absorbable gallium(III) ion, is anti-proliferative to cancer and some bacteria that take it instead of ferric iron (Fe3+), and is being tested for cancer, infectious, and inflammatory diseases. When gallium ions replace iron(III) in bacteria like Pseudomonas, they disrupt respiration because iron is redox-active while gallium is not. A complex amine-phenol Ga(III) compound MR045 is selectively toxic to chloroquine-resistant malaria parasites by inhibiting hemozoin crystallization. Gallium-67 salts such as gallium citrate and gallium nitrate are used as radiopharmaceuticals in gallium scans, where the radioactive isotope 67Ga is used and the gallium compound is unimportant. The body handles Ga3+ as if it were iron(III).

text: Ferric iron (Fe³⁺) is a key component in biological respiration, and researchers are investigating a compound containing gallium in clinical and preclinical trials for treating cancers, infectious diseases, and inflammatory conditions. When gallium ions substitute for iron(III) in bacteria like Pseudomonas, they disrupt respiration because iron is redox-active and facilitates electron transfer, whereas gallium is redox-inactive, leading to bacterial death. A complex amine-phenol Ga(III) compound, MR045, is selectively toxic to malaria parasites resistant to chloroquine, as both compounds inhibit the crystallization of hemozoin, a byproduct of blood digestion in parasites. Gallium-67 salts, such as gallium citrate and gallium nitrate, are used in nuclear medicine imaging (gallium scan) where the radioactive isotope ⁶⁷Ga is employed; the specific gallium compound is unimportant because Ga³⁺ behaves like Fe³⁺ in the body, concentrating in areas of inflammation or rapid cell division, enabling imaging of these sites. Gallium-68, a positron emitter with a half-life of 68 minutes, is used in PET-CT diagnostics when linked to pharmaceuticals like DOTATOC (for neuroendocrine tumors) and DOTA-TATE (for neuroendocrine metastasis and lung neuroendocrine cancers, including certain microcytomas); it is produced via chemical extraction from germanium-68 in gallium-68 generators. Gallium is used in neutrino detection, notably in the SAGE experiment at the Baksan Neutrino Observatory in Russia, which contains 55–57 tonnes of liquid gallium, and in the earlier GALLEX experiment in Italy, which used 12.2 tons of watered gallium-71; solar neutrinos caused a few ⁷¹Ga atoms to become radioactive ⁷¹Ge, detected in the experiment, revealing a 40% deficit in solar neutrino flux compared to theory—later explained by improved detectors and theories (e.g., SNO). Gallium serves as a liquid metal ion source in focused ion beams, such as in creating the world's smallest book, Teeny Ted from Turnip Town. It is also an additive in glide wax for skis and low-friction materials. Materials scientists consider gallium promising for flexible and wearable electronics. Gallium disrupts the protective oxide layer on aluminum, enabling water to react with aluminum in AlGa to produce hydrogen gas. A common chemist joke involves using gallium spoons to serve tea, as gallium resembles aluminum in appearance, and the spoons melt in hot tea. Advances in trace element analysis have detected dissolved gallium in the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans, with concentrations in the Beaufort Sea recently reported; typical dissolved gallium levels in the Pacific at depths <~150 m are 4–6 pmol/kg, while in the Atlantic at depths >~350 m, they are 25–28 pmol/kg. Gallium enters oceans primarily via aeolian input and is geochemically similar to aluminum, being less reactive; due to its similar dissolved profile and longer surface water residence time, gallium acts as a tracer for aluminum and for aeolian inputs of iron, particularly in the northwest Pacific, south and central Atlantic Oceans; for instance, low gallium surface waters in the subpolar northwest Pacific suggest low dust input, explaining high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll conditions. Metallic gallium is not toxic, but several gallium compounds are; gallium halide complexes are toxic, and the Ga³⁺ ion in soluble gallium salts forms an insoluble hydroxide when injected in large doses, causing nephrotoxicity in animals; at lower doses, soluble gallium is well-tolerated, does not accumulate, and is excreted mainly through urine in two phases: a first phase with a biological half-life of 1 hour and a second phase with a half-life of 25 hours. Inhaled Ga₂O₃ particles are likely toxic.

text: Gang Chen, born in China and known in Chinese as 陈刚 (pinyin: Chén Gāng), is a Chinese-born American mechanical engineer and nanotechnologist. At the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), he holds the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering position and served as head of the Department of Mechanical Engineering from July 2013 to June 2018. He directs the Solid-State Solar-Thermal Energy Conversion Center, an energy frontier research center previously funded by the United States Department of Energy. Chen was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 2010 and to the National Academy of Sciences in 2023. He earned a Bachelor of Engineering in 1984 and a Master of Engineering in 1987, both in power engineering, from the Huazhong University of Science and Technology, and a Doctor of Philosophy in mechanical engineering from the University of California, Berkeley in 1993. He worked as an assistant professor at Duke University from 1993 to 1997 and as a tenured associate professor at the University of California, Los Angeles from 1996 to 2001 before joining MIT in 2001. Chen has made significant contributions to thermoelectricity, nanotechnology, and thermal engineering. In 2022, he and colleagues discovered that cubic boron arsenide is a highly effective semiconductor with potential applications in electronics. He has received the K.C. Wong Education Foundation fellowship and the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation fellowship (2002–2003), the NSF Young Investigator Award, an R&D 100 award (2008), and the ASME Heat Transfer Memorial Award (2008). He is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Physical Society, and the American Society of Mechanical Engineers. In 2010, he was elected to the National Academy of Engineering for contributions to heat transfer at the nanoscale and thermoelectric energy conversion technology; in 2014, he was elected an academician of Academia Sinica in the Division of Engineering Science and received the Nukiyama Memorial Award of the Heat Transfer Society of Japan. He was elected a Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in April 2018 and of the National Academy of Sciences in 2023. On January 14, 2021, Chen was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation and charged under the now-abolished China Initiative for allegedly failing to disclose connections to several Chinese educational programs in a U.S. Department of Energy grant application and for omissions in IRS filings, including allegations of wire fraud, failure to file a foreign bank account report (FBAR), and false statements on tax returns. The wire fraud charge stemmed from alleged omissions in an electronically submitted federal grant proposal form (Current and pending support). The FBI documents alleged that Chen received $19 million from China's Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech). In response, MIT President L. Rafael Reif stated the news was "surprising, deeply distressing and hard to understand," and on January 21, 2021, over 100 MIT faculty signed a letter protesting Chen's arrest, citing "deeply flawed and misleading statements" and ending with "we are all Gang Chen," which was shared on Twitter. On January 22, 2021, MIT's president clarified that the funds went to MIT, not Chen, to support a departmental research collaboration with SUSTech that Chen directed on MIT's behalf. The charges provoked widespread criticism, with many MIT faculty joining the protest, stating the defense of Chen was the defense of the scientific enterprise. Bloomberg noted that U.S. science has historically flourished by attracting international talent, and an MIT researcher stated the Department of Justice's China Initiative fundamentally misunderstands research and international collaboration. On January 14, 2022, the Wall Street Journal reported that federal prosecutors recommended dropping the charges, and the Washington Post reported that the DOE forms did not require Chen to disclose his connections to Chinese educational programs, undermining the basis of the charges. On January 20, 2022, federal prosecutors filed a motion to dismiss the charges "in the interests of justice," and the U.S. District Court dismissed the case. In a New York Times interview after his exoneration, Chen described the experience as "traumatic and deeply disillusioning" and stated, "I didn't do anything wrong." After the charges were filed, he was banned from the MIT campus and from contacting MIT employees, and his postdocs were moved to other labs. He lost his research group and funding and worked alone on other topics until the charges were dropped, after which he returned to his MIT office the day following the dismissal of the case.

In 2018, Gazprom agreed to a settlement that dropped all contractual barriers to the free flow of gas in Central and Eastern European markets, granted customers explicit rights to trigger price reviews when prices diverged from competitive benchmarks, and allowed more frequent and efficient reviews. Gazprom agreed not to seek damages from its Bulgarian partners after the South Stream project ended. Had the case gone to court, it could have resulted in fines of up to $12 billion. In 2020, Gazprom agreed to reimburse Poland's PGNiG nearly $1.5 billion for years of compelling overpayment for gas supplies.
