text: PJSC Gazprom, a Russian majority state-owned multinational energy corporation headquartered in the Lakhta Center in Saint Petersburg, derives its name from the Russian phrase gazovaya promyshlennost (gas industry). In January 2022, Gazprom surpassed Sberbank to become the largest company in Russia by market capitalization. In 2023, the company reported a revenue of 8.5 trillion rubles, a significant drop from 11.7 trillion rubles in 2022. Gazprom is vertically integrated and operates in all segments of the gas industry, including exploration and production, refining, transport, distribution, marketing, and power generation. In 2018, it produced 497.6 billion cubic meters of natural and associated gas and 15.9 million tonnes of gas condensate, accounting for 12% of global natural gas output. That year, Gazprom had proven reserves of 35.1 trillion cubic meters of gas and 1.6 billion tons of gas condensate. It exported gas via pipelines it builds and owns, such as Power of Siberia and TurkStream, producing 359 billion cubic meters of natural and associated gas in 2018, a 13% decline from the prior year. Gazprom Neft, a subsidiary, produces about 41 million tons of oil with reserves of 2 billion tons. The company also holds stakes in finance, media, and aviation. Gazprom was established in 1989 when the Soviet Ministry of Gas Industry was converted into a corporation, becoming the first state-run corporate enterprise in the Soviet Union. After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, Gazprom retained its Russian assets and secured a monopoly in the gas sector, while other national companies like Naftogaz and Turkmengaz took over assets abroad. In December 1992, following a presidential decree and government resolution, Gazprom became a joint-stock company and began distributing shares via vouchers, with 33% of shares acquired by the public by 1994 and 15% allocated to employees, while the state retained 40%, later reduced to 38%. Foreign ownership was limited to 9% until 1996, when 1% of equity was offered as Global Depository Receipts, and a $2.5 billion bond issue was launched in 1997. Under Viktor Chernomyrdin, who became Prime Minister in 1992, Gazprom evaded taxes, engaged in asset stripping, and shared assets with its executives and relatives, including the company Itera. Chernomyrdin was removed from office in 1998 and later became Gazprom's chairman. In 2000, Vladimir Putin, aiming to increase state control over key companies, replaced Chernomyrdin and Rem Viakhirev with Dmitry Medvedev and Alexei Miller, both of whom were Putin’s prior associates in Saint Petersburg. Miller and Medvedev were tasked with halting asset stripping and recovering losses, leading to Itera being denied access to Gazprom pipelines and nearly going bankrupt, with Itera eventually agreeing to return stolen assets in 2006. In April 2001, Gazprom acquired NTV, Russia’s only nationwide independent television station, from Vladimir Gusinsky’s Media-Most Holdings, after Gusinsky criticized the Kursk submarine disaster and the Second Chechen War and fled Russia. In June 2005, Gazprom subsidiaries sold a 10.7399% stake to Rosneftegaz for $7 billion, completing the sale by December 2005, which, combined with the state’s 38% share, gave the Russian government full control. The government then lifted the 20% foreign ownership cap, allowing foreign investment. In September 2005, Gazprom bought 72.633% of Sibneft for $13.01 billion, renaming it Gazprom Neft and using a $12 billion loan; the deal valued the company at £69.7 billion (US$123.2 billion) on the day of completion. In July 2006, the State Duma passed the On Gas Export law, granting Gazprom exclusive rights to export Russian natural gas. In December 2006, Gazprom signed an agreement with Royal Dutch Shell, Mitsui, and Mitsubishi to take a 50% plus one share stake in Sakhalin Energy. In June 2007, TNK-BP agreed to sell its stake in the Kovykta field to Gazprom after the Russian government questioned BP’s export rights. On 1 August 2007, Gazprom’s Sergey Kuprianov threatened Belarus with a 300% price increase on gas if debts were not paid, which was later resolved. On 23 June 2007, Russia and Italy signed a memorandum to build a 558-mile (900 km) South Stream pipeline to deliver 1.05 trillion cubic feet (30 km³) of gas annually to Europe, with a south fork to Italy and a north fork to Hungary. On 18 December 2007, Frank-Walter Steinmeier and Dmitry Medvedev signed an agreement with BASF to exploit a gas field, despite German academic warnings about overreliance on Russian gas. On 11 February 2008, Kuprianov threatened Ukraine with a gas flow halt, which was implemented in January 2009, beginning the 2009 Russia–Ukraine gas dispute. In December 2014, during a visit to Turkey, Putin announced the South Stream project would not proceed and instead committed to shipping 63 billion cubic meters per year (bcm/y) to Turkey, citing Bulgaria’s EU contract violations. In September 2012, the European Commission launched an anti-trust investigation into Gazprom, citing concerns about its dominant market position in upstream gas supply. In November 2013, Gazprom acquired Profmedia from Vladimir Potanin to expand its media interests. In May 2014, Gazprom and China National Petroleum Corporation signed a $400 billion contract for 38 billion cubic meters of natural gas annually to China starting in 2018. Construction of the Power of Siberia pipeline began in August 2014 with pipe deliveries to Lensk, Yakutia, and gas supply to China began on 20 December 2019 as part of the energy pact; Beijing and Moscow are now negotiating a second Far Eastern gas pipeline. In June 2014, Gazprom negotiated a 24.9% stake in OMV with the Abu Dhabi-based IPIC. In July 2014, Gazprom acquired Central Partnership, one of Russia’s largest film distributors. In September 2015, Nord Stream 2 contracts were signed and the pipeline was commissioned by July 2021. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Gazprom’s export market shrank from 185 bcm in 2021 to 100 bcm in 2022 and further declined in 2023, leading to a revenue collapse and a 34% price increase in the domestic market over three years. Gazprom has also faced compensation claims for failing to supply gas under long-term contracts. In April 2025, Gazprom announced it would begin producing home appliances. In 2011, Gazprom produced 513.17 billion cubic meters of natural gas—17% of global output and 83% of Russian production—with Yamburg producing 41%, Urengoy 23.6%, Nadym 10.9%, Noyabrsk 9.3%, and others 15.2%. It also produced 32.28 million tons of oil and 12.07 million tons of gas condensate. The majority of Gazprom’s fields are in the Nadym-Pur-Taz region of Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug in Western Siberia, with the historically largest fields being Medvezhe, Urengoy, and Yamburg. After over two decades of production, these fields are in decline, with annual production dropping by 20 to 25 bcm. Production at Zaporliarnoe, Gazprom’s fourth-largest field, increased until 2004, offsetting the decline in others. Since 2004, Gazprom has maintained production by activating new smaller fields and purchasing assets from other companies. Gazprom Neft was acquired in 2005 for $13.1 billion, purchasing 75% of its shares. Gazprom’s domestic and reexport gas supply relies heavily on imports from Central Asia: 42.6 bcm from Turkmenistan, 8.5 bcm from Kazakhstan, and 9.6 bcm from Uzbekistan in 2007, with 75% of Turkmenistan’s gas exports purchased to supply Ukraine. In 2008, Gazprom paid $130/mcm to $180/mcm for Central Asian gas. In 2015, Gazprom’s proved and probable natural gas reserves were 23.705 trillion cubic meters (837.1 trillion cubic feet), a 3.8% increase from 2011, representing 18.4% of global reserves; crude oil reserves were 1.355 billion tons and gas condensate reserves were 933.3 billion tons. Of these, 59.8% of natural gas reserves (Categories A+B+C1) were in the Urals Federal District (decreasing), 20.5% in the Arctic shelf (increasing), and 8.3% in the Southern Federal District and North Caucasus Federal District. Gazprom invested approximately 480 billion rubles ($20 billion) in new major projects to maintain supply. Nearly 37% of its reserves are located in the Yamal Peninsula and the Barents Sea. One of its major projects is the Blue Stream Pipeline, which delivers natural gas to Turkey via the Black Sea; the agreement was signed in 1997, the first joint was welded in 2000, and it transports 16 billion cubic meters annually. Exploration in the Yamal Peninsula has found over 10 trillion cubic meters of natural gas and over 500 million tons of oil and gas condensate, with about 60% located in Bovanenkovo, Kharasavey, and Novoportovo. The Bovanenkovo field has an estimated annual production capacity of 115 billion cubic meters (4.1 trillion cubic feet), with potential for increase.

## 🌟 Origin Story Method: The "How It All Began" Strategy

The **origin story method** involves reconstructing a clear, narrative-driven timeline of how something came into being — not just facts, but *why*, *when*, *who*, and *how* it started. It turns dry information into a compelling, human-centered story that helps with memory, understanding, and emotional connection.

We’ll use this method to tell the **origin story of Fort Oglethorpe**, Georgia — from land to name to community.

---

## 📖 The Origin Story of Fort Oglethorpe

### 🏁 Chapter 1: The Land — A Place of Travel and Legacy  
Long before soldiers marched or flags flew, the land that would become Fort Oglethorpe was home to a quiet, well-known family: **William Hamilton Hargrave and his wife, Amelia Cecilia Strange-Hargrave**.  

In the 19th century, travelers on the road from LaFayette, Georgia, to Ross’s Landing on the Tennessee River passed through this area. The Hargraves were respected locals — landowners who welcomed travelers, hosted them, and helped shape the early life of the region. Their home and land became a familiar landmark.  

But when the U.S. Army arrived in the early 20th century, they needed a strategic location near the Chickamauga National Battlefield. The existing settlement — named **Hargrave** after the family — was seen as ideal.  

👉 *So, the first chapter of Fort Oglethorpe’s story begins not with a soldier, but with a family who built a legacy on the land.*

---

### ⚔️ Chapter 2: The Army Arrives — A Military Post is Born  
In **1902**, the U.S. Army established a cavalry post at the site of Hargrave. This became known as the **Chickamauga Post**.  

The land, once owned by the Hargraves, was taken by the government — not through force, but through a practical decision: the Army needed a base for the **6th Cavalry**. The Hargraves, like other landowners, were asked to sell their property.  

👉 *This marks the official beginning of the military presence — a shift from a peaceful settlement to a strategic military outpost.*

---

### 🏛️ Chapter 3: The Name Changes — From Hargrave to Oglethorpe  
Even though the post was originally named after the local family, it wasn’t long before the name changed.  

In the early 20th century, the post was renamed **Fort Oglethorpe** in honor of **James Oglethorpe**, the founder of the Colony of Georgia.  

Why? Because Oglethorpe was a foundational figure in American history — a visionary who established Georgia as a haven for English settlers and a symbol of American ideals. Naming the post after him gave it a sense of **historical continuity, patriotism, and regional pride**.  

👉 *The name change wasn’t just administrative — it was symbolic. It transformed a local settlement into a place of national significance.*

---

### ⚖️ Chapter 4: The Human Cost — Detention and War  
During **World War I (1917–1920)**, the fort became a **detention camp** for civilian internees and prisoners of war.  

Then, during **World War II**, it served as a **war-time induction and processing center** — where young men were brought in, tested, and prepared for military service.  

And crucially, it became a **major training center for the Women’s Army Corps (WAC)** — a groundbreaking moment in American military history. Women trained here, breaking gender barriers and shaping the future of the armed forces.  

👉 *The fort didn’t just serve soldiers — it served the nation’s evolving values, including inclusion and equality.*

---

### 🏡 Chapter 5: From Military to Community — The Birth of a Town  
By **1947**, the post was declared **surplus** — no longer needed by the military.  

The land was returned to civilian use. And from that land, a new town began to grow.  

In **1949**, the town of **Fort Oglethorpe** was officially incorporated.  

👉 *The origin story ends not with a soldier’s march, but with a community’s rise — a place built on land, memory, and transformation.*

---

text: Gazprom invested approximately 480 billion rubles ($20 billion) in new major projects to maintain its supply. Nearly 37 percent of Gazprom's reserves are located in the Yamal Peninsula and in the Barents Sea. Exploration in the Yamal Peninsula has found reserves of over 10 trillion cubic metres of natural gas and over 500 million tons of oil and gas condensate, with about 60 percent of these reserves in Bovanenkovo, Kharasavey, and Novoportovo. The Bovanenkovo field has an estimated natural gas production capacity of 115 billion cubic metres per annum (4.1 trillion cubic feet per annum), with potential to increase to 140 billion cubic metres per annum (4.9 trillion cubic feet per annum). The Shtokman field, located 650 kilometres (400 mi) northeast of Murmansk and 1,000 kilometres (620 mi) west of the Yamal Peninsula in the central part of the Barents Sea, is estimated to contain up to 3.7 trillion cubic metres (130 trillion cubic feet) of gas, with potential production of 71 billion cubic metres per annum (2.5 trillion cubic feet per annum) in initial phases and up to 95 billion cubic metres per annum (3.4 trillion cubic feet per annum). Gazprom, TotalEnergies (France), and Statoil (Norway) formed Shtokman Development AG for the field's development. In 2013, in Amsterdam, Alexey Miller, chairman of Gazprom's management committee, and Jorma Ollila, chairman of Royal Dutch Shell's board, signed a memorandum outlining cooperation in Arctic shelf hydrocarbons exploration and development, in the presence of Putin and Mark Rutte. In 2008, Gazprom conducted 284.9 kilometres (177.0 mi) of explorative well drilling, 124,000 kilometres (77,000 mi) of 2D seismic, and 6,600 square kilometres (2,500 sq mi) of 3D seismic survey, resulting in a 583.4 billion cubic metre (20.60 trillion cubic feet) increase in gas reserves and a 61 million ton increase in crude oil and gas condensate reserves. Gazprom conducts prospecting in India, Pakistan, Algeria, Venezuela, Vietnam, Libya, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan. Its Unified Gas Supply System (UGSS) includes 158,200 kilometres (98,300 mi) of gas trunklines and branches and 218 compressor stations with a 41.4 GW capacity, making it the world's largest gas transmission system; in 2008, it transported 714.3 billion cubic metres (25.23 trillion cubic feet) of gas, and Gazprom has claimed the UGSS has reached its capacity. Major transmission projects include Nord Stream pipelines and internal Russian pipelines. In 2021, Russia had two large LNG production plants, Yamal LNG and Sakhalin-2 LNG, both of which Gazprom has an interest in. In March 2021, the Russian Government authorized a long-term programme to develop and expand the LNG industry with nine additional LNG plants to meet the growing global LNG market. In August 2021, Russia's first LNG bunkering vessel, Dmitry Mendeleev, was completed for Gazprom. In October 2021, Gazprom and RusGazDobycha announced the construction of Baltic LNG at Ust-Luga, with access to the Baltic Sea for westward sea transportation, processing ethane-containing natural gas with a capacity of 13 million tons of LNG per year. In 2024, Gazprom faced a significant LNG tanker shortage, leading it to use the Marshal Vasilevskiy floating storage and regasification unit (FSRU) for exporting LNG from its Portovaya facility, as its regular tankers like the Pskov were engaged in extended voyages to Asia, avoiding the Suez Canal and Red Sea due to Houthi attacks. In 2006, Gazprom sold 316 billion cubic metres (11.2 trillion cubic feet) to domestic customers, 162 billion cubic metres (5.7 trillion cubic feet) to Europe, and 101 billion cubic metres (3.6 trillion cubic feet) to CIS countries and the Baltic states; about 60 percent of its revenue came from European sales. In 2008, the average gas price for Russian industrial customers was $71/mcm, while households paid $54/mcm. Natural gas prices fluctuated since 2000; in late 2007, the NYMEX price was $7.53 per million Btu ($25.7/MWh), equivalent to $285 per 1,000 cubic metres, while German customers paid $250 per m3, Polish customers $290 per m3, Ukrainian customers $130 per m3, and Russian customers $49 per m3. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, due to falling export revenue, the domestic market is expected to see price increases of 34% by July 2025. Gazprom delivered gas to 25 European countries; its main export arm, Gazprom Export LLC (founded in 1973, previously known as Gazexport until November 1, 2006), holds a monopoly on gas exports to countries outside the former Soviet Union and sells most Russian gas in Europe under 25-year contracts. In late 2004, Gazprom was the sole gas supplier to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Estonia, Finland, Macedonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia, and Slovakia, providing 97 percent of Bulgaria's gas, 89 percent of Hungary's, 86 percent of Poland's, nearly 75 percent of the Czech Republic's, 67 percent of Turkey's, 65 percent of Austria's, about 40 percent of Romania's, 36 percent of Germany's, 27 percent of Italy's, and 25 percent of France's gas. By December 2010, Italy's gas supply from Russia increased from 25 percent in 2004 to 70 percent with support from Alexander Medvedev and Antonio Fallico. In May 2006, the European Union received about 25 percent of its gas supply from Gazprom, and Gazprom entered several long-term gas contracts with European companies, with prices mainly linked to oil. In 2014, Europe accounted for 40% of Gazprom's revenue, and the proportion of gas bought in the spot market in Europe rose from 15 percent in 2008 to 44 percent in 2012. In September 2013, during the G20 summit, Gazprom signed an agreement with China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) to exclude the Henry Hub index from price settlements. In May 2014, Putin met with Xi Jinping and negotiated a $400 billion deal, under which Russia would supply 38 billion cubic metres annually over 30 years at $350 per thousand cubic metres starting in 2018. In 2013, the average price of Gazprom's gas in Europe was about $380 per thousand cubic metres. China offered a $50 billion loan to finance gas field development and pipeline construction to the Chinese border, with China building the remaining pipeline. In January 2023, due to sanctions following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Gazprom's gas exports fell 45% from 185 billion cubic metres (Bcm) to 101 Bcm, mainly due to the loss of the European market; in 2023, Europe purchased only 28 Bcm, the lowest level since the 1970s. On 3 April 2006, Gazprom announced a threefold price increase for gas to Belarus after 31 December 2006; on 1 January 2007, it threatened to cut supply unless Belarus increased payments from $47 to $200 per 1,000 cubic metres or ceded control of its distribution network. Some analysts suggested the penalty was aimed at President Lukashenko for failing to pursue closer integration with Russia, while others noted Armenia paid similar prices. Gazprom requested $105, but Belarus refused; it responded that cutting supplies would deny Gazprom access to its pipelines, impairing gas transport to Europe. On 1 January 2007, a last-minute agreement was signed, with Belarus paying $100 per 1,000 cubic metres and allowing Gazprom to purchase 50 percent of Beltransgaz shares; immediately after, Belarus imposed a $42/ton transportation tax on Russian oil passing through its pipelines. On 13 March 2008, after halving gas supplies to Ukraine for three days, Gazprom agreed to supply it for the remainder of the year, removing intermediary companies. On 1 April 2014, Gazprom increased the gas price to Ukraine from $268.50 to $385.50 (£231.00) per 1,000 cubic metres; Ukraine's unpaid gas bills stood at $1.7 billion (£1.02 billion). On 30 October 2014, Russia agreed to resume gas supplies to Ukraine over winter through a deal brokered by the European Union. Gazprom is a vertically integrated company, owning its supply and distribution activities, including all main gas processing facilities in Russia, operating high-pressure pipelines, and since 2006 holding a legal export monopoly; other producers like Novatek are required to use Gazprom's facilities for processing and transport. At the end of 2008, Gazprom had 221,300 employees across subsidiaries in production, transportation, storage, and processing, with 9.5 percent in management, 22.9 percent as specialists, 63.4 percent as workers, and 4.2 percent as other employees. Gazprom's headquarters were in the Cheryomushki District, South-Western Administrative Okrug, Moscow until 2021, when they moved to the Lakhta Center in Saint Petersburg. Gazprom is a national champion, a concept promoted by Putin, where strategic companies serve national interests, such as selling gas domestically at prices below the global market; in 2008, Gazprom's activities accounted for 10 percent of Russia's GDP. Due to large-scale projects including Nord Stream 1 and Turkish Stream, Gazprom was a major revenue source for domestic suppliers and contractors. As of 2017, Gazprom's main shareholders were the Federal Agency for State Property Management (38.37%) and Rosneftegaz (10.97%), with Rosgazifikatsiya holding 0.89%, giving the Russian government majority control; the rest were held by investors, including 25.20% by ADR holders and 24.57% by other legal entities and individuals. Gazprom is listed on the Moscow and Karachi stock markets and is the top component of the MICEX and RTS indices; it was previously listed on London, Berlin, Frankfurt, and Singapore markets before 2022 sanctions. Gazprom has several hundred subsidiaries in Russia and abroad, directly or indirectly owned, including Gazprom International UK Ltd and Gazprom International Projects BV. Gazprom is the owner and sponsor of FC Zenit Saint Petersburg and its sports departments (basketball, volleyball), VC Zenit-Kazan, Gazprom-Ugra Surgut, and SKA St Petersburg of the KHL. On 1 January 2007, Gazprom became a sponsor of FC Schalke 04 at a cost of up to €25 million per year, extending the partnership for five years in November 2009; the sponsorship was suspended after the Russian invasion of Ukraine and was worth $150 million over five years. On 9 July 2010, Gazprom became a sponsor of Red Star Belgrade in the Serbian SuperLiga. In 2010, Gazprom was a Gold Partner of Team Katusha, alongside Itera and Rostekhnologii. In April 2021, Gazprom became a sponsor of the International Amateur Boxing Association (AIBA, now International Boxing Association) as a "general partner," a sponsorship that became controversial due to the IBA's increased Russian involvement.

text: Gender-affirming surgery (GAS) is a surgical procedure or series of procedures that alter a person's physical appearance and sexual characteristics to align with their gender identity. It is most commonly associated with transgender health care but is also pursued by cisgender individuals. The term is also known as sex reassignment surgery (SRS), gender confirmation surgery (GCS), and other names; however, "sex change" is generally considered offensive. Feminizing surgeries, such as vaginoplasty, vulvoplasty, and breast augmentation, result in female-looking anatomy, while masculinizing surgeries, including phalloplasty, mastectomy, and hysterectomy, result in male-looking anatomy. Patients often require lifelong hormone replacement therapy to support their endocrine system. Professional medical organizations, such as the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH), have established Standards of Care that require psychological evaluation and a period of real-life experience living in the desired gender before surgery is considered. Sweden became the first country to allow transgender people to change their legal gender after reassignment surgery and provide free hormone treatment in 1972, followed by Singapore in 1973 as the first in Asia. GAS is sometimes referred to as bottom surgery (in contrast to top surgery on the chest), and WPATH defines it broadly to include any surgical procedure for gender dysphoria. For trans women, genital reconstruction typically involves vaginoplasty using techniques like penile inversion, rectosigmoid vaginoplasty, or peritoneal pullthrough vaginoplasty; a less invasive option is vulvoplasty, which creates external female genitalia without a vaginal canal. For trans men, procedures may include phalloplasty or metoidioplasty to construct a penis, with metoidioplasty using the clitoris and resulting in a sensation-perceiving penis head, and scrotoplasty with possible testicular implants. Bigenital operations, such as androgynoplasty or vagina-preserving phalloplasty, allow individuals to retain original organs and are rarely performed. Gender nullification, which removes all external genitalia except the urethral opening, is pursued by some individuals assigned male at birth. GAS is also pursued by cisgender people for procedures like mammaplasty, penile implants, or testicular implants after orchiectomy. The term is often misrepresented by anti-trans activists as "genital-mutilation surgery." WPATH lists medically necessary procedures as including complete hysterectomy, bilateral mastectomy, chest reconstruction or augmentation, genital reconstruction, and certain facial plastic reconstructions, as well as facial hair electrolysis. Historical cases include Roman Emperor Elagabalus (2nd century), Alan L. Hart (1917), Dora Richter (1922–1931), and Lili Elbe (1930–1931), who underwent multiple surgeries including orchiectomy, penectomy, vaginoplasty, and an experimental uterine transplant that was rejected. In 1951, Harold Gillies developed a phalloplasty technique that became a standard. In 1971, Roberto Farina performed Brazil’s first male-to-female surgery, and in 1984, Jalma Jurado developed a technique used in over 500 surgeries. In 1999, Lebovic and Laub developed metoidioplasty. In 2003, the European Court of Human Rights ruled in favor of Carola van Kück, affirming access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy. In 2011, Christiane Völling won a landmark case against a surgeon for non-consensual sex reassignment. As of 2017, some European countries require forced sterilization for legal gender recognition, and Japan requires sterilization as of 2020. The prevalence of transgender-related surgeries is difficult to measure, with a 2015 U.S. survey reporting that 25% of respondents had undergone such surgery. Medical conditions like diabetes, asthma, and HIV can complicate treatment, and patients typically require a multidisciplinary healthcare team, including endocrinologists and pharmacists, for medication management and education. Fertility is a key consideration, as orchiectomy or oophorectomy results in irreversible infertility. Surgery is generally not performed on children under 18, though rare exceptions exist with long-term mental health counseling and parental or court consent. Infants with intersex conditions may undergo early interventions, which are controversial due to human rights concerns. Negative outcomes, including PTSD and suicide, can occur when the surgically assigned gender does not match gender identity. Milton Diamond recommended delaying surgery until children can give informed consent and suggested introducing them to others with differences of sex development to reduce stigma. Access to GAS is limited by financial barriers, insurance coverage, and provider availability, with many surgeons trained under Standards of Care, particularly WPATH’s, which are widely recognized but criticized for being rigid and restrictive. Many surgeons require two letters of recommendation, one from a mental health professional with over a year of experience diagnosing gender dysphoria, confirming surgery is appropriate. While many medical professionals oppose requiring surgery for legal gender change, many jurisdictions still require a physician’s letter attesting to surgery for legal recognition. In the U.S., an increasing number of insurance plans cover GAS, including genital reconstruction, chest reconstruction, breast augmentation, and hysterectomy, with some requiring proof of psychological evaluation and real-life experience (RLE). In June 2008, the American Medical Association stated that denying treatment for gender dysphoria constitutes discrimination and supports insurance coverage as recommended by physicians. In 2017, the U.S. Defense Health Agency approved payment for sex reassignment surgery for an active-duty trans woman, performed at a private hospital due to lack of expertise in military facilities. Long-term quality-of-life research is limited by small sample sizes and baseline mental health disparities. A 2020 meta-analysis found low-quality evidence that chest reconstruction improves quality of life; a 2022 review found reduced suicide attempts, anxiety, depression, and gender dysphoria, along with higher life satisfaction; a 2024 review found genital surgeries improved depression and dissociation, with mixed results for other mental health outcomes and less conclusive evidence of improvement compared to hormonal therapy. A secondary analysis of the U.S. Transgender Survey found that gender-affirming surgery was significantly associated with lower rates of psychological distress, smoking, and suicidal ideation among those who underwent it compared to those who desired but did not undergo surgery.

text: Cyprus is an island in the Eastern Basin of the Mediterranean Sea, ranking as the third-largest island in the Mediterranean after Sicily and Sardinia and the 80th-largest island globally by area. It lies south of the Anatolian Peninsula and is part of the Cyprus Arc. Geographically, it is classified in West Asia, though it is considered a European country in political geography. The island has experienced prolonged periods of Greek influence, along with intermittent Anatolian, Levantine, Byzantine, Ottoman, and Western European influence. It is dominated by two mountain ranges—the Troodos Mountains and the Kyrenia Mountains (also known as Pentadaktylos)—with the central plain, the Mesaoria, lying between them. The Troodos Mountains cover about half the island and stretch from Pomos Point in the northwest to Larnaca Bay in the east, featuring a complex, fragmented structure with steep valleys and stepped foothills in the southwest. The Kyrenia Range, a narrow limestone ridge along the northern coast, rises suddenly from the plains and extends into the Karpas Peninsula, which points toward Asia Minor, reflecting Cyprus’s geological connection to that region. The Kyrenia Range is known for its jagged, Gothic-like peaks and is less than half the height of Mount Olympus (1,952 m or 6,404 ft), the highest point in Cyprus, which is located in the Troodos Mountains. The Kyrenia Range is also referred to as the Pentadactylon Mountains due to its five-fingered summit shape. Ancient copper deposits were found on the Troodos slopes, originating from massive sulphide deposits within an ophiolite complex formed at a spreading centre under the Mediterranean Sea and uplifted during the Pleistocene. Access to year-round water is difficult across much of the island, traditionally attributed to deforestation and erosion, though Grove and Rackham challenge this view; instead, winter rivers originate in the Troodos and flow in various directions, including the Yialias and Pedhieos rivers flowing eastward into Famagusta Bay and the Serraghis River flowing northwest through the Morphou plain, all of which dry up in summer. An extensive network of dams and waterways has been built to supply farming areas. The Mesaoria plain is the island’s agricultural heartland, with crop productivity depending heavily on winter rainfall, and other crops grown under irrigation. Historically, the island was richly forested, especially in the Troodos and Kyrenia ranges and in the Mesaoria, though ancient conquerors removed much of the timber for shipbuilding, leaving little evidence today. About 12% of the island is classified as woodland, with shrub communities like golden oak, strawberry tree, terebinth, olive, kermes oak, and styrax found in non-forested areas, though maquis is uncommon. Most untended land is covered by garrigue, composed of low bushes such as Cistus, Genista sphacelata, Calicotome villosa, Lithospermum hispidulum, Phagnalon rupestre, and locally Pistacia lentiscus; excessive grazing leads to impoverished batha with stunted herbs. The island has a Mediterranean climate with warm, dry summers (mid-May to mid-September) and mild, rainy winters (November to mid-March), with temperature and rainfall variations influenced by altitude and distance from the coast. The total area of Cyprus is 9,251 km², of which 5,896 km² are under the Republic of Cyprus and 3,355 km² under the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus; land area is 9,241 km² and water area is 10 km². The island has no land boundaries and a coastline of 648 km. Its maritime claims include a territorial sea of 12 nmi (22.2 km; 13.8 mi), a continental shelf extending to 200 m depth or to the depth of exploitation, and an exclusive economic zone of 98,707 km² (38,111 mi²). The elevation extremes are 0 m at sea level and 1,952 m at Mount Olympus. Natural resources include copper, pyrite, asbestos, gypsum, timber, salt, marble, and clay earth pigment. Land use in 2012 shows 9.90% arable land, 3.24% permanent crops, and 86.86% other land. Irrigated land was 457.9 km² in 2007, and total renewable water resources were 0.78 km³ in 2011. Freshwater withdrawal in 2009 was 0.18 km³ per year (10% domestic, 3% industrial, 86% agricultural), with a per capita rate of 164.7 m³/year. Natural hazards include moderate earthquake activity and droughts. Current environmental issues involve water resource problems due to the lack of natural reservoirs, seasonal rainfall disparities, seawater intrusion into the island’s largest aquifer, increased salinization in the north, water pollution from sewage and industrial waste, coastal degradation, and loss of wildlife habitats from urbanization. Cyprus is a party to international environmental agreements including Air Pollution, Air Pollution-Persistent Organic Pollutants, Biodiversity, Climate Change, Climate Change-Kyoto Protocol, Endangered Species, Environmental Modification, Hazardous Wastes, Law of the Sea, Marine Dumping, Nuclear Test Ban, Ozone Layer Protection, Ship Pollution, and Wetlands, with no signed but unratified agreements.

text: The Gerbrandy Tower (Dutch: Gerbrandytoren) is a radio tower located in IJsselstein, the Netherlands, and is also known as the Lopik tower due to its proximity to the town of Lopik. It was constructed in 1961 and is used for directional radio services, FM- and TV-broadcasting. The tower features a concrete structure 100 meters (328') high, upon which a guyed aerial mast is mounted. Its original total height was 382.5 metres (1,255 ft), but it was reduced to 375 metres (1,230 ft) in 1987. On August 2, 2007, its analog antenna was replaced with a digital one, reducing its height by another 9 metres (30 ft), bringing its current height to 366.8 metres (1,203 ft). This structure is a partially guyed tower, combining a lower free-standing concrete tower with an upper guyed mast. If counted as a tower, it is the tallest in Western Europe. A similar but smaller partially guyed tower exists in the Netherlands—the Zendstation Smilde radio tower—consisting of an 80-metre (260 ft) concrete tower with a 223.5-metre (733 ft) guyed mast. This tower collapsed after a fire on July 15, 2011, and was rebuilt starting in late 2011, completed in October 2012, with the replacement structure now standing at 303 metres (994 ft). The tower is named after Pieter Gerbrandy, who served as Prime Minister of the Netherlands during World War Two. Nearby, the KNMI-mast Cabauw is used for meteorological measurements, and the 196-metre (643 ft) high mediumwave transmitter Lopik was demolished on September 4, 2015. On July 15, 2011, a small fire occurred in the Gerbrandy Tower, prompting the immediate shutdown of all transmitters in the tower as a precaution, resulting in large parts of the Netherlands losing FM-radio and digital TV (DVB-T) reception, as the Smilde tower also caught fire and collapsed shortly after. Ownership of the tower is complex: the concrete main structure and the first three meters (10') of ground around the base are owned by Alticom, a company established in 2007 that acquired assets from KPN and was part of the European TDG Group; in June 2011, all Alticom shares were acquired by Infracapital, an infrastructure specialist of Prudential plc. The metal mast is owned by NOVEC, a subsidiary of TenneT. The ground surrounding the base, excluding the first three meters (10'), remains owned by KPN. Annually, from December 6 to January 6, the tower is decorated with 120 LED lamps attached to its 12 guy-wires, creating the appearance of a giant Christmas tree at night. In 1998, it was awarded by The Guinness Book of Records as the tallest Christmas tree in the world in a construction. The Mount Ingino Christmas Tree is also noted as the largest Christmas tree, though it is constructed on a hill slope.

text: Gerhard Heinrich Friedrich Otto Julius Herzberg, PC CC FRSC FRS, born on December 25, 1904, in Hamburg, Germany, to Albin H. Herzberg and Ella Biber, was a German-Canadian physicist and physical chemist who won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1971 "for his contributions to the knowledge of electronic structure and geometry of molecules, particularly free radicals." He is renowned for his work in atomic and molecular spectroscopy, using these techniques to determine the structures of diatomic and polyatomic molecules, including free radicals, and for the chemical analysis of astronomical objects. Herzberg served as Chancellor of Carleton University in Ottawa from 1973 to 1980. He had an older brother, Walter, born in January 1904, and his family was atheist, a fact they kept hidden. His father died in 1914 at age 43 due to dropsy and complications from a prior heart condition. Herzberg attended Vorschule (pre-school) late after contracting measles and graduated shortly after his father's death. He married Luise Herzberg (née Oettinger), a spectroscopist and fellow researcher, in 1929; Luise died in 1971. In 1933, the Nazi Party enacted a law banning men with Jewish wives from teaching at universities; as Luise was Jewish, Herzberg and his wife began planning to leave Germany. With help from John Spinks, a visiting physical chemist from the University of Saskatchewan, Herzberg secured a position at the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon. When they left Germany in 1935, the Nazis allowed them to take only the equivalent of $2.50 each and personal belongings. Initially considering a career in astronomy, Herzberg was rejected by the Hamburg Observatory due to lack of private financial support. After completing high school at the Gelehrtenschule des Johanneums, he studied at Darmstadt University of Technology with a private scholarship and earned his Dr.-Ing. degree under Hans Rau in 1928. His most significant recognition was the 1971 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, during which he was described as "generally considered to be the world's foremost molecular spectroscopist." Herzberg received numerous honors, including being elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1951, winning the Frederic Ives Medal from the OSA in 1964, and being named an Honorary Member of the Society. The NSERC Gerhard Herzberg Canada Gold Medal for Science and Engineering, Canada's highest research award, was established in his honor in 2000. The Canadian Association of Physicists also has an annual award named after him, and the Herzberg Institute of Astrophysics is named for him. An asteroid, 3316 Herzberg, bears his name. At Carleton University, Herzberg Laboratories, belonging to the Physics and Mathematics/Statistics Departments, is named after him. The main building of John Abbott College in Montreal and a public park in Saskatoon's College Park neighborhood are also named after him. Herzberg authored influential works, including Atomic Spectra and Atomic Structure and the four-volume encyclopedic series Molecular Spectra and Molecular Structure, often referred to as the spectroscopist's bible. The first three volumes were re-issued by Krieger in 1989 with extensive new footnotes by Herzberg, and Volume IV, "Constants of diatomic molecules," is a reference work compiling known spectroscopic constants of diatomic molecules up to 1978. Gerhard Herzberg fonds are held at Library and Archives Canada and the National Research Council Canada.

text: The German Air Force, known in German as Luftwaffe (literally "air weapon," pronounced [ˈlʊftvafə]), is the aerial warfare branch of the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces. It was established in 1956 during the Cold War as part of the Bundeswehr, the armed forces of West Germany, following West Germany's accession to NATO in 1955. After German reunification in 1990, the Luftwaffe integrated elements of the former East German air force, the Luftstreitkräfte der NVA, which had been founded in 1956 as part of the National People's Army. There is no organizational continuity between the current Luftwaffe and the pre-1945 Wehrmacht Luftwaffe, which was disbanded in 1945/46 after World War II. The term Luftwaffe is used generically in German for any air force. The commander of the German Air Force is Lieutenant General Holger Neumann. As of 2015, the Luftwaffe operates from eleven air bases, two of which host no flying units, and maintains a presence at three civil airports. In 2012, it had an authorized strength of 28,475 active airmen and 4,914 reservists. After World War II, military aviation in Germany was banned by the Allied Control Commission, which disbanded the Nazi-era Luftwaffe in August 1946. The new Luftwaffe began operations in January 1956 with its first volunteers arriving at Nörvenich Air Base and receiving the US-made Republic F-84 Thunderstreak. Initially, it was divided into two operational commands: one in Northern Germany aligned with the British-led Second Allied Tactical Air Force and one in Southern Germany aligned with the American-led Fourth Allied Tactical Air Force. In 1957, the Luftwaffe took command of Army Air Defence Troops in Rendsburg and began expanding its air defense missile capabilities. The first operational unit was Air Transport Wing 61 at Erding Air Base, followed by the 31st Fighter-Bomber Squadron at Büchel Air Base. In 1958, the Luftwaffe received its first conscripts. In 1959, the 11th Missile Group in Kaufbeuren, armed with MGM-1 Matador surface-to-surface tactical nuclear cruise missiles, became operational. That same year, Fighter Wing 71 (Jagdgeschwader 71) equipped with Canadair CL-13 fighters became operational at Ahlhorner Heide Air Base. All aircraft, including current ones, feature the Iron Cross on the fuselage, a symbol from pre-March 1918, and the national flag of West Germany on the tail. In 1960, the Luftwaffe received its first Lockheed F-104 Starfighter jets, which remained in service until 1991. A total of 916 Starfighters were acquired, 292 of which crashed, resulting in 116 pilot deaths. This led to the Starfighter crisis in 1966, following 27 crashes and 17 casualties in 1965 alone. The West German public referred to the F-104 as the Witwenmacher (widow-maker), fliegender Sarg (flying coffin), Fallfighter (falling fighter), and Erdnagel (tent peg). On 25 August 1966, Defence Minister Kai-Uwe von Hassel relieved Chief Inspector Werner Panitzki and appointed Colonel Erich Hartmann, commander of the 71st Fighter Squadron, as Chief Inspector, due to public criticism of the Starfighter acquisition. On 2 September 1966, Johannes Steinhoff, with Günther Rall as deputy, became Chief Inspector. Steinhoff and Rall concluded that the non-German F-104s were safer and visited the US to study the aircraft, identifying deficiencies in training—such as lack of mountain and foggy-weather training and the aircraft's handling characteristics, including rapid, high-G turns—which contributed to accidents. They revised the training regimen, reducing accident rates to those comparable or better than other air forces and establishing a culture of high professionalism and tactical combat training outside Germany. Despite this, the F-104 retained its "widow-maker" reputation and was replaced earlier than in other nations by the McDonnell Douglas F-4 Phantom II and the Panavia Tornado. On Steinhoff's initiative, the Luftwaffe established the German Air Force Command USA/Canada in Fort Bliss for missile and air defense training and pilot basic training, and a Tactical Training Command in Beja, Portugal, for Close Air Support training. Between 1967 and 1970, the Luftwaffe reorganized its forces, dissolving the two operational commands and dividing the four mixed Air Force divisions into two flying and two air defense divisions, with the remainder forming functional commands. Over the next decade, it received new equipment: in 1968, the first C-160 Transall transport planes; in 1974, the F-4 Phantom II fighter-bombers; in 1978, the first Alpha Jet Version A light attack jets; and in 1979, the first of 212 Panavia Tornado fighters. In 1986, the air defense forces began replacing Nike Hercules missiles with the MIM-104 Patriot and Roland short-range missile systems. Germany participates in NATO's nuclear sharing concept, allowing member nations without nuclear weapons to participate in nuclear weapon delivery. The Luftwaffe began training with the US Seventeenth Air Force in handling, arming, and delivering nuclear weapons. Initially, the F-104 was intended as a nuclear delivery platform with nuclear air-to-air and air-to-surface missiles and bombs. The Tornado became the second aircraft capable of delivering nuclear weapons, limited to B61 bombs. From 1965 to 1970, Missile Wings 1 and 2 operated 16 Pershing 1 missile systems with nuclear warheads under US Army custody, upgraded to Pershing 1a with 72 missiles in 1970. Although not directly affected by the 1988 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, the Luftwaffe removed the Pershing 1a missiles from its inventory in 1991 and destroyed them. At the end of the Cold War, over 100,000 soldiers served in the Luftwaffe. The United States continues to lend nuclear weapons for hypothetical use under the nuclear sharing agreement. In 2007, 22 B61 nuclear bombs were stored at Büchel Air Base for use with Tornado IDS fighter-bombers of Tactical Air Force Wing 33. American nuclear weapons previously stored at Nörvenich, Ramstein, and Memmingen were withdrawn during the mid- to late-1990s. By international treaties with the "Big Four" powers—United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, and France—East Germany was a nuclear-free zone; the latter three no longer have nuclear weapons in Germany. After reunification in October 1990, the aircraft and personnel of the former East German air force were integrated into the Luftwaffe. The remnants were placed under the newly formed 5th Air Force Division (5. Luftwaffendivision) in Strausberg, renamed in 1993 to the 3rd Air Force Division (3. Luftwaffendivision), moved to Gatow in Berlin, and assigned to NATO in 1995. By 1990, East German aircraft markings were replaced by the Air Force Iron Cross, marking the first time Soviet-built aircraft served in a NATO air force. However, due to incompatibility with Western NATO equipment, most of the East German aircraft—such as the Sukhoi Su-17, MiG-21, MiG-23, and MiG-29—were retired and sold or transferred to NATO members in Eastern Europe, including Poland and the Baltic states. An exception was Fighter Wing 3 "Vladimir Komarov" (Jagdfliegergeschwader 3 "Vladimir Komarov") at Preschen Air Base, which flew new MiG-29 fighters. On 1 June 1993, it was renamed Fighter Wing 73 (Jagdgeschwader 73) and moved to Laage Air Base on 1 October 1994. The pilots were among the world's most experienced MiG-29 operators and served as aggressor pilots for dissimilar combat training. The United States sent fighter pilots to Germany during the Red October exercise to practice tactics against MiG-29s. The MiG-29s were fully integrated into the Luftwaffe's air defense structure and became the first Soviet Bloc aircraft to be operationally deployed within NATO. With the introduction of the Eurofighter Typhoon, the decision was made to withdraw the MiG-29s. All MiG-29s, except one, were sold to Poland for €1 each. On 9 August 2004, the last MiG-29s arrived in Poland and continue to serve in the 41st Tactical Squadron of the Polish Air Force. The Luftwaffe experienced its first combat action since World War II in September 1995 during Operation Deliberate Force, when six IDS Tornado fighter-bombers, equipped with forward-looking infrared devices, and escorted by eight ECR Tornados, supported NATO artillery missions against Bosnian Serb positions near Sarajevo. In March 1999, during the Kosovo War, the Luftwaffe participated directly in combat with Fighter Bomber Wing 32, equipped with ECR Tornados, which conducted missions to suppress enemy air defenses in Kosovo. These aircraft were equipped with an electronic countermeasures pod, one AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missile, and an AGM-88 HARM air-to-ground missile. The wing flew 2,108 hours and 446 sorties, firing 236 HARM missiles at hostile targets, with no manned aircraft lost. In 2005 and 2008, Luftwaffe F-4F Phantom II fighters participated in the Baltic Air Policing operation, supplemented in 2009 by Typhoon units. In 2006, the Luftwaffe deployed several Panavia Tornado reconnaissance planes from the 51st Reconnaissance Wing "Immelmann" stationed in Mazar-i-Sharif, Afghanistan, and German Army helicopters also operated from the Luftwaffe air base there. Additionally, C-160 Transall transport aircraft conducted missions in and around Afghanistan. Since the 1970s, the West German and post-reunification German Luftwaffe, along with other European air forces, has pursued the development of European-made warplanes, including the Panavia Tornado and the Eurofighter Typhoon, introduced in 2006. On 13 January 2004, Minister of Defence Peter Struck announced plans to reduce the number of fighter planes from 426 in early 2004 to 265 by 2015. Assuming full implementation of the order for 180 Typhoons and the removal of all F-4 Phantoms, the number of Tornado fighter-bombers would be reduced to 85. Previously, the Bundesmarine's naval air wing (Marineflieger) operated 112 Tornado IDS aircraft; however, the last unit was disbanded in late 2004, and the entire maritime combat role was transferred to the Luftwaffe, with one unit equipped to carry Kormoran II and American HARM missiles. As of 2014, a significant portion of Germany's military aircraft was unserviceable, with approximately half of the Eurofighters and Tornados not airworthy, and the aging C-160 fleet operating in limited service while awaiting the introduction of the Airbus A400M, the first of which was delivered in December 2014. Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged that due to the poor state of Bundeswehr equipment, Germany could no longer fulfill its NATO commitments. The Luftwaffe was one of the founding members of the European Air Transport Command (EATC) headquartered in Eindhoven, Netherlands, and most of its transport and tanker assets are managed under EATC. In 2018, the replacement of four Airbus A310 MRTTs with Airbus A330 MRTTs was approved, with four units acquired by the Royal Netherlands Air Force. Future plans include replacing the aging Sikorsky CH-53 Sea Stallion, acquired in the 1970s, with Boeing CH-47 Chinook or Sikorsky CH-53K King Stallion. A bid for a heavy transport helicopter (STH) program was initiated in 2018 but suspended in 2020 due to high costs. The Luftwaffe also participated in the Israeli Air Force's "Blue Flag" exercise, the country's largest international air combat exercise, simulating extreme combat scenarios. The German Air Force contributed six Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets from Tactical Air Force Squadron 73 Steinhoff based in Rostock.

text: The German Air Force is one of the founding members of the European Air Transport Command (EATC), headquartered in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, and most of its Transport & Tanker assets are now under EATC management. In 2018, the German Air Force approved the replacement of four Airbus A310 MRTT aircraft with four Airbus A330 MRTT aircraft, a decision made in conjunction with the Royal Netherlands Air Force. Future plans include replacing the aging Sikorsky CH-53 Sea Stallion, acquired in the 1970s, with either the Boeing CH-47 Chinook or the Sikorsky CH-53K King Stallion. A bid for a heavy transport helicopter program (STH) was initiated in 2018 but suspended in 2020 due to high costs. The Luftwaffe participated in the Israeli Air Force's "Blue Flag" exercise, the country's largest international air combat exercise, for the first time, with six Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets from Tactical Air Force Squadron 73 Steinhoff based in Rostock. In 2018, the Air Force issued a request for information on four aircraft to replace the Panavia Tornado—Eurofighter Typhoon, F-15 Advanced Eagle, F/A-18E/F Super Hornet, and F-35 Lightning—before dropping the F-35 in January 2019, leaving the Eurofighter Typhoon and Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornet as options. The German Air Force will acquire three C-130J Super Hercules transport and three KC-130J tanker aircraft, with deliveries planned for 2020–2021, jointly operated with the French Air Force’s two C-130J and two KC-130J aircraft (delivered 2018–19). The Super Hornet was selected for its compatibility with nuclear weapons and availability of an electronic attack variant, though as of March 2022, it had not been certified for the B61 Mod 12 nuclear bombs, with Boeing stating it believed it could meet German requirements with U.S. government support. In December 2021, Air Transport Wing 63 at Hohn Air Base, including the last remaining German C-160 Transalls, was disbanded, with the A400M and C-130J now serving as the primary tactical transport aircraft. In March 2022, Minister of Defence Christine Lambrecht announced Germany would buy 35 Lockheed Martin F-35A Lightning II fighter jets instead of Super Hornets, the only aircraft capable of carrying U.S. nuclear weapons, with an additional ten potentially added; Germany also planned to order 15 Eurofighter Typhoon electronic warfare aircraft to replace Growlers. In April 2022, Germany selected the CH-47F Chinook to replace its CH-53 Sea Stallion fleet as part of the STH program, with a contract worth approximately €5 billion (US$5.40 billion) for 60 aircraft. In August 2022, Germany deployed six Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets, three Airbus A330 MRTT tankers, and four Airbus A400M Atlas transports to Exercise Pitch Black in Australia, its largest peacetime deployment. From 12 to 23 June 2023, the German Air Force hosted Air Defender 23, the largest NATO air exercise since its creation, involving 25 nations and up to 10,000 troops. The current commander of the German Air Force is Lieutenant General Holger Neumann. This command, similar to the U.S. Air Force Air Staff, is a force-providing command, not an operational one, responsible for ensuring combat readiness of combat units, which during operations are commanded by NATO or the Joint Operations Command of the Bundeswehr. The Air Force Command directly controls three higher commands. The creation of the Air Force Command was part of a 2011 Bundeswehr reorganization announced by Thomas de Maizière, which reduced the Air Force to 23,000 personnel and led to the disbanding of the three air divisions, Air Force Training Command, and Air Force Weapon Systems Command. The three surface-to-air missile units merged into a single wing at Husum, fielding 14 MIM-104 Patriot and 4 MANTIS systems. The Luftwaffe will field three Multirole Eurofighter Wings, each with two squadrons for a total of 143 Eurofighter Typhoons. A fighter-bomber wing with Panavia Tornado IDS remains at Büchel Air Base, and Reconnaissance Wing 51 at Schleswig Air Base will retain its Tornado ECR squadron and add one drone squadron. The Kommando Luftwaffe has two main elements: individual units fall under the Air Force Operational Forces Command or Support Forces Command, and only come under Air Operations Command during deployment or EU/NATO attachments. This system was replaced in 1968 with a four-digit registration code, separated by an Iron Cross: the first two digits identify the aircraft type, the last two are sequential per type. text: Gertrude Katherine Lathrop (December 24, 1896–March 16, 1986) was an American sculptor renowned for her medallion work and sculptures of small animals. She was born in Albany, New York, to artist Ida Pulis Lathrop and Cyrus Clark Lathrop, and her sister Dorothy P. Lathrop was also an artist. Lathrop studied at the Art Students League in 1918 and at the School of American Sculpture, both under Gutzon Borglum. Her first exhibition was at the National Academy of Design in 1921. In 1924, she traveled to Gloucester, Massachusetts to study with Charles Grafly. She received an Honorable Mention from the Art Institute of Chicago in 1924, as well as the Helen Foster Barnett prize and the National Academy of Design award in 1928. In 1936, she designed the Albany Charter half dollar, and in 1938, she was commissioned by the Westchester County Coin Club of New Rochelle, New York, to design the New Rochelle 250th Anniversary half dollar. In 1964, she was awarded the Allied Artists of America's Medal of Honor; in 1967, she received the Pen and Brush Club's silver medal; and in 1970, she won the John Sanford Saltus Gold Medal from the British Numismatic Society. Lathrop was skilled in medal design and portrait modeling, but her primary passion was sculpting animals, a choice she explained by stating, "I chose to model animals because of their infinite variety of form and texture and their great beauty, for even the lowliest of them have beauty, yes even the ward bug, with his magnificent tusks." In 1954, she moved to Falls Village, Connecticut with her sister, a noted illustrator of children's books, where she resided for the rest of her life. Her works are held in the collections of the Seattle Art Museum, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the National Gallery of Art in Washington, the Albany Institute of History & Art, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art. She died in Falls Village, Connecticut in 1986.

text: The northernmost part of Ghana is Pulmakong, located near the Burkina Faso border, while the southernmost point is Cape Three Points. Ghana has a tropical climate with distinct wet and dry seasons and lies at the intersection of three hydro-climatic zones: the eastern coastal belt is warm and comparatively dry, the south-west corner is hot and humid, and the north is hot and dry. Climate change is significantly affecting Ghana, with rising temperatures, altered rainfall, extreme weather, drought, wildfires, floods, and sea-level rise negatively impacting infrastructure, hydropower, food security, water supply, and coastal and agricultural livelihoods such as farming and fisheries. These changes threaten climate-sensitive sectors like agriculture, energy, and forestry, and are expected to increase diseases such as malaria, dengue fever, and cholera due to shifting water conditions. Ghana signed the Paris Agreement in 2016 and aims to avoid 64 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to a business-as-usual scenario, with a commitment to net zero by 2060. The country's geography includes low coastal plains, forested hills in the center, and savanna in the north, with Mount Afadja (885 m) in the Akwapim-Togo Range being the highest point. The Volta River system is dominant, with the White Volta and Black Volta converging in the north and flowing into Lake Volta, one of the world's largest artificial reservoirs created by the Akosombo Dam in 1965. The Volta exits into the Gulf of Guinea east of Accra, and other major rivers include the Pra, Ankobra, and Tano. Ghana is a unitary presidential constitutional democracy with a parliamentary multi-party system dominated by the National Democratic Congress (NDC) and the New Patriotic Party (NPP), having transitioned to the Fourth Republic in 1993 after civilian elections. Presidents are limited to two four-year terms; Nana Akufo-Addo won the 2016 and 2020 elections, defeating John Mahama, and his presidency ended in January 2025, after which Mahama became president. In 2012, Ghana ranked 67th least fragile globally and fifth least fragile in Africa, 64th least corrupt globally and fifth least corrupt in Africa, and seventh in Africa on the Ibrahim Index of African Governance. According to the 2023 V-Dem Democracy Index, Ghana is ranked 67th as an electoral democracy worldwide and 10th in Africa. Since independence, Ghana has adhered to nonalignment and is a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement, actively participating in the United Nations and African Union. Ghana has strong ties with the United States, with three U.S. presidents—Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama—and Vice President Kamala Harris having visited officially. Notable Ghanaian figures such as Kofi Annan, Akua Kuenyehia, Jerry John Rawlings, and John Agyekum Kufuor have held international diplomatic roles. In 2010, President John Atta Mills visited China to mark the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations, and China reciprocated in 2011 with a visit by Zhou Tienong. China has become a top investor in Ghana, focusing on infrastructure, natural resources, and manufacturing, though concerns remain about sustainability, environmental impacts, and transparency. In 2013, Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad met with Mahama to discuss the Non-Aligned Movement and co-chair a bilateral meeting at Flagstaff House. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are integrated into Ghana’s development agenda and budget through a decentralized planning approach involving UN agencies, traditional leaders, civil society, and academia. President Akufo-Addo noted that Ghana was the first Sub-Saharan African country to halve poverty as per Goal 1 of the Millennium Development Goals. In 1957, the Ghana Armed Forces (GAF) consisted of headquarters, support services, three infantry battalions, and a reconnaissance squadron; by 1964, it had expanded to six battalions, including a parachute unit. Today, Ghana is considered a regional power and hegemon, with Canadian Forces commander Roméo Dallaire highly praising its military personnel. Military operations are guided by the constitution, the Law on Armed Force Military Strategy, and agreements with the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre, executed under the Ministry of Defence. Despite being relatively peaceful, Ghana has experienced political violence, with an upward trend in politically motivated incidents in 2017. The Ghana Police Service and the Criminal Investigation Department are the primary law enforcement agencies, operating in 12 divisions, including specialized units such as a Militarized Rapid Deployment Force and Marine Police Unit, which handles offshore oil and gas issues. The Ghana Prisons Service and the Borstal Institute for Juveniles manage incarceration, and Ghana retains the death penalty for treason, corruption, robbery, piracy, drug trafficking, rape, and homicide. The UN's new SDGs emphasize promoting the rule of law, equal access to justice, reducing corruption, and building accountable, transparent institutions. Ghana is a key transshipment point for narcotics, primarily from South America and some African nations, with drug cartels exploiting weak border controls and porous borders. In 2013, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime stated that drug cartels from Colombia and Latin America use Africa as a route to Europe. Narcotics trafficking remains underground, and seizures declined in 2011; the Narcotics Control Board has impounded container ships at Sekondi Naval Base carrying thousands of kilograms of cocaine with a street value in billions of cedis. Drug cartels are using new methods to evade security agencies. President Mills initiated efforts to reduce the role of airports in drug trafficking. Homosexual acts are illegal in Ghana, and a 2013 Pew Research Center survey found that 96% of Ghanaians believe homosexuality should not be accepted. In rural areas, especially in northern Ghana, witchcraft accusations are common, with so-called "witch camps" housing around 1,000 people accused, and the government has announced plans to close them. Ghana possesses industrial minerals, hydrocarbons, and precious metals and is an emerging digital economy with a mixed economy. The "Ghana Vision 2020" economic plan aims for Ghana to become the first African country to become developed between 2020 and 2029 and a newly industrialized country between 2030 and 2039, excluding South Africa. Ghana has economic ties to the Chinese yuan renminbi, with the Bank of Ghana beginning to circulate renminbi as a second national trade currency in 2013. Between 2012 and 2013, 38% of rural dwellers lived in poverty compared to 11% of urban dwellers, with 94% of rural poor households engaged in agriculture. The Volta River Authority and the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation are the two major electricity producers. The Akosombo Dam (1965), Bui Dam, Kpong Dam, and other hydroelectric dams provide hydropower, and the government plans to build a second nuclear power plant in Africa. The Ghana Stock Exchange is the fifth largest in continental Africa and third largest in Sub-Saharan Africa with a market capitalization of GH¢57.2 billion (CN¥180.4 billion) in 2012, and was the second best-performing exchange in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2013. Ghana produces high-quality cocoa and is the second largest global producer, supported by ICCO membership. It is classified as a middle-income country, with services accounting for 50% of GDP, manufacturing 24.1%, extractive industries 5%, and taxes 20.9%. text: Ghana exports gold, silver, timber, diamonds, bauxite, and manganese, and has other mineral deposits; it ranks 9th globally in diamond export and reserve size. The government has planned to nationalize the mining industry to increase government revenue. Electricity shortages in 2015 and 2016 led to "dumsor," defined as persistent, irregular and unpredictable power outages, increasing interest in renewable energy; as of 2019, there is a surplus of electricity. The judicial system addresses corruption, economic malpractice, and lack of economic transparency; according to Transparency International’s 2018 Corruption Perceptions Index, Ghana was ranked 78th out of 180 countries with a score of 41, where 0–9 indicates highly corrupt and 90–100 very clean. Ghana launched a cellular mobile network in 1992, later connecting it to the Internet and introducing ADSL broadband services. In 2025, Ghana was ranked 101st in the Global Innovation Index. The Ghana Space Science and Technology Centre (GSSTC) and Ghana Space Agency (GhsA) oversee space exploration and programs; they worked to launch a national security observational satellite into orbit in 2015. Ghana spends 1% of its GDP annually on space exploration to support science and technology research. In 2012, Ghana was elected to chair the Commission on Science and Technology for Sustainable Development in the South (Comsats) and has a joint space exploration effort with the South African National Space Agency. In 2011, tourist arrivals numbered 1,087,000, including South Americans, Asians, Europeans, and North Americans; tourist attractions include waterfalls such as Kintampo and Wli (the largest waterfall in West Africa), coastal palm-lined sandy beaches, caves, mountains, rivers, reservoirs, lakes like Lake Bosumtwi and Lake Volta (the largest human-made lake by surface area), forts and castles, World Heritage Sites, nature reserves, and national parks. Notable castles are Cape Coast Castle and Elmina Castle, which mark sites of bloodshed during the slave trade and preserve African heritage; UNESCO named the Castles and Forts of Ghana World Heritage Monuments, stating they shaped Ghana’s and the world’s history over four centuries as centers of the gold and slave trades and as symbols of European–African encounters and the African Diaspora. In 2010, Ghana ranked 108th out of 139 countries in the World Economic Forum’s list of favorite tourist destinations, moving two places from 2009; in 2011, Forbes ranked Ghana as the 11th most friendly country in the world, based on a 2010 traveler survey, with the highest rank among African countries included. Tourism is the fourth highest earner of foreign exchange. In 2024, Ghana ranked 55th most peaceful country globally. Surfing spots have been identified and developed along the coastline by locals and international surfers, who have brought their boards on traditional fishing vessels. According to Destination Pride, Ghana’s Pride score is 22 out of 100. As of 2024, the United Nations reports Ghana’s population is 34,581,288; as of 2018, 29% of the population is under 15, and 57.8% are aged 15–64; the 2010 census identified the largest ethnic groups as Akan (47.3%), Mole-Dagbani (18.5%), Ewe (13.9%), Ga-Dangme (7.4%), Gurma (5.7%), and Guan (3.7%); the median age is 21 years, and Ghana contributes 0.42% to the world population. There is a small population of Chinese, Malaysian, Indian, Middle Eastern, and European nationals due to recent skilled worker immigration; in 2010, the Ghana Immigration Service reported 14.6% (3.1 million) of the population as economic migrants or undocumented immigrants, mostly Nigerians, Burkinabe, Togolese, and Malians; in 1969, under the "Ghana Aliens Compliance Order" enacted by Prime Minister Kofi Abrefa Busia, over 3 million aliens and undocumented immigrants were deported in three months, representing 20% of the population at the time; in 2013, more than 4,000 undocumented miners, mostly Chinese nationals, were deported. English is the official language; eleven languages are government-sponsored, with Asante Twi being the most widely spoken. Due to its proximity to French-speaking countries, French is widely taught in schools and used in commercial and international economic exchanges; Hausa is widely spoken in the north, especially among Muslim communities. Since 2005, Ghana has been an associate member of the Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (84 nations); over 350,000 Ghanaian children studied French in schools, and it has become mandatory in all junior high schools, with efforts underway to make it an official language. Ghanaian Pidgin English, known as Kru English or kroo brofo, is a variety of West African Pidgin English spoken in Accra and southern towns, divided into "uneducated" and "educated" varieties, the latter used in institutions like universities. Christianity is the largest religion, with 71.3% of the population as members of various Christian denominations (2021 census); Islam is practiced by 16.8%, with 60.71% Sunni, 9.52% Shia, and 29.76% non-denominational Muslims; there is no significant link between ethnicity and religion; approximately 16% belong to the Ahmadiyya religion, and 8.7% are in other religions. There are about 150,000 Jehovah’s Witnesses. The Grand Orange Lodge of Ghana is a Protestant fraternal organization within the Orange Order; its most famous lodge, The Loyal Leopold Lodge No. 907, was founded in 1894 by Dr. A.D. MacDonald and initially served European administrators, military officers, and merchants; it later admitted local African members, a significant shift from British and Irish lodges; today, members participate in events like The Twelfth and engage in community and charitable work. In 1994, Emmanuel Aboki Essien, a Ghanaian Orangeman, was elected President of the Imperial Orange Council, becoming the first African to hold the office, a milestone that elevated African lodges’ recognition in the international Orange Order. Ghana has a universal health care system, the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS), strictly for Ghanaian nationals; in 2012, over 12 million were covered; urban areas have most hospitals, clinics, and pharmacies; there are over 200 hospitals, and Ghana is a destination for medical tourism; in 2010, there were 0.1 physicians per 1,000 people and 0.9 hospital beds per 1,000 people; in 2010, 5.2% of GDP was spent on health; in 2020, Ghana achieved "maturity level 3" in the WHO’s national medicines regulatory system, the second-highest in the African region. Life expectancy in 2021 was 68.6 years for females and 63.7 for males; in 2013, infant mortality was 39 per 1,000 live births; WHO estimated life expectancy in 2016 as 62 years for men and 64 for women; the fertility rate declined from 3.99 (2000) to 3.28 (2010), with 2.78 in urban and 3.94 in rural areas; the UN reported a decline from 6.95 (1970) to 4.82 (2000) to 3.93 live births per woman in 2017. As of 2012, HIV/AIDS prevalence among adults aged 15–49 was estimated at 1.40%. The education system includes basic education (11 years, ages 4–15), divided into kindergarten (2 years), primary school (two modules of three years), and junior high (three years), ending with the Basic Education Certificate Examination; after certification, students proceed to secondary education, with options for general or vocational education; senior high school lasts three years and leads to the West African Senior School Certificate Examination, required for university enrollment. A bachelor’s degree takes four years, followed by a one- or two-year master’s and a PhD of at least three years; polytechnic programs last two or three years. Ghana has colleges of education; universities include the University of Ghana, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, and University of Cape Coast. Over 95% of children are in school; youth literacy (ages 15–24) was 81% in 2010 (82% males, 80% females); the education system attracts foreign students, especially at the university level. Ghana has a free six-year primary education beginning at age 6; the government funds basic education, including public primary and junior high schools; senior high schools were subsidized until September 2017/2018, after which education became free; at higher education, the government funds over 80% of public universities, polytechnics, and teacher training colleges. Under the Free Compulsory Universal Basic Education (FCUBE), the government supplies all basic education schools with textbooks and supplies like exercise books; senior high schools receive textbook requirements; private schools obtain materials from private suppliers. Ghanaian cuisine features soups and stews with varied seafoods, most using vegetables, meat, poultry, or fish; fish is important, with tilapia, roasted and fried whitebait, smoked fish, and crayfish common; banku (akple), a starchy food made from ground corn, and cornmeal staples kɔmi (kenkey) and banku are served with fried fish (chinam) or grilled tilapia and a spicy pepper sauce made from raw red and green chillies, onions, and tomatoes; banku and tilapia is a common restaurant combo; fufu is the most exported Ghanaian dish and a delicacy in the African diaspora; rice is a staple, with variants including waakye, plain rice and stew (kontomire or tomato gravy), fried rice, and jollof rice. Ghanaian literature has roots in a long oral tradition, was influenced by Western literature during colonial rule, and became prominent with a post-colonial nationalist movement in the mid-20th century; the current literary community includes diverse voices in film, theatre, and digital formats like blogging. Prominent authors include J. E. Casely Hayford (Ethiopia Unbound, 1911), Ayi Kwei Armah (The Beautyful Ones Are Not Yet Born, 1968), and Nii Ayikwei Parkes (Tail of the Blue Bird, 2009). Other literary forms such as theatre and poetry have developed with notable playwrights and poets like Joe de Graft and Efua Sutherland. The Ghanaian national literature radio program Voices of Ghana (1955–1957) was one of the earliest on the African continent and helped establish the scope of Ghana’s contemporary literary tradition. Scholarship in Anglophone Africa sometimes favors literature from other regions, such as Nigeria. In the 13th century, Ghanaians developed adinkra printing; hand-printed and hand-embroidered adinkra clothes were used exclusively by royalty in devotional ceremonies; each motif has a name and meaning derived from proverbs, historical events, human attitudes, ethology, plant life, or shapes of objects; meanings fall into categories of aesthetics, ethics, human relations, and concepts; adinkra symbols serve as tattoos and convey traditional wisdom, life aspects, or environmental messages, acting as a means of transmitting complex beliefs in pre-literate societies, as noted by Anthony Appiah. Alongside adinkra cloth, various traditional fabrics are used; the most well-known is Kente cloth, a ceremonial hand-woven cloth on a horizontal treadle loom, made from strips about 4 inches wide sewn together into larger pieces; different colors and symbols carry distinct meanings; Kente is the most famous Ghanaian clothing and is used in both traditional and modern attire.
